And when Abimelech came claiming they had done him nothing but good, though his people had stopped the wells and sent him away, he answered plainly and asked why they came to him, seeing they hated him (Genesis 26:26-27). Words can be smoother than butter while war is in the heart, and he dealt with their covenant with his eyes open. Then Isaac sowed in that land and received in the same year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him; the man waxed great and went forward and grew until he became very great (Genesis 26:12-13). The Philistines envied him and stopped up all his wells with earth; the nations envy the prosperity of Israel, and it is not for anything done to them, for the blessing itself is what is hated (Genesis 26:14-15). The king of the country came to him seeking terms, and gave his reason: they had seen certainly that the Lord was with him (Genesis 26:28). The blessing was public and legible to outsiders. He made them a feast, exchanged an oath and sent them away in peace without pretending he had been well treated, and that same day his servants came and told him of the well (Genesis 26:30-33). The Lord had appeared to him the night before at Beersheba as the God of Abraham his father, told him not to fear, and promised to be with him and bless him and multiply his seed for his servant Abraham’s sake; and he builded an altar there, called upon the name of the Lord and pitched his tent (Genesis 26:24-25). He lived an hundred and fourscore years and died old and full of days, and his two sons buried him (Genesis 35:28-29).

name: Laban and the changed wages
text: Changing his hired servant’s wages ten times, and giving the elder daughter in place of the younger. Laban of the house of Nahor, an idolater as his fathers were, received Jacob as his own bone and flesh, then took seven years of work for Rachel and delivered Leah, charged seven more, and changed the wages ten times over twenty years while the Lord blessed him for Jacob’s sake. When Jacob left, he pursued him seven days with the power in his hand to hurt him, and God came to him in a dream by night and told him to speak to Jacob neither good nor bad. Jacob went up out of Canaan north and then east to Haran, back to the family Terah had left there when he brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldees, and Laban said he was surely his bone and his flesh, which in the scriptures means, we are family (Genesis 29:1-5, 14; Genesis 11:26-31). Jacob loved Rachel, beautiful and well favoured, and served seven years for her, and they seemed to him but a few days for the love he had to her; men gather gold and silver and every goodly thing and then let it all go and fix their eyes fast on a comely woman, and many have run out of their wits for a woman and become servants for their sakes (Genesis 29:16-20; 1 Esdras 4:18-26). In the evening Laban brought him Leah, and in the morning it was Leah; his answer, that it must not be so done in their country to give the younger before the firstborn, was a rule he had known before he took the seven years (Genesis 29:23-26). He required seven other years (Genesis 29:27-30). Laban had learned by experience that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob’s sake, and Jacob reminded him how little he had before he came, and that it was now increased to a multitude, and asked when he should provide for his own house also (Genesis 30:27-30). Jacob asked no gift. He set terms that could be checked in the open, the speckled and the spotted and the brown to be his hire, so that his righteousness would answer for him in time to come; and Laban agreed and that same day removed those very cattle into the hand of his own sons and set three days journey between them (Genesis 30:31-36). Then he changed the wages ten times. Jacob’s account, which Laban does not deny, is that but for the God of his father he would have been sent away empty: twenty years, the drought consuming him by day and the frost by night, and his sleep departing from his eyes (Genesis 31:7, 38-42). When Laban’s sons said Jacob had taken away all that was their father’s, Laban’s countenance was not toward him as before (Genesis 31:1-2). The Lord told Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and to his kindred, and he would be with him (Genesis 31:3). Laban pursued him seven days journey and asked why he had stolen his gods. That question tells what Laban was: an idolater of the house of Nahor, whose fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood and served other gods, the very kindred the Most High had separated Abram from (Genesis 31:23, 30; Joshua 24:2; Genesis 12:1). The pursuer was restrained before he could use the power he had. God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night and warned him to take heed that he speak not to Jacob either good or bad (Genesis 31:24). He admitted it to Jacob’s face: he had the power to do Jacob harm, but the God of Jacob’s father had spoken to him the night before (Genesis 31:29). He searched every tent and found nothing. Jacob answered that God had seen his affliction and the labour of his hands, and had rebuked him the night before (Genesis 31:42). They made a covenant at the heap and the pillar, that neither would pass over it to the other for harm, and Laban rose up early, kissed his sons and his daughters, blessed them and returned to his place (Genesis 31:44-55). The record does not reduce him to poverty, and it does not need to. It shows a man with the power and the numbers to take everything, stopped in his sleep by one sentence, and Jacob walking away with the household and with the substance the Most High had preserved for him out of twenty years of changed wages.

name: Rachel and the stolen teraphim
text: Stealing her father’s images, and hiding them under her while she sat upon them. Rachel stole the images that were her father’s, hid them in the camel’s furniture and sat upon them, and told her father she could not rise up before him, so he searched and found them not. Jacob, not knowing, had said that whoever was found with them should not live. No sentence for the theft is announced. The strange gods stayed hidden in the household until Jacob commanded them put away before Bethel, and the beguiling of the mothers from Eve to Rachel is the warning the record leaves. When Laban went to shear his sheep, Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s (Genesis 31:19). Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that fears the Lord shall be praised: she was fine, and she was a thief (Proverbs 31:30). Laban’s own question, why he had stolen his gods, tells what house she came out of: an idolater of the line of Nahor, whose fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time and served other gods, and that is why the Most High had told Abram to get out from his country and from his kindred (Genesis 31:30; Joshua 24:2). Jacob, who did not know that Rachel had stolen them, answered that with whoever his gods were found, let him not live, and invited Laban to search before their brethren (Genesis 31:32). She had taken the images and put them in the camel’s furniture and sat upon them, and said to her father, let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before you, for the custom of women is upon me; and he searched all the tent and found not the images (Genesis 31:34-35). Idolatry was carried hidden into the covenant household, and a lie covered it, and her own husband had unknowingly pronounced a sentence over her head. No sentence for the theft is recorded, and Jacob’s oath was spoken in ignorance. The images stayed in the camp. Before going up to Bethel, Jacob said to his household and to all that were with him, put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean, and change your garments; the strange gods were there because she had stolen them and hidden them, and she gave them up then, and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem (Genesis 35:1-4). Idolatry hidden in a household has to be put away before a man can stand at Bethel. What followed was protection, not punishment: the terror of God was upon the cities round about, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob, for the angel of the Lord encamps round about them that fear him and delivers them (Genesis 35:5; Psalms 34:7). From Eve to Rachel the scriptures show how sin comes into a house through the household, for of the woman came the beginning of sin, and the warning left here is for the mothers of Israel to guard against the same beguiling (Ecclesiasticus 25:24). Rachel died in hard labour bearing Benjamin in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem, and Jacob set a pillar upon her grave (Genesis 35:16-20); the record does not name that death as the penalty for the theft, and it is not given as one. Delay is not acquittal.

name: Jacob at Peniel
text: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. Facing the brother who had purposed to slay him, Jacob prayed humbly, pleaded the covenant, sent his present before him, and was left alone at the ford. A man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day and had to put his thigh out of joint to stop him, and with his thigh out of joint Jacob still held on and would not let go without a blessing. He was named Israel, a prince that has power with God, and Hosea says he had power over the angel and prevailed. The angels of God met him as he went on his way from Laban, and he called the place Mahanaim, which is two hosts; when the scriptures speak of the Lord of hosts, the hosts are the armies of angels that stand before his throne with trembling (Genesis 32:1-2; 2 Esdras 8:21). His messengers returned saying that Esau was coming to meet him and four hundred men with him, and he was greatly afraid and distressed. The fear was rightful, for the last word he had of his brother was that Esau purposed to slay him, and the violent man imagines mischiefs in his heart and is continually gathered together for war (Genesis 32:3-7; Genesis 27:41-42; Psalms 140:1-2). He prayed humbly and was not too proud to confess the fear: he was not worthy of the least of all the mercies and of all the truth shown to his servant, and he asked to be delivered from the hand of his brother. Then he pleaded the covenant, that the Lord had said he would make his seed as the sand of the sea. That is the pattern for prayer: plead the promise made to the fathers (Genesis 32:9-12). And then he moved. He sent droves before him, spaced apart, every servant instructed what to say, to appease him with the present that went before him, for a man’s gift makes room for him and brings him before great men (Genesis 32:13-20; Proverbs 18:16). Jacob was left alone, and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. That was no light matter; it went the whole night, and the man had to touch the hollow of his thigh and put it out of joint, because Jacob would not be beaten. With his thigh out of joint he still held on and would not let go until he was blessed (Genesis 32:24-26). That is faith with works. The forefathers knew how to handle themselves: Abraham had three hundred and eighteen trained servants born in his own house, and armed them and went after four kings to bring his brother’s son back, and that strength ran down the line to David and to Samson (Genesis 14:14-16). Ecclesiasticus says to cleave to him and not depart away, so as to be increased at the last end; Paul says to fight the good fight of faith and lay hold on eternal life (Ecclesiasticus 2:3; 1 Timothy 6:12). His name should be called no more Jacob, but Israel, for as a prince he had power with God and with men, and had prevailed (Genesis 32:27-28). Israel means a prince that has power with God, and the God of Israel is the one who gives strength and power to his people; he is the power source. When Israel went astray and served other gods the name and the power were taken, and the nations called the people by every other name; returning to the Most High is how the name and the power come back, and not by carnal weapons (Psalms 68:35). The one he wrestled was an angel: Hosea says that by his strength he had power with God, that he had power over the angel and prevailed, and that he wept and made supplication to him (Hosea 12:3-4). He asked the man his name and was given none, and was blessed there, and called the name of the place Peniel, because he had seen God face to face and his life was preserved (Genesis 32:29-30). The word God, Elohim, is plural, which clears up the passages where men are said to have seen God and yet no man has seen the Father. The sun rose upon him as he halted upon his thigh, which is why the children of Israel do not eat of the sinew which shrank, upon the hollow of the thigh, to this day (Genesis 32:31-32). The name was confirmed again at Bethel, with the promise of a nation and a company of nations, and kings out of his loins (Genesis 35:10-11).

name: Shechem son of Hamor
text: Taking Dinah and defiling her; then seeking to marry into the house he had wronged and make the two peoples one. Dinah, Jacob’s only daughter, went out to see the daughters of the land without supervision, and Shechem the son of Hamor, prince of the country, took her and defiled her: stranger rape, which the law sets beside murder. He did it backwards, taking first and loving after, and his father came proposing that the two peoples intermarry and become one, the offer the nations always make. Jacob’s sons answered deceitfully, and on the third day Simeon and Levi took the city with the sword. Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land without supervision, and Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, took her, lay with her and defiled her (Genesis 34:1-2). That was stranger rape, and rape is a violent act; the law sets it beside murder, for as when a man rises against his neighbour and slays him, even so is this matter. The man only that lay with her shall die, and to the damsel nothing is to be done, for in her there is no sin worthy of death (Deuteronomy 22:25-27). Under it is a covetous spirit, a man desiring what is not his, which is the tenth commandment broken (Exodus 20:17). Judith remembers the act exactly: they loosened the girdle of a maid to defile her, discovered her thigh to her shame and polluted her virginity to her reproach (Judith 9:2). The lesson stands for every generation: a man with daughters is to have a care of their body and keep a sure watch over them, for the father wakes for the daughter when no man knows, and the care for her takes away sleep, lest she be defiled and made a byword and a reproach; do not give overmuch liberty (Ecclesiasticus 7:24; Ecclesiasticus 26:10; Ecclesiasticus 42:9-11). Shechem’s soul clave to Dinah after he had defiled her; he did it backwards, taking first and loving after, which is the world’s pattern and not righteousness (Genesis 34:3). When Jacob’s sons heard it, the men were grieved and very wroth, because he had wrought folly in Israel in lying with Jacob’s daughter, which thing ought not to be done; the laws were in place and kept long before they were written in stone at Sinai (Genesis 34:7). Hamor proposed the exact opposite of the law: that the two houses should make marriages together, give their daughters and take his people’s daughters, dwell with them and become one people (Genesis 34:8-10, 16). Assimilation and intermarriage is the offer the nations always make, and Moses would forbid it by name (Deuteronomy 7:3). The sons of Jacob answered deceitfully, saying they could not give their sister to one that was uncircumcised, for that were a reproach to them, and requiring every male of the city to be circumcised (Genesis 34:13-15). The city’s own reasoning was written down: their cattle, their substance and every beast of Jacob’s house would be theirs (Genesis 34:23). On the third day, when they were sore, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brethren, took each man his sword, came upon the city boldly and slew all the males; they slew Hamor and Shechem his son with the edge of the sword, and took Dinah out of Shechem’s house (Genesis 34:25-26). Two men do not take a city alone. Judith says the sword of Simeon was given him of God to take vengeance of the strangers that defiled the maid, that their rulers were given to be slain and the servants smitten with their lords, and that the brothers were moved with the zeal of the Most High (Judith 9:2-4). Jacob was troubled and said they had made him to stink among the inhabitants of the land, and feared that the nations round about would gather themselves against his house while he was few in number (Genesis 34:30). The brothers answered by asking whether he should deal with their sister as with a harlot: the daughters of Israel are not handled so, and the law allows no whore of the daughters of Israel (Genesis 34:31; Deuteronomy 23:17). His desire to marry her after the fact did not acquit him, and the marriage offer did not lessen the charge; it added to it. Jacob afterward judged the fierce anger of his sons, which is entered under their names.

name: Simeon and Levi at Shechem
text: Deceitful covenant; slaughter of a city in their anger. Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land without supervision, and Shechem the prince of the country took her and defiled her. Her brothers answered Shechem and Hamor deceitfully, required that every male of the city be circumcised, and on the third day Simeon and Levi slew the males with the sword. Judith remembers that sword as vengeance given of God for the maid. Jacob on his deathbed cursed their anger and divided them in Jacob and scattered them in Israel, and the two are brethren sharing one island to this day. Dinah, Jacob’s only daughter, went out to see the daughters of the land without supervision, and Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, took her and defiled her (Genesis 34:1-2). This was stranger rape, and the lesson the fathers drew from it stands for every generation: have a care of the body of your daughters, do not give overmuch liberty, for the father wakes for the daughter when no man knows, and the care of her takes away sleep (Ecclesiasticus 7:24; Ecclesiasticus 42:9-11). His soul clave to her after he had defiled her, taking first and loving after, which is the world’s pattern and not righteousness. When Jacob’s sons heard it they were grieved and very wroth, because he had wrought folly in Israel in lying with Jacob’s daughter, a thing that ought not to be done (Genesis 34:7): the laws were in place and kept long before they were written in stone at Sinai. Hamor then proposed the exact opposite of the law, that the two peoples give and take daughters, dwell together and become one people (Genesis 34:8-10). Assimilation and intermarriage is the offer the nations always make, and it is the offer the law forbids. The sons of Jacob answered deceitfully: every male of the city must be circumcised before they would consent. Hamor and Shechem carried it to the gate of their city by the profit in it, reasoning that the cattle and the substance of Jacob’s house would become theirs, and every male was circumcised (Genesis 34:13-24). On the third day, when they were sore, Simeon and Levi each took his sword, came on the city boldly, and killed all the males; they took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and the sons of Jacob spoiled the city and carried away the substance and the households (Genesis 34:25-29). Two men do not take a city alone. Judith names what was behind it: the sword of Simeon was given him of God to take vengeance on the strangers who defiled the maid, and they were moved with the zeal of the Most High (Judith 9:2-4). Jacob was troubled that they had made him to stink among the inhabitants of the land, being few in number, and feared the nations round about would gather against his house. They answered with the law: should he deal with our sister as with a harlot, when there is to be no whore of the daughters of Israel (Genesis 34:30-31; Deuteronomy 23:17). The offense against Dinah was real; so was the anger their father held them answerable for. When Jacob gathered his sons to tell them what should befall them in the last days, the sentence came with the blessing: Simeon and Levi are brethren, with instruments of cruelty in their habitations; his soul was not to come into their secret nor his honour be joined to their assembly, because in their anger they slew a man and in their selfwill they dug down a wall; their anger was cursed for being fierce and their wrath for being cruel, and he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Genesis 49:1, 5-7). The scattering is on the record: Levi had no whole portion but cities scattered throughout all the tribes, and Simeon’s inheritance lay inside the inheritance of Judah (Joshua 21:1-8; Joshua 19:1-9). As Judah was scattered to the four corners of the earth so was Levi, for Judah, Benjamin and Levi made up the southern kingdom. The blessings are twofold, speaking to each tribe in their own day and in the last days, and they tell who the tribes are now. Simeon is the so-called Dominican and Levi the so-called Haitian today, brethren dwelling together on the one island of Hispaniola. The instruments of cruelty in their habitations are the witchcraft practised there, the voodoo of Haiti and the sorcery of the other side; and because of those practices the Most High does not unite them, so the two nations stay divided on one island even though Levi helped free Simeon from slavery. The anger cursed at Shechem did not end the tribe of Levi. The same sword was taken up lawfully at the golden calf, and that day is entered in this volume as a blessing, not a curse.

name: Reuben
text: Lying with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. Jacob’s firstborn went up to his father’s bed and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it. Paul calls that a fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles, and the law had already forbidden it, because a father’s wife is the father’s own nakedness. Nothing more is said until the deathbed, where it cost Reuben the birthright: unstable as water, he would not excel. While Israel dwelt in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it (Genesis 35:22). Paul names the same offense among the Corinthians and calls it a fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles, that a man should have his father’s wife (1 Corinthians 5:1). The law had already forbidden it: the nakedness of a father’s wife is the father’s own nakedness, and the wicked mind that reasons she is not the biological mother is answered before it opens its mouth (Leviticus 18:8). The chapter sets it in the middle of a household being cleaned up. Before going up to Bethel, Jacob had told his house to put away the strange gods among them and be clean, and the terror of God was on the cities round about so that they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob (Genesis 35:2-5). Sin entering the household is the running warning of the chapter. The brief report on Reuben is not an acquittal by silence. Jacob called him his firstborn, his might and the beginning of his strength, the excellency of dignity and the excellency of power; then, unstable as water, he would not excel, because he went up to his father’s bed and defiled it (Genesis 49:3-4). The firstborn is the father’s posterity, and dignity and power belonged to him. The chronicle states the transfer plainly: because he defiled his father’s bed his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, and the genealogy is not reckoned after the birthright; Judah prevailed above his brethren, and of him came the chief ruler (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). The firstborn lost the place of the heir, as Esau came out first and did not keep it.

name: Joseph’s brothers
text: Envy, conspiracy to murder, selling their brother to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and deceiving their father with the bloodied coat. Joseph was seventeen when he brought his father the evil report of his brothers, as the law of the witness required, and dreamed the dreams that showed his brethren and his father bowing to him. His brothers envied him, conspired to kill him, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and lied to their father with a kid’s blood. Years later the dream came true in Egypt, they confessed their guilt, and Joseph spared them, because what they meant for evil God meant for good. Joseph was seventeen years old when he brought his father the evil report of his brothers (Genesis 37:2). That was law, not tale bearing: the soul that hears swearing and is a witness and does not utter it bears his iniquity, and the law was already around, and Joseph kept it (Leviticus 5:1). Israel loved him more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours, and his brethren hated him and could not speak peaceably to him (Genesis 37:3-4). That is real hatred among brothers, and the same spirit is on Israel today, where a brother cannot even receive a greeting in peace. He dreamed, and the sheaves of his brethren bowed to his sheaf, and then the sun, the moon and the eleven stars bowed to him; his father caught the second dream at once (Genesis 37:5-10). The Lord speaks by the prophets in visions and similitudes, and the vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, as the likeness of a face to a face, so dreams are not to be chased but read (Hosea 12:10; Ecclesiasticus 34:1-3). The same figures mark the nation: the woman clothed with the sun, crowned with twelve stars, is the daughter of Zion, and the stars are the tribes (Revelation 12:1). His brethren understood that he was to reign over them, and hated him the more. They envied him, and consuming envy has no fellowship with wisdom; when envy takes over, wisdom leaves (Genesis 37:11; Wisdom of Solomon 6:23). When they saw him afar off they conspired to slay him, mocking him as the dreamer. That is the same spirit Cain had and the same spirit Esau had, and the apostle names it: a man who hates his brother is a murderer (Genesis 37:18-20; 1 John 3:15). Reuben delivered him out of their hands to the pit, meaning to return him to his father, and Judah asked what profit there was in slaying their brother and concealing his blood. They sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, the people known today as the Arab man; the Midianites and the Ishmaelites, Abraham’s children by Keturah and by Hagar, roamed and worked and traded together, which is why the account names both (Genesis 37:21-28; Genesis 25:1-4, 12-16). The law puts to death the man who steals a man and sells him (Exodus 21:16). Then, unable to explain his absence, they dipped the coat in the blood of a kid and let their father believe an evil beast had devoured him, dealing falsely and lying against the law (Genesis 37:31-35; Leviticus 19:11). They were spared, and the sparing is the case. The psalm says he sent a man before them, Joseph, sold as a servant, his feet hurt with fetters and laid in iron, until the time that his word came (Psalms 105:17-19). The dream came true: in the famine the whole house of Jacob came down to Joseph in Egypt and bowed before him with their faces to the earth, and he placed them in the best of the land and nourished them with bread (Genesis 42:6; Genesis 47:11-12). Their own verdict was spoken before they knew who was listening, for he had made himself a stranger and spoke to them by an interpreter: they were truly guilty concerning their brother, because they had seen the anguish of his soul when he begged them and would not hear; and Joseph turned himself about and wept, because he still loved them (Genesis 42:21-24). Judah, who had proposed the sale, afterward offered himself as a bondman in Benjamin’s place (Genesis 44:33). When Jacob died the brothers were afraid Joseph would repay them, and sent begging forgiveness; he wept, and told them not to fear, for he was not in the place of God: they thought evil against him, but God meant it for good, to save much people alive (Genesis 50:15-20). Only a spiritual man can look back on that and see it. Joseph sat with all that had happened to him and understood it was the Lord’s design, though he could not have understood it while he was in the middle of it. Had he never gone down to Egypt the whole house of Israel would have died in the famine (Genesis 45:5-7). All things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose (Romans 8:28). He comforted them and nourished them and their little ones.

name: Er and Onan
text: Er: wickedness in the sight of the Lord. Onan: refusing to raise up seed to his brother. Judah took the daughter of Shuah the Canaanite and had Er, Onan and Shelah. Er, his firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord slew him. Onan was told to go in to his brother’s wife and raise up seed for his brother, and he refused, spilling it on the ground, and the Lord slew him also. The sin was the refusal to raise up his brother’s name, not the act itself, and what happened here afterward became law in Israel. Judah took the daughter of Shuah, a Canaanite, and she bore Er, Onan and Shelah; Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, whose name was Tamar, and Er was wicked in the sight of the Lord (Genesis 38:1-7). There is nothing wrong with a father taking a wife for his son; that is a good thing. But men pray and fast and intercede for children and can still get unprofitable ones, and Judah had two. Judah then told Onan to go in to his brother’s wife, marry her, and raise up seed for his brother. Onan knew the seed would not be his, and when he went in to his brother’s wife he spilled it on the ground rather than give seed to his brother (Genesis 38:8-9). He took the woman and kept the use of her and withheld the one thing the arrangement existed for. The sin was refusing to raise up seed to his brother, not the act itself; do not build a doctrine on the wrong point, and this is not a verse about contraception. What happened here later became law: when brethren dwell together and one dies with no child, the husband’s brother goes in to her and performs the duty of a husband’s brother, and the firstborn she bears succeeds in the name of the dead, so that his name is not put out of Israel (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). The succeeding in the name is the inheritance in the land staying in the dead man’s name, so the portion is not lost. The Most High puts stock in a name; a good name is better than precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1). A brother who will not build up his brother’s house has broken the law of loving the neighbour as himself (Leviticus 19:18). The law even guards the other end of it: a man who has taken a new wife does not go out to war nor is charged with any business for one year, so that he can raise up seed in Israel (Deuteronomy 24:5). Both died at the Lord’s hand. Er was wicked in the Lord’s sight and the Lord slew him; the thing Onan did displeased the Lord, and he slew him also (Genesis 38:7, 10). The muster of Judah keeps the record: the sons of Judah were Er and Onan, and Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan (Numbers 26:19). Under the law the man who refused was brought before the elders of his city, and if he stood to it, his brother’s wife loosed the shoe from off his foot and spat in his face and declared that this is what is done to the man who will not build up his brother’s house; and his house was named in Israel after the loosed shoe (Deuteronomy 25:7-10). That is a humiliation title, carried by the house and not only by the man. In Ruth the nearer kinsman would not redeem for fear of marring his own inheritance, and the right passed to Boaz, who performed the kinsman’s part and raised up the name of the dead on his inheritance (Ruth 3:10-13; Ruth 4:1-6). Judah’s house did not end with these two deaths: Tamar bore Pharez and Zarah, and through them the line ran on, down into Egypt, where Judah died with his brethren (Genesis 38:27-30; Exodus 1:6).

name: Judah and Tamar
text: Withholding Shelah from his brother’s widow; going in to a woman he took for a harlot by her attire. Judah promised Tamar to Shelah and never performed it. She put off her widow’s garments, covered herself with a veil and sat where Judah would pass, and he took her for a harlot by the attire and went in to her for the price of a kid, leaving his signet, bracelets and staff. When her pregnancy came to light he ordered her burnt, until she produced the pledge. He judged himself: she had been more righteous than he. Judah went down from his brethren, saw there the daughter of a certain Canaanite named Shuah, and took her (Genesis 38:1-2). The forefathers were not all the most righteous men; he did what Israel was forbidden to do, and the trouble in the chapter follows from that house. After Er and Onan died, he sent Tamar back to her father’s house to remain a widow until Shelah was grown, because with her husband dead her father was her head again and would keep her as before; and Shelah was still a child (Genesis 38:11). Then Judah did not perform it. When she saw that Shelah was grown and she had not been given to him to wife, she took off her widow’s garments, covered herself with a veil, wrapped herself, and sat in an open place on the road to Timnath (Genesis 38:12-14). Judah thought her to be a harlot because of the attire; a harlot was always known by her dress, as the woman in Proverbs with the attire of a harlot and a subtle heart (Genesis 38:15; Proverbs 7:10). He went in to her for the price of a kid of the flock, and she took his signet, his bracelets and his staff as a pledge, and conceived by him (Genesis 38:16-18). When his friend could not find her to redeem the pledge, Judah said to let her keep it, lest they be shamed (Genesis 38:20-23): he knew what he had done was wrong and wanted no noise made about it. Three months later, when it began to show, he was told his daughter in law had played the harlot and was with child by whoredom, and he ordered her brought out and burnt (Genesis 38:24). The sentence was that heavy because a woman promised in the covenant who plays the harlot and brings in an heir by another has disobeyed the law of the Most High, and her reproach is not blotted out (Ecclesiasticus 23:22-26). He condemned her before he looked at his own part in it. When she was brought out she sent word to her father in law that she was with child by the man who owned the signet, the bracelets and the staff, and asked him to discern whose they were. Judah acknowledged them and said she had been more righteous than he, because he had not given her to Shelah his son; and he knew her again no more (Genesis 38:25-26). No sentence fell on Tamar. Judah stopped it himself, and his own confession names the withheld duty as the cause. That is the whole weight of the case: the man holding the authority to burn her was the man who had broken the law of the brother’s name first. Twins were in her womb. One put out his hand and the midwife bound a scarlet thread on it to mark the elder, but he drew his hand back and his brother came out first, and she said, how have you broken forth; so his name was called Pharez, which is a breach, and afterward came his brother with the scarlet thread on his hand, Zarah (Genesis 38:27-30). The line through Pharez is the line kept in the genealogy of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:18-22; Matthew 1:3). Judah’s house went down into Egypt, and Judah died there with his brethren (Exodus 1:6).

name: Joseph
text: Refusing his master’s wife day by day: how can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?. Sold by his brothers at seventeen and bought by Potiphar, Joseph was faithful in that which was least, and the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for his sake. Tempted day by day by his master’s wife, he refused, naming adultery a great wickedness and a sin against God long before any law was written at Sinai; when she caught his garment he fled from sin as from a serpent. Lied on and imprisoned, he found the Lord with him in the prison as in the house, and the favour followed him until he stood where he could save the whole house of Israel alive. The Lord was with Joseph in his captivity, and his master saw that the Lord made everything he did to prosper; Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake (Genesis 39:1-6), the same theme as when Laban was blessed for Jacob’s sake. The Most High deals with his people even in captivity and gives them compassion before those who carried them away captive (1 Kings 8:50). Christ said a man faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10). That is the explanation of Joseph: he was a slave, and he was faithful to Potiphar in it, and Potiphar raised him up. The same measure is on us. We are in captivity as he was in captivity, and being in captivity is no licence to steal or lie or rob on the little jobs out here; deal right on them, because the Most High is watching what a man does with the least thing. His master’s wife cast her eyes on Joseph and told him to lie with her. He refused: no one in the house was greater than he, and his master had kept back nothing from him except her, because she was his wife; how then could he do this great wickedness and sin against God (Genesis 39:7-9). Adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai: Abraham kept the commandments, the statutes and the laws, and Abimelech the heathen king knew that one of his people lying lightly with another man’s wife would have brought guiltiness upon them (Genesis 26:5, 10). Note also what he did not say. He did not blame God for being in slavery. The Egyptians did not marry plain women, and she was not hard to look at, and there was no one watching him; and he still said no. She spoke to him day by day, wearing him down, and he would not listen, to lie by her or to be with her; then, on a day when none of the men of the house were within, she caught him by his garment, and he left it in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:10-12). That is the example: flee from sin as from the face of a serpent, for if a man comes too near it, it will bite him, and the teeth of it are as the teeth of a lion (Ecclesiasticus 21:2). He saw sin like a snake and ran like a rabbit; thirty more seconds of entertaining her would have been the bite. He understood the rule his father had taught him: a man who comes to serve the Lord is to prepare his soul for temptation, to take cheerfully whatever is brought upon him and be patient when he is changed to a low estate (Ecclesiasticus 2:1, 4). Jacob was a wealthy man, and Joseph was taken from all of it into a dungeon. She lied, and held his garment as evidence, and his master’s wrath was kindled and he put Joseph into the prison without seeking any understanding, for jealousy is the rage of a man, and he will not spare in the day of vengeance nor accept any ransom (Genesis 39:13-20; Proverbs 6:34-35). But the Lord was with Joseph, showed him mercy, and gave him favour with the keeper of the prison, who committed everything in the prison to his hand, and whatever he did the Lord made it to prosper (Genesis 39:21-23). When a man’s ways please the Lord, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). Everywhere Joseph went the favour followed, because the Most High was ordering his steps the whole way. From the dungeon he asked the butler only to make mention of him to Pharaoh, saying he had been stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews and had done nothing there to deserve the pit; and the butler forgot him (Genesis 40:14-15, 23). Before Pharaoh he claimed no interpretation as his own, saying it was not in him and that God would give Pharaoh an answer of peace (Genesis 41:16). He was raised to govern the country that had bought him (Genesis 41:41), and he became the means by which the family that sold him lived through the famine: they thought evil against him, but God meant it for good, to save much people alive (Genesis 50:20). From seventeen he endured slavery, a false accusation and years in the prison without blaming God, and came out where he could save the whole house of Israel alive.

name: Potiphar’s wife
text: Soliciting her husband’s servant day by day, and bearing false witness against him when he fled. She set her eyes on Joseph and asked him day by day to lie with her, and he refused, naming it a great wickedness and a sin against God. When she caught his garment and he fled, she kept the garment and turned it into evidence, and cried that the Hebrew had come in to mock her. The innocent man went to prison on her lie, and the record never gives her sentence. His master’s wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, lie with me (Genesis 39:7). She spoke to him day by day, trying to wear him down, and he would not listen to her, to lie by her or even to be with her (Genesis 39:10). His refusal names the offense before any law was written at Sinai: how could he do this great wickedness and sin against God (Genesis 39:9). Adultery was known as sin from the beginning; Abraham kept the commandments, the statutes and the laws, and a heathen king knew that lying with another man’s wife brought guiltiness on a people (Genesis 26:5, 10). The wisdom books mark the approach for what it is: do not sit at all with another man’s wife, nor banquet with her, lest the heart incline to her and the desire lead into destruction (Ecclesiasticus 9:9). On a day when none of the men of the house were within, she arranged the empty house, caught him by his garment, and he left it in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:11-12). When she saw that he had fled, she lied. She called the men of her house and told them her husband had brought in a Hebrew to mock them, that he came in to lie with her and she cried with a loud voice; and she laid up his garment by her until his lord came home, and told him the same (Genesis 39:13-18). She could not get her way, so she lied, and she kept his clothes as false evidence. Her sort is drawn out in the books: the lips of a strange woman drop as a honeycomb and her mouth is smoother than oil, but her end is bitter as wormwood and her ways are moveable; and the woman whose heart is snares and nets and whose hands are bands is more bitter than death, though the man who pleases God escapes from her (Proverbs 5:3-6; Ecclesiastes 7:26). The same mouth that flattered turned and accused. A backbiting tongue has disquieted many and overthrown the houses of great men, and more have fallen by the tongue than by the edge of the sword (Ecclesiasticus 28:14, 18). Our people have met that spirit before: in this captivity men were put to death on a woman’s lie, and the young man Emmett Till is one of many cases like it. The judgment recorded fell on the innocent man. His master’s wrath was kindled, and he took Joseph and put him into the prison where the king’s prisoners were bound; he did not seek understanding, for jealousy is the rage of a man, and he will not spare in the day of vengeance nor regard any ransom (Genesis 39:19-20; Proverbs 6:32-35). Against the woman no sentence is recorded. Her offense is double, the solicitation and the false witness, and both stand written with no penalty set against them. What the record does report is where the favour went: the Lord was with Joseph, showed him mercy, and gave him favour with the keeper of the prison, so that the prison became the road to the throne of Egypt; his feet were hurt with fetters and he was laid in iron until the time that his word came (Genesis 39:21-23; Psalms 105:18-19). Joseph’s deliverance did not make her accusation true, and delay is not acquittal.

name: Job
text: Perfect and upright, fearing God and eschewing evil; and in all his loss he sinned not with his lips. Job lived in the land of Uz but was not of that nation; he was a son of God, of the lineage of Adam, as Israel lives among the nations today and is not of them. He sanctified his children after every one his day and offered for them in case they had sinned. Satan, who took his orders from the Lord and needed his permission, was given all that Job had and then his flesh, and Job blessed the name of the Lord and answered his wife that we receive both good and evil at the hand of God. When the Lord answered him he repented in dust and ashes and prayed for his friends, and the Lord turned his captivity. Job was a man of the land of Uz, blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned from evil, the greatest of all the men of the east (Job 1:1-3). Living in the land of Uz did not make him of that nation, for he was a son of God, of the lineage of Adam. Some say he was an Edomite on the strength of a paragraph the Greek copy adds at the end of the book out of a Syriac writing, making him Jobab of the kings of Edom; the Hebrew, the Latin and the English all end at the same place, and that addition is commentary, not scripture. Job settles it himself: his skin was black upon him (Job 30:30). The law of sacrifice was never given to Esau, yet the Lord sends three men at the end of the book to offer through Job (Numbers 28:1-2); Ezekiel ranks him with Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14, 20). Job 29 shows who he was before the trial: he prepared his seat in the street as a judge, delivered the poor and the fatherless, and broke the jaws of the wicked (Job 29:4-17; Deuteronomy 16:18). His sons feasted in their houses, every one his day, which is their birthdays, the only birthdays the scriptures record being kept by the heathen; and Job offered burnt offerings for each of them, in case they had sinned in their hearts (Job 1:4-5; Job 8:4). When the sons of God came before the Lord, Satan came among them (Job 1:6); the sons of God are the lineage of Adam, also called angels, for another word for angel is messenger. The Lord asked Satan whether he had considered his servant Job, since there was none like him. The more good works a man does, the harder Satan comes at him. Satan asked whether Job feared God for nothing, and whether a hedge had not been made about him; the hedge is the angel of the Lord that encamps round about them that fear him (Job 1:8-10; Psalms 34:7). He is subject to God and took his orders: all Job had was put in his power, but not Job himself (Job 1:12). Both good and evil come from the Lord, who makes peace and creates evil (Isaiah 45:7). In one day the Sabeans, fire from heaven, the Chaldeans and a great wind took his herds, his servants and all ten children (Job 1:13-19). Job tore his mantle, fell to the ground and worshipped: he had come naked and would return naked, the Lord had given and the Lord had taken away, and he blessed the name of the Lord; in all this he did not sin or charge God with wrong (Job 1:20-22). Then the Lord bragged on him, that he still held fast his integrity; Satan was given his flesh but not his life (Job 2:3-7). His wife told him to curse God and die: if Satan cannot get to a man he comes through his woman, as he went to Eve. Job answered that she spoke as one of the foolish women, and asked whether they should receive good at God’s hand and not evil (Job 2:9-10). When the Lord answered out of the whirlwind, Job laid his hand on his mouth; he had uttered what he did not understand, and having now seen with his eye what he had heard by the ear, he repented in dust and ashes (Job 40:4; Job 42:3-6). The Lord’s wrath was kindled against the three friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, and the sacrifice for their sin had to be carried to the righteous one in the matter (Job 42:7-9). The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before, and seven sons and three daughters, Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, the fairest women in all the land, to whom he gave inheritance among their brothers. He lived a hundred and forty years and saw four generations (Job 42:10-16). James points to the patience of Job and the end the Lord gave, to show that the Lord is full of compassion and tender mercy (James 5:11). And Job looked past the restoration: he knew that his redeemer lived and would stand at the latter day upon the earth, and that though worms destroyed his body, in his flesh he would see God, with his own eyes (Job 19:25-27). His life is the pattern for every son of God: prepare the soul for temptation, for the trial comes by the Lord’s permission and inside his limits, and he will not suffer a man to be tempted above what he is able (Ecclesiasticus 2:1; 1 Corinthians 10:13).

name: Job’s three friends
text: Speaking of God the thing that is not right; condemning the righteous, having found no answer. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite came from their own places by appointment to mourn with Job and comfort him, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word. Then they reasoned from his suffering back to his guilt, and Eliphaz at last invented the sins outright. The Lord answered them by name: they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had, and he sent them with sacrifice to the man they had condemned, that he might pray for them. When Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had come on him, each came from his own place by appointment to mourn with him and to comfort him. They lifted up their voice and wept, rent every man his mantle, sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven, and sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word, for they saw that his grief was very great (Job 2:11-13). Friends who come to a man’s affliction with correction and hard truth are not the fault here. What is wanted is people who give straight facts and not people who butter a man up while he is in the wrong. The fault is the conclusion they reached and would not abandon. Eliphaz began where it cuts deepest: Job had instructed many, strengthened the weak hands, upheld him that was falling and strengthened the feeble knees, and now that it had come on him, he fainted (Job 4:3-5). There is one that is wise and teaches many and yet is unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19): you were the man who comforted everybody, and now your own turn has come and you want to give up. That much was fair warning. Then he went further and asked who ever perished being innocent, or where the righteous were cut off (Job 4:7), which turns every affliction into proof of sin. Bildad asked whether God perverts judgment, pointed at Job’s dead children as cast away for their transgression, and promised a latter end that would greatly increase if Job were pure and upright, on the false premise that he was not already upright (Job 8:3-7; Job 1:1, 5). Zophar told him God exacted of him less than his iniquity deserved (Job 11:6). Then Eliphaz stopped inferring and began inventing: he said Job’s wickedness was great, that he had taken a pledge from his brother for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing and withheld bread from the hungry (Job 22:5-7), none of which the record supports. Job named it while it was being done: they were forgers of lies and physicians of no value and miserable comforters, and he asked whether they would speak wickedly for God and talk deceitfully for him (Job 13:4, 7; Job 16:2). Defending God with false accusations against his servant is the thing this case is entered for. Elihu’s wrath was kindled against the three because they had found no answer and yet had condemned Job (Job 32:3); and it was Elihu who spoke the word that reaches to our own day, that by reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry, and they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty (Job 35:9). The Lord told Eliphaz the Temanite that his wrath was kindled against him and against his two friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had (Job 42:7). The remedy was sacrifice and intercession, and it had to be carried to the man they had accused: seven bullocks and seven rams, brought to his servant Job, a burnt offering offered for themselves, and Job would pray for them, for the Lord would accept him, or else he would deal with them after their folly (Job 42:8). That is how the priesthood always worked in Israel: the sacrifice is brought to the righteous one and offered on the sinner’s behalf, and the man who does not bring it is not forgiven. The three who had argued so long for Job’s guilt now depended on the prayer of the man they had condemned, and the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much (James 5:16). It was not the prayer by itself, but the prayer of a righteous man; the Most High deals with those who are dealing in righteousness. They did as the Lord commanded them, and the Lord also accepted Job; and it was in the praying for these friends that his own captivity was turned (Job 42:9-10). Afterward his brethren and sisters and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him and comforted him, every man bringing him a piece of money and an earring of gold (Job 42:11). The friends were restored along with everything else.

name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
text: Dealing wisely with Israel: hard bondage, the sons cast into the river, and refusing the Lord’s command through ten plagues. A new kingdom arose over Egypt that did not know Joseph, and resolved to deal wisely with Israel: institutional slavery, taskmasters, treasure cities Israel built and did not dwell in, and the sons cast into the river. To the Lord’s command he answered that he did not know the Lord, and hardened his heart through ten plagues that mocked every god of Egypt, until the firstborn died and the sea covered his host. What ancient Egypt did to Israel is what spiritual Egypt does, and the plagues are the pattern of what comes on it. Seventy souls came out of the loins of Jacob into Egypt, and the children of Israel were fruitful, increased abundantly and grew exceeding mighty, and the land was filled with them (Exodus 1:5-7). Then a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph (Exodus 1:8). That is not merely one man but a new kingdom, the New Kingdom of Egypt, the eighteenth dynasty; everyone who knew what Joseph had done for the previous dynasty was dead, and the new house did not care. He told his people that the children of Israel were more and mightier than they, and that they should deal wisely with them before they multiplied and joined their enemies (Exodus 1:9-10). Dealing wisely was institutional slavery: taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens, the treasure cities Pithom and Raamses which Israel built and did not dwell in, and lives made bitter with hard bondage in mortar and in brick and in all manner of service in the field (Exodus 1:11-14). Those are the curses by name: build a house and not dwell in it, the stranger within getting up very high and Israel coming down very low, and they that hate us reigning over us (Deuteronomy 28:30, 43-44; Leviticus 26:17). The mural of that bondage is still on the wall of the Theban tomb of Rekhmire. The more they were afflicted, the more they multiplied and spread. When the midwives would not kill the sons, Pharaoh charged all his people to cast every newborn son into the river (Exodus 1:22). The same wise dealing works on Israel in the land spiritually called Egypt today, where the taskmaster is no longer the overseer in the field but the governor, the politician and the boss (Revelation 11:8). When Moses and Aaron delivered the word of the Lord God of Israel, that he let his people go to hold a feast to him in the wilderness, Pharaoh asked who the Lord was that he should obey his voice, said he did not know the Lord, and refused (Exodus 5:1-2). The feast was the Passover. He sent them back to their burdens and called them idle, took away the straw and kept the tale of bricks, and the officers of Israel set over their own brethren were beaten (Exodus 5:4-19). The Lord had said he would harden his heart, and told him why: he had been raised up so that the Lord’s power might be shown in him and his name declared throughout all the earth (Exodus 9:16; Romans 9:17). After each plague he hardened it again; under the hail he admitted that he had sinned that time, and when it ceased he sinned yet more (Exodus 9:27, 34). The Lord declared that he would execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4), and every plague put one of them to shame. The river turned to blood mocked Sobek, the crocodile god of the rivers, who could not defend his own waters; the frogs mocked Heqet, so that Pharaoh had to beg Moses and not her to take them away; the lice and the swarms of biting flies mocked Beelzebub, the lord of flies, and the flies bit them and destroyed them (Wisdom of Solomon 16:9); the murrain mocked Hathor; the boils that broke out on the magicians themselves mocked Sekhmet, the goddess of health; the darkness that could be felt showed that Ra the sun god is no god at all; and at midnight the death of every firstborn, from the throne to the dungeon, showed that Osiris and Isis control neither life nor death, for to God the Lord belong the issues from death (Psalms 68:20). Israel’s quarter in Goshen was severed from the plagues (Exodus 8:22; Exodus 9:26). Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where there was not one dead; and Israel went out with the silver, the gold and the raiment of the Egyptians and spoiled them (Exodus 12:29-36). He pursued them into the sea, and the waters returned and covered the chariots, the horsemen and all the host that came after them, and not so much as one of them remained (Exodus 14:27-28). What came out of Egypt was not merely a people delivered but an army brought forth by great judgments (Exodus 7:4). And the sentence is not finished. The Lord has said that he will not suffer his people to dwell in the land of Egypt any longer, but will bring them out with a mighty hand and a stretched out arm and smite Egypt with plagues as before, and destroy all the land of it (2 Esdras 15:10-12).

name: Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives
text: Fearing God and not doing as the king of Egypt commanded them. Pharaoh commanded the Hebrew midwives to kill every son at the birthstool: the fruit of the body attacked at the source. They feared God more than the king and saved the men children alive, and answered that the daughters of Israel are not as the women of the nations. Because they feared God, he dealt well with them and made them houses. The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other Puah, and told them that when they did the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women and saw them upon the stools, if it were a son they were to kill him, and if a daughter, she should live (Exodus 1:15-16). This is what dealing wisely looks like when it reaches the cradle: the male children killed at birth, the fruit of the body cursed at the source, which is one of the named curses on the nation (Deuteronomy 28:18). Spiritual Egypt does the same thing by other means, through abortion and through a system built to take the sons, with poverty and drugs brought into the community and the school to prison pipeline waiting at the end of it. They are trying to stop the prophets from ever coming up. But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive (Exodus 1:17). That is the apostles’ rule long before the apostles: we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Two women stood between a king’s order and a nation’s sons. Called to account for why they had saved the men children alive, they answered that the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women, being lively, and delivered before the midwives come in to them (Exodus 1:18-19): the daughters of Israel are not as the women of the nations. The record does not rebuke the answer. Therefore God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very mighty; and it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses (Exodus 1:20-21). The blessing and the reason for it are stated in the same breath: not because the plan worked, but because they feared God. The increase they risked their own lives to protect is set down in the same verse as their reward, and the whole nation that came out of Egypt came through the hands they refused to use. Pharaoh’s plot did not succeed. His next order, that every son born be cast into the river, is what put the deliverer into his own house, where Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out of the water and paid his own mother to nurse him (Exodus 1:22; Exodus 2:5-10). The names of these two women are written in the book; the name of the Pharaoh who commanded them is not.

name: Moses, and the Egyptian in the sand
text: Slaying the Egyptian that smote his brother, and hiding him in the sand. Raised in Pharaoh’s house but nursed by his own mother, Moses always knew who he was. At forty it came into his heart to visit his brethren, and he looked on their burdens and saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and killed him. He did not merely marvel at the oppression; he used his position for his people, supposing his brethren would understand that God would deliver them by his hand. They did not understand, the man in the wrong threw the killing in his face, and Moses fled to Midian a stranger in a strange land forty years, until the God of his fathers sent back the man they had refused. A man of the house of Levi took to wife a daughter of Levi, Amram and Jochebed, and the child was goodly, exceeding fair; by faith his parents hid him three months and were not afraid of the king’s commandment (Exodus 2:1-2; Exodus 6:20; Acts 7:20; Hebrews 11:23). Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out of the river and knew at once that this was one of the Hebrews’ children, because the Most High puts a difference between the Egyptians and Israel, though both peoples were dark of skin (Exodus 2:5-6; Exodus 11:7). His sister Miriam was crafty, and by her offer his own mother was called and paid wages to nurse him, so that his first years were spent with her (Exodus 2:7-9). He was raised in the royal court and received one of the finest educations in the world, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words and in deeds (Acts 7:22). When he was full forty years old it came into his heart to visit his brethren, the children of Israel; he went out to them and looked on their burdens, and he spied an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, one of his brethren (Exodus 2:11; Acts 7:23). He did not act as though the palace had made him something else. This was not ordinary correction on a work site; it was an abuse of power in which his brother’s life was in danger. He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand (Exodus 2:12). He did not kill out of hatred, and the law weighs the other side of it: if a man forbears to deliver them that are drawn to death and those that are ready to be slain, and says he did not know it, the one that ponders the heart considers it, and he that keeps the soul knows it, and renders to every man according to his works (Proverbs 24:11-12). He did not merely marvel at the matter as the preacher warns (Ecclesiastes 5:8); he used his position for his people, supposing his brethren would have understood that God by his hand would deliver them, but they did not understand (Acts 7:25). The second day two men of the Hebrews strove together, and he asked the one that did the wrong why he smote his fellow. The man answered by asking who made him a prince and a judge over them, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian (Exodus 2:13-14). When a people is oppressed they take the oppression out on one another, and the same spirit answers correction among our people now, pointing the finger at the one who corrects. Moses was afraid, and knew that the thing was known. When Pharaoh heard of it he sought to slay Moses, but Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and dwelt in the land of Midian (Exodus 2:15). By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:24-26). At the well he stood up for the seven daughters of the priest of Midian against the shepherds and watered their flock, a man of war and not a weak man, and they told their father that an Egyptian had delivered them, for Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same colour as the Egyptians (Exodus 2:16-19). He married Zipporah and named his son Gershom, because he had been a stranger in a strange land (Exodus 2:21-22). No sentence upon the killing is recorded. Forty years later, at eighty, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire in a bush at Sinai, and the man they had refused with the question, who made him a ruler and a judge over them, is the same man God sent to be a ruler and a deliverer (Acts 7:30-35). The people he had tried to help turned on him; the God of his fathers sent him back to deliver them.

name: Moses and the uncircumcised son
text: Neglecting the token of the covenant in his own house, on the road to demand the release of God’s firstborn. Sent back to Egypt with the rod of God in his hand and the message that Israel was the Lord’s son, his firstborn, whom Pharaoh must release or lose his own firstborn, Moses went with his wife and his sons. On the way, at the inn, the Lord met him and sought to kill him, because his own son was uncircumcised. Zipporah took a sharp stone and circumcised the child, and the Lord let him go. The laws did not begin at Sinai, and the covenant of circumcision still stands. Circumcision was not a Sinai ordinance. It was given to Abraham as the token of the covenant: every man child in every generation circumcised at eight days, and the uncircumcised man child whose flesh is not circumcised cut off from his people, because he has broken the covenant (Genesis 17:10-14). Moses had spent forty years in Midian and had married Zipporah, a daughter of the priest of Midian and not a daughter of Israel, and the son of that house carried no token of the covenant. The Egyptians did not practise it either; they were a nation of uncleanness, and Israel was afterward told plainly not to do after the doings of the land of Egypt where they had dwelt (Leviticus 18:3). The word he was carrying makes the neglect weigh more. He was to tell Pharaoh that Israel is the Lord’s son, even his firstborn, and that Pharaoh must let that son go to serve him, and if he refused, the Lord would slay Pharaoh’s son, his firstborn (Exodus 4:22-23). Israel was not the first nation created; Israel was the first nation the Most High chose, the apple of his eye from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob down, and the firstborn is the heir. Moses was going to demand another man’s firstborn on pain of death while his own son bore no token of the very covenant he was invoking. That is why he was worthy of death. By the way in the inn, the Lord met him and sought to kill him (Exodus 4:24). Zipporah took a sharp stone and cut off the foreskin of her son and cast it at his feet, and called him a bloody husband; so the Lord let him go, and she said again that he was a bloody husband because of the circumcision (Exodus 4:25-26). Bloody because she had to take the stone and do it herself. The thing had to be set right in his own house before he could carry a word from God into Pharaoh’s house. This shows the laws did not begin at Sinai, and the covenant still stands. A son of Israel is circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), and a man who comes to the truth grown is still circumcised at forty, fifty or sixty years, as Abraham himself was circumcised at ninety and nine, and as Paul took Timothy, whose father was a Greek, and circumcised him (Genesis 17:24; Acts 16:3). Joshua had to circumcise again the generation born in the wilderness before they took the land (Joshua 5:2-5). Romans does not do away with circumcision of the flesh: circumcision profits if a man keeps the law, and the man circumcised who breaks the law has made his circumcision uncircumcision, while the uncircumcised who keeps the righteousness of the law is counted for circumcision (Romans 2:25-29). The circumcision of the heart is commanded alongside it and not instead of it, Israel being told to circumcise themselves to the Lord and take away the foreskins of their heart (Jeremiah 4:4; Deuteronomy 10:16). Nothing that defiles enters the kingdom (Revelation 21:27).

name: The magicians of Egypt
text: Withstanding Moses with their enchantments, and hardening Pharaoh in his refusal. The Lord made Moses a god to Pharaoh and Aaron his prophet, and it was Aaron’s rod that became a serpent and swallowed up the rods of the magicians. They matched the blood and the frogs with their enchantments, but could only add to the plagues and never lift one. At the lice they could not, and told Pharaoh it was the finger of God; at the boils they could not stand before Moses, because the boil was upon them. Every plague mocked a god of Egypt, and the magicians served what was being mocked. The Lord told Moses that he had made him a god to Pharaoh, with Aaron his brother as his prophet (Exodus 7:1). It was Aaron who cast down the rod before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a serpent; a great many people still say it was Moses holding the rod, because they do not read the account. Then Pharaoh called the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did in like manner with their enchantments, and every man cast down his rod, and they became serpents (Exodus 7:10-11). What they did was witchcraft, which the law names among the abominations for which the nations were cast out, and which is not to be suffered to live in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Exodus 22:18). There was real spiritual power at work; some of them dealt with Satan on a high level. Mark the limit of the craft: they could copy a plague and they could never lift one. They turned water into blood and could not turn it back clear, so the fish still died and the river still stank and the Egyptians could not drink (Exodus 7:22). They brought up frogs on the land of Egypt and could not take away a single frog, so that Pharaoh had to send for Moses and entreat the Lord, and not Heqet, to have them destroyed (Exodus 8:7-8). Every imitation added to the affliction of their own country and handed the king a reason to refuse, and the record gives that reason each time: Pharaoh’s heart was hardened and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said. Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods before the contest had properly begun (Exodus 7:12). Then the plagues came down on the very things the magicians served: the river to blood mocked Sobek, the god of the rivers; the frogs mocked Heqet; the lice and the biting flies mocked Beelzebub, the lord of flies and uncleanness; the murrain mocked Hathor; the boils mocked Sekhmet, the goddess of health; the hail and the fire mocked the sky and the earth; and the darkness mocked the sun god, for the Lord executed judgment against all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4). At the third plague the craft ran out. The magicians tried with their enchantments to bring forth lice out of the dust and could not, and they told Pharaoh that this was the finger of God (Exodus 8:18-19). At the sixth they could not so much as stand in the room before Moses, because the boil was upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians (Exodus 9:11). The men who claim now that none of this ever happened refuse it for the same reason: to admit it is to admit that the idols they call gods and goddesses were powerless before the God of Israel, and that those idols do not exist at all. Paul names the two and gives the standing sentence on every imitator after them: as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so these also resist the truth, but they shall proceed no further, for their folly shall be made manifest to all men (2 Timothy 3:8-9).

name: Israel at the first Passover
text: Doing as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron: the lamb, the blood on the door, the flesh roast with fire, the unleavened bread and bitter herbs. On the night the destroyer went through Egypt, every house of Israel that did as it was told was passed over. The month was made the beginning of months, the lamb without blemish was the shadow of Christ, the bitter herbs were the bondage and the unleavened bread the life without sin, and the ordinance was made perpetual on the spot: Christ our passover is sacrificed for us, and the feast is still to be kept. The Lord made this month the beginning of months, the first month of the year for Israel (Exodus 12:1-2). The month is Abib, its name before the exile; afterward it was called Nisan, and it falls between March and April (Exodus 13:4; Deuteronomy 16:1). The year of the nation begins in the spring, in the month Israel came out of Egypt, not on the first of January in the dead of winter. On the tenth day every man took a lamb according to the house of his fathers, and if the household was too little for the lamb he and his neighbour next to his house took it according to the number of the souls; the lamb was without blemish, a male of the first year, kept up until the fourteenth day and killed by the whole assembly of the congregation in the evening (Exodus 12:3-6). The feast days and the sacrifices are a shadow of things to come, and the body is of Christ; the lamb without blemish and without spot is Christ, foreordained before the foundation of the world and manifest in these last times (Colossians 2:16-17; 1 Peter 1:19-20). They took a bunch of hyssop, used like a brush, dipped it in the blood in the bason and struck the lintel and the two side posts, and none went out at the door of his house until the morning (Exodus 12:7, 22). A Hebrew who refused the blood would have died with the Egyptians. They ate the flesh that night roast with fire, not raw nor boiled at all with water, with unleavened bread and with bitter herbs, and let nothing remain until the morning (Exodus 12:8-10): the bitter herbs are the bitter bondage of Egypt, and the unleavened bread is being without sin. They ate it with their loins girded, their shoes on their feet and their staff in their hand, in haste, because the Lord was passing through Egypt that night to deliver them (Exodus 12:11). By faith Moses kept the passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them (Hebrews 11:28). The children of Israel went away and did exactly as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron (Exodus 12:28, 50). The Lord said he would pass through the land of Egypt that night and smite all the firstborn, man and beast, and execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt; the blood would be a token on the houses where Israel was, and when he saw the blood he would pass over them (Exodus 12:12-13). The destroyer was the almighty word of God, which the book of Wisdom describes leaping down out of heaven from the royal throne, in the quiet silence of that night, as a fierce man of war into the land of destruction; and upon the destruction of the firstborn the Egyptians acknowledged this people to be the sons of God (Wisdom of Solomon 18:13-16; John 1:1). At midnight every firstborn in Egypt died, from the throne to the dungeon, and Osiris and Isis controlled neither life nor death, for to God the Lord belong the issues from death; against the children of Israel not so much as a dog moved his tongue (Exodus 12:29; Exodus 11:7; Psalms 68:20). They went out the selfsame day, at the end of four hundred and thirty years, with the silver, the gold and the raiment of the Egyptians, and the hosts of the Lord went out by their armies (Exodus 12:35-41). The day was made a memorial and kept as a feast to the Lord throughout their generations, by an ordinance for ever. Seven days unleavened bread, the leaven put out of the houses on the first day, and the soul that eats leaven cut off from Israel; and the leaven to be purged is the sin within, for the body is the temple of God (Exodus 12:14-20; 1 Corinthians 3:16-17). No stranger eats of it unless all his males are circumcised, and then he is as one born in the land, with one law for the homeborn and the stranger; and not a bone of the lamb is broken, as not a bone of Christ was broken on the cross (Exodus 12:43-48; John 19:36). It was not done away. On the Passover night Christ took the bread and the cup and named them his body and the blood of the new testament shed for many for the remission of sins, which is why we do not kill a lamb and paint a doorpost today (Matthew 26:26-28). Christ our passover is sacrificed for us, so the feast is to be kept, not with old leaven nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:7-8).

name: Amalek
text: Smiting the hindmost, the feeble and faint and weary, when Israel came out of Egypt; and he feared not God. Amalek, the grandson of Esau, was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt. He did not meet the mighty men in front; he crept up behind and smote the hindmost, the feeble, the faint and the weary, and he did not fear God. The Lord swore war with Amalek from generation to generation and had it written for a memorial: Saul spared Agag, Samuel hewed him in pieces, Haman the Agagite rose in Persia, and the war runs on to the end of the world, when Jacob bruises the head. Then came Amalek and fought with Israel in Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). This was no stranger’s war. Timna was concubine to Eliphaz, Esau’s son, and bore him Amalek, and Amalek is named a duke among the dukes that came of Eliphaz in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:12, 16). That is the elite of Esau’s line, and the battle between the two brothers carried into the next generation. The manner of the attack is the charge, and Moses rehearsed it forty years later so it could not be forgotten: remember what Amalek did to Israel by the way when they came forth out of Egypt, how he met them by the way and smote the hindmost of them, even all that were feeble behind, when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). In a caravan the strong men walk in front; in the back are the old, the women, the babies and the lame. Rather than meet the mighty men head on, Amalek came up from behind, killed the feeble, and waited until Israel was tired and worn out to do it. They knew exactly who Israel was; those were their cousins. That same spirit works against the young and the old of this nation to this day. When Moses held up his hand Israel prevailed, and when he let down his hand Amalek prevailed; so they put a stone under him, and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side and the other on the other side, until the going down of the sun, and Joshua discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword (Exodus 17:11-13). Moses was about eighty years old holding a rod above his head all day; the fathers were mighty men. The sign showed the people whose hand their life was in. Then the Lord told Moses to write it for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, because he would utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven, and had sworn to have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exodus 17:14-16).
