Balaam pronounced the end of it: Amalek was the first of the nations, meaning the first nation to make war on Israel coming out of Egypt, but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever (Numbers 24:20). Hundreds of years later the Lord still remembered what Amalek did to Israel and how he laid wait for him in the way, and sent Saul by Samuel to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had (1 Samuel 15:2-3). Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High said remember; the law against bearing a grudge is toward the children of a man’s own people (Leviticus 19:18). Israel were no tyrants in it either: the Kenites were warned to depart from among the Amalekites before the sword came, for the kindness they had showed Israel coming up out of Egypt (1 Samuel 15:6). Saul spared Agag, and Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal (1 Samuel 15:33); of that seed Haman the Agagite rose in Persia to destroy the whole nation, and was hanged on his own gallows (Esther 3:1; Esther 7:10). The war runs from generation to generation. Today that seed says they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, and the Lord will make them come and worship before Israel’s feet and know that he has loved us (Revelation 2:9; Revelation 3:9). The enmity was set in the garden between the serpent’s seed and the woman’s seed; they bruised Christ’s heel, and at the end of the world the God of peace will bruise Satan under the feet of his people (Genesis 3:15; Romans 16:20; 2 Esdras 6:7-10). The command to blot out Amalek belongs to the kingdom and to the Lord’s timing, written in his book; it is not a licence for any man’s hand now, for Israel is to live peaceably with all men (Deuteronomy 25:19; Romans 12:18).

name: Moses
text: Refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; faithful in all the Lord’s house; very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth. Things were not bad for Moses in Egypt; he made them bad for himself by choosing his people. By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, chose affliction with the people of God over the pleasures of sin for a season, and led a stiffnecked house forty years. The Lord’s testimony on him is unmatched: his servant Moses was faithful in all his house, and he spoke with him mouth to mouth. He was very meek, above all the men on the face of the earth, and God buried him. By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he had respect to the recompence of the reward (Hebrews 11:24-26). Everybody in ancient Egypt was not badly off. Some of our people had money and standing and were comfortable with the oppression they lived under, like the officers of the children of Israel whom the taskmasters had set over their own brethren, until the beatings came to them too (Exodus 5:14); the same men live in spiritual Egypt now. In Egypt his head was shaved, his beard cut, his dress and his customs Egyptian, and he laid every bit of it down to be what he was called to be. He was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words and in deeds (Acts 7:22). He did not stutter, as is commonly taught; he was not fluent in the Hebrew of his brethren, having been raised in Pharaoh’s court and then spent forty years in Midian, and a language moves on in forty years, so Aaron was given him for a mouth and he stood to Aaron instead of God (Exodus 4:10-16). From the royal court he went to keeping his father in law’s flock for forty years, and when the Lord called him out of the bush his answer was, who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh (Exodus 3:11). A man’s goings are of the Lord (Proverbs 20:24). He built the tabernacle exactly as the Lord commanded him (Exodus 40:16), bore a congregation that murmured at every stage, and stood between the people and the wrath they provoked, asking to be blotted out of the Lord’s book if their sin was not forgiven (Exodus 32:11-14, 32). The man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3). When Miriam and Aaron spoke against him because of the Ethiopian woman, who was Zipporah the daughter of the priest of Midian, and asked whether the Lord had spoken only by Moses and not also by them, the Lord heard it, came down in the pillar of the cloud, and declared the difference: to a prophet among them he would make himself known in a vision and speak in a dream, but his servant Moses was not so, being faithful in all his house; with him he would speak mouth to mouth, even apparently and not in dark speeches, and Moses beheld the similitude of the Lord; why then were they not afraid to speak against his servant (Numbers 12:1-8). They that despise government and speak evil of dignities are presumptuous and selfwilled (2 Peter 2:10). Miriam became leprous, white as snow, and was shut out of the camp seven days, and the people did not journey until she was brought in again. The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11). He was refused the land for Meribah, which is entered separately, and the Lord buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, and no man knows of his sepulchre to this day (Deuteronomy 34:5-6). He was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, and his eye was not dim nor his natural force abated (Deuteronomy 34:7): he was not a weak, sickly old man; he was in full strength, and still he had to go up and die, because he could not enter. There arose not a prophet since in Israel like him, whom the Lord knew face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10). That verse also answers a doctrine. Some say Joshua was the prophet raised up like Moses, and therefore there is no Christ; but the same passage that says Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom says in the next breath that there arose not a prophet like Moses. Joshua was a mighty prophet, and he did not fit that word; Christ did (Deuteronomy 18:18). And Moses himself stood on the mount with Elijah at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

name: The manna hoarders
text: Keeping manna overnight; going out to gather on the Sabbath. The whole congregation murmured for the flesh pots of Egypt, and the Lord answered with bread from heaven and a test: a daily portion, to prove whether they would walk in his law or not. Some kept it till morning and it bred worms and stank. Told that the sixth day’s double portion was for the sabbath, some went out on the seventh day to gather and found none. The sabbath was already binding in the wilderness. The whole congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, wishing they had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt when they sat by the flesh pots and ate bread to the full (Exodus 16:2-3). When deliverance does not come easy, the people turn on the man sent to them. Moses answered that their murmurings were not against him and Aaron but against the Lord: complaining against the leadership the Most High sets up is murmuring against the Most High himself (Exodus 16:8). The Lord said he would rain bread from heaven, and the people would go out and gather a certain rate every day, that he might prove them, whether they would walk in his law or not (Exodus 16:4). They did not know what it was and said one to another, it is manna, which means, what is it; and Moses told them it was the bread the Lord had given them to eat (Exodus 16:15). Every man gathered according to his eating, and he that gathered much had nothing over and he that gathered little had no lack (Exodus 16:17-18): the portion was measured to the appetite and the household, because nourishment is not the same for everybody. Man does not live by bread only, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord, and that is what the Lord was proving by a daily portion (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4). The manna is the bread from heaven that speaks of Christ, and our fathers all ate the same spiritual meat and drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ (John 6:31-33; 1 Corinthians 10:1-4). Moses told them that no man was to leave any of it until the morning; some did not listen and left it until the morning, and it bred worms and stank (Exodus 16:19-20). Yesterday’s portion is not enough for today. Job esteemed the words of his mouth more than his necessary food, and Jeremiah found the words and ate them, and they were the joy and rejoicing of his heart (Job 23:12; Jeremiah 15:16). On the sixth day they gathered twice as much, and Moses said the next day was the rest of the holy sabbath to the Lord, so they were to bake and seethe that day what they would and lay up the rest; and what was laid up for the sabbath did not stink nor breed a worm (Exodus 16:22-24). Some of the people went out on the seventh day to gather, and found none (Exodus 16:27). The hoarded bread rotted, and Moses was wroth with them (Exodus 16:20). To the sabbath gatherers the Lord asked how long they refused to keep his commandments and his laws, and set the reason beside it: because the Lord had given them the sabbath, he gave them on the sixth day the bread of two days, and every man was to abide in his place and not go out on the seventh day (Exodus 16:28-29). The sabbath was binding before Sinai. Abiding in his place is about not going out to gather food on the sabbath, and it does not undo the holy convocation of the seventh day in all your dwellings, which is a gathering (Leviticus 23:3). The sentences were small and exact, a stink and an empty basket, given so that the daily portion and the sabbath would be understood before the greater tests came. An omer of the very manna that spoiled overnight was laid up before the Testimony and kept for the generations, that they might see the bread the Lord fed Israel with in the wilderness (Exodus 16:32-34), and Israel ate manna forty years, until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan (Exodus 16:35). The petition for daily bread sits in a prayer that is otherwise wholly about the kingdom, and it is that same lesson set where it cannot be missed (Matthew 6:11). These things are our examples, so that we should not lust after evil things as they lusted; they were not overthrown by an enemy in the wilderness, but by their own appetite (1 Corinthians 10:5-6).

name: Bezaleel and Aholiab
text: Making all that the Lord commanded, and no more; and teaching others to do it. The Lord called Bezaleel of Judah by name and filled him with the spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge and all manner of workmanship, gave him Aholiab of Dan, and put wisdom in the hearts of all that were wise hearted. God sets every member in the body as it pleases him. They made every piece to the pattern and taught their brethren, and Moses looked upon all the work and blessed them. The Lord told Moses that he had called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and had filled him with the spirit of God in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge and in all manner of workmanship, to devise cunning works in gold, in silver and in brass, in cutting of stones and in carving of timber; and that he had given him Aholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, and had put wisdom in the hearts of all that were wise hearted, that they might make everything he had commanded (Exodus 31:1-6). The first men in scripture said to be filled with the spirit of God were filled for the work of their hands. Bezaleel most likely never thought God had given him anything; in his own mind he was just good at something. The talent was given for that purpose, so that the tabernacle, the ark, the mercy seat, the garments and the vessels could be made. The Most High still works the same way. He sets the members, every one of them, in the body as it has pleased him, and there are diversities of operations but the same God working all in all, and the body is not one member but many (1 Corinthians 12:6-11, 14, 18). Carpenters, builders, painters, cooks and craftsmen come into the congregation, and the Lord sends the souls in so that the work gets done; a school goes from a folding table with a cloth on it to a built stage because the Lord brought builders in. But no man appoints himself, and no man sits on his hands or on somebody else’s gift. Everyone whose heart stirred him up and whose spirit made him willing brought the Lord’s offering, both men and women, and all the women that were wise hearted did spin with their hands (Exodus 35:21-26). The Lord had put it in his heart that he may teach, both he and Aholiab (Exodus 35:34): the two men the Most High dealt with in workmanship trained their brethren how to do it, so Israel put its talents together and built. They worked to the pattern and added nothing, and the children of Israel did according to all that the Lord commanded Moses (Exodus 39:42). Moses looked upon all the work, and they had done it as the Lord had commanded, and Moses blessed them (Exodus 39:43). The breastplate carried four rows of stones, twelve according to the names of the children of Israel, every one with his name like the engravings of a signet, and the shoulders of the ephod carried the same for a memorial: when the priest stepped on the scene you already knew what nation he was, because nationality mattered to the Lord and he took it seriously. The bells and the pomegranates went upon the hem of the robe round about, and the account keeps saying round about. The plate of the holy crown was of pure gold, written like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD (Exodus 39:8-14, 24-26, 30). Our forefathers the priests wore crowns of real gold; that is the heritage. Then the cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle they had made (Exodus 40:34). That spirit of workmanship on Israel is why the tabernacle, and afterward the house Solomon built, outshined anything the world had seen. Their skill was taught out and not held privately, and in the kingdom, though the sons of strangers shall build up our walls, it will be Israel directing how the Lord wants it done (Isaiah 60:10). Every case in Leviticus and Numbers takes place inside or around what these men built.

name: Aaron and Israel at the golden calf
text: Idolatry within weeks of the covenant: the spirit of Egypt still in Israel. Not forty days after they heard the voice from the mount, the people told Aaron to make them gods, since they did not know what had become of this Moses. Aaron, who had seen every plague, made the calf and proclaimed a feast to the Lord, and the people feasted and rose up to play. The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left. Moses stood in the breach, the sons of Levi drew the sword, and the Lord plagued the people because of the calf that Aaron made. When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, they gathered to Aaron and told him to make them gods to go before them, since as for this Moses they did not know what had become of him (Exodus 32:1). Any time deliverance did not come when Israel wanted it, the nation turned, and the leadership got the blame; the same spirit works against the leadership of Israel to this day. Aaron told them to break off the golden earrings in the ears of their wives, their sons and their daughters, which men and women both wore in the scriptures and which is not the sin here; he received the gold, fashioned it with a graving tool and made a molten calf, and they declared it the god that had brought them up out of the land of Egypt, and he built an altar before it and proclaimed a feast to the Lord for the next day (Exodus 32:2-5). Aaron had seen the miracles in Egypt and was set up as high priest, and he still succumbed to the pressure of the people. The people rose up early, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play; that play was fornication, the same play as at Peor (Exodus 32:6; 1 Corinthians 10:7-8). The Lord told Moses that they had turned aside quickly out of the way he commanded them, and that he had seen this people and it is a stiffnecked people (Exodus 32:8-9). Not forty days gone from the mount, and they had already left his commandments. The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left, and the same holds coming into this truth: the evil carried in from the world will corrupt a man and turn him from the Lord if it is not put off (Ecclesiastes 5:1). They had broken the first two commandments that had just been given at Sinai (Exodus 20:3-5). The Lord told Moses to let him alone, that his wrath might wax hot against them and consume them, and he would make of Moses a great nation; Moses was of Levi and of the seed of Jacob, so the Lord could have started over with him (Exodus 32:10). Moses stood in the middle and pleaded the name and the oath: why should the Egyptians say that for mischief he brought them out to slay them in the mountains; and he asked the Lord to remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel, to whom he swore by his own self. And the Lord repented of the evil which he thought to do to his people (Exodus 32:11-14). He was never going to break that covenant, for consuming the people would have destroyed the very seed he had sworn to, and his counsel stands from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10). Joshua heard the noise of the people and said there was a noise of war in the camp, and Moses answered that it was not the voice of them that shout for mastery nor the voice of them that cry for being overcome, but the noise of them that sing (Exodus 32:17-18): they were feasting and dancing around the idol, and Joshua’s loyalty at the mount is one of the main reasons the Lord chose him to follow Moses. When Moses came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, his anger waxed hot; he brake the tables beneath the mount, burnt the calf, ground it to powder, strawed it on the water and made the children of Israel drink of it (Exodus 32:19-20). Aaron answered exactly as Saul would answer afterward, blaming the congregation: they are set on mischief, I cast the gold into the fire, and there came out this calf (Exodus 32:22-24). A leader cannot blame the people he was left in charge of. The people were naked, for Aaron had made them naked to their shame among their enemies, the same nakedness of the garden, sin uncovered (Exodus 32:25). The sons of Levi answered the call to the Lord’s side, and about three thousand men fell that day, entered separately as their blessing (Exodus 32:26-28). Moses returned to mediate, asking to be blotted out of the Lord’s book if the sin was not forgiven, and the Lord answered that the man who sinned against him is the man he would blot out, and that in the day of his visitation he would visit their sin upon them; and the Lord plagued the people because they made the calf, which Aaron made (Exodus 32:32-35). They changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eats grass, and forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt (Psalms 106:19-21).

name: The sons of Levi at the golden calf
text: Answering, Who is on the Lord’s side? and executing the sentence on their own brethren. When Moses stood in the gate of the camp and asked who was on the Lord’s side, all the sons of Levi gathered to him, took every man his sword, and went through the camp from gate to gate without hesitating. Three thousand fell. For that day Levi was consecrated, taken instead of the firstborn, and given the charge of the sanctuary and the teaching of the law; the last blessing of Moses names the cause: they observed his word and kept his covenant. Moses stood in the gate of the camp and asked who is on the Lord’s side, and all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together to him (Exodus 32:26). The command was the hardest in the law: every man was to put his sword by his side, go in and out from gate to gate throughout the camp, and slay his brother, his companion and his neighbour (Exodus 32:27). They did according to the word of Moses without hesitating, and about three thousand men of the people fell that day (Exodus 32:28). The Lord chose those particular ones to die; that spirit would have wrecked the nation down the road, so he moved it out of the congregation. This is the zeal Levi had for the Most High, and his blessing states it: he said of his father and of his mother that he had not seen him, neither did he acknowledge his brethren nor know his own children, because they observed the Lord’s word and kept his covenant (Deuteronomy 33:9). They did not care who it was; if you broke the law of the Most High, Levi came. Moses told them to consecrate themselves that day to the Lord, every man upon his son and upon his brother, that he might bestow upon them a blessing that day (Exodus 32:29). The Most High took the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn, which were his from the day he smote the firstborn of Egypt, and gave them the charge of the sanctuary, and the stranger that came near was to be put to death (Numbers 3:10-13). The last blessing of Moses sets their office: the Thummim and the Urim with the Lord’s holy one; they were to teach Jacob his judgments and Israel his law, and put incense before him and whole burnt sacrifice upon his altar; and the Lord was asked to bless his substance, accept the work of his hands, and smite through the loins of them that rose against him and of them that hated him, that they rise not again (Deuteronomy 33:8-11). That is why Levi had no land of his own but dwelt among all the tribes: he made the sacrifices and taught the laws to the people, and the tithes were his substance (Ecclesiasticus 45:16-17; Deuteronomy 14:27-29).

name: Nadab and Abihu
text: Offering strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. The law of the incense had already been given, with specificity, to their own father: a perpetual sweet incense, and no strange incense on that altar. The two sons of Aaron took their censers and offered strange fire, which he had not commanded them, and the same fire that had consumed the lawful offering came out from the Lord and devoured them. Their father was not permitted to mourn them, because they died in the midst of sin. Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, put fire in it and incense on it, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not (Leviticus 10:1). The instructions had already been given, and given to their own father: Aaron was to burn sweet incense upon the altar every morning and at even, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout their generations, and no strange incense was to be offered on it (Exodus 30:7-9). There were instructions on what could be burned and what could not. When the Most High gave instructions on what to sacrifice and how, it was with specificity; a man did it exactly the way he was told. They were also not the men authorized to burn it. In the tabernacle service a man was appointed to his service and could not take a service upon himself, and the pattern held through the generations: Zacharias executed the priest’s office in the order of his course, and his lot, his appointed job, was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord (Luke 1:8-9). Aaron and his sons were appointed to wait on the priest’s office, and the stranger that came near was to be put to death (Numbers 3:10). Fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord (Leviticus 10:2). It was the same fire that had come out from before the Lord and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar while the people shouted and fell on their faces (Leviticus 9:24). Moses said this is what the Lord spoke: I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified; and Aaron held his peace (Leviticus 10:3). Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, carried them in their coats out of the camp (Leviticus 10:4-5). Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar were told not to uncover their heads nor rend their clothes, lest they die and wrath come upon all the people. They were not to mourn them, because Nadab and Abihu died in the midst of sin, though the whole house of Israel might bewail the burning the Lord had kindled; the same standard fell on Ezekiel, told to make no mourning when the desire of his eyes was taken with a stroke, and on Jehoiakim, for whom no man was to lament (Leviticus 10:6; Ezekiel 24:16-18; Jeremiah 22:18). They could not go out from the door of the tabernacle, for the anointing oil of the Lord was upon them (Leviticus 10:7; Leviticus 21:12). Then came the standing rule for the priests on duty: neither Aaron nor his sons were to drink wine or strong drink when they went into the tabernacle of the congregation, so that they could put a difference between holy and unholy and between unclean and clean and teach the children of Israel all the statutes (Leviticus 10:9-11). Ezekiel lays out the same working rules: the sons of Zadok entering the gates of the inner court are clothed in linen and girded with nothing that causes sweat, they change garments before going out to the people, they drink no wine in the inner court, they teach the difference between the holy and the profane, and in controversy they stand in judgment (Ezekiel 44:17-24). The chapter ends on the other side of the same law. Moses diligently sought the goat of the sin offering and found it burnt, and was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, because it should have been eaten in the holy place to bear the iniquity of the congregation. Aaron answered that this day they had offered their sin offering and their burnt offering, and such things had befallen him, and asked whether it would have been accepted in the sight of the Lord if he had eaten the sin offering that day; and when Moses heard that, he was content (Leviticus 10:16-20). The law that killed the sons was not applied blindly to the father.

name: The blasphemer in the camp
text: Blaspheming the Name of the Lord, and cursing, in a quarrel. The son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian, fought with a man of Israel in the camp and blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed: he spoke ill of the Lord, and it was heard. He was held in ward until the mind of the Lord was shown, and his case became the statute: the man that blasphemes the name of the Lord is surely put to death, the stranger as well as the home born. The son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the children of Israel, and he and a man of Israel strove together in the camp (Leviticus 24:10). His mother was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan; his father being an Egyptian shows he was conceived while Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, when some of the daughters of Israel had children by them (Leviticus 24:11). On his own standing there is no such thing as being half Israelite or a quarter Israelite: if the parent is Israel, the child is Israel. The strife itself most likely arose from a man of Israel correcting him concerning the law. In the striving the Israelitish woman’s son blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed. Blasphemy is the expressing of contempt, scorn or profound disrespect toward the divine, whether in speech, in writing or in action, and it has levels to it. The cursing here is not modern curse words; it means he spoke ill of the Lord, insulting the divine aloud in the camp, and the two words are naming the same thing. The offense was against God directly, and it was heard. They put him in ward, that the mind of the Lord might be shewed them (Leviticus 24:12): the accused held, and the sentence sought rather than assumed. The Lord’s answer became the statute. The man that had cursed was to be brought outside the camp, all that heard him were to lay their hands upon his head, and all the congregation was to stone him; the man that curses his God shall bear his sin, and he that blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death, all the congregation stoning him, the stranger as well as he that is born in the land (Leviticus 24:14-16). Under Moses, blaspheming the Lord was an immediate death sentence, and one manner of law stood for the stranger and for one of your own country (Leviticus 24:22). The witnesses laid their hands on his head because their testimony was the ground of the death, and the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses (Leviticus 24:23). The same charge is named elsewhere in the record, so its weight can be measured. When Rabshakeh stood on the wall and told Judah that no god of the nations had delivered his land and that the Lord would not deliver them either, Hezekiah called that day a day of trouble and of rebuke and of blasphemy, and the answer came back that the king of Assyria had reproached and blasphemed the Holy One of Israel (2 Kings 19:3-4, 22). It can also be provoked by a man’s own conduct: Nathan told David that by his deed he had given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme (2 Samuel 12:14). In the same breath as the sentence came the law of recompense, breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth (Leviticus 24:19-20); and when Christ came he magnified that law for dealing inside the nation. They had heard that it was said, an eye for an eye, and he told them not to resist evil, but to turn the other cheek, to let the man who sues for the coat have the cloak, and to go two miles with the man who compels one (Matthew 5:38-42). Inside the nation the walk is forgiveness, patience and longsuffering, because these are brothers with a conscience.

name: The complainers at Taberah and the lusters at Kibroth-hattaavah
text: Complaining against the Lord after the deliverance, and lusting after the food of Egypt behind the mixed multitude. The Most High hates it when his people complain. He had just destroyed Egypt for them, and at the first trial on the far side of the sea they complained, and the fire of the Lord burnt in the outskirts of the camp. Then the mixed multitude fell a lusting, and Israel followed them and wept for the fish and the cucumbers and the garlick of the house of bondage, despising angels’ food that agreed to every taste. Quail came, and with the quail a plague, and the graves of lust are the name of the place. When the people complained it displeased the Lord, and he heard it, and his anger was kindled (Numbers 11:1). He had just destroyed Egypt for Israel, its land, its firstborn and its army in the sea, and at the first trial on the other side they jumped off his bandwagon. Nothing spoken behind closed doors is hidden. Inquisition is made into the counsels of the ungodly, the ear of jealousy hears all things, and a murmuring that is unprofitable is to be refrained from, for no word so secret shall go for nothing, and the mouth that lies slays the soul (Wisdom of Solomon 1:8-11). A problem with the leadership the Most High set up is a problem with the Most High himself. Then the mixed multitude that was among them fell a lusting, and the children of Israel also wept again (Numbers 11:4). The mixed multitude were the other nations sprinkled in among Israel that went up with them out of Egypt, and the law appointed what they were to be, bondmen and bondmaids, not Israel’s example (Exodus 12:38; Leviticus 25:44-45). It was not Israel complaining first. The nations lusted after the food of Egypt, and the children of Israel, gullible and assimilated as always, followed right after them, remembering the fish they ate freely in Egypt, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlick (Numbers 11:5). They wept for the diet of the house of bondage weeks after the bondage ended, and they had just watched the fire consume the complainers in the outermost parts of the camp and went back and did the same thing. And what they despised was angels’ food, sent from heaven without their labour, which they had only to pick up, able to content every man’s delight and agreeing to every taste, tempering itself to every man’s liking, so that whatever the tongue craved that day the manna tasted like it (Psalms 78:25; Wisdom of Solomon 16:20-21). They tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust (Psalms 78:18). The same spirit is on the people in this captivity, comfortable with the entertainments and the table of the oppressor. At Taberah the fire of the Lord burnt among them and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp; the people cried to Moses, and when Moses prayed to the Lord the fire was quenched, and the place was named for the burning (Numbers 11:1-3). The weight of carrying them fell on Moses, who asked the Lord why he had afflicted his servant and laid the burden of all this people upon him, and whether he had conceived them all, that he should carry them in his bosom as a nursing father, and said that if this was how it was to be, let him be killed out of hand (Numbers 11:11-15). He was carrying grown people who behaved like children. The reason for the second judgment was stated plainly: because they had despised the Lord which is among them and had wept before him, asking why they came out of Egypt, they would eat flesh not one day nor two nor five nor ten nor twenty, but a whole month, until it came out at their nostrils and was loathsome to them (Numbers 11:18-20). When Moses asked how it could be done for six hundred thousand footmen, the Lord answered by asking whether the Lord’s hand had waxed short (Numbers 11:23). A wind from the Lord brought quails from the sea and let them fall by the camp, two cubits high upon the face of the earth, and while the flesh was yet between their teeth, before it was chewed, the wrath of the Lord was kindled and he smote the people with a very great plague; and the place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of lust, because there they buried the people that lusted (Numbers 11:31-34). He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul (Psalms 106:15). The lesson also stands in nature: excess of meat brings sickness, and many have perished by surfeiting, but he that takes heed prolongs his life (Ecclesiasticus 37:29-31). These things were our examples, to the intent that we should not lust after evil things as they also lusted (1 Corinthians 10:6).

name: Eldad and Medad
text: Prophesying in the camp when the spirit rested on them, and being defended by Moses. Moses told the Lord he was not able to bear the people alone, so the Lord took of the spirit that was on him and put it on seventy elders, and they prophesied. Two of the written men stayed in the camp, and the spirit rested on them there, and they prophesied in the camp. Joshua asked Moses to forbid them; Moses corrected the envy and wished that all the Lord’s people were prophets. Moses said he was not able to bear all this people alone, because it was too heavy for him, and the Lord told him to gather seventy men of the elders of Israel, men he knew to be elders and officers over them, and bring them to the tabernacle; He would take of the spirit that was on Moses and put it on them, so that they would bear the burden of the people with him (Numbers 11:14-17). The spirit on the head is meant to come down to the men under him. Leadership still works that way, and the teaching says so plainly: the deacons, the captains and the officers teach the way they teach because of what was taught to them and because the spirit on the man over them was put on them, not because any one of them worked it out on his own. That is why the leaders have to be right according to the scriptures, since it is their spirit the Most High takes and lets rest on the others. The Lord came down in a cloud, took of the spirit that was on Moses and gave it to the seventy elders, and when the spirit rested on them they prophesied and did not cease (Numbers 11:24-27): they taught, and they did not stop. It was the same with Elijah and Elisha, when Elisha asked for a double portion of his master’s spirit before Elijah was taken up and the sons of the prophets said that the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha (2 Kings 2:9, 15), and the same in the time of Christ, when men could tell that spirit was on the apostles. But two of the men remained in the camp, Eldad and Medad, and the spirit rested on them; they were among those written, but had not gone out to the tabernacle, and they prophesied in the camp. They prophesied where the people were, not at the tabernacle with the rest, and they did not conceal it or wait for permission before speaking. A young man ran and told Moses, and Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses and one of his young men, asked Moses to forbid them (Numbers 11:28-29). Joshua was carrying a spirit of envy, and Moses corrected it: he asked whether Joshua envied for his sake, and wished that all the Lord’s people were prophets and that the Lord would put His spirit on them. The Most High wants all His people to be prophets. Do not envy the gift on another brother or sister; glean from it. A brother may be the better teacher and a sister the better labourer, so go and learn from them rather than rolling in envy. Christ answered John the same way when John forbade a man casting out devils because he did not follow with them: forbid him not, for the man who is not against us is for us (Luke 9:49-50). The teaching reads Joshua’s word a second way as well. He was the servant of Moses, being moulded and trained to lead, and he never once tried to overthrow him; he was not vainglorious, he was loyal, and his concern was for his master and not for himself. What he saw in the camp Moses had not seen as yet, because a man can carry the spirit and still teach the scriptures for vainglory and for preeminence, which is what the seventy princes would show soon enough. The lesson drawn for a man waiting on his own ministry is the same: learn to be a disciple first, hold post, hand out a flyer, learn to read, and then learn to teach, the way Elisha would not leave his master’s side. So the blessing was defended by the one man whose standing it might have threatened, and what Moses wished for is what Joel prophesied and Peter cited at Pentecost as fulfilled: the spirit poured out on all flesh, with sons and daughters prophesying (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:16-18).

name: Aaron and Miriam
text: Speaking against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, and claiming an equal standing: hath he not spoken also by us?. Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, who was Zipporah the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom the Lord had allowed him. The woman was the excuse; what they actually said was a claim of equal standing with the man God had set over them, and the Lord heard it. He came down and declared the difference to their faces, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow: a father’s spit in her face, seven days without the camp, while the whole nation waited. Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman he had married (Numbers 12:1). This is still Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom Moses married in the forty years he dwelt outside Egypt, when he was in a land by himself with none of his own people around him, and whom the Lord allowed him (Exodus 2:16, 21); a place being called Midian and the woman being called an Ethiopian is no contradiction. They had said nothing about her when Moses was saving them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women; the murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of what was at hand. The woman was the excuse. The charge is what they actually said: they asked whether the Lord had spoken only by Moses, and not also by them, and the Lord heard it (Numbers 12:2). Was the Most High dealing with Aaron and Miriam? He was. He was dealing with Moses more, and that is what could not be borne, so the real matter was a covetousness for his standing dressed up as a complaint about his wife. The teaching names the pattern: a man who has a problem with the leadership goes looking for something in the leadership to hold up, so that when he gossips and murmurs about the body he looks like the righteous one; pull the curtain back and it was never about the thing he named, it was about power. The man Moses was very meek, above all the men on the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3), so this was no hard man provoking them. Those who despise government are presumptuous and selfwilled, and are not afraid to speak evil of dignities (2 Peter 2:10). The Lord spoke suddenly to Moses, Aaron and Miriam, calling the three of them out to the tabernacle; He came down in the pillar of the cloud, called Aaron and Miriam forward, and declared the difference: to a prophet among them He would make Himself known in a vision and speak in a dream, but His servant Moses was not so, being faithful in all His house; with him He spoke mouth to mouth, plainly and not in dark speeches; so why were they not afraid to speak against His servant Moses (Numbers 12:4-5, 6-10). He had to let them know that He does not deal with everyone the same. They were a prophet and a prophetess and He spoke with them, but in visions and dreams; some spirits are greater than others, and a nation has to learn to accept it. The anger of the Lord was kindled, the cloud departed from the tabernacle, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow. Aaron pleaded that the sin not be laid on them, and Moses cried to the Lord to heal her (Numbers 12:11, 13-15). The Lord answered that if her father had only spat in her face she would have been ashamed seven days, so she was to be shut out of the camp seven days and then received in again. The spit is correction, a father putting his child in her place; had she been raised to respect the men of the Lord, this would not have come on her. Miriam was shut out, and the people did not journey until she was brought in again: a whole nation held in place over one tongue. This is a charge to raise the children in the fear of the Lord and teach them to respect the elders and the men of the Lord. Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, and fathers are not to provoke their children to wrath but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:1-4); parents who let their children speak evil to the men of the Lord bring the judgment on their own household. Moses made it a standing warning: Israel was to remember what the Lord their God did to Miriam by the way (Deuteronomy 24:9).

name: The ten spies
text: Bringing up an evil report of the land the Lord had given; making the congregation to murmur. Twelve rulers, heads of the children of Israel, searched the land the Lord was giving them for forty days and brought back the fruit. Ten put a nevertheless after the promise: the people were strong, the cities walled, they had seen the giants, and they were as grasshoppers in their own sight. Doubt and fear are Satan’s playground, and the evil report carried that spirit through the whole camp in a night. The ten died by the plague before the Lord. The Lord told Moses to send men to search the land of Canaan, which He was giving to the children of Israel, a ruler of every tribe of their fathers (Numbers 13:1-2). Which I give: the land was already given and the fight was already the Lord’s. The men sent were not regular brothers either; every one was a ruler among them, a head of the children of Israel, a man of renown able to lead other men, and that is what makes the report so heavy. Sending spies to learn the landscape, the people and their strength is the wisdom of war, which Moses had learned as a leader in Egypt. They searched the land forty days and cut down a branch with one cluster of grapes so great that two men carried it between them on a staff, and brought pomegranates and figs (Numbers 13:23-25), for the earth was younger then and brought forth greater stature in its fruit and in its men (2 Esdras 5:52-55). They reported that the land surely flowed with milk and honey, and showed the fruit. Then the report turns on one word: nevertheless, the people who dwelt in the land were strong, the cities walled and very great, and they had seen the children of Anak there (Numbers 13:27-28). Doubt entered on the heels of the promise. Caleb stilled the people before Moses and urged them to go up at once and possess it, because they were well able to overcome it (Numbers 13:30). But the men who went up with him said they were not able to go up against the people, who were stronger than they, and they brought up an evil report of the land, calling it a land that eats up its inhabitants, where they had seen the giants, the sons of Anak, and had been as grasshoppers in their own sight and in the giants’ sight (Numbers 13:31-33). Rulers and leaders, shook with doubt and fear, who had watched Egypt destroyed and forgot that the Most High had already brought down mightier nations than these. Doubt and fear are Satan’s playground. An evil report spreads a spirit of fear, and God has not given His people the spirit of fear but of power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7). The giants they feared were famous from the beginning, of great stature and expert in war, yet the Lord chose them not and they were destroyed because they had no wisdom (Baruch 3:26-28), and by the law of war the fearful are sent home, lest they put their fear on the other men (Deuteronomy 20:8; 1 Maccabees 3:56). The spirit of fear jumped from the leaders onto everybody: all the congregation lifted up their voice and cried, the people wept that night, and they talked of making a captain and returning to Egypt, forgetting there was nothing to return to, since Pharaoh and his army were at the bottom of the sea (Numbers 14:1-4). When Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes and spoke for the land, all the congregation called for them to be stoned, and the glory of the Lord appeared in the tabernacle before all the children of Israel (Numbers 14:6-10). It is the same today: bring the truth that the Most High loves this people and has something great for them if they repent, and they will not believe it and are ready to kill the messenger. The men Moses had sent to search the land, who returned and made all the congregation murmur against him by bringing up a slander on the land, died by the plague before the Lord; but Joshua and Caleb, of the men who went to search the land, lived on (Numbers 14:34-38). The nation’s sentence, entered separately, was measured from their search: forty days searching the land, each day for a year, forty years bearing their iniquities. The Most High deals in numbers, and the forty matched the forty exactly. Forty-five years later Caleb, at eighty-five, asked for the mountain of the very giants the ten had feared, and took it (Joshua 14:10-12).

name: Caleb and Joshua
text: Wholly following the Lord when ten spies and the whole congregation would not. Twelve men saw the same land, the same walled cities and the same giants. Ten said they were not able. Two rent their clothes before a congregation reaching for stones and said the Lord was with them and they need not fear the people. The Most High had already said He would deliver the enemy into their hands, so the stature of the giants did not matter. Caleb had another spirit with him and followed the Lord fully; of six hundred thousand, these two walked into the land. Twelve rulers walked the same ground and came back with the same facts; the difference was not information. Caleb stilled the people before Moses and urged them to go up at once and possess the land, because they were well able to overcome it (Numbers 13:30). The Most High had said that the land was His gift to the children of Israel (Numbers 13:2), so the stature of the men in it did not matter. Caleb was not playing any games and was not shook; he was about that business, ready to go and take the land, because he understood the land had already been promised. When the whole congregation wept and spoke of a captain to take them back to Egypt, Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes and spoke to all the company: the land they had passed through was an exceedingly good land; if the Lord delighted in them He would bring them into it; they were only not to rebel against the Lord or fear the people of the land, who were bread for them, because their defence had departed from them and the Lord was with Israel (Numbers 14:6-9). All the congregation called for them to be stoned, and the glory of the Lord appeared in the tabernacle (Numbers 14:10). That is what the obedience cost: public contradiction of a settled majority, faith and courage while the leaders around them were shook with doubt and fear. There has to be something different about a man in the matter of faith, because a faithless spirit does not profit the nation at all, and a man cannot keep company with men who will not go up. The Lord’s own words fix the standard: His servant Caleb had another spirit with him and had followed Him fully (Numbers 14:24). None of that generation would come into the land except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun (Numbers 14:30). Every other man numbered from twenty years old and upward died in the wilderness at a year for a day, and their children went in (Numbers 14:29-33). Out of all the people who came out of Egypt, only these two saw the land. Caleb at eighty-five asked for the mountain with the giants on it: he was as strong that day as on the day Moses sent him, as his strength was then so was it for war, and he asked for the mountain the Lord had spoken of that day, where Joshua had heard the Anakims were and the cities great and fenced; if the Lord was with him he would drive them out. Hebron became Caleb’s inheritance because he wholly followed the Lord God of Israel (Joshua 14:10-14). The record praises the source of that strength rather than the man: the Lord gave strength also to Caleb, and it remained with him to his old age, so that he entered upon the high places of the land, and his seed obtained it for a heritage, so that all the children of Israel might see that it is good to follow the Lord (Ecclesiasticus 46:9-10). Everybody does not get that, and strength is shown when a man is going through something, not when everything is good. Joshua succeeded Moses, a man in whom the spirit was, was set before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation and given some of the honour of Moses in their sight, and he divided the land he had been the first to say could be taken (Numbers 27:18; Joshua 14:6). Mattathias recalled both of them at the end of his life: Caleb received the heritage of the land for bearing witness before the congregation, and Joshua was made a judge in Israel for fulfilling the word (1 Maccabees 2:55-56).

name: The generation that died in the wilderness
text: Tempting the Lord ten times; unbelief at Kadesh-barnea; a captain to return into Egypt. Those numbered from twenty years old who had seen the signs in Egypt and at the sea tempted the Lord ten times, from the Red Sea to the report of the spies, and at the border of the land talked of making a captain and returning to Egypt: a slave mentality that called the house of bondage home. The Lord said He would do to them exactly as they had spoken in His ears. Their carcases fell in the wilderness at a year for a day, and only Caleb and Joshua of them entered. The charge is a count, and the Lord gave the number Himself: all the men who had seen His glory and the miracles He did in Egypt and in the wilderness had tempted Him ten times and had not listened to His voice (Numbers 14:22). The teaching writes the ten down, because the Most High deals in numbers and nothing in the Bible is insignificant. At the Red Sea, because there were no graves in Egypt; at Marah, over the bitter water; in the wilderness of Sin, for the flesh pots; the hoarding of the manna against a plain instruction; the gathering on the sabbath after two days of bread had been given; Massah and Meribah, when they chode with Moses over water and he was almost stoned; the golden calf, and the disrespect in the words, as for this Moses, we know not what is become of him; Taberah; the lusting for flesh at Kibroth-hattaavah, weeping for the fish and the cucumbers and the melons and the leeks and the onions and the garlick; and the tenth and last, the report of the spies (Exodus 14:11-12; Exodus 15:23-24; Exodus 16:2-3, 19-20, 27-29; Exodus 17:2-7; Exodus 32:1-10; Numbers 11:1-6, 34; Numbers 14:1-4). The Lord was patient when they asked for water and for food, and gave it, and it was not enough. At the border of the land the whole congregation wept, wishing they had died in the land of Egypt or in this wilderness, and said one to another that they should make a captain and return to Egypt (Numbers 14:2-4). Were they loved by the Egyptians? They were hated there as they are hated in this land. They had cried to the Most High under the taskmasters, and now they wanted to go back to master. That is a slave mentality; the teaching recalls Harriet Tubman saying she could have saved thousands more had they known they were slaves. Making a captain was a vote against the men God appointed, a search for somebody who would give heed to their itching ears, and it is the same mentality that calls the land of captivity home when it is exile and not home. And do not say it would have been different: some will say the same thing when the Most High brings this people out again, and the murmuring is heard every year in the tents at the feast. Unbelief is why they could not enter (Hebrews 3:19). The Lord asked how long He should bear with this evil congregation that murmured against Him, and swore that as they had spoken in His ears, so He would do to them: their carcases would fall in this wilderness, and all who were numbered from twenty years old and upward who had murmured against Him would not come into the land, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun; but their little ones, whom they said would be a prey, He would bring in, and they would know the land their fathers had despised (Numbers 14:28-35). After the number of the days they searched the land, forty days, each day for a year, they would bear their iniquities forty years, and the forty matched the forty exactly. Told the sentence, they mourned, then rose early and presumed to go up to the hill top without the ark and without Moses, and the Amalekites and the Canaanites came down and smote them as far as Hormah (Numbers 14:40-45). All they had to do was follow counsel, and their refusal was written so that we would learn to follow the counsel of the men the Most High sets up instead of leaning on our own presumption. From Kadesh-barnea to the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until all the generation of the men of war had been wasted out from among the host (Deuteronomy 2:14-16). Six hundred thousand footmen, hardened in heart and gathered together, whom He did not pity (Ecclesiasticus 16:10). Paul draws the warning for us: do not murmur as some of them murmured and were destroyed of the destroyer, for these things happened to them for examples and are written for our admonition, so harden not your hearts as in the provocation, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief (1 Corinthians 10:10-11; Hebrews 3:8-12).

name: The man gathering sticks on the Sabbath
text: Gathering sticks on the Sabbath day to kindle a fire: the presumptuous sin. The sabbath had already been given as the sign between the Lord and Israel, and its breach already carried death. The law had just separated the sin of ignorance, which an offering covered, from the sin done presumptuously, which is a man thinking about it before he does it; the man found gathering sticks is the example the chapter gives. He was held in ward until the manner of the death was declared, and all the congregation stoned him. The fringes were given in the same breath, so that Israel would look and remember. Israel was to keep the Lord’s sabbaths, for it was a sign between Him and them throughout their generations, so that they would know that He was the Lord who sanctified them; everyone who defiled it was surely to be put to death, and anyone who did work on it was to be cut off from among his people (Exodus 31:13-14, 15). It is more than a day of rest; it is the sign of who the God of Israel is. No fire was to be kindled throughout their habitations on the sabbath day (Exodus 35:2, 3), and kindling fire goes to cooking: what was to be baked was baked the day before and the rest laid up, for the sabbath food is cooked the day before (Exodus 16:23). The chapter sets the two sins side by side. If a soul sinned through ignorance, without knowing what he was doing, he brought a she goat of the first year, the priest made an atonement for him, and it was forgiven him, and one law covered the man born in Israel and the stranger alike (Numbers 15:27-29). But the soul that does anything presumptuously, whether born in the land or a stranger, reproaches the Lord and is cut off from among his people; because he has despised the word of the Lord and broken His commandment, that soul is utterly cut off, and his iniquity is on him (Numbers 15:30-31). Presumptuously means wilfully: he thought about it before he did it, and there was no offering written for that. While the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the sabbath day (Numbers 15:32). He is the example of the sin just described. He was not picking up sticks for the sake of sticks; he was gathering them to kindle a fire and cook on a day he was commanded to rest. He never even reached the act; he had the intention, and the case stands as a warning against every man excusing his own trade on that day. Those who found him brought him to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation, and they put him in ward, which is to say they locked him up, because it had not been declared what should be done to him: the fact of the death was already written, and the manner was what was sought (Numbers 15:33-34). The Lord told Moses that the man was surely to be put to death, all the congregation stoning him with stones outside the camp; and all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him with stones, and he died, as the Lord commanded Moses (Numbers 15:35-36). He was killed without mercy, and he was made an example. Because of that act the Most High gave Israel the fringes: they were to make fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, with a ribband of blue on the fringe, so that they would look on it and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them, and not seek after their own heart and their own eyes, after which they used to go astray (Numbers 15:37-41). The fringe is worn on the border where it can be seen. When a man thinks of sin he looks at the fringes and remembers the law, instead of going out and picking up sticks. The stoning was done away in Christ, but the judgment for breaking the sabbath still stands, and the mercy is not a licence. Anyone who despised the law of Moses died without mercy under two or three witnesses; of how much sorer punishment is the man counted worthy who has trodden the Son of God underfoot and used the grace period to stay in the same sin (Hebrews 10:28-29). The sabbath was made for man, the children of Israel, and the Son of man is Lord of it, so that it is lawful to do well on that day and grace is given for what is out of a man’s control, never for what he plans (Mark 2:27-28; Matthew 12:8-12).

name: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram
text: Rebellion against the men the Lord chose; seeking the priesthood also. Korah of Levi, with Dathan, Abiram and On of Reuben and two hundred and fifty princes, famous in the congregation and men of renown, charged Moses and Aaron with lifting themselves above the congregation. The Most High was the one who chose them. They had the service of the tabernacle and it was not enough; they sought the priesthood also. The earth opened her mouth and swallowed them, and fire consumed the two hundred and fifty at their censers. Korah, the son of Izhar, of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, of Reuben, rose up before Moses with two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown (Numbers 16:1-2). Two hundred and fifty three in all, and they were known and powerful men; their influence, because of who they were, is how they were able to persuade the people. The teaching will not let that detail pass. When division, heresies and offences come, the man who brings them is never the regular soldier or the regular officer; it is a brother who is well known and loved by the people, a man in a high position who was not faithful over the little he was given, and the ones who admire him leave with him. Of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them (Acts 20:30). They told Moses and Aaron that they took too much on themselves, since all the congregation was holy, every one of them, and the Lord was among them, so why did they lift themselves above the congregation of the Lord (Numbers 16:3). They thought Moses and Aaron carried themselves as better than the rest, when the Most High was the one who chose them. Moses answered by asking whether it seemed a small thing to them that the God of Israel had separated them from the congregation to bring them near to Himself to do the service of the tabernacle, and whether they sought the priesthood also (Numbers 16:9-10). Only Levi could do the service of the tabernacle, and it was a heavy job in itself, and still it was not enough for them. Dathan and Abiram would not come up when called, because they wanted Moses’ spot: they accused him of bringing them up out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill them in the wilderness, and of making himself altogether a prince over them (Numbers 16:12-13). Those same spirits are around today; what went on in the old time goes on now. The test was censers, since the dispute was over who might come near: the man whom the Lord chose would be holy (Numbers 16:5-7). Moses put the proof on the Most High: if these men died the common death of all men, the Lord had not sent him; but if the Lord made a new thing, and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up, then they would understand that these men had provoked the Lord (Numbers 16:28-30). As he finished speaking, the ground under them split apart, and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up, with their houses, all the men that belonged to Korah, and all their goods; they went down alive into the pit, and all Israel round about fled at the cry of them (Numbers 16:31-34). Fire came out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who offered incense (Numbers 16:35). Their censers were taken out of the burning, because they had been offered before the Lord and were hallowed, and were beaten into broad plates for a covering of the altar, a memorial and a sign that no stranger who was not of the seed of Aaron should come near to offer incense before the Lord, and be as Korah and his company (Numbers 16:38-40). They envied Moses in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord, and the earth swallowed Dathan and covered the company of Abiram; they despised order and structure (Psalms 106:16-18). Peter calls such men natural brute beasts made to be taken and destroyed, who speak evil of the things they do not understand (2 Peter 2:12), and the teaching takes that at its word: they were made to be an example to us, so that we would not go against the leadership God set before us. Jude places everyone who follows them under the same sentence, perishing in the gainsaying of Core (Jude 1:11).

name: The congregation, the day after Korah
text: Murmuring that Moses and Aaron had killed the people of the Lord. The earth had swallowed Korah’s company the day before and the fire had consumed the two hundred and fifty, and on the very next day the whole congregation gathered against Moses and Aaron and called the dead the people of the Lord. Wrath went out from the Lord and the plague began before any warning. Aaron, the high priest they had said was no better than themselves, ran with a censer and stood between the dead and the living. Fourteen thousand seven hundred died, and his rod that budded was laid up as a token against the rebels. On the next day the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying that they had killed the people of the Lord (Numbers 16:41). After they had just seen the earth open and swallow men alive and fire come out and consume the rest, they still would not let it go. Look at who was blamed. Who opened the earth? Moses did not open it; God did, and they laid the dead at the feet of the two men who had pleaded for them. That is our habit as a people: when a man is checked for his own fault, he looks for somebody else to blame. And the ones who stood by were glad their names had not been in the first company, not understanding that the Most High had their number too, and had it the very next day. The judgment they had watched became the grievance, and the Most High saw what was going on: the cloud covered the tabernacle, and the glory of the Lord appeared (Numbers 16:42-45). He came down ready to put them to death again, telling Moses and Aaron to get up from among the congregation so that He could consume them in a moment; and Moses and Aaron fell on their faces, still pleading for their people. That is the character of the man: no matter what was said against him, he loved his people and stood up for them. Paul warns not to murmur as some of them murmured and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10). Wrath had gone out from the Lord and the plague was begun before any test or warning. Moses told Aaron to take a censer, put fire in it from off the altar and incense on it, and go quickly to the congregation to make an atonement for them (Numbers 16:46). Aaron ran into the midst of the congregation, put on incense, and made an atonement for the people; he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 16:47-48). The high priest they had said was no better than themselves stood in the gap with the very fire the two hundred and fifty had died for offering. Those who died in the plague were fourteen thousand seven hundred, besides those who died in the matter of Korah (Numbers 16:49-50). Then the Lord settled the question so that it would not have to be settled with bodies again. Every prince wrote his name on his rod according to the house of his fathers, twelve rods, with Aaron’s name on the rod of Levi, and they were laid up before the testimony where the Lord met with them; the man whose rod blossomed was the man He had chosen (Numbers 17:2-9). On the morrow the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi had budded, brought forth buds, bloomed blossoms and yielded almonds, and every man took back his own rod. Aaron’s rod was brought again before the testimony to be kept as a token against the rebels, to take their murmurings away from the Lord so that they would not die, and Moses did as he was commanded (Numbers 17:10-11). The children of Israel cried that they were dying and perishing, all of them, and that any man who came near the tabernacle of the Lord would die (Numbers 17:12-13). A man had to be of Levi to go near it; that had to be his office.

name: Moses at the waters of Meribah
text: Failing to sanctify the Lord before the people: must we fetch you water out of this rock?. There was no water, and the people chode with Moses, loud and angry, wishing they had died when their brethren died. Moses had to deal with all twelve tribes at once, and a stomach can only take so much of a rebellious people. Told to speak to the rock, he called them rebels, asked whether he and Aaron must fetch them water out of this rock, and smote it twice. That we is how the record shows he was out of the spirit: he put himself in the place of the One giving the water. The water still came, and the sentence with it. The congregation came into the desert of Zin in the first month and abode in Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried there (Numbers 20:1). There was no water for the congregation, and they gathered together against Moses and against Aaron. The people chode with Moses, which is to say they raised their voices in a loud, angry, shouting argument: they wished they had died when their brethren died before the Lord, and asked why they had been made to come up out of Egypt into this evil place, with no seed, figs, vines or pomegranates, and no water to drink (Numbers 20:2-5). Taken out of Egypt by the hand of the Most High and headed to the promised land, they forgot so quickly how they were brought out, and anything out of the ordinary they complained about. Moses had to deal with twelve tribes at once, twelve personalities and twelve attitudes, and that brother deserves all the honour he is given. The command was exact: take the rod, gather the assembly with Aaron, and speak to the rock before their eyes, and it would give forth its water for the congregation and their beasts (Numbers 20:7-8). At this point Moses got out of the spirit; a stomach can only take so much of a rebellious people. He called them rebels and asked, must we fetch you water out of this rock? The Lord never told him to say that. That we is how you know he was off: he put himself alongside the One who was giving the water. Then he lifted up his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod (Numbers 20:9-11). The psalm gives the cause: they provoked his spirit, so that he spoke unadvisedly with his lips (Psalms 106:32-33). Anger is what clouds a man’s judgment; it takes him out of the spirit, and then he leans on his own understanding instead of trusting the Lord with all his heart and keeping to the instruction he was given (Proverbs 3:5). A wrathful man stirs up strife, but the man slow to anger appeases it (Proverbs 15:18). The water came out abundantly, and the congregation and their beasts drank; the people lost nothing by it (Numbers 20:11). The Lord told Moses and Aaron that because they had not believed Him, to sanctify Him in the eyes of the children of Israel, they would not bring this congregation into the land He had given them (Numbers 20:12-13). This is the water of Meribah, which means strife, because the children of Israel strove with the Lord, and He was sanctified in them. Set beside it the war with Og a short time later, when the people said that the Lord their God delivered the king of Bashan into their hands (Deuteronomy 3:3): they were doing the fighting, and they gave the praise, the glory and the victory to the Most High, and did not boast in their own swords. That is what sanctifying Him looks like, and at the rock Moses did the opposite. Forty years of carrying the nation ended with the two men kept out of the land for a sentence spoken out of the spirit. At mount Hor, by the coast of the land of Edom, the Lord said Aaron would be gathered to his people because they had rebelled against His word at the water of Meribah; Moses stripped him of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son, and Aaron died there on the top of the mount, and all the house of Israel mourned him thirty days (Numbers 20:23-29). Moses was told to go up into mount Abarim and see the land, and then be gathered to his people as Aaron was, for the same cause (Numbers 27:12-14). He begged to go over and see the good land beyond Jordan, and the answer was final: let it suffice, and speak no more of this matter (Deuteronomy 3:23-26), the way a parent tells a child who keeps asking that the matter is closed. His charge was to strengthen and encourage the man appointed to take the people over in his place.

name: Israel and the fiery serpents
text: Speaking against God and against Moses; loathing the bread from heaven. Edom had refused them passage, and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way. They spoke against God and Moses: no bread, no water, and their soul loathed this light bread, which was angels’ bread. The Lord sent fiery serpents and many of the people of Israel died. The brass serpent on the pole was for the Israelites, to heal the Israelites, and Christ brought it to Nicodemus, one Israelite to another: the Son of man must be lifted up the way Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness. They journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea to compass the land of Edom, and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way; since Edom refused passage and came out against them with a strong hand, Israel had to go around, and the way was longer than they wanted it to be (Numbers 21:4; Numbers 20:18-21). The people spoke against God and against Moses, asking why they had been brought up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness with no bread and no water, and saying that their soul loathed this light bread (Numbers 21:5). The bread they loathed was angels’ bread, rained on them from heaven every morning, prepared without their labour and able to agree with every taste (Psalms 78:25). No other nation on this earth takes its food as seriously as Israel; even the complaints over bread and water are a familiar mark of this people to this day, and you cannot put another nation in these scriptures. Paul sets it among the warnings: do not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted and were destroyed of serpents (1 Corinthians 10:9). The Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, and many of the people of Israel died (Numbers 21:6). Fiery means poisonous, and the words of the verse should be read with the nation in view: the people bitten, the people dying, all of it is Israel. That detail settles an argument. A mixed multitude had come up with them, but the dying named here is Israel, because He gave His word to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel, and He has not dealt so with any nation (Psalms 147:19-20). The biting brought them back into the spirit at once: they confessed that they had sinned in speaking against the Lord and against Moses, and asked him to pray that the Lord would take away the serpents; and Moses prayed for the people (Numbers 21:7).

name: Sihon and Og
text: Refusing Israel passage on the king’s highway and coming out to battle against them. Israel was forbidden to meddle with Esau, Moab or Ammon, for the Most High had appointed their possessions. To Sihon king of the Amorites Moses sent words of peace: only pass through on the highway, buying meat and water for money. The Lord hardened his spirit as He had hardened Pharaoh’s, that He might deliver him into Israel’s hand, for the Amorites’ iniquity was full. Og, of the remnant of giants, came out after him. Both kingdoms were utterly destroyed, and the land east of Jordan became the first inheritance. Israel had compassed mount Seir long enough, and was charged to turn northward and pass through the coast of their brethren the children of Esau, the people called the white man today, and not meddle with them, for mount Seir was given to Esau for a possession and not so much as a foot breadth of it was Israel’s; and the same for Moab and Ammon, the children of Lot, whose lands the Most High had appointed (Deuteronomy 2:2-9, 19). Then the word changed: they were to rise up and pass over the river Arnon, for the Lord had given Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land into their hand, and that day He would begin to put the dread and the fear of Israel on the nations under the whole heaven, so that they would tremble and be in anguish (Deuteronomy 2:24-25). Moses sent messengers to Sihon with words of peace: let Israel pass through his land along the highway, turning neither to the right hand nor to the left, buying meat and water for money, only passing through on foot, exactly as they had passed the children of Esau in Seir and the Moabites in Ar (Deuteronomy 2:26-29; Numbers 21:21-22). But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let them pass, for the Lord their God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate so that He might deliver him into their hand: the same dealing as with Pharaoh, the heart hardened so the judgment could land, for the iniquity of the Amorites was full and their land was appointed to Israel (Deuteronomy 2:30; Genesis 15:16). He gathered all his people, went out against Israel into the wilderness, and fought at Jahaz (Numbers 21:23). Then Og the king of Bashan came out against them with all his people at Edrei (Deuteronomy 3:1). Og was an Amorite, and the Amorite came of Canaan the son of Ham (Genesis 10:6, 16); the Hamitic nations were known for great stature, which is why the tallest peoples on the earth to this day are of that line. He remained of the remnant of giants, and his bedstead of iron was nine cubits long and four broad, about thirteen feet by six, near the size of two king beds set together (Deuteronomy 3:11). The Lord delivered Sihon before Israel, and they smote him, his sons and all his people, took all his cities at that time, and utterly destroyed the men, women and little ones of every city, leaving none to remain; only the cattle and the spoil of the cities they took as a prey for themselves (Deuteronomy 2:33-35; Numbers 21:24-26). That is how thorough the judgment of the Most High was for Israel’s sake, and how privileged this people was, and still they struggled to believe Him. Of Og the Lord said not to fear him, for He had delivered him and all his people and his land into their hand; so they smote him, his sons and all his people until none was left alive, and possessed his land (Numbers 21:33-35). Threescore cities were taken, all fenced with high walls, gates and bars, beside a great many unwalled towns, and not one was left (Deuteronomy 3:4-6). The giants were famous from the beginning, of great stature and expert in war, yet the Lord chose them not and gave them no way of knowledge; they were destroyed because they had no wisdom and perished through their own foolishness (Baruch 3:26-28). From Aroer by the brink of the river Arnon to Gilead there was not one city too strong for them, and the Lord delivered all of it; only they did not come to the land of the children of Ammon, nor to anything the Lord their God had forbidden (Deuteronomy 2:36-37). And when it was over, the people did not boast in their own swords: they said that the Lord their God delivered the king of Bashan into their hands (Deuteronomy 3:3). Always remember that the battle is the Lord’s, and that this fight is spiritual; Israel needs no weapons of mass destruction, because the Bible is the weapon, and when the commandments are kept the Most High fights for His people. Joshua was made to look at these two kings and told that so the Lord would do to all the kingdoms he passed into, so he was not to fear them (Deuteronomy 3:21-22). The psalm keeps the record: He smote great kings, Sihon king of the Amorites and Og the king of Bashan, and gave their land as a heritage to Israel His servant, for His mercy lasts for ever (Psalms 136:17-22).

name: Balaam
text: Divination for hire; counselling Balak to make Israel curse itself through the women of Moab. Hired by Balak to curse Israel, Balaam was told at the first asking that he was not to curse the people, because they were blessed.
