There is no enchantment against Jacob, so the spell could not land, and the soothsayer turned to the counsel that is the best the enemy can ever do: throw another god in front of Israel and send the women to bring them to it. It worked at Peor, and the war it caused killed him among the kings of Midian. Balak the king of Moab sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor to curse Israel, and the answer was given at the first asking: he was not to go with them or curse the people, because they were blessed (Numbers 22:5-7, 12). God will not allow what He has blessed to be cursed, and the reason runs deeper than one refusal: there is no enchantment against Jacob and no divination against Israel (Numbers 23:23). No spell cast at this people lands while they keep His commandments. Balaam asked again when the princes came back with more honour, and the going was permitted in anger; the angel of the Lord stood in the way as an adversary with a drawn sword, and the ass saw what the prophet could not (Numbers 22:20-23). Peter says Balaam loved the wages of unrighteousness but was rebuked for his iniquity when the dumb ass spoke with a man’s voice and forbade the madness of the prophet (2 Peter 2:15-16). He was a soothsayer, a diviner, a witch, a man who went after the lust of greed (Joshua 13:22). He could not curse them, and blessed them four times against his will, so he found another way. He told Balak plainly that he could not curse them, but he could tell him how to make them fall: get the daughters of Moab and Midian among the men of Israel, and those women will bring them to their gods. That is what the scripture calls a wile, a stratagem, a thing well planned out whose result does not have to come right away. Moses names it after the war: through Balaam’s counsel these women caused the children of Israel to trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor (Numbers 31:16), and Christ names it in the churches, where Satan’s seat was, as the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, idol sacrifices and fornication (Revelation 2:13-14). The offense was not the failed curse. It was teaching the enemy how to make Israel curse itself. He was killed in the war his own counsel caused. When the Lord sent Israel to avenge themselves of the Midianites, they slew the five kings of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, and Balaam the son of Beor they slew with the sword (Numbers 31:1-8). Joshua sets him among the slain and calls him the soothsayer, killed among those slain by Israel (Joshua 13:22). He chased the reward and he ended up put to death for it. Jude gives the sentence on everyone who follows him: running greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perishing in the gainsaying of Core (Jude 1:11). His own words are left standing as the verdict on his life. He asked to die the death of the righteous and to have his last end like theirs (Numbers 23:10), which is the one thing he did not get, and it is worth knowing what he was asking for: the last end of Israel is a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, the land married, double for our shame, everlasting joy, and a seed acknowledged among the nations as the seed the Lord has blessed (Isaiah 62:3-4; Isaiah 61:7-9). The counsel he sold outlives him, because the same stratagem is still run. As long as Israel continues in whoredom it does not build the marriages that raise a nation, and without those marriages the children do not come up in the right frame of mind and the generational curses keep going; the strength is to come back to the laws of God, and the marriage bed is where allegiance is decided (Numbers 25:1-2; Numbers 31:15-16).

name: Israel at Baal-peor
text: Whoredom with the daughters of Moab, eating the sacrifices of their gods, and joining themselves unto Baal-peor. Balaam could not curse Israel, so his counsel was the best the enemy can ever do: throw another god in front of Israel and send the women. In Shittim the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, who called them to the sacrifices of their gods; the people ate and bowed down, and Israel joined himself to Baal-peor. It was sex that got the people to worship another god. The judges slew every man his men, the plague took twenty-four thousand, and it was stayed by the javelin of Phinehas. Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, who called them to the sacrifices of their gods; the people ate and bowed down to their gods, Israel joined himself to Baal-peor, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel (Numbers 25:1-3). Balaam could not curse what God had blessed, so he taught Balak the one thing that works: put another god in front of Israel and send the women to bring them to it; through his counsel these women caused the children of Israel to trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14). The worship of Baal-peor went into whoredom, orgy worship; the whoredom and the worship were one sin, and Israel joined himself to it as a man is joined to a wife. What would make this people bow to another nation’s god? It was sex that got them there. The nations knew what they were doing. The Lord said they had vexed Israel with their wiles, beguiling them in the matter of Peor (Numbers 25:18), and a wile is a clever, seductive trick, a stratagem planned out in advance whose result need not come right away. Crafty counsel is taken against His people and consulted against His hidden ones by nations confederate against Him (Psalms 83:3-5), and the same counsel is still run today through an entertainment industry that oversexualises everything the young ones see, until what was shocking a generation ago is not shocking at all. Hosea says they went to Baal-peor and separated themselves to that shame, and their abominations were according to what they loved (Hosea 9:10). The psalm says they joined themselves to Baal-peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead (Psalms 106:28). It was the golden calf again: the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play, and that play means what it means (1 Corinthians 10:7-8). The sentence began with the leadership: the Lord told Moses to take all the heads of the people and hang them up before the Lord against the sun, so that His fierce anger might be turned away from Israel; and Moses told the judges of Israel each to slay his men who were joined to Baal-peor (Numbers 25:4-5). Every one his man means every judge by his rank, the officer over ten taking his ten and the officer over fifty his fifty, the men under their own hands put down and set facing the sun so that all could see. With the Most High there were two options only, life and death; under the old covenant there was no winking at ignorance and judgment was instant. The only reason the gods Israel served in this captivity are not judged that way now is the grace given through Christ: God winked at the times of that ignorance, but now commands all men everywhere to repent, because He has appointed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness by the man He has ordained (Acts 17:29-31). Do not take that mercy lightly and do not frustrate it. A plague ran through the camp while the sentence was being carried out, and those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:9): in one day, because of sin. It was stayed by Phinehas, who is entered separately as a blessing. Moses set the outcome before the next generation: their eyes had seen what the Lord did because of Baal-peor, for the Lord their God had destroyed from among them all the men who followed Baal-peor, but those who clung to the Lord their God were all alive that day (Deuteronomy 4:3-4). Then the judgment turned outward against the nation that had supplied the women, entered under the Midianites.

name: The Midianites, in the matter of Peor
text: Beguiling Israel with their wiles into fornication and the worship of Baal-peor. On Balaam’s counsel the daughters of Midian and Moab drew Israel to the sacrifices of their gods, and twenty-four thousand died in the plague. The Lord commanded Israel to vex the Midianites and smite them, because they had vexed Israel with their wiles. Twelve thousand went out with Phinehas and the holy instruments, slew the five kings of Midian and Balaam with the sword, and burnt their cities and their goodly castles. Moses was wroth that the women who had caused the trespass were kept alive. Through Balaam’s counsel these women caused the children of Israel to trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor, and there was a plague among the congregation of the Lord (Numbers 31:16). The women of Midian and Moab called the people to the sacrifices of their gods; the people ate and bowed down, and Israel joined himself to Baal-peor (Numbers 25:2-3). It was not done at a distance either: Cozbi, the daughter of Zur, head over a people of a chief house in Midian, was brought into the camp itself in the sight of Moses and all the congregation (Numbers 25:6, 15). The Lord told Moses to vex the Midianites and smite them, because they vexed Israel with their wiles, wherewith they had beguiled them in the matter of Peor and in the matter of Cozbi (Numbers 25:16-18). The wile is the charge: a planned seduction aimed at making a people sin against their own God, because their enemies understood that this was the one way to get at them. Midian comes from the line of Abraham by Keturah and dwelt with the children of Ishmael, the people known today as the Arab man (Genesis 25:1-4). That is worth holding on to, because the nation that supplied the women was not a stranger to Israel by blood, and the closeness is part of how the stratagem worked. The Lord told Moses to avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites, after which he would be gathered to his people (Numbers 31:1-2). A thousand of every tribe, twelve thousand armed for war, went out with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the holy instruments and the trumpets to blow in his hand, the same Phinehas who had thrust through the man of Israel and the Midianitish woman (Numbers 31:3-6). They warred against the Midianites as the Lord commanded Moses, and slew all the males and the five kings of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, and Balaam the son of Beor they slew with the sword (Numbers 31:7-8). They took the women of Midian captive with their little ones and the spoil of all their cattle, flocks and goods, and burnt all their cities and all their goodly castles with fire (Numbers 31:9-10). Esau was not the one who first came up with castles; the ones seen in the movies were conquered from other nations. Israel also took all the prey both of men and of beasts, because the Midianites had captives of their own, and those passed over when Israel overcame them. Moses was angry with the officers of the host for saving all the women alive, since these were the ones who, through Balaam’s counsel, had caused the children of Israel to trespass against the Lord; so every male among the little ones was to be killed, and every woman who had known a man by lying with him (Numbers 31:14-18). The men of war and their captives purified themselves outside the camp seven days, on the third day and on the seventh, by the law that puts anyone defiled by the dead outside the camp, and the metal that could abide the fire went through the fire and the rest through the water (Numbers 31:19-24; Numbers 19:11-12). The prey was then divided between the army that went to battle and the congregation that stayed, because the nation looked out for each other, and a tribute of the Lord was levied out of both parts and given to Eleazar the priest and to the Levites who kept the charge of the tabernacle, since the heave offerings belong to the priesthood by a statute for ever and Levi has no inheritance in the land (Numbers 31:25-30; Numbers 18:19-21).

name: Phinehas
text: Zealous for his God at Peor; making an atonement for the children of Israel. While the whole congregation wept before the door of the tabernacle and the plague was running, a prince of Simeon brought a Midianite woman past them all into the camp, a man who did not care about his people. Phinehas the son of Eleazar rose up from among the congregation, took a javelin, and thrust them both through, and the plague was stayed. He stands third in glory: because he had zeal in the fear of the Lord, a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood was made with him, and it was counted to him for righteousness to all generations. The plague was already running and the whole congregation was weeping before the door of the tabernacle of the congregation when one of the children of Israel came and brought a Midianitish woman to his brethren in the sight of Moses and of all the congregation (Numbers 25:6). Everybody around him was mourning and praying while the Most High was passing judgment, and this man came through with no fear and no shame, caring only to fulfil his lust. He did not care about his people. When Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from among the congregation, took a javelin in his hand, went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly (Numbers 25:7-8). The words of the verse tell what he walked in on: one thrust went through the man and on through the woman, both of them taken in the act. The psalmist asks who will rise up for the Lord against the evildoers and stand up against the workers of iniquity (Psalms 94:16); Phinehas rose up. In the praise of famous men he is set third in glory, because he had zeal in the fear of the Lord and stood up with good courage of heart when the people were turned back, and made reconciliation for Israel; and for that a covenant of peace was made with him, that he and his posterity should have the dignity of the priesthood for ever (Ecclesiasticus 44:1; Ecclesiasticus 45:23-24). Mattathias set him before his sons at the end of his own life: Phinehas their father, in being zealous and fervent, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, and they were to be zealous for the law and give their lives for the covenant of their fathers (1 Maccabees 2:50, 54). So the plague was stayed from the children of Israel, and those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:8-9). The Lord gave the motive Himself: Phinehas had turned His wrath away from the children of Israel by being zealous for His sake among them, so that He did not consume the children of Israel in His jealousy; therefore He gave him His covenant of peace, for him and his seed after him, the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and made an atonement for the children of Israel (Numbers 25:10-13). The psalm says he stood up and executed judgment and the plague was stayed, and that it was counted to him for righteousness to all generations for evermore (Psalms 106:30-31), the same phrase used of Abraham’s faith. That covenant of peace is what this nation is striving for, rest from this servitude of bondage, and the wisdom of the case is that a man must be zealous for the law of the Most High to obtain it. Being zealous today is confessing Christ before men, and a man confesses him chiefly through his actions: Christ suffered for us and left us an example that we should follow his steps, and those steps were the keeping of the commandments, so the first way a man denies him is by rejecting them (1 Peter 2:21). Anyone who confesses him before men he will confess before his Father, and he came not to send peace on earth but a sword, setting a man at variance against his own household, so that the man who loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:32-37). We stay zealous by letting nothing separate us from following in those steps.

name: Zimri and Cozbi
text: Bringing a Midianite woman into the camp in the sight of the congregation, while the plague ran. While the whole congregation wept at the tabernacle door over the plague, Zimri the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites, walked Cozbi the daughter of Zur, a princess of Midian, past them into his tent: a man who did not care about his people while everyone around him mourned. Phinehas followed with a javelin and thrust them both through, and the plague was stayed. The charge stands to Simeon to this day. The people had already joined themselves to Baal-peor, called to the sacrifices of their gods and eating and bowing down, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel (Numbers 25:2-3). Then, while the whole congregation was weeping before the door of the tabernacle and the plague was running, one of the children of Israel came and brought a Midianitish woman to his brethren in the sight of Moses and of all the congregation of the children of Israel (Numbers 25:6). The Israelites at that door were trying to repent, praying that the judgment would be lifted, and this man came through the middle of it with the woman, hopping and skipping, clueless, without fear. That is what it looks like when a thing has been going on so long that a man no longer cares who sees it; all he cared about was fulfilling his lust, in the middle of a national mourning, while the Most High was passing judgment. The record names them both deliberately: the Israelite who was slain was Zimri, the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites, and the Midianitish woman who was slain was Cozbi, the daughter of Zur, who was head over a people and of a chief house in Midian (Numbers 25:14-15). A prince of Israel brought a princess of the other nations into the camp, which is why the two houses are named. It is the mixing the fathers forbade from the beginning: no covenant with those nations and no marriages with them, because they turn a son away from following Him to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4), and a man is to take a wife of the seed of his fathers, because the fathers from the beginning all married wives of their own kindred (Tobit 4:12). The charge stands to Simeon to get it together, and Simeon is coming back with the rest of the tribes. Phinehas rose up from among the congregation with a javelin in his hand, went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly; so the plague was stayed from the children of Israel, and those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:7-9). The Lord said that Phinehas had turned away His wrath, being zealous for His sake among them, so that He did not consume the children of Israel in His jealousy (Numbers 25:10-11). Then Phinehas stood up and executed judgment, and so the plague was stayed (Psalms 106:30-31). The judgment then ran outward to the nation that had supplied the women: Israel was to vex the Midianites and smite them, because they vexed Israel with their wiles, wherewith they had beguiled them in the matter of Peor and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, who was slain in the day of the plague for Peor’s sake (Numbers 25:16-18). Her own people are charged with her, which is how the case is remembered: not one man’s private sin but a stratagem working through a prince and a princess in the sight of the whole congregation.

name: The daughters of Zelophehad
text: Asking rightly for their father’s inheritance, and marrying within their tribe as commanded. Five sisters with no brother stood at the door of the tabernacle and asked the question of the lineage: why should their father’s name be done away from among his family because he had no son? Moses did not do his own thing; he brought their cause before the Lord, and the Lord said that the daughters of Zelophehad spoke right, and set the order of inheritance for all Israel. When the chief fathers of Gilead raised the question of the tribe, the daughters married within their father’s tribe as commanded, and the inheritance stayed in Manasseh. The daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes and all the congregation, by the door of the tabernacle (Numbers 27:1-2). They set out the facts: their father had died in the wilderness, not in the company of those who gathered together against the Lord in the company of Korah, but in his own sin, and he had no sons (Numbers 27:3). Their question was the question of the lineage, since the man puts the seed in the woman: why should their father’s name be done away from among his family because he had no son? So they asked for a possession among their father’s brethren (Numbers 27:4). They brought a gap in the law to the only authority who could fill it, in the proper form and at the proper place, before the whole congregation and not behind anyone’s back. Moses brought their cause before the Lord (Numbers 27:5); he did not do his own thing, he sought counsel and asked the Most High what to do in this instance. The second question came from the other side. The chief fathers of the families of Gilead came near and said that if these daughters married into any of the other tribes, their father’s inheritance would be taken from the inheritance of their fathers and added to the tribe they married into, and at the jubilee it would be fixed there for good, so Manasseh would lose that land for ever (Numbers 36:1-4). Their concern was real, because the jubilee would not undo a marriage. That question went to Moses as well, and the daughters accepted the ruling and married their father’s brothers’ sons, within the families of the sons of Manasseh, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of the family of their father (Numbers 36:10-12). The Lord did not merely grant the request; He endorsed the reasoning: the daughters of Zelophehad speak right, and they were surely to be given a possession of an inheritance among their father’s brethren, and their father’s inheritance was to pass to them (Numbers 27:6-7). Their case became the order for the whole nation: if a man died with no son, his inheritance passed to his daughter; if no daughter, to his brethren; if no brethren, to his father’s brethren; and if his father had no brethren, to the next kinsman of his family; and it was to be a statute of judgment for the children of Israel (Numbers 27:8-11). Israel always had questions, just as we do when we read, and the Lord put the statutes in place to answer them, covering every angle so the inheritance stayed within the tribe. The second ruling ran the same way: the tribe of the sons of Joseph had said well, and the daughters could marry whom they thought best, only within the family of the tribe of their father, so that the inheritance of the children of Israel would not remove from tribe to tribe (Numbers 36:5-9). That boundary belonged to the land inheritance, and it is why the law was given. Israel has no inheritance in the lands of this captivity, and no man knows his exact tribe with certainty, since a Judahite could have been dropped anywhere in it; so what stands now is marrying within the nation of Israel, taking a wife of the seed of the fathers and not a strange woman, because the fathers from the beginning all married wives of their own kindred and were blessed in their children (Tobit 4:12). Read without the history of Numbers 36, that verse gets twisted into a doctrine that a man may marry only his own tribe, and that is a heresy born of not knowing why the law was given. What never happened is an inheritance in Israel passing to an Edomite, an Ammonite or a Moabite. Joshua gave the five their portion among their father’s brethren according to the commandment of the Lord, and the chronicler still names them (Joshua 17:3-4; 1 Chronicles 7:15).

name: Rahab
text: Receiving the spies with peace, and believing that the Lord had given Israel the land. A harlot of Jericho, a Canaanite in a city under the ban, hid two spies under the flax on her roof and confessed what the report had done to the whole city: their hearts had melted, because the Lord, the God of Israel, is God in heaven above and in earth beneath. Faith and fear go hand in hand; what she feared was not the king of Jericho but the judgment of the God of this people, and that fear gave her the faith to put her life on the line. She bound the scarlet line in the window, her house alone stood when the wall fell, and she is in the line of Christ. Joshua sent two men out of Shittim to spy secretly and view the land, even Jericho, and they came into the house of a harlot named Rahab and lodged there (Joshua 2:1). When the king of Jericho sent to bring them out, she had already taken the two men and hidden them on the roof under the stalks of flax she had laid in order there; she told the king’s men the truth in part and misdirection in the rest, saying the men had gone out about the time of the shutting of the gate and urging a quick pursuit (Joshua 2:2-7). The pursuers chased toward Jordan after men who had gone nowhere, the gate was shut behind them, and the spies had clearance. A heathen woman looked out for Israel. Her faith came by report before it came by sight: she knew the Lord had given them the land, that the terror of Israel had fallen on the city, and that its inhabitants fainted because of them, for they had heard how the Lord dried up the Red sea and what Israel did to Sihon and Og, and as soon as they heard it their hearts melted and no courage remained in any man, because the Lord God of Israel is God in heaven above and in earth beneath (Joshua 2:8-11). That is faith and belief, a heathen acknowledging that the God of Israel had ordained this people to conquer her land, and it is the word of the Most High fulfilled: that day He would begin to put the dread and the fear of Israel on the nations who heard the report (Deuteronomy 2:25). Faith and fear go hand in hand. She knew the Lord is not to be played with where this people is concerned, and that fear is what gave her the faith to put her life on the line; she might be caught by her own king for hiding the spies, but what she really feared was the judgment of their God if she did not help them. It is the same spirit as the woman of Canaan who answered that the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table, and was told that her faith was great (Matthew 15:27-28). She asked them to swear to her by the Lord, since she had shown them kindness, that they would show kindness to her father’s house and save her father, mother, brethren and sisters alive; and the men answered with their own lives for hers, on the condition that she kept their business quiet (Joshua 2:12-14). Rahab the harlot was justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way (James 2:25), and works in the Bible’s own dictionary is keeping His commandments (Psalms 78:7), for the Lord is a God of knowledge and by Him actions are weighed (1 Samuel 2:3). The token was the line of scarlet thread bound in the window by which she let them down, for her house was on the town wall; anyone who went out of her doors into the street would answer for himself, and anyone who stayed in the house would be Israel’s charge, and she bound the scarlet line in the window (Joshua 2:17-21). The spies hid three days in the mountain until the pursuers turned back, then came to Joshua and reported that the Lord had delivered the whole land into their hands, because all the inhabitants of the country fainted because of them (Joshua 2:22-24). When the wall fell down flat, her house stood, and Joshua sent the two spies into the harlot’s house to bring out Rahab, her father, her mother, her brethren and all that she had, as they had sworn to her, while everything else in the city was devoted; Joshua saved Rahab the harlot alive and her father’s household, and she dwelt in Israel from then on, because she hid the messengers (Joshua 6:22-25). A Canaanite and a heathen was blessed, because she did it to benefit Israel, and that is still the only help Israel wants from the other nations: not welfare and not reparations, but telling this people who they are and that they must keep the commandments of the Most High. By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with those who did not believe, because she had received the spies in peace (Hebrews 11:31), and Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, so the woman spared from the ban stands in the line of David and of Christ (Matthew 1:5). Set beside her is Achan, an Israelite of Judah, who lacked faith and was put to death while the Canaanite harlot was saved alive for hers.

name: Achan
text: Israel trespassed in the accursed thing: Achan saw, coveted, took of the devoted spoil of Jericho, and hid it in his tent. Who committed the trespass? The first sentence says the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing, for Achan took of it. One man’s secret sin sent faintness into the hearts of the whole nation, and thirty-six died before Ai; the Lord said Israel had sinned, and He would not be with them until the accursed thing was destroyed from among them. Taken by lot, Achan confessed that he saw, he coveted, he took: he was stealing from the Most High. He and all that he had were stoned and burned in the valley of Achor. The children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing, for Achan of the tribe of Judah took of the accursed thing, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against the children of Israel (Joshua 7:1). Many will answer that Achan committed the trespass; the record says the children of Israel. A man’s individual sins can hurt the rest of the nation. He can be the hindrance to why his camp is not growing, why his family, his marriage or his children have issues, when he carries a spirit he knows about and keeps it secret, not praying and not fasting over it. That is the spirit of Achan, and the nation pays for it, because wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good (Ecclesiastes 9:18). Joshua had charged them plainly at Jericho to keep themselves from the accursed thing, for all the silver, gold and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated to the Lord and went into His treasury, and nobody was to gain personally from that war (Joshua 6:18-19). Achan’s confession gives the sequence: he saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, two hundred shekels of silver and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels, then he coveted them, took them, and hid them in the earth in the midst of his tent (Joshua 7:20-21). He was not stealing from men; he was stealing from the Most High, and he found the time to do it in the middle of a war. Covetousness is the last of the ten commandments, the weightiest warning kept for last (Exodus 20:17), and there is not a more wicked thing than a covetous man, for he sets his own soul to sale (Ecclesiasticus 10:9). Confident after viewing Ai, they sent about three thousand men, who fled before the men of Ai; thirty-six fell, and the hearts of the people melted like water (Joshua 7:2-5). The Lord is the one who wins the battles, not us: however strong Israel is physically, if the people are not right with Him He will make them lose, because this fight is not carnal. Hearts melting is the curse written for disobedience: a faintness sent into their hearts, so that the sound of a shaken leaf chases them and they fall when none pursues (Leviticus 26:36). Joshua tore his clothes and fell before the ark until evening, afraid the Canaanites would cut off their name, and asked what the Lord would do for His great name (Joshua 7:6-9). The Lord told him to get up: Israel had sinned, transgressed the covenant, stolen, dissembled, and put the accursed thing among their own stuff; therefore they could not stand before their enemies, and He would not be with them any more unless they destroyed the accursed from among them (Joshua 7:10-12). It does not say Achan sinned; it says Israel. As a father who finds mischief chastens all his children together when none confesses, so the Most High deals with His children as one house. The lot narrowed by tribe, then family, then household, then man by man, and Achan was taken; Joshua told him to give glory to the Lord God of Israel, make confession, and hide nothing (Joshua 7:16-19). It was a secret sin and no man had seen him, but no man can hide himself in secret places where the Lord does not see him (Jeremiah 23:24), and be sure your sin will find you out (Numbers 32:23). Joshua and all Israel took Achan, the silver, the garment, the gold, his sons and daughters, his cattle, his tent and all he had to the valley of Achor; Joshua asked why he had troubled them and said the Lord would trouble him that day, and all Israel stoned him and burned them (Joshua 7:22-25). Why the whole household? The teaching asks it and answers it: they had to have known about it, and they said nothing, so none of them was innocent. A man who sees sin or hears of sin has to speak up, because silence is agreement. They were destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6), and that knowledge is the law, which the priest’s lips are to keep and the people are to seek at his mouth (Malachi 2:7). The law bound a witness who had seen or known of a sin to speak, or bear the iniquity himself (Leviticus 5:1): had they kept the law, they would not have been silent. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31). They raised over him a great heap of stones, the Lord turned from the fierceness of His anger, and the place was called the valley of Achor to this day (Joshua 7:26).

name: The Gibeonites, and Israel’s oath
text: Obtaining a covenant by fraud; and Israel making it without asking counsel at the mouth of the Lord. The Hivites of Gibeon, Hamites of the land Israel was commanded to destroy, came to Gilgal in old sacks, rent wine bottles and mouldy bread, leaning on the fame of the Most High and claiming to come from a far country. They knew Israel’s own law of war, and they built the lie on it. The men of Israel were suspicious, asked the right questions, and then took of their victuals and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord. That one omission became a snare to the nation for centuries. The princes held the oath, and the Gibeonites were cursed to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. When the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, Hamites better known as Nilotic Africans, gathered to fight Joshua and Israel with one accord, the inhabitants of Gibeon worked wilily: they made as if they had been ambassadors, with old sacks on their asses, old wine bottles rent and bound up, old clouted shoes, old garments, and bread dry and mouldy (Joshua 9:1-5). Israel was commanded to destroy all the inhabitants of the land, the very nations listed in the first verse, so their only hope was to pretend they were not of them. And the lie was built on Israel’s own law of war: a city very far off was to be offered peace first, and if it answered peace its people became tributaries and served Israel, while the cities of these nations were to be utterly destroyed (Deuteronomy 20:10-15, 16-17). They knew the rule, so they claimed the far country and asked for a league (Joshua 9:6). They leaned on the fame of the Most High to sell it, saying they had come because of the name of the Lord Israel’s God, having heard all He did in Egypt and to Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan beyond Jordan (Joshua 9:9-10). The props sold the story. The men of Israel were suspicious at first, saying the strangers might dwell among them, and Joshua pressed them on who they were and where they came from (Joshua 9:7-8). Israel’s fault is set down in one clause: the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord (Joshua 9:14-15). The Most High says let reason go before every enterprise and counsel before every action (Ecclesiasticus 37:16); they reasoned it out among themselves instead of inquiring. The league forbidden with the inhabitants of the land (Exodus 23:32; Deuteronomy 7:2) was made through not asking, and it became a snare to the nation for centuries after. At the end of three days Israel heard that they were their neighbours and dwelt among them, and the children of Israel smote them not, because the princes of the congregation had sworn to them by the Lord God of Israel; all the congregation murmured against the princes, but the princes held the line: they had sworn by the Lord God of Israel and could not touch them, and would let them live, so that wrath would not be on them because of the oath (Joshua 9:16-21). Our fathers were wrong in one situation, but they were upright men in holding to their word: when a man vows a vow to God, he is not to defer to pay it, for it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6). A vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile. Joshua called for them, asked why they had beguiled him by saying they were very far off when they dwelt among them, and pronounced them cursed: none of them would be freed from being bondmen, hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of his God (Joshua 9:22-23). Hewers of wood and drawers of water means servants, according to the law of the Most High pertaining to the other nations: the bondmen and bondmaids of Israel are to be of the heathen round about, taken as an inheritance for the children after them, while over their own brethren the children of Israel were not to rule with rigour (Leviticus 25:44-46). There was no equality among the nations then and there is none now; they were made for a purpose, and the reason they are not in it today is that Israel sinned and failed. The Gibeonites themselves answered honestly that it had been told them how the Lord commanded Moses to give Israel all the land and to destroy all its inhabitants, so they were sore afraid of their lives, and Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the Lord (Joshua 9:24-27). The oath bound Israel harder than it bound Gibeon: when Saul broke it, the Lord sent three years of famine in David’s day for Saul and his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1), entered under Rizpah. The same ordeal plays out again when Christ returns: the sons of strangers will build up Israel’s walls and their kings will minister to her, and the nation and kingdom that will not serve her will perish and be utterly wasted (Isaiah 60:10-12), for to the man who overcomes and keeps His works to the end He gives power over the nations (Revelation 2:26). There is nothing new under the sun.

name: The five kings at Makkedah
text: Confederating against Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Five kings of the Amorites joined to punish Gibeon for making peace with Joshua, and Gibeon sent to Gilgal for help. The Lord told Joshua not to fear them, for He had delivered them into his hand. Israel came up all night, the Lord cast down great stones from heaven and killed more with hailstones than Israel killed with the sword, and the sun stood still until the people had avenged themselves. The five hid in a cave, and Joshua brought them out, had the captains put their feet on their necks, and hanged them until evening, saying that so the Lord would do to all their enemies. What we read in Joshua is future prophecy. When Adoni-zedec king of Jerusalem heard how Joshua had taken Ai and utterly destroyed it as he had done to Jericho, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them, they feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, as one of the royal cities, greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty (Joshua 10:1-2). The five kings of the Amorites, of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, gathered themselves with all their hosts, encamped before Gibeon, and made war against it (Joshua 10:5). Gibeon’s only offense was making peace. The men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at Gilgal, asking him not to slack his hand from his servants but to come up quickly and save them from all the kings of the Amorites gathered against them (Joshua 10:6). Israel was bound by the oath, entered separately, so the whole campaign is Israel keeping a covenant it had been tricked into. The Lord told Joshua not to fear them, for He had delivered them into his hand and not a man of them would stand before him (Joshua 10:8). Joshua went up from Gilgal all night and came on them suddenly, and the Lord discomfited them before Israel and slew them with a great slaughter at Gibeon; as they fled, the Lord cast down great stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and more died from the hailstones than the children of Israel slew with the sword (Joshua 10:9-11). The Most High was aiming from heaven and nobody could get away from it; He had done the same in Egypt, where the elements themselves were changed to fight for Israel (Wisdom of Solomon 19:18-20). These are the wars of the Lord, in which He killed more than His people killed. Then Joshua spoke to the Lord in the sight of Israel and told the sun to stand still on Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Ajalon, and the sun stood still and hasted not to go down about a whole day, until the people had avenged themselves on their enemies; it is written in the book of Jasher, and there was no day like it before or after, that the Lord hearkened to the voice of a man, for the Lord fought for Israel (Joshua 10:12-14). Time stopped, and the reason it stopped for him is his faith: he believed the Lord would do it. The Lord is a man of war, and that is His name (Exodus 15:3). The five kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah; Joshua had great stones rolled on its mouth and men set to keep them, while the people pursued and smote the hindmost until they were consumed, and none moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel (Joshua 10:16-21). Not a dog would move his tongue against the children of Israel (Exodus 11:7), and the dogs are the nations, as Christ used the same word when he said he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24-26). Then he brought out the five kings and told the captains of the men of war to come near and put their feet on the necks of those kings, and said, fear not, be strong and of good courage, for so the Lord would do to all their enemies (Joshua 10:22-25). They hid in caves, and the nations will do it again: in the day of the Lord men will go into the holes of the rocks and the caves of the earth for fear of the Lord, when He arises to shake terribly the earth (Isaiah 2:19-21). What we read in Joshua is future prophecy. Joshua smote them and hanged them on five trees until evening, and at the going down of the sun took them down according to the law, for a man hanged is accursed of God and his body is not to remain all night on the tree, so that the land is not defiled, and they were cast into the cave and great stones laid in its mouth (Joshua 10:26-27; Deuteronomy 21:22-23). So Joshua smote all the country of the hills, the south, the vale and the springs, and all their kings, and left none remaining, but utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the Lord God of Israel commanded, because the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel (Joshua 10:40-42). Do not think the Most High unjust in it. No one taught Him or counselled Him; all nations before Him are as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance, counted to Him less than nothing, and vanity (Isaiah 40:13-17), and He increases the nations and destroys them (Job 12:23).

name: Othniel and Achsah
text: Taking Kirjath-sepher at Caleb’s word; and asking for the springs as well as the land. Caleb, given Hebron for wholly following the Lord, drove out the three sons of Anak and offered his daughter to whoever smote Kirjath-sepher. Othniel the son of Kenaz, his younger brother, took it and was given Achsah. She moved him to ask her father for a field, and asked well: he had given her a south land, so she asked also for springs of water, and Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs. When Israel served Chushan-rishathaim eight years, the Spirit of the Lord came on Othniel, and he judged Israel and went out to war, for the Lord is a man of war. Caleb the son of Jephunneh was given a part among the children of Judah according to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua, the city of Arba the father of Anak, which is Hebron, and Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai (Joshua 15:13-14). He had been promised that mountain and he went and claimed it. He went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir, whose name before was Kirjath-sepher, and promised his daughter Achsah as wife to the man who smote it and took it; Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, took it, and Caleb gave him Achsah (Joshua 15:15-17). He took a fortified city on the strength of a word. Achsah’s obedience is one of speech. When she came to him she moved him to ask her father for a field, then got down off her ass, and when Caleb asked what she wanted she asked for a blessing, because he had given her a south land, and asked also for springs of water (Joshua 15:18-19). Given a lawful portion in the dry south, she did not resent it; she asked the right person, at the right moment, framing it as a blessing rather than a complaint, and asked for the one thing the land needed. The record carries the whole account twice, at the opening of Judges as at the end of Joshua, because the history is worth reviewing (Judges 1:12-15). Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs (Joshua 15:19): more than she had asked for. Then the Lord left nations in the land to prove Israel, nations that had not known the wars of Canaan, so that the generations of the children of Israel might know war and be taught it, and so that it would be seen whether they would hearken to His commandments (Judges 3:1-4). They did not. The children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, the very people they had been told to destroy, took their daughters to wife and gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods; so the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel and He sold them into the hand of Chushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, whom they served eight years (Judges 3:5-8). When the children of Israel cried to the Lord, He raised up a deliverer, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother; the Spirit of the Lord came on him, and he judged Israel and went out to war, and the Lord delivered Chushan-rishathaim into his hand, and his hand prevailed (Judges 3:9-10). He judged Israel, and today our people say that no one can judge them. And he went out to war, because the Lord is a man of war, and that is His name (Exodus 15:3); that also answers the question asked of the men out on the street about where their women are. The war now is spiritual: though we walk in the flesh we do not war after the flesh, and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:3-5). The weapon is this Bible. The land had rest forty years, until Othniel the son of Kenaz died (Judges 3:11). The first deliverer in the book of Judges came out of the household of the man who wholly followed the Lord, where a daughter asked well and a father gave more than was requested.

name: Adoni-bezek
text: Mutilating seventy kings and feeding them under his table. After the death of Joshua, Judah went up first at the Lord’s word, with Simeon his brother, and slew ten thousand Canaanites and Perizzites in Bezek. Their king fled and was caught, and Judah cut off his thumbs and his great toes. He confessed it himself: seventy kings with their thumbs and great toes cut off had gathered their meat under his table, and as he had done, so God had requited him. After the death of Joshua the children of Israel asked the Lord who should go up first for them against the Canaanites to fight against them, and the Lord said Judah, for He had delivered the land into his hand; Judah asked Simeon his brother to come up with him into his lot and promised to go with him likewise into Simeon’s, so Simeon went with him (Judges 1:1-3). The Lord delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they slew ten thousand men in Bezek (Judges 1:4). The king who fled from that field had made a practice of mutilation and counted it his glory. He gives the number himself: seventy kings with their thumbs and their great toes cut off had gathered their meat under his table (Judges 1:7). Seventy kings maimed so that they could neither hold a sword nor stand in a rank, kept alive to eat scraps on the floor as a display of his power. The law of Israel keeps punishment to measure: breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and as a man causes a blemish in another, so it is done to him (Leviticus 24:19-20; Exodus 21:23-25). Adoni-bezek had exceeded all measure seventy times over. They pursued after him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes (Judges 1:6): the same mutilation, once. The record does not soften what Israel did in those wars. When Israel went to war terrible things were done to people, and they were done at the commandment of the Most High and by His measure, and the scripture leaves them in plain sight rather than hiding them. The verdict here is pronounced by the condemned man himself, and the record leaves it in his mouth: as he had done, so God had requited him (Judges 1:7). A Canaanite king read the measure of the God of Israel off his own case and named it justice. They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died; and the children of Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, smote it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire (Judges 1:7-8). Christ states the rule he fell under as a rule for everyone: with what measure you mete, it will be measured to you again (Matthew 7:2). David dealt with the Ammonites by the same principle when he put the people of their cities under saws and harrows and axes of iron and made them pass through the brickkiln (2 Samuel 12:31), giving back what had been done. And the same measure stands written against the nations that stole a man and sold him: a man who steals a man and sells him, or is found with him in his hand, is to be put to death (Exodus 21:16). That is judgment and justice, and the judgment for it has not been paid.

name: Jabez
text: Calling on the God of Israel to bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil. Among the families of Judah the record stops on one man. Jabez was more honourable than his brethren, and his mother called his name Jabez because she bore him with sorrow. He called on the God of Israel and asked that He would bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil, that it might not grieve him. And God granted him what he requested. The chapter gathers more of the families of Judah, the sons that came from him and the line of Hur the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem, and keeps the households in order down to the sons of Coz (1 Chronicles 4:1-8). The names in that stretch carry meaning, which is why the scribe keeps them. In the middle of the list the record stops on one man: Jabez was more honourable than his brethren, and his mother called his name Jabez because she bore him with sorrow (1 Chronicles 4:9), the meaning of the name matching the scripture itself. Jabez called on the God of Israel and asked that He would bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil, so that it might not grieve him (1 Chronicles 4:10). He did not call on the gods of the land around him; he called on the God of Israel, and he asked for four things: the blessing itself, land, the hand of the Lord with him, and to be kept from evil. It is the same ground Achsah stood on when she asked her father for the springs as well as the south land (Joshua 15:18-19), and the same calling on the name of the Lord that men began in the days of Enos (Genesis 4:26). And God granted him that which he requested (1 Chronicles 4:10). The Most High gave him what he asked for, and the record says no more about him. It gives no offense, no judgment and no chronology; it gives a man of Judah, born in sorrow, who called on the God of Israel and was heard, and it sets him in the middle of a genealogy rather than in a history of his deeds. The teaching of the chapter around him is that the blessing rested heavily on Judah. When the same chapter turns to the sons of Simeon it notes that Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brethren had not many children, and Simeon did not multiply like the children of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:24-27). The blessing of increase was on Judah, and Jabez stands inside it as a single name the scribe would not pass over. Simeon was not left without mercy either: the princes of Simeon, whose houses increased, went to seek pasture for their flocks and found fat and quiet pasture in a land where the sons of Ham had dwelt of old, and smote those habitations in the days of Hezekiah; and five hundred of them went to mount Seir, smote the remnant of the Amalekites that had escaped, and dwelt there (1 Chronicles 4:38-43).

name: Israel in the days of the Judges
text: Making leagues with the inhabitants of the land; marrying their daughters and serving their gods; every man doing that which was right in his own eyes. An angel came up from Gilgal to Bochim and rehearsed the covenant: the Lord had said He would never break it, and Israel was to make no league with the inhabitants of the land and to tear down their altars, and they had not listened. The sentence was that He would not drive those nations out, but leave them as thorns in Israel’s sides and their gods as a snare. A generation arose that did not know the Lord, lived among the very nations it had been commanded to destroy, married their daughters and served their gods, and was sold into the hands of one oppressor after another. The key to the whole book is one verse: there was no king in Israel, and every man did what was right in his own eyes. An angel of the Lord came up from Gilgal to Bochim and reminded Israel of the covenant: the Lord had brought them out of Egypt into the land promised to their fathers, with a plain command to make no league with the people of the land and to tear down their altars, and they had not listened (Judges 2:1-5). The law had said it before they crossed over: no covenant with those nations or their gods, and no room for them in the land, or they would lead Israel into sin (Exodus 23:32-33). Living among them breeds curiosity about their gods, and that curiosity is the snare: how did these nations serve their gods, what is that thing they are doing with that tree, what are they hanging on it (Deuteronomy 12:30). Tearing down their altars meant burning the carved images and not even wanting the silver or gold on them (Deuteronomy 7:25). The same is true where we are scattered. We have made leagues with the inhabitants of the land, in their sports leagues and bowling leagues and at their dinner parties, when the scripture warns against envying the violent man or copying any of his ways (Proverbs 3:31). When Joshua and his generation died, another generation grew up that did not know the Lord or what He had done for Israel, and they served the Baals and Ashtaroth, the gods of the nations around them (Judges 2:10-13). A pattern starts there: when a judge in Israel dies, the people just go off. It shows we are a people that need leadership, which is why we are told to trust the Lord and not rely on our own understanding (Proverbs 3:5-6). Brothers and sisters today come with theories they think are their own thoughts, but those thoughts were given to them, mostly by the television. Israel lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, the very nations they were told to utterly destroy, married their daughters and served their gods (Judges 3:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:1-4; Deuteronomy 20:16-18). Joshua had warned that if they intermarried with what was left of these nations, the Lord would stop driving them out and they would become snares and traps (Joshua 23:12-13). The key to the whole book is one verse: there was no king in Israel, and every man did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 17:6). With no king and no government Israel was sheep without a shepherd, and the same individual spirit is around today in those who say join no camp and let no man teach you. The sentence at Bochim was that the Lord would not drive those nations out; they would be thorns in Israel’s sides and their gods a snare, and the people wept aloud. In His anger He handed Israel over to raiders and to their enemies, until they could no longer stand against them (Judges 2:14-15). Look at us today, hands up and do not shoot, begging our enemies to see us as people. That is the curse written for disobedience, a curse that follows a man out of his house and back into it (Deuteronomy 28:19). We wonder why we cannot get anywhere as a people, with individual millionaires and no farms, no distribution, no hospitals, no textiles, none of the things a nation needs to sustain itself. Our people do not think we are at war, but when the enemy hands you a false image, a false religion and a false education, slums to live in and bad food to eat, he is at war with you. The Lord has withdrawn to His place until we acknowledge our offence (Hosea 5:15). Still He raised up judges who rescued them from the raiders, because He was moved by their groaning under those who oppressed them (Judges 2:16-19), as in Egypt, where He said He had seen the affliction of His people (Exodus 3:7). Israel is the apple of His eye, and to touch them is to touch Him (Zechariah 2:8). The Most High does not want to see us on the bottom, but we broke His commandments and had to be punished for it. Yet they would not listen to their judges, and when a judge died they became more corrupt than their fathers. As soon as we came out of the condition we were in, we went right back to it. So He left the nations Joshua had not driven out, to test whether Israel would keep His way as their fathers had, and to teach the younger generations war (Judges 2:20-23; Judges 3:1-4). Judges is the record of that affliction beginning to come upon our people for turning their backs on the one true living God.

name: Eglon king of Moab
text: Possessing the city of palm trees and holding Israel in servitude eighteen years. Israel did evil again, and the Lord made Eglon king of Moab strong against them; Eglon allied with Ammon and Amalek, took the city of palm trees, and held Israel in service eighteen years. The same nations whose hearts melted at the report of Israel in Joshua’s day were now being strengthened against Israel for breaking the commandments. When the people cried, the Lord raised up Ehud the son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, with a double-edged dagger under his clothes and a message from God. Moab was subdued that day, and the land had rest eighty years. Israel did evil again in the Lord’s sight, and the Lord made Eglon king of Moab strong against Israel because of the evil they had done (Judges 3:12-14). Read that carefully: the record says the Lord strengthened him. In Joshua’s day the hearts of those same nations melted at the report of what the Lord had done for Israel, and Rahab told the spies that terror of Israel had fallen on them and no man had any courage left (Joshua 2:9-11). Now the same Lord was strengthening a heathen king against His own people for breaking His commandments. Eglon joined with Ammon and Amalek, attacked Israel, took the city of palm trees, and Israel served him eighteen years. The king’s dominion was real, but it was never power held outside the hand of the Most High; Israel’s own disobedience had set them under him. This is one servitude out of many. We had captivity after captivity, and there is not one nation that has nothing to answer for. While our people want to hold hands and sing along with everybody, every one of these nations played its part in our demise, and plays it to this day. Moab was not an accident of politics; Moab was a rod the Most High picked up because Israel had given Him cause. When Israel cried to the Lord, He raised up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite (Judges 3:15-26). Notice how the Lord raised up judges out of different tribes: Othniel of Judah before him, now Ehud of Benjamin. Ehud made a double-edged dagger a cubit long, strapped it under his clothes on his right thigh, and carried the tribute to Eglon, who was a very fat man. Saying he had a secret errand for the king, he got him alone in his cool upper room, told him he had a message from God for him, and drove the dagger into his belly with his left hand, and the fat closed over the blade so that he could not pull it out. He shut and locked the doors of the room and went out. The servants found the doors locked and supposed the king was relieving himself in the inner room; they waited until they were embarrassed, then took a key and found him dead on the floor. Ehud escaped to Seirath, blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim, and led Israel down, telling them to follow him because the Lord had given their enemies the Moabites into their hand. They seized the fords of the Jordan toward Moab and killed about ten thousand men, all strong and able fighters, and not one escaped; so Moab was subdued that day under Israel’s hand, and the land had rest eighty years (Judges 3:27-30). The same Lord who strengthened Eglon took his dominion away the moment His people cried. After Ehud came Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad, a farm tool ten feet long with a sharp point, and he also delivered Israel (Judges 3:31).

name: Jabin and Sisera
text: Mightily oppressing Israel twenty years with nine hundred chariots of iron. When Ehud was dead the children of Israel again did evil, and the Lord handed them over to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor, whose captain was Sisera of Harosheth of the Gentiles. Nine hundred chariots of iron, and twenty years of harsh oppression, until Israel cried. The Lord drew Sisera to the river Kishon and routed him and all his army before the sword; heaven itself fought against him and the river swept his army away. He fled on foot and died in a tent, and God subdued Jabin before the children of Israel. When Ehud was dead the children of Israel again did evil in the Lord’s sight, and He handed them over to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor; his captain was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles (Judges 4:1-3). Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron and harshly oppressed Israel for twenty years, and they cried to the Lord. That is the cycle already laid down in chapter two, running one more turn: Israel does evil, is sold into an oppressor’s hand, cries out, and a deliverer is raised up. The song of that day describes what the servitude did to ordinary life. The highways were empty and travellers kept to back paths, and village life ceased in Israel until Deborah arose, a mother in Israel; and it names the cause underneath it, that the people took up new gods and war arrived at their gates, with forty thousand in Israel and no shield or spear among them (Judges 5:6-8). The iron chariots account for the terror of it; they do not account for how Israel came to be under them. Sisera is the general of the Canaanite host, and Israel had been told plainly not to fear horses and chariots and an army larger than their own, because the Lord their God was with them (Deuteronomy 20:1). The fear came in because the faith had gone out. Deborah gave Barak the Lord’s command: march to mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and the Lord would draw Sisera with his chariots and his army to the river Kishon and give him into Barak’s hand (Judges 4:6-7). Sisera gathered all nine hundred chariots of iron and all his people to the river, and Deborah told Barak the day had come and the Lord had gone out ahead of him. The Lord threw Sisera, his chariots and his whole army into a rout before Barak’s sword, so that Sisera jumped down from his chariot and fled on foot, and the whole army fell by the sword until not one man was left (Judges 4:12-16). The song tells how it was done. The kings of Canaan fought by the waters of Megiddo and carried off no silver as plunder; heaven itself fought, the stars from their courses battled Sisera, and the ancient river Kishon swept them away (Judges 5:19-21). Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, because Jabin king of Hazor was at peace with Heber’s house, and he died there with a tent peg through his temple; so God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan that day before Israel, and Israel pressed harder and harder against him until they had destroyed him (Judges 4:17-24). The song closes at a window in Harosheth: Sisera’s mother looked out and cried, asking why his chariot was so slow in coming, and her wisest ladies answered her with imagined victory, that they were dividing the spoils. She was looking for a son who was never coming home; he lay dead in Jael’s tent. The song ends by wishing ruin on the Lord’s enemies and the strength of the rising sun on those who love Him; and the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:28-31).

name: Deborah
text: Judging Israel under the palm tree; delivering the commandment of the Lord to Barak, and going up with him. Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, judged Israel at that time, sitting under the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim, where the children of Israel came to her for judgment. She sent for Barak and reminded him of what the Lord had already commanded him, and when he would not go without her, she went, telling him the journey would not be for his honour. She did not put on armour and lead the charge; she was the motivating factor to men who were shaky, a mother in Israel, and her heart was with the leaders of Israel who volunteered themselves. The land had rest forty years. Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, judged Israel at that time; she sat under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim, and the children of Israel came to her for judgment (Judges 4:4-7). A prophetess in scripture is not a woman in a pulpit over men. Miriam the prophetess took a timbrel and led the women out in song (Exodus 15:20). Anna the prophetess never left the temple, serving God with fasting and prayer night and day (Luke 2:36-37). That is the office, and the woman who claims the title of prophetess to teach and mislead the servants of God is the one the scripture rebukes (Revelation 2:20). The order did not change in the letters, where the woman is to learn quietly in full subjection and is not to teach or take authority over the man (1 Timothy 2:11-12). Deborah was a married woman in subjection to a husband, set by the Most High to judge matters between the children of Israel, and Israel respected her. She called Barak the son of Abinoam and asked whether the Lord God of Israel had not already commanded him to march to mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, since the Lord would draw Sisera to the river Kishon and hand him over. Mark the wording: she is confirming an order Barak already had, because the Lord reveals His secret to His servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). Barak said he would go only if she went with him; she agreed, but told him the journey would not be for his honour, because the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman (Judges 4:8-10). She went up with him, and when the day came she told him to rise, for this was the day the Lord had given Sisera into his hand (Judges 4:14-16). She was used as a vessel to get a fearful man off his seat so the will of God could be done. This passage is for all the closet feminists who think Deborah justifies women leading men. She did not lead men into any kind of war; she did not put on body armour and a breastplate, rise up on a horse, and lead the charge. She was the motivating factor to men that were shaky and fearful in that time, a mother in Israel, a guiding light, one of the ones who had to rise up when the brothers were not handling business. Her own song proves it: her heart was with the leaders of Israel who volunteered themselves among the people (Judges 5:1-11). Judith did the same in her day; she heard the governors speak wrongly before the people and did not stay quiet, but told them plainly it was not right and called them to seek the Lord, and they answered that she had spoken rightly. That is a righteous sister in her place, and our people are still in captivity today, paying for the iniquities of their fathers (Baruch 3:8). Deborah and Barak sang that day, praising the Lord for avenging Israel when the people offered themselves willingly. That is what the Most High wants from us, a willing heart in keeping the commandments, the feast days, and His praise, the same willing heart that brought gold for the tabernacle, men and women alike (Exodus 35:22). How do we offer ourselves now? By giving up whatever stands between us and the Lord, whether father, mother, husband, wife or children, for Christ said His coming would divide households, and love for family must not outrank love for Him (Matthew 10:34-37), and every man carries his own load (Galatians 6:5). The song counts who came and who stayed home: Reuben sat second guessing itself, Gilead stayed across the Jordan, Dan stayed with the ships, Asher stayed on the coast; but Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives to the death on the heights of the field, and Meroz was bitterly cursed by the angel of the Lord for failing to come to the Lord’s help against the mighty (Judges 5:15-23). Sitting out the battle of the Lord brings a curse. The opening of the song, the Lord marching out of the field of Edom with the earth trembling and the mountains melting, has not happened yet; it is the same picture as the figure coming out of Edom with his clothes stained red, treading the winepress alone in the day of vengeance (Isaiah 63:1-4). And the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:31).

name: Barak
text: Going down from Tabor at the word of the Lord against nine hundred chariots of iron; and going only on condition that Deborah went. The Lord had already commanded Barak to march to mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and Deborah was sent to remind him of it. He answered that he would go only if she went with him; she went, and told him the journey would not be for his honour, for the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman. He went down anyway against nine hundred chariots of iron, and the Lord routed Sisera and all his army before him, until not a man was left. The record still counts him among the faithful. Deborah called Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and asked whether the Lord God of Israel had not commanded him to march to mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, since the Lord would draw Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his troops to the river Kishon and give him into his hand (Judges 4:6-9). Read her words again. She is not handing him a new errand; she is asking whether God has not already told him to do this. The Lord had spoken to him, Barak was slow and fearful about it, and so the Lord spoke to His prophetess and sent her to confirm it to his face. Barak answered that he would go if she went with him, and if she would not go, he would not go. She said she would certainly go, but the journey would not be for his honour, because the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman. The promise of victory stood; only the honour of the day was taken from him. He called Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh and went up with ten thousand men behind him, and Deborah went up with him (Judges 4:6-10). When she told him the day had come and asked whether the Lord had not gone out ahead of him, Barak went down from mount Tabor with ten thousand men after him. That was the test: horses, chariots and an army larger than his, and the word of the Lord telling him not to fear them, because the Lord his God was with him (Deuteronomy 20:1). The song remembers who stood with him. Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives to the death on the heights of the field; those tribes are warriors. Set against them are the clans of Reuben, full of deep thoughts and heart searching, second guessing themselves, and Gilead staying across the Jordan, and Dan with the ships, and Asher on the coast (Judges 5:15-21). The Lord routed Sisera, all his chariots and all his army before Barak’s sword, and Barak chased the chariots and the army to Harosheth of the Gentiles, and the whole army of Sisera fell by the sword until not a man was left (Judges 4:14-16). Heaven itself fought; the stars from their courses battled Sisera, and the river Kishon swept them away (Judges 5:19-21). The pursuit was real work, but the victory was not in the arm that did it. When Barak came in pursuit, Jael came out to meet him and showed him the man he was looking for, lying dead with the tent peg in his temple (Judges 4:22). Both words spoken over him were fulfilled in one day: the army was given into his hand, and the honour of the captain went to a woman. His hesitation cost him the honour; it did not cost Israel the deliverance, and it did not cost him his name. The record of the faithful still counts Barak among those who by faith conquered kingdoms, grew strong in battle, and put foreign armies to flight (Hebrews 11:32-34). That is worth weighing by any brother who has been called to something and is dragging his feet: the calling was already on him, the word came to him twice, and when he finally moved, God did exactly what He said He would do. Then Deborah and Barak sang that day, praising the Lord for avenging Israel when the people offered themselves willingly (Judges 5:1-2). The song ends by wishing ruin on the Lord’s enemies and the strength of the rising sun on those who love Him; and the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:31).

name: Jael
text: Blessed above women in the tent: the nail, the hammer, and Sisera. Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, because Jabin king of Hazor was at peace with Heber’s house. She covered him with a rug, gave him milk when he asked for water, and when he was sound asleep from exhaustion she took a tent peg and a hammer, crept up to him, and drove the peg through his temple into the ground. The word Deborah had spoken was fulfilled by her hand, that the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman. The song of Deborah puts the blessing on her: most blessed of the women in tents. Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, because Jabin king of Hazor was at peace with the house of Heber the Kenite (Judges 4:17-22). Heber, of the descendants of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had separated from the Kenites and pitched his tent near Kedesh (Judges 4:11). Jael went out to meet Sisera, told him to come in and not be afraid, and covered him with a rug; he asked for a little water because he was thirsty, and she opened a skin of milk, gave him a drink and covered him again. He told her to stand in the tent door and, if anyone asked, say no man was there. The captain who had commanded nine hundred chariots of iron was now depending on a woman to hide him. Then Jael took a tent peg and a hammer, crept up to him as he lay sound asleep from exhaustion, and drove the peg through his temple into the ground, and he died. When Barak came in pursuit, she came out to meet him and showed him the man he was looking for, lying dead with the peg in his temple. The word Deborah had spoken to Barak was fulfilled by her hand: the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman (Judges 4:9). So God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan that day before Israel (Judges 4:17-23). The song of Deborah and Barak pronounces it: Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite is most blessed of women, most blessed of the women in tents. He asked for water and she gave him milk, cream in a bowl fit for nobles; she reached for the peg with one hand and the workman’s hammer with her right, and he collapsed dead at her feet (Judges 5:24-27). Set immediately before that blessing is the curse on Meroz, bitterly cursed by the angel of the Lord because its people did not come to help the Lord against the mighty (Judges 5:23-31). The song puts the two side by side on purpose: a city in Israel that sat out the battle of the Lord and drew a curse, and a woman in a tent who acted and drew a blessing. It was counted a shame in that day for a man of war to die by a woman’s hand, and the shame followed the next man who earned it. When the millstone crushed Abimelech’s skull at Thebez he quickly called his armourbearer to draw his sword and kill him, so that no one would say a woman had killed him (Judges 9:53-54). Sisera got no such cover. The song then turns to his mother at her window, asking why his chariot is so slow in coming while her wisest ladies answer her with imagined victory and dividing of spoils; she is looking for a son who is never coming home, and Jael has already ended his flight (Judges 5:28-30). The song ends by wishing ruin on the Lord’s enemies and the strength of the rising sun on those who love Him (Judges 5:31).

name: Gideon
text: Throwing down his father’s altar of Baal; going against Midian with three hundred, as the Lord said. Israel hid in dens and caves in the mountains of their own land while Midian, Amalek and the eastern peoples swarmed in like locusts and destroyed the crops. An angel sat under an oak in Ophrah while Gideon threshed wheat in the winepress to hide it, and greeted him as a mighty man of valour with the Lord at his side; the Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat. He tore down his father’s altar of Baal by night, sent home thirty-one thousand seven hundred men because the Lord said the army was too big, and broke the host of Midian with three hundred, with pitchers, lamps and trumpets. The victory of battle comes from the Lord. Israel did evil, and the Lord handed them to Midian for seven years; they hid in dens, caves and strongholds in the mountains of their own land (Judges 6:1-16). Whenever Israel planted, Midian, Amalek and the eastern peoples swarmed in like locusts, destroyed the crops, and left no food and no livestock: the curse of blight and mildew gone into famine (Deuteronomy 28:21-22). When Israel cried, the Lord first sent a prophet to remind them that He had brought them out of bondage and told them not to fear the gods of the Amorites, and that they had not listened; the judgment came with a reason attached, and those Amorites trace back through Canaan into the Hamites (Genesis 10:15-16). Then an angel of the Lord sat under an oak in Ophrah while Gideon threshed wheat in the winepress to hide it from Midian, and greeted him as a mighty man of valour with the Lord at his side.
