The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat. Gideon asked why, if the Lord was with them, all this had happened, and where were the miracles their fathers told of. Many of us ask the same today, watching our people judged in the streets over and over. But God has not forsaken us; we forsook Him, abandoning the spring of living water for broken cisterns that hold nothing (Jeremiah 2:13), and the Lord disciplines those He loves (Hebrews 12:6). Sent to save Israel, Gideon answered with his pedigree: his family the poorest in Manasseh, himself the least in his father’s house. That is a defeated mentality, and every one of us has to overcome it. God calls few of the wise, mighty or noble; He chooses the foolish, weak and lowly to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:26-28), and what men prize is detestable to Him (Luke 16:15). Fire rose out of the rock to consume his offering, and the same night the Lord told him to tear down his father’s altar of Baal and cut down the grove beside it (Judges 6:17-32). The tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal before the kingdom split, which made Jeroboam’s golden calves an easy transition (1 Kings 12:28). He did it by night, and when the men of the city demanded his death, Joash told them to let Baal defend himself if he was a god, He asked the fleece sign twice (Judges 6:34-40), but we do not ask for signs like that any more, for Christ called sign seeking the mark of a wicked and unfaithful generation (Matthew 12:39). The Lord said the army was too large, or Israel would boast that its own hand had saved it (Judges 7:1-8). That is Israel: look at what I did. They had been warned before entering the land not to credit their own power and strength for their wealth (Deuteronomy 8:14-18). The fearful were sent home, and twenty-two thousand left; the Lord tested the rest at the water, and kept the three hundred who lapped from the hand, men still upright and alert with their eyes on what was around them. You have to be willing to let go of some people, as the Lord told Abraham to leave his country and kindred (Genesis 12:1), and as Christ came to set a man against his own household (Matthew 10:34-36). That night the Lord sent Gideon down to the edge of the camp. There he overheard a man tell a dream of a barley loaf tumbling into the camp and flattening a tent, and his companion say it could only be the sword of Gideon, into whose hand God had given Midian. The Lord put that dream in the enemy’s mind and sent Gideon to hear it, so he would go in without doubt (Judges 7:9-25). Look around us and it is the same picture, enemies as far as the eye can see. He split the three hundred into three companies with trumpets and lamps hidden in empty pitchers, and struck at the start of the middle watch, right as the watchmen changed; they blew the trumpets, smashed the pitchers, and shouted a battle cry for the Lord and for Gideon, and the Lord turned every man’s sword against his companion. The enemy destroyed itself. The trumpets go into the law: when Israel goes to war against an oppressor they sound an alarm, and the Lord remembers and saves them (Numbers 10:9). Midian was subdued and never raised its head again, and the land was quiet forty years (Judges 8:28). Victory does not come by numbers, by how many guns or bullets; it is easy for many to be delivered into the hands of a few, for strength comes from heaven (1 Maccabees 3:18-19).

name: The men of Succoth and Penuel
text: Refusing bread to the army of the Lord, faint yet pursuing, and upbraiding them with it. Gideon and the three hundred crossed the Jordan exhausted but still pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian, and asked the men of Succoth for bread. The princes of Succoth asked whether he already had the two kings in hand, that they should feed his army, and the men of Penuel answered the same way, both cities playing neutral for fear the kings might come back on them. He told each of them what he would do when the Lord had given the kings into his hand, and he came back with the kings in hand. He taught the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers and tore down the tower of Penuel. Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed with his three hundred men, exhausted but still pursuing, and asked the men of Succoth for bread for the people with him, because they were worn out while he chased Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian. The princes of Succoth sneered, asking whether he already had the two kings in hand, that they should feed his army; and when he went on to Penuel and asked the same, the men of Penuel gave the same answer (Judges 8:4-6). Both cities were playing neutral ground out of fear that the kings of Midian might come against them for helping. Two cities of Israel watched the army of the Lord come through faint and weary from the deliverance of the whole nation, and made their help depend on a victory that was not finished yet. Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that remained of the eastern armies, for a hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen (Judges 8:4-12). Three hundred men against those numbers on an empty stomach, and you know God was with them. Those two kings are the princes named in Asaph’s prayer, which asks that God’s enemies be made like Oreb and Zeeb and their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna (Psalms 83:11). Gideon promised Succoth that when the Lord had given Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand he would thresh their flesh with the thorns and briers of the wilderness, and promised Penuel that when he came back in peace he would tear down their tower (Judges 8:7-9). He came around by the road of the tent dwellers, struck the camp while it felt safe, chased down the two kings, captured them, and routed the whole army. On the way back he caught a young man of Succoth who gave him the names of the princes and elders of the city, and he came back with the kings in hand and showed the men of Succoth the very prisoners they had mocked him about. He took the elders of the city and taught the men of Succoth with the thorns and briers of the wilderness (Judges 8:13-16). He taught them a lesson: when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn it away. And he tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city. Then he asked Zebah and Zalmunna what the men they had killed at Tabor looked like, and they said each one looked like a king’s son, just like him; they were his own brothers, his mother’s sons, and he told the kings that if they had spared them he would have spared the kings (Judges 8:13-21). He told Jether his firstborn to get up and kill them, but the boy did not draw his sword, because he was afraid, being still young. We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from our father and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but look at what Gideon was doing, taking his son to the war and teaching him the way he must walk, which is exactly what we have to do with our young men, training a boy early in the path he is to keep (Proverbs 22:6). Zebah and Zalmunna told Gideon to do it himself, since a man’s strength matches the man; they wanted to die quickly at the hand of a warrior rather than suffer under the sword of a boy. So Gideon killed them and took the ornaments from their camels’ necks.

name: Gideon’s ephod
text: Making an ephod of the golden earrings of the spoil, and putting it in Ophrah; all Israel going a whoring after it. The men of Israel asked Gideon to rule over them, and his son and grandson after him, for saving them from Midian, and he refused: the Lord would rule over them. Then he asked every man for the earrings from his plunder, because the enemy were Ishmaelites and wore gold earrings, and made an ephod of seventeen hundred shekels of gold and set it up in his city. All Israel went after it there in spiritual whoredom, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house. As soon as he was dead the people went after the Baals again and made Baal-berith their god. The men of Israel asked Gideon to rule over them, he and his son and his grandson, because he had saved them from Midian (Judges 8:22-27). Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep and wander off the path without somebody to guide us in the way we must go. Gideon refused the throne for himself and his son, because the Lord was their ruler. He knew that if thrones were set up in Israel the people would put their trust and their faith in the king instead of in the Most High. Those were right words, and the man who spoke them had already torn down his father’s altar of Baal and cut down the grove beside it (Judges 6:25-27). The test did not end when he refused the crown. He made one request: that every man give him the earrings from his plunder, since the enemy, being Ishmaelites, wore gold earrings. They gave gladly, spreading a garment and throwing the earrings on it, and the gold weighed seventeen hundred shekels, not counting the ornaments, pendants and purple garments of the Midianite kings and the chains from their camels’ necks. Gideon made an ephod of it and set it up in his city of Ophrah, and all Israel went after it there in spiritual whoredom, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house. Paul names the love of money as the root of evil (1 Timothy 6:10); the gold Gideon gathered turned into the very snare that trapped his own house. The judgment is already in the word the record chooses: a snare. No sentence is passed on Gideon in the chapter, and none needed to be written; the man who had pulled down one idol furnished the people with another object to go after, and his own house was caught in it. Midian stayed subdued and the land was quiet forty years in Gideon’s days; he fathered seventy sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem also bore him a son he named Abimelech, and Gideon the son of Joash died at a good old age (Judges 8:28-35). As soon as Gideon was dead, the children of Israel turned again to spiritual whoredom after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god (Judges 8:33-35). Baal means lord and berith means covenant, so the god they set up was the lord of the covenant, a counterfeit put over the people in place of the One who had just delivered them. They forgot the Lord their God who had rescued them from all the enemies around them, and showed no kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, that is Gideon, for all the good he had done Israel. The same cycle turned again the moment the judge was gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. The son born of the concubine in Shechem, and the silver out of the house of Baal-berith, are the next case.

name: Abimelech son of Gideon
text: Slaying his seventy brethren upon one stone with silver out of the house of Baal-berith; making himself king at Shechem. Gideon’s son by his concubine in Shechem went to his mother’s kin and told them to remember he was their own flesh and blood, and they chose him by kinship rather than by righteousness. With seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith he hired worthless, reckless men and killed his seventy brothers on one stone; only Jotham, the youngest, escaped, and stood alone on mount Gerizim and prophesied the fire. Three years later God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and both sides were destroyed. A woman in a tower at Thebez broke his skull with a piece of a millstone. Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to his mother’s kin in Shechem and had them ask the men of the city whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to rule them or one man, reminding them he was their own blood (Judges 9:1-6). His very name means my father is king; the ambition was carried in what he was called. When people remind you that blood is thicker than water, they want you to back them whether or not the thing is right. The men of Shechem leaned toward him because he was their brother: they chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol’s house, and with it he hired worthless, reckless men to follow him. At Ophrah he killed his seventy brothers on one stone; only Jotham the youngest survived, by hiding. Then the men of Shechem and the house of Millo made him king, endorsing the man who had used their money to murder his seventy brothers. When Jotham heard, he stood on the top of mount Gerizim and shouted for the men of Shechem to listen to him, so that God would listen to them (Judges 9:7-21). This young brother was fearless, standing alone to rebuke them. In his parable the trees went out to anoint a king. The trees are Israel; the olive tree is Gideon, who would not give up his richness to rule over the trees; the fig tree and the vine are Gideon’s sons, who would not give up their sweetness and their wine. Only the bramble accepted, a thistle that pricks and tears, and its answer carried a threat of fire. Jotham applied it: their father had risked his life for them, and they had killed his sons on one stone and made the slave woman’s son king because he was their brother. If they had acted in good faith, let them enjoy Abimelech; if not, let fire come out of Abimelech and consume Shechem, and fire out of Shechem consume Abimelech. That was a prophecy, and it came to pass. After Abimelech had ruled Israel three years, God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, and they betrayed him, so that the blood of the seventy sons of Jerubbaal would fall on Abimelech who killed them and on the men of Shechem who helped him (Judges 9:22-24). Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody’s spirit suddenly turns against you, we tend to think it is just that person. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, not karma, not mother nature; the Lord of hosts musters the army for battle (Isaiah 13:4), both peace and evil come from His hand as light and darkness do (Isaiah 45:7), and He put a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets (1 Kings 22:22-23). Abimelech ran three years and everything looked good, and he was not getting away with it. Gaal the son of Ebed came to Shechem and, with wine in him, talked big against Abimelech (Judges 9:22-49). Zebul the ruler of the city sent word to Abimelech, strung Gaal along, then asked him where his big mouth was now. All the big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Abimelech drove him out, took the city, killed its people, razed it and sowed it with salt; and when the men of the tower of Shechem took refuge in the stronghold of the temple of Berith, he burned the stronghold over them with branches from mount Zalmon, so that about a thousand men and women died. The people who made him king were burned by him; the fire out of the bramble was doing exactly what Jotham said. At the tower of Thebez a woman dropped a piece of millstone on his head and cracked his skull; he quickly told his armourbearer to kill him so no one would say a woman had done it, and the young man ran him through (Judges 9:50-57). It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by a woman’s hand, as when Jael drove the peg into Sisera’s temple (Judges 4:21). Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull. So God repaid Abimelech and the men of Shechem for their evil, and Jotham’s curse came upon them. Trace the pattern in the man and you can name it anywhere: preeminence, manipulation, hatred, murder. It begins in wanting to be the head and it ends in blood, and the warning to us is plain: do nothing out of rivalry or conceit (Philippians 2:3), and know that your sin will catch up with you (Numbers 32:23).

name: Jephthah’s vow
text: A vow uttered before the Lord, and paid in his only daughter. The son of a harlot, driven out of his father’s house by his half brothers, was brought back by the elders of Gilead when Ammon made war, and asked them why they came to him now in their trouble after hating him and throwing him out. He knew the history and would not let the king of Ammon lie about it. Before the battle he vowed that whatever came out of his house to meet him first would belong to the Lord, and his only daughter came out with tambourines and dancing. He did not burn her; Israel did not do human sacrifice. She was given over to the Lord and knew no man. Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, the son of a harlot. His father’s wife’s sons drove him out, saying he would inherit nothing in their father’s house because he was the son of a strange woman; strange there does not mean his mother was of another nation, for the scripture says only that she was a harlot. He fled to the land of Tob, and worthless men gathered around him (Judges 11:1-11). When the ones trying to do right do not get love and support from their own family, they go looking for it in the wrong places, and you see the kind of men they end up around. We all have a background, and none of it puts a man outside the use of the Most High. When Ammon made war on Israel, the elders of Gilead came to fetch him as their captain. Jephthah did not forget: he asked whether they had not hated him and thrown him out, and why they came now that they were in trouble. He set the terms, and the people made him head and captain. The king of Ammon claimed Israel had taken his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan when it came up from Egypt, and demanded it back. That claim was a lie, and Jephthah sent back the whole history (Judges 11:12-28). Israel took no land from Moab or Ammon; Edom and Moab refused passage (Numbers 20:21), and Israel went around their territory and never crossed the border of Moab. Sihon king of the Amorites refused passage and fought, and the Lord gave his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok into Israel’s hand (Deuteronomy 2:30-37). Israel never touched Ammon’s land, and for three hundred years nobody came to claim those cities. This is why we must know our history: the king of Ammon could have pulled that on somebody ignorant and been handed the land, and people try the same thing on us in the street. Ask the former generations and learn what the fathers found out (Job 8:8); remember the days of old and ask your father and your elders (Deuteronomy 32:7); devote yourself to reading (1 Timothy 4:13). The Lord is in the midst of every battle, telling the end from the start, and His purpose stands (Isaiah 46:10); the king of Ammon would not listen, his heart hardened as Sihon’s had been. Then the Spirit of the Lord came on Jephthah, and he vowed that if the Lord gave him Ammon, whatever came out of his house to meet him on his return would belong to the Lord (Judges 11:29-33). The Lord gave them into his hand. When he came home to Mizpeh, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dancing, and she was his only child. He tore his clothes and told her she had crushed him, for he had made a vow to the Lord and could not take it back (Judges 11:34-40). Whoever swears rashly with his lips, for good or evil, is guilty in it (Leviticus 5:4-6); a vow to God is to be paid without delay, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). She did not plead for her life; since the Lord had avenged him on his enemies, she told him to do as he had vowed. She asked one thing, two months to wander the mountains with her companions and mourn her virginity. Jephthah did not burn his daughter as a human sacrifice. Israel did not do human sacrifice; that was Molech worship among the Canaanites. Read the end of the passage: after two months she returned to her father, he did with her as he had vowed, and she knew no man. If she had been put to death there would be no reason for the record to say she knew no man, and no reason to mourn her virginity if she were about to die. The sorrow was that, given over to the Lord, she could never marry or bear children, and in those days our women wanted to bring children into the world and continue the lineage; to be childless was counted a shame among the daughters of Israel, which is why Rachel told Jacob she would die if he did not give her children (Genesis 30:1). Her life was committed to the Lord to serve Him, and the difficulty people trip over is a translation difference around the word offering. It became a custom that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah four days a year. Let your yes be yes and your no be no, for anything more comes from evil (Matthew 5:37).

name: Manoah and his wife
text: Asking, how shall we order the child? and observing all that the angel commanded. The angel of the Lord appeared to a barren woman of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, and told her she would bear a son who would be a Nazarite to God from the womb, with a rule laid on her as well: no wine, no strong drink, and nothing unclean. She told her husband, and Manoah prayed that the man of God would come again and teach them how to raise the child, and the Lord heard him. They offered a young goat on a rock, the angel rose in the flame, and they fell on their faces. His wife reasoned rightly: if the Lord had meant to kill them He would not have accepted an offering from them. Israel did evil again in the Lord’s sight, and He gave them into the hand of the Philistines forty years. A man of Zorah of the family of Dan named Manoah had a wife who was barren (Judges 13:1-7). This is one of many places where our foremothers went through barrenness, and when the Most High was ready He enabled them to conceive; He settles the childless woman in her home as a happy mother of children (Psalms 113:9). Sisters who have tried for years should be patient, take comfort in the scriptures, and believe what the Bible says. The angel of the Lord told the woman she would conceive and bear a son, and laid the rule on her as well as on the child: no wine or strong drink, nothing unclean, and no razor on his head, because the child would be a Nazarite to God from the womb and would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Even in the womb he was to be kept pure. That is the vow set out in the law, the separation of a man or woman to the Lord, with nothing from the grapevine, seeds or skins, and no razor on the head while the hair grows long (Numbers 6:2-5). Understand the difference between a Nazarite and a Nazarene: Christ was a Nazarene because He was of the city of Nazareth, and He drank wine, which a Nazarite could not do. Samson was a Nazarite from birth, and so were Samuel and John the Baptist after him. The locks also witness to who Israel is; the hair of Israel naturally grows that way. The woman told her husband that a man of God had come to her, looking like an angel of God, very frightening. The popular pictures of angels as babies with smooth cheeks and little white wings do not match scripture at all; to see an angel of the Most High was terrifying, blazing like lightning in snow-white clothes (Matthew 28:3). Manoah prayed that the man of God would come again and teach them how to raise the child, and God heard him; the angel came again to the woman in the field, and she ran to fetch her husband (Judges 13:8-14). Manoah asked how the child should be raised, and the angel only repeated what he had already told the woman, that she must keep all of it. Their task was not to invent a manner of upbringing for an extraordinary child. It was to receive the instruction and keep it. Manoah tried to keep the angel and prepare a young goat for him; the angel refused to eat, and said that if they offered a burnt offering it must be to the Lord, for Manoah did not know he was an angel of the Lord (Judges 13:15-25). The angel knew Manoah might try to offer it to him, since he appeared like a god, so he directed the offering where it belonged. Israel is quick to worship anything that looks like it could be God, which is why the letters warn against being cheated by false humility and the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18), and why, when John fell at the angel’s feet to worship, the angel stopped him, calling himself a fellow servant, and told him to worship God (Revelation 22:8-9). Manoah asked his name, and the angel asked why he wanted to know, since it was secret. Manoah offered a young goat with a grain offering on a rock to the Lord, and the angel did a wonder: as the flame went up from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the Lord rose in the flame and was gone, and Manoah and his wife fell face down to the ground (Judges 13:19-23). Angels are made of that fire; they have bodies, they walk, they eat, they come and go, and one of them can take the flame off an altar and rise in it. Manoah said they would surely die, because they had seen God. The contradictors point to this, since the Bible says no man has seen God; but the word there is Elohim, which is plural and speaks of heavenly beings. They saw an angel, not the Most High; no flesh can look upon Him, and the furthest anybody got was Moses seeing His back. His wife reasoned rightly: if the Lord had wanted to kill them He would not have accepted their offerings or shown them all these things. She bore a son and named him Samson, the child grew and the Lord blessed him, and the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol.

name: Samson
text: Lusting after Philistine women: a wife at Timnath against his parents’ counsel, a harlot at Gaza, and Delilah, to whom he told all his heart. A Nazarite to God from the womb, with a lust for heathen women that is the infamy his story is known for. His parents answered him rightly, asking whether no woman among his own people would do, but he insisted, and the Lord used the flaw as an occasion against the Philistines who ruled Israel. Three times Delilah tried to have his life taken and he stayed with her; then he told her everything in his heart, woke shaven in her lap, and did not know that the Lord had left him. Blinded and grinding grain in the prison at Gaza, he prayed once more, and killed more Philistines in his death than in his life. Samson saw a Philistine woman at Timnath and told his parents to get her for him. This brother had a lust issue with heathen women. His parents answered him rightly, asking whether no woman among his own people would do; there were twelve tribes and no shortage of women in Israel, and the forefathers always charged their sons against it, as Isaac charged Jacob not to marry a Canaanite (Genesis 28:1). Samson insisted, because she pleased him (Judges 14:1-6). His parents did not know it was from the Lord, who sought an occasion against the Philistines then ruling Israel. The Most High was using Samson’s own flaw to destroy the nation oppressing His people, and that is the basis of the whole story. His thinking is higher than ours (Isaiah 55:8-9); both the one misled and the one misleading are under His rule (Job 12:16); no counsel stands against the Lord (Proverbs 21:30); no calamity comes on a city unless the Lord has done it (Amos 3:6). At the wedding feast his thirty companions threatened to burn his wife and her father’s house unless she got his riddle out of him. She turned to tears and manipulation, crying through the feast that he did not love her, until he gave in and she passed it to her people (Judges 14:15-18). This big strong mighty brother caved in under the tears of a woman, and knew it, saying they had plowed with his heifer. Never trust the enemy. Her loyalty belonged to her husband, and she carried his business straight to her heathen people, which is why it makes no sense to marry the enemy. Later he slept with a harlot at Gaza and carried off the city gate at midnight (Judges 16:1-14). Then he loved Delilah, and each Philistine lord offered her eleven hundred pieces of silver to learn the secret of his strength. It was a setup. Once they learn where a man’s strength lies they can bind him and plunder his goods, and that is the method used on this whole nation, the same reason Holofernes wanted to know what held Israel up. The weapon they used on Samson was his weakness for sex. She asked him outright how he could be bound and subdued, asking for the formula to get him killed. Three times she tried it with men waiting in the room, and a man of war should have recognised the setup and cut her off; he was still there. She nagged him daily, asking how he could say he loved her when his heart was not with her, until he told her everything: he was a Nazarite from the womb, and if shaved his strength would leave him (Judges 16:15-22). That is where he messed up. This is the scriptural example of why a man does not tell his wife every single thing in his heart; we do not go by the philosophies of men that say your wife is your best friend you tell everything to. Scripture says to guard your words even from the woman who lies in your arms (Micah 7:5); counsel on those things belongs among the brothers. His downfall was compromise: emotional attachment, a physical relationship, and every warning sign ignored. She lulled him to sleep on her knees and had his seven locks shaved, and he woke not knowing the Lord had left him. They gouged out his eyes and set him grinding in the prison at Gaza, a blind slave put on show; but his hair began to grow back. The Philistine lords gathered to sacrifice to Dagon, crediting their god with delivering Samson to them (Judges 16:23-31). They gave the glory to an idol that had not done a thing; it was Samson’s own transgression that caused the Most High to allow them to afflict him, and that praise to a fake god did not please Him. They brought Samson out to entertain them and stood him between the pillars, with all the lords in the house and about three thousand on the roof. He called on the Lord to strengthen him just this once, to be avenged for his two eyes, pushed on the two middle pillars with all his might, and the house fell, so that he killed more in his death than in his life. Even with all his failings the Most High used him as a vessel of vengeance on the oppressor who gave the glory of the victory to a devil. Israel’s salvation in scripture is always joined with the destruction of the enemy, the two received together (Wisdom of Solomon 18:7). He had judged Israel twenty years. When Satan whispers to a fallen man that God cannot use somebody like him, remember that He used Samson.

name: Micah’s idols and the tribe of Dan
text: A house of gods, a hired Levite, and a tribe that stole both and set up the graven image in Dan. A man of mount Ephraim stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his own mother, and when he gave it back she blessed him and had it made into a graven image and a molten image instead of rebuking him. He kept a house of gods, consecrated one of his own sons, then hired a wandering Levite for ten shekels a year, and expected the Lord to do him good because he had a Levite for his priest. Six hundred Danites passing through took the gods and the priest, burned Laish, and the first thing they did in their new land was set up the graven image. Dan stayed heavy in idolatry all through history and is not named among the sealed tribes. A man of mount Ephraim named Micah stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his own mother, and when he heard her cursing over it he confessed and gave it back. Instead of rebuking her son she blessed him, said she had dedicated the silver to the Lord for him to make a graven image and a molten image, and had two hundred shekels made into idols for his house (Judges 17:1-6). A mother buying her son idols was nothing new in Israel; later king Ahaziah followed the ways of Ahab’s house because his mother counselled him in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:3). Micah kept a house of gods, made an ephod and teraphim, and consecrated one of his own sons as priest: a counterfeit priesthood serving counterfeit gods. Then stands the key verse of the book: there was no king in Israel, and every man did what was right in his own eyes. With no king Israel was sheep without a shepherd, and every time the scripture shows Israel without a leadership structure, all manner of wickedness follows, primarily idolatry. A young Levite from Bethlehem-judah came wandering through, and Micah offered him ten shekels of silver a year, clothing and food to live with him as father and priest (Judges 17:10-13). Nothing says the Levite was already in idolatry, but when money was offered he went right along with it; being corrupted for reward was always the Levites’ weakness. Then Micah was sure the Lord would bless him now that a Levite was on the payroll, with a house full of idols and a hired priest over them. That is how sick in the mind Israel had become. The tribe of Dan was still looking for territory, because its inheritance had not yet come into its hand (Judges 18:1-14; Joshua 19:47). Five scouts lodging at Micah’s house recognised the young Levite and asked what he was doing there, because a Levite serving in a house of idols raised questions. At Laish they found a quiet, secure people with no ruler, far from Zidon and with no dealings with anyone: no judicial system, no neighbour, no ally. When six hundred armed men went up, the scouts pointed out Micah’s images. The first time they lodged there they saw his expensive looking gods and got covetous; on the way to one lick they had spotted another. Do not bring just anybody into your house, even brethren, for the deceitful man has many tricks (Ecclesiasticus 11:29). While the six hundred stood armed at the gate, the scouts took the images (Judges 18:14-20). When the priest objected they told him to keep quiet and asked whether it was better to be priest to one man’s house or to a whole tribe in Israel, and the priest was glad. Already sold out to serve idols for Micah’s silver, he dropped the man who treated him as a son the moment a bigger position was offered. Micah and his neighbours caught up with the Danites, and he complained that they had taken the gods he made and his priest, and what did he have left (Judges 18:22-31). Examine how foolish that sounds: the gods I made. How can a man make his own god? That is how simple we had become without leadership. The Danites warned him to be quiet, or hot-tempered men would attack him and he would lose his life and his household’s, and Micah went home. Neither his images nor his hired priest delivered him from anything. At Laish they put the people to the sword and burned the city, and no one came to rescue it, exactly as the spies had scoped out; they rebuilt it as Dan. The first thing the Danites did in the land the Most High allowed them to take was set up the graven image, a god made by the hands of a man they had just robbed, with Jonathan the son of Gershom and his sons as its priests until the captivity. Dan stayed heavy in idolatry all the way through history and never changed. After the kingdom split, Jeroboam feared the people would turn back to Rehoboam if they kept going to Jerusalem, so he made two golden calves, set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and it became a sin (1 Kings 12:28-30). The prophet says those who swear by the sin of Samaria and by the god of Dan as a living god will fall and never rise again (Amos 8:14). It is an idol made with hands, and they called it living. That is why, when the tribes are sealed, Dan is not named among them (Revelation 7:5-8); the tribe that set up the graven image was discontinued as a tribe of itself.

name: The men of Gibeah, and Benjamin
text: Sons of Belial demanding the man; the gang rape and death of his concubine; and a tribe that would not deliver up the guilty. A Levite heading home would not lodge in Jebus, a city of foreigners, and turned in to Gibeah of Benjamin, where no one took them in but an old man who knew what the streets of that city held at night. Sons of Belial surrounded the house and pounded on the door demanding the man, a rerun of Sodom; they were given his concubine, and abused her all night until she fell dead at the door with her hands on the threshold. He cut her into twelve pieces and sent them throughout the territory of Israel. Benjamin would not hand over the men of Gibeah, and four hundred thousand men went to war behind one woman; twenty-five thousand Benjamites fell in a day, and six hundred were left. With no king in Israel, a Levite living in the hill country of Ephraim took a concubine from Bethlehem-judah, the house of bread; a concubine was a wife of secondary rank. She was unfaithful to him and went back to her father’s house for four months, and her husband went after her to win her back (Judges 19:1-12). By the law a woman who leaves and becomes another man’s is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back pollutes the land (Deuteronomy 24:4; Jeremiah 3:1); but with no king and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did. The day drawing toward evening as they left is the Bible’s own witness that a day runs from evening to evening. Passing Jebus, which is Jerusalem, still held by the Jebusites whom Judah could not drive out (Joshua 15:63) until David took the stronghold of Zion (2 Samuel 5:6-7), he refused to lodge in a city of foreigners and went on to Gibeah, which means a hill town. Even then he would lodge only with his brothers. At Gibeah of Benjamin they sat in the street and no one took them in (Judges 19:14-21). The Benjamites were not so friendly. An old man of Ephraim living there took them in, knowing the men of that city. Hospitality to strangers is commanded (Hebrews 13:1-2); a stranger there is a brother travelling, and that hospitality was owed. That night sons of Belial, children of the devil, surrounded the house demanding that the man be brought out so they could know him (Judges 19:22-30). To know in that context is sexual; the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. It is a rerun of Sodom at Lot’s door (Genesis 19:4-5), and the letters name the vile thing (Romans 1:26-27). Like Lot, the old man offered his daughter and the concubine instead, and the Levite put his concubine out to them, and they abused her all night. That is plural: a gang rape, forced, nothing voluntary about it. At dawn she fell at the door with her hands on the threshold; in the morning he told her to get up, and there was no answer. The scripture is plain that rape is a sin worthy of death, like murder (Deuteronomy 22:25-26), and God will judge the sexually immoral (Hebrews 13:4). He cut her into twelve pieces and sent them through all Israel, and all said nothing like it had been seen since Egypt. All Israel gathered as one man at Mizpeh, four hundred thousand armed men (Judges 20:1-17). Israel got ready for war behind one woman. There is no hatred of women in this truth; a crime against one sister moved the whole nation to arms. The Levite testified that the men of Gibeah had surrounded the house to kill him and forced his concubine until she died (Judges 20:4-7). Forced is the Bible’s own word for rape, and nowhere can it be called lawful; be very mindful of sick, perverted camps that teach otherwise. The tribes demanded that Benjamin hand over the men of Gibeah for death (Judges 20:12-13), but Benjamin refused, riding for their own no matter the crime. Some of our people do not know we had a civil war in Israel. This is it. Benjamin had twenty-six thousand swordsmen and seven hundred chosen left-handed slingers who could hit a hair and not miss, against four hundred thousand (Judges 20:18-35). You would think a landslide. But Benjamin cut down twenty-two thousand Israelites the first day and eighteen thousand the second. Then the whole nation wept, fasted and offered sacrifices at the house of God; this time Israel humbled itself, and through Phinehas at the ark the Lord promised them Benjamin the next day. No more going head up against slingers they could not beat straight on. They set an ambush, drew Benjamin out onto the highways by feigned flight, and burned Gibeah behind them as a signal; the Benjamites looked back and knew disaster had come. Twenty-five thousand one hundred fell that day (Judges 20:40-48). Six hundred fled to the rock of Rimmon; only that remnant kept the tribe from being wiped out. The Most High pushed the reset button on the tribe for what came out of Gibeah, and drastic measures had to be taken afterward so Benjamin could continue. That war is why Saul later called himself a Benjamite, of the smallest tribe of Israel (1 Samuel 9:21). There have been mighty and righteous Benjamites since, Paul chief among them; but we learn the history as it is written, and the book closes on the same key it turned on: there was no king in Israel, and every man did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25).

name: Ruth and Boaz
text: Ruth: cleaving to Naomi and joining herself under Israel and Israel’s God. Boaz: the law of the land conducted at the gate before witnesses, and love thy neighbour as thyself. In the days when the judges ruled, a Moabite widow would not go back to her people and to Chemosh, but bound herself to Naomi’s road, Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God. She came to Bethlehem with a mother in law who called herself Mara, gleaned in the field of Boaz, and called herself what she was to Israel, a stranger. Boaz went up to the gate, called ten elders as witnesses, carried out the law of inheritance and the law of the husband’s brother, and bought the field and Ruth with it, to keep the dead man’s name alive. Their son was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David. When the judges ruled, famine drove Elimelech of Bethlehem-judah to Moab with Naomi and their two sons, who married the Moabite women Orpah and Ruth and died there (Ruth 1:1-9). Were the sons of Israel supposed to marry the women of Moab? No. A Moabite was not to enter the congregation of the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:3), and Israel had already gone whoring with the daughters of Moab at Shittim (Numbers 25:1-2); but this was the era of no king, when every man did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25), and even in Ezra’s day the Moabites had not been put away (1 Esdras 8:69). Naomi prayed that each daughter in law find rest in a husband’s house. That rest is an inheritance; a good man leaves one to his children’s children, not a gang of bills (Proverbs 13:22). Behind her words stands the law of the husband’s brother, the widow’s firstborn carrying on the dead man’s name (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). We are not under that law now, having no land inheritance in this captivity, and it is wicked to pull that scripture today to get with a brother’s widow; but we are still to build a legacy and pass it down. Orpah went back to her people and her gods, to Chemosh (Numbers 21:29), for all the gods of the nations are idols (Psalms 96:5). Ruth clung to Naomi, her people and her God until death (Ruth 1:14-22). Does that make her an Israelite, or an heir of the kingdom? No. Both daughters in law knew exactly what they were, and Ruth never claimed otherwise. She joined herself under Israel and acknowledged her place, like the woman of Canaan who accepted the crumbs from the masters’ table (Matthew 15:24-28), and like Rahab, who knew the God of Israel was the true living God (Joshua 6:25). Naomi came home to Bethlehem calling herself Mara, bitter. Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Elimelech, who kept her with his young women and charged his men not to touch her (Ruth 2:1-16). She asked why he took notice of her, since she was a stranger, the word the law uses for the nations round about (Leviticus 25:44-46). Boaz had heard how she left her own parents and land for her mother in law, prayed that the Lord under whose wings she had taken refuge would reward her, and had handfuls dropped on purpose for her. Naomi then sought that same rest for her, sending her to lie at Boaz’s feet on the threshing floor (Ruth 3:1-18), where Ruth asked him to spread his skirt over her as near kinsman. The skirt is male clothing, the edge of the garment; she was asking the near kinsman to take her under his covering. He blessed her for not going after young men: even as a Moabitess she was keeping the customs of Israel, seeking her dead husband’s kinsman to keep his name in the earth. Boaz sat at the gate with the nearer kinsman and ten elders as witnesses, for the record (Ruth 4:1-12). The kinsman had first right to redeem Elimelech’s land, under the law that no inheritance pass from tribe to tribe (Numbers 36:5-9); a man could marry outside his own tribe but not outside the nation. But whoever took the land took the dead man’s wife with it, to keep his name on his inheritance, the duty of the husband’s brother and the loosed shoe. The kinsman declined and drew off his shoe, and Boaz bought all that was Elimelech’s and took Ruth, Mahlon’s widow, as his wife. What law was Boaz exercising in all of that? Loving his neighbour as himself (Leviticus 19:18). That is why he is mentioned in the scriptures. The elders blessed the marriage, naming Rachel and Leah who built the house of Israel and Pharez whom Tamar bore to Judah; in that blessing they were prophesying of David to come. Ruth bore a son, and Naomi took the child to her bosom and became his nurse (Ruth 4:13-22). Why? Because it is not the custom of Israel to allow a child to be raised under the hand of a heathen. A child’s first teacher is the mother; he takes on her ways, which is what Nehemiah found among the children of the wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, who could not speak the Jews’ language (Nehemiah 13:23-24). Ruth was brought in to keep Mahlon’s name alive in Israel, and she had no hand in raising the child; Naomi raised him so he would learn the ways of Israel. His name was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David, the line of Judah running down to the king and on to Christ (Matthew 1:5-6).

name: Hannah
text: Pouring out her soul before the Lord, vowing a son to him, and lending him to the Lord as long as he liveth. Elkanah had two wives; Peninnah had children, and Hannah had none, for the Lord had closed her womb, and her rival taunted her year after year at the house of the Lord until she wept and would not eat. In deep anguish she vowed that if the Lord gave her a son she would give him to the Lord for life, and no razor would touch his head. Eli thought she was drunk; she answered him, believed his word, went and ate, and was no longer downcast. She bore Samuel, weaned him, and brought him up to give him to the Lord, and the Lord gave her three sons and two daughters more. Elkanah of mount Ephraim had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah; Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none (1 Samuel 1:1-8). Each year at Shiloh he gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her, but the Lord had closed her womb, and her rival taunted her year after year until she wept and would not eat. The women of Israel have not changed one bit; even in the days of Samuel there was a sister vexing a barren woman and rubbing it in her face. Her husband asked why she wept, and whether he was not better to her than ten sons. At Shiloh Hannah prayed in anguish and wept, and vowed that if the Lord of hosts would look on her affliction and give her a son, she would give him to the Lord for life, and no razor would touch his head (1 Samuel 1:9-18). Sometimes you have to go before the Lord and just let it go, and that is what this sister did. That vow goes back to the law of the Nazarite, no razor on the head and the locks let grow (Numbers 6:5); the locks are hair braided so that it locks into place as it grows, the same seven locks on Samson’s head (Judges 16:13). Her lips moved but no sound came, so Eli took her for drunk and told her to put her wine away. She said she had drunk nothing but had poured out her soul before the Lord. Eli blessed her request, and she went and ate and was no longer downcast. She believed when she heard the word. And why was the petition granted? It was the will of the Most High for Samuel to come through Hannah, in His own time, and she was granted it because of what she did before she ever asked: we receive what we ask because we keep His commandments and do what pleases Him (1 John 3:22), and we can be confident that He hears whatever we ask according to His will (1 John 5:14-15). A lot of us pray for things the Lord has not given us; He knows what is best, so some things He keeps back, and we have to accept that. The Lord remembered her, and she bore a son and named him Samuel, because she had asked the Lord for him (1 Samuel 1:19-28). Hannah stayed home from the yearly sacrifice until the child was weaned, about three or four years old; the law required only the males to appear before the Lord (Deuteronomy 16:16). Then she brought him to Eli and said this was the child she had prayed for, and she was giving him to the Lord for as long as he lived. That is great faith, and she kept her end of it; Hannah was an upright and honest woman. A vow to God is to be paid without delay, and not excused afterward as a mistake (Ecclesiastes 5:4); let your yes be yes and your no be no (Matthew 5:37). Hannah’s prayer rejoices in the Lord’s salvation: the Lord alone is holy, and no rock compares with our God (1 Samuel 2:1-10). She warns the proud, for the Lord weighs actions: if it came out of your mouth, are you going to do it? Why call Him Lord and not do the things He says (Luke 6:46)? Men will give account in the day of judgment for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). The mighty are broken and the stumbling made strong; the barren woman bears seven while the mother of many wastes away, and she is speaking of herself there, with the Lord prophesying through her. The Lord puts to death and brings to life, sends down to the grave and raises up (Deuteronomy 32:39). He lifts the poor from the dust and the beggar from the dunghill to seat them with princes and give them a throne of glory. Why beggars? Because we are the ones always begging another race of people for reparations, for jobs, for services, instead of building with our own. And the dunghill is not one poor country; wherever we live in this captivity has been made a dunghill compared to what we came from, because we came from ruling. From the dunghill to the throne of glory is planet rulership. He gives strength to His king and lifts up His anointed, which is Christ. Samuel served before the Lord as a child, his mother bringing him a small robe each year, and the Lord gave Hannah three sons and two daughters more (1 Samuel 2:18-21).

name: Eli and his sons
text: Sons of Belial in the priest’s office, strong-arming the offering of the Lord and lying with the women at the tabernacle door; and a father who honoured his sons above the Lord. The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they did not know the Lord. Levites and priests in the house of the Lord, doing the work of the Lord, and yet they did not know Him, because they kept the commandments only on the surface where men could see. They sent a servant with a three-pronged fork to take the priest’s portion raw before the fat was burned, by force if the man refused, so that men despised the offering of the Lord; and they lay with the women who served at the door of the tabernacle. Eli said something, but he took no action. In one day both sons died, the ark was taken, and the old man fell backward from his seat and broke his neck. The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they did not know the Lord (1 Samuel 2:12-17). They were the devil. Priests in the house of the Lord, they still did not know Him, because they kept the commandments on the surface where you can see it and not true in their spirit. They looked the part, the fringes, the beard, showing up on the sabbath day, and their spirit was not right with the Lord. Do not let that be you, Israel. The custom was that while a man’s sacrifice was boiling, the priest’s servant plunged a three-pronged fork into the pot and the priest took whatever it brought up. That is how the Lord took care of Levi, who had no land inheritance among the tribes; He provided for them out of Israel’s sacrifices, so that they needed nothing. But these men would not wait. Before the fat was even burned the servant demanded raw meat, by force if the worshipper objected. So the young men’s sin was very great before the Lord, for men came to despise the Lord’s offering. Devils serving in the house of the Lord, strong-arming the offerings of the people. Eli was very old, and he heard everything his sons did to Israel, and that they lay with the women serving at the door of the tabernacle, the harlots hanging around the temple (1 Samuel 2:22-25). He asked why they did such things, and told them they were making the Lord’s people sin. The Levites were the leaders, so the people followed their actions, saying it must be all right, look at how they live in the temple. But the sons would not listen to their father, because the Lord meant to put them to death. Eli said something to his children, but he did not remove them from the priesthood. He did not go further than words, and you have to watch what happened to his children. A man of God reminded Eli that the Lord had chosen his father’s house out of all the tribes as priests and given it Israel’s offerings (1 Samuel 2:27-36). Why then did they scorn His sacrifices, and why did Eli honour his sons above Him? Take that into account: do you honour your children above what the Lord says to do? Can they do no wrong, even when they keep no commandments and never show up on the sabbath day while living grown under your roof? Joshua resolved that he and his house would serve the Lord (Joshua 24:15), and the Lord dealt with Abraham as He did knowing he would command his children and household after him to keep the way of the Lord (Genesis 18:19). The Lord had promised Eli’s house would serve before Him for ever, but now He said He would honour those who honour Him, and those who despise Him would be lightly esteemed. Lightly esteemed means He is not looking out for you: you are not thinking about me, so I am not thinking about you. He would cut off the strength of Eli’s house, so that no man in it would reach old age. Cutting off the arm is cutting off the strength, and the strength was his children. Why judge the generations after? Not because a son dies for his father; each son lives or dies by his own doings (Ezekiel 18:10-17). Because Eli did not reprove his sons, the generations after them were going to follow in the same footsteps. The sign was that his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, would both die on one day, and the Lord would raise up a faithful priest who would act according to His heart and mind. That is the same man we all have to be, not leaning on our own understanding or our own emotions (Proverbs 3:5). Whoever was left in Eli’s house would come begging for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread: Levi had no inheritance of land, and cut off from the priesthood there was nothing left but to beg. The Lord confirmed it to the child Samuel: Eli’s house was judged because his sons disgraced themselves and he did not stop them, and Eli accepted it as the Lord’s will (1 Samuel 3:13-18). When the Philistines fought Israel again, thirty thousand Israelite soldiers fell, the ark was taken, and both sons of Eli were killed (1 Samuel 4:10-22). When the news reached Shiloh that the ark was taken, Eli fell backward off his seat, broke his neck and died, for he was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years. His daughter in law named her newborn Ichabod, for the glory had departed from Israel.

name: The Philistines and the captured ark
text: Setting the ark of God in the house of Dagon, and carrying it from city to city seven months. The Philistines took the ark of God from Ebenezer to Ashdod and had the audacity to bring it into the house of Dagon and set it beside him. In the morning Dagon lay face down before the ark; they stood him up again, and the next morning his head and both hands lay broken off on the threshold. The hand of the Lord came down hard on Ashdod, then on Gath, then on Ekron, with emerods and deadly panic, until after seven months their own priests warned them not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh did. They sent the ark home with a trespass offering on a new cart. Israel had lost the ark by bringing it into the camp as a charm, with the two sons of Eli walking beside it under sentence; the Philistines heard the shout and were afraid, remembering what these Gods did to the Egyptians with all the plagues, but they steeled themselves, fought the harder, and took the ark (1 Samuel 4:3-11). The lesson Samuel would drive home later was already in the ground: there were still Israelites with idols among them, and the ark of the covenant among us does nothing so long as other gods are among us. The Philistines carried the ark from Eben-ezer to Ashdod and set it beside Dagon in his temple (1 Samuel 5:1-7). They had the audacity to set the ark of the God of Israel beside a fake god the Lord had already exposed once: Samson had pulled Dagon’s house down on the lords of the Philistines (Judges 16:29-30), and they rebuilt him. Capturing the ark did not make them masters of the God of Israel. He had judged His own people; He had not handed His power to an idol. Early next morning the people of Ashdod found Dagon face down on the ground before the ark of the Lord. This was no little souvenir you could knock over; it was a large statue, and nobody had been in there to touch it. They stood him up again, as if maybe the wind had blown a little harder, and the next morning he was down again, his head and both hands broken off on the threshold and only the stump left. No man did that. Then the hand of the Lord came down hard on Ashdod, striking them with emerods, what we know today as hemorrhoids; the Most High was not playing games with the heathen, and He struck His enemies from behind and put them to lasting shame (Psalms 78:66). Ashdod wanted the ark gone, and the lords of the Philistines moved it to Gath, where the Lord struck young and old with the same plague (1 Samuel 5:8-12). Moving it changed nothing; the affliction went with it. When it reached Ekron the people cried out that it had been brought to kill them, deadly panic filled the city, and its cry went up to heaven. The nations and their gods have no power against our God, and just as in Egypt, everybody got it. After seven months the Philistines asked their priests and diviners how to send it back, which is itself a thing Israel is forbidden to do (1 Samuel 6:1-9). The priests said not to send it empty but with a trespass offering, and then they would be healed. A trespass offering acknowledges that you did wrong: five golden emerods and five golden mice, one for each lord’s city, Ashdod, Gaza, Askelon, Gath and Ekron, images of the very things that ruined the land, giving glory to the God of Israel. Their own priests warned them out of Israel’s history not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh and the Egyptians did, who let the people go only after God had worked His wonders on them. They did not want to end up like Egypt. The test was a new cart drawn by two nursing cows that had never been yoked, with their calves shut up at home: if the cows went toward Beth-shemesh, the God of Israel had done this; if not, it was chance. The cows went straight to Beth-shemesh down the highway, lowing all the way and never veering, with the lords of the Philistines following to the border (1 Samuel 6:12-18). Cows with no yoke, separated from their calves, walking a straight line home to Israel: that settled it. The five lords went back to Ekron understanding it really was the Lord that had afflicted them. What Israel had to understand came later at Mizpeh, when Samuel told them that if they were returning to the Lord with all their hearts they must get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth and serve Him only, and He would deliver them from the Philistines; and when they did, the Lord thundered against the Philistines that day and routed them (1 Samuel 7:3-10).

name: The men of Beth-shemesh
text: Looking into the ark of the Lord. The people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley when they looked up and saw the ark coming home on the cart, and they rejoiced. The Levites took it down and set it on a great stone, the wood of the cart was split and the cows offered as a burnt offering. Then they got nosy and looked into the ark of the Lord, and He struck down fifty thousand and seventy men. The people mourned and asked who could survive in the presence of so holy a God, and sent for the men of Kirjath-jearim to come and take it up. The people of Beth-shemesh were reaping wheat in the valley, and when they looked up and saw the ark they rejoiced (1 Samuel 6:13-15). As soon as the ark crossed that border coming home it was rejoicing time in Israel. The cart stopped in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh beside a great stone; they split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the Lord, the Levites set the ark and the chest of gold objects on the great stone, and the five lords of the Philistines watched and went back to Ekron the same day. Then the men of Beth-shemesh looked into the ark of the Lord (1 Samuel 6:19-21). It was not only the other nations that had to keep discretion with the ark of the covenant. The law had been laid on Levi itself: they were not to go in and look at the holy things even for a moment, or they would die (Numbers 4:20). No matter what tribe a man came from, even Levi, it was forbidden to touch it or to look into it unless the Lord gave him authority. These men got too excited and got nosy, taking a peek to see what the writing of God looked like. He struck down the men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the ark of the Lord, fifty thousand and seventy men, and the people mourned the great slaughter (1 Samuel 6:19-21). Fifty thousand and seventy men, just for peeking. That shows us we have to have a level of discipline over our eyes; with these devices in every hand it is very easy to take a two second look at what you know you should not be looking at, so guard your eyes. And it answers those who say the Lord does not kill. He said it Himself: life and death, wounding and healing, are His, and no one escapes His hand (Deuteronomy 32:39). The Bible acknowledges the Most High as the king of terrors, before whom the wicked man’s confidence is torn away (Job 18:14); His works are awesome toward the children of men (Psalms 66:5), heathen and wicked Israelite alike. The men of Beth-shemesh asked who could survive in the presence of so holy a God, and where the ark should go from them, and sent messengers to Kirjath-jearim to come and take it. The men of Kirjath-jearim brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill and consecrated Eleazar his son to keep it (1 Samuel 7:1-4): appointed custody, and no crowd about it. The ark stayed in Kirjath-jearim a long time, twenty years, and all Israel mourned after the Lord. Having the ark back did not finish the nation’s return. That came when Samuel told all Israel that if they were returning to the Lord with all their hearts they must get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth, set their hearts on the Lord and serve Him only, and He would deliver them from the Philistines; and Israel put away the Baals and Ashtaroth and served the Lord only. That is repentance.

name: Samuel
text: Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth: telling Eli every whit and hiding nothing; and an accounting no man could contradict, whose ox have I taken?. Given to the Lord as a child, he served before Eli in days when the word of the Lord was precious and visions were rare. The Lord came and stood and called him by name, and the child did not yet know the Lord until Eli taught him how to answer. His first test as a judge was to carry a judgment against the house that raised him, and he told Eli all of it and held nothing back. The Lord made every one of his words come to pass; he judged Israel all the days of his life, established the kingdom, and by his faithfulness was found a true prophet. The child Samuel served the Lord under Eli when the word of the Lord was precious and visions were rare (1 Samuel 3:8-14). Precious means the Lord was not dealing with everybody; not with the priests, and there were no prophets around saying what the Lord had spoken. Twice the Lord called and the child ran to Eli, because Samuel did not yet know the Lord. He had been in the house of the Lord since he was weaned, and he still did not know the Lord. That goes in on those playing church with their children: just because your children come and sit and listen does not mean they know the Lord; they are there because you brought them. Your job is the training, raising a child in the path he should keep (Proverbs 22:6); the revealing belongs to the Most High, for only the Son knows the Father, and He reveals Him to whom He chooses (Matthew 11:27). The third time Eli understood, and taught the child to answer that the Lord’s servant was listening. The Lord came and stood and called as before, Samuel, Samuel. He did not simply call out of the heavens; He came down and stood by him. Samuel could not see Him, but he heard Him, and that is what happens in the spirit to all of us. The Lord is merciful with us even in this wickedness, standing at the door and knocking, calling numerous times until we wake up (Revelation 3:20). Those who heed His correction receive His spirit and His words; those who refuse, and the day comes when they call and He will not answer (Proverbs 1:23). The word given to the child was a judgment against the house that raised him: Eli’s house judged for ever, its sin beyond the reach of any sacrifice. When the Lord is angry, He is angry; do not sin a sin so great that it cannot be prayed for. In the morning Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision, but Eli charged him to hide nothing, and Samuel told him all of it (1 Samuel 3:18-21). He was going to be a judge of Israel, and this was his first test: do not sugarcoat what the Lord has said, and do not trim your words to seek love. Years later he put his own record before the nation, and the people agreed he had taken nothing from anyone (1 Samuel 12:3-4). Nor did he abandon them: he would count it a sin against the Lord to stop praying for them, and he would keep teaching them the good and right way (1 Samuel 12:23). Marinate on that. For a leader of Israel, ceasing to pray for the nation is itself a transgression. Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him. What Samuel said, it came to pass. All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew he was confirmed as a prophet of the Lord (1 Samuel 3:18-21). At Mizpeh he told Israel that if they were returning to the Lord with all their hearts they must get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth and serve Him only, and they did (1 Samuel 7:3-6). That is repentance. When the Philistine lords came up and Israel was afraid, this time the people did not run for the ark; they begged Samuel not to stop crying to the Lord for them, because they knew the earnest prayer of a righteous man is powerful and effective (James 5:16). Samuel offered a lamb and cried to the Lord for Israel, and as the Philistines closed in, the Lord thundered against them and routed them (1 Samuel 7:8-13). That was no regular thunder; that was the Lord entering the battle Himself. They had repented and put away the false gods, and the prayer of a righteous man reached His ears. Samuel set up a stone and named it Ebenezer, and the Philistines were held back all his days. He judged Israel all his life, circling each year through Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpeh and home to Ramah (1 Samuel 7:15-17). That yearly circuit is leadership making its rounds, establishing the people and coming back to check on them, as Paul went back to visit the brethren in every city (Acts 15:36). Ecclesiasticus remembers him as beloved of his Lord, proved a true prophet by his faithfulness (Ecclesiasticus 46:13-15). Faithfulness translates loyalty. He came up under Eli, watched Eli’s sons go wicked, watched Eli die and the nation take losses, and stayed loyal to the Most High. Prayer is a superpower, and that is how our forefathers rolled, from Moses to Samuel all the way to Christ. What was written before was written to teach us (Romans 15:4).

name: Joel and Abiah, the sons of Samuel
text: Turning aside after lucre, taking bribes, and perverting judgment in the seat of the judge. When Samuel was old he made his sons judges over Israel in Beersheba, and they did not follow his ways: they chased dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice. The elders of Israel used them as the reason to demand a king like all the nations. No sentence upon the two men is recorded anywhere in the chapter; the sentence that is recorded fell on the nation that used them as an excuse. When Samuel was old he made his sons judges over Israel, Joel the firstborn and Abiah the second, judging in Beersheba. But his sons did not follow his ways: they chased dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:1-3). The law for the judges in the gates was plain. They were to judge the people justly, not twist judgment, not show partiality, and take no gift, because a bribe blinds even the wise and corrupts the cause of the righteous (Deuteronomy 16:18-20; Exodus 23:8). That gift is what goes into the pocket of a judge and comes back out as a perverted sentence against the man who could not pay. We see that same thing going on now in this political climate, and even in the church system. It is why the churches will not teach us who we are or teach the commandments of the Most High, and why, when riots and unrest break out, it is those same pastors who are sent out to calm the people down. The contrast with their father was public and undeniable. Samuel could stand before all Israel and ask whose ox or donkey he had taken, whom he had cheated, and from whom he had taken a bribe, and the whole congregation answered that he had taken nothing from anyone (1 Samuel 12:3-4). The sons made the seat of judgment serve their own increase. Then all the elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah, saying he was old and his sons did not follow his ways, and asking him to appoint a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-5). Your sons are not righteous like you, so instead of them judging us, give us a ruler like the other nations have. The corruption was real and the complaint was real; the remedy the people insisted on is its own case, entered next, because the Lord told Samuel that they had not rejected him but had rejected the Lord as their king (1 Samuel 8:7). No penalty upon Joel or Abiah is recorded. Their own end is not written, and the silence does not turn bribery into righteousness. If a man sees the poor oppressed and justice violently perverted in a province, he is not to be astonished, for a higher official watches over the high one, and One higher still is over them both (Ecclesiastes 5:8). What the record does show is the damage: an office handed down without the character the office requires, a nation that had been delivered by judges for four hundred years handed its excuse, and a demand made at Ramah that cost Israel far more than two corrupt men in Beersheba ever took in bribes.

name: Israel asking for a king
text: Rejecting the Lord, that he should not reign over them, to be like all the nations. The elders came to Samuel at Ramah asking for a king to judge them like all the nations. It displeased Samuel, and the Lord told him the people had not rejected the prophet but had rejected Him as their king. Samuel told them the ways of the king who would reign over them, that he would take their sons, their daughters, their fields and a tenth of their grain, and that they would cry out in that day and the Lord would not answer them; and they answered that they would have a king anyway. The ways of the king came to pass under Solomon and Rehoboam, and the door of the covenant was left open to the nation still. The elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah, saying he was old and his sons did not follow his ways, and asked for a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-9). Moses had prophesied it: Israel would come into the land and want a king like the nations around them, and the king was to be one the Lord chose, from among their brethren, never a foreigner (Deuteronomy 17:14-15). Moses was shown from the beginning to the end; he saw Israel rejecting the Lord and wrote it down for us to read. Where do we see it today? Voting. We say the same thing when we vote, looking to a ruler like the nations instead of to the Most High, and the answer we hear is that this one is the lesser of two evils, when they are both evil. We reject Him also by keeping their holidays and walking in their ways; we have made a covenant with them. It displeased Samuel, and he prayed; the Lord told him to listen to the people, for they had not rejected him but had rejected the Lord as their king, as they had done ever since Egypt, forsaking Him for other gods. Joshua had warned us about this at Shechem, where Israel made the covenant with its own mouth and became witnesses against itself that it had chosen the Lord (Joshua 24:21-22). Asking for a king was breaking the choice we ourselves made. Christ gave the same picture in the nobleman who went away to receive a kingdom, whose citizens sent word after him that they refused to have him as their king (Luke 19:12-14). The spirit that said set a king over us is the same spirit that says it of Christ. Samuel told the people what the king would do (1 Samuel 8:11-20). He would take their sons for his chariots and horsemen, to plough his ground, reap his harvest and make his weapons; their daughters as perfumers, cooks and bakers; the best of their fields, vineyards and olive groves for his servants; a tenth of their grain, vineyards and flocks; their servants, their finest young men and their donkeys for his work, and they would be his slaves. And they would cry out in that day because of the king they had chosen, and the Lord would not answer them. The repeated word is take. Still the people refused to listen and insisted on a king, to be like all the nations, with a king to judge them and fight their battles. Samuel repeated the people’s words to the Lord, and the Lord told him to give them a king (1 Samuel 8:19-22). He gave them exactly what they asked for. At Mizpeh Samuel set the choice before them once more in the Lord’s words: He had brought Israel out of Egypt and rescued them from every kingdom that oppressed them, and that day they had rejected the God who saved them from all their troubles and demanded a king (1 Samuel 10:18-19). Remember what they had just come out of. Every time one of the judges rose up and delivered us from oppression, we got right during the life of that judge, and when the judge died we went right back into our falling; and now they wanted a man on a throne in place of the God who had done all the delivering. It all came to pass as Samuel said. Solomon conscripted thirty thousand men from all Israel and sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand, a month there and two months home (1 Kings 5:13-14). Rehoboam made the yoke heavier still, rejecting the counsel of the old men for the young men he grew up with and answering the people harshly (1 Kings 12:13-14). We rejected the Lord and wanted a king like all the other nations, and this is what we got, and look at our condition now, ruler after ruler and nothing getting any better for us. At the wheat harvest Samuel called on the Lord for thunder and rain on a day they expected clear skies, and the people, terrified, begged him to pray for them so they would not die, for they had added to all their sins the evil of asking for a king (1 Samuel 12:14-19). Yet the door was left open. If they would fear the Lord, serve Him, obey His voice and not rebel, both they and their king would continue following the Lord; if not, His hand would be against them as it was against their fathers. A crown did not move Israel outside the covenant. The nation still had to obey the King whose rule it had tried to trade away.

name: King Saul
text: Offering the burnt offering himself at Gilgal; sparing Agag and the best of the spoil; and stubbornness, which is as iniquity and idolatry. The first king of Israel began to show his simplicity at Gilgal: told to wait seven days until Samuel came, he panicked when the people scattered, offered the burnt offering that was not his office to offer, and answered the prophet with excuses. Sent to wipe out Amalek, he spared Agag and the best of the flocks, greeted Samuel claiming he had carried out the Lord’s command while the sheep were bleating in the prophet’s ears, and laid it on the people. Obeying counts for more than sacrifice, and rebellion ranks with witchcraft. The kingdom was torn from him that day, and it ended on mount Gilboa. Chapter thirteen is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the proof he was not fit to be king. Samuel had told him to wait seven days at Gilgal (1 Samuel 10:8). When the Philistines massed, the chosen nation hid in caves and pits, though the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for them; the spirit God gives is not fear but power, love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:7). With Samuel not yet come and the people scattering, Saul offered the burnt offering himself, Samuel’s office, not his, and Samuel arrived as he finished (1 Samuel 13:8-14). Brothers do the same today: leadership said ten o’clock, it is five past, so we go home. Wait as you were instructed; the Lord may be testing your patience, and a man is not to rush in time of trouble (Ecclesiasticus 2:2). Then came the excuses: the people scattering, Samuel late, the Philistines gathering. That is the pattern of the man; he never holds himself accountable, he always deflects, going out to meet the man before he gets to where he messed up. Samuel told him he had acted foolishly and his kingdom would not last, for the Lord had sought a man after His own heart (Acts 13:22). Disobeying the prophet’s instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. Then Saul was sent to destroy Amalek completely for what it did to Israel on the way out of Egypt (1 Samuel 15:3), the war sworn from generation to generation (Exodus 17:16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Christianity says forgive and forget; the Most High said remember. But Saul spared Agag and the best of the flocks, destroying only what was worthless (1 Samuel 15:9), killing what looked like it deserved killing so he could say he did some killing. Saul did most of it, and the Lord counted that as not carrying out His commands at all (1 Samuel 15:10-11). Whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given to you. At Carmel he raised a monument to himself, then claimed he had obeyed while sheep bleated nearby, and blamed the people, as at Gilgal. The Lord’s commands are kept with nothing added or taken away (Deuteronomy 12:32). Still insisting he had obeyed, he boasted of bringing back Agag; a man who justifies himself is condemned by his own mouth (Job 9:20). Samuel made it plain: the Lord delights in obedience more than in burnt offerings (1 Samuel 15:22). Spoil taken against His will made the offering ridiculous; the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, worse when brought with evil intent (Proverbs 21:27).
