Rebellion ranks with witchcraft and stubbornness with idolatry, and because Saul rejected the Lord’s word, the Lord rejected him as king (1 Samuel 15:23). A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway, and according to this verse that rebellion is witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction is the Lord’s commandment carried by leadership, and stubbornness against it puts what I want before what God wants. The confession finally came and was still not sincere: he feared the people and did what they said (1 Samuel 15:24). Fear of man is a trap, but whoever trusts the Lord is safe (Proverbs 29:25); a leader in fear of his people is being led by them. Saul tore Samuel’s robe, and Samuel told him the Lord had torn the kingdom from him that day for a better man; God does not lie or change His mind (Numbers 23:19). Then he asked to be honoured before the elders anyway, hiding the demotion: the spirit of vanity, caught up in a title and forgetting it came for pleasing the Lord. Samuel mourned for him, for he had seen his potential. The Spirit of the Lord left Saul and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him (1 Samuel 16:14), and instead of repenting he went down into envy of David. It all traces back to bashfulness: he looked in the mirror and saw a kitty cat where God had said there was a lion, self-willed because he was afraid, and would not ask, wait or take counsel with the prophet at his side. A man can ruin his own soul through bashfulness and bring himself down by respecting persons (Ecclesiasticus 20:22). At the end, with the Lord silent, he consulted a medium, the very thing he had driven out of the land, and heard that he and his sons would die the next day (1 Samuel 28:19). They fell on mount Gilboa, Saul on his own sword (1 Samuel 31:4-6), dying for his unfaithfulness and for seeking a medium, and the kingdom went to David (1 Chronicles 10:13).

name: David
text: A man after the Lord’s own heart: twice sparing the Lord’s anointed, leaving vengeance with the Lord, and repenting when he fell. Samuel named the replacement at Gilgal before he had ever met him: the Lord had sought a man after His own heart and commanded him to be captain over His people. Twice Saul was delivered into David’s hand, in the cave at Engedi and in the trench at Hachilah, and twice David would not stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed, leaving the judgment with the Most High. He reverenced the man who was hunting him, and he judged the men who shed blood in his name. When he fell he had godly sorrow and rose again; his one great fall is its own case, and this is the rest. Samuel told Saul at Gilgal that his kingdom would not continue, because the Lord had sought a man after His own heart and commanded him to be captain over His people (1 Samuel 13:14); the prophet said it without ever having met the replacement, and the apostle repeated the testimony, that the Lord had found in David the son of Jesse a man after His own heart who would fulfil all His will (Acts 13:22). What that heart looks like is shown while Saul hunted him. Saul took three thousand chosen men to the rocks of the wild goats and went into a cave to cover his feet, which is the scripture’s way of saying he was in there relieving himself, and David and his men were staying in the sides of it (1 Samuel 24:2-13). David rose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily, the corner of a man’s garment where the fringes are attached, and afterward his heart smote him even for that, and he stayed his servants, saying the Lord forbid that he should do such a thing to his master, the Lord’s anointed (1 Samuel 24:4-7). Then he went out after him, called him his lord the king, bowed with his face to the earth, laid the proof in his hand, and left the case with the Most High to judge between them, since his own hand would not touch him. Saul wept and admitted that David was more righteous, having repaid him good for evil, and that he knew well David would surely be king (1 Samuel 24:16-20). A king shall reign in righteousness (Isaiah 32:1); that is what Saul was acknowledging. It happened again in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul lay sleeping in the trench with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster and Abner and the people round about him, and Abishai asked leave to pin him to the earth with one stroke and not need a second. David answered that no man could stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be guiltless; as the Lord lived, the Lord would smite him, or his day would come to die, or he would go down into battle and perish (1 Samuel 26:7-11). These were warriors and they were itching for it, but David took the bigger position: this man was chosen before me, so let God deal with him. Saul had men around him whispering that David thought himself better and wanted the throne,, and he fed into it instead of saying that David was a man of God. David cried from the hill that if the Lord had stirred Saul up against him, let Him accept an offering, but if it was the children of men, let them be cursed before the Lord, and Saul confessed that he had played the fool and erred exceedingly (1 Samuel 26:19-21). The same spirit met Shimei on the road out of Jerusalem, and David let him curse, saying it might be that the Lord would look on his affliction and repay him good for the cursing that day (2 Samuel 16:10-12). The Lord built him a house: his house and his kingdom would be established for ever before Him, and his throne established for ever (2 Samuel 7:16). When a stranger claimed the crown of Saul, and when two captains carried in the head of Ish-bosheth, he did not accept wickedness done in his name; both were put to death for taking a life not ordained of the Lord nor commanded by the king (2 Samuel 1:14-16; 2 Samuel 4:9-12), because all things are to be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40). When Nathan told him he was the man, he confessed that he had sinned against the Lord (2 Samuel 12:13), and his sorrow was the godly sorrow that works repentance to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10); a just man falls seven times and rises up again (Proverbs 24:16). Fleeing from Absalom he sent the ark back into the city in faith: if he found favour in the eyes of the Lord, He would bring him again to see it, and if not, let Him do what seemed good (2 Samuel 15:25-26). The Lord took away his sins and exalted his horn for ever, giving him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel (Ecclesiasticus 47:11). The throne stands on the stipulation he gave Solomon at the last, to keep the charge of the Lord his God and walk in His ways and keep His statutes and commandments as written in the law of Moses (1 Kings 2:3-4); and the throne of his father David is the one given to Christ, whose kingdom shall have no end (Luke 1:32-33).

name: Saul’s rash oath, and the people at the blood
text: A strange oath that distressed the army; the people eating flesh with the blood; the king ready to kill the son who had wrought the salvation. Jonathan and his armourbearer climbed a rock face on their hands and feet and took a Philistine garrison, and the Lord sent a trembling through the host until the Philistines turned their swords on one another. In the middle of that deliverance Saul bound the army with a curse on any man who ate before evening, and the men of Israel were distressed. Jonathan, who had not heard the charge, tasted honey and argued against the order, and the famished people fell on the spoil and ate flesh with the blood. When the lot fell on Jonathan the king swore he should die, and the people would not let him kill the man who had wrought with God that day. Jonathan told the young man who bore his armour to come over to the garrison of the uncircumcised, since it might be that the Lord would work for them, for there is no restraint on the Lord to save by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6). The Most High put that spirit on him; He loves to show His power by having a small number defeat a very large number, and that is why it will be the hundred and forty-four thousand taking over the whole world. Judas Maccabeus said the same thing, that with the God of heaven it is all one to deliver with a great multitude or a small company (1 Maccabees 3:18-19). Jonathan climbed up on his hands and his feet with his armourbearer after him, and that first slaughter was about twenty men within half an acre of land. Some hold a doctrine that Jonathan was a homosexual; scaling a rock face to rush a garrison two deep is a bold, manly act of war that most men are not cut out for. There was trembling in the host and in the field, the earth quaked, the Philistines went on beating down one another, the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines turned back to Israel, and the men who had hidden in mount Ephraim followed hard after them; so the Lord saved Israel that day (1 Samuel 14:13-23). In the middle of that deliverance the king adjured the people with a curse on any man who ate food before evening, until he was avenged on his enemies, and the men of Israel were distressed that day (1 Samuel 14:24-30). A vow is not a light thing: a man that vows a vow to the Lord is not to break his word, but to do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth (Numbers 30:2), and it is better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay, for God has no pleasure in fools (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). They came into a wood where honey dropped on the ground, and no man put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath; but Jonathan had not been there when the charge went out, and he dipped the end of his rod in a honeycomb, and his eyes were enlightened. He said his father had troubled the land, and argued that the slaughter of the Philistines would have been far greater if the people had eaten freely of the spoil. The scripture says to fear the Lord and the king and to meddle not with them that are given to change (Proverbs 24:21); the king’s order was folly, but the talk against it led the people into a worse thing. Very faint, they flew on the spoil, took sheep, oxen and calves, slew them on the ground, and ate them with the blood (1 Samuel 14:29-32). When they told Saul that the people were sinning against the Lord, he answered that they had transgressed, had a great stone rolled to him, and made every man bring his ox and his sheep and kill them there and eat, and not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood; and he built an altar to the Lord, the first altar he ever built to Him (1 Samuel 14:31-35). Then he proposed to go down after the Philistines by night, and when he asked counsel of God, God did not answer him that day. When the Lord ignores a man the scriptures give only one reason: if a man regards iniquity in his heart the Lord will not hear him (Psalms 66:18), and our iniquities have separated between us and our God, and our sins have hid His face so that He will not hear (Isaiah 59:2). Saul swore by the Lord who saves Israel that the guilty man would surely die, even if it were his own son; the lot fell between him and Jonathan, and Jonathan was taken. Jonathan said he had only tasted a little honey with the end of the rod in his hand, and Saul swore that God should do so and more to him if Jonathan did not surely die (1 Samuel 14:36-46). The people would not have it: should the man who had wrought this great salvation in Israel die? Not one hair of his head would fall to the ground, for he had wrought with God that day, and so the people rescued him. Weigh it as they weighed it: yes, he crossed the order, but he had just saved all their lives. Judgment without mercy comes on the man who has shown no mercy, and mercy rejoices against judgment (James 2:13).

name: Agag king of the Amalekites
text: The sword that made women childless; and the sworn war with Amalek from generation to generation. Amalek, Esau’s grandson, was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt, and he did not meet the mighty men in front: he struck the rearmost, the feeble, when Israel was faint and weary, and he did not fear God. The Lord swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation, and hundreds of years later He sent Saul to finish it. Saul spared the king, presuming to find something good in what God had condemned. Agag came to Samuel delicately, saying surely the bitterness of death was past, and the old prophet hewed him in pieces before the Lord at Gilgal. Then came Amalek and fought with Israel in Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). Amalek was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt, and he was Esau’s grandson, born to Eliphaz by Timna the concubine, and a duke in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:12). Moses gave the detail of the attack, and it was written to stir Israel up: remember what Amalek did by the way, how he met them and smote the hindmost, all that were feeble behind, when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God; and when the Lord gave them rest from all their enemies round about they were to blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven and not forget it (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). In a caravan the strong men walk in front; at the back are the elderly, the women, the babies and the lame. Amalek did not come at the front; he came up behind and waited until Israel was worn out. The Lord told Moses to write it in a book for a memorial and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, and He swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exodus 17:14-16). God does not forget; we do. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High said remember, and the law against bearing a grudge is toward the children of our own people, not toward the nations He has sworn against (Leviticus 19:18). Hundreds of years later the Lord sent Saul by Samuel, saying that He remembered what Amalek did to Israel when they came up from Egypt, and commanding him to go and smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had and spare them not (1 Samuel 15:1-3). The generation under that sword had not personally done the deed in the wilderness, which answers the argument heard today, that I never did anything to you; the Most High Himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. He also discriminates righteously: the Kenites were told to get down from among the Amalekites, because they had shown kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fatlings and the lambs, and destroyed only what was vile and refuse (1 Samuel 15:6-9). Agag was an Edomite king out of the line of the dukes of Esau, and Saul presumed to find something good in what God had condemned; he kept the one they liked, as men today keep the one Edomite at work who smiles at them. Agag’s own charge is written into his sentence: his sword had made women childless. Samuel called for Agag the king of the Amalekites to be brought to him, and Agag came to him delicately, saying surely the bitterness of death was past (1 Samuel 15:32). With Saul under rebuke he figured nobody was angry at the Amalekites any more and he was safe. Never trust an enemy; though he humble himself and go crouching, his wickedness is as rusting brass, so take good heed and beware of him (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-11). Saul trusted the enemy; Samuel did not. The prophet told him that as his sword had made women childless, so his mother would be childless among women, and he hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal, measure for measure, finishing the commandment himself (1 Samuel 15:33). Samuel followed instructions; Saul played games. Because the line was not finished, in Esther’s day Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite rose out of that same seed and sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus (Esther 3:1); the war truly runs from generation to generation, and Esau keeps the records while we forget. Slaughter is prepared for the children of the wicked for the iniquity of their fathers, that the name and the remnant be cut off (Isaiah 14:21), and the same seed now says it is Jews and is not, but is the synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9). Understand the frame: as much as lies in us, we live peaceably with all men (Romans 12:18), we lay hands on no one, and we neither incite nor condone violence. The day when the man who rewards Babylon as she served us is called happy has not come (Psalms 137:8); it belongs to the return of the Lord, and it is His judgment written in His book, not a licence for any man’s hand now. The war continues, and it is more spiritual than ever.

name: Goliath of Gath
text: Defying the armies of the living God, morning and evening, forty days. Out of the Philistine camp came a champion six cubits and a span high, in a coat of mail of five thousand shekels of brass, with a spear like a weaver’s beam and a man to carry his shield, and for forty days morning and evening he defied the armies of Israel and demanded a man. Saul and all Israel were dismayed and greatly afraid, measuring his height and his reach in a carnal spirit. A shepherd sent with bread and cheese for his brothers asked who this uncircumcised Philistine was, that he should defy the armies of the living God. He came to him in the name of the Lord of hosts, and took his head off with the giant’s own sword. The Philistines gathered their armies and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, and Israel pitched by the valley of Elah, the two hosts on mountains on either side with a valley between them. Out of their camp came a champion named Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span high, in a helmet of brass, a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels of brass, greaves of brass, a target of brass between his shoulders, and a spear with a staff like a weaver’s beam, and one bearing a shield went before him. He cried to the armies of Israel to choose a man and send him down: if that man prevailed the Philistines would serve Israel, and if he prevailed Israel would serve them; and he defied the armies of Israel that day and demanded a man to fight (1 Samuel 17:4-11). When Saul and all Israel heard those words they were dismayed and greatly afraid. They were in a carnal spirit, measuring his height, his armour and his reach. God has not given us the spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7); who is a man of the living God, that he should be afraid of a man who shall die and be made as grass? (Isaiah 51:12). The law of battle was in the book: when they went out and saw horses and chariots and a people more than they, they were not to be afraid, for the Lord their God was with them (Deuteronomy 20:1). The Philistine drew near morning and evening and presented himself forty days, and the men of Israel fled from him and were sore afraid, David’s three eldest brothers among them, the same three the Lord had refused at Bethlehem. Who will rise up for the Lord against the evildoers? (Psalms 94:16). That is the spirit the Most High looks for. David, sent on an errand with corn and loaves for his brethren, heard the same words and asked what would be done for the man who killed this Philistine and took away the reproach from Israel, for who was this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:23-26). The soldiers themselves did not understand that they were the armies of the living God; a sheep keeper on an errand knew it. The Most High calls the children of Israel His armies (Exodus 7:4). Saul told him he was but a youth against a man of war from his youth; no man is to despise a young man for his youth, who is to be an example of the believers in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith and in purity (1 Timothy 4:12). David gave his resume: when a lion or a bear took a lamb out of the flock he went after it, smote it and delivered the lamb out of its mouth, and the Lord who delivered him from the paw of the lion and the bear would deliver him from the hand of this Philistine. He played with lions as with kids and with bears as with lambs (Ecclesiasticus 47:3). Saul armed him with his own armour and David put it off, because he had not proved it, and took his staff, five smooth stones out of the brook, and his sling; what he put on instead was the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6:16-17). The Philistine disdained him and cursed him by his gods, and David answered that he came with a sword and a spear and a shield, but David came in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom he had defied; that day the Lord would deliver him into his hand, so that all the earth would know there was a God in Israel, and all that assembly would know that

name: Jonathan
text: Stripping himself of his robe for the man whom the Lord would make king; standing between his father and David’s innocent blood; thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee. Jonathan’s soul was knit with David’s, and he loved him as his own soul; the same word describes the church, hearts knit together in love. The king’s son and heir stripped off his own robe and gave it to the shepherd, with his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle. He warned David of his father’s intent, spoke good of him to Saul and had a javelin cast at him for it, and went out to him in the wood at Ziph to strengthen his hand in God. His loyalty exceeded his own desires, and the kindness he asked for reached his lame son at the king’s table. When David had made an end of speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul; they made a covenant, and Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him and gave it to David, with his garments, even to his sword, his bow and his girdle (1 Samuel 18:1-4). Souls being knit is not speaking of anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church, whose hearts are comforted by being knit together in love (Colossians 2:2), and the body, knit together by joints and bands (Colossians 2:19). Note the estate of the two men: Jonathan was the prince and the heir, David was an armourbearer out of Bethlehem, and a true friend does not rejoice in standing higher. A faithful friend is a strong defence and the medicine of life, and he that has found such a one has found a treasure (Ecclesiasticus 6:14). Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants that they should kill David; the Philistines could not get him, so now the king wanted Israelites to kill an Israelite. But Jonathan delighted much in David and told him plainly that his father sought to kill him, and told him to take heed until the morning, abide in a secret place and hide himself (1 Samuel 19:1-7). Jonathan would have been next in line for the throne, and you would think his loyalty lay with his father, but he saw that the spirit was not on his father, it was on his brother David. Do not be ashamed to defend a friend, nor hide from him in the time of his trouble (Ecclesiasticus 22:25). He spoke good of David to Saul: let not the king sin against his servant, who had not sinned against him and whose works toward him had been very good, for he put his life in his hand and slew the Philistine and the Lord wrought a great salvation for all Israel, which Saul saw and rejoiced at; so why sin against innocent blood and slay David without a cause? The innocent and righteous are not to be slain (Exodus 23:7), and hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-17). Saul listened and swore that David would not be slain, and Jonathan brought him back. At the new moon, when David’s seat was empty and Jonathan covered for him, Saul’s anger was kindled against his own son, telling him that as long as the son of Jesse lived on the ground neither he nor his kingdom would be established, and he cast a javelin at him to smite him; by that Jonathan knew it was determined of his father to slay David (1 Samuel 20:30-33). He would not buy a throne with his friend’s blood. When David was hunted in the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan rose up and went to him into the wood and strengthened his hand in God, telling him not to fear, for the hand of Saul his father would not find him, and David would be king over Israel and Jonathan would be next to him, and Saul his father knew it too (1 Samuel 23:16-17). Jonathan had asked that the kindness of the Lord continue toward his house and never be cut off from it (1 Samuel 20:12-17). The covenant outlived him. The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons and slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua on mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2). David lamented over them in the spirit, a eulogy and a prophecy: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives and in their death they were not divided, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions; and he was distressed for his brother Jonathan, whose love to him was wonderful, passing the love of women (2 Samuel 1:23-26). There is a friend that sticks closer than a brother (Proverbs 18:24); that is what Jonathan was. When David was king he asked whether any of the house of Saul was left, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, fetched Mephibosheth, lame on both his feet, out of Lo-debar, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually (2 Samuel 9:1-13). When seven of Saul’s house were delivered to the Gibeonites, the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan because of the oath of the Lord that was between them (2 Samuel 21:7). Jonathan did not live to stand next to David, but his bones were gathered with his father’s into the sepulchre of Kish (2 Samuel 21:12-14), and the kindness he asked for was still being served at the king’s table years after he died.

name: Saul and Doeg at Nob
text: Slaughter of the priests of the Lord on an Edomite’s report. Saul had set an Edomite over his servants. Doeg reported that Ahimelech had enquired of the Lord for David, given him the hallowed bread and the sword of Goliath, and Saul, who by then read any loyalty to David as treason against himself, would not hear the priest’s defence. The king’s own footmen would not put forth their hand against the priests of the Lord, so he got the Edomite to do what his own men would not: Doeg slew eighty-five men that wore a linen ephod and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword. David wrote the Edomite’s sentence in a psalm. David came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest, three days out in the field and fearful of king Saul, and the priest gave him hallowed bread, for there was no bread there but the shewbread that had been taken from before the Lord (1 Samuel 21:6-7). Christ recounted this very history when the Pharisees challenged his disciples for plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day, asking whether they had never read what David did when he had need and was an hungred (Mark 2:25-26); precept it in your bibles if it is not there already. A certain servant of Saul was detained before the Lord that day: Doeg, an Edomite, the chief of Saul’s herdmen (1 Samuel 21:7). The scriptures tell us never to trust an enemy (Ecclesiasticus 12:10), yet here is a king of Israel with an Edomite set over his servants. Doeg answered and reported that he had seen the son of Jesse come to Nob to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, who enquired of the Lord for him, gave him victuals, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine (1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul sent for Ahimelech and all his father’s house, the priests in Nob, and charged them with conspiracy; Ahimelech answered that no one among all the king’s servants was as faithful as David, the king’s son in law, who went at his bidding and was honourable in his house, and that it was hardly the first time he had enquired of God for him, and the king should impute nothing to his servant nor to all his father’s house (1 Samuel 22:13-16). Saul had become so desperate that he read loyalty to David as betrayal of himself, because he wanted everybody against David. That is no new thing under the sun: men put slander out to turn whole congregations against a man they have never sat down with and broken bread with. The king told the footmen standing about him to turn and slay the priests of the Lord, because their hand also was with David, but the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the Lord. So the king said to Doeg, turn and fall upon the priests; and Doeg the Edomite turned and fell upon them and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod, and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, oxen, asses and sheep (1 Samuel 22:13-19). Saul was able to get the Edomite to do what his own men would not do. Go back to Genesis and see the spirit that has been on this man from the beginning: Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing, and comforted himself with the purpose of slaying his brother (Genesis 27:41). That comfort in killing is the same thing seen in Doeg; when Saul appointed him to the task you can best believe he found pleasure in it. Eighty-five priests and a whole city destroyed because they showed affinity to David, all out of hatred and envy. The servant is not greater than his lord, and if they persecuted Christ they will persecute us (John 15:20), and not only by the heathen but by our own kinsmen.

name: Nabal
text: Railing on the Lord’s anointed and his men who had been a wall to his shepherds; who is David?. A very great man in Maon, three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, churlish and evil in his doings, and such a son of Belial that a man could not speak to him. David’s men had been a wall to his shepherds by night and by day, and at sheepshearing David sent ten young men in peace to ask for whatever came to his hand. Nabal asked who David was, and said there were many servants nowadays that break away from their masters. His wife turned the sword back on the road; when the wine had gone out of him and she told him, his heart died within him, and about ten days later the Lord smote him. There was a very great man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel, three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel. His name was Nabal, and his wife was Abigail, a woman of good understanding and of a beautiful countenance, but the man was churlish and evil in his doings, and he was of the house of Caleb (1 Samuel 25:2-3). David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing, and sent ten young men to greet him in peace, peace to him and to his house and to all that he had: his shepherds had been with David’s men and were not hurt, and nothing of theirs was missing all the while they were in Carmel; he could ask his own young men, and they would tell him; so let him give whatever came to his hand to his servants and to his son David (1 Samuel 25:4-8). The request was righteous, and loyalty is a two way street: David’s men had given protection and were asking a favour back in a good day. Nabal answered by asking who David was, and who the son of Jesse was, since there were many servants nowadays that break away every man from his master, and was he to take his bread, his water and the flesh he had killed for his shearers and give it to men he knew not? (1 Samuel 25:10-11). He was talking much smack, as though he did not even know who David was; he was rich and he was feeling himself, and an arrogant spirit often comes with that. One of the young men told Abigail that David had sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute their master and he railed on them, though the men had been very good to them and nothing was hurt or missed as long as they were conversant with them, for they were a wall to them both by night and day; so she should know and consider what to do, because evil was determined against their master and all his household, for he was such a son of Belial that a man could not speak to him (1 Samuel 25:14-17). Some of us know people like that; you cannot talk to them and they will not reason with you. David told his men to gird on every man his sword, and about four hundred men went up after him while two hundred abode by the stuff. He said he had kept all that this fellow had in the wilderness in vain, for he had requited him evil for good, and he swore to leave alive by the morning light none of all that belonged to him (1 Samuel 25:13-22). He was coming with intent to destroy the men of that house. Abigail met him on the road with the provision, and that speech is her own case, entered next; David blessed her advice and blessed her for keeping him that day from coming to shed blood and from avenging himself with his own hand (1 Samuel 25:33).

name: Abigail
text: Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be: keeping David from shedding blood and avenging himself with his own hand. A woman of good understanding attached to a son of Belial. When she heard that David was coming with four hundred swords for her husband’s railing, she made haste with two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, raisins and figs, and went down to meet him without telling her lord. She fell at his feet, took the iniquity upon herself, named her husband’s folly without defending it, and told the coming king what the Lord would do for him. David blessed her advice; about ten days later the Lord smote Nabal, and David sent for her. One of the young men told Abigail what Nabal had done and what David’s men had been to the shepherds, a wall to them both by night and by day, and that evil was determined against their master and all his household. She made haste and took two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five measures of parched corn, a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, laid them on asses, and sent her servants on before her; but she told not her husband Nabal (1 Samuel 25:14-19). When she saw David she hasted, lighted off the ass, fell before him on her face and bowed to the ground, fell at his feet, and said, upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be. She was not the one who did anything wrong, and she took that iniquity on herself; she was being the pillar of her house, using wisdom to protect it. She did not turn her lord over to be destroyed, as some women today would be ready to do, and she did not defend him either: let not my lord regard this man of Belial, she said, for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him (1 Samuel 25:23-31). Belial means a child of Satan; she said openly that her husband was the devil the Bible speaks of, and she asked pardon for a trespass that was not hers. Then she told the coming king who he was: the Lord had withheld him from coming to shed blood and from avenging himself with his own hand; the Lord would certainly make her lord a sure house, because he fought the battles of the Lord; his soul would be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord his God, and the souls of his enemies would be slung out as out of the middle of a sling; and when the Lord had appointed him ruler over Israel it would be no grief nor offence of heart to him that he had shed blood causeless or avenged himself. This is a woman who knows what to say, when to say it, and how to say it. David said, blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent her that day to meet him, and blessed be her advice, and blessed be she, which had kept him that day from coming to shed blood and from avenging himself with his own hand. He received of her hand what she had brought, and told her to go up in peace to her house, for he had hearkened to her voice and accepted her person (1 Samuel 25:32-35). The Lord put the spirit on her, she spoke eloquently, and the king changed his mind. That is the lesson for wives: be in subjection to your own husbands, so that if any obey not the word they may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives, beholding a chaste conversation coupled with fear (1 Peter 3:1). Her chaste conversation was her behaviour, not her mouth; when she heard that David was coming she made that feast and carried it down herself. And the scripture that tells servants to be subject not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward covers the house she was in: enduring grief wrongfully for conscience toward God is thankworthy (1 Peter 2:18-19).

name: Saul and the witch of Endor
text: Seeking a woman with a familiar spirit after he had himself put them out of the land. Samuel was dead, Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land, and when he saw the host of the Philistines his heart greatly trembled. He enquired of the Lord and was not answered, not by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets, so he asked his servants to find him a woman with a familiar spirit: that is necromancy, and it was the very thing he had outlawed. He disguised himself, went by night, and heard from Samuel that the Lord had become his enemy and that the next day he and his sons would be with him. Chronicles names this as the cause of his death. Samuel was dead and buried in Ramah, and Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land. When the Philistines gathered and pitched in Shunem, Saul was afraid and his heart greatly trembled (1 Samuel 28:3-7). This is the king; if the king is afraid, so goes every man under him. As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers, and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein (Ecclesiasticus 10:2). Fear is nothing else but a betraying of the succours which reason offers (Wisdom of Solomon 17:12): a man tricks himself into being afraid of what is not there, because his faith is in what his eyes can see. Saul had been bashful from the beginning, little in his own sight, and bashfulness made him self willed, full of excuses, and easy to manipulate. When Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. Then he told his servants to seek him a woman that had a familiar spirit, that he might go to her and enquire of her, and they told him of one at Endor (1 Samuel 28:3-7). He had just rid the land of the familiar spirits and the wizards, and now he says, find me one; his mind was all over the place, double minded. What he was doing is called necromancy, and the commandment he broke is written plainly: there shall not be found among the people any that uses divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a necromancer, for all that do these things are an abomination to the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); and the law says not to suffer a witch to live (Exodus 22:18). Saul disguised himself and came to the woman by night with two men, asking her to divine by the familiar spirit and bring up whoever he named. She answered that he knew what Saul had done, cutting off those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land, and asked why he was laying a snare for her life; and Saul swore to her by the Lord that no punishment would happen to her for it (1 Samuel 28:8-14). He swore by the name of the Lord to protect her in the doing of what the Lord calls abomination. Samuel asked why he had disquieted him, and Saul answered that he was sore distressed: the Philistines made war on him and God was departed from him and answered him no more, so he had called Samuel to make known what he should do. Samuel asked why he asked of him, seeing the Lord was departed from him and was become his enemy (1 Samuel 28:15-19). Imagine that: the Lord is your enemy now. The Lord had done to him as He spoke by Samuel, rending the kingdom out of his hand and giving it to his neighbour David, because he obeyed not the voice of the Lord nor executed His fierce wrath upon Amalek; that is the law concerning Amalek he did not carry out (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Moreover the Lord would deliver Israel with him into the hand of the Philistines, and the next day he and his sons would be with Samuel: a prophecy from the grave that he and his sons would die. Saul fell straightway all along on the earth, sore afraid, and there was no strength in him (1 Samuel 28:15-20). The Philistines followed hard upon Saul and his sons and slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua; the archers hit Saul and he was sore wounded, and rather than be taken and abused by the uncircumcised he asked his armourbearer to thrust him through, and when the man would not, Saul took a sword and fell upon it; so Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together (1 Samuel 31:2-6), exactly as Samuel said. The chronicle states the cause: Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the Lord, against the word of the Lord which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it, and enquired not of the Lord; therefore He slew him and turned the kingdom to David the son of Jesse (1 Chronicles 10:13-14). The Philistines cut off his head, put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth and fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan, until the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead went all night, took down the bodies and buried the bones at Jabesh (1 Samuel 31:8-13).

name: The Amalekite who claimed to kill Saul
text: Claiming to have slain the Lord’s anointed, and bringing his crown for a reward. A young man came out of the camp of Israel to Ziklag with his clothes rent and earth upon his head, and fell before David with the crown and the bracelet of Saul: he said he had come by chance upon mount Gilboa, found Saul leaning on his spear, and slew him at his own asking. The earlier chapter says Saul fell on his own sword. He was an Amalekite, of the seed of Esau, the nation written of as fearing not God, and he expected a reward for the deed. His own mouth testified against him, and David had him slain. After the death of Saul, when David had returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and abode two days in Ziklag, a man came out of the camp from Saul with his clothes rent and earth upon his head and fell to the earth before David. He said the people were fled from the battle, many were fallen and dead, and Saul and Jonathan his son were dead also. Asked how he knew it, he said he happened by chance upon mount Gilboa and found Saul leaning upon his spear with the chariots and horsemen following hard after him; Saul asked who he was, and he answered that he was an Amalekite; then Saul asked him to stand upon him and slay him, because anguish was come upon him while his life was yet whole in him, so he stood upon him and slew him, being sure he could not live after he was fallen, and took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm and brought them to his lord (2 Samuel 1:2-10). The earlier account says Saul took a sword and fell upon it (1 Samuel 31:3-5). The man was an Amalekite: Amalek came of Eliphaz the son of Esau (Genesis 36:12). He carried the crown and the bracelet as tokens of a deed he expected to be paid for. David took hold on his clothes and rent them, and so did all the men with him, and they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul, for Jonathan his son, and for the house of Israel, because they were fallen by the sword. The renting of garments was the sign of mourning, but the Most High looks for a rent heart and not rent garments only, for true repentance is inward (Joel 2:13). The opening of the throne was no occasion for celebration, and the man who brought the crown had misjudged the king he brought it to. David asked the young man where he was from, and he answered that he was the son of a stranger, an Amalekite. Then David asked how he was not afraid to stretch forth his hand to destroy the Lord’s anointed (2 Samuel 1:13-16). The answer to that question is written in the law: Amalek met Israel by the way, smote the hindmost when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:18). That nation has had a perpetual hatred and has shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity (Ezekiel 35:5), pursuing his brother with the sword, casting off all pity, and keeping his wrath for ever (Amos 1:11). The man who had twice refused to put forth his hand against Saul, saying the Lord forbid it (1 Samuel 26:11), was not going to reward a stranger for claiming the act. David called one of his young men and told him to go near and fall upon him, and he smote him that he died; his blood was upon his own head, for his own mouth had testified against him. Whether or not he had done what he claimed, his mouth condemned him; he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword (Revelation 13:10). David remembered this messenger when Rechab and Baanah brought him the head of Ish-bosheth: the man who thought he brought good tidings of Saul was taken hold of and slain in Ziklag, and that was the reward he got for his tidings (2 Samuel 4:10). Then David lamented over Saul and over Jonathan, and bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, which is written in the book of Jasher (2 Samuel 1:17-18). The book of Jasher is not in the canon because the Most High did not will us to have it; He put in the book exactly what His people need in the last days. And this walk is not by the bow nor by the gun: not by might, nor by power, but by His spirit (Zechariah 4:6); here is the patience of the saints, they that keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus (Revelation 14:12). There is nothing wrong with knowing how to defend yourself, but the redemption of Israel does not come by force of arms. The lament itself is prophecy given in the spirit: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions (2 Samuel 1:23). Before the devil jumped on Saul he was a good man, and the forefathers died only when the Most High said it was time; the man who boasted of hastening it lost his own life for it.

name: Joab
text: Shedding the blood of war in peace: Abner in the gate of Hebron, and Amasa with a kiss. Abner had slain Asahel in open battle, after warning him twice to turn aside. When Abner came to David to bring all Israel under him and was sent away in peace, Joab, without the king’s knowledge, sent messengers after him, took him aside in the gate to speak quietly, and smote him under the fifth rib for his brother’s blood. Years later he took Amasa by the beard as though to kiss him and shed his bowels on the ground at one stroke. David said the sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him and left it with the Lord; the payback came through Solomon, and the horns of the altar were no refuge for a man who killed with guile. Abner sent messengers to David offering to bring all Israel over to him, and came to Hebron with twenty men; David made them a feast and sent him away, and he went in peace (2 Samuel 3:12-27). Joab came in from pursuing a troop, heard of it, and demanded of the king why he had sent Abner away, saying the king knew that Abner came to deceive him and to know his going out and his coming in. It was not true, and Joab knew it; there was already blood between them, because Abner had smitten Asahel his brother under the fifth rib at Gibeon after twice telling him to turn aside and take another man’s armour (2 Samuel 2:21-23). That was war, and the man had been warned. What Joab did was another matter. When he came out from David, he sent messengers after Abner without David’s knowledge, brought him back from the well of Sirah, took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother (2 Samuel 3:26-30). That is premeditated murder, not the avenger of blood and not manslaughter: the law provides a city of refuge for the man who kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when the axe head slips from the helve, but if a man comes presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, he is to be taken from the altar of the Lord that he may die (Exodus 21:14). When David heard it he declared himself and his kingdom guiltless before the Lord for ever from the blood of Abner and laid it on the head of Joab and all his father’s house; he made Joab and all the people rend their clothes and gird with sackcloth and mourn before the coffin, and lamented over Abner in the spirit, asking whether he died as a fool dies, his hands not bound nor his feet put in fetters, but falling as a man falls before wicked men (2 Samuel 3:28-39). The king said he was weak that day though anointed king, and that the sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him, but the Lord would reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness (2 Samuel 3:38-39). Joab had his own squad of hard men and did what he wanted; David knew what kind of man his captain was, stayed quiet, and waited for the right time. Years later, when David made Amasa captain of the host in Joab’s place, Joab met him at the great stone in Gibeon with a sword secretly fastened on his loins, and took him by the beard as though to kiss him; Amasa took no heed to the sword, and Joab smote him in the fifth rib and shed his bowels to the ground at one stroke (2 Samuel 20:8-10). David gathered both into one charge at the last: Solomon knew what Joab had done to him, and to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he slew, shedding the blood of war in peace (1 Kings 2:5). The only reason Asahel died was that a war was on; Joab turned a peaceful meeting into a killing. Joab had turned after Adonijah, though he turned not after Absalom. When the tidings came he fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and caught hold on the horns of the altar, and when Benaiah came with the king’s word he refused and said he would die there (1 Kings 2:28-35). Men would grab the horns of the altar and sometimes get mercy, but wilful murder found no refuge there. Solomon told Benaiah to do as Joab had said and fall upon him, that the innocent blood he shed might be taken away from Solomon and from the house of his father. The Lord would return his blood upon his own head, because he fell upon two men more righteous and better than he and slew them with the sword without David’s knowledge; their blood would return upon the head of Joab and upon his seed for ever, but upon David and upon his seed and upon his throne there would be peace for ever from the Lord. So Benaiah went up and fell upon him, and the king set Benaiah over the host in his place. Joab had kept his rank for years after both killings, and the delay did not cancel the bloodguilt; the doer of evil was rewarded according to his wickedness, exactly as David said. Neither his service in every war David fought nor his hold on the altar made the blood of Abner and Amasa disappear.

name: Mephibosheth
text: What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am? and, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, because a new king customarily killed the descendants of the old one, and in her haste he fell and became lame. David fetched him out of Lo-debar for Jonathan’s sake, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually. When David fled from Absalom, his servant Ziba slandered him and took the estate; when the king came again in peace, Mephibosheth met him unwashed and unshaven and said, let him take all. Jonathan the son of Saul had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she made haste to flee he fell and became lame; his name was Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4). She fled because a new king taking over would customarily kill the descendants of the former king, so that none could overthrow him. But David asked whether there was yet any left of the house of Saul, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, because they had made a covenant, loving each other as their own souls (1 Samuel 18:3). Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, told him that Jonathan had yet a son, lame on his feet, in Lo-debar, and the king sent and fetched him. When Mephibosheth came he fell on his face and did reverence, and David told him to fear not, for he would surely show him kindness for Jonathan his father’s sake, restore him all the land of Saul, and have him eat bread at the king’s table continually; and he bowed and asked what his servant was, that the king should look upon such a dead dog as he (2 Samuel 9:1-8). His standing rested on a covenant between his father and the king, not on anything he could do. During Absalom’s rebellion Ziba met David past the top of the hill with asses saddled and bread and raisins and summer fruits and wine; when the king asked where his master’s son was, Ziba said he abode in Jerusalem, saying that the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father that day. It was not true, and on that word David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16:1-4). When the king came again, Mephibosheth came down to meet him, having neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace: he had mourned the whole time. He told the king that his servant had deceived him, for he was lame and had asked for an ass to be saddled that he might ride to the king, and Ziba had slandered him; but the king was as an angel of God, and all his father’s house were but dead men before the king, yet he had set his servant among them that ate at his own table, so he had no right to cry any more to the king. When David said that he and Ziba should divide the land, Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take all, forasmuch as his lord the king was come again in peace to his own house (2 Samuel 19:24-30). The king called Ziba and told him he had given his master’s son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house; Ziba, his sons and his servants were to till the land and bring in the fruits, that his master’s son might have food, but Mephibosheth would eat bread always at the king’s table. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Samuel 9:9-13). That shows the riches Israel had as a nation: Saul’s servant had servants of his own, all set to work the land for a lame man out of the respect David had for Jonathan. So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem and did eat continually at the king’s table, and was lame on both his feet. This is what we need to bring back into Israel, that same love and care for the people we lose: we take care of their family as if they were there themselves. That is a large part of why the Most High called David a man after His own heart. When the famine came for Saul’s bloody house and the Gibeonites required seven of his sons, the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, because of the oath of the Lord between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). Set the two houses side by side. Saul had given his word to the Gibeonites and gone back on it, and the whole house paid for it, because when a man vows a vow to God he must not defer to pay it, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). David had given his word to Jonathan and kept it, and Jonathan’s crippled son was pulled out of that judgment by the promise. Jonathan was gone, Saul’s rule was gone, the kingdom had passed; the word of kindness had not passed, and a lame man at the king’s table made a kept promise visible every day.

name: Baanah and Rechab
text: Murder of Ish-bosheth on his bed at noon, and carrying his head to David for a reward. When Saul’s son heard that Abner was dead in Hebron his hands were feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled. Two captains of his own bands came about the heat of the day as though they would fetch wheat, smote him under the fifth rib as he lay on his bed at noon, beheaded him, and carried the head all night through the plain to David at Hebron, calling it the head of the king’s enemy. They did too much. David required the blood of a righteous person slain in his own house upon his bed, and they were slain, dismembered and hanged up over the pool. When Saul’s son Ish-bosheth heard that Abner was dead in Hebron his hands were feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled. He had two men that were captains of bands, Baanah and Rechab, the sons of Rimmon a Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin (2 Samuel 4:1-2). The sons of Rimmon came about the heat of the day to the house of Ish-bosheth, who lay on a bed at noon in the hottest part of the day; they came into the midst of the house as though they would have fetched wheat, and smote him under the fifth rib, and escaped. They beheaded him, took his head, and got away through the plain all night (2 Samuel 4:5-12). His own captains, who had a right to be in the house, used that access to kill him while he rested. They brought the head to David at Hebron and presented it as the head of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul his enemy, who sought his life, and said that the Lord had avenged the king that day of Saul and of his seed (2 Samuel 4:8). They did too much; they went overboard. Israel being out of order took the matter into their own hands. David had no quarrel with Saul’s sons; it was Saul who sought his life. They called murder the vengeance of the Lord, and expected the new king to pay them for it. David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, swearing by the Lord who had redeemed his soul out of all adversity: when one told him Saul was dead, thinking to have brought good tidings, he took hold of him and slew him in Ziklag, and that was the reward he gave him for his tidings; how much more, when wicked men had slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed, should he not require his blood of their hand and take them away from the earth? (2 Samuel 4:9-12). The man was at rest, asleep, and it was not even a contest between men for the kingdom; that is not how the Most High brings His purpose to pass. So David commanded his young men, and they slew them, cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up over the pool in Hebron; but they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the sepulchre of Abner. The murderers were publicly judged, and the head they had carried as a token for reward was given a burial.

name: Uzzah and the ark
text: Putting forth his hand to the ark of God, which was carried on a new cart and not on the shoulders of the Levites. David gathered thirty thousand chosen men to bring up the ark of God from the house of Abinadab, where it had been left since the days of the judges, and they set it upon a new cart with Uzzah and Ahio driving and all Israel playing before the Lord. At Nachon’s threshingfloor the oxen shook it, Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark, and God smote him there for his error, and he died by the ark. Grabbing it was a natural reaction, but the Most High had already declared it holy and untouchable. When David came back for it, none carried it but the Levites, upon their shoulders, after the due order. The congregation agreed to bring the ark again, because they had not enquired at it in the days of Saul, and the thing was right in the eyes of all the people (1 Chronicles 13:3-4). The purpose was right and the joy was real. They set the ark of God upon a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio the sons of Abinadab drove the cart, with Ahio going before the ark, while David and all the house of Israel played before the Lord on all manner of instruments of fir wood, on harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets and cymbals (2 Samuel 6:3-5). But the manner of carrying it had already been commanded, and a cart was not it. This is the third of three: touch not, taste not, handle not. The staves were to stay in the rings of the ark and never be taken out of them, so that it was always borne and never handled (Exodus 25:15). The sons of Kohath were the movers of the sanctuary, but when Aaron and his sons had made an end of covering the holy things, the Kohathites came to bear them and were not to touch any holy thing, lest they die (Numbers 4:15). Only the Levites chosen for it could come near. A new cart was what the Philistines used to send the ark home; it was not an improvement on obedience. When they came to Nachon’s threshingfloor, the oxen shook the cart and Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it. The anger of the Lord was kindled against him, and God smote him there for his error, and he died there by the ark of God (2 Samuel 6:6-9). It was a natural reaction; the beast bumped the cart and he reached for it. It does not matter. That was the most holy thing and it was not his place to touch it, and even a man who meant well did not get away with it. The Lord had warned Aaron himself, through Moses, not to come at all times into the holy place within the vail before the mercy seat that is upon the ark, so that he die not, and that warning came after the two sons of Aaron died for offering strange fire (Leviticus 16:1-2). Everything in that day had to be done to a T, and we owe thanks that there is mercy through Christ, because the Lord was not playing about His commandments. If it falls, let it fall, and get a Levite to lift it.

name: Obed-edom the Gittite
text: Keeping the ark of God in his house three months, after it had killed Uzzah. Uzzah had just died for putting forth his hand to the ark, and David was afraid of the Lord that day and asked how the ark should come to him. He carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, and it remained there three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household because of the ark. The blessing was so plain that it was told the king, and David came back for it with sacrifices and dancing. The ark blesses when it is with Israel and afflicts those who hold it wrongly. David was afraid of the Lord that day and asked how the ark of the Lord should come to him; he would not remove it to himself into the city of David, but carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, and it continued there three months (2 Samuel 6:6-11). The same ark before which judgment had just stopped the procession now stood inside an ordinary household. The holiness of the Lord had not changed, and neither had His power to bless. The ark blesses when it is with Israel and afflicts those who hold it wrongly: the Philistines were smitten with emerods for taking it and begged Israel to carry it away (1 Samuel 5:6-9), and Uzza died for putting his hand to it (1 Chronicles 13:9-10). Obed-edom received into his house what the king had become afraid to bring any nearer, and he kept it as it was to be kept. When the ark went on to the city of David it went the way it should have gone the first time: the Levites sanctified themselves and bare the ark of God upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded according to the word of the Lord (1 Chronicles 15:14-15). Receiving holy things and keeping the order of the service belong together, and this household did both. His name appears again among the porters, where Shemaiah the firstborn and seven more sons of Obed-edom are listed, with the note that God blessed him, and his sons and his brethren, able men for strength for the service, threescore and two of Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:4-8). The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household (2 Samuel 6:11), the house of Obed-edom and all that he had (1 Chronicles 13:13-14; 1 Chronicles 13:14). It was told king David that the Lord had blessed the house of Obed-edom and all that pertained to him because of the ark of God, so David went and brought up the ark from that house into the city of David with gladness; when they that bare it had gone six paces he sacrificed oxen and fatlings, and he danced before the Lord with all his might (2 Samuel 6:12; 2 Samuel 6:12-14). Judgment on the first journey had taught fear; the blessing in this house showed that the Lord had not forbidden Israel to draw near in obedience. The blessing was not only goods inside a private house; it was a family equipped for service. When the lots were cast for the gates, the south gate fell to Obed-edom, and to his sons the house of Asuppim (1 Chronicles 26:15). Strength received from God was put to work in an appointed charge. And do not let anyone claim the ark is in Ethiopia or anywhere else on show: the prophet Jeremiah hid the tabernacle, the ark and the altar of incense in a cave, and the place is to remain unknown until the time that God gathers His people together again (2 Maccabees 2:5-7). The Lord who smote beside the cart is the same Lord who blessed the house where the ark rested.

name: Michal
text: Despising the king in her heart for dancing before the ark; how glorious was the king of Israel to day. As the ark came into the city of David with shouting and the sound of the trumpet, Michal the daughter of Saul looked through a window, saw the king leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despised him in her heart. She had once been a tower against death to him, letting him down through a window out of her father’s reach; now she met him at the door with sarcasm. In the midst of pure righteousness she was out of the spirit, hating him instead of rejoicing. Michal had no child to the day of her death. David danced before the Lord with all his might, girded with a linen ephod, and he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet; and as the ark came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked through a window, saw king David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:14-16; 1 Chronicles 15:29). He was happy and he was in the spirit, because the Lord had chosen him to bring the ark back among the people, and he was clothed with a robe of fine linen along with the Levites and the singers (1 Chronicles 15:27). The people were dressed well and the day was holy. This is the same Michal who had loved him and saved his life when her father sent messengers to slay him in the morning, letting him down through a window and laying an image in the bed; a married woman is a tower against death to her husband, and that night she was one (1 Samuel 19:11-17). But here is a spirit to be careful of: coming out of the spirit on the Lord’s day and murmuring against a brother who is rejoicing in the Most High. David set the ark in the tabernacle he had pitched for it, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts, and dealt to every one, both men and women, a cake of bread, a good piece of flesh and a flagon of wine (2 Samuel 6:17-19). Then he returned to bless his own household, still in a good mood, and Michal came out to meet him and said sarcastically how glorious the king of Israel had been that day, uncovering himself in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself (2 Samuel 6:17-20; 2 Samuel 6:20). She had watched from a distance and could think of nothing but the king dancing with his clothes flying, on the day the ark of God came home to Israel. She forgot the greatness of the day and let a murmuring spirit take her. David answered that it was before the Lord, who chose him before her father and before all his house to appoint him ruler over the people of the Lord, therefore he would play before the Lord; and he would yet be more vile than this and base in his own sight, and of the maidservants she had spoken of he would be had in honour (2 Samuel 6:21-22; 2 Samuel 6:21-23). The office was a gift from the One before whom he was dancing, not a reason to hold himself too great to rejoice. Her real quarrel was older than the dance: the man leaping before the ark was the man who had replaced her father on the throne, and she was the daughter of Saul. Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:20-23; 2 Samuel 6:23). The Lord shut her womb. Do not play with the Most High. The earth is disquieted by an odious woman when she is married (Proverbs 30:23), and the adulterous woman of the proverb eats and wipes her mouth and says she has done no wickedness (Proverbs 30:20); the common thread is a woman who will not hold herself accountable. It is better to keep house where there is an evil wife than to bring her among the people (Ecclesiasticus 42:6). The king came home to bless his household, and the household met the blessing with reproach; the record closes her account not with her dignity preserved but with a childless house.

name: David and Bathsheba
text: Adultery with the wife of Uriah, and setting Uriah up to be murdered on the battlefield to cover it. In the season when kings went out to war, David stayed behind in Jerusalem, saw a woman bathing from his roof, was told plainly that she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and sent for her anyway. When she conceived he called Uriah home to cover it, and when Uriah would not go down to his house he sent him back carrying his own death warrant. Nathan came with a parable, David pronounced sentence on himself, and Nathan told him he was the man. The Lord took away his sin, but the sword never left his house, and the child died. While Joab and all Israel were sent to destroy the Ammonites and besiege Rabbah, David stayed in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 11:1). Walking on the roof of his house in the evening he saw a woman bathing, asked after her, and was told she was Bath-sheba the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 11:2-3). He was told plainly that she was a married woman, and he had known the law from his youth up. He sent for her and lay with her, and she conceived and sent him word that she was pregnant (2 Samuel 11:4-5). Bath-sheba was not innocent either; when the king called she went, and she did not refuse. David sent for Uriah and told him to go down to his house, with a gift of food following him from the king; but Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with the servants and did not go home (2 Samuel 11:6-9). He answered that the ark and Israel and Judah were living in tents and his lord’s servants were camped in the open field, so how could he go into his own house (2 Samuel 11:11). David made him drunk, and even drunk he would not go down (2 Samuel 11:13). That loyalty was killing David all the more. In the morning David wrote to Joab and sent the letter by Uriah’s own hand, ordering that he be put at the front of the fiercest fighting and abandoned there to be killed (2 Samuel 11:14-15). Joab placed him where he knew the valiant men were, and Uriah died along with some of David’s servants (2 Samuel 11:16-17); other men of Israel died with that sin. The curses at Ebal are for this: a curse lies on the man who strikes his neighbour in secret and on the man who takes a reward to kill an innocent person, and the reward here was the woman (Deuteronomy 27:24-25). David sent word to Joab not to be troubled, since in battle the sword kills this man or that one (2 Samuel 11:25). When the mourning was over he married her, but the Lord was displeased with what David had done (2 Samuel 11:27). The Lord sent Nathan with a parable of a rich man with many flocks who took a poor man’s one ewe lamb, dear to him as a daughter, to feed a traveller. David burned with anger and swore the man deserved to die, because he had no pity (2 Samuel 12:1-5); judging that man, he was pronouncing sentence on himself. Nathan told him he was the man: the Lord had anointed him, delivered him from Saul, given him his master’s house and all Israel and Judah, and would have given him more; why then had he despised the Lord’s commandment, killing Uriah and taking his wife (2 Samuel 12:7-9)? If he had only asked, the Lord would have given him anything. So the sword would never leave his house; the Lord would raise up trouble from within it and give his wives to another man in broad daylight, because he had acted in secret and this would be done before all Israel (2 Samuel 12:10-12). It came to pass exactly, on a roof, by Ahithophel’s counsel. David confessed his sin against the Lord, and Nathan told him the Lord had taken it away and he would not die, but because the deed had given the Lord’s enemies great cause to blaspheme, the child would die (2 Samuel 12:13-14). That child was the judgment: the Lord shows mercy and forgives iniquity, yet does not clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7). He was pardoned; he was not cleared. He fasted and lay on the ground all night while the child lived; when it died he rose, washed, worshipped and ate, saying he would go to the child but the child would not come back to him (2 Samuel 12:16-23). His was the godly sorrow that leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10); a just man who falls seven times gets up again (Proverbs 24:16). Through the judgment Solomon was still born and the Lord loved him (2 Samuel 12:24-25). People who want to justify wrongdoing run straight to this history; but you are not King David, and this is the mess up, not the licence.

name: Uriah the Hittite
text: The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; shall I then go into mine house? as thou livest, I will not do this thing. One of David’s mighty men, recalled from the siege of Rabbah so that the king’s sin could be covered. He would not go down to his house, but slept at the door of the king’s house with the servants of his lord; asked why, he answered that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents and Joab and the servants were encamped in the open fields, and swore he would not do this thing. Made drunk, he still would not go, and was sent back carrying the letter that ordered his death. The king could command his movements, but he could not make the blood innocent: Nathan named him, and the record of the kings and the ancestry of Christ still name him. David sent to Joab for Uriah the Hittite, and when he came the king asked him how Joab did and how the people did and how the war prospered, and then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, and a mess of meat from the king followed him; but Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord and went not down to his house (2 Samuel 11:6-9). Uriah was no ordinary soldier; he is numbered among the thirty and seven mighty men of David (2 Samuel 23:39), one of the men Joab had at the front, and the small talk from the king was out of the ordinary for him. The name Hittite does not make him a Hamite in David’s army; men in that record carry the names of the lands they dwelt in after Israel removed the nations from those coasts. When David was told that he had not gone down, he asked why, since he had come from a journey, he went not down to his house; and Uriah answered that the ark, and Israel, and Judah abode in tents, and his lord Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields, so how could he go into his house to eat and to drink and to lie with his wife, and he swore by the king’s life that he would not do this thing (2 Samuel 11:6-11; 2 Samuel 11:10-11). He remembered the men still carrying the burden he had been briefly recalled from, and he remembered the ark in a tent. David kept him there another day, called him to eat and drink before him and made him drunk, and at evening he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house (2 Samuel 11:12-13). Even drunk, when a man might just go home and sleep it off, he would not go. That loyalty was killing David all the more, because he could not deceive this man into lying with his own wife. In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that he be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and that they retire from him, that he might be smitten and die (2 Samuel 11:14-17; 2 Samuel 11:14-15). He carried his own death warrant to the captain without opening it. Joab assigned him to a place where he knew valiant men were, the men of the city came out and fought, some of the servants of David fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also (2 Samuel 11:16-17). His death exposed no failure of duty in him; it exposed the treachery of the command set over him. The king tried to hide him among the ordinary losses of war, saying the sword devoureth one as well as another (2 Samuel 11:25), and Joab knew what the king really wanted and charged the messenger to name Uriah the Hittite as dead also (2 Samuel 11:21-25; 2 Samuel 11:21-24). The Lord did not let him disappear in the casualty list. Nathan named him to his face in the judgment on the king: David had killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and taken his wife to be his wife, and slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:9). The curse that fell was the curse written for the man who did it: a curse lies on the man who strikes his neighbour in secret and on the man who takes a reward to kill an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:24-25). The record of the kings keeps his name in it: David did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord and turned not aside from any thing that He commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5). The ancestry of Christ keeps his name in it too: David the king fathered Solomon by the woman who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6). He was not delivered from the fatal order, and his faithfulness is not measured by whether he escaped it. The account honours the conduct of the servant and condemns the king who exploited it.

name: Amnon
text: Forcing his sister Tamar, then hating her and putting her out. David’s firstborn was so tormented over his half sister that he made himself ill, and his crafty friend Jonadab told him how to get her alone: play sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for him where he could watch. He cleared the room so there would be no witnesses. She begged him not to force her, because Israel does not do such things, and called it folly; being the stronger, he forced her, then hated her more than he had loved her and had her thrown out and the door bolted. David was very angry and did nothing. Two years later Absalom had him killed at a sheepshearing. Amnon the son of David was so tormented over Tamar, Absalom’s beautiful sister, that he fell ill, because she was a virgin and it seemed impossible for him to do anything to her; but he had a friend, Jonadab the son of David’s brother Shimeah, a very crafty man (2 Samuel 13:1-2; 2 Samuel 13:1-3). He was the grimy sort who knows exactly how to get over on somebody, and Tamar was Amnon’s sister by another mother. Jonadab told him to lie in bed and pretend to be sick, and when his father came, to ask for Tamar to prepare food in front of him so he could eat from her hand (2 Samuel 13:5). David sent Tamar, and she made cakes where he could see; he refused to eat and sent every man out (2 Samuel 13:7-9). He emptied the room so there would be no witnesses, then took hold of his own sister and told her to lie with him.
