She begged her brother not to force her, because Israel does not do such things, and not to commit this folly; she would have nowhere to carry her shame, and he would be counted among the fools of Israel; let him rather speak to the king, who would not keep her from him. He would not listen, and he overpowered her and forced her (2 Samuel 13:6-14; 2 Samuel 13:12-14). Tamar herself calls it folly and sin. Any man talking about forcing a woman is wicked, and the law is plain: if a man forces a betrothed young woman in the field, only the man dies and nothing is done to her, for the case is like a man attacking his neighbour and killing him (Deuteronomy 22:25-26). Rape is murder, and it falls under the commandment against killing. On top of that it was his sister, whose nakedness the law forbids uncovering (Leviticus 18:9), and a curse stands on the man who lies with his sister (Deuteronomy 27:22). Then Amnon’s hatred for her was greater than his love had been, and he told her to get out; she answered that sending her away was a worse wrong than the first, but he would not listen, and had his servant put her out and bolt the door behind her (2 Samuel 13:15-19; 2 Samuel 13:15-18; 2 Samuel 13:15-17). She wore a robe of many colours, the dress of the king’s virgin daughters (2 Samuel 13:18), part of the order of the kingdom, and it is why we wear garments today. Tamar put ashes on her head, tore her robe and went away crying. Absalom asked whether Amnon had been with her, told her to keep quiet for now, since he was her brother, and she stayed desolate in his house. David was very angry when he heard, and Absalom said nothing at all to Amnon, for he hated him for forcing his sister (2 Samuel 13:19-22). David was upset at what happened to Tamar and did nothing about it; Absalom was one of those men who holds a grudge for years just to get somebody back, and these are people who know the law and know they are Israel. After two full years Absalom held a sheepshearing at Baal-hazor and pressed the king until Amnon and all the king’s sons came; he ordered his servants to wait until Amnon was merry with wine and then strike him down at his word, and they did (2 Samuel 13:23-29; 2 Samuel 13:23-33). He was killed for what he did to Tamar, by a brother’s revenge and not by a hearing under the law; his guilt did not make every act against him righteous. Word reached David that all his sons were slain, and he tore his clothes and lay on the ground, until Jonadab told him only Amnon was dead, and that Absalom had settled on it from the day Amnon forced Tamar (2 Samuel 13:30-33). The king and his servants wept bitterly, Absalom fled to Talmai king of Geshur, and David mourned for his son every day (2 Samuel 13:36-37). The sword Nathan had announced was working inside the house: Tamar desolate, Amnon dead, Absalom gone.

name: Absalom
text: Murder of Amnon; stealing the hearts of the men of Israel; conspiracy and rebellion against the king his father; lying with his father’s concubines before all Israel. David’s son killed his brother, fled, was brought home, then provided himself chariots, horses and fifty runners and stood by the road to the gate, telling every man who came for judgment that his case was good and right but the king had appointed no one to hear it. He kissed their hands and stole the hearts of the men of Israel. Under cover of a vow at Hebron he raised a rebellion, drove his father out barefoot and weeping up Olivet, and by Ahithophel’s counsel lay with the royal concubines on the roof in the sight of all Israel. He was left hanging by his head in an oak, and Joab drove three darts through his heart. Absalom took his sister into his house after Amnon forced her, nursed his hatred two full years, had Amnon killed at his sheepshearing, and fled to Geshur (2 Samuel 13:11-14; 2 Samuel 13:15-22; 2 Samuel 13:23-29; 2 Samuel 13:20-38). Joab brought him home by the wise woman of Tekoah; he lived two years in Jerusalem without seeing the king, and when Joab would not come he set Joab’s barley field on fire to force a meeting (2 Samuel 14:23-33). His complaint was that his father had rendered no justice for Tamar, but he had already taken that justice into his own hand, and now he wanted the seat. He then provided himself chariots and fifty runners, stood early by the gate, and told every man bringing a case to the king that his cause was good and right but no one was appointed to hear it, wishing aloud that he were judge in the land. When anyone bowed to him he took his hand and kissed him, and so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel (2 Samuel 15:1-6; 2 Samuel 15:1-12). That is the sneakiness: instead of going to the king and resolving the matter, he got into the king’s good graces and then went around patting people on the back behind his back. That is what the bishop calls friendish, showing people friendship without being a true friend. After forty years he asked leave to pay a vow at Hebron, and sent spies through all the tribes to proclaim at the trumpet that Absalom reigned in Hebron; two hundred men went with him in their simplicity, knowing nothing, and with Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, the conspiracy grew strong (2 Samuel 15:7-12). That is the simplicity of a lot of brothers: a man who says all the nice things goes completely out of order against leadership, and men follow him carnally because he kissed their hand and told them their cause was good. Others follow for what they can get, grumblers and faultfinders driven by their own desires, flattering people to gain an advantage (Jude 1:16). When word came that Israel’s heart was with Absalom, the king fled barefoot and weeping up Olivet (2 Samuel 15:13-30). Ahithophel then counselled Absalom to go in to the concubines David had left to keep the house, so all Israel would know he had made himself odious to his father; they pitched a tent on the roof and he did it in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:21-22). That fulfilled exactly what the Lord said by Nathan, that David’s wives would be given to another in broad daylight (2 Samuel 12:11); and the son who fulfilled it fell under the curse himself, which lies on a man who lies with his father’s wife (Deuteronomy 27:20). David prayed that the Lord would turn Ahithophel’s counsel to foolishness and sent Hushai back to defeat it (2 Samuel 15:31-34), and the Lord had determined to overthrow that counsel so as to bring evil on Absalom (2 Samuel 17:1-14). David divided the army under Joab, Abishai and Ittai and charged them in everyone’s hearing to deal gently with the young man for his sake; even after the concubines and the stolen hearts, the father still sought to make amends with his son (2 Samuel 18:1-5). In the battle in the wood of Ephraim the forest took more lives than the sword. Absalom, riding a mule, was caught by the head in the thick branches of a great oak and left hanging between heaven and earth as the mule went on (2 Samuel 18:6-9). The man who saw it would not touch him for a thousand shekels, because of the king’s charge; Joab took three darts and drove them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive in the oak, and ten of his armour bearers finished him (2 Samuel 18:10-15; 2 Samuel 18:1-15). Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought him back alive for his father to make amends, and he did what he wanted. In his lifetime he had set up a pillar in the king’s dale and named it after himself, because he had no son to keep his name alive (2 Samuel 18:17-18). He sought a monument and a kingdom, and his rebellion ended in a pit under stones. When Cushi brought the news, the king went up to the room over the gate and wept for his son, wishing he had died in his place (2 Samuel 18:31-33). Promotion comes from the Most High, who places every member in the body as He pleases (1 Corinthians 12:18), and not from a man stealing hearts at the gate.

name: Ahithophel
text: Treason against David; counselling Absalom to lie with his father’s concubines; asking for twelve thousand men to smite the king; suicide. David’s counsellor, whose advice was received as though a man had asked of God Himself, was among the conspirators at Hebron. His first counsel in Jerusalem was that Absalom go in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel; his second was to give him twelve thousand men to pursue David that night and strike down the king alone. He had a reason he had carried for years: Bath-sheba was his granddaughter. David prayed that his counsel be turned to foolishness, and the Lord had determined to defeat it; when he saw that it was not followed, he put his household in order and hanged himself. Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, from his city Giloh while he offered sacrifices, and the conspiracy grew strong as the people kept joining Absalom (2 Samuel 15:12). His counsel in those days was received as if a man had inquired of God, both with David and with Absalom (2 Samuel 16:23). This man was so persuasive that his advice sounded almost biblical, like talking to an angel of the Most High. He was David’s own counsellor turned traitor; the enemies a man of Israel must forgive are the ones risen up out of his own people (Micah 2:8). When David heard he was among the conspirators, he prayed that the Lord would turn his counsel to foolishness (2 Samuel 15:31). Asked what to do, Ahithophel told Absalom to go in to the concubines his father had left to keep the house, so all Israel would hear that he had made himself odious to his father; a tent was pitched on the roof and it was done in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:20-23; 2 Samuel 16:20-22). Politically calculated and morally corrupt: the counsel carried out the very word spoken against David, that it would be done in broad daylight (2 Samuel 12:11), and the counsellor answers for advising the abomination. Then he asked for twelve thousand men to pursue David that night while he was weary and weak, scatter the people with him, strike down the king alone and bring the rest back (2 Samuel 17:1-3). He wanted the victory and the bragging rights of being the man who killed King David. Why would a man do that to the king he had served from a young man? The record names his son: Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite is listed among the mighty men (2 Samuel 23:34), and Bath-sheba was the daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3). Ahithophel was her grandfather. He was in that throne room when Uriah was called home, and he carried it for years. When he saw an opening he used Absalom to disgrace David’s household in front of all Israel, exactly as his own had been disgraced in secret. That is what bitterness does: it lies in wait, and at the end it is the ruin of the man who keeps it. Absalom wanted a second opinion and called Hushai the Archite. There is safety in a multitude of counsellors, but only where the counsel is according to the word of the Lord; a counsellor who does not go to the scriptures is not one to want. Hushai said Ahithophel’s advice was not good this time: David and his men were mighty and enraged like a bear robbed of her cubs, his father was a man of war who would not sleep among the people, and if some fell at the first attack even the bravest would lose heart; so all Israel should be gathered from Dan to Beer-sheba, countless as the sand, with Absalom leading them in person (2 Samuel 17:5-14; 2 Samuel 17:5-11). It was deliberately inaccurate counsel that would waste time gathering troops and give David room to escape; Hushai was a man planted in righteousness, always siding with the king. Absalom and the men of Israel preferred it, for the Lord had determined to defeat Ahithophel’s good counsel so as to bring evil on Absalom (2 Samuel 17:14). Hushai sent word by the priests, a maidservant and two men hidden in a well under a covering of grain, and David crossed the Jordan by morning (2 Samuel 17:15-23; 2 Samuel 17:15-22). When Ahithophel saw his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, went home to his city, put his household in order and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). The evil counsel he devised reared around and bit its author: evil hunts down sinners, while the righteous are repaid with good (Proverbs 13:21). To be righteous is to keep all the commandments before the Lord (Deuteronomy 6:25), and every unrighteous act is sin (1 John 5:17). David was righteous and did not even want to war against his own son, and good was repaid to him, while the sinner was pursued by his own device to a rope. A man’s heart holds many plans, but it is the Lord’s counsel that stands (Proverbs 19:21). Ahithophel had reputation, access and practical wisdom, and none of it could establish a purpose the Lord had appointed to overthrow.

name: Ittai the Gittite
text: As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be. As David fled from Absalom, all his servants passed on beside him, and with them the Gittites, six hundred men that came after him from Gath. David told Ittai to go back, because he was a stranger and an exile who had come only yesterday, and the king would not make him go up and down with him when he himself did not know where he was going. Ittai swore by the Lord and by the king’s life to be with him in death or in life, and passed over with all his men and all the little ones. When the army was set in array, a third part of it was under his hand. All his servants passed on beside him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king. The king asked Ittai the Gittite why he went with them too, and told him to return to his place and abide with the king, for he was a stranger and also an exile; he came but yesterday, and should the king this day make him go up and down with them, seeing the king himself was going wherever he could? He told him to return and take back his brethren, and mercy and truth be with him (2 Samuel 15:18-19; 2 Samuel 15:18-20). The king gave him leave to go and made him no promise of what would come of staying. Ittai answered with an oath by the Lord and by the life of the king, that in what place the king should be, whether in death or life, even there also would his servant be. David said, go and pass over, and Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him (2 Samuel 15:20-22; 2 Samuel 15:21-22). Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected, and so David let him come; that loyalty in the face of trouble is the thing seen all through Israel’s story. His oath named death as well as life, so it was not a bargain made on a guaranteed reward. All the country wept with a loud voice as the people passed over the brook Kidron toward the wilderness (2 Samuel 15:18-23; 2 Samuel 15:23), and the contrast is sharp: the king’s own son, who came forth of his bowels, was seeking his life, while a stranger the king had offered to release bound himself to the king’s danger. David numbered the people that were with him and set captains of thousands and captains of hundreds over them, and sent forth a third part under the hand of Joab, a third under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under the hand of Ittai the Gittite (2 Samuel 18:1-2; 2 Samuel 18:2). The man who had pledged to stay with the king in death or in life was trusted with a third of the army. When David said he would surely go forth with them himself, the people answered that he should not go, for he was worth ten thousand of them, and it was better that he succour them out of the city; and the king hearkened to their counsel and said he would do what seemed best to them (2 Samuel 18:2-4). He did not run a dictatorship, and in a time when he could not trust his own flesh and blood he trusted the proven men he had warred with for years. Then the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai to deal gently for his sake with the young man Absalom, and all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge concerning him (2 Samuel 18:1-5; 2 Samuel 18:5). Of the three captains it was Joab, and not the stranger out of Gath, who broke that charge. The road out of Jerusalem showed who would stand when the favour of the throne no longer promised anything, and Ittai gave his word on that road, before any honour was in sight.

name: Shimei son of Gera
text: Cursing the king and casting stones at him: come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial. As David reached Bahurim on the road out of Jerusalem, a man of Saul’s family came out cursing him all the way, throwing stones and dust, and saying the Lord had paid him back for all the blood of Saul’s house. Saul was the wicked one who had tried to kill David, and it was the hand of the Most High that stopped him, yet Shimei cursed the king as though David were in the wrong. David would not let Abishai take his head, but said to let him curse, because the Lord had told him to. He swore Shimei would not die, and left the case to Solomon. When David reached Bahurim, Shimei the son of Gera, of the family of Saul’s house, came out cursing him all the way and throwing stones at David and his servants, though the people and the mighty men surrounded the king. He called David a man of blood and a man of Belial and told him to get out; the Lord, he said, had paid him back for all the blood of Saul’s house, whose throne he had taken, and had handed the kingdom to his son Absalom, and he was caught in his own evil because he was a man of blood (2 Samuel 16:5-13; 2 Samuel 16:5-8). Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David, and it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed; yet Shimei cursed him as though David were the one in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw the king in a low state and went to rub it in his face. He truly thought he was right in it. The law forbids reviling the gods or cursing the ruler of the people (Exodus 22:28), and the gods there are the leaders set over the people, for the Most High called the judges gods and children of the Most High (Psalms 82:6). Paul obeyed that very verse when he was checked for speaking against the high priest (Acts 23:5). Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and asked leave to go over and take off his head. The king asked what he had to do with them, the sons of Zeruiah: if the Lord had told Shimei to curse David, who could question him? If his own son was seeking his life, how much more this Benjamite. He told them to leave him alone and let him curse, for the Lord had told him to, and perhaps the Lord would look on his affliction and repay him with good for that day’s cursing (2 Samuel 16:9-13). David rolled with mighty men of war and Abishai was ready to take the man’s head off his shoulders, but if it was of the Most High, then let it come; the same as when people come into our forums to bicker and bring confusion, sometimes to try the patience of men who prayed for patience. So David went on his way while Shimei kept pace along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones and flinging dust (2 Samuel 16:13). To endure suffering patiently after doing well is what pleases God (1 Peter 2:20). When the king came back over the Jordan, Shimei hurried down with a thousand men of Benjamin, fell before him, and begged him not to hold against him the wrong he had done the day the king left Jerusalem, for he knew he had sinned. Abishai said he should die for cursing the Lord’s anointed; David again rebuked the sons of Zeruiah and asked whether anyone should be put to death in Israel the day he was king again. So he swore to Shimei that he would not die (2 Samuel 19:18-23; 2 Samuel 19:16-23). David understood grace long before the New Testament; grace has always been around. Mercy gave the man his life; it did not make the curse true. At the last David charged Solomon concerning Shimei, who had cursed him bitterly on the day he went to Mahanaim and then met him at the Jordan, where David swore by the Lord not to kill him; Solomon was not to count him innocent, but as a wise man he would know what to do (1 Kings 2:8-9). Solomon had him build a house in Jerusalem and stay there, warning him that on the day he crossed the brook Kidron he would die and the blame would be his own; Shimei called the terms good and agreed (1 Kings 2:36-46; 1 Kings 2:36-38). Three years later he rode to Achish king of Gath after two servants who had run off, and brought them back (1 Kings 2:39-40). Solomon asked why he had not kept the oath of the Lord and the command he had called good, told him he knew all the wickedness he had done to David, and said the Lord would bring it back on him (1 Kings 2:42-44). Benaiah the son of Jehoiada struck him down, and Solomon’s kingdom was made secure (1 Kings 2:46). He had been given a condition for his life and had agreed to it, and two runaway servants proved more urgent to him than the word his safety stood on; the pardon of the father did not entitle him to break the charge of the son.

name: Barzillai the Gileadite
text: Providing the king with sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man. When David came to Mahanaim on the run from his son, Shobi, Machir and Barzillai brought beds, basons, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched corn, beans, lentiles, honey, butter, sheep and cheese of kine, because they said the people were hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness. After the rebellion the aged man of fourscore years came down from Rogelim to conduct the king over Jordan, and declined the king’s table in Jerusalem because at eighty he could no longer taste what he ate nor hear the singing men and women. He sent Chimham in his place; the king kissed him and blessed him, and charged Solomon to keep his sons at the table. When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim brought beds, and basons, and earthen vessels, and wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse, and honey, and butter, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David and for the people that were with him to eat, for they said the people were hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27-29). The provision answered the actual condition of men who had fled Jerusalem barefoot, and it was brought before the battle in the wood of Ephraim, while the outcome was still open and the hearts of the men of Israel were after Absalom. Barzillai was a very aged man, even fourscore years old, and he had provided the king with sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man (2 Samuel 19:32). His wealth became provision at the moment the kingdom hung in the balance. When the king came again, Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and went over Jordan with the king to conduct him over. The king invited him to come over with him and be fed in Jerusalem, and Barzillai asked how long he had to live that he should go up with the king; he was fourscore years old that day, and could no longer discern between good and evil, nor taste what he did eat or drink, nor hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women, so why should his servant be yet a burden to his lord the king? He asked leave to turn back again and die in his own city and be buried by the grave of his father and of his mother, and he offered his servant Chimham to go over with the king, to do to him what should seem good (2 Samuel 19:31-39; 2 Samuel 19:31-37). The Most High set man’s days at a hundred and twenty years (Genesis 6:3), and the days of our years are threescore years and ten, or by reason of strength fourscore years, and even then their strength is labour and sorrow (Psalms 90:10); the Lord kept cutting the lifespan down because of sin, so that a man of ninety is called very aged in the days of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 6:24). At eighty Barzillai knew exactly where he stood, and his service had not been a hidden bid for a place at court; he could decline the honour for himself without refusing the king’s kindness toward another. The king answered that Chimham should go over with him, and he would do to him what should seem good, and whatsoever Barzillai required of him he would do for him. All the people went over Jordan, and when the king was come over, the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place (2 Samuel 19:38-39). The king did not treat the provision of his troubled days as a debt forgotten once the throne was secure. The remembrance went into the next reign: in the charge he gave Solomon at the end of his life, David told him to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite and let them be of those that eat at his table, because so they came to him when he fled because of Absalom his brother (1 Kings 2:7). Barzillai did not move to Jerusalem, and his sons ate at the king’s table there for what their father did when the king was hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.

name: Sheba son of Bichri
text: Insurrection: we have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse. After Absalom’s revolt, while the men of Israel and the men of Judah quarrelled over who had the right to bring the king home, Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite and a man of Belial, blew a trumpet, declared that Israel had no part in David, and drew the men of Israel away after him (2 Samuel 19:41-43; 2 Samuel 20:1-2). Joab pursued him to Abel of Beth-maachah and laid siege to the city. A wise woman of Abel spoke with Joab, and the people of the city delivered Sheba’s head over the wall, so that one rebel died and the city was spared (2 Samuel 20:14-22). The quarrel came first. When the tribes debated bringing David back, the men of Judah claimed the king as their near kin, the men of Israel claimed ten parts in him and more right in David, and the words of Judah were the fiercer (2 Samuel 19:41-43). The study notes mark this as the tribal strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel. Into that quarrel stepped Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite. Scripture calls him a man of Belial, and the notes say plainly what that means: a devil. He blew a trumpet, declared that they had no part in David and no inheritance in the son of Jesse, and sent every man of Israel to his tents. The men of Israel went up from following David to follow Sheba, while the men of Judah held to their king from Jordan to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 20:1-2). A quarrel between brethren became a banner of rebellion against the king the Lord had set over them, and David weighed it at once. He told Abishai that Sheba would now do them more harm than Absalom had done, and sent him out with Joab’s men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites and all the mighty men, to pursue Sheba before he could reach fenced cities and escape (2 Samuel 20:6-7). On the road Joab murdered Amasa, the man David had named captain in his place, taking him by the beard as if to kiss him and striking him with a sword he had fastened out of sight; the notes call Joab grimy and shady (2 Samuel 20:8-10). The pursuit went on through all the tribes to Abel of Beth-maachah, where Sheba shut himself in. Joab’s army cast up a bank against the city and battered the wall to throw it down (2 Samuel 20:14-15). One man’s rebellion had put a whole city of Israel under siege. The end came through a woman. A wise woman called from the wall and asked that Joab come near so she could speak with him. The teaching on this passage draws out her manner. She had enough respect to come to the leader who was bringing the harm on the city and ask him for a hearing. She made sure she knew who he was, which showed that she recognised his authority. She asked him to hear his handmaid, humbling herself and speaking respectfully, not loud and not up in his space. She reminded him of the old saying that men would ask counsel at Abel and so settle a matter. She told him she was one of the peaceable and faithful in Israel, so that he knew her character and her good reputation among her people. Only then did she ask why he would destroy a city that was a mother in Israel and swallow up the inheritance of the Lord (2 Samuel 20:16-19). A man in the heat of war wants to take the head, so she calmed him first and spoke to him reasonably and peaceably. Joab answered that he had no wish to destroy. His matter was with one man of mount Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri, who had lifted up his hand against King David; if the city delivered him alone, Joab would leave. She promised that Sheba’s head would be thrown over the wall, went to all the people in her wisdom, and they cut off his head and threw it out to Joab (2 Samuel 20:20-22). She negotiated with the captain and stopped the onslaught on the city. The sentence fell on the rebel alone. Joab blew the trumpet, the army withdrew from the city every man to his tent, and Joab returned to the king at Jerusalem (2 Samuel 20:22). Sheba had used a trumpet to scatter Israel from David, and a trumpet ended his revolt. Joab stayed over all the host of Israel, and David’s officers stood in their places again (2 Samuel 20:23-26). The teaching carries the lesson into the house of Israel today. The Most High puts that kind of spirit on sisters who know how to speak to men and become peacemakers, and a man who is supposed to have wisdom should be able to recognise it rather than bring down a whole house because of one loud mouth. That is why wise women are lifted up and honoured among the people and not kept beneath: the people know the history of their foremothers, and there are sisters with gifts that can do what the brothers cannot.

name: Rizpah
text: Spreading sackcloth upon the rock from the beginning of harvest until water dropped out of heaven, suffering neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night to touch them. Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, lost her two sons when seven of Saul’s house were delivered to the Gibeonites and hanged before the Lord at the beginning of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:8-9). She spread sackcloth on the rock and kept the birds off the bodies by day and the beasts by night until the rain came (2 Samuel 21:10). When David heard what she had done, he brought home the bones of Saul and Jonathan and buried them with the hanged in the sepulchre of Kish, and after that the Most High was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:11-14). Her sons died for their father’s sin. Three years of famine had come on Israel because Saul broke the oath Israel had sworn to the Gibeonites and killed them, and the lesson the Most High was teaching the nation was to pay what you vow; that matter is entered as its own case (2 Samuel 21:1-6). The king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan because of the oath between David and Jonathan. He took the two sons Rizpah had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal, and delivered them to the Gibeonites, who hanged them in the hill before the Lord. All seven fell together, put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:7-9). Rizpah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, and stayed there from the beginning of harvest until the rain fell on the bodies from heaven. By day she let no bird of the air settle on them, and by night no beast of the field (2 Samuel 21:10). She could not save her sons, but she would not let them be eaten. The day and the night brought different dangers, and she kept watch against both through the whole season. The record gives her no speech; her endurance was her testimony, and it made the condition of the dead known to the king. The law cared even for the body of a man put to death. One hanged on a tree for a sin worthy of death was not to remain there all night but was to be buried the same day, because a hanged man lies under the curse of God, and burying him kept the land the Lord gave Israel for an inheritance from being defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). Rizpah’s watch did not replace that burial. It kept the bodies whole until the matter reached David and the burial could be done. It was told David what Rizpah had done. He went to the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the street of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them after Saul fell on Gilboa (2 Samuel 21:11-12). The history behind that wall matters. The Philistines cut off Saul’s head, sent word round to publish it in the house of their idols, put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth, and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan, where the Canaanites and the Philistines, Hamites in league together, dwelt. The valiant men of Jabesh-gilead went all night, took the bodies down from that defiled idol place, buried the bones under a tree at Jabesh and fasted seven days (1 Samuel 31:9-13). The study notes add that Jonathan’s body had been hung in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites. David brought the bones of Saul and Jonathan up from there, the bones of the seven who had been hanged were gathered with them, and they were buried in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish, Saul’s father. They did all that the king commanded, and after that God was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:13-14). Saul and his sons were taken down from a heathen wall and laid in the land of their own inheritance. Rizpah’s sons were not given back to her. What her vigil won was burial for the whole house of Saul and the lifting of the judgment from the land after three years of famine. She kept faith with those who could no longer speak for themselves until the king acted.

name: Saul’s house and the Gibeonites
text: Breaking the oath Israel sware to the Gibeonites by slaying them in zeal for Israel and Judah. A famine of three years sent David to enquire of the Lord, who answered that it was for Saul and his bloody house, because Saul had slain the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn by the Lord in Joshua’s day to let live (2 Samuel 21:1-2; Joshua 9:15-20). The lesson the Most High was teaching Israel through the famine was to pay what you vow. The Gibeonites refused silver and gold and asked for seven of Saul’s sons; David spared Jonathan’s son for his own oath, delivered the seven, and after the burial of Saul’s house the Lord was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:3-14). There was a famine in the days of David, three years, year after year, and David enquired of the Lord. The answer was that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he killed the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1). The Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Israel had sworn to them, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 21:2). Saul broke his word. The oath went back to the conquest. The Gibeonites heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai and worked by craft: old sacks, torn wine skins, worn shoes and garments, dry and mouldy bread, and a story that they came from a far country. Israel was commanded to destroy the nations of the land, so their only hope was to pretend they were not of it. The men of Israel took of their provisions and did not ask counsel of the Lord. That was the first mistake, and it became a snare to the people, for the Most High says counsel before every action (Joshua 9:3-14). Joshua made peace with them and a league to let them live, and the princes of the congregation swore to it (Joshua 9:15). When the deceit came out three days later the congregation murmured, but the princes held the line: they had sworn by the Lord God of Israel, so they could not touch them, and would let them live lest wrath come on Israel for the oath (Joshua 9:16-20). Our forefathers were wrong in one situation, but upright men in holding to their word. A vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile. The Gibeonites were made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God (Joshua 9:21-27). Saul undid what the princes had kept. When a vow is made to God it is not to be put off; He has no pleasure in fools, it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay, and a man is not to tell the angel afterward that it was a mistake (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6). Christ made it simple: let your yes be yes and your no be no (Matthew 5:37). The teaching on this says your word is your bond, and it is better not to swear at all than to cause yourself to sin by an oath you cannot live up to. Saul gave his yes to the Amorites and went back on it, and the whole house paid for it. Blood defiles the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood shed in it except by the blood of the one who shed it (Numbers 35:33). David asked the Gibeonites what he should do for them and how he could make atonement, so that they would bless the inheritance of the Lord. The study notes are careful here: the blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through the famine. The Gibeonites would take no silver or gold of Saul or his house, and did not ask for any man in Israel to be killed for them. They asked for seven sons of the man who had consumed them and plotted to wipe them out of every border of Israel, to be hanged before the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, and the king agreed (2 Samuel 21:3-6). David kept his own oath while he settled Saul’s broken one. He spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the oath of the Lord between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). David did not go back on his word; he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David’s table. The king delivered the two sons of Rizpah and the five sons of Michal to the Gibeonites, who hanged them in the hill before the Lord, all seven together, at the beginning of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:8-9). Rizpah kept watch over the bodies until the rain, which is entered as her own case, and when David heard it he gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan with the bones of the hanged and buried them in the sepulchre of Kish; after that God was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:10-14). Saul’s death on Gilboa did not wipe the breach out of the land. The king who came after him had to enquire into the cause and settle what lay beneath three years of famine.

name: David’s numbering of the people
text: Numbering Israel and Judah against Joab’s counsel; seventy thousand men dead of the pestilence. The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David to number Israel and Judah; the Chronicles account says Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to do it (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The king’s word prevailed over Joab’s objection, and when the count came in David’s conscience struck him. Offered three judgments by the prophet Gad, he chose to fall into the hand of the Lord, and seventy thousand men died of the pestilence before the Lord stayed the angel at the threshing floor of Araunah, which David bought for an altar (2 Samuel 24:10-25). Two accounts tell one event. Second Samuel says the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel and he moved David against them to number Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 24:1). First Chronicles says Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number Israel (1 Chronicles 21:1). The teaching reconciles them: it is all saying the same thing. The Most High wanted to judge Israel, and he used David and used Satan to do it. Satan cannot come into a man’s life without the okay from God: God chooses him, and Satan uses him. The Lord already knew the lust that was in David, and it was Satan’s work to feed that desire and keep tempting him until he carried it out. The lust was pride, the desire of a man in power to know how many he is over. Only God is supposed to know the number of his people. Numbering was not the king’s work but the Levites’, and when Israel was counted under the law, every man from twenty years old and up gave a ransom for his soul, half a shekel, rich and poor alike, so that no plague would come on them (Exodus 30:11-16). Joab tried to talk sense into the king. He asked why the king took delight in this thing when God already knew the number, but the king’s word prevailed against Joab and the captains of the host (2 Samuel 24:3-4). Chronicles adds that Joab called it a cause of trespass to Israel and left Levi and Benjamin uncounted, because the king’s word was abominable to him (1 Chronicles 21:3-6). The count took nine months and twenty days from Dan to Beer-sheba, and Joab brought back eight hundred thousand valiant men of Israel who drew the sword and five hundred thousand of Judah, not counting the women and children (2 Samuel 24:5-9). The teaching sets this beside the census of today. The powers that control the earth count the people not for their good but to know what level of force to use against them. A leader aligned with God does as Joab said and keeps the number to God. As soon as it was done it hit him. David’s conscience struck him; he confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly, and asked the Lord to take away his servant’s iniquity (2 Samuel 24:10). In the morning the word came to Gad, David’s seer, with three judgments and a choice of one: famine in the land, three months fleeing before his enemies, or three days of pestilence (2 Samuel 24:11-13). Samuel gives the famine as seven years and Chronicles as three (1 Chronicles 21:11-12). David was in a great strait and chose to fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great, rather than into the hand of man, knowing that man would not show him the mercy the Most High would (2 Samuel 24:14; 1 Chronicles 21:13). The pestilence ran from the morning to the time appointed, and seventy thousand men died from Dan to Beer-sheba (2 Samuel 24:15). God killed seventy thousand because David decided to number the people, and the same way God used the nations back then to correct us when we were disobedient, it is the same thing today. The notes send the reader back to the first verse: the reason for the seventy thousand is that the Most High was angry at Israel. When the angel stretched out his hand over Jerusalem, the Lord repented of the evil and told him it was enough. David saw the angel, something we cannot see today, for this walk is by faith and the keeping of the commandments. He and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces, and he pleaded that he alone had sinned and that the sheep had done nothing (2 Samuel 24:16-17; 1 Chronicles 21:16-17). Gad sent him to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. Araunah offered the floor, the oxen and the threshing tools as a free gift, but David would not offer the Lord burnt offerings that cost him nothing. He paid, built the altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the plague was stayed from Israel (2 Samuel 24:18-25). Samuel gives the price as fifty shekels of silver for the floor and the oxen; Chronicles gives six hundred shekels of gold for the place, and adds that the Lord answered by fire from heaven and the angel put up his sword (1 Chronicles 21:25-27). True worship costs us something. That threshing floor on mount Moriah is where Solomon later built the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 3:1).

name: Adonijah
text: Exalting himself, saying, I will be king; and after his pardon, asking for Abishag the Shunammite. While David lay old and failing, his son Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying he would be king, drew Joab and Abiathar to his side, and held a feast for his party without Solomon, Nathan, Zadok or Benaiah (1 Kings 1:5-10). David confirmed his oath that Solomon would reign, Solomon was anointed at Gihon, and Adonijah fled to the horns of the altar and was spared on condition that he show himself a worthy man (1 Kings 1:29-53). After David’s death he asked for Abishag the Shunammite to wife, and Solomon, discerning the request as a reach for the kingdom, had him put to death (1 Kings 2:13-25). King David was old and could get no heat, so his servants found Abishag the Shunammite, a very fair young woman, to lie in his bosom and keep him warm, but he did not know her (1 Kings 1:1-4). That happens with age, and two who lie together have heat (Ecclesiastes 4:11); that he did not know her means he had no relations with her. Then Adonijah exalted himself, saying he would be king, and prepared chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him, and his father had never once crossed him by asking why he did so (1 Kings 1:5-6). David was still alive, and this son was already seeking power. He took the throne to himself rather than receiving it from the Most High; the teaching calls it a vainglorious and covetous spirit, seeking preeminence as Absalom his brother had. He conferred with Joab and with Abiathar the priest, while Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, Shimei, Rei and David’s mighty men would not follow him (1 Kings 1:7-8). Joab had been David’s right hand, loyal and a warrior, but always doing underhanded things, and David knew it and kept quiet; Joab had not turned after Absalom, but he turned after Adonijah (1 Kings 2:28). Adonijah killed sheep and oxen at the stone of Zoheleth and called all the king’s sons and the men of Judah, but not Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men or Solomon (1 Kings 1:9-10). He left out Solomon because he knew what he was doing was wrong and knew Solomon was meant to be king, and he left out Nathan because he knew he would be checked. Nathan warned Bathsheba that her life and her son’s were at stake; she went in to the king, and Nathan came in after her to confirm her words, two witnesses establishing the matter (1 Kings 1:11-27). David swore by the Lord who had redeemed his soul out of all distress, the distress of a life of war and of his own sons rising against him, that Solomon would reign in his place that very day (1 Kings 1:29-30). The throne was Solomon’s by that sworn word and by the Lord’s choice among David’s sons (1 Chronicles 28:5). Solomon rode the king’s own mule to Gihon, the king’s own property, which was the king confirming him, and Zadok and Nathan anointed him while the people rejoiced until the city rang (1 Kings 1:32-40). Adonijah’s guests heard it, rose up and scattered, and Adonijah, afraid of Solomon, caught hold of the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:41-50). Solomon showed mercy. If Adonijah would show himself a worthy man, not a hair of him would fall to the earth; but if wickedness were found in him, he would die. They brought him down from the altar, he bowed before King Solomon, and Solomon sent him to his house (1 Kings 1:51-53). The pardon was real, and it was conditional: Solomon was watching him. After David died, Adonijah came to Bathsheba, and she asked whether he came peaceably. He said he did, then told her she knew the kingdom had been his and all Israel had set their faces on him to reign, but it had turned about and become his brother’s, for it was his from the Lord; he had one request, that she ask Solomon to give him Abishag the Shunammite to wife (1 Kings 2:13-17). The teaching hears bitterness in his mouth: you know the kingdom was mine. There were many women he could have asked for; he asked for the one who had lain in the king’s bosom. Like riding the king’s mule, taking the king’s woman would be claiming the king’s place. Bathsheba did not discern it and carried the request to her son (1 Kings 2:18-21). Solomon discerned it at once. He told his mother she might as well ask the kingdom for Adonijah too, since he was the elder brother, and for Abiathar the priest and Joab with him (1 Kings 2:22). He read the reasoning of men, the discernment he had asked of God, and saw that the request came with guile. He swore that Adonijah had spoken this word against his own life, and sent Benaiah, who fell on him so that he died (1 Kings 2:23-25). Abiathar was thrust out of the priesthood, fulfilling the word against the house of Eli, and Joab died at the altar for the innocent blood of Abner and Amasa (1 Kings 2:26-34). The mercy at the altar was not leave to reach for the throne by another road. The teaching draws the lesson for the congregation: those who seek preeminence reveal themselves over a process of time, and it never fails.

name: Solomon at Gibeon
text: Asking for an understanding heart to judge thy people, and not long life, nor riches, nor the life of his enemies. At Gibeon the Lord appeared to the young king in a dream and told him to ask what He should give him. Solomon called himself a little child set over a people too many to count, and asked for an understanding heart to judge them and to discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:5-9). The request pleased the Lord, who gave him a wise and understanding heart like none before or after him, added the riches and honour he had not asked for, and promised length of days on condition that he walk in the commandments as David had (1 Kings 3:10-14). The chapter opens on the setting. Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and took his daughter, and the people still sacrificed in high places because no house had yet been built to the name of the Lord. Solomon loved the Lord and walked in the statutes of David his father, only he too sacrificed and burnt incense in high places, and he went to Gibeon, the great high place, and offered a thousand burnt offerings there (1 Kings 3:1-4). The study notes read this as a king who loved the Lord in a time before the temple. The classes press the other side of the same verses: marrying Pharaoh’s daughter went against the law that forbade marriages with the nations because they would turn the heart to other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4), so the Lord came to him while he was already mixing, and History in the AM counts Gibeon as the first of the two times the Lord appeared to him to admonish him (1 Kings 11:9). God said to ask. Solomon began with the great mercy shown to David, who had walked before the Lord in truth, righteousness and uprightness of heart, and the kindness of giving him a son to sit on his throne. He said he was only a little child who did not know how to go out or come in, set in the midst of a chosen people too great to be numbered, and he asked for an understanding heart to judge them, that he might discern between good and bad, for no one could judge so great a people without it (1 Kings 3:6-9). The teaching hears a young man saying, Lord, how do I guide these people; tell me what to do. This is what we still need to pray for: that the Most High endows our leadership with wisdom, and that we ourselves learn wisdom in these scriptures and how to judge matters among one another. The saints will judge the world and even angels, so they ought to be able to judge the smallest matters of this life (1 Corinthians 6:1-3). The speech pleased the Lord. Because Solomon had not asked for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies, but for understanding to discern judgment, God gave him a wise and understanding heart, so that there was none like him before him and none would arise after him, and added what he had not asked, riches and honour above all the kings of his days (1 Kings 3:10-13). Length of days was conditional: if he would walk in God’s ways and keep His statutes and commandments as his father David had, the Lord would lengthen his days (1 Kings 3:14). The gift did not cancel the command. Solomon woke, came to Jerusalem, and offered before the ark of the covenant (1 Kings 3:15). The wisdom was seen in judgment. When the two women came before him, which is entered as its own case, all Israel feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:28). It was seen in government: princes and twelve officers, each man in his position of order, the same pattern of captains and officers set up in the days of Moses (1 Kings 4:1-7). Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and fig tree from Dan to Beer-sheba, because the wars of David had put down the surrounding nations and put them to tribute (1 Kings 4:20-25). God gave him wisdom and understanding exceeding much and largeness of heart like the sand on the seashore. His wisdom excelled all the children of the east country and all the wisdom of Egypt; he spoke three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, and people of all nations came to hear him (1 Kings 4:29-34). Since his wisdom already excelled Egypt’s, there is no need to dabble in Egyptology or any doctrine outside the scriptures; the classes ask whether we do not want our own understanding to pass the nations the same way, by keeping the Lord’s ways, statutes and commandments. The Most High gave him knowledge of how the world was made, the working of the elements, the natures of living creatures, the diversities of plants and the virtues of roots, and the reasonings of men (Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-21). The reasonings of men is what would be called psychology today, spiritual discernment, and it is the gift he used to see through the claims brought to his throne. The Lord appeared to him a second time after the temple was finished with the same condition (1 Kings 9:2-5); what he did with his wives when he was old is another case.

name: The two women before Solomon
text: Two harlots, one living child, and a claim that only a sword could sort out. Two harlots who lived in one house each bore a son three days apart; one woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it, and she exchanged it for the living child while the other slept (1 Kings 3:16-22). There was no witness, and before the king each claimed the living child. Solomon called for a sword and ordered the child divided; the true mother gave up her claim to save the child’s life, the other would have it cut in two, and the king gave the child to its mother, so that all Israel saw the wisdom of God in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:23-28). The case came before the throne soon after Gibeon, when Solomon had asked for an understanding heart to judge the people and to discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:9). Two women who were harlots stood before the king. The first said that she and the other woman lived in one house, that she gave birth there, and that three days later the other woman gave birth as well, with no one else in the house but the two of them. The other woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it. She rose at midnight, took the living son from beside the first woman while she slept, laid him in her own bosom, and laid her dead child in the first woman’s bosom. In the morning the first woman rose to nurse her child and found him dead, but when she looked closely in the light she knew it was not the son she had borne (1 Kings 3:16-21). The teaching notes that a child dying under its sleeping mother is something that happens, and it hurts the mothers greatly; and that to an untrained eye one small baby can look like another, but a mother knows her own. The other woman answered that the living child was hers and the dead one belonged to the first, and the first said the opposite, and so they argued before the king (1 Kings 3:22). How was Solomon to know who was lying and who was telling the truth? He was king over all Israel and did not know these women. There was no stranger in the house to bear witness, both women claimed the same right, and both laid the dead child on the other. The classes add that during the time of Solomon, the Kingdom of Heaven on earth, there were still harlots, and they came to the king in a pair: all flesh keeps company with its own kind. The king repeated both claims back to them, called for a sword, and when it was brought he ordered the living child divided in two and half given to each (1 Kings 3:23-25). Then the woman whose child it was spoke, because her heart yearned over her son. She begged the king to give the other woman the living child and by no means kill it. The other said to let it be neither hers nor her rival’s, but divided (1 Kings 3:26). The teaching reads the second woman plainly: she did not care whether the baby was put to death, because she had already lost her own; she wanted company in her misery. It compares her spirit to that of women today who have abortion after abortion and have no love for the child. The king answered that the living child was to be given to the first woman and by no means killed, for she was its mother (1 Kings 3:27). The Jurisprudence class asks what law Solomon had to go on, since no statute covers one woman taking another’s baby, and answers that he went on the strength of common sense. From the moment he called for the sword he knew the real mother would react in a way the false one would not; he judged by what he had seen of a mother’s love for her child. Wisdom knows things of old and can conjecture aright what is to come; she knows the subtleties of speeches (Wisdom of Solomon 8:8). Conjecture is a conclusion formed on incomplete information, and Solomon had only each woman’s version of the story; by wisdom, experience and the law he reached a right conclusion and recognised the subtlety in the false woman’s speech. Most in the congregation will never be judges, the class says, but they still have to understand judgment, and study is how that wisdom is gained. All Israel heard of the judgment the king had judged, and they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:28). This was the answer to what he had asked at Gibeon, made visible to the whole nation through a household dispute between two women. The Lesser and the Greater class then turns to Christ, the greater Solomon, who did not need anyone to testify of man, for he knew what was in man (John 2:24-25). Solomon had to hear the women out and watch their countenance; Christ perceives the thoughts of men before they speak (Luke 5:22). The record gives no separate punishment for the false claimant. It ends with the living child given to his mother.

name: King Solomon
text: Loving many strange women of the nations the Lord had forbidden; multiplying wives against the law of the king; building high places for Chemosh and Molech. Solomon, the wisest of kings, loved many strange women besides Pharaoh’s daughter, from the very nations the law said would surely turn Israel’s heart after their gods, and he had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (1 Kings 11:1-3). When he was old they turned his heart, and he built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill before Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:4-8). The Lord, who had appeared to him twice, said He would rend the kingdom out of his son’s hand, leaving one tribe for David’s sake, and stirred up adversaries against him (1 Kings 11:9-40). Sirach sums up his life: he reigned in a peaceable time, was as wise as a flood of understanding, gathered gold as tin and silver as lead, and then bowed his loins to women, was brought into subjection by his body, stained his honour and polluted his seed (Ecclesiasticus 47:13-20). History in the AM calls the lesson Simping Solomon, from his own words. He knew better. He wrote that understanding would deliver a man from the strange woman who flatters with her words, whose house leads down to death (Proverbs 2:16-19); that her lips drip honey but her end is bitter as wormwood, and a man should not embrace the bosom of a stranger (Proverbs 5:3-20); that many strong men have been slain by her (Proverbs 7:24-27). His own mother told him not to give his strength to women (Proverbs 31:3). One may be wise and teach many and yet be unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19). The law was plain. Israel was to make no marriages with the nations, for they would turn their sons away to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4), and their daughters would lead Israel’s sons after their gods (Exodus 34:16). The study notes stress that it was not a maybe but a will. The king in particular was not to multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away, nor greatly multiply silver and gold (Deuteronomy 17:17). Tobit told his son to take a wife of the seed of his fathers, for despising the sons and daughters of your people by not taking a wife of them is pride, and pride is destruction (Tobit 4:12-13). Nehemiah later saw children who could not speak the Jews’ language because their mothers were of Ashdod, and reminded the people that even Solomon, beloved of his God, was caused to sin by outlandish women (Nehemiah 13:23-26). Solomon clung to these in love, and when he was old his wives turned his heart after other gods, and it was not perfect with the Lord as David’s had been. David sinned, but he repented and turned back; Solomon kept going. He went after Ashtoreth of the Zidonians, the fertility goddess behind Easter, and Milcom of Ammon, and built high places for Chemosh and Molech and for all his strange wives to burn incense to their gods (1 Kings 11:3-8). He did this after building the Lord’s house. The six-pointed star belongs here: the star of their god that Israel carried with Molech (Amos 5:26), the star of Remphan still carried in the apostles’ day (Acts 7:43), not a star of David. His sin was not his alone, for he was the greatest influence on the earth. He gave his heart to know madness and folly, and kept nothing from his eyes (Ecclesiastes 1:17; Ecclesiastes 2:10). The Lord was angry, because Solomon’s heart had turned from Him who had appeared to him twice and commanded him not to go after other gods (1 Kings 11:9-10). The teaching sets it beside the rule for a heretic, to be rejected after a first and second admonition (Titus 3:10): the third time is judgment. The Lord said He would surely rend the kingdom from him and give it to his servant, not in his days for David’s sake, but out of his son’s hand, leaving one tribe for David and for Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:11-13). The study notes call this the pivotal moment in Israel’s history, the sin that divided the kingdom under Jeroboam and Rehoboam. Peace had held while he kept the commandments; when he broke them, the Lord gave strength to his enemies. He stirred up Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a child when Joab cut off every male in Edom, for Esau was always the first hater of Israel, and Rezon, who reigned in Damascus and was an adversary all Solomon’s days (1 Kings 11:14-25). Then the prophet Ahijah tore Jeroboam’s new garment into twelve pieces and gave him ten, for ten tribes; Solomon sought to kill him, and he fled to Shishak in Egypt until Solomon died (1 Kings 11:26-40). Sirach says he left behind him the foolishness of the people and a son without understanding who turned the people away (Ecclesiasticus 47:23); the classes observe that a king searching out every folly had no time to raise Rehoboam in the law. Had he walked in the way of God, he would have dwelt in peace forever (Baruch 3:13). At the end he came full circle: he found more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares (Ecclesiastes 7:26), called it all vanity, and gave the conclusion of the whole matter, to fear God and keep his commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

name: Rehoboam
text: Forsaking the counsel of the old men for the young men he grew up with; and forsaking the law of the Lord when the kingdom was established. All Israel came to Shechem to make Solomon’s son king and asked him to lighten the heavy yoke his father had laid on them (1 Kings 12:1-4). Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men who had served Solomon, took the counsel of the young men he grew up with, and answered the people roughly, and ten tribes left the house of David that day, for the cause was from the Lord (1 Kings 12:6-20). Once his kingdom was strong he forsook the law of the Lord and all Israel with him, and Shishak of Egypt came up against Jerusalem until king and princes humbled themselves (2 Chronicles 12:1-12). Sirach names him plainly: Solomon left behind him even the foolishness of the people, one that had no understanding, who turned away the people through his counsel (Ecclesiasticus 47:23). Rehoboam went to Shechem, where all Israel came to make him king; Jeroboam came back from Egypt, and the congregation asked Rehoboam to lighten the grievous service and heavy yoke his father had put on them, and they would serve him (1 Kings 12:1-4). The study notes say the yoke was the labour of the building; Solomon did not enslave his own people as he did the nations, but they had to put in that work. Our Hidden History reads it as the taxes Solomon laid on the people to finance his wives’ temples. He told them to come back in three days, which was wisdom, for it is right to take time and get counsel before giving an answer (1 Kings 12:5). He consulted the old men who had stood before Solomon, and they told him that if he would be a servant to the people that day and speak good words to them, they would be his servants forever. He forsook their counsel and turned to the young men who had grown up with him (1 Kings 12:6-8). Solomon was the wisest man on earth and still had counsellors, yet Rehoboam forsook the counsellors of the wisest man for his peers; the problem is getting counsel from those on your own level rather than from your elders. The classes call it pride, and add that his father, busy with his own pleasures, had not been there to guide him. The young men told him to say that his little finger would be thicker than his father’s loins, and that where his father chastised them with whips he would chastise them with scorpions (1 Kings 12:9-11). On the third day he spoke to the people roughly in just those words (1 Kings 12:12-14). You are where you are based on the decisions you made. The study notes on Chronicles show the second offense. When Rehoboam had established the kingdom and strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him (2 Chronicles 12:1). One who leads goes astray and carries many with him. Judah built high places, images and groves on every high hill, and sodomites were in the land (1 Kings 14:22-24). He did evil because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14); Solomon had prepared his heart at Gibeon, and his son did not follow those footsteps. The king did not listen to the people, for the cause was from the Lord, that the word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam might come to pass (1 Kings 12:15). Israel answered that they had no portion in David, and went to their tents; Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute, and all Israel stoned him to death, and the king fled in his chariot to Jerusalem. So Israel rebelled against the house of David to this day, and only Judah followed the house of David (1 Kings 12:16-20). Rehoboam gathered a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men to bring the kingdom back, but the word came through Shemaiah not to fight their brethren, for this thing was from the Lord, and they listened and went home (1 Kings 12:21-24). In his fifth year, because they had transgressed, Shishak king of Egypt came up with a great host and took the fenced cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 12:2-4). Shemaiah told them that because they had forsaken the Lord, He had left them in Shishak’s hand. The princes and the king humbled themselves and said the Lord is righteous (2 Chronicles 12:5-6). When correction comes, the right response is to confess that the Most High is righteous in what He does. Because they humbled themselves He would not destroy them, but they would be Shishak’s servants, to learn the difference between His service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chronicles 12:7-8). If Israel confesses its iniquity and accepts the punishment, He remembers His covenant (Leviticus 26:40-42). The people today must likewise humble themselves and accept their condition as righteous judgment. Shishak carried off the treasures of the Lord’s house and the king’s house and all the shields of gold Solomon had made, and Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place, a fall from gold to brass (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Because he humbled himself, the wrath turned from him, and in Judah things went well (2 Chronicles 12:12). There was war with Jeroboam all his days, and after seventeen years Abijah his son reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:13-16).

name: Jeroboam son of Nebat
text: Two calves of gold, behold thy gods, O Israel; priests of the lowest of the people; a feast devised of his own heart. Given ten tribes by the word of Ahijah, with the promise of a sure house if he would keep the commandments as David had, Jeroboam feared that if the people went up to sacrifice at Jerusalem their hearts would turn back to Rehoboam (1 Kings 11:29-38; 1 Kings 12:26-27). He made two calves of gold, set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, made priests of the lowest of the people, and devised a feast of his own (1 Kings 12:28-33). He did not turn even after the altar was rent and his hand dried up, and the Lord cut off his house and gave Israel up because of the sins by which he made Israel to sin (1 Kings 13:33-34; 1 Kings 14:7-16). Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite whose mother was a widow, was Solomon’s servant, a mighty man of valour, and so industrious that Solomon made him ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph (1 Kings 11:26-28). Our Hidden History adds that he grew up without a father’s restraint and used Ephraim’s old discontent against Judah. Ahijah the Shilonite tore his new garment into twelve pieces and gave him ten, for ten tribes, with a plain condition: if he would hearken to all the Lord commanded and keep His statutes as David did, the Lord would build him a sure house as He built for David (1 Kings 11:29-38). When the tribes made him king, he did not trust the promise. He said in his heart that if the people went up to sacrifice in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, their heart would turn again to Rehoboam, and they would kill him (1 Kings 12:26-27). He knew the law: three times a year all the males were to appear before the Lord in the place He would choose (Deuteronomy 16:16). So he took counsel and made two calves of gold, told the people it was too much for them to go up to Jerusalem, and presented the calves as their gods that brought them out of Egypt (1 Kings 12:28). It was the same thing Israel did in the wilderness (Exodus 32:4), when the people died for it, and History in the AM says he doubled that sin. He set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this thing became a sin (1 Kings 12:29-30). From its birth as a separate nation the northern kingdom was given over to idolatry. He made a house of high places and priests of the lowest of the people, not of the sons of Levi. He ordained a feast in the eighth month, a feast he devised of his own heart, and sacrificed on the altar at Bethel to the calves he had made (1 Kings 12:31-33). Devising your own holy days is the same error men make today. A man of God came out of Judah and cried against that altar; when Jeroboam stretched out his hand to seize him, it dried up, and the altar was rent as the sign declared. He begged the man of God to entreat the Lord for him, and his hand was restored (1 Kings 13:1-6). After all these signs he did not return from his evil way, but made whoever wanted it a priest of the high places (1 Kings 13:33). The punishment of the proud has no remedy, for the plant of wickedness has taken root in him (Ecclesiasticus 3:27-28). This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, to cut it off and destroy it from the face of the earth (1 Kings 13:34). When his son Abijah fell sick, the same hard man sent his wife in disguise to the old, blind prophet Ahijah at Shiloh; the Lord makes the heart soft through trouble (Job 23:16). The Lord told Ahijah she was coming, and at the sound of her feet he called her the wife of Jeroboam and said he was sent to her with heavy tidings (1 Kings 14:1-6). The Lord had exalted Jeroboam and rent the kingdom from David’s house to give it to him, yet he made other gods and molten images and cast the Lord behind his back; therefore every male of his house would be cut off, and the rest swept away as dung until it was all gone (1 Kings 14:7-11). The child would die as soon as she entered the city, and he alone of Jeroboam’s house would come to the grave, because some good thing toward the Lord was found in him; and the child died at the threshold (1 Kings 14:12-13; 1 Kings 14:17). The sentence reached the nation. The Lord would smite Israel as a reed shaken in the water, root them out of the good land, and scatter them beyond the river because of their groves, giving Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, who sinned and made Israel to sin (1 Kings 14:15-16). Against Abijah of Judah his great army and its golden calves could not prevail, and he never recovered strength (2 Chronicles 13:8-20). Baasha killed Nadab his son and left none that breathed of his house, according to Ahijah’s word (1 Kings 15:29). Every northern king after him walked in his sins, until Israel was carried away to Assyria (2 Kings 17:21-23). Dan, where the second calf stood, stayed in idolatry, swearing by the sin of Samaria (Amos 8:14), and is not named when the tribes are sealed (Revelation 7:5-8).

name: Amaziah the priest of Bethel
text: Forbidding Amos to prophesy at the king’s chapel; sending to Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him. When Amos, a herdman of Tekoa, prophesied at Bethel that the sanctuaries of Israel would be laid waste and the Lord would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword, Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to King Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him and the land could not bear his words (Amos 7:7-11). He told the prophet to go and prophesy in Judah and never again at Bethel, the king’s chapel (Amos 7:12-13). Amos answered that the Lord had taken him from the flock to prophesy to Israel, and pronounced the judgment on Amaziah’s house and on Israel’s land (Amos 7:14-17). Amos prophesied in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel (Amos 1:1). History in the AM stresses that this is Jeroboam the second, not Jeroboam the son of Nebat of the split, though he departed not from the sins of the first Jeroboam, who made Israel to sin (2 Kings 14:23-24). The Lord showed Amos grasshoppers eating the grass of the land and a fire devouring the great deep, and twice Amos pleaded for Jacob because he was small, and the Lord relented (Amos 7:1-6). Then the Lord stood on a wall with a plumbline in His hand, a builder’s instrument for measuring, and said He would set it in the midst of His people Israel and not pass by them any more: the high places of Isaac would be desolate, the sanctuaries of Israel laid waste, and He would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword (Amos 7:7-9). Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel, where Jeroboam the son of Nebat had set his calf, sent to the king that Amos had conspired against him in the midst of Israel and the land could not bear all his words, for Amos was saying that Jeroboam would die by the sword and Israel would surely be led away captive out of their land (Amos 7:10-11). The teachers read the report two ways. One class takes it as Amos’s own directness and fearlessness, telling a king to his face that he would die. History in the AM, on the reign of Jeroboam the second, says Amaziah was saucing it up to slander him to the king: Amos had not said Jeroboam would die by the sword, but that the northern kingdom would go into captivity if it did not repent. Either way, the priest tried to put a charge of treason on the prophet to get him put to death. Our own people will do this to us; the time comes when whoever kills you will think he does God service (John 16:2). Amaziah also told Amos, calling him a seer, to flee into the land of Judah, eat bread and prophesy there, and never prophesy again at Bethel, for it was the king’s chapel and the king’s court (Amos 7:12-13). The class of 2026-07-18 draws the point: Amaziah was more concerned with protecting the king’s institution than with hearing the word of the Lord, and the same thing goes on today. Instead of correcting leaders and teachers with their ridiculous doctrines, they prefer that we not speak at all. It was the northern kingdom’s habit from the beginning: they gave the Nazarites wine to drink and commanded the prophets not to prophesy (Amos 2:11-12), and that goes into lies and deceit, doing anything to stop the word of the Most High. Amos answered that he was no prophet and no prophet’s son, but a herdman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit, and the Lord took him as he followed the flock and told him to go and prophesy to His people Israel (Amos 7:14-15). The prophet did not choose himself; the Lord chose him and ordained him, as He ordained Jeremiah before he was born (Jeremiah 1:5). The Most High gives His word to the prophets, and the prophet’s job is to carry out the word of the Lord, no more, no less; if you do not like it, too bad. Because Amaziah said not to prophesy against Israel nor drop a word against the house of Isaac, the Lord said his wife would be a harlot in the city, his sons and daughters would fall by the sword, his land would be divided by line, he would die in a polluted land, and Israel would surely go into captivity out of its land (Amos 7:16-17). Amaziah was trying to get the brother to stop prophesying, and judgment came on him for that. The priest of the king’s chapel could protect none of it: not his wife, his children, his inheritance, nor the ground he would be buried in. The judgment came as spoken. Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria took Gilead, Galilee and all the land of Naphtali and carried them captive, and in the ninth year of Hoshea Samaria fell and Israel was carried away to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 17:6). They did not want to hear it, but it happened, because they sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes, and in that day the mighty would not deliver himself (Amos 2:6; Amos 2:14).

name: The man of God from Judah
text: Turning back to eat bread and drink water at Bethel against the word of the Lord, on the word of a prophet who lied. A man of God came out of Judah by the word of the Lord to Bethel and cried against Jeroboam’s altar, naming Josiah, a child of David’s house, who would burn the priests of the high places on it; the altar was rent and the king’s hand dried up as the sign declared (1 Kings 13:1-6). He refused the king’s reward and meal because the Lord had charged him to eat no bread, drink no water and go home another way (1 Kings 13:7-10). Then an old prophet of Bethel lied to him, claiming an angel’s word, and he turned back and ate; on the road a lion killed him, and his body lay in the way with the ass and the lion standing by it (1 Kings 13:11-26). Jeroboam stood by his altar at Bethel burning incense to his calf when the man of God cried against the altar: a child named Josiah would be born to the house of David and would offer the priests of the high places on it and burn men’s bones on it. He gave a sign that same day, that the altar would be rent and its ashes poured out (1 Kings 13:1-3). The prophecy came hundreds of years before the child was born. When Jeroboam stretched out his hand to have him seized, the hand dried up so that he could not draw it back, and the altar was rent (1 Kings 13:4-5).
