The Lord reproves kings for the sake of His anointed and lets no man do His prophets harm (Psalms 105:14-15). Pain changed the king’s thoughts: he wanted the man put to death a few minutes before, and now he wanted him to pray for him, and the hand was restored (1 Kings 13:6). The king invited him home to refresh himself and receive a reward. The man of God answered that even for half the king’s house he would not go in, eat bread or drink water in that place, for so the word of the Lord had charged him, and not to return by the way he came; and he went home another way (1 Kings 13:7-10). The Lord had told him what to do and what not to do, and so far he was doing right. Then an old prophet of Bethel, told by his sons what had happened, rode after him and found him sitting under an oak. The man of God repeated his charge. The old man said he was a prophet too, and an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord to bring him back to eat and drink; but he lied to him (1 Kings 13:11-18). The study notes say the man of God, giving reverence to the older prophet, went back and ate (1 Kings 13:19); a man is not to let reverence for any person cause him to fall (Ecclesiasticus 4:22). The teachers press the warning. The Lord is not wishy-washy; He does not tell a man one thing and then send word by someone else to do the opposite. The Lord speaks to His prophets in visions and dreams, and mouth to mouth only with Moses (Numbers 12:6-8), so a claim of an angel’s new message deserved suspicion. The Lord proves His people by such voices, to know whether they love Him with all their heart (Deuteronomy 13:3-4). Some come into your life for blessings and some for cursings, but ultimately it is to try each one of us. As they sat at the table, the word of the Lord came to the very prophet who had lied, and he cried to the man of God that because he had disobeyed the Lord’s command and eaten and drunk where he was forbidden, his body would not be buried in the tomb of his fathers (1 Kings 13:20-22). A lion met him on the road and killed him, and his body was thrown in the way, with the ass standing by it and the lion standing by it, neither eating the body nor tearing the ass (1 Kings 13:23-25). History in the AM calls this plainly spiritual: a lion left to itself would have eaten both the man and the donkey, but this lion was sent to take vengeance on a disobedient man and then stood watch until the old prophet came. There are spirits created for vengeance, and among them are the teeth of wild beasts (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-30). The Most High used the deceiver to prove whether the man would keep the charge; the deceived and the deceiver are His (Job 12:16). The old prophet said it was the man of God who had been disobedient, buried him in his own grave, mourned him as his brother, and told his sons to lay his bones beside him, for the word cried against the altar of Bethel would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:26-32). Even though he disobeyed, he was a real prophet, and the test of a true prophet is that the thing he speaks comes to pass (Deuteronomy 18:22). It did. Josiah broke down the altar at Bethel, burned bones from the sepulchres on it to pollute it according to the word of the man of God, and when shown his tomb said to let him alone, so his bones were not moved (2 Kings 23:15-18). The warning for today is simple: do not deviate from the instructions for a voice that makes itself equal to them.

name: The old prophet of Beth-el
text: Lying in the name of the Lord, claiming an angel’s word, to turn a prophet from his charge. An old prophet living in Bethel heard from his sons what the man of God from Judah had done at Jeroboam’s altar, rode after him, and brought him back to eat and drink by claiming that an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord; but he lied to him (1 Kings 13:11-19). At the table the true word came through the liar himself, the man of God was killed by a lion on the road, and the old prophet buried him in his own grave and asked to be laid beside him, confessing that the word against Bethel would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:20-32). No sentence on the old prophet is recorded. The man of God had kept his charge before the king: no bread, no water, and home by another way (1 Kings 13:7-10). Then there dwelt an old prophet in Bethel, the city of Jeroboam’s calf. His sons told him all the works the man of God had done and the words he had spoken to the king, and showed him which way he had gone. He had them saddle the ass, rode after him, and found him sitting under an oak, and asked whether he was the man of God who came from Judah (1 Kings 13:11-14). He invited him home to eat bread. The man of God repeated the word of the Lord to him: he could not return, go in, eat or drink in that place (1 Kings 13:15-17). The old man answered that he was a prophet also, and an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord to bring him back to eat bread and drink water; but he lied to him (1 Kings 13:18). So the man of God went back with him and ate (1 Kings 13:19). The teaching hears the voice of the serpent with Eve: first a little resistance, then the voice that talks a man out of a plain command. He came with a claim no one could check, an angel’s word, but the Lord speaks to His prophets in visions and dreams and mouth to mouth only with Moses (Numbers 12:6-8); this man said an angel came to him, and he was lying. A prophet who presumes to speak a word in the name of the Lord which He has not commanded him to speak is condemned by the law (Deuteronomy 18:20). When a student asked in class who the old prophet was, the answer was that the moral is not who he was but what he did to the man of God: he made himself equal to him, so the man let his guard down. That is why the congregation does not hook up with every other camp that quotes the same scriptures and claims the Lord is working with them too, for such a man will get you killed. The class note sets it beside Jeremiah’s warning not to put blind trust in a brother, because brothers supplant one another (Jeremiah 9:4). The word of the Lord came to the old prophet at his own table, and he had to cry out the sentence on the man he had deceived: because he disobeyed the Lord’s command, his body would not be buried in the tomb of his fathers (1 Kings 13:20-22). A lion killed the man of God on the road and stood by the body with the ass, and when men told it in the city, the old prophet said it was the man of God who had been disobedient to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 13:23-26). The study notes say the Most High used the deceiver to prove whether the man would keep his charge, for the deceived and the deceiver are His (Job 12:16). He went, found the body untouched, brought it back on the ass, laid it in his own grave, and mourned over him as his brother. He told his sons that when he died they should bury him in the same sepulchre and lay his bones beside the bones of the man of God, for the word cried against the altar in Bethel and against the high places of Samaria would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:27-32). History in the AM notes the point for Jeroboam: the Lord had shown him that the word was real, first by the sign on the altar and then by the death of the man who disobeyed it. Scripture records no punishment for the old prophet. What it records is that his confession came true. Josiah burned the bones of Bethel on its altar, and when he came to the tomb of the man of God he said to let him alone; so they let his bones alone, together with the bones of the prophet who had asked to lie beside him (2 Kings 23:17-18).

name: Baasha
text: Walking in the way of Jeroboam after being exalted out of the dust to destroy Jeroboam’s house. Baasha conspired against Nadab the son of Jeroboam, killed him, and destroyed all the house of Jeroboam as Ahijah had foretold, then reigned twenty-four years walking in the same way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:27-34). He built Ramah to stop the people of the north from going over to Asa and the Lord (2 Chronicles 16:1). The word came by Jehu the son of Hanani that the Lord, who had lifted him out of the dust, would make his house like the house of Jeroboam, and it was fulfilled when Zimri killed his son Elah and all his kin (1 Kings 16:1-13). Nadab the son of Jeroboam reigned two years and did evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him and struck him down at Gibbethon, reigned in his place, and struck all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word the Lord spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite, because of the sins by which Jeroboam made Israel to sin (1 Kings 15:25-30). The study notes mark it as the fulfilment, years later, of the judgment on Jeroboam’s descendants. Then he reigned twenty-four years in Tirzah and did evil in the sight of the Lord, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin he made Israel commit (1 Kings 15:33-34). The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming. He also made war on Judah. There was war between Asa and Baasha all their days, and Baasha came up and built Ramah to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah (1 Kings 15:16-17). The study notes on Chronicles give the reason: tribes out of Israel had been turning their hearts back to the Most High and joining Asa, and Baasha was trying to stop the northern kingdom from coming down to Judah (2 Chronicles 16:1). Asa, instead of crying to the Most High as he had against Zerah, hired Benhadad of Syria with the treasures of the Lord’s house to break his league with Baasha; Benhadad struck the cities of Israel, and Baasha left off building Ramah (2 Chronicles 16:2-6). The word of the Lord came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha: the Lord had exalted him out of the dust and made him prince over His people Israel, and he had walked in the way of Jeroboam and made Israel sin, provoking Him with their sins. Therefore He would take away the posterity of Baasha and make his house like the house of Jeroboam; the dogs would eat those of his who died in the city, and the birds those who died in the field (1 Kings 16:1-4). The same judgment falls because the same sin is repeated, just as descendants keep the pattern of their fathers though they saw the ruin it brought. The word came against him both for all the evil he did in walking like Jeroboam and because he killed him (1 Kings 16:7). Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned (1 Kings 16:6). Elah reigned two years. His servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, killed him while he was drunk in a steward’s house, and as soon as Zimri sat on the throne he killed all the house of Baasha, leaving not one male, nor his kinsfolk nor his friends, according to the word spoken by Jehu (1 Kings 16:8-12). It all came for the sins of Baasha and of Elah his son, who provoked the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:13). Moses saw it in the spirit: Israel grew fat and kicked, forsook the God who made him, and provoked Him to jealousy with strange gods (Deuteronomy 32:15-21). A generation later the same sentence was pronounced on Ahab, that his house would be made like the house of Jeroboam and like the house of Baasha (1 Kings 21:22).

name: Zimri
text: Conspiring against his master Elah as he drank himself drunk; slaying all the house of Baasha; seven days on the throne. Zimri, captain of half the chariots of Elah the son of Baasha, killed his king while he lay drunk in a steward’s house in Tirzah, took the throne, and killed all the house of Baasha, fulfilling the word spoken by Jehu the prophet (1 Kings 16:8-13). He reigned seven days. The army encamped at Gibbethon made Omri king, besieged Tirzah, and when Zimri saw the city taken he burnt the king’s house over himself and died for his sins and his treason (1 Kings 16:15-20). Years later Jezebel threw his name at Jehu from her window (2 Kings 9:31). Elah the son of Baasha reigned over Israel two years in Tirzah. His servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him while he was getting drunk in Tirzah in the house of Arza, his steward, went in, struck him down and killed him, and reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:8-10). He waited until the king was helplessly drunk. As soon as he sat on the throne he killed all the house of Baasha; he left not one male, neither of his kinsfolk nor of his friends, according to the word the Lord spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet, for the sins of Baasha and of Elah his son, who provoked the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:11-13). The 2013 class on the wants and needs of the people sets Zimri beside Achan and his Babylonish garment. Not everyone covets clothing, because not everyone has the same covetous spirit; some covet power and preeminence. Zimri’s covetousness was power. He wanted to be king, it was good to be the king, and so he killed the king to sit on the throne. When you read Kings and Chronicles you read about a lot of conspiracy among our people. The class carries the same spirit into the New Testament with Diotrephes, who loved to have the preeminence among the brethren, would not receive the apostles, and prated against them with malicious words (3 John 1:9-10), and calls it the same evil seen today, when men want to be known as number one. Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. The people were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, and when they heard that he had conspired and slain the king, all Israel made Omri, the captain of the host, king over Israel that day in the camp. Omri went up from Gibbethon with all Israel and besieged Tirzah (1 Kings 16:15-17). When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the palace of the king’s house, burnt the house over himself with fire, and died (1 Kings 16:18). His death came for his sins, for he too walked in the way of Jeroboam, and the record names the treason he committed (1 Kings 16:19-20). The study notes stress that point: treason was punishable by death in that time. Years later his name came up again. When Jehu rode into Jezreel as the Lord’s instrument against the house of Ahab, Jezebel painted her face, looked out of a window, and called down to ask whether Zimri, who killed his master, had peace (2 Kings 9:30-31). It did not save her; Jehu called for anyone on his side, and she was thrown down and trodden under foot, as Elijah had said (2 Kings 9:32-37).

name: Omri
text: Doing worse than all that were before him; walking in all the way of Jeroboam. After Zimri’s seven days Israel was split between Tibni and Omri, the captain of the host; Omri’s side prevailed, and he reigned twelve years (1 Kings 16:21-23). He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built the city that became the capital of the northern kingdom, yet he did worse than all before him, walking in all the way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 16:24-26). His son Ahab brought in Baal, and the prophets later named the whole corruption after them both: the statutes of Omri and the works of the house of Ahab (Micah 6:16). When Zimri burnt the palace over himself, the people of Israel were divided in two: half followed Tibni the son of Ginath to make him king, and half followed Omri. Those who followed Omri prevailed, Tibni died, and Omri reigned (1 Kings 16:21-22). In the thirty-first year of Asa he began to reign over Israel, twelve years, six of them in Tirzah (1 Kings 16:23). He bought the hill Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, built a city on it, and named it after Shemer, the owner of the hill (1 Kings 16:24). The Samaritan Woman teaching begins its whole account here: from that time Samaria was the capital city of the northern kingdom, the head of Ephraim (Isaiah 7:9), and the land of the ten tribes that revolted from the house of David. When Christ met the woman at the well in Sychar, a city of Samaria near the ground Jacob gave to Joseph, he was speaking to a daughter of that kingdom (John 4:4-9). But Omri did evil in the eyes of the Lord, worse than all who were before him, for he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat and in the sin he made Israel commit, provoking the Lord God of Israel with their vanities (1 Kings 16:25-26). The teachers observe that there were no righteous kings in the northern kingdom from Jeroboam all the way down; every time a king of Israel is named, the record says he did evil in the sight of the Lord. History in the AM counts Omri as the sixth king of the north, after Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah and Zimri. Omri died and was buried in Samaria, the city he had bought, and Ahab his son reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:27-28). History in the AM says Omri built Samaria into a rich city, a northern Jerusalem, through an alliance with the Zidonians of Tyre and Zidon, and sealed it by marrying his son to their daughter. Ahab did evil above all before him, and as if the sins of Jeroboam were a light thing, he married Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians and served Baal, raising an altar to Baal in the house of Baal he built in Samaria (1 Kings 16:30-32). So idol worship was established in the very city Omri built. Generations later Micah gave the verdict by name. The rich were violent and the people liars, so the Lord would strike them and leave them desolate; they would sow and not reap and press olives without oil, because they still kept the statutes of Omri and all the works of the house of Ahab and followed their counsel, and so they would carry the reproach of His people (Micah 6:12-16). Injurious Practices in the Kingdom asks why Micah names Omri and Ahab, and answers that the works of idolatry, marriage to the heathen and every other wickedness set up in their days were still being kept in the land. Amos warned that those who swear by the sin of Samaria and say the god of Dan lives would fall and never rise again (Amos 8:14). The land of Samaria that Omri bought was the land the northern kingdom was carried away out of, when the king of Assyria besieged it three years and took it in the ninth year of Hoshea (2 Kings 17:5-6).

name: Ahab
text: Marrying Jezebel and serving Baal above all the kings before him; letting go Ben-hadad whom the Lord appointed to destruction; selling himself to work wickedness. Ahab the son of Omri did evil above all the kings before him: he married Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, served Baal, and built him an altar and a house in Samaria (1 Kings 16:30-33). He blamed Elijah for the drought his own sin brought, spared Ben-hadad whom the Lord had appointed to destruction, and took Naboth’s vineyard after Jezebel had him murdered, selling himself to work wickedness (1 Kings 18:17-18; 1 Kings 20:31-42; 1 Kings 21:19-25). His humbling delayed the ruin of his house to his son’s days, but he died at Ramoth-gilead and the dogs licked his blood (1 Kings 21:27-29; 1 Kings 22:34-38). As if walking in the sins of Jeroboam were a light thing, he took Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians to wife, served and worshipped Baal, reared an altar for Baal in the house of Baal he built in Samaria, and made a grove, provoking the Lord more than all the kings of Israel before him (1 Kings 16:29-33). The study notes see Solomon in it, whose wives turned his heart after Ashtoreth of the Zidonians (1 Kings 11:4-5), against the law on marriage outside the people (Deuteronomy 7:3). History in the AM adds that Omri had made the alliance with the Zidonians of Tyre and Zidon by marrying his son to their daughter, so that Samaria became a little Zidon in Israel. The teachers call Ahab the weak, woman-led king: the Jezebel spirit cannot exist without a man who enables it, and Ahab let Jezebel reign through him, kill the prophets, and feed Baal’s prophets at her table. When Elijah appeared after three years of drought, Ahab asked whether he was the one who troubled Israel. That is the mind of a wicked person: he blamed the ordained prophet of God for the trouble instead of his own wickedness. Elijah answered that Ahab and his father’s house had troubled Israel by forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). Into a malicious soul wisdom will not enter; sin comes in and wisdom goes out, so Ahab had thoughts without understanding (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4-5). When Ben-hadad besieged Samaria, the study notes call it Ahab’s judgment for trying to kill Elijah, serving Baal, and letting Jezebel run him. Yet a prophet told him the Lord would deliver that great multitude into his hand that he might know He is the Lord, and He did it twice, the second time because the Syrians said the Lord was a god of the hills and not of the valleys (1 Kings 20:13; 1 Kings 20:28). The Most High was giving Ahab a chance to repent, but he did not check Jezebel or destroy the idols. When Ben-hadad’s servants came in sackcloth with ropes on their heads, Ahab called him his brother, took him into his chariot, and sent him away with a covenant (1 Kings 20:31-34). Look at his wickedness: this Syrian had just tried to kill him. A prophet in disguise drew from Ahab his own sentence, that because he let go a man appointed to utter destruction, his life would go for that man’s life (1 Kings 20:39-42). Then he coveted Naboth’s vineyard and when Jezebel had Naboth stoned on false witness he rose up and went down to take it; he shares the guilt, for he let her commit the crime and went to claim the reward (1 Kings 21:1-16). Elijah met him in the vineyard. Ahab called him his enemy, and Elijah answered that he had found him because he had sold himself to work evil in the sight of the Lord; the Lord would cut off every male of his house and make it like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and dogs would lick his blood where they licked Naboth’s (1 Kings 21:19-24). There was none like Ahab, stirred up by Jezebel his wife (1 Kings 21:25). When he heard it he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted and walked humbly, and the Lord said He would not bring the evil in his days but in his son’s days (1 Kings 21:27-29). The judgment was not cancelled but delayed and moved to the next generation; genuine humbling before the Most High moves His hand. Three years later he wanted Ramoth-gilead, and four hundred prophets told him with one mouth to go up. Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Ahab admitted there was Micaiah, but he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him (1 Kings 22:6-8). Micaiah saw Israel scattered on the hills as sheep with no shepherd, and a lying spirit put in the mouths of all Ahab’s prophets; the Most High used the lie to bring the judgment He had already declared (1 Kings 22:17-23). Ahab jailed Micaiah and went into battle in disguise (1 Kings 22:27-30). An arrow drawn at a venture struck him between the joints of his armour, he died at evening propped up in his chariot, and when they washed it in the pool of Samaria the dogs licked up his blood, according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:34-38). In Jehu’s day the rest came: seventy sons of Ahab beheaded and every one of his house cut off, that nothing of the word spoken by Elijah would fall to the ground (2 Kings 10:7-11).

name: Jezebel
text: Cutting off the prophets of the Lord; feeding eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the groves at her table; whoredoms and witchcrafts. Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians became Ahab’s wife and brought Baal into Israel; she cut off the prophets of the Lord and fed eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and of the groves at her table (1 Kings 16:31; 1 Kings 18:4; 1 Kings 18:19). After Carmel she swore to take Elijah’s life, and she had Naboth murdered by false witness so Ahab could take his vineyard (1 Kings 19:1-2; 1 Kings 21:8-16). Jehu was anointed to avenge the blood of the prophets at her hand; she was thrown from a window at Jezreel and the dogs ate her, as Elijah had said (2 Kings 9:7-10; 2 Kings 9:30-37). Ahab took Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians to wife and went and served Baal (1 Kings 16:31). History in the AM explains the marriage as the price of Omri’s alliance with Tyre and Zidon; with Jezebel came the images and priests of Baal, and Samaria became a little Zidon in Israel. When Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah hid a hundred of them by fifty in a cave and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4). Ahab searched every nation and kingdom for Elijah to slay him; the study notes say that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead, so she got Ahab to do her bidding (1 Kings 18:10). The four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves ate at Jezebel’s table: she was the one feeding eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her (1 Kings 18:19). Walking in Elijah’s Footsteps puts it bluntly: she was the boss at that time, and Ahab was just there for show. The Giving the Sense class on Thyatira adds that the Jezebel spirit cannot exist without a man who enables it. When Ahab told her all that Elijah had done and how he had slain her prophets with the sword, she sent a messenger swearing by her gods to make his life as one of theirs by that time the next day (1 Kings 19:1-2). The fire from heaven did not bring her to repentance. Elijah, remembering that she had killed prophets before him, ran for his life (1 Kings 19:3). Her hand is in Naboth’s death, which is entered as its own case. When Ahab sulked because Naboth would not sell his fathers’ inheritance, she mocked his weakness, asked whether he governed the kingdom of Israel, and promised him the vineyard. She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal, the signet of the king’s authority, told the elders to proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high, and set two sons of Belial, children of the devil, to witness that he blasphemed God and the king; they stoned him, and she told Ahab to take possession (1 Kings 21:5-15). Injurious Practices in the Kingdom says that really Jezebel was the king: she ruled through his power. The record says Ahab did very abominably, stirred up by Jezebel his wife (1 Kings 21:25). Of Jezebel the Lord said that the dogs would eat her by the wall of Jezreel (1 Kings 21:23). The charge given to Jehu named her: he was anointed to smite the house of Ahab, that the Lord might avenge the blood of His servants the prophets and of all the servants of the Lord at her hand, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it continue; the dogs would eat her in the portion of Jezreel, and none would bury her (2 Kings 9:6-10). When Joram rode out and asked whether it was peace, Jehu answered that there could be no peace while the whoredoms and witchcrafts of his mother Jezebel were so many (2 Kings 9:22). When Jehu came to Jezreel she painted her face, dressed her head, and looked out at a window, returning to her seductive ways, and she called down to ask whether Zimri, who killed his master, had peace (2 Kings 9:30-31). Jehu asked who was on his side, two or three eunuchs looked out, and at his word they threw her down; her blood spattered the wall and the horses, and he trod her under foot (2 Kings 9:32-33). When they went to bury her as a king’s daughter they found only the skull, the feet and the palms of her hands, fulfilling the word by Elijah that dogs would eat her flesh and her body would be as dung on the field (2 Kings 9:34-37). The house of Ahab was then cut off to the last of its sons, and Jehu took vengeance on the priests and servants of Baal (2 Kings 10:11; 2 Kings 10:18-28). Christ still names her. To the church in Thyatira He says that He has a few things against its angel, because he allowed that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce His servants to commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols (Revelation 2:20). The teachers apply it to the Jezebel spirit today: women who call themselves prophetesses out of the order the scriptures set, and the men who let them lead.

name: Hiel the Bethelite
text: Building Jericho again under the oath Joshua adjured before the Lord. When the walls of Jericho fell and the city was burned, Joshua laid an oath on Israel before the Lord: the man who rose up and rebuilt Jericho would lay its foundation at the cost of his firstborn and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son (Joshua 6:20-26). The study notes put it plainly: the city was not to be rebuilt. In the days of Ahab, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt it, laying the foundation in his firstborn Abiram and setting up the gates in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord by Joshua (1 Kings 16:34). Jericho was shut tight against Israel, with its garrison and walls, and the battle was decided before it began: the Lord told Joshua He had given the city, its king and its mighty men into his hand (Joshua 6:1-2). The people compassed it as the Lord commanded, the priests blew the trumpets, the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat (Joshua 6:20). They took the city and utterly destroyed all that was in it, burnt it with fire, brought the silver, gold, brass and iron into the treasury of the house of the Lord, and saved Rahab and her household because she hid the messengers (Joshua 6:21-25). History in the AM reads Joshua’s charge that the city and all in it were devoted to the Lord, and that Israel must keep itself from the accursed thing lest it trouble the camp (Joshua 6:17-19). Then Joshua adjured them at that time: cursed before the Lord would be the man who rose up and built the city of Jericho; he would lay its foundation in his firstborn, and set up its gates in his youngest son (Joshua 6:26). The study notes give the plain sense: the city was not to be rebuilt. A word spoken before the Lord binds. When a man vows a vow to the Lord or swears an oath to bind his soul, he is not to break his word but do all that he said (Numbers 30:2); the notes on that law add that a vow cannot simply be gone back on with a request for forgiveness afterward. Generations later, in the days of Ahab, when the northern kingdom had gone after Baal above all the kings before, Hiel of Bethel built Jericho (1 Kings 16:34). The study notes set his building in the same passage as Ahab’s marriage to Jezebel, his altar to Baal and his grove. He came out of Bethel, where Jeroboam had set up his calf, and he set his hand to a city the Lord had put under a curse. He laid the foundation of Jericho in Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord which He spoke by Joshua the son of Nun (1 Kings 16:34). The two ends of the work answered the two parts of the curse exactly as Joshua had spoken it: the firstborn when the foundation was laid, the youngest when the gates were hung. The record gives the names of his sons beside the report that the city was built. Joshua himself had warned Israel how the word of the Lord works. Near his death he had them acknowledge in all their hearts that not one thing had failed of all the good things the Lord spoke concerning them; all came to pass. The other side is a heavy scripture: as all the good things had come, so the Lord would bring on them all the evil things, until He had destroyed them from the good land, if they transgressed the covenant and served other gods (Joshua 23:14-16). The study notes press it on those who come out of Christianity told that God is good all the time: the Most High also promised to destroy His people when they go off, and that is why Israel is not at home today. Hiel’s sons fell under a word spoken generations before him.

name: Elijah
text: As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand: shutting the heaven by prayer, standing alone against eight hundred and fifty at Carmel, and running before the king in the hand of the Lord. Elijah the Tishbite of Gilead stood before Ahab and declared, by the Lord God of Israel before whom he stood, that there would be no dew nor rain but by his word (1 Kings 17:1). The Lord fed him by ravens and by a widow of Zarephath, raised her son at his prayer, and at Carmel answered him by fire before all Israel and the prophets of Baal, then sent rain (1 Kings 17:2-24; 1 Kings 18:17-46). Fleeing Jezebel, he asked to die, but the Lord fed him, spoke to him at Horeb in a still small voice, told him seven thousand had not bowed to Baal, and gave him Elisha; he was taken up by a whirlwind (1 Kings 19:1-19; 2 Kings 2:11-13). The session on these chapters frames everything on the power of the Most High, set on display through His prophet. Elijah told Ahab there would be no dew nor rain those years but according to his word; he prayed, and it did not rain (1 Kings 17:1). The history the class reads calls him a man of tempestuous nature, guided by no consideration of expediency, who thundered against the weak, woman-led Ahab and was gone before anyone could seize him; he wore a leather girdle and a hairy cloak, unlike the effeminate dress of the worshippers of Baal, and he was known by it (2 Kings 1:8). The Lord sent him to hide by the brook Cherith, where the ravens brought him bread and flesh morning and evening, for He can command the animals to feed a man (1 Kings 17:2-6). When the brook dried up He sent him to a widow at Zarephath, whose meal and oil did not fail, and at his prayer her dead son revived (1 Kings 17:7-22). She said that now she knew he was a man of God and the word of the Lord in his mouth was truth (1 Kings 17:24): a man of God is known because the word in his mouth is the word of truth. In the third year he showed himself to Ahab, and when Ahab called him the troubler of Israel, he answered that Ahab and his father’s house were, for forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). At Carmel he asked the people how long they would halt between two opinions; if the Lord is God, follow Him. They answered not a word (1 Kings 18:21). It is a call for us to examine ourselves and not keep one foot in and one foot out, for the lukewarm are spewed out (Revelation 3:15-16). The prophets of Baal cried from morning until past noon, leaped on their altar and cut themselves till the blood gushed out, and Elijah mocked them; no one answered, because the Lord will not give His glory to another and the gods of the nations are idols (1 Kings 18:26-29; Isaiah 42:8; Psalms 96:5). He repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones for the twelve tribes, drenched the sacrifice three times until the trench was full, and at the evening sacrifice prayed that the people would know the Lord is God in Israel and that He had turned their heart back again (1 Kings 18:30-37). The fire of the Lord fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the dust, and licked up the water. The people fell on their faces crying that the Lord, He is the God, and at Elijah’s word the prophets of Baal were taken down to the brook Kishon and slain (1 Kings 18:38-40). The false shepherds of today stand under the same woe (Jeremiah 23:1-2). Then he prayed on the top of Carmel with his face between his knees until a cloud like a man’s hand rose from the sea, and there was a great rain; the hand of the Lord was on him and he ran before Ahab to Jezreel (1 Kings 18:41-46). When Jezebel swore to take his life he fled, sat under a juniper tree, and asked to die, saying he was no better than his fathers (1 Kings 19:1-4). The notes say our forefathers had ultimate faith and understood regeneration, trusting the Most High to raise them when He chose. An angel fed him twice, and in the strength of that food he went forty days and nights to Horeb (1 Kings 19:5-8). The Lord passed by in wind, earthquake and fire, and was not in them, and then came a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11-12); we do not know who we are dealing with. He said he alone was left, and the Lord sent him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha in his place, and told him He had left Himself seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:14-18). Elijah was not by himself; the Lord had people reserved who had not yet awakened, and the classes say that is why we pray for more labourers and preach, for we never know which flyer or video will wake one. He cast his mantle on Elisha (1 Kings 19:19), founded a circle of disciples who kept the ancient law alive, and was taken up by a whirlwind while Elisha cried after him as his father (2 Kings 2:11-13). Christ said Elias had come already, and the disciples understood He spoke of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:11-13), who came in his spirit before the great day (Malachi 4:5).

name: The widow of Zarephath
text: Making the man of God a little cake first, out of the last handful of meal, according to the word. When the brook Cherith dried up, the Lord sent Elijah to Zarephath of Zidon, where He had commanded a widow to sustain him; she had only a handful of meal and a little oil, and was gathering sticks to make a last meal for herself and her son (1 Kings 17:7-12). Elijah told her to make him a little cake first, and the meal and oil did not fail until the rain came (1 Kings 17:13-16). When her son died, Elijah prayed and the child revived, and she confessed that he was a man of God and the word of the Lord in his mouth was truth (1 Kings 17:17-24). Christ named her in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:25-26). The brook dried up for want of rain, and the word of the Lord sent Elijah to Zarephath, which belonged to Zidon, where He had commanded a widow woman to sustain him (1 Kings 17:7-9). The study notes stress the distance: from the east side by Jordan to the west by Sidon on the coast was a hard walk, with no water anywhere. The Jubilee class places Zarephath in Lebanon, the northern bound named when the captivity of Israel returns to possess the land of the Canaanites (Obadiah 1:20). The Lord who had commanded the ravens now commanded a widow; the class on temptation calls it a show of how mighty the prophets were, for God said, I commanded the animals, and now a woman is going to feed you. At the gate of the city she was gathering sticks. Elijah asked her for a little water, and as she went he asked for a morsel of bread. She answered, by the Lord his God, that she had no cake, only a handful of meal in a barrel and a little oil in a cruse, and she was gathering two sticks to dress it for herself and her son, that they might eat it and die (1 Kings 17:10-12). Elijah told her not to fear, but to go and do as she had said, only to make him a little cake first and bring it to him, and afterward make for herself and her son; for the Lord God of Israel said the meal and the oil would not run out until the day He sent rain (1 Kings 17:13-14). She went and did according to the saying of Elijah (1 Kings 17:15). The study notes draw a precept from the order: feed the man of God first; the man eats first. Sisters must trust in the Lord when He tells them to reverence their husbands and be submissive in all things, and not lean to their own understanding; the wife is to see that she reverences her husband (Ephesians 5:33), and that reverence goes into the honour of feeding the man first, as the widow did. She was asked to give out of her last handful before she saw any increase, and for trusting the Lord and obeying she was sustained. She and Elijah and her house ate many days, and the meal and the oil did not run out, according to the word the Lord spoke by Elijah (1 Kings 17:15-16). The little she had did not run out until God sent rain on the earth again; that is the power God gave His prophets to do what is not natural. After these things her son fell sick, so severe that there was no breath left in him. She asked Elijah whether he had come to bring her sin to mind and kill her son; her thought was that the child was paying for the parent’s sins (1 Kings 17:17-18). Elijah took the child up to the loft where he lodged, laid him on his own bed, stretched himself on him three times, and cried to the Lord to let the child’s soul come into him again. The Lord heard the voice of Elijah, the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived, and Elijah brought him down and gave him to his mother (1 Kings 17:19-23). The notes give praise that Elijah was there to call on the Lord, for it was not the young man’s time to go. A man’s days are determined, his months are numbered with the Most High, and he cannot pass the limit set for him; because the child’s day had not come, the Lord let his soul return (Job 14:1-5). She said that now she knew he was a man of God and that the word of the Lord in his mouth was truth (1 Kings 17:24). Christ brought her up in the synagogue at Nazareth. There were many widows in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut three years and six months, but Elias was sent to none of them except a widow of Sarepta, a city of Sidon; and none of the many lepers of Israel was cleansed in Elisha’s time but Naaman the Syrian. At this the synagogue was filled with wrath and tried to cast him headlong from the hill (Luke 4:25-29). Giving the Sense reads Christ’s point this way: he was not sent to everybody, just as Elijah was sent to one widow.

name: Obadiah, who hid the prophets
text: Taking an hundred prophets and hiding them by fifty in a cave, and feeding them with bread and water, while governor of Ahab’s house. Obadiah was governor of Ahab’s house and feared the Lord greatly; when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, he took a hundred of them, hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water through a severe famine (1 Kings 18:3-4). Sent out by Ahab to search for grass, he met Elijah on the road and was afraid to carry his message, lest the Spirit carry the prophet away and Ahab kill him; Elijah swore he would show himself that day, and Obadiah went (1 Kings 18:5-16). His errand brought Ahab to Elijah and set the stage for Carmel (1 Kings 18:17-19). In the third year of the drought the word came to Elijah to show himself to Ahab, and there was a severe famine in Samaria. Ahab called Obadiah, the governor of his house; and Obadiah feared the Lord greatly, for when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, he took a hundred prophets, hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:1-4). The study notes say he put his own life in danger to save them. He was the ruler of the house of the very king whose wife was killing them. Cutting off the prophets, the teaching says, is not cutting someone off in their speech; she killed them, and a faithful man had to hide them. The Systemic Starvation class sets him among the righteous men of the famines, like Joseph in Egypt: in a time when rain meant everything, a man who feared the Lord greatly did not sit on his hands but kept something alive. The famine was so sore it was hitting the animals, and Ahab sent Obadiah through the land to every fountain and brook to find grass to save the horses and mules, the two of them dividing the land between them (1 Kings 18:5-6). That was the fruit of the drought Elijah had pronounced. On the road Elijah met him; Obadiah knew him, fell on his face, and asked whether he was his lord Elijah, and Elijah told him to go and tell his master that Elijah was there (1 Kings 18:7-8). Obadiah was afraid. Ahab had searched every nation and kingdom for Elijah and made them swear they had not found him; that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead. If Obadiah went and the Spirit of the Lord carried Elijah off, Ahab would kill him for a false report. So he pleaded his own record: he had feared the Lord from his youth, and had hidden a hundred of the Lord’s prophets by fifty in a cave and fed them (1 Kings 18:9-14). Walking in Elijah’s Footsteps hears him saying, you are putting my life in danger, for Elijah was always here today and gone tomorrow. Elijah swore by the Lord of hosts that he would surely show himself to Ahab that day, and Obadiah went and told Ahab, and Ahab came to meet Elijah (1 Kings 18:15-16). A hundred prophets of the Lord lived through Jezebel’s killing and the famine because one man inside Ahab’s house feared the Lord. The class of 2026-07-18 draws out what she was really after: she was not trying merely to destroy one prophet; she was trying to stop the whole prophetic voice out of Israel, the whole movement, as the enemies of the congregation do today when they speak against one person, for the scripture says to smite the shepherd and the sheep will scatter (Zechariah 13:7). His errand then brought the king face to face with Elijah, and from that meeting came the gathering of all Israel to Carmel with the eight hundred and fifty prophets who ate at Jezebel’s table (1 Kings 18:17-19). When Elijah later sat under the juniper tree and said he alone was left, the Lord answered that He had left Himself seven thousand in Israel whose knees had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:10; 1 Kings 19:18). Walking in Elijah’s Footsteps notes that in his panic Elijah had forgotten what Obadiah told him about the hundred prophets he had hidden; he was not alone, and neither are the faithful today, for there are many out there waiting to call on the name of the Lord.

name: The prophets of Baal at Carmel
text: Prophesying in the name of Baal and eating at Jezebel’s table; crying from morning to noon to a god that could not answer. The four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, with the four hundred prophets of the groves, ate at Jezebel’s table, and Elijah called them to Mount Carmel before all Israel (1 Kings 18:19-24). They dressed their bullock and cried to Baal from morning until past noon, leaped on their altar and cut themselves till the blood gushed out, but no one answered (1 Kings 18:25-29). When Elijah prayed, the fire of the Lord fell, the people confessed that the Lord is God, and the prophets of Baal were taken down to the brook Kishon and slain (1 Kings 18:36-40). Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel to Carmel with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel’s table (1 Kings 18:19). The study notes say Jezebel was the one feeding these eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her. The Revelation 2 teaching on Thyatira adds that these prophets were men, weak men under the authority of an evil woman, taking orders from her and eating at her table, while she killed the real prophets of God. Walking in Elijah’s Footsteps calls Baal what he is: the devil. Elijah asked the people how long they would halt between two opinions: if the Lord is God, follow Him; if Baal, follow him. The people answered not a word (1 Kings 18:21). He said he alone remained a prophet of the Lord against four hundred and fifty, and proposed the test: each side would lay a bullock on wood with no fire under it, and the God who answered by fire, let Him be God; the people said it was well spoken (1 Kings 18:22-24). The Mantle class notes that the other nations also sacrificed, but they sacrificed to devils, for God never made a covenant with them. The prophets of Baal dressed their bullock and called on Baal from morning until noon, crying for him to hear them, but there was no voice and no one answered, and they leaped on the altar they had made (1 Kings 18:25-26). The notes ask the reader to picture it: eight hundred and fifty men running wild while Elijah sat back and watched. At noon Elijah mocked them, telling them to cry louder, for he is a god; perhaps he was talking, or chasing someone, or on a journey, or asleep and must be woken (1 Kings 18:27). They cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets after their manner until the blood gushed out (1 Kings 18:28). Cutting was part of their false worship whenever they called on Baal, and it is why the law says no cuttings in the flesh for the dead nor marks printed on the body (Leviticus 19:28); the Mantle class calls it a Hamitic thing that some tribes still practise as tradition. From midday past the evening sacrifice there was neither voice nor answer nor anyone who paid attention (1 Kings 18:29). No one answered because the Most High will not give His glory to another nor His praise to graven images (Isaiah 42:8), and all the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens (Psalms 96:4-5). The gods of the nations are made up by people who have no God, so when they call on them the idols cannot answer. Elijah repaired the altar of the Lord that was broken down with twelve stones for the twelve tribes, for the whole book is about the twelve tribes of Israel. He had the sacrifice drenched three times until the water filled the trench, and at the evening sacrifice he prayed to the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel that the people might know He is God in Israel and that He had turned their heart back again (1 Kings 18:30-37). The fire of the Lord fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench; the people fell on their faces and said the Lord, He is the God (1 Kings 18:38-39). Elijah told them to take the prophets of Baal and let not one escape, and he brought them down to the brook Kishon and killed them there (1 Kings 18:40). The law had said that the prophet who speaks in the name of other gods shall die (Deuteronomy 18:20). The study notes carry it forward: in the last days it will be the same, and when the Most High rains down fire again by the hand of Christ, no false prophet of Baal will escape, for those who feed the sheep of God lies will not be able to flee. Woe to the pastors who destroy and scatter the sheep of His pasture; He will visit on them the evil of their doings (Jeremiah 23:1-2). When Jezebel heard that all her prophets had been slain with the sword, she swore to take Elijah’s life (1 Kings 19:1-2).

name: Elisha
text: Leaving the oxen and following; asking a double portion of the spirit; and refusing Naaman’s reward, as the Lord liveth, before whom I stand. Elijah found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and cast his mantle on him; Elisha killed his oxen, fed the people with them, and followed (1 Kings 19:19-21). He would not leave his master, asked for a double portion of his spirit, saw him taken up, and parted the Jordan with his mantle (2 Kings 2:1-15). The spirit of Elijah worked through him in healings, provision and deliverance; he refused Naaman’s gifts, and after his death a dead man who touched his bones revived (2 Kings 5:15-16; 2 Kings 13:20-21). Elijah passed by Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and cast his mantle on him without a word. Elisha left the oxen, ran after him, and asked to kiss his father and mother first. Then he went back, killed a yoke of oxen, boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, gave it to the people, and went after Elijah and ministered to him (1 Kings 19:19-21). The Mantle class draws the lesson. The mantle was the prophets’ garment, and the spirit in Elisha told him this was a special calling. He had faith: husbandry was his living, yet he destroyed the oxen and the instruments and did not turn back. No man who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom (Luke 9:57-62). Twelve oxen under one goad are the twelve tribes, and guiding them takes the tunnel vision of a straight furrow, and the class asks where that faith is in brothers today who give up their post when home life pulls at them. When the Lord was about to take Elijah up, at Gilgal, Bethel and Jericho Elijah told him to stay behind, and each time Elisha swore he would not leave him. The sons of the prophets, a prophetic order and not blood sons, told him his master would be taken, and he told them he knew it. Elijah struck the Jordan with his mantle and they crossed on dry ground, and when Elijah asked what he should do for him, Elisha asked for a double portion of his spirit (2 Kings 2:1-10). He saw him go up in a whirlwind with a chariot and horses of fire, cried after him as his father, took up the mantle that fell from him, struck the waters, and they parted; the sons of the prophets said the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha and bowed before him (2 Kings 2:11-15). Walking in Elijah’s Footsteps, reading the history of the prophetic schools, says Elisha then placed himself at the head of Elijah’s disciples at Bethel, Gilgal and Jericho, lived at first on Mount Carmel, and later roused the man who destroyed the house of Omri and ended the worship of Baal. The spirit that was on Elijah worked through him where the people were in need. He healed Jericho’s waters with salt (2 Kings 2:19-22). For a widow of the sons of the prophets whose sons were to be taken for her dead husband’s debt, the oil ran until every borrowed vessel was full, and she paid the debt and lived on the rest (2 Kings 4:1-7). The Shunammite who made him a chamber bore a son at his word, and when the child died, Elisha shut the door, prayed, and stretched himself on him until he sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (2 Kings 4:8-37). He took the death out of the pot at Gilgal and fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, with some left over, according to the word of the Lord (2 Kings 4:38-44). When Naaman the Syrian was cleansed and came back confessing that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, Elisha swore by the Lord before whom he stood that he would receive nothing, though Naaman urged him (2 Kings 5:15-16). Gehazi ran after the gifts and went out a leper, for that was not the time to receive (2 Kings 5:20-27; Ecclesiastes 3:6). When Syria sent a host by night to Dothan for one prophet, he told his servant that those with them were more than those against them, and the Lord opened the young man’s eyes to a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire; the angel of the Lord encamps round those who fear Him (2 Kings 6:15-17; Psalms 34:7). He led the blinded Syrians into Samaria and had them fed and sent home, and their raids stopped (2 Kings 6:18-23). On his deathbed King Joash wept over him as the chariot of Israel, and Elisha put his hands on the king’s hands for the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance from Syria; the king struck the ground only three times, and Elisha was angry, for he would now beat Syria only three times (2 Kings 13:14-19). Elisha died and was buried, and when a dead man was thrown into his sepulchre and touched his bones, he revived and stood on his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). History in the AM reads Sirach on him: filled with Elijah’s spirit, he was not moved by any prince, no one could bring him into subjection, and after his death his body prophesied (Ecclesiasticus 48:12-14).

name: Ben-hadad and the Syrians at Aphek
text: Saying, the Lord is God of the hills, but he is not God of the valleys. After a small company of Israel’s young men routed the Syrians before Samaria while Ben-hadad sat drinking with his allied kings, his servants told him that Israel’s God ruled only the hills and could be beaten on level ground (1 Kings 20:16-23). He rebuilt his army and came back in the spring to Aphek, and a man of God told Ahab that because the Syrians had made the Lord a god of the hills and not of the valleys, the whole host would be handed over (1 Kings 20:26-28). A hundred thousand fell in a day and a wall killed twenty-seven thousand more; Ahab let go the king the Lord had marked for destruction, and Ben-hadad later died by the hand of his own servant Hazael (1 Kings 20:29-42; 2 Kings 8:15). Ben-hadad king of Syria gathered his whole army, with thirty-two kings, horses and chariots, and laid siege to Samaria. He demanded Ahab’s silver, gold, wives and children, and then the right to search his house and carry off whatever pleased him (1 Kings 20:1-6). The study notes teach that this siege was Ahab’s judgment from the Lord for seeking Elijah’s life, for serving Baal, and for letting Jezebel run him and kill the prophets. When the elders told Ahab to refuse the second demand, Ben-hadad swore to grind Samaria into handfuls of dust, and Ahab sent back that a man putting his armor on should not boast like a man taking it off (1 Kings 20:7-11). While Ben-hadad sat drinking in the tents, a prophet brought Ahab the word that the Lord would give that great multitude into his hand that day, so that he would know that He is the Lord. Two hundred and thirty-two young men of the princes of the provinces went out at noon with seven thousand behind them; each killed his man, the Syrians fled, and Ben-hadad escaped on a horse (1 Kings 20:13-21). The Most High gave the victory though Israel’s numbers were small. The prophet warned Ahab to strengthen himself, because the king of Syria would come again at the return of the year (1 Kings 20:22). The return of the year is the spring, the season when the kings of the ancient East went out to war. Ben-hadad’s servants then gave him their reading of the defeat: Israel’s gods were gods of the hills, so fight them on the plain; take the kings out of command and put captains in their places; raise an army equal to the one lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot (1 Kings 20:23-25). He took their advice. The Syrians changed the ground and the officers, but not the error under the whole war, that the God of Israel could be fenced into one kind of country. In the spring Ben-hadad mustered at Aphek, and Israel camped opposite like two small flocks of goats while the Syrians covered the land (1 Kings 20:26-27). A man of God came to Ahab with the answer: because the Syrians had said the Lord was God of the hills and not of the valleys, He would deliver the whole multitude into Ahab’s hand, and they would know that He is the Lord (1 Kings 20:28). The armies faced each other seven days; on the seventh the battle was joined, and Israel killed a hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in one day. The rest fled into Aphek, and a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of the men who were left (1 Kings 20:29-30). Seven thousand against a hundred thousand, and the numbers did not matter, because the Lord was with Israel. The study notes add that the Most High was also giving Ahab a chance to repent by showing His power with fewer numbers; Ahab still did not check Jezebel or destroy the idols of Baal, for his sin had blinded him. Ben-hadad hid in an inner room. His servants had heard that the kings of Israel were merciful kings, so they put sackcloth around their waists and ropes on their heads and went out to beg for his life. Ahab asked whether he was still alive, called him his brother, took him up into his own chariot, and sent him away on a covenant of restored cities and trading streets in Damascus (1 Kings 20:31-34). The teaching calls this an old fault of our people: showing mercy to a people the Lord had said to destroy, to a man who had tried to kill Ahab the year before. A prophet brought the sentence: because Ahab had let go the man the Lord had marked for destruction, his life would go for that man’s life and his people for that people (1 Kings 20:42). The teacher sets it beside the wicked men of Israel who urged a covenant with the heathen round about (1 Maccabees 1:11), and those who boasted of a covenant with death (Isaiah 28:15). Ben-hadad of Damascus and Ahab the Israelite both appear in the Assyrian record of Shalmaneser III at the battle of Qarqar, about 853 BC, and the teaching identifies him as the Ben-hadad of the scriptures. When he later lay sick and sent Hazael to ask Elisha whether he would recover, Hazael went back, spread a thick wet cloth over his face until he died, and reigned in his place (2 Kings 8:7-15). The king who made the Lord a god of the hills died in his own bed by his own servant’s hand, as the word to Elijah had already set Hazael over Syria (1 Kings 19:15).

name: The man who refused the prophetic command
text: Refusing to smite the prophet when commanded in the word of the Lord. One of the sons of the prophets told his neighbour, by the word of the Lord, to strike him, and the neighbour refused. The prophet told him that because he had not obeyed the voice of the Lord a lion would kill him as soon as he left, and a lion met him and killed him (1 Kings 20:35-36). The blow was needed for the sign that would bring Ahab to pronounce his own sentence for sparing Ben-hadad. The man who gave the command was one of the sons of the prophets (1 Kings 20:35). The sons of the prophets were schools of instruction that go back to the spirit the Lord took from Moses and put on the seventy elders (Numbers 11:25). Samuel stood as the appointed head over a company of them (1 Samuel 19:20), and there were schools at Ramah, at Jericho and at Bethel, where Elijah and Elisha often went and where the people came on Sabbaths and new moons for public lessons in the law of Moses. So when this man spoke to his neighbour in the word of the Lord, it came with the weight of the Lord’s appointed teachers, not as a private whim. The command belonged to a prophetic act aimed at the king. Ahab had just sent Ben-hadad away on a covenant, though the Lord had marked him for destruction (1 Kings 20:34, 42). The prophet needed to stand before the king wounded and disguised with ashes, as a soldier who had lost a prisoner put in his charge on pain of his own life, so that the king would judge the case and pass sentence on himself (1 Kings 20:37-40). The neighbour was not asked to decide whether the message should go forward, only to do his part in it. His refusal may have looked like kindness toward a prophet, but the prophet named it for what it was: he had not obeyed the voice of the Lord (1 Kings 20:36). The sentence was spoken at once: as soon as he left, a lion would kill him; and as soon as he left, a lion found him and killed him (1 Kings 20:36). The judgment fell before the message ever reached the king. The prophet found another man and told him to strike him, and that man struck and wounded him (1 Kings 20:37). The work went on without the one who refused. The prophet waited for the king by the road with ashes on his face and told his story; the king ruled that the soldier had decided his own sentence; and when the ashes came off, the king saw that he was one of the prophets and heard that his own life would go for Ben-hadad’s life, and his people for Ben-hadad’s people (1 Kings 20:38-42). He went home to Samaria sullen and angry (1 Kings 20:43), crying again over a just judgment because he would not obey the voice of the Lord. The chapter holds two refusals of a received command: the neighbour who would not strike, and the king who would not destroy. The same thing had happened to the man of God out of Judah, who turned back to eat at Bethel against the word given him, and a lion met him on the road and killed him (1 Kings 13:21-24). Under that dispensation disobedience to the mouth of the Most High carried the penalty of death. The study notes draw the lesson for us: we are to do as it is written, that we may be justified and our life not be taken from us for rebellion against the Lord.

name: Jezebel and Naboth’s vineyard
text: Letters in the king’s name under the king’s seal; a fast, two sons of Belial, and a stoning, to take a man’s inheritance. Naboth would not sell Ahab the vineyard beside the palace in Jezreel, because it was the inheritance of his fathers and the land belonged to the Lord (1 Kings 21:1-3; Leviticus 25:23). Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name under his seal, had the elders proclaim a fast, set two sons of Belial to swear that Naboth had cursed God and the king, and had him stoned; then she told Ahab to go and take the vineyard (1 Kings 21:8-16). Elijah met Ahab in the stolen field with the sentence on his house and on Jezebel, and it was carried out to the letter (1 Kings 21:17-24; 2 Kings 9:30-37). Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard right against the palace of Ahab in Jezreel. Ahab asked for it as a garden of herbs, offering a better vineyard or its worth in money, and Naboth answered that the Lord forbid him to give away the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kings 21:1-3). He could not simply hand off an inheritance given to him: the land was not to be sold for ever, because it was the Lord’s and they were only tenants on it (Leviticus 25:23). The teaching asks the obvious question: if the other vineyard was better, why did the king want this one? The law says do not covet, and a king who already had the whole kingdom under him was eyeing what belonged to his neighbour. Ahab went home heavy and displeased, lay on his bed, turned his face to the wall, and would not eat (1 Kings 21:4). The study notes call it a fit: a grown man sulking because a subject would not surrender his inheritance. Jezebel asked why he was so sad, mocked his weakness by asking whether he was king in Israel or not, and promised him the vineyard (1 Kings 21:5-7). The teaching marks the pattern: the Jezebel spirit looks for the mild-mannered man she can control, and there is a difference between a strong woman and a mean-spirited one. She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal, the signet that carried the king’s own authority, as when a king sealed Daniel’s den so the decree could not be changed (1 Kings 21:8; Daniel 6:17). She told the elders and nobles of his city to proclaim a fast, as though the matter were holy, set Naboth up high before the people, and seat two sons of Belial opposite him to swear that he had cursed God and the king, and then stone him (1 Kings 21:9-10). She had to find two men willing to lie for money, which is exactly what the commandment against false witness forbids (Exodus 20:16). The elders did it. There was no true judgment and no true witness, only a plot; they stoned Naboth and sent word to Jezebel, who was not even there (1 Kings 21:11-14). She told Ahab to get up and take the vineyard, since Naboth was dead, and Ahab went down to take possession (1 Kings 21:15-16). This is extortion, seizing what another holds by violence, the dishonest gain the Lord strikes His hand against (Ezekiel 22:12-13). Ahab shares the guilt: he sat by, let Jezebel commit the crime because he coveted the field, and went to collect the reward. Following a multitude to do evil made him an accomplice to murder and theft (Exodus 23:2). The word of the Lord sent Elijah to meet Ahab in Naboth’s vineyard, the very place he had gone to possess; nothing is hidden from the Lord. Elijah was to ask him whether he had killed and also taken possession, and tell him that where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood they would lick his own (1 Kings 21:17-19). The teaching titles it plainly: selfishness is the spirit of murder. Ahab called Elijah his enemy, as the men who would not believe Christ because he told them the truth (John 8:45). Elijah said he had found him because he had given himself over to evil before the Lord. Every male of Ahab’s house would be cut off, his house made like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and the dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel; those of his house who died in the city the dogs would eat, and those in the field the birds, the curse of the law on the disobedient (1 Kings 21:20-24; Deuteronomy 28:26). He lost everything over one vineyard. One sinner destroys much good (Ecclesiastes 9:18). When Ahab heard it he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted and went about quietly, and because he humbled himself the evil was moved to his son’s days (1 Kings 21:27-29). The judgment was not cancelled, only delayed; the sentence against an evil work is not always carried out speedily, but the Lord will get to it (Ecclesiastes 8:11-13). The dogs licked Ahab’s blood when his chariot was washed in Samaria (1 Kings 22:38). Jehu shot Joram through the heart and threw his body onto Naboth’s portion of ground, as the Lord had said (2 Kings 9:24-26). Jezebel painted her face and looked out a window at Jezreel; she was thrown down, and when they went to bury her, only her skull, her feet and the palms of her hands were left, as the Lord had spoken by Elijah (2 Kings 9:30-37).

name: Micaiah the son of Imlah
text: As the Lord liveth, what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak: against four hundred prophets, two kings, a slap, and a prison. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat sat on their thrones at the gate of Samaria and four hundred prophets told them with one voice to go up to Ramoth-gilead, Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Ahab named Micaiah and said he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him (1 Kings 22:6-8). Coached to agree with the others, Micaiah answered that he would speak only what the Lord told him, saw Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd and a lying spirit in the mouths of the four hundred, and was struck and imprisoned on short rations (1 Kings 22:13-27). He staked his word on the outcome, and Ahab did not come back (1 Kings 22:28-38). After three years without war, Jehoshaphat king of Judah came down to Ahab, who wanted Ramoth-gilead back from the king of Syria; Jehoshaphat agreed to go, but first asked that they inquire at the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:1-5). Ramoth-gilead, a Levitical city of refuge east of the Jordan, had been lost to Aram-Damascus. Ahab gathered about four hundred prophets, and they all said go up, the Lord would deliver it into the king’s hand (1 Kings 22:6). After the split the northern kingdom fell into idolatry and forsook the Levites, and a prophet of the Most High wanted nothing to do with their manner of worship, as Elisha later told a king of Israel to go to the prophets of his father and mother (2 Kings 3:13). Jehoshaphat saw something in the spirit: four hundred men agreeing was not the counsel of God, and he asked whether there was not a prophet of the Lord besides (1 Kings 22:7). Ahab said there was one more, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but he hated him, because he never prophesied good concerning him, only evil (1 Kings 22:8). The teaching presses the point: Ahab already knew where true counsel was, and chose four hundred who would tell him what he wanted to hear. He called the counsel of God evil because it went against his flesh. They acknowledged the spirit of the Lord was on Micaiah and hated him for the words of the law that came out of his mouth; he did not preach what they wanted, and they did not like it. The messenger sent to fetch him tried to prepare him: all the prophets spoke good to the king with one voice, so let his word be like theirs (1 Kings 22:13). In plain terms, lie to the king and make it sound good. Micaiah swore by the living Lord that whatever the Lord said to him, that he would speak (1 Kings 22:14). To the law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to that word, there is no light in them (Isaiah 8:20). At first he answered the king in the words of the others, until Ahab demanded the truth in the name of the Lord, wanting to be told the truth and lied to at the same time. Then Micaiah said he saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep with no shepherd, and the Lord said they had no master and should go home in peace (1 Kings 22:15-17). It was counsel to save Ahab’s life, and mercy from God, and Ahab heard it as evil. Micaiah told him the rest: he saw the Lord on His throne with the host of heaven on either side, and a spirit offered to go and speak lies through all Ahab’s prophets, and the Lord sent it (1 Kings 22:19-23). The deceived and the deceiver both belong to Him (Job 12:16), and it is the Lord’s counsel that stands (Proverbs 19:21). Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah struck Micaiah on the cheek, and Ahab had him taken to Amon the governor and Joash the king’s son, to be kept in prison on the bread and water of affliction until the king came back in peace (1 Kings 22:24-27). They put him in prison because they did not like what he spoke; not for adultery, not for striking a brother, not for stealing. His light shone on their darkness, and roaches scatter when the light turns on. Micaiah answered that if the king came back in peace at all, the Lord had not spoken by him, and called all the people to hear it (1 Kings 22:28). Ahab disguised himself for the battle and had Jehoshaphat wear his robes. The Syrian captains chased Jehoshaphat and turned back when they saw he was not the king of Israel, and a man drew his bow at random and struck Ahab between the joints of his armor. God makes no mistakes; when the counsel of the Lord is rejected, judgment finds its mark. Ahab died at evening, and the dogs licked his blood when the chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria, according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:29-38). The four hundred were exposed by the test the law gives: when the thing does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it (Deuteronomy 18:22). The record does not say Micaiah was released; his vindication did not depend on his comfort. He was not afraid of four hundred men, and that is how we must be; Christ said not to be ashamed of him, and the same hatred falls today on those who speak the laws.

name: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, and the four hundred prophets
text: Horns of iron and a lying spirit: prophesying victory at Ramoth-gilead in the name of the Lord, and smiting Micaiah on the cheek. Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made himself horns of iron and told Ahab in the name of the Lord that with these he would push the Syrians until they were finished, and all four hundred prophets said the same (1 Kings 22:10-12). When Micaiah revealed the lying spirit in their mouths, Zedekiah struck him on the cheek and asked which way the Spirit of the Lord had gone from him to speak to Micaiah (1 Kings 22:23-24). Micaiah told him he would find out on the day he ran into an inner room to hide, and Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:25, 34-37). Ahab gathered about four hundred prophets and asked whether to go up against Ramoth-gilead, and they told him to go, for the Lord would deliver it into his hand (1 Kings 22:6). These were the king’s prophets in a kingdom that had cast out the priests of the Lord, the sons of Aaron, and made priests after the manner of the nations, so that any man could consecrate himself to serve gods that are no gods (2 Chronicles 13:9). Jehoshaphat already sensed that God was not in that council. The two kings sat each on his throne in their robes at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets prophesied before them. Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made horns of iron and declared in the name of the Lord that with these Ahab would push the Syrians until they were consumed, and the whole company joined in, telling the king to go up and prosper (1 Kings 22:10-12). A man claimed to speak for the Most High and gave his false word a solid sign, and the rest hopped on the bandwagon. They told the king what made him feel good and did not care whether he died. The teacher sets them beside the rebellious and lying children who tell the seers not to see and the prophets to speak smooth things (Isaiah 30:8-10), and beside the false apostles of whom Paul warned: Satan himself is made over into an angel of light, so it is no surprise that his ministers pass for ministers of righteousness, and their end will match their works (2 Corinthians 11:13-15). When Micaiah told them the Lord had set a lying spirit to speak through all these prophets (1 Kings 22:23), Zedekiah went up and struck him on the cheek, and asked which way the Spirit of the Lord had gone from him to speak to Micaiah (1 Kings 22:24). In other words: who do you think you are? God talks to me too. That is what men do, spiritually, when they reject counsel from the man of the Lord: they slap him. Micaiah answered that Zedekiah would see on the day he went into an inner room to hide himself (1 Kings 22:25). The confidence shown before two kings would end in running. Ahab went up to Ramoth-gilead, was struck by an arrow drawn at random, and died at evening, and the army scattered every man to his own city, as Micaiah had seen (1 Kings 22:34-37). The iron horns pushed no Syrians anywhere. The law gives the test: when a prophet speaks in the name of the Lord and the thing does not follow or come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; that prophet has spoken presumptuously and is not to be feared (Deuteronomy 18:22). The four hundred failed it. The record does not follow Zedekiah into his inner room; it leaves him under the word that sent him there. The deceived and the deceiver both belong to the Most High (Job 12:16), who used the lie in their mouths to bring the judgment He had already declared on Ahab, and the men who carried the lie were not made righteous by being useful to it. False prophets and religious leaders who lie to the people still put them in harm’s way, and people who do not read are the ones who bleed.

name: Ahaziah of Israel
text: Sending to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron, as though there were not a God in Israel. Ahab’s son Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and sent to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover, and Elijah met the messengers with the Lord’s question: was there no God in Israel (2 Kings 1:2-3)? Two captains of fifty who ordered the prophet down were burned up by fire from heaven, and the third fell on his knees and begged for his life (2 Kings 1:9-14). Ahaziah died in his bed according to the word Elijah spoke (2 Kings 1:16-17). After Ahab died, Moab rebelled against Israel (2 Kings 1:1). The nations David had subdued and put under tribute began to break away, because Israel no longer walked in the blessing that came from serving the Most High (2 Samuel 8:2). If Israel listened diligently and did His commandments, the Lord would set them on high and strike down their enemies before them; if not, they would be struck down before their enemies and their bodies left to the birds, the same judgment spoken on the house of Ahab (Deuteronomy 28:1, 7, 15, 25-26). Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper chamber and lay sick, and he sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub the god of Ekron whether he would recover (2 Kings 1:2). Baal-zebub is the lord of the flies, and the teaching calls him plainly Satan, a god of the Hamites at Ekron. It frames the act as a choice, like Joshua’s call to choose whom they would serve (Joshua 24:15): Ahaziah thought God was not listening and went to another nation’s god, and he could not blame God for that. He should have known the history. When the ark of God was brought to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out that it had come to kill them, and the hand of God was heavy there; the god of Ekron could not even defend his own people (1 Samuel 5:10-11). The angel of the Lord sent Elijah to meet the messengers and ask whether it was because there was no God in Israel that they were going to inquire of Baal-zebub; the Lord’s word was that the king would never rise from his bed; he would die (2 Kings 1:3-4). Elijah was quick to the point, and left. The messengers described a hairy man with a leather belt, a man in a garment of hair like the camel’s hair John the Baptist later wore, and the king knew it was Elijah (2 Kings 1:7-8; Mark 1:6). Then he sent a captain with his fifty men, who found Elijah on top of a hill and told the man of God that the king ordered him to come down (2 Kings 1:9). Elijah answered that if he was a man of God, fire would come down from heaven and consume the captain and his fifty, and it did. The king sent another captain with fifty, who spoke the same way, and fire from heaven consumed them too (2 Kings 1:10-12).
