This is our history, not a Marvel movie: Elijah brought down fire three times, once on Carmel and then on the captains back to back (Ecclesiasticus 48:3). The Lord did not let His prophet’s words fall to the ground (1 Samuel 3:19). The third captain was a wise one. Having heard that a hundred men had been burned, he humbled himself quickly, went up, fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged that his life and the lives of his fifty be precious in the prophet’s sight (2 Kings 1:13-14). The angel of the Lord told Elijah to go down with him and not be afraid (2 Kings 1:15). The teaching draws the lesson: humble yourself and seek the prayers of the Lord’s leaders rather than scorning correction. Elijah went to the king himself and delivered the same word: because he had sent to ask Baal-zebub as though Israel had no God to ask, he would never rise from that bed; he would die (2 Kings 1:16). He died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken, and since he had no son, Jehoram reigned in his place (2 Kings 1:17). The prophet brought kings to destruction and honored men from their beds (Ecclesiasticus 48:6). The same Ahaziah had joined with Jehoshaphat king of Judah to build ships, and because Jehoshaphat joined himself with a king who did very wickedly, the Lord broke the ships (2 Chronicles 20:35-37). If we join with the wicked, the Lord breaks our works.

name: The young mockers of Bethel
text: Mocking the prophet of the Lord: go up, thou bald head. As Elisha went up to Bethel, just after the Lord healed Jericho’s waters through him, young children came out of the city and jeered at him, telling him to go up, bald head (2 Kings 2:19-23). He turned, looked at them, and cursed them in the name of the Lord, and two she bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:24). The teaching uses it to warn that God brings every work into judgment, even the works of children, and that elders are to be honored as fathers. Elisha had just come from Jericho, where the men of the city told him the water was bad and the land barren; he threw salt into the spring and said the Lord had healed the waters (2 Kings 2:19-22). The sign showed that the spirit that had been on Elijah now worked through Elisha, the double portion coming into effect. He was not a man to be played with. From there he went up to Bethel, and as he went up the road, young children came out of the city and mocked him, telling him to go up, bald head (2 Kings 2:23). The baldness shows he had some age on him. They saw a prophet and did not care. This is the child behaving proudly against the elder, as Isaiah described a people under judgment (Isaiah 3:5). Honor your father and mother, and do not dishonor a man in his old age (Matthew 15:4; Ecclesiasticus 8:6); an elder is to be entreated as a father (1 Timothy 5:1), and the eye that mocks a father the ravens of the valley will pick out (Proverbs 30:17). The elders over the congregation are to be honored as fathers, and these children’s parents had not taught them right. Children disrespecting elders is a sin, and it is the same lack of home training that fills the gangs today. Do not judge a man by his looks; you might be dealing with an Elisha. He turned back, looked at them, and cursed them in the name of the Lord, and two she bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the children (2 Kings 2:24). He cursed them in the name of the Lord, so whatever happened next was of the Lord. Two bears could not have caught forty-two children scattering in every direction unless it was a spiritual thing; the Lord put the spirit on those bears. There are spirits created for vengeance, and the teeth of wild beasts are among them (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-30). It is one of the curses of the law on a people who walk contrary to Him, that He will send wild beasts among them to rob them of their children (Leviticus 26:22). The teachers speak of the forty-two as put to death, though the text says only that the bears tore them. Elisha went on to Mount Carmel and from there returned to Samaria (2 Kings 2:25). God brings every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil (Ecclesiastes 12:14), and that includes the works of children. The teaching charges parents to read these judgments to their children and put the fear of the Lord in them before it is too late. It is a harsh judgment, and one teacher says plainly that we do not know all the Lord’s reasons; the lesson he draws is to leave vengeance to the Lord, whose judgment this was.

name: The prophet’s widow, and the pot of oil
text: Borrowing empty vessels of her neighbours, not a few, shutting the door, and pouring, as the prophet said. The widow of one of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha that her husband, who had feared the Lord, was dead, and the creditor had come to take her two sons as bondmen (2 Kings 4:1). She had nothing in the house but a jar of oil; Elisha told her to borrow empty vessels from all her neighbours, not a few, shut the door on herself and her sons, and pour, and the oil ran until every vessel was full (2 Kings 4:2-6). She sold the oil, paid the debt, and lived on the rest with her sons (2 Kings 4:7). The sons of the prophets were not the literal sons of prophets but a prophetic order, students in the schools that went back to Samuel, at Naioth, Bethel, Jericho and Gilgal. This woman’s cry shows that some of them were married (2 Kings 4:1). Her husband, Elisha’s servant, had feared the Lord and died in debt, and the creditor was coming to take her two sons to work off what was owed. The teaching applies it to men who fear what will happen to their wives and children if they stand firm: God already had a plan, and nothing here belongs to us. Elisha asked what he should do for her and what she had in the house, and she said she had nothing but a jar of oil (2 Kings 4:2). He told her to go out and borrow empty vessels from all her neighbours, not just a few, then go in and shut the door behind herself and her sons, and pour oil into all those vessels, setting each full one aside (2 Kings 4:3-4). She went and did exactly as the prophet said (2 Kings 4:5). Even this woman showed faith in what Elisha told her. She shut the door, her sons brought her the vessels, and she poured. When the vessels were full she asked her son for another, and he told her there were no more, and the oil stopped (2 Kings 4:5-6). The oil ran until every vessel was full, and only then stayed. The empty vessels she borrowed from her people, the children of Israel, were filled through the spirit of the Lord. She came and told the man of God, and he told her to sell the oil, pay her debt, and live with her children on what was left (2 Kings 4:7). Elisha multiplied what she had, so the debt that distressed her was paid and her sons were kept. This was not the only time the Lord multiplied a little in the hands of His servants. The miracles the Most High allowed Elisha came through his faith and his obedience, and by the same spirit that was in the prophets the Lord did marvelous works through them (1 Peter 1:10-11). The teaching pairs the widow’s oil with Christ feeding the multitude from five loaves (Luke 9:12-17): what Christ did was not happening for the first time. In the same chapter Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42-44).

name: The Shunammite woman
text: Constraining the man of God to eat bread, and building him a little chamber on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick. A great woman of Shunem pressed Elisha to eat at her house, saw that he was a holy man of God, and had her husband build him a small room on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool and a lamp (2 Kings 4:8-10). Offered a word to the king, she answered that she lived among her own people; promised a son, she could hardly believe it, as Sarah had not, but he was born at the time set (2 Kings 4:13-17; Genesis 18:12-14). When the boy died she laid him on the prophet’s bed and went for Elisha, who prayed and raised him; and when she came home from the famine he had warned her to flee, the king restored her house, her land and all its produce (2 Kings 4:32-37; 2 Kings 8:1-6). As Elisha passed through Shunem, a great woman there urged him to eat bread, and after that he turned in whenever he passed (2 Kings 4:8). She told her husband she perceived that this was a holy man of God, and asked that they make him a small room on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool and a lamp, so he could stay when he came (2 Kings 4:9-10). When Elisha sent Gehazi to ask what could be done for her for all her care, whether she wanted to be spoken for to the king or the captain of the army, she answered that she lived among her own people (2 Kings 4:11-13). Gehazi noted that she had no son and her husband was old, and Elisha told her that about that time next year she would hold a son; she begged the man of God not to deceive his servant (2 Kings 4:14-16). Like our mother Sarah, she did not believe it, and the Lord had asked Abraham whether anything was too hard for Him (Genesis 18:11-14). She conceived and bore a son at the time Elisha had said (2 Kings 4:17). When the child had grown, he went out to his father among the reapers, cried that his head hurt, was carried to his mother, sat on her knees till noon, and died, of what seemed only a headache (2 Kings 4:18-20). She carried him up, laid him on the bed of the man of God in the room she had made, shut the door, and asked her husband for a servant and a donkey to go to the man of God (2 Kings 4:21-22). He asked why she would go that day, when it was neither new moon nor Sabbath (2 Kings 4:23); the people went to the prophets on Sabbaths and new moons for instruction. She said it would be well, rode to Mount Carmel, told Gehazi it was well, and caught Elisha by the feet; when Gehazi came to push her away, Elisha said her soul was bitter and the Lord had hidden it from him (2 Kings 4:24-27). She asked whether she had asked him for a son, and whether she had not said not to deceive her. Elisha sent Gehazi ahead with his staff, but she swore she would not leave him, and he got up and followed her (2 Kings 4:28-30). Gehazi laid the staff on the child’s face, and there was no voice and no response (2 Kings 4:31). Elisha came in, found the child dead on his bed, shut the door on the two of them, and prayed to the Lord first (2 Kings 4:32-33). Then he lay on the child, mouth on mouth, eyes on eyes, hands on hands, and the child’s flesh grew warm; he walked the house, stretched himself on him again, and the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (2 Kings 4:34-35). The teaching likens it to the breath of resuscitation, which the world got from our book, and sets it beside Elijah and the widow’s son (1 Kings 17:20-22). The prayer of faith saves the sick (James 5:15), and a prayer from a poor man’s mouth reaches the ears of God (Ecclesiasticus 21:5). He called the Shunammite and told her to take up her son, and she fell at his feet, bowed to the ground, took her son, and went out (2 Kings 4:36-37). This is another act of the Most High through Elisha, a miracle of his faith and obedience. Later Elisha told her to rise and go with her household and live wherever she could, because the Lord had called for a famine that would last seven years (2 Kings 8:1). The Lord summons the famine for His purpose; a famine purges evil, and in affliction people seek the Lord. The teaching compares the leadership’s warning to prepare now with Elisha’s warning to her. She lived in the land of the Philistines seven years, and when she came back she went to appeal to the king for her house and land (2 Kings 8:2-3). At that very moment the king was asking Gehazi to tell him the great things Elisha had done, and Gehazi was telling how he had restored a dead child to life when the mother came in; Gehazi said this was the woman and this her son (2 Kings 8:4-5). The timing was of the Most High. The king appointed an officer to restore all that was hers, with all the produce of the field since the day she left (2 Kings 8:6).

name: Naaman the Syrian
text: Going down and dipping himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God, after his anger. Naaman, the Syrian commander through whom the Lord had given Syria its victories, was a leper, and an Israelite girl taken captive into his house sent him to the prophet in Samaria (2 Kings 5:1-3). Told by Elisha’s messenger to wash seven times in the Jordan, he went off in a rage because the cure was not the show he expected, until his servants reasoned with him; then he went down and dipped seven times as the man of God had said, and his flesh came back like a child’s (2 Kings 5:10-14). He returned confessing that the only God in all the earth was the God of Israel (2 Kings 5:15). Naaman was captain of the army of the king of Syria, a great and honored man, because by him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria; he was a mighty man of valor, but a leper (2 Kings 5:1). A little girl carried captive out of Israel waited on his wife, and she said that if her master were with the prophet in Samaria, he would be healed (2 Kings 5:2-3). An Israelite sister serving in a foreign house pointed a great commander to the prophet. The Syrians had their own gods, yet their king sent to Israel with a letter and a fortune in silver, gold and clothing, and the king of Israel tore his clothes and asked whether he was God, to kill and to make alive (2 Kings 5:5-7; Deuteronomy 32:39). The king was shaken, but the man of God stood up: Elisha sent word to let the man come to him, and he would know there was a prophet in Israel (2 Kings 5:8). Naaman came with his horses and chariot to Elisha’s door, and Elisha did not come out; he sent a messenger to tell him to wash in the Jordan seven times and his flesh would be restored (2 Kings 5:9-10). Naaman was furious. He had expected the prophet to come out, call on his God, wave his hand over the place and heal him; he wanted a big performance and was given something simple. Were not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? He turned away in a rage (2 Kings 5:11-12). That was pride. The process was not what he expected, and his mind was carnal, thinking of a bodily washing rather than a spiritual one, and the muddy Jordan was beneath him. We often want God to do things the way we want them done; when the Lord says do, be quiet and obey. His pride almost kept him from being healed. His servants came near and reasoned with him: if the prophet had told him to do some great thing, he would have done it; how much more when he only said wash and be clean (2 Kings 5:13). He humbled himself once his servant spoke to him, went down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God (2 Kings 5:14). His flesh came back like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (2 Kings 5:14). Seven is completion, as with the seventh-day rest and Jericho compassed seven times. The spirit of Christ did the healing through Elisha, and what healed Naaman was that he believed and obeyed. The true washing is not a dip in water but putting away evil and learning to do well, action and not speech (Isaiah 1:16-17). The same Jordan is where John preached the baptism of repentance, with confession of sins, and where Christ came to be baptized (Luke 3:3; Matthew 3:6, 13). Naaman came back with all his company, stood before Elisha, and confessed that now he knew the only God in all the earth was the God of Israel (2 Kings 5:15). This is the heathen speaking, like Jethro before him confessing that the Lord is greater than all gods (Exodus 18:11), so that the peoples of the earth might know the hand of the Lord (Joshua 4:24). Elisha refused his gift (2 Kings 5:16). Naaman asked for two mules’ load of earth, because from then on he would offer sacrifice to no god but the Lord, and asked pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon when his master leaned on his arm; in asking it he was saying he knew Rimmon was no god, for all the gods of the nations are idols (2 Kings 5:17-18; Psalm 96:5). Elisha told him to go in peace (2 Kings 5:19). Christ reached back and named him: there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha’s time, and none of them was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian, and the synagogue was filled with wrath to hear it (Luke 4:27-28).

name: Gehazi
text: Running after Naaman to take what his master refused; lying to Naaman and then to the prophet’s face. When Elisha refused Naaman’s gifts, his servant Gehazi ran after the Syrian’s chariot, invented a message from his master asking silver and clothing for two young prophets, and hid the two talents and the garments in the house (2 Kings 5:20-24). He lied again to Elisha’s face, and Elisha told him his heart had gone with him; Naaman’s leprosy would cling to him and his descendants for ever, and he went out a leper white as snow (2 Kings 5:25-27). Elisha had refused Naaman’s gifts, swearing by the Lord before whom he stood (2 Kings 5:16). Gehazi, his servant, told himself his master had let this Syrian off too lightly, and swore by the Lord to run after him and get something from him (2 Kings 5:20). He had been Elisha’s understudy and seen all the miracles, and he was still looking at all that glitter. When Naaman saw him running he got down from his chariot and asked whether all was well. Gehazi said it was, and that his master had sent him to ask a talent of silver and two changes of clothing for two young men of the sons of the prophets just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim (2 Kings 5:21-22). Naaman told him to be content and take two talents, and pressed them on him; Gehazi should have woken up then (2 Kings 5:23). At the hill he took the bags from Naaman’s servants, hid them in the house like a thief, and sent the men away (2 Kings 5:24). Then he went in and stood before his master, and when Elisha asked where he had been, he said he had gone nowhere (2 Kings 5:25). Covetousness makes a man lie, and Gehazi lied twice, adding sin to sin, because he would not control it. The study notes say it shows how Israel thought then and how the nation still thinks, hasty to grasp things by unjust means. Elisha had asked Elijah for a double portion of his spirit, not for money and clothes. The real men of God do not do the Lord’s work for a reward; they trust Him to provide. Elisha asked whether his heart had not gone with him when the man turned from his chariot to meet him (2 Kings 5:26). God sees it all; the spirit of the Lord reveals what is done in secret, so do not lie before righteous men, but come correct. He asked whether this was a time to take money and clothes, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, and servants (2 Kings 5:26). There is a season for everything, a time to get and a time to lose (Ecclesiastes 3:1, 6), and Elisha explained that there was a time to receive, and this was not it. The leprosy of Naaman would cling to Gehazi and to his descendants for ever, and he went out from Elisha’s presence a leper, white as snow (2 Kings 5:27). The same sickness that had just left Naaman came on him. He was judged immediately. Many think they are fine because judgment is slow, but the money they love will destroy them. The work of one sinner cost his whole lineage: he destroyed not only himself but his children. The teaching applies it to generational curses, telling the hearers to examine whether they are paying for the sins of their parents. The class on generational curses reads the leprosy white as snow as the whole skin with its pigment gone, which the law calls the clean leprosy when it covers the body from head to foot (Leviticus 13:12-13). It teaches that this is how Cain was cursed from the ground and how Esau was born, and that the look of white people is that curse. Because it was laid on his seed for ever, the class teaches that Gehazi’s descendants are here today and carry it. The remedy the law gives for a generational curse is to confess the iniquity of the fathers and accept its punishment, and then the Lord remembers His covenant (Leviticus 26:40-42).

name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned
text: Doubting the word of the Lord by Elisha in the famine of Samaria: if the Lord would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?. In the famine of the Syrian siege, when mothers in Samaria were eating their children, Elisha declared that by the same time the next day flour and barley would sell for a shekel in the gate (2 Kings 6:28-29; 2 Kings 7:1). The officer on whose arm the king leaned answered that even if the Lord opened windows in heaven it could not happen, and Elisha told him he would see it with his own eyes and never taste it (2 Kings 7:2). The Syrians fled at a noise the Lord sent, the food came as spoken, and the officer was trampled to death in the gate (2 Kings 7:6-7, 16-20). Ben-hadad besieged Samaria until a donkey’s head sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a woman cried to the king that she and her neighbour had agreed to boil and eat their sons, and she had given hers (2 Kings 6:24-29). This was the curse of the law on a disobedient Israel, that in the siege they would eat the fruit of their own body (Deuteronomy 28:53). The king saw the Lord’s hand in it and said he could do nothing, and then he and his messenger blamed the Lord for the evil and lost patience waiting for His deliverance (2 Kings 6:27, 33). The teaching warns those who have never known real hunger not to say what they would never do, and to prepare now. Elisha answered with the word of the Lord: by about this time tomorrow a measure of fine flour would sell for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria (2 Kings 7:1). The prophet speaks the word of the Most High plainly, without fear and without doubting, whether the message is blessing or judgment. A lord on whose arm the king leaned answered the man of God that even if the Lord made windows in heaven, this could not be (2 Kings 7:2). He heard the word of the Lord from the Lord’s prophet and called it impossible. Elisha told him he would see the food with his own eyes and never taste it (2 Kings 7:2). Four leprous men at the gate reasoned that they would die whether they went into the city or sat where they were, and went out to the Syrian camp. The Lord had made the Syrians hear the noise of chariots and horses and a great army, and they fled in the twilight, thinking the king of Israel had hired the kings of the Hittites and of Egypt against them, and left their tents, horses and food as they stood (2 Kings 7:3-7). The lepers ate and hid silver and gold, then told each other they were not doing right to keep quiet on a day of good news, and went and told the king’s household (2 Kings 7:8-11). The people went out and plundered the camp, and fine flour and barley sold for a shekel, according to the word of the Lord (2 Kings 7:12-16). The king had put the lord on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him there, and he died, as the man of God had said (2 Kings 7:17). He saw the plenty and did not eat of it, and the word fell out to the letter (2 Kings 7:18-20). The study notes picture it as a crowd stampeding after goods, hating one another over things, and that crowd became the judgment on the man who doubted the word. The whole chapter stands on one point: the certainty of the word of the Most High spoken by His prophets.

name: Hazael king of Syria
text: Smothering his master with a wet cloth to take the throne, and doing to Israel the evil Elisha wept over. When Ben-hadad lay sick and sent Hazael with forty camel loads of gifts to ask Elisha whether he would recover, the prophet fixed his eyes on him and wept, because he saw the evil Hazael would do to Israel: burning their strongholds, killing their young men, dashing their children and ripping open pregnant women (2 Kings 8:7-12). Hazael went back, smothered his master with a wet cloth, and took the throne, and the Lord used him to cut Israel short (2 Kings 8:15; 2 Kings 10:32). By Amos the Lord said He would send fire on the house of Hazael and carry Syria captive to Kir (Amos 1:3-5). At Horeb the Lord told Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu over Israel, and Elisha as prophet, and whoever escaped the sword of Hazael, Jehu would kill (1 Kings 19:15-17). The Most High had things set up, and Syria would come against the northern kingdom. When Elisha came to Damascus, Ben-hadad was sick and sent Hazael with a present of every good thing of Damascus, forty camels’ load, to ask whether he would recover (2 Kings 8:7-9). The word of a prophet was precious in those days. The Syrians had their own gods, yet their king sent to the God of Israel; they knew there was only one true and living God, and that did not stop them fighting against us. Elisha told him to tell the king he could recover, though the Lord had shown him that he would surely die; then he fixed his gaze on Hazael until the man was ashamed, and wept (2 Kings 8:10-11). Asked why, he said he knew the evil Hazael would do to the children of Israel: set their strongholds on fire, kill their young men with the sword, dash their children, and rip open their women with child (2 Kings 8:12). Hazael had done none of it yet. The prophet saw years ahead that he would be an instrument of terror; prophecy has no time clock, and leadership can discern a spirit at work in a man that the man cannot see in himself. Hazael asked whether he was a dog, to do such a thing, and Elisha answered that the Lord had shown him Hazael would be king over Syria (2 Kings 8:13). Hazael went back, told his master he would recover, and the next day took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king’s face until he died, and reigned in his place (2 Kings 8:14-15). The teaching names the murdered king Ben-hadad the second. What Elisha wept over came. Jehu destroyed Baal but kept Jeroboam’s calves and did not walk in the law with all his heart, and in those days the Lord began to cut Israel short: Hazael struck them in all the land east of the Jordan, Gilead, Gad, Reuben and Manasseh, from Aroer by the Arnon to Bashan (2 Kings 10:31-33). When we sin, the Lord brings an adversary, other nations, to correct us. Hazael took Gath and set his face against Jerusalem, and Jehoash of Judah bought him off with the hallowed things of the house of the Lord (2 Kings 12:17-18). The Lord’s anger gave Israel into the hand of Hazael and his son all the days of Jehoahaz, yet He was gracious to them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (2 Kings 13:3, 22-23). The teacher sets the ripping open of pregnant women beside what was done to our people in American slavery; no nation has suffered as Israel has under the curses of the law (Daniel 9:11-12). Even though the Lord used him, He would judge him. Through Amos the Lord said that for three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, He would not turn back its punishment, because they had threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron; He would send fire into the house of Hazael to devour the palaces of Ben-hadad, break the bar of Damascus, and send the people of Syria captive to Kir (Amos 1:3-5). Threshing Gilead means they thrashed it and took the whole east side of the Jordan. Prophecy is fulfilled in layers. Hazael died and his son Ben-hadad reigned, and Jehoash of Israel beat him three times and took back the cities; then Jeroboam the second recovered Damascus and Hamath, which the teachers read as the fire on Hazael’s house (2 Kings 13:24-25; 2 Kings 14:28). The captivity came when Tiglath-pileser took Damascus, carried its people to Kir and killed Rezin (2 Kings 16:9). One teacher adds a further layer still to come on the nations at the end.

name: Jehu
text: Executing the house of Ahab and destroying Baal out of Israel, and then not departing from the golden calves at Bethel and Dan; taking no heed to walk in the law of the Lord with all his heart. Anointed at Ramoth-gilead by one of the sons of the prophets, Jehu was charged to strike the house of Ahab and avenge the blood of the prophets shed by Jezebel, and he did it to the last man, from Joram and Jezebel to Ahab’s seventy sons and the worshippers of Baal (2 Kings 9:1-10; 2 Kings 10:11, 25-28). The Lord commended him and promised his sons the throne to the fourth generation, but Jehu kept Jeroboam’s golden calves at Bethel and Dan and took no care to walk in the law with all his heart, and in his days the Lord began to cut Israel short (2 Kings 10:29-32). Elisha sent one of the sons of the prophets to Ramoth-gilead with a flask of oil to anoint Jehu king over Israel and then flee (2 Kings 9:1-3). The charge was to strike the house of Ahab and avenge the blood of the prophets and of all the servants of the Lord at the hand of Jezebel, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it go on (2 Kings 9:6-10). Omri had built Samaria through his alliance with the Zidonians and married his son to Jezebel, making it a little Zidon in Israel, and none of the men had the fortitude to set right what was wrong; so God anointed a soldier to execute the judgment. His fellow captains asked why the mad fellow had come, then spread their garments under him on the stairs, blew the trumpet, and proclaimed Jehu king (2 Kings 9:11-13). Joram came out asking whether it was peace, and Jehu answered that there could be no peace as long as his mother Jezebel’s harlotry and sorcery went on: no peace as long as a wicked woman holds power. He drew his bow with full strength, shot Joram through the heart, and had him thrown onto Naboth’s portion of ground, requital for Naboth’s blood (2 Kings 9:22-26). Ahaziah of Judah, complicit through the house of Ahab, was struck down as he fled (2 Kings 9:27). Jezebel painted her face and looked out a window, trying to entice men with a superficial beauty; at Jehu’s word she was thrown down, and the dogs left only her skull, her feet and her palms, as Elijah had spoken (2 Kings 9:30-37). The rulers of Samaria beheaded Ahab’s seventy sons, and Jehu killed all that remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, his great men, his friends and his priests (2 Kings 10:1-11). Forty-two brothers of Ahaziah were killed for their ties to the house of Ahab (2 Kings 10:12-14). Then, by a trick, saying that Ahab had served Baal a little but Jehu would serve him much, he called a solemn assembly for Baal, as Jezebel had once called a fast against Naboth, gave out vestments to every worshipper, and had them all killed; he burned the images, broke down the house of Baal, and made it a latrine (2 Kings 10:18-27). The images were to be burned as a cursed thing (Deuteronomy 7:25-26), and the teaching adds that idols come with clothing, the robes of false clergy then and now. So Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel (2 Kings 10:28). But he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan (2 Kings 10:29). The teacher offers a reason: Baal was a foreign Zidonian god, but the calves were stamped into their own heritage, the gods of their fathers, and Jehu was not concerned with the law. The Lord told Jehu that because he had done well in carrying out what was right in His eyes against the house of Ahab, his sons to the fourth generation would sit on the throne of Israel (2 Kings 10:30). That was the mercy shown him. But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart, for he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 10:31). There were never any righteous kings of the northern kingdom; all the kings were defective except David, Hezekiah and Josiah (Ecclesiasticus 49:4). A man may do great things and still turn away and stay in sin. Whoever thinks he is standing must watch that he does not fall, and God provides a way out (1 Corinthians 10:12-13), and not everyone who calls Christ Lord will enter the kingdom, but the one who does the will of the Father (Matthew 7:21-23). Jehu was righteous in the beginning, and then he went wicked. In those days the Lord began to cut Israel short, and Hazael struck them throughout the land east of the Jordan (2 Kings 10:32-33), as the word to Elijah had set Hazael’s sword and Jehu’s side by side (1 Kings 19:17); prophecy has no time clock. Jehu reigned twenty-eight years (2 Kings 10:36). His line held the throne to the fourth generation as promised, until Shallum killed Zachariah after six months (2 Kings 15:8-12), and Hosea named Jezreel, where the house of Jehu would be punished for the blood it shed and the kingdom of Israel brought to an end (Hosea 1:4). The walk is a marathon, not a sprint; the difference is whether a man gets back up and repents, or stays down and departs from the law.

name: Athaliah
text: Destroying all the seed royal of the house of Judah to reign herself; crying treason when the rightful king was crowned. Athaliah of the house of Ahab counselled her son Ahaziah king of Judah in wickedness, and when Jehu killed him she destroyed all the royal seed of Judah to keep the power that had come to her through him (2 Chronicles 22:2-3; 2 Kings 11:1). Jehosheba hid the infant Joash in the house of the Lord six years; in the seventh, Jehoiada the priest crowned him under guard, and when Athaliah tore her clothes and cried treason, she was taken out and killed (2 Kings 11:2-16). Jehoiada renewed the covenant, and the people tore down the house of Baal (2 Kings 11:17-18). Ahaziah king of Judah was the son of Athaliah, of the house of Omri and Ahab, and he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, because his mother counselled him in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:2-3; 2 Kings 8:18, 26). He went to his mother for counsel instead of to the priests and the judges; a woman with a grudge can rule a kingdom through her son. A mama’s boy is not ready to rule, and the Lord does not deal with men who follow behind a woman into sin. When Jehu killed Ahaziah and Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she rose and destroyed all the royal seed (2 Kings 11:1). A mother gave orders to kill anyone next in line, because her power came through her son and she meant to keep it; to stay in power, such women will destroy the men. She did not do it alone; she had weak men helping her run over everything. The teaching reads her as the Jezebel of Thyatira, with the children who follow her (Revelation 2:20-23). But Jehosheba, daughter of king Joram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, took Joash the son of Ahaziah from among the king’s sons who were being murdered, and hid him and his nurse in a bedroom, and he stayed hidden with her in the house of the Lord six years while Athaliah reigned over the land (2 Kings 11:2-3; 2 Chronicles 22:11-12). The rightful king was kept hidden the whole time the usurper sat on the throne. Her sons, meanwhile, broke up the house of God and gave its dedicated things to the Baals (2 Chronicles 24:7). In the seventh year Jehoiada brought the captains of hundreds and the guard into the house of the Lord, made a covenant with them, showed them the king’s son, and set armed men around him on every side with King David’s spears and shields, with orders to kill anyone who came within the ranks (2 Kings 11:4-11). That was order and strategy. He brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, gave him the testimony, and anointed him, and the people clapped and cried, God save the king (2 Kings 11:12). The saying comes from our forefathers, not from Europe: the priest had to establish a king against a wicked woman who had interfered with the rulership of men. Athaliah heard the noise and came into the house of the Lord, saw the king standing by the pillar as the custom was, with the trumpeters and all the people rejoicing, and tore her clothes and cried, Treason, treason (2 Kings 11:13-14). She had just killed all the royal seed, and when the rightful king was anointed she screamed treason. When someone tries to restore order, that is how some look at it, as treason against them; they do not see that they are out of order. Jehoiada ordered her taken out between the ranks, and anyone who followed her killed with the sword, because she was not to be slain in the house of the Lord; they seized her, and at the horse entrance to the king’s house she was killed (2 Kings 11:15-16). Twice in the history, when wicked women rose up in power to devour, Jezebel and Athaliah, God sent men of the Lord to remove them for not listening to Him. Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord, the king and the people, that they should be the Lord’s people; the people tore down the house of Baal, smashed its altars and images, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars, and the city was quiet (2 Kings 11:17-20). This same covenant is what happens today: as a person repents, keeps the commandments and comes out of idolatry, they become the Lord’s people again. The weapons then were physical; today Israel’s weapon is the scriptures.

name: Jehoahaz of Israel
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord and following the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, departing not therefrom; beseeching the Lord under the oppression of Syria, and not departing from the sins of the house of Jeroboam when the saviour came. Jehu’s son Jehoahaz reigned seventeen years in Samaria and kept Jeroboam’s sins, and the Lord gave Israel into the hand of Hazael and his son Ben-hadad all his days (2 Kings 13:1-3). He pleaded with the Lord, and the Lord heard him, because He saw how Syria oppressed Israel, and gave Israel a saviour; but the people still did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, and the king was left with fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers (2 Kings 13:4-7). The teaching reads the saviour as coming after his death, in the reigns of his son and grandson (2 Kings 13:22-25; 2 Kings 14:25-27). In the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years; the teaching dates it about 814 to 798 BC (2 Kings 13:1). He did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin (2 Kings 13:2). His father had cut off Baal but kept the calves (2 Kings 10:28-31), and the son walked in them. The Lord’s anger burned against Israel, and He gave them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and Ben-hadad his son all their days (2 Kings 13:3). When we sin, the Lord brings an adversary, other nations, to correct us. Jehoahaz pleaded with the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, because He saw the oppression of Israel (2 Kings 13:4). Even though he was wicked, the Lord hears the prayer of the oppressed (Ecclesiasticus 35:13). Yet they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam but walked in them, and the grove also stood in Samaria (2 Kings 13:6). The prayer was heard; the idolatry stayed. Syria left Jehoahaz no army but fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust of threshing (2 Kings 13:7). Fifty horsemen is what remains after a people takes a major loss: the curse of the law, to go out against the enemy one way and flee seven (Deuteronomy 28:25). Threshing here means thrashing. Hazael oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 13:22). The saviour is written ahead of time. What is read there is not what was happening in his reign but what was going to happen: the Lord heard him in his lifetime and answered in the days of his son and his grandson, as the commentators the teacher reads explain it, when Jehoash took back the cities and Jeroboam the second restored Israel’s border (2 Kings 13:5, 24-25; 2 Kings 14:25-27). He gave them saviours when they cried to Him in their trouble, as the Levites later confessed (Nehemiah 9:27). The Lord put a plan of salvation in place; He did not send a Clark Kent. The mercy is named with its reason: the Lord was gracious to them and had compassion and regard for them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and would not destroy them or cast them from His presence as yet (2 Kings 13:23). God has a chosen people and has regard for His chosen (Wisdom of Solomon 4:15), but He is no respecter of persons in judging them. The words as yet carry the rest of the story, for the northern kingdom was later cast off (2 Kings 17:18). Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, was buried in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place (2 Kings 13:8-9).

name: Jehoash of Israel and the arrows
text: Doing evil and departing not from the sins of Jeroboam; smiting the ground thrice with the arrows and staying, when the man of God had put his hands on his hands. Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz kept Jeroboam’s sins, yet he came down and wept over the dying Elisha, who put his hands on the king’s hands to shoot the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance from Syria (2 Kings 13:10-17). Told to strike the ground with the arrows, he struck three times and stopped, and the prophet was angry: five or six strokes would have finished Syria, and now he would beat Syria only three times (2 Kings 13:18-19). He beat Ben-hadad three times and took back Israel’s cities, and the calves stayed (2 Kings 13:25). In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria, sixteen years, about 798 to 782 BC in the teaching’s dating; he is not to be confused with Joash of Judah (2 Kings 13:10). He did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 13:11). When Elisha fell sick with the sickness he would die of, the king came down and wept over his face, crying, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen (2 Kings 13:14), the same cry Elisha had made when Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:12). Elisha told him to take bow and arrows and put his hand on the bow, and put his own hands on the king’s hands; he told him to open the window eastward and shoot, and when he shot, Elisha called it the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance, the arrow of deliverance from Syria, for he would strike the Syrians at Aphek until he had finished them (2 Kings 13:15-17). The arrow proved what had been written of his father’s reign: the deliverance had not come under Jehoahaz, and here it was being given. Then Elisha told him to take the arrows and strike the ground, and he struck three times and stopped (2 Kings 13:18). Elisha did not tell him how many times; he stopped on his own. The man of God was angry with him and said he should have struck five or six times, and then he would have struck Syria until it was finished; now he would strike Syria only three times (2 Kings 13:19). The three strokes stood for the wars against Ben-hadad. Three victories would not bring back all the land, so it would take another generation; a man will only do so much in his time. Aram and the Arameans came of Aram the son of Shem, brother of our forefather Arphaxad, and Jehoash got as far as Aphek. Elisha died and was buried, and when raiders from Moab came in the spring, men burying a man threw the body into Elisha’s tomb, and when it touched Elisha’s bones the man came to life and stood up (2 Kings 13:20-21). After his death his body prophesied (Ecclesiasticus 48:13-14). Yet Elisha died a natural death, so Elijah, who was taken up, was still the greater. Hazael died, and Jehoash took back from Ben-hadad his son the cities Hazael had taken from his father; three times he beat him and recovered the cities of Israel (2 Kings 13:24-25). He also fought Amaziah king of Judah. Amaziah had hired soldiers out of Israel and then sent them home, and they raided Judah’s cities; after he beat Edom and set up Edom’s gods, he challenged Jehoash, who answered with the parable of the thistle and the cedar and told him to stay home (2 Chronicles 25:6-14; 2 Kings 14:8-10). It came of God, because Judah had sought the gods of Edom (2 Chronicles 25:20). Jehoash beat Judah at Beth-shemesh, broke down the wall of Jerusalem, and carried the gold, silver, vessels and hostages to Samaria (2 Kings 14:11-14). There was civil war between us. The cities came back, the brother kingdom was humbled, and the calves stayed in Bethel and Dan.

name: Jeroboam the son of Joash
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord forty-one years; departing not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Jeroboam the son of Joash reigned forty-one years in Samaria and did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, yet the Lord used him to restore Israel’s border from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the plain, as Jonah had prophesied, because He saw how bitter Israel’s affliction was (2 Kings 14:23-27). The prosperity of his reign bred luxury, oppression and violence, and Amos and Hosea prophesied the sword against his house and captivity for Israel (Amos 7:9-11; Hosea 1:4). The sentence fell on his son Zachariah, killed after six months, the end of Jehu’s fourth generation (2 Kings 15:8-12). In the fifteenth year of Amaziah king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash began to reign in Samaria and reigned forty-one years, one year longer than David; the teaching dates him about 793 to 753 BC (2 Kings 14:23). He did evil and did not depart from any of the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat (2 Kings 14:24). Like Omri, he looms large in secular history and gets about six verses in scripture; the Lord does not care about carnal accolades. His reign was prosperous, and riches bred trouble: more money, more problems. Amos railed against the rich who sold the upright for money and the needy for the price of sandals, and against those at ease in Zion (Amos 2:6-8; Amos 6:1); they were about making their bread, impatient for the Sabbath to end so they could sell (Amos 8:5). Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his riches will come to want (Proverbs 22:16). Hosea described the land in those days: no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God, but swearing, lying, killing and stealing, and blood touching blood (Hosea 4:1-2). The Lord eased the pressure from outside, and the northern kingdom decided to relax too. Amos prophesied that the sanctuaries of Israel would be laid waste and the Lord would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent word to the king that Amos was conspiring against him and the land could not bear his words, and told the prophet to go back to Judah and prophesy there (Amos 7:9-13). He misreported him: Amos said the sword would come on the house of Jeroboam, not that Jeroboam himself would die by it. The prophet’s job is the word of the Lord, no more and no less, and Amos was telling the northern kingdom they were going into slavery soon. He restored Israel’s border from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the plain, according to the word the Lord spoke by His servant Jonah the son of Amittai of Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25). The entrance of Hamath is the northern border of the land given in Numbers, reached under David and Solomon, and the sea of the plain is the Salt Sea (Numbers 34:8; Deuteronomy 3:17). Jonah of Gath-hepher was of Zebulun, and he, Hosea and Amos prophesied in the same days. The Lord saw that Israel’s affliction was very bitter, with no one left, bond or free, and no helper, and He had not said He would blot out the name of Israel, so He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:26-27). It was not because they were righteous, but because He saw their oppression. He recovered Damascus and Hamath and made Syria tributary (2 Kings 14:28). The sentence was deferred, not lifted. Hosea’s first child was named Jezreel, because the Lord would soon punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel and end the kingdom of Israel (Hosea 1:1, 4). Jeroboam slept with his fathers, and his son Zachariah reigned six months, doing evil as his fathers had, until Shallum conspired against him and killed him before the people; that was the word the Lord spoke to Jehu, that his sons would sit on the throne to the fourth generation (2 Kings 14:29; 2 Kings 15:8-12). After him came violence, men slaying each other for the throne; an unwise king destroys his people (Ecclesiasticus 10:3). The teacher applies it to America: destruction is coming to this land.

name: Hosea the prophet
text: Taking a wife of whoredoms at the Lord’s command as a sign against Israel; prophesying the scattering and the return. In the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, the Lord told Hosea to take a wife of whoredoms, because the land had left the Lord for other lovers, and he took Gomer and named her children Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi as the sentence on the northern kingdom (Hosea 1:1-9). Told again to love an adulteress, he bought her back and kept her many days, a sign that Israel would live many days without king or sacrifice and afterward return to the Lord and David their king (Hosea 3:1-5). The same prophet carried the promise that the children of Israel would be as the sand of the sea and be called sons of the living God (Hosea 1:10-11). The word of the Lord came to Hosea the son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel (Hosea 1:1); he and Isaiah shared the same four kings of Judah. The Lord told him to go and take a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms, because the land had left the Lord for other lovers, and he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim (Hosea 1:2-3). He took a whore because it was a picture of how the people committed spiritual fornication against the Most High, devising idols and keeping the customs of other nations (Wisdom of Solomon 14:12). God was showing Hosea that he would go through what God goes through, with Israel as the bride. The Lord named the children. The first son was Jezreel, for in a little while He would punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel and end the kingdom of the house of Israel, breaking Israel’s bow in the valley of Jezreel (Hosea 1:4-5). The daughter was Lo-ruhamah, for He would no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, though He would have mercy on Judah and save them by the Lord their God, not by bow or sword (Hosea 1:6-7). The second son was Lo-ammi, for they were not His people and He would not be their God (Hosea 1:8-9). The names say cut off three times, and they were fulfilled when Assyria carried Israel away (2 Kings 17:6). When a people are no longer God’s people they become strangers, heathen, Gentiles; the Gentiles all through Paul’s letters are this chapter. Then the Lord told him to go again and love a woman loved by another, an adulteress, as the Lord loves the children of Israel though they turn to other gods; he bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and a measure and a half of barley, and told her she would stay with him many days and not play the harlot or belong to another man (Hosea 3:1-3). By the law a man could not take back a wife who had gone to another, yet the Lord lets Israel return (Jeremiah 3:1). The captivity itself is mercy compared with being cut off altogether. Yet the number of the children of Israel would be as the sand of the sea, beyond measuring or counting, and where it was said to them that they were not His people, it would be said that they were sons of the living God (Hosea 1:10). Paul reads it of the called (Romans 9:24-26): Ephraim was cast down but not cast away. The study notes teach that the sand of the sea is the blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans, not the so-called white man calling himself a Jew, and that the multitude is one sign of who the people of God are. Then Judah and Israel would be gathered together, appoint themselves one head, and come up out of the land, for great would be the day of Jezreel (Hosea 1:11): the northern and southern kingdoms coming together under God’s laws with one head, Christ, needing no other nation to put its stamp on it. The children of Israel would live many days without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an image, without an ephod and without household gods (Hosea 3:4). Without a king is political sovereignty, lost when Europe colonized Africa and the slave ships took us. Without a sacrifice is no religious establishment teaching us our God; the slave master taught us his. Without an image, our image was destroyed, and worshipping a god who does not look like you destroys the way you see yourself. Without an ephod is no priest to guide. The classes set the many days beside the time, times and a half of Daniel, reckoned as three hundred and fifty years, until the power of the holy people is scattered (Daniel 12:7); other teaching speaks of the many days as centuries. Afterward the children of Israel would return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, and come trembling to the Lord and His goodness in the last days (Hosea 3:5). David their king is Christ, the king the Lord said He would raise up to them when He breaks the yoke from their neck and saves them from the land of their captivity (Jeremiah 30:8-10). The afterward is today: we are returning.

name: Menahem king of Israel
text: Ripping up all the women with child in Tiphsah; buying Assyria with a thousand talents of silver exacted from Israel. Menahem the son of Gadi killed Shallum, who had reigned a month, took the throne, and when Tiphsah would not open its gates he struck it and ripped open all its pregnant women (2 Kings 15:14-16). He did evil ten years, and when Pul king of Assyria came against the land he paid him a thousand talents of silver, taxed from Israel’s men of wealth at fifty shekels a head, to hold the kingdom in his hand (2 Kings 15:17-20). Assyria turned back for the moment; under Pekah it carried off Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali (2 Kings 15:29). Shallum had killed Zachariah and reigned a full month in Samaria, and Menahem went up from Tirzah, killed Shallum, and reigned in his place (2 Kings 15:13-14). He took the throne the way Shallum had, by killing. Tirzah was the old capital before Omri built Samaria, and Tiphsah here is not the Tiphsah on the Euphrates of Solomon’s day but a town on his road; when it would not open to him, he struck it and all its territory and ripped open every woman in it who was with child (2 Kings 15:16). He met resistance and made an example of those people to spread fear. It is what Elisha wept to foresee from Hazael, and what Amos charged against Ammon, who ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead to enlarge their border (2 Kings 8:12; Amos 1:13). Menahem did the same as the heathen, against his own people. The cruel man troubles his own flesh (Proverbs 11:17), and a man is punished by the very thing he sins with (Wisdom of Solomon 11:16). He reigned ten years in Samaria and did evil, not departing all his days from the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 15:17-18). Pul king of Assyria, who is Tiglath-pileser, came against the land, and Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to buy his support and secure his hold on the throne. He raised it from all the men of great wealth in Israel, fifty shekels from each, to pay the king of Assyria (2 Kings 15:19-20). Instead of calling on God he paid Pul off, and Israel became a tributary vassal. The wealthy he taxed were the ones who had been fleecing the poor in the prosperity under Jeroboam the second (Amos 8:4-6); wealth gotten by vanity dwindles (Proverbs 13:11), and the heavy tax was the Lord’s way of getting it back. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay in the land (2 Kings 15:20). It was the beginning of the end, the first time Assyria reached into Israel. When Ephraim saw his sickness he went to the Assyrian, but that king could not heal him or cure his wound (Hosea 5:13); Assyria was a physician of no value (Job 13:4), and they could not stop what was coming, because they stayed in sin. Assyria was the rod of the Lord’s anger against a hypocritical nation (Isaiah 10:5-6). Because of unrighteous dealings and riches got by deceit, a kingdom is taken from one people and given to another (Ecclesiasticus 10:8), and an unwise king destroys his people (Ecclesiasticus 10:3). Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned two years, kept paying, and did evil, until Pekah his captain conspired against him with fifty men of Gilead and killed him in the palace: a trusted captain killing the king (2 Kings 15:22-25). In the days of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and took Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). When Israel sins, God sends nations who are not going to be their friends (Deuteronomy 28:48). No sentence on Menahem himself is written in the chapter; the silver bought him time on the throne, and what he put off fell on the nation after him.

name: Hoshea, last king of Israel
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord, though not as the kings before him; conspiring with So king of Egypt and withholding the tribute. Hoshea the son of Elah, the last king of Israel, did evil though not as the kings before him; he became Shalmaneser’s servant and paid him tribute, then sent to So king of Egypt and stopped the payments (2 Kings 17:1-4). The king of Assyria bound him in prison, besieged Samaria three years, took it in Hoshea’s ninth year, and carried Israel away to Halah, to Habor by the river of Gozan, and to the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:4-6). It came because they would not obey the voice of the Lord their God (2 Kings 18:12). Pekah had killed Pekahiah and lost half the land to Assyria, and Hoshea conspired against Pekah and killed him the same way (2 Kings 15:25, 29-30); what a man sows he reaps (Galatians 6:7). In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea began to reign in Samaria nine years, about 732 to 722 BC in the teaching, and did evil in the sight of the Lord, though not as the kings of Israel before him (2 Kings 17:1-2). Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against him, and Hoshea became his servant and paid tribute (2 Kings 17:3); he was a puppet king. The splitting of the kingdom was one thing and the cutting off was another: the north still had a kingdom until 722 BC, and that is when the northern kingdom became Gentiles. Then the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no tribute as he had year by year (2 Kings 17:4). He turned to Egypt, the first nation that enslaved them, instead of to the Lord. Ephraim was like a silly dove without sense, calling to Egypt and going to Assyria (Hosea 7:11), and the teaching reads king Jareb as no person but the great king, Shalmaneser (Hosea 5:13; Hosea 10:6). Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and trust in its shadow instead of looking to the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 30:1-3; Isaiah 31:1). The teacher applies it to trusting in America’s politics, and Zedekiah later repeated the same pattern. The king of Assyria shut Hoshea up and bound him in prison, came up through all the land, and besieged Samaria three years; in Hoshea’s ninth year he took Samaria, carried Israel away to Assyria, and placed them in Halah and Habor by the river of Gozan and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:4-6; 2 Kings 18:9-11). A siege meant the famine the law had warned of, until they ate the fruit of their own bodies (Deuteronomy 28:52-53). This Shalmaneser is the Enemessar of Tobit, who carried Tobit of Naphtali to Nineveh (Tobit 1:2). The captives were led away with hooks (Amos 4:2) along a long road through Damascus and Hamath, across the Euphrates to the Habor and Media, which is why northern Israelites turn up later in Corinth, Galatia and Macedonia. The captivity came in waves: Tiglath-pileser had already taken Galilee and Naphtali (2 Kings 15:29), and a remnant stayed in the land, the ones Hezekiah called to his Passover (2 Chronicles 30:6). It came because they did not obey the voice of the Lord their God but broke His covenant and all that Moses commanded, and would neither hear it nor do it (2 Kings 18:12). That is what Amos was telling them was going to happen; they did not want to hear it, and it happened (2 Kings 17:23). The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the children of Israel (2 Kings 17:24). Yet the Lord would sift the house of Israel among all nations like grain in a sieve, and not the least kernel would fall to the ground (Amos 9:9). Because of the promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob He will always bring them back, for there cannot be twelve tribes if ten of them are missing.

name: The captivity of Israel (the northern kingdom)
text: Fearing other gods; walking in the statutes of the heathen; two calves, a grove, the host of heaven, Baal; sons and daughters through the fire; divination and enchantments; selling themselves to do evil. The northern kingdom was carried into Assyria because Israel feared other gods, walked in the customs of the heathen and of its own kings, built high places and groves on every hill, made two calves, worshipped the host of heaven, served Baal, passed its children through the fire and gave itself over to evil, though the Lord warned it by every prophet (2 Kings 17:7-17). The Lord removed them from His sight until only Judah was left, and Judah walked the same way (2 Kings 17:18-19). Assyria planted foreigners in Samaria in their place, and the teaching follows the scattered tribes to the nations of the west (2 Kings 17:24; 2 Esdras 13:40-45). The children of Israel sinned against the Lord who brought them out of Egypt, feared other gods, and walked in the statutes of the heathen the Lord had driven out and in the statutes their own kings had made (2 Kings 17:7-8). They did in secret what was not right, built high places in all their cities from the watchtower to the fortified city, set up images and groves on every hilltop and under every leafy tree, and burned incense there as the heathen had (2 Kings 17:9-12). The law had commanded them to destroy every such place, not build them (Deuteronomy 12:2-3). The Lord warned Israel and Judah by all the prophets and seers to turn from their evil ways and keep His commandments, but they would not listen, and stiffened their necks as their fathers had, who did not trust the Lord their God (2 Kings 17:13-14). To believe in Him is to take heed to the commandments (Ecclesiasticus 32:24); those who claim belief while breaking the law do not truly believe. They rejected His statutes and His covenant, chased emptiness and became empty, and copied the nations around them; they made two calves and a grove, worshipped all the host of heaven, served Baal, passed their sons and daughters through the fire, used divination and enchantments, and gave themselves over to evil before the Lord (2 Kings 17:15-17). The law had warned them not to lift their eyes and worship the sun, moon and stars (Deuteronomy 4:19). For about two hundred years the northern kingdom kept the sins of Jeroboam, every king and the people with him. The teaching carries the same idolatry into today, Christmas and birthdays, horoscopes and palm reading, the divination the law forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10). There was no truth and no mercy in the land, only swearing, lying and killing, and blood touching blood (Hosea 4:1-2). So the Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them from His sight; none was left but the tribe of Judah, and Judah also did not keep His commandments but walked in the statutes Israel had made, so the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, afflicted them, and gave them to plunderers (2 Kings 17:18-20). God was angry with all twelve tribes. This rejection is why the seed of Israel is called heathen and Gentiles in the New Testament; He would move them to jealousy with those who were not a people (Deuteronomy 32:21), and Galilee of the Gentiles and the Samaritans were the northern kingdom (Matthew 4:15; Matthew 10:5). They walked in Jeroboam’s sins until the Lord removed them as He had said by all His prophets, and Israel was carried away to Assyria (2 Kings 17:21-23). When we get destroyed, we have no one to blame but ourselves. Assyria moved peoples to erase their national identity. It settled men from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim in the cities of Samaria, squatters in the land; the Lord sent lions among them, a priest was brought back to teach them, and they feared the Lord while serving their own gods (2 Kings 17:24-33). The covenant had been made with the children of Jacob, whom He named Israel, charging them to fear no other gods, and the settlers kept serving their images (2 Kings 17:34-41). No nation or treaty can redeem Israel, only turning to the Most High, and as a nation Israel today serves the gods of the nations it was scattered into. The teachers follow the tribes from the cities of the Medes, and by the second book of Esdras the ten tribes took counsel to go to a farther country where no one had ever lived, Arsareth, which they identify as the Americas (2 Esdras 13:40-45). The tribal charts taught in the classes place Ephraim in Puerto Rico, Manasseh in Cuba, Simeon among the Dominicans, Issachar in Mexico and Gad among the American Indians, with others through the islands and Central and South America, and some still in Iraq, Syria and Turkey. The punishment is living in the lands of the enemy under the slave masters’ names and a language that is not ours (Leviticus 26:38-41). His people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because they forgot the law of their God, He would forget their children (Hosea 4:6). How is knowledge rejected? By not taking it in daily; the whole northern kingdom forgot all that was established.

name: Hezekiah
text: Trusting in the Lord God of Israel, so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah; cleaving to him and keeping his commandments; breaking the brasen serpent; opening the doors of the house of the Lord and keeping the passover. Hezekiah trusted in the Lord God of Israel so that no king of Judah before or after him was like him; he broke down the high places and the bronze serpent the people burned incense to, and kept the commandments given to Moses (2 Kings 18:3-7). In his first month he reopened and cleansed the house of the Lord, and he called all Israel and Judah to a second-month Passover whose joy had not been seen since Solomon (2 Chronicles 29:3-5; 2 Chronicles 30:1, 26). The teaching calls him a king of God’s mercy: the Lord heard him for the people, for the city, and on his sickbed (2 Chronicles 30:20; 2 Kings 20:5). Hezekiah son of Ahaz began to reign in the third year of Hoshea, Israel’s last king, and did right in the sight of the Lord, as David had (2 Kings 18:1-3). Unlike his father, who multiplied idols even in the holy place, Hezekiah, whose name the teaching gives as the strength of God, refused to serve the king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:7). He removed the high places, broke the images, cut down the groves, and smashed Moses’ bronze serpent, to which the people burned incense, calling it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4). The Lord was with him and he prospered (2 Kings 18:5-7). Prospering here is not a mansion or luxury; it is the blessing that comes from keeping the covenant and doing it (Deuteronomy 29:9). Of all the kings, only David, Hezekiah and Josiah were not found defective (Ecclesiasticus 49:4). In the first month of his first year he opened the doors of the house of the Lord, repaired them, and told the priests and Levites to sanctify themselves and carry the filth out of the holy place (2 Chronicles 29:3-5). He named the sin plainly: their fathers had shut the doors, put out the lamps and stopped the offerings of an everlasting statute, so wrath had come on Judah and Jerusalem, and they could see it (2 Chronicles 29:6-9; Leviticus 24:2-8). The confession came before the offerings, a broken spirit before sacrifice (Psalm 51:16-17), and he set his heart on a covenant with the Lord because Judah was about to go the way of the northern kingdom (2 Chronicles 29:10). The cleansing ran past the Passover, so he sent letters through all Israel and Judah, Ephraim and Manasseh too, to keep it at Jerusalem in the second month, as the law allows for the unclean and those far off (2 Chronicles 29:17; 2 Chronicles 30:1-5; Numbers 9:10-11). Tiglath-pileser had carried off most of the north, and the letters called the remnant that escaped Assyria to turn back; it was their last chance, some six years before Samaria fell (2 Chronicles 30:6-9). The runners went from city to city and were laughed to scorn, the same mockery Israel meets today when the truth is preached; yet some of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came (2 Chronicles 30:10-11). Many who came had not cleansed themselves and ate the Passover otherwise than written, and Hezekiah prayed that the good Lord would pardon everyone who set his heart to seek Him; the Lord listened and healed the people (2 Chronicles 30:18-20). Grace and mercy were already there. They kept the feast seven days with gladness and chose seven more, and there had been no joy like it in Jerusalem since Solomon (2 Chronicles 30:21-26). In every work he began he sought his God with all his heart, and prospered (2 Chronicles 31:21); no one can halfway walk in the truth and expect to grow. The teaching calls him a king of God’s mercy. The Lord had said He would no longer have mercy on the house of Israel but would have mercy on Judah and save them without bow or sword (Hosea 1:6-7), and the king who trusts in the Lord will not be moved (Psalm 21:7). Hoshea was moved; Hezekiah was not. When the nation was threatened, he went to the house of the Lord and to the man of God, and Isaiah brought word that God had heard; the deliverance from Assyria is entered as its own case (2 Kings 19:1-7, 14-20). He made a pool and a conduit and brought water into the city, which the study notes call vision and planning like no other: nation building (2 Kings 20:20). The class reads the same works through Isaiah: when Sennacherib came they stopped the fountains, gathered the lower pool and broke down houses for the wall, but did not look to their Maker; they did everything but return to the Lord (2 Chronicles 32:2-4; Isaiah 22:9-11). Sick to death and told to set his house in order, that is, settle his inheritance, he did not trust the physicians as Asa had (2 Chronicles 16:12). He turned his face to the wall and prayed and wept, and the Lord heard his prayer, saw his tears, and added fifteen years (2 Kings 20:1-6). A lump of figs was laid on the boil, for remedies go together with prayer, but it was the Lord’s word that healed him (2 Kings 20:7; Wisdom of Solomon 16:12). For a sign the shadow went back ten steps on the dial of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:8-11): the Lord, who can turn back time itself, showed that everything is subject to the Most High. After such mercy he did not repay the benefit done to him (2 Chronicles 32:25), a failing entered under the envoys of Babylon.

name: Shebna the treasurer
text: Hewing himself a sepulchre on high in the rock, as if Jerusalem were his to be buried in; a shame to his lord’s house. Isaiah was sent to Shebna, the treasurer over the king’s house, to ask what right he had to cut himself a tomb high in the rock of Jerusalem, in a city the Lord had called to weeping and that had answered with feasting (Isaiah 22:12-16). The Lord would toss him like a ball into a wide country to die there, a shame to his master’s house, and give his robe, his authority and the key of the house of David to Eliakim the son of Hilkiah (Isaiah 22:17-22). The teaching reads Shebna as the rulers of Israel carried into captivity, and Eliakim as a figure of Christ. The burden of the valley of vision is the burden of Jerusalem. When the Assyrian came, the city counted its breaches, gathered the waters of the lower pool, pulled down houses to strengthen the wall, and built a reservoir between the two walls, but did not look to the One who made it (Isaiah 22:9-11; 2 Chronicles 32:2-4). They did everything but return to the Lord. The Lord called for weeping, mourning and sackcloth, and they killed oxen and sheep and feasted, telling one another to eat and drink because tomorrow they would die; and the Lord of hosts declared that this iniquity would not be purged from them until they died (Isaiah 22:12-14). He would go back to His place until they acknowledged their offence (Hosea 5:15). Into that city the Lord sent Isaiah to one man, Shebna, the treasurer who was over the house, to ask what he had there and whom he had there, that he had cut out a tomb for himself high up and carved a resting place for himself in the rock (Isaiah 22:15-16). This was an actual man. The teacher reads from a Bible dictionary that Shebna was Hezekiah’s steward and scribe who carved himself an elaborate rock tomb, and that an inscription on a tomb in the Siloam hillside is believed to be his. But Shebna also represents the leadership, and the word is double, for the rulers of that day and of ours. While the city stood under judgment, the man over the king’s house was preparing a monument to himself. The Lord would carry him off in a mighty captivity, roll him up and throw him like a ball into a wide country, and there he would die, and there the chariots of his glory would be the shame of his master’s house; he would be driven from his office and pulled down from his post (Isaiah 22:17-19). Being thrown into a large country is captivity: the rulers and the people with them enslaved, turned and tossed into a strange land. The teacher notes that the chariots of glory can be read as vessels, ships, the fleets of Solomon and Jehoshaphat, and at last the ships that carried Israel back into bondage (Deuteronomy 28:68). A carved tomb in Jerusalem could not keep him from dying in a foreign land. In that day the Lord would call His servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, dress him in Shebna’s robe, bind on his sash, and put his authority into his hand; he would be a father to the people of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah, and the key of the house of David would be laid on his shoulder, so that the doors he opened no one could close, and the doors he closed no one could open (Isaiah 22:20-22). The teaching makes Eliakim, whose name it gives as God raises up, a figure of Christ: the government is on his shoulder (Isaiah 9:6-7), he is a father to both kingdoms reunited under Christ, and he holds the key of David (Revelation 3:7). That key opens the understanding of the scriptures, and when the Lord shuts that door on one who falls away, nobody can open it. Eliakim was to be fastened like a nail in a sure place and be a throne of glory to his father’s house (Isaiah 22:23), which the teaching sets beside Christ the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). When Rabshakeh stood at the conduit of the upper pool, Eliakim was the one over the household and Shebna was the scribe (2 Kings 18:18). The office Shebna held was a trust over the king’s house, and when he used it for himself, the Lord gave it to another.

name: Sennacherib and Rabshakeh
text: Reproaching the living God; setting the Holy One of Israel among the gods of the nations that could not save. After Assyria carried the northern kingdom away, Sennacherib came against the fenced cities of Judah, and his captain Rabshakeh stood at the conduit of the upper pool and shouted in the Jews’ language that Hezekiah could not make them trust in the Lord, since no god of the nations had delivered his land from Assyria (2 Kings 18:13-35). Hezekiah spread the blasphemous letter before the Lord, and the answer came through Isaiah that Sennacherib had reproached the Holy One of Israel (2 Kings 19:14-22). That night one angel killed a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib was later killed by his own sons in the house of his god (2 Kings 19:35-37). Assyria was a rising empire. It had carried the northern kingdom away in stages, and in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib came up against all the fenced cities of Judah and took them (2 Kings 18:9-13). Judah seems to have joined a revolt against the tribute; Hezekiah admitted he had offended and, to pay it, cut the gold off the doors of the temple (2 Kings 18:14-16). Tribute did not satisfy the king of Assyria. He wanted the land, and sent Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh with a great host to Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17). Rabshakeh asked what confidence Hezekiah was trusting in. He called Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of the man who leans on it, and then turned Hezekiah’s own reform against him: was this not the God whose high places and altars Hezekiah had taken away, and whose house he had just stripped to pay Assyria? He even claimed the Lord had sent him to destroy the land (2 Kings 18:19-25). Asked to speak in the Syrian language, he stood and cried in the Jews’ language so the people on the wall would hear: Hezekiah could not deliver them and should not make them trust in the Lord; make an agreement, eat from your own vine, until I come and take you to a land like your own (2 Kings 18:26-32). It is the same thing they try with us now: the enemy threatens your food and water, because once that is cut off most people will turn their backs on God. He asked whether any of the gods of the nations had delivered his land, where the gods of Hamath, Arpad and Sepharvaim were, and whether they had saved Samaria (2 Kings 18:33-35), and his letter set the living God among the idols Assyria had burned (2 Kings 19:9-13). This is the puffed-up spirit the Lord allows the heathen to reach just before He destroys them, when their rulers say there is none other but us (Ecclesiasticus 36:10). Assyria was only the rod of His anger (Isaiah 10:5). The people held their peace and did not answer him a word, for the king had commanded it (2 Kings 18:36). Let him talk; that is why we do not do interviews with these people. Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, went into the house of the Lord and sent to Isaiah, calling it a day of trouble, rebuke and blasphemy. Isaiah answered that he should not fear the words of the Assyrian servants; the Lord would send a blast on the king, he would hear a rumour, return to his own land, and fall by the sword there (2 Kings 19:1-7). While Rabshakeh was running his mouth, the Lord had already set an ambush on another front (2 Kings 19:8-9). Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord and prayed that He would save them, so that all the kingdoms of the earth would know He alone is God (2 Kings 19:14-19). That is a righteous prayer, praying for the downfall of the enemy and for righteous judgment. The answer came back through Isaiah: the virgin daughter of Zion laughed him to scorn, for he had lifted his eyes against the Holy One of Israel (2 Kings 19:20-22). The Lord had formed Assyria’s conquests long before; now He would put His hook in Sennacherib’s nose and His bridle in his lips and turn him back the way he came (2 Kings 19:25-28). He would not shoot an arrow into the city, for the Lord would defend it for His own sake and for His servant David’s sake (2 Kings 19:32-34). That is why we honour our forefathers: God had a relationship with them before us. That night the angel of the Lord struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and in the morning they were all dead (2 Kings 19:35). This was a celestial being, part of the army from heaven, and Judah did not lift a sword, for it is not by might nor by power but by His spirit (Zechariah 4:6).
