Ben Sira records that Sennacherib lifted his hand against Zion and boasted proudly, and the Holy One heard His people out of heaven and delivered them by the ministry of Isaiah (Ecclesiasticus 48:17-21). Sennacherib went home to Nineveh and took out his rage on the northern kingdom captives there, whom Tobit buried in secret, and within fifty-five days his own sons killed him as he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god (2 Kings 19:36-37; Tobit 1:18-21). The man who said no god could save Jerusalem could not be saved in the house of his own god. God sends strange punishments to the proud, even from inside their own house.

name: Hezekiah and the ambassadors of Babylon
text: Rendering not again according to the benefit done unto him, for his heart was lifted up; shewing all his treasures to the men of Babylon. Healed of a mortal sickness, given fifteen years, and shown the shadow going back ten degrees, Hezekiah did not repay the benefit done to him, for his heart grew proud (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). When the king of Babylon sent letters and a present, Hezekiah showed his envoys everything in his treasuries and armoury, and Isaiah declared that all of it would be carried to Babylon and some of his sons made eunuchs in the palace there (2 Kings 20:12-18). Hezekiah humbled himself, and the wrath did not come in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). Hezekiah was sick to death, and Isaiah told him to set his house in order. He turned to the wall and wept, and asked the Lord to remember how he had walked before Him in truth, and before Isaiah had left the middle court the word came back: fifteen years added, and the city defended for David’s sake (2 Kings 20:1-6). A lump of figs was laid on the boil, for remedies go together with prayer, though it is the word of the Lord that heals (2 Kings 20:7; Wisdom of Solomon 16:12). For a sign the shadow went back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz, reversing the course of the sun (2 Kings 20:8-11). Sickness humbles the mightiest man; in his writing afterward Hezekiah said the grave cannot praise the Lord, but the living will, and the father will make the truth known to the children (Isaiah 38:9-19). Yet he did not repay the kindness shown him, for his heart swelled with pride, and wrath came on him and on Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). When things go well, do not get puffed up and make it about yourself. Berodach-baladan king of Babylon, then only a province under Assyria, sent letters and a present because he had heard Hezekiah had been sick. Hezekiah was glad of them and showed them the whole house of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the spices, the ointment and all his armour; nothing in his house or dominion was held back (2 Kings 20:12-13; Isaiah 39:1-2). A flattering letter and a gift, and he gave the heathen a tour of everything, not knowing they were scouting what they meant to take. A gift destroys the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:7). This was a trial. In the business of the ambassadors who came to enquire of the wonder done in the land, God left him, to try him and know all that was in his heart (2 Chronicles 32:31). The Lord does the same with us: you have been doing well, and then a strange scenario is before you, and you have to stop and ask whether the Lord is trying you right now, and not get carried away in the moment. He tried Abraham, Isaac and Jacob the same way (Judith 8:25-27). Isaiah asked what the men had said and what they had seen, and Hezekiah answered that they had seen everything. Then came the word: the days would come when all in his house, and all his fathers had stored up, would be carried to Babylon with nothing left, and some of his own descendants would be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (2 Kings 20:14-18; Isaiah 39:3-7). It is like a family that left you houses, and you show a stranger all the deeds; everything you showed them you are going to lose. It was fulfilled when Nebuchadnezzar carried out the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house (2 Kings 24:13), and when Daniel and his companions, of the king’s seed and the princes, were taken to stand in the palace of Babylon under the master of the eunuchs (Daniel 1:3-6). Some are made eunuchs by men (Matthew 19:12). Each time we were conquered we were made to take on another tongue and customs not our own. Hezekiah called the word of the Lord good and took comfort that there would be peace and truth in his own days (2 Kings 20:19). He did not argue or justify himself. He humbled himself for the pride of his heart, he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so the wrath of the Lord did not come on them in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). That is how to take correction: when your elders show you that what you did was foolish, say you are right and fix it. The humbling held the judgment back for his lifetime, but the prophecy still came to pass. He slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place (2 Kings 20:21).

name: Isaiah
text: Here am I; send me: a prophet unto a people whose heart was made fat, who walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign, and stood beside the king when Assyria blasphemed. In the year king Uzziah died Isaiah saw the Lord on His throne, confessed himself a man of unclean lips, was cleansed by a coal from the altar, and answered the call to go (Isaiah 6:1-8). He was sent to a people who would hear and not understand, until the land was desolate; he walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia; and when Assyria blasphemed he told Hezekiah not to fear, and the word came to pass exactly (Isaiah 6:9-12; Isaiah 20:2-4; Isaiah 37:5-7, 36-38). Isaiah the son of Amoz prophesied concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1), in the same period as Hosea and Micah, which is why so much of what is read in one is found in the others. In the year Uzziah died he saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and His train, His garment, so long that it filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims, high ranking angels that cover the throne as the cherubims covered the mercy seat, each with six wings, crying to one another that the Lord of hosts is holy and the whole earth full of His glory (Isaiah 6:1-4). The King he saw, the Lord of hosts, is Christ. Isaiah cried that he was undone, a man of unclean lips living among a people of unclean lips, the Israelites (Isaiah 6:5). When men see the Most High or the day of the Most High, terror comes on them. A seraphim took a live coal from the altar with the tongs and laid it on his mouth, and his iniquity was taken away. Then the Lord asked whom He should send, and Isaiah offered himself (Isaiah 6:6-8). Nowhere in that scripture does it say he was sent to be liked. That is not the job and not the mission: he was sent to wake up the people, to tell them how evil they are, to repent and come back to Messiah. His message was hard. The people would hear and not understand, see and not perceive; their heart was made fat and their ears heavy, lest they turn and be healed (Isaiah 6:9-10). Christ spoke in parables for the same reason, fulfilling this prophecy, because it is not meant for everybody to get the understanding (Matthew 13:13-14). When he asked how long, the answer was until the cities were wasted and the land desolate, and the Lord had removed men far away, yet a tenth would return, and the holy seed would be its substance (Isaiah 6:11-13). In the year Tartan took Ashdod for Sargon, the Lord told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and take off his shoes, and he walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign that Assyria would lead Egypt and Ethiopia away captive, young and old, uncovered to their shame (Isaiah 20:1-4). An 1844 history by a coloured man, R. B. Lewis, reads it as a sign that went further: as the prophet was naked, so the people were led away barefoot into captivity, and their descendants from Africa are led away by a wicked people into slavery even to this day. When Rabshakeh blasphemed, Hezekiah sent to Isaiah for prayer, and Isaiah answered that he should not fear, for the king of Assyria would hear a rumour, return home and fall by the sword in his own land (Isaiah 37:1-7). The Lord would defend Jerusalem for His own sake and for David’s sake; not an arrow would be shot into it; and the angel of the Lord struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand in one night, and Sennacherib was killed by his own sons in the house of his god (Isaiah 37:33-38). Every word Isaiah spoke stood. Ben Sira says the Holy One delivered them by the ministry of Isaiah, who was great and faithful in his vision; in his days the sun went backward, and by an excellent spirit he saw what would come to pass at the last and comforted those who mourned in Sion (Ecclesiasticus 48:20-24). The answer Here am I is also a prophecy that Isaiah would return. Long after he was dead, the Lord said by Esdras that for the help of Jerusalem He would send His servants Isaiah and Jeremiah (2 Esdras 2:17-18), and He named the prophets He would give as leaders to the people coming from the east (2 Esdras 1:37-40). John too was told he must prophesy again before many peoples and nations (Revelation 10:11). We do not know who is who, but those prophets are back in these last days, grown up in a grimy state and now coming to the fulfilment of their spirit, and no amount of money spent against this awakening can stop what the Most High Himself is doing.

name: Manasseh
text: Building again the high places his father destroyed; altars to all the host of heaven in the two courts of the Lord’s house; his children through the fire; observing times, enchantments, witchcraft, familiar spirits and wizards; a carved image in the house of God; Jerusalem filled with innocent blood from one end to another. Manasseh began to reign at twelve and reigned fifty-five years, undoing his father Hezekiah’s reform and leading Judah to do worse than the heathen the Lord had cast out: altars to the host of heaven in the temple courts, his son through the fire, sorcery, a carved image in the house of God, and Jerusalem filled with innocent blood (2 Kings 21:1-16). The captains of Assyria carried him in fetters to Babylon, where he humbled himself and prayed, and the Lord restored him (2 Chronicles 33:11-13). The sentence on the nation stood, and Judah later went into captivity for the sins of Manasseh (2 Kings 24:3-4). Manasseh was the son of a righteous king whose life the Lord had lengthened, and the people assumed the son must be good too. He was not. He rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had broken down, reared altars for Baal, made a grove as Ahab did, worshipped all the host of heaven, and built altars for them in the two courts of the very house where the Lord had put His name (2 Kings 21:1-5; 2 Chronicles 33:1-5). That is wickedness with zero fear of the Most High. People did not serve idols for nothing but for the self-gratification in it, the same as men keep pagan feasts today for the gifts, the food and the revelling. He made his son pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom, observed times, used enchantments and witchcraft, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards (2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chronicles 33:6). Passing a child through the fire is child sacrifice, the same spirit as abortion today, and his own firstborn, the heir to the throne, went in. Every one of these things was a commandment he broke (Deuteronomy 18:10-13). He set a carved image in the house of God (2 Kings 21:7), and seduced Judah to do more evil than the nations the Lord destroyed (2 Kings 21:9). Those nations were driven out for witchcraft, wicked sacrifices, merciless murders of children and feasts of blood (Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-6); we took their land and did the same and worse. How do you become more pagan than the pagans? He also shed very much innocent blood, until Jerusalem was full of it from one end to the other (2 Kings 21:16), and the Lord hates hands that shed innocent blood (Proverbs 6:16-17). The Lord spoke to him and his people through the prophets, and they would not listen (2 Chronicles 33:10). The prophets declared that the Lord would bring such evil on Jerusalem that the ears of all who heard of it would tingle, the kind of famine and disease written in the curses (2 Kings 21:10-12). He would stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab: since they worshipped Baal as Ahab did, they would get the same judgment Samaria got from Assyria. He would wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish and turns it upside down, and give the remnant of His inheritance to their enemies as a prey (2 Kings 21:13-15). In Manasseh’s own day the Lord brought the captains of Assyria, who took him among the thorns, bound him in fetters and carried him to Babylon, then under Assyria (2 Chronicles 33:11). The king they set over themselves was brought into a nation they had not known, as the curse said (Deuteronomy 28:36). In affliction, locked up, his ear was finally opened to discipline, as Job says the Lord does with kings bound in fetters (Job 36:7-10). He humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers and prayed, and the Lord heard him and brought him back to his kingdom; then Manasseh knew that the Lord was God (2 Chronicles 33:12-13). His prayer is written among the sayings of the seers (2 Chronicles 33:18-19), and it is in the Apocrypha, which proves those books belong: he calls on the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob who made heaven and all its host, the very host he had worshipped, and confesses sins above the number of the sands of the sea (Prayer of Manasses 1:1-9). Repentance is not appointed for the just, who keep the law, but for sinners (1 Timothy 1:9). He showed his repentance in works: he threw the strange gods and the idol out of the house of the Lord, repaired the altar, offered peace offerings and thank offerings, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord (2 Chronicles 33:15-16). This is the pattern of a people called by His name who humble themselves and are heard (2 Chronicles 7:14). Repentance is always possible; our people are repenting, not repented, so no man should judge before the time. Yet the Lord does not forget. Jeremiah, generations later, said Judah would be removed into all kingdoms because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 15:4), and the bands of the Chaldees came in the days of Jehoiakim for his sins and the innocent blood, which the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:2-4). The iniquity was visited on the third and fourth generation.

name: Amon
text: Sacrificing to all the carved images his father had made; humbling not himself as his father had humbled himself, but trespassing more and more. Amon began to reign at twenty-two, reigned two years, and brought back all the idols his father Manasseh had served, without the humbling his father came to at the end (2 Kings 21:19-22; 2 Chronicles 33:21-23). He trespassed more and more, and his own servants conspired against him and killed him in his house; the people of the land killed the conspirators and made his son Josiah king (2 Kings 21:23-24). Every time a king tried to remove the idolatry, Israel found its way back to folly; the Lord speaks peace to His people, but they are not to turn again to folly (Psalm 85:8). Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, and at most the last few were spent trying to put things right. Amon was twenty-two when he took the throne, so most of his life had been spent under his father’s worst years, watching the rituals and the orgies of Baal worship. That was what he was raised in, and as soon as his father died he brought it all back as if Manasseh had never tried to undo it. He did evil as his father had done, walked in all his ways, served the idols his father served, and forsook the Lord God of his fathers (2 Kings 21:19-22). Chronicles sets him beside his father on purpose: he sacrificed to all the carved images Manasseh had made, and did not humble himself as his father had, but trespassed more and more (2 Chronicles 33:22-23). Ezekiel describes exactly this: a just man who has a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, who eats on the mountains and lifts his eyes to idols. It does not matter that the father repented; that son will surely die, and his blood is on himself (Ezekiel 18:10-13). The idols Amon served are named in Josiah’s cleansing: vessels made for Baal, for the grove and for all the host of heaven, idolatrous priests burning incense to the sun, moon and planets, and houses of the sodomites by the house of the Lord (2 Kings 23:4-7). Baal worship came with sexual rites, and it is thriving today under the name of Christianity and liberty, down to the daily horoscope beside the scripture. The worship of idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil, and with it come blood, theft, adultery and men slaying one another treacherously (Wisdom of Solomon 14:23-27). Because sentence against an evil work is not carried out speedily, men’s hearts are set to do evil (Ecclesiastes 8:11), and his sins abounded to his own destruction. The servants of Amon, the people he kept close, conspired against him and killed the king in his own house (2 Kings 21:23). That was the fruit of his own work: the idolatry he enforced brought with it the spirit of slaying one another treacherously, and it came back on him. The traitors did not escape either; the people of the land killed all who had conspired against the king and made Josiah his son king in his place (2 Kings 21:24). Treason was not tolerated. The power of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time He sets over it one that is profitable (Ecclesiasticus 10:4). Wicked rulership lasts only so long. The throne passed to a boy of eight who, while he was still young, began to seek the God of David his father (2 Chronicles 34:1-3). Ben Sira says that all the kings of Judah were defective, for they forsook the law, except David, Hezekiah and Josiah (Ecclesiasticus 49:4). Grandfather, father and son stood in a row: the one who went past the Amorites and then humbled himself, the one who saw it and trespassed more and more, and the one who turned to the Lord with all his heart.

name: Josiah
text: A tender heart at the reading of the book; rending his clothes; turning to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses. Josiah began to reign at eight, sought the God of David while still young, and in his eighteenth year, while the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was found (2 Chronicles 34:1-3; 2 Kings 22:8). When it was read to him he tore his clothes, and Huldah answered that the curses written in it would come, but because his heart was tender he would go to his grave in peace (2 Kings 22:11-20). He read the book to all the people, made a covenant, cleansed the land from the temple to Samaria, and kept a passover like none since the judges (2 Kings 23:1-25). Manasseh began to reign at twelve, Amon at twenty-two and Josiah at eight, and the youngest was the wisest; better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished (Ecclesiastes 4:13). He did what was right and turned neither to the right hand nor to the left, the charge given to Joshua (2 Kings 22:1-2; Joshua 1:7). In his eighth year he began to seek the God of David, and in his twelfth to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, groves and images (2 Chronicles 34:3-7). Jeremiah, a Levite and a priest’s son of Anathoth, was called in his thirteenth year, and Zephaniah prophesied in his days against the remnant of Baal (Jeremiah 1:1-2; Zephaniah 1:1-4). In his eighteenth year he sent Shaphan to have the silver given to the carpenters and masons repairing the house, and he made sure the workmen were paid, for the workman is worthy of his hire (2 Kings 22:3-7). Hilkiah the high priest found the book of the law in the house of the Lord (2 Kings 22:8). Manasseh and Amon had been so wicked the very book was lost. When Shaphan read it, the king tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). The king was meant to read the law all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-19), and the wicked kings had not. Josiah had been seeking the Lord for years and still had not heard the curses; what shook him was the wrath written for a people that will not listen (Deuteronomy 28:15). The same is true on the street today: people in Bible study their whole life know the Exodus, but never heard that the slave ships and the iron yoke are in the Bible. He sent to enquire of the Lord, for great was the wrath kindled because the fathers had not kept the book (2 Kings 22:13). To enquire of the Lord you go to one who has the word. They went to Huldah the prophetess, who lived in Jerusalem in the college, the school where the sons of the prophets were trained in the scriptures, as the brothers go to the school on the Sabbath now. She answered that all the curses in the book would come on the place, as Micah had said Zion would be ploughed as a field for the sake of its heads, priests and prophets (2 Chronicles 34:22-25; Micah 3:9-12). But because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the evil (2 Kings 22:18-20). He gathered all the people, small and great, read in their ears the whole book of the covenant, stood by a pillar and made a covenant to keep the commandments with all their heart and soul, and all the people stood to it (2 Kings 23:1-3). Our forefathers had the Bible, and the king read it openly. Then he cleaned house: the vessels of Baal and the host of heaven burned at the Kidron, the idolatrous priests put down, the grove burned to powder, the houses of the sodomites by the temple broken down, Topheth defiled so no child could be passed through the fire to Molech, the horses given to the sun taken away, and Solomon’s high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom defiled (2 Kings 23:4-14). He burned bones on Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel as the man of God had foretold by name (2 Kings 23:15-16; 1 Kings 13:2). The priests of the high places in Samaria he killed on their own altars (2 Kings 23:19-20). It was a bloody path to redemption: the king who will set no wicked thing before his eyes destroys early all the wicked of the land (Psalm 101:3-8). This is repentance in action, cleaning house of every idol that brings a people under punishment. He commanded the passover as written in the book, and none like it had been kept since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-22); reading the law brought the nation back to the appointed feasts in order, as the feast is kept in order today. No king before or after him turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul and might (2 Kings 23:25). His memory is like perfume and like honey in every mouth; he behaved uprightly in the conversion of the people, and in a time of the ungodly he established the worship of God. All the kings except David, Hezekiah and Josiah were defective, for they forsook the law (Ecclesiasticus 49:1-4). Yet the Lord did not turn from His wrath over Manasseh’s provocations (2 Kings 23:26-27); the promise to Josiah was that the evil would not come in his days.

name: Jehoahaz (Shallum) of Judah
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord according to all that his fathers had done. After Josiah fell at Megiddo the people of the land anointed his son Jehoahaz, called Shallum, and in three months he did evil according to all his fathers had done (2 Kings 23:30-32). Pharaoh Necho put him in bands at Riblah, laid a tribute on the land, set his brother Eliakim on the throne as Jehoiakim, and carried Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:33-34). Jeremiah told the people to weep not for the dead king but for the one who went away, for he would never see his native land again (Jeremiah 22:10-12). Josiah was carried dead from Megiddo, and the people of the land took Jehoahaz his son, anointed him and made him king in his father’s place (2 Kings 23:30). The people did this themselves, and they passed over the elder brother: Jehoahaz was twenty-three and Jehoiakim twenty-five (2 Kings 23:31, 36). The curse had said the Lord would bring them and the king they set over themselves into a nation they had not known (Deuteronomy 28:36), and this king is an example of it. He reigned three months and did evil according to all that his fathers had done (2 Kings 23:31-32). He followed the wicked kings, not his father who had turned to the Lord with all his heart. Ezekiel took up a lamentation for the princes of Israel: their mother was a lioness who raised a whelp among the young lions, and he learned to catch the prey and devoured men; the nations heard of him, he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains to the land of Egypt (Ezekiel 19:1-4). That is Jehoahaz. Like Nimrod, the mighty hunter, he led men, the nation, into evil. Jeremiah was sent to the king’s house in those days with the terms on which the house of David would stand: execute judgment and righteousness, deliver the oppressed, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless or the widow, and shed no innocent blood; if they would not hear, the house would become a desolation (Jeremiah 22:1-5). Pharaoh Necho put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, in Syria, so that he could not reign in Jerusalem, and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. He made Eliakim, Josiah’s other son, king and changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:33-34; 2 Chronicles 36:3-4). Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh by taxing the people, exacting silver and gold from every man according to his assessment (2 Kings 23:35), and he too did evil like his forefathers. The word concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, who reigned in place of his father, was that the people should not weep for the dead, but weep bitterly for the one who went away: he had gone out of that place and would not return, but would die where they led him captive and see the land no more (Jeremiah 22:10-12). Shallum means retribution. Josiah was buried among his fathers; his son was buried in Egypt, the house of bondage the Lord had brought Israel out of. A father’s crown could not keep a son who would not keep his father’s course.

name: Jehoiachin (Coniah)
text: Doing evil as his father Jehoiakim had done; a signet plucked from the Lord’s right hand. Jehoiachin, called Coniah and Jeconiah, reigned three months and did evil as his father Jehoiakim had done (2 Kings 24:8-9). Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin went out to him with his mother, servants, princes and officers; he was carried to Babylon in the second wave of the conquest with the temple treasures, the mighty men and the craftsmen (2 Kings 24:10-16). Jeremiah said that though Coniah were the signet on the Lord’s right hand he would be plucked off, and written childless as to the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24-30). Babylon took Judah in three waves. In the first, in the days of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar came up and Jehoiakim served him three years and rebelled, and the Lord sent bands of the Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah, as He had spoken by the prophets, for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:1-4); Daniel and his companions were taken then (Daniel 1:1-6). Jehoiakim built his house by unrighteousness, used his neighbour’s service without wages, and set his eyes on covetousness and innocent blood, so he was buried with the burial of an ass, dragged out beyond the gates (Jeremiah 22:13-19). Jehoiachin his son was eighteen when he began to reign, reigned three months, and did evil according to all his father had done (2 Kings 24:8-9); Chronicles gives eight years, and three months and ten days (2 Chronicles 36:9). His mother, Nehushta, is named with him, as the mothers of these evil kings are named, and the teaching reads Isaiah’s word over them: children are their oppressors and women rule over them (Isaiah 3:12). Jeremiah was told to say to the king and the queen to humble themselves and sit down, for the crown of their glory would come down (Jeremiah 13:18). The queen in our custom was the king’s mother, not his wife, and the king and the queen went into captivity together (Jeremiah 29:2). The Lord said that though Coniah were the signet on His right hand, the closest place a man can hold, He would pluck him off and give him to Nebuchadnezzar, whose face he feared, and cast him and his mother into a country where they were not born (Jeremiah 22:24-26). This was the second wave. Nebuchadnezzar’s servants besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his princes and his officers, and was taken in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign. All the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house were carried out, and the vessels of gold Solomon made were cut in pieces, as the Lord had said (2 Kings 24:10-13), the word to Hezekiah fulfilled (Isaiah 39:6). Those who plunder stripped the land and ruined its vines (Nahum 2:2); the Lord turned away the excellency of Jacob, and Judah was like Jeremiah’s linen girdle hidden by the Euphrates, marred and good for nothing (Jeremiah 13:1-11). He carried away the princes and the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, seven thousand men of might, and a thousand craftsmen and smiths, all strong and fit for war; none remained but the poorest sort (2 Kings 24:14-16). They took the best of the best, the men who built in their own land, to build for Babylon. America did the same: it did not bring illiterate people to build a country; it had to pass laws against our reading and writing, because the dumbing down was made here. Among those captives was Ezekiel, whose visions by the river Chebar are dated by the years of king Jehoiachin’s captivity (Ezekiel 1:1-3), and to them Jeremiah wrote his letter after Jeconiah and the craftsmen had departed (Jeremiah 29:1-2). The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, his father’s brother, king and changed his name to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). Over Coniah the Lord asked whether he was a despised and broken vessel, and had him recorded as childless: no descendant of his would prosper on the throne of David or rule in Judah again (Jeremiah 22:28-30). In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity Evil-merodach lifted his head out of prison, spoke kindly to him, changed his prison garments and gave him a daily allowance for life (2 Kings 25:27-30), a mercy at the close of the account that did not put him back on the throne of David.

name: Asa in his first years
text: Taking away the altars of the strange gods, the high places, the images and the groves; commanding Judah to seek the Lord and to do the law; crying to the Lord against a thousand thousand Ethiopians. Asa son of Abijah, one of the better kings to reign in Judah, took away the strange altars, high places, images and groves, and commanded Judah to seek the Lord and do the law (2 Chronicles 14:1-5). He used the years of rest to build fenced cities, and when Zerah the Ethiopian came against him with a thousand thousand, he cried to the Lord and the Ethiopians were overthrown (2 Chronicles 14:6-15). At the word of Azariah son of Oded he put away the idols, led the people into a covenant, and removed his own mother from being queen for her idol (2 Chronicles 15:1-16). Abijah slept with his fathers and Asa reigned, and the land was quiet ten years. Asa did what was good and right: he took away the altars of the strange gods and the high places, broke the images, cut down the groves, and commanded Judah to seek the Lord God of their fathers and to do the law and the commandment (2 Chronicles 14:1-4). Rehoboam had walked three years in the way of David and then, once his kingdom was strong, forsook the law and all Israel with him (2 Chronicles 11:17; 2 Chronicles 12:1); that pattern is the warning over every strong king. Because the Lord had given rest, Asa built fenced cities with walls, towers, gates and bars while the land was still before them, and raised an army of mighty men out of Judah and Benjamin (2 Chronicles 14:6-8). Rest is not idleness; by much slothfulness the building decays (Ecclesiastes 10:18). When Zerah the Ethiopian, a Cushite, came out against him with a thousand thousand and three hundred chariots, Asa cried to the Lord that it was nothing with Him to help, whether with many or with those who have no power, for they rested on Him and went in His name (2 Chronicles 14:9-11). Faith in the Most High, not the numbers of the enemy, wins the battle; those with us are more than those with them (2 Kings 6:15-17). Then the Spirit of God came on Azariah the son of Oded, who told Asa and all Judah and Benjamin that the Lord is with you while you are with Him; if you seek Him He will be found, but if you forsake Him He will forsake you. Israel had long been without the true God, without a teaching priest and without law, but when they turned in their trouble and sought Him, He was found (2 Chronicles 15:1-7). That is discipline: as long as we walk in God’s discipline He is with us, and as soon as we step out of it, He forsakes us. Asa heard it and took courage, put away the abominable idols out of all the land, and renewed the altar of the Lord (2 Chronicles 15:8). Hearing the word gives courage still, for faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and we teach our people who they are. He gathered Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers out of Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon who fell to him in abundance when they saw the Lord was with him; those strangers were Israelites whose hearts turned back (2 Chronicles 15:9). They entered a covenant to seek the Lord with all their heart and soul, that whoever would not seek Him should be put to death, and swore it with a loud voice and trumpets (2 Chronicles 15:12-14). He removed Maachah his own mother from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, and cut it down and burned it at the brook Kidron (2 Chronicles 15:16). Neither family nor royal rank sheltered the abomination. The Lord struck the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah; they fled to Gerar and were destroyed before the Lord and His host so that they could not recover, and the fear of the Lord came on all the cities round about, and Judah carried away very much spoil (2 Chronicles 14:12-15). All Judah rejoiced at the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and sought Him with their whole desire, and He was found of them and gave them rest round about (2 Chronicles 15:15). The high places were not all taken away, yet the heart of Asa was perfect all his days; he brought the dedicated silver and gold into the house of God, and there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of his reign (2 Chronicles 15:17-19). The word that gave him courage, that the Lord forsakes those who forsake Him, is the word his latter years would answer to.

name: Asa in his latter years
text: Relying on the king of Syria and not on the Lord; putting the seer in a prison house for the rebuke; in his disease seeking not to the Lord, but to the physicians. In Asa’s thirty-sixth year Baasha of Israel built Ramah to cut Judah off, and instead of crying to the Lord as he had against Zerah, Asa took silver and gold out of the house of the Lord and hired Ben-hadad of Syria to attack his brothers in the north (2 Chronicles 16:1-6). Hanani the seer rebuked him for relying on Syria and not on the Lord, and told him he would have wars from then on; Asa put the seer in prison and oppressed some of the people (2 Chronicles 16:7-10). Diseased in his feet, he sought not the Lord but the physicians, and died (2 Chronicles 16:12-13). Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah and built Ramah so that none could go out or come in to Asa (2 Chronicles 16:1). Tribes out of Israel had been turning their hearts back to the Most High and joining Asa, and Baasha was trying to stop them. This was internal beef within the nation of Israel, and there are internal battles among us still. Asa brought silver and gold out of the treasuries of the house of the Lord and of his own house and sent it to Ben-hadad king of Syria at Damascus, asking him to break his league with Baasha. Ben-hadad sent his captains against the cities of Israel, Baasha stopped building, and Asa carried off the stones of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah (2 Chronicles 16:2-6). He went into his treasury and paid the heathen to fight his brother. That is a sick mindset: rejoicing when the heathen come against your own people, even people in error, instead of hoping the Most High has mercy on them. Cursed is the man who trusts in man. Hanani the seer came and told him that because he had relied on the king of Syria and not on the Lord, the host of Syria had escaped his hand. Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host with many chariots? Yet because he relied on the Lord, the Lord delivered them to him. The eyes of the Lord run to and fro through the whole earth to show Himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward Him; in this he had done foolishly, and from then on he would have wars (2 Chronicles 16:7-9). God wants the glory. The help comes with conditions: the heart has to be right. Many today go to therapists, spiritual healers and lying churches instead of asking what the Bible says to do. Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in a prison house, for he was in a rage over it, and he oppressed some of the people at the same time (2 Chronicles 16:10). He did not ask how to get right with God; he locked up the man of God who told him the truth and took it out on everyone around him. In his thirty-ninth year he was diseased in his feet until the disease was exceeding great, as diabetics lose toes and their legs swell, yet in his disease he sought not the Lord but the physicians (2 Chronicles 16:12). Who do you seek first and foremost when you are sick? The Lord, not the physician first. The rebuke is not against physicians: honour the physician, for the Lord created him, but healing comes from the Most High, and in sickness you pray, leave off from sin and cleanse your heart, and then give place to the physician (Ecclesiasticus 38:1-2, 9-12). Job called his comforters physicians of no value (Job 13:4). The host of Syria escaped his hand, and from then on he had wars (2 Chronicles 16:7, 9). You want to know why some problems never go away: the same wrong decision keeps being made, and nothing changes in the house. He bought temporary relief and lost the greater deliverance that relying on God would have brought. His disease grew exceeding great, and Asa slept with his fathers in the forty-first year of his reign. They buried him in the sepulchre he had made in the city of David, on a bed of sweet odours and spices, with a very great burning (2 Chronicles 16:13-14). His acts first and last are written in the book of the kings (2 Chronicles 16:11), and they were written for our learning, so that we would have hope through the scriptures and not through a loan from the bank or a therapist (Romans 15:4). The heart of Asa was perfect all his days (2 Chronicles 15:17), yet he ended relying on Syria and on physicians with the seer in prison. The Lord is with you while you are with Him, and if you forsake Him He will forsake you (2 Chronicles 15:2).

name: Jehoshaphat
text: Walking in the first ways of his father David and seeking not unto Baalim; sending princes and Levites with the book of the law to teach in all the cities of Judah; and setting singers before the army. The Lord was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the first ways of David and did not seek Baal; he took away the high places and groves and in his third year sent princes, Levites and priests through all the cities of Judah with the book of the law to teach the people (2 Chronicles 17:3-9). The fear of the Lord fell on the kingdoms round about so that they made no war with him (2 Chronicles 17:10). When Moab, Ammon and mount Seir came against him he fasted and prayed, was told the battle was not his but God’s, sent singers before the army, and found the enemy dead (2 Chronicles 20:1-24). Jehoshaphat reigned in his father Asa’s place, strengthened himself against Israel, and set garrisons in the fenced cities, securing the land before trouble came (2 Chronicles 17:1-2). The Lord was with him because he walked in the first ways of David and sought the God of his fathers and His commandments, not the doings of Israel (2 Chronicles 17:3-4). David was a man after God’s own heart because he kept the commandments, and the way we must walk is set by the ordinances and laws we are taught (Exodus 18:20). His heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord, not in pride but in devotion, and he took the high places and groves out of Judah, the false idols and their little churches (2 Chronicles 17:5-6). In the third year of his reign he sent his princes, and with them Levites and priests, and they taught in Judah with the book of the law of the Lord, going through all the cities and teaching the people (2 Chronicles 17:7-9). What Christ did in sending out the twelve was not new, and what is done in the streets today is not new. In Jehoshaphat’s day our people were worshipping Molech, Chemosh and Baal, and the remedy was to tear down the groves and send teachers through the land with the book. Christ said to go into the highways and hedges and compel them to come in (Luke 14:23), and wisdom cries at the gates and the entry of the city, calling to men (Proverbs 8:1-4). He also went out himself from Beer-sheba to mount Ephraim bringing the people back to the Lord, and set judges city by city, telling them they judged not for man but for the Lord, with whom there is no iniquity, no respect of persons and no taking of gifts (2 Chronicles 19:4-7). These judges are soldiers with biblical education; it is easy to get caught up in popular persuasion even among our own people, and God says take heed and do what the book says. When Moab, Ammon and those with them came against him, Jehoshaphat feared, set himself to seek the Lord, proclaimed a fast and stood in the congregation and prayed that they had no might against this great company and did not know what to do, but their eyes were on Him (2 Chronicles 20:1-12). Then the spirit of the Lord came on Jahaziel, a Levite, in the midst of the congregation. The spirit is not always there; the Lord watches how His people respond and then sends the right word. Jahaziel told them not to fear the great multitude, for the battle was not theirs but God’s; they would not need to fight, but should stand still and see the salvation of the Lord (2 Chronicles 20:14-17). Do not be scared of armies and people; teach the word no matter what they threaten, for those with us are more than those with them (2 Kings 6:15-17). Jehoshaphat bowed with his face to the ground and all Judah worshipped, the Levites praised with a loud voice, and in the morning he told them to believe in the Lord and be established, believe His prophets and prosper, and set singers before the army to praise the beauty of holiness (2 Chronicles 20:18-21). The fear of the Lord fell on all the kingdoms round about so that they made no war against him; Philistines brought presents and tribute silver and Arabians brought flocks, and he built castles and cities of store (2 Chronicles 17:10-12). Teaching the law had a real effect on the nations: wisdom is better than weapons of war (Ecclesiastes 9:18), and strengthens the wise more than ten mighty men in a city (Ecclesiastes 7:19). Cities of store are cities of provision, like Joseph’s storehouses; the diligent tend to plenty. When they began to sing and praise, the Lord set ambushments against Ammon, Moab and mount Seir, and they turned on one another until every one was destroyed; when Judah came to the watchtower the multitude were dead bodies on the ground and none escaped (2 Chronicles 20:22-24). They spent three days gathering the spoil, blessed the Lord in the valley of Berachah, and returned to the house of the Lord with harps and trumpets; the fear of God was on all the kingdoms when they heard that the Lord fought against the enemies of Israel, and his realm was quiet (2 Chronicles 20:25-30). Some battles you have to let the Lord fight; your job on this earth is to fear God and keep His commandments. His affinity with the house of Ahab, and what it cost him, is the next case.

name: Jehoshaphat’s alliances
text: Joining affinity with Ahab and going up with him to Ramoth-gilead against the word of the prophet; joining himself with Ahaziah to make ships. Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord and taught the law through Judah, joined affinity with Ahab by marrying his son to Ahab’s daughter, and went up with him to Ramoth-gilead after the true prophet Micaiah had foretold defeat (2 Chronicles 18:1-16). Ahab disguised himself and sent Jehoshaphat into the battle in his royal robes, and only the Lord’s help saved him (2 Chronicles 18:29-31). Jehu the son of Hanani rebuked him for helping the ungodly, and when he later joined with Ahaziah to build ships, the Lord broke his works (2 Chronicles 19:1-3; 2 Chronicles 20:35-37). Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:1): he married his son Jehoram to Ahab’s daughter, and through that marriage the daughter of Jezebel brought Baal worship into the southern kingdom, where even righteous kings after that could never fully purge it out. After some years he went down to Samaria, and Ahab killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, good northern kingdom hospitality, and persuaded him to go up to Ramoth-gilead, a war Judah had nothing to do with. Jehoshaphat answered that he was as Ahab was and his people as Ahab’s people (2 Chronicles 18:2-3). You cannot join affinity with people just because they are your people; this was a war God had not sanctioned. Some men are friends for their own occasion and will not stay in the day of your trouble (Ecclesiasticus 6:7-8), and a friend cannot be known in prosperity (Ecclesiasticus 12:8). He was making a bad decision in being with the wicked, yet the spirit was still on him: he asked to enquire of the Lord first, and when four hundred prophets said go up, he asked whether there was not a prophet of the Lord besides. Ahab said there was one, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him, which meant he told the truth (2 Chronicles 18:4-7). A rebellious people tell the seers to prophesy smooth things (Isaiah 30:9-11), and the time comes when men will not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:3-4). Micaiah told them he saw all Israel scattered on the mountains as sheep with no shepherd (2 Chronicles 18:16), and Jehoshaphat went up anyway. At the point of no return Ahab told him that he would disguise himself, but Jehoshaphat should wear his robes. The king of Syria had ordered his captains to fight no one but the king of Israel, and Ahab knew it; he was setting Jehoshaphat up for the kill. The captains saw the robes, took him for the king of Israel and surrounded him, and if it had not been for the Lord he would have died in Ahab’s place (2 Chronicles 18:28-31). Beware of a counsellor who counsels for himself, who tells you your way is good and then stands on the other side to see what will happen to you (Ecclesiasticus 37:8). After Ahab was dead he did it again, joining himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly, to make ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:35-36). The Lord helped him and moved the Syrians away from him (2 Chronicles 18:31), but his rescue was mercy, not approval. When he returned in peace, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and asked whether he should help the ungodly and love those who hate the Lord; therefore wrath was on him from before the Lord. Nevertheless good things were found in him, for he had taken away the groves and prepared his heart to seek God (2 Chronicles 19:1-3). We have to be careful not to bring wrath on ourselves or on the congregation; the Lord does not like that thing right there. Do not strive in a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10). Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah prophesied that because he had joined himself with Ahaziah, the Lord had broken his works, and the ships were wrecked and never went to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:37). Good works are being done, and all praise for the leadership that labours before us; but the scripture says that if we join with those doing wickedness, the Lord will break our works. The marriage he made outlived him: Jehoram his son took the daughter of Ahab, walked in the way of the kings of Israel and killed all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4-6), and Athaliah later destroyed the seed royal (2 Chronicles 22:10). The judgment on his alliances was written in his ships and in his grandchildren.

name: Jehoram of Judah
text: Slaying all his brethren with the sword as soon as he was strengthened; walking in the way of the house of Ahab, for he had the daughter of Ahab to wife; making high places and compelling Judah to fornication. As soon as Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat had the throne he killed all his brothers; married to Ahab’s daughter, he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, made high places and compelled Judah to fornication (2 Chronicles 21:1-11). Edom and Libnah revolted, a writing from Elijah pronounced a plague on his house and a disease of his bowels, and Philistines and Arabians carried off his goods, wives and sons (2 Chronicles 21:8-17). After two years his bowels fell out, and he died without being desired (2 Chronicles 21:18-20). Jehoshaphat gave his other sons great gifts of silver, gold and fenced cities, but the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn. As soon as Jehoram had risen up and strengthened himself, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and some of the princes of Israel too (2 Chronicles 21:1-4). This is a pattern to watch: as soon as some among Israel get power, they turn and hurt everyone around them; at thirty-two, all he could think of was killing anyone he saw as a threat. He reigned eight years and walked in the way of the kings of Israel as the house of Ahab did, for he had Ahab’s daughter to wife (2 Chronicles 21:5-6). A wicked man is given a wicked woman: her mother was the one who had Naboth killed for his vineyard. Second Chronicles is the same history as 2 Kings 8, told again the way the gospels retell one story (2 Kings 8:16-18). He made high places in the mountains of Judah, caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication and compelled Judah to it (2 Chronicles 21:11). High places are places of worship that have nothing to do with the God of Israel. Dealing with other gods is spiritual fornication, but physical fornication is built into these false worships; the pagan holidays passed down to our people are built on it, and that is what draws the people. Then a writing came to him from Elijah the prophet: because he had not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat or Asa, but had led Judah into the same spiritual whoredom as the house of Ahab, and had killed his brothers who were better than himself, the Lord would strike his people, his children, his wives and all his goods with a great plague, and he would have a disease of the bowels until they fell out day by day (2 Chronicles 21:12-15). Everyone who follows an evil man shares in it when judgment comes on him, and the Lord touches whatever sustains you. This is what it looks like to mess with the Most High: every sickness not written in the book of the law He brings on a disobedient people (Deuteronomy 28:61), and many are weak and sickly for disobedience (1 Corinthians 11:30). In his days Edom revolted from under Judah and made itself a king, and Libnah revolted at the same time, because he had forsaken the Lord God of his fathers (2 Chronicles 21:8-10). When we obey the Most High the nations are subject to us; when we come out from under the commandments they rise up. We had Esau on lockdown around Petra, and this was the word to Esau coming due, that when he had the dominion he would break Jacob’s yoke from his neck (Genesis 27:40). From that revolt Edom increased in numbers and strength and spread its colonies far and wide. The Lord stirred up the Philistines and the Arabians near the Ethiopians, and they broke into Judah, carried away all the substance of the king’s house, his sons and his wives, and left him only Jehoahaz, the youngest (2 Chronicles 21:16-17). Ham and Ishmael raided Judah together, and the scholars note that it accords with Joel, where the children of Judah were sold to the Grecians (Joel 3:4-6); the same peoples later held our people in the trans-Saharan slave trade. Then the Lord struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease, and after two years his bowels fell out and he died of grievous diseases, the sickness working from within like the cancers of today. His people made no burning for him as for his fathers; he departed without being desired, buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 21:18-20). Many were glad to see him go. A good name is better than precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1); a man cannot rule wickedly and shame the people and expect them to stand by him when disease comes. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31). Yet the Lord would not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant He made to give a light to him and his sons for ever (2 Chronicles 21:7). The Most High keeps His promises, to David as to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. That is why a man who wakes up to the truth must not go off: a righteous father’s walk preserves his lineage, and a wicked one can destroy a whole line.

name: Ahaziah of Judah
text: Walking in the ways of the house of Ahab, his mother being his counsellor to do wickedly; going down to Jezreel to see Joram. Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son, reigned one year and walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:1-4). He went with Joram son of Ahab to war at Ramoth-gilead and then down to Jezreel to visit him, and so came into the path of Jehu, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:5-7). Jehu’s men killed him, and his mother then destroyed the seed royal (2 Chronicles 22:8-10). The Arabians had killed all the elder sons, so the people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah king. He reigned one year, and his mother was Athaliah, called the daughter of Omri (2 Chronicles 22:1-2); scripture often calls a grandparent father, and the other translations make it plain that she was Omri’s granddaughter, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. As is the mother, so is her daughter (Ezekiel 16:44). Jezebel was a heathen, but her daughter was an Israelite with the same wicked spirit, the spirit that works through weak men. He walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly, and after his father died the house of Ahab were his counsellors, to his destruction (2 Chronicles 22:3-4). As Jezebel stirred up Ahab, Athaliah stirred up Ahaziah. This is a warning against being ruled by the wrong counsel: instead of going to the priests and the judges, as the law set for hard matters (Deuteronomy 17:9-11), he went to his mother, and a woman with a grudge ruled a kingdom through her son. He was the son-in-law of the house of Ahab (2 Kings 8:27), a picture of the curse passed from father to son. He walked after their counsel and went with Joram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead; the Syrians wounded Joram, who went back to Jezreel to be healed, and Ahaziah went down to see him (2 Chronicles 22:5-6; 2 Kings 8:28-29). His descent from Jehoshaphat did not make his own conduct righteous; he joined the cause of Ahab’s house at the hour its judgment was arriving. The destruction of Ahaziah was of God, by his coming to Joram, for he went out with Joram against Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:7). Joram asked Jehu whether it was peace, and Jehu answered, what peace, so long as the whoredoms and witchcrafts of his mother Jezebel were so many? There is no peace as long as a wicked woman is in power. Joram turned and fled, crying treachery to Ahaziah, and Jehu drew his bow and shot him through the heart (2 Kings 9:22-24). Ahaziah fled by the garden house and was struck in his chariot at the going up to Gur, and died at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27). Jehu also found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who served him, and killed them; they caught Ahaziah hiding in Samaria, brought him to Jehu and killed him, and buried him because he was the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord with all his heart. The house of Ahaziah had no power to keep the kingdom (2 Chronicles 22:8-9). The remembered faithfulness of his grandfather bought him a grave, not a deliverance, and the same hand the Most High anointed to avenge Israel on Ahab cut off the king of Judah who rode with Ahab’s son. When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah (2 Chronicles 22:10), killing her own grandsons, or so she thought, because her power had come through her son and she meant to rule. Back then a woman was only empowered through the man. The counsellor to do wickedly finished the ruin she had counselled, and only one child, hidden in the house of God, was left of the house of David.

name: Jehoiada the priest
text: Hiding the king’s son in the house of God six years; crowning him with the testimony; making a covenant that they should be the Lord’s people; doing good in Israel, both toward God, and toward his house. When Athaliah destroyed the seed royal, Jehoshabeath the wife of Jehoiada the priest stole the infant Joash and hid him in the house of God six years (2 Chronicles 22:10-12). In the seventh year Jehoiada made a covenant with the captains and Levites, armed them with king David’s spears and shields, crowned and anointed the boy, and had Athaliah put to death outside the temple (2 Chronicles 23:1-15). He made a covenant that the people should be the Lord’s, the house of Baal was broken down, the service of the temple set in order, and at a hundred and thirty he was buried among the kings (2 Chronicles 23:16-21; 2 Chronicles 24:15-16). When Athaliah saw her son was dead she arose to destroy all the seed royal, a mother giving orders to kill anyone next in line, because her power had come through her son. But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of king Jehoram, the sister of Ahaziah and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, stole Joash from among the king’s sons who were being slain and hid him and his nurse in a bedchamber, and he was hidden in the house of God six years while Athaliah reigned (2 Chronicles 22:10-12). Jehoiada was righteous, and his wife, one flesh with him, did the righteous thing and preserved the child. They had to hide that little boy, because a wicked woman who means to stay in power will destroy the men. In the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself and took the captains of hundreds into covenant; they gathered the Levites and the chief of the fathers out of all Judah, and the congregation made a covenant with the king in the house of God, for the king’s son would reign as the Lord had said of the sons of David (2 Chronicles 23:1-3). He set a third of the priests and Levites at the doors, a third at the king’s house and a third at the gate of the foundation, let none but the ministering priests and Levites into the house, and had the Levites surround the king with weapons in hand (2 Chronicles 23:4-7). He did not dismiss the courses of the Levites but kept them at their work with security added for the king. He gave the captains king David’s spears and shields from the house of God, set the people round the king from one side of the temple to the other, brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, gave him the testimony, and he and his sons anointed him and cried, God save the king (2 Chronicles 23:8-11). This was the proper custom, a priest anointing the king as Samuel anointed Saul and David, and that is where the saying comes from. Athaliah heard the noise, came into the house of the Lord, tore her clothes and cried treason. She had just killed the royal seed, and when the rightful king is anointed she calls it treason; when you try to restore order, some look at it as treason against them and do not see that they are out of order. Jehoiada commanded that she be taken out between the ranks and anyone who followed her be killed, but not in the house of the Lord, and she was slain at the entrance of the horse gate (2 Chronicles 23:12-15). Twice in the history, when wicked women rose up in power to devour, God sent men of the Lord to remove them. Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, the people and the king that they should be the Lord’s people, and they broke down the house of Baal, smashed its altars and images and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars; just as Jezebel had prophets at her table, Athaliah had a priest of Baal who answered to her, and they had to wipe that clean (2 Chronicles 23:16-17). He appointed the offices of the house of the Lord by the priests and Levites as David had distributed them, offered the burnt offerings as written in the law of Moses with singing, and set porters so that none unclean should enter; then they brought the king down and set him on the throne, and the city was quiet (2 Chronicles 23:18-21). Before a king takes his position he is under tutors and governors (Galatians 4:1-2); young Joash was king in rank and still a learner under Jehoiada. Athaliah had no place ruling Israel; being the king’s mother did not make her the ruler, and even Deborah, a mother in Israel, set her heart toward the governors (Judges 5:7-9). Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada, because that is what he was taught, and under him the house of the Lord was repaired and the burnt offerings offered continually (2 Chronicles 24:2, 14). Jehoiada grew old and full of days and died at a hundred and thirty, and they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel toward God and toward His house (2 Chronicles 24:15-16). That a priest was buried among the kings shows the respect and diligence this man had earned. What Joash did after Jehoiada died is the next case.

name: Joash of Judah
text: Hearkening to the princes after Jehoiada’s death; leaving the house of the Lord to serve groves and idols; stoning Zechariah the son of Jehoiada in the court of the house of the Lord. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest and repaired the house of the Lord, but after Jehoiada died he listened to the princes of Judah, who left the house of the Lord to serve groves and idols (2 Chronicles 24:1-18). When the spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada and he asked the people why they broke the commandments so that they could not prosper, the king had him stoned in the court of the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). A small Syrian company destroyed the princes, and Joash’s own servants killed him on his bed for the blood of the priest’s son (2 Chronicles 24:23-25). Joash was seven when he began to reign and reigned forty years, and he did right all the days of Jehoiada, because that is what he was taught; he had seen the wicked try to kill him, and he followed the man who showed him the ropes (2 Chronicles 24:1-2). He did well under the tutelage of the priest, and after that he dropped the ball. He set out to repair the house of God, which the sons of Athaliah had broken up and whose dedicated things they had given to Baalim; a chest was set at the gate, the collection Moses laid on Israel was brought in with rejoicing, and the money paid the masons, carpenters and workers in iron and brass, for the workman is worthy of his hire and we dealt righteously with our people (2 Chronicles 24:4-13). Then Jehoiada died, and the princes of Judah came and bowed to the king, and he listened to them. They left the house of the Lord and served groves and idols, and wrath came on Judah and Jerusalem. The Lord sent prophets to bring them back, and they would not listen (2 Chronicles 24:17-19). As soon as Jehoiada died Israel went off again, because the king was weak and listened to those who served other gods. Lust drives Israel to idolatry, and the Most High always sends prophets to warn. The spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, who stood above the people and asked why they broke the commandments of the Lord and so could not prosper: because they had forsaken the Lord, He had forsaken them (2 Chronicles 24:20). He was not condemning or harassing anyone; he asked a question. We could have had our own again and been out from under the hand of the oppressor, if we had kept the commandments, and as soon as tragedy comes we march and ask God why. If you seek Him He will be found, but if you forsake Him He forsakes you (2 Chronicles 15:2). They conspired against him and stoned him at the king’s command in the court of the house of the Lord. So Joash did not remember the kindness Jehoiada had shown him, but killed his son, and as Zechariah died he asked the Lord to look on it and require it (2 Chronicles 24:21-22). You cannot get more evil than that. When the prophet came to correct the king, the king killed him for telling the truth, the same spirit our people show when a labourer brings the medicine and is met with violence. Zechariah prayed for vengeance on his murderer, and it is scripture. At the end of the year a small company of Syrians came against Judah and Jerusalem, destroyed all the princes of the people, the same princes who had drawn the king to the groves, and sent the spoil to Damascus; the Lord delivered a very great host into their hand because they had forsaken Him, and so they executed judgment on Joash (2 Chronicles 24:23-24). They left him in great diseases, and his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada and killed him on his bed; he was buried in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 24:25). His son Amaziah would follow the same course, doing right for a time with a heart that was not perfect, and die by conspiracy as his father did. Joash began by doing right under Jehoiada, repairing the house and clearing out the idols, and none of it was remembered because of the wickedness he turned to after he was warned: when the righteous turns from his righteousness, it will not be remembered (Ezekiel 3:20; Ezekiel 18:24). The Lord sends the prophet to turn the hearts of fathers and children lest He smite the earth with a curse (Malachi 4:6), and our own sword devoured the prophets (Jeremiah 2:30). Christ counted that blood when He said that on that generation would come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from Abel to Zacharias, slain between the temple and the altar (Matthew 23:34-35). In Babylon the great is found the blood of prophets and saints (Revelation 18:24): the same prophets are back, and they will be treated the same way.

name: Amaziah
text: Bringing home the gods of the children of Seir, setting them up to be his gods, and bowing down before them; threatening the prophet sent to him; provoking Israel to his hurt. Amaziah did right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart; he punished his father’s murderers but spared their children as the law commands, and at the word of a man of God sent home the hundred thousand men he had hired out of Ephraim (2 Chronicles 25:1-10). After the Lord gave him victory over Edom he brought home the gods of Seir and worshipped them, and threatened the prophet sent to rebuke him (2 Chronicles 25:11-16). He then provoked Joash of Israel, was defeated and captured, saw Jerusalem’s wall broken and the temple plundered, and was later killed by conspirators at Lachish (2 Chronicles 25:17-27). Amaziah was twenty-five when he began to reign, and he did right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart (2 Chronicles 25:1-2). Kings says he did right, yet not like David his father, but according to all his father Joash did (2 Kings 14:3), and Joash did right only while Jehoiada instructed him. David praised the Lord with his whole heart (Psalm 111:1), while Solomon’s heart was not perfect with the Lord (1 Kings 11:4). Do not come to the Lord with a double heart (Ecclesiasticus 1:28): when circumstances change, a double heart changes on the Lord. When the kingdom was established he took vengeance on the servants who had killed his father, but did not kill their children, as written in the law of Moses that every man dies for his own sin (2 Chronicles 25:3-4; Deuteronomy 24:16). That is a foundational law: a man answers for his own sin. He mustered three hundred thousand of Judah and Benjamin and hired a hundred thousand mighty men out of Israel for a hundred talents of silver, like mercenaries. A man of God told him not to take them, for the Lord was not with Israel, with all the children of Ephraim; if he went with them, God would make him fall. When he asked about the hundred talents, the man of God answered that the Lord could give him much more than that, and he sent them home (2 Chronicles 25:5-10). Moses had warned Israel the same way not to go up when the Lord was not among them (Numbers 14:41-43). The hired men went home in great anger and fell on the cities of Judah while he was at war, and a brother offended is harder to win than a strong city (2 Chronicles 25:13; Proverbs 18:19). He went to the valley of salt and struck ten thousand of the children of Seir, and cast another ten thousand from the top of the rock (2 Chronicles 25:11-12). Then he brought home the gods of the children of Seir, set them up to be his gods, bowed down to them and burned incense to them (2 Chronicles 25:14). It makes no sense: the Lord gave him the victory, and he took the gods of the people who had just lost while praying to them. The law said to consume those nations and not serve their gods, for that would be a snare (Deuteronomy 7:16). In mercy the Lord sent a prophet to ask why he sought gods that could not deliver their own people out of his hand, and the king asked whether he had been made the king’s counsellor and told him to stop before he was struck. The prophet stopped, and said he knew God had determined to destroy him because he had done this and would not listen to counsel (2 Chronicles 25:15-16). Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18), and there is more hope for a fool than for a man wise in his own conceit (Proverbs 26:12). Someone boosted his head, and he sent to Joash king of Israel to meet him face to face. Joash answered with the parable of the thistle in Lebanon that asked the cedar for his daughter and was trampled by a wild beast: he had struck Edom and his heart was lifted up; why stir up trouble to his own harm? Amaziah would not listen, for it came of God, to deliver them into the hand of their enemies because they had sought the gods of Edom (2 Chronicles 25:17-20). Judah was routed at Beth-shemesh, Amaziah was captured, four hundred cubits of the wall of Jerusalem were broken down, and the gold, silver and vessels of the house of God and the king’s treasures were carried to Samaria with hostages (2 Chronicles 25:21-24). The spoil taken from Edom was snatched away, brother stripping his own brother’s temple. He lived fifteen years after Joash, and from the time he turned away from following the Lord they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; he fled to Lachish, and they sent after him and killed him there (2 Chronicles 25:25-27). Like father, like son: he did right for a time without a whole heart, went off, and his own people conspired against him as they had against his father. Power is given by the Lord, who will search out the counsels of kings who do not walk after the counsel of God, and a sharp judgment comes to those in high places (Wisdom of Solomon 6:1-5). When a man departs from the Most High, the protection departs with him.

name: Uzziah
text: Going into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense, which appertaineth not unto the king but to the priests the sons of Aaron; and raging at the priests who withstood him. Uzziah was made king at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years; as long as he sought God in the days of Zechariah, God made him prosper, against the Philistines, Arabians and Mehunims, in towers, wells, husbandry and a great army with engines of war (2 Chronicles 26:1-15). When he was strong his heart was lifted up, and he went into the temple to burn incense, which belonged only to the priests (2 Chronicles 26:16). When Azariah and eighty priests withstood him he raged with the censer in his hand, and leprosy broke out on his forehead; he lived as a leper, cut off from the house of the Lord, until he died (2 Chronicles 26:17-21). All the people of Judah made Uzziah king at sixteen in place of Amaziah, and he did right and sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God; as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper (2 Chronicles 26:1-5). This Zechariah was a different man from the priest Joash killed. Uzziah is like Joash, who did well while he had the guidance of Jehoiada. All the wise kings consulted with spiritual men; David consulted with every leader (1 Chronicles 13:1), and by wise counsel you make your war (Proverbs 24:5-6). Prosperity comes from the Most High, and it lasts only as long as a man keeps seeking Him. He broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod and built cities among the Philistines, God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabians and the Mehunims, the Ammonites paid gifts, and his name spread to the entrance of Egypt (2 Chronicles 26:6-8). Jehoram had lost Edom and Elath; Uzziah restored Elath to Judah (2 Chronicles 26:2). He built towers, dug wells for his cattle and loved husbandry, a picture of the blessings of Deuteronomy 28 as the Lord made the land fruitful. His army numbered three hundred and seven thousand five hundred, with shields, spears, helmets and slings, and engines invented by cunning men to shoot arrows and great stones; his fame spread far, for the Lord helped him wonderfully until he became strong (2 Chronicles 26:9-15). Together with Jeroboam II in the north, the two kingdoms held borders close to those of David and Solomon; the Lord was giving His people another chance before He began to unleash judgments. But when he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense (2 Chronicles 26:16). He got big-headed, a Judahite acting like a Levite. The king was to write a copy of the law and read it all the days of his life, so that his heart would not be lifted up above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18-20); the greater you are, the more you should humble yourself (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). Only the seed of Aaron could offer incense, lest a man end like Korah (Numbers 16:40), and the stranger who came near the priest’s office was to die (Numbers 18:7). Azariah the priest and eighty valiant priests withstood him and told him it did not belong to him, to leave the sanctuary, for he had trespassed and it would not be for his honour. Then Uzziah was angry, with a censer in his hand (2 Chronicles 26:17-19). He had beaten nations and would not be corrected by men he counted lower than himself, and he was ready to set fire to the priests of God. While he was angry with the priests, the leprosy rose up in his forehead before them beside the incense altar. The priests saw it and thrust him out, and he hurried out himself, because the Lord had struck him (2 Chronicles 26:19-20). He that is soon angry deals foolishly (Proverbs 14:17); one act out of a quick temper cost him a lifetime. The fear of the Lord goes before the obtaining of authority, but roughness and pride is the losing of it, and the Lord brings strange calamities on the proud (Ecclesiasticus 10:13, 21). He was a leper to the day of his death and lived in a separate house, cut off from the house of the Lord, and Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people (2 Chronicles 26:21). The law said the leper must dwell alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46); he was still king in name but could no longer sit on the throne, and leprosy is not merely white skin but a slow deterioration of the whole body. The Lord puts down the mighty from their seats (Luke 1:52). Isaiah wrote the rest of his acts, and they buried him in the field of burial belonging to the kings, not in their sepulchres, because they said he was a leper (2 Chronicles 26:22-23). Stay in the spirit, stay humble, and never forget who put you in the position you are in. In the year king Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1).

name: Jotham
text: Preparing his ways before the Lord his God; doing according to all that his father Uzziah did, howbeit he entered not into the temple of the Lord. Jotham, son of Uzziah, reigned sixteen years and did right as his father had done, but he did not go into the temple as his father had; the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, cities, castles and towers, and put the Ammonites under tribute (2 Chronicles 27:3-5). He became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6). Jotham judged the people from the king’s house while his father lived as a leper in a separate house, so the last years counted to Uzziah were really his son’s (2 Chronicles 26:21). He was twenty-five when he began to reign in his own right and reigned sixteen years; he did right according to all his father Uzziah did, except that he did not enter the temple of the Lord (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He was like his father, industrious and a builder, but he did not make his father’s mistake of going in to burn incense as though he were a Levitical priest. Yet the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:2). The high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there (2 Kings 15:35); since Solomon brought in the gods of his wives, the land was never the same. Micah began to prophesy in the days of Jotham, and this is the corruption he describes: they built up Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity, the heads judged for reward, the priests taught for hire, the prophets divined for money, and still they leaned on the Lord and said no evil could come on them; therefore Zion would be ploughed as a field (Micah 1:1; Micah 3:10-12). A righteous king in Jerusalem did not mean the whole realm was clean, any more than the lower parts of the capital are clean today. He built the high gate of the house of the Lord and much on the wall of Ophel, and cities in the mountains of Judah, and castles and towers in the forests (2 Chronicles 27:3-4). He cut down the forests and made towns; we always built castles, that is Judah. He fought the king of the Ammonites and prevailed, and they paid him a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand measures each of wheat and barley that year and the next two, putting the heathen under tribute as his father had done (2 Chronicles 27:5).
