So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6). That is what Ezra did when he prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach it in Israel (Ezra 7:10), and it is the opposite of Rehoboam, who did evil because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14). That is why he had favour during his reign. The Most High was with our forefathers when they followed the commandments. In those days the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah (2 Kings 15:37). Syria had been the northern kingdom’s oppressor, and now the two were joining against Judah; it began under Jotham and came to its height under his son. Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, not in the field where his leper father lay, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 27:7-9). A good reign does not pass to the next by blood, and the son who followed him would burn his children in the fire.

name: Ahaz
text: Molten images for Baalim; burning his children in the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom; hiring Assyria with the treasure of the Lord’s house; sacrificing to the gods of Damascus that smote him; cutting the vessels in pieces and shutting up the doors of the house of the Lord. Ahaz son of Jotham walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, made molten images for Baalim and burned his children in the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom (2 Chronicles 28:1-4). The Lord gave him into the hands of Syria and of Pekah, and instead of believing Isaiah he sent the Lord’s treasure to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, who distressed him and did not help him (2 Chronicles 28:5-21). In his distress he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, cut up the vessels of God’s house, shut its doors and set up altars on every corner of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 28:22-25). Ahaz was twenty when he began to reign and did not do right like David his father, but walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and made molten images for Baalim (2 Chronicles 28:1-2). His grandfather and father had Judah making progress, and he came on the scene and set them five steps back. He burned incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom and burned his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen the Lord had cast out (2 Chronicles 28:3). Hinnom was a place of burning south of Jerusalem, where Tophet stood and children were sacrificed to Molech; its Greek name, Gehenna, became the word for hell. The Lord said He never commanded it, nor did it come into His heart (Jeremiah 7:31). The Canaanites were driven out for their witchcraft, wicked sacrifices and merciless murders of children (Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-6), and Ahaz did the very thing that got them evicted. Baal was worshipped as the sun and storm god who gave power, crops and children, with ritual prostitution and the sacrifice of the firstborn; wealth and power for a sacrifice, and it sounds familiar today. When Rezin of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah came against Jerusalem they could not overcome him, as Isaiah said, for within sixty-five years Ephraim would be broken; but if Ahaz would not believe, he would not be established (2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:7-9). He did not believe the Lord; he believed the king of Assyria. He sent to Tiglath-pileser saying he was his servant and his son, and asked him to save him (2 Kings 16:7). That is the mind of the Negro today, wanting the one who enslaved him to save him. Isaiah pronounced woe on the rebellious children who seek counsel and protection anywhere but from the Lord and His spirit, adding sin to sin (Isaiah 30:1). He took the silver and gold of the house of the Lord and sent it as a present (2 Kings 16:8). At Damascus he saw a heathen altar that captivated him and had Urijah the priest build one on its pattern to replace the altar the Lord had designed (2 Kings 16:10-16). In the time of his distress he trespassed yet more: he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had struck him, reasoning that since the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, they would help him; but they were the ruin of him and of all Israel (2 Chronicles 28:22-23). Why not serve your own God? He cut the vessels of the house of God in pieces, shut up the doors of the house of the Lord, made altars in every corner of Jerusalem and high places in every city of Judah (2 Chronicles 28:24-25). The Lord delivered him to the king of Syria, who carried a great multitude captive to Damascus, and to the king of Israel: Pekah killed a hundred and twenty thousand valiant men of Judah in one day because they had forsaken the Lord, and Israel carried away two hundred thousand of their brethren, women and children, to Samaria (2 Chronicles 28:5-8). It was brother against brother. The prophet Oded met the army and told them they had slain their brethren in a rage that reached to heaven and now meant to make them bondmen, with sins of their own; the heads of Ephraim agreed, and they clothed, fed and anointed the captives, carried the feeble on asses and brought them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). A brother sold for poverty was not to serve as a bondservant (Leviticus 25:39-41); even in the division these men feared the Most High. The Edomites struck Judah and the Philistines took the cities of the low country, for the Lord brought Judah low because of Ahaz, who made Judah naked (2 Chronicles 28:17-19). Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and killed Rezin, as Amos had foretold (2 Kings 16:9; Amos 1:3-5), but he came to Ahaz and distressed him and did not strengthen him, though Ahaz stripped the house of the Lord, the king’s house and the princes to pay him (2 Chronicles 28:20-21). Never trust your enemy. Running to another nation with the Lord’s treasure bought only distress, and Isaiah warned that the Assyrian would overflow Judah up to the neck (Isaiah 8:6-8). This history shows why we went into captivity: despite every warning of the prophets we begged the Most High to send us there. Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem but not in the sepulchres of the kings, and Hezekiah his son reigned (2 Chronicles 28:27).

name: Josiah at Megiddo
text: Going out against Necho king of Egypt who had no quarrel with him; hearkening not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God; disguising himself to fight. Some years after his great passover, Josiah went out against Necho king of Egypt, who was marching to Carchemish on the Euphrates to fight the Babylonians and told him plainly that his quarrel was not with Judah and that God was with him (2 Chronicles 35:20-21). Josiah would not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, disguised himself, and was shot by the archers in the valley of Megiddo; he died in Jerusalem and all Judah mourned him (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). He got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it. Josiah’s passover was right on time, on the fourteenth day of the first month as Moses instituted it (2 Chronicles 35:1), and it was greater than any since the days of Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:18); his works were upright, with a heart full of godliness (1 Esdras 1:23). It shows what order and unity in righteousness can restore, even after all we had done and suffered. The same history shows the other lesson: you can know all the precepts and be righteous and still get high minded, and you have to mind your God-given business. The power of Assyria was slipping, and Babylon and Egypt were contending for what it had held. Nineveh had fallen to the Babylonians and Medes, and Pharaoh Necho led his army north to help what was left of Assyria at Carchemish, passing through Josiah’s kingdom on the way (2 Kings 23:29). Josiah went out against him (2 Chronicles 35:20). Necho sent ambassadors asking what he had to do with the king of Judah: he had not come against him but against the house he was at war with, for God had commanded him to make haste, and Josiah should stop meddling with God, who was with him, lest God destroy him (2 Chronicles 35:21). The Lord is not restricted in whom He speaks through; He spoke through a donkey and through Balaam, and He had spoken to Pharaoh. That did not mean He wanted Egypt to stop Babylon, for He had already foretold in Hezekiah’s day that Babylon would take Judah (Isaiah 39:5-7). Pharaoh was telling his Israelite brother to fall back, because this had nothing to do with him. In Josiah’s eyes he was standing up to possible Egyptian oppression. Nevertheless he would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself to fight, and did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God (2 Chronicles 35:22). Esdras says he did not regard the words of the prophet Jeremiah spoken by the mouth of the Lord (1 Esdras 1:28). Ben Sira warns not to strive in a matter that does not concern you, for if you meddle much you will not escape (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10), and the one who meddles with strife not belonging to him is like a man who takes a dog by the ears (Proverbs 26:17). Grab a pit bull by the ears and you are going to get torn up. He went into the battle in disguise, yet the archers shot at king Josiah himself. Pharaoh had warned that God would destroy him if he meddled, and among all the soldiers the Lord put it on the archers to find the king. He told his servants to take him away, for he was badly wounded; they moved him to his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in the sepulchres of his fathers (2 Chronicles 35:23-24). Megiddo is the place of troops, the place the Lord will gather all nations again in the last days. After Megiddo the Egyptians and Assyrians were destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, Assyria ceased to be, and Babylon rose to take Judah as the prophets had said; the Bible is real history. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah; Jeremiah, who began to prophesy in the same years as Josiah’s reform, lamented for him, and the singing men and women spoke of him in their lamentations and made it an ordinance in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:24-25). The promise through Huldah that he would be gathered to his grave in peace concerned the evil coming on Jerusalem, which he did not live to see (2 Kings 22:20). He meddled in a matter that did not belong to him, but he never went after another god, and he left a very good example. Virtue leaves a memorial that is immortal: when it is present men take example from it, and when it is gone they desire it (Wisdom of Solomon 4:1-2). Like David, whose righteous legacy stands over his transgressions, Josiah’s is praised among the famous men whose bodies are buried in peace and whose name lives for evermore (Ecclesiasticus 44:1-15). His death opened Judah’s last years: the people made Jehoahaz king, and within three months Pharaoh had him in bands (2 Chronicles 36:1-4).

name: Zedekiah
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord; humbling not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the Lord; rebelling against Nebuchadnezzar who had made him swear by God; stiffening his neck and hardening his heart from turning unto the Lord God of Israel. Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah king as Zedekiah and bound him by an oath sworn by God; Zedekiah did evil, did not humble himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord, and rebelled, sending to Egypt for horses and men (2 Chronicles 36:11-13; Ezekiel 17:12-15). Jeremiah told him to the end that if he surrendered to Babylon’s princes he would live and the city would not burn, but he was afraid of the Jews who had already gone over (Jeremiah 38:17-19). After a two-year siege he fled by night, was caught in the plains of Jericho, saw his sons killed, and was blinded and carried in chains to Babylon (2 Kings 25:1-7). The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king and changed his name to Zedekiah; he reigned eleven years and did evil like Jehoiakim, and through the anger of the Lord he rebelled against the king of Babylon (2 Kings 24:17-20). He did not humble himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord, and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar who had made him swear by God, stiffening his neck and hardening his heart (2 Chronicles 36:12-13). In his days false prophets told the captives in Babylon they would soon return and told those in the land that Babylon would not come; Jeremiah said seventy years, and called the people left with Zedekiah the evil figs, marked for sword, famine and pestilence. Babylon took the true king and the mighty men so the kingdom would be low, set up a puppet king, and made a covenant with him under oath, so that by keeping it the kingdom might stand (Ezekiel 17:12-14). Jeremiah told him to submit to the yoke of Babylon and live, rather than die with his people by sword, famine and pestilence (Jeremiah 27:12-13). In his ninth year he sent ambassadors to Egypt for horses and much people, with Tyre and Ammon behind him. The Lord asked whether a man who breaks the covenant shall escape, and called it His own oath that Zedekiah despised (Ezekiel 17:15-19). Rebelling against Nebuchadnezzar, he was rebelling against the Lord. When Pharaoh’s army came out and the Chaldeans lifted the siege, Jeremiah told him not to be deceived: Egypt would go home, and the Chaldeans would return, take the city and burn it (Jeremiah 37:5-10). The princes beat Jeremiah and imprisoned him on a false charge, then let him down into the mire of Malchiah’s dungeon, and the king said he could do nothing against them (Jeremiah 37:15; Jeremiah 38:4-6). Secretly Zedekiah sent for him and asked for a word, and got the same one: surrender to the king of Babylon’s princes and your soul will live and the city will not burn; refuse, and you will cause this city to be burned. Zedekiah answered that he was afraid of the Jews who had gone over to the Chaldeans, lest they mock him (Jeremiah 38:14-23). You give people the solution from the Lord and there is always a rebuttal. He kept Jeremiah locked up in the court of the prison until the day the city was taken (Jeremiah 38:28; Jeremiah 32:1-5). Ezekiel, already in Babylon, carried his stuff out through a wall at twilight as a sign: the prince in Jerusalem would do the same, and the Lord would spread His net on him and bring him to Babylon, yet he would not see it, though he would die there (Ezekiel 12:1-13). On the very day the final siege began, in the ninth year, tenth month, tenth day, the word came to Ezekiel to write the date (Ezekiel 24:1-2; 2 Kings 25:1). The city was besieged until his eleventh year, and the famine prevailed (2 Kings 25:2-3). The Lord said He would gather them into Jerusalem as dross into a furnace and melt them in His fury (Ezekiel 22:17-22). When the city was broken up Zedekiah fled by night between the two walls, ready to leave everyone behind to burn, and the Chaldeans overtook him in the plains of Jericho. At Riblah the king of Babylon killed his sons before his eyes, then put out his eyes and bound him in chains to be carried to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7; Jeremiah 39:4-7). That was how he came to Babylon and did not see it: the last thing his eyes saw was his sons dying. Then the house of the Lord, the king’s house and the houses of Jerusalem were burned and the walls broken down (Jeremiah 39:8). The crown fell from our head (Lamentations 5:16). When the prophets were living, the people played with them; after every word came to pass, they wanted to honour them. Jeremiah had said his soul would weep in secret places for their pride (Jeremiah 13:17), and the Lord had set before them the way of life and the way of death (Jeremiah 21:8-9).

name: The captivity of Judah
text: All the chief of the priests and the people transgressing very much after all the abominations of the heathen, and polluting the house of the Lord; mocking the messengers of God, despising his words, and misusing his prophets, till there was no remedy; the land’s sabbaths not kept. The chief of the priests and the people followed all the abominations of the heathen and polluted the house of the Lord; He sent His messengers again and again out of compassion, but they mocked them, despised His words and misused His prophets until there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:14-16). The king of the Chaldees killed young and old in the sanctuary, carried the treasures to Babylon, burned the house of God and broke down the walls (2 Chronicles 36:17-19). The survivors served Babylon until Persia, while the land enjoyed the sabbaths it had been denied, seventy years as Jeremiah said (2 Chronicles 36:20-21). All the chief of the priests and the people transgressed very much after all the abominations of the heathen and polluted the house the Lord had hallowed. The Lord God of their fathers sent His messengers to them again and again, early and persistently, because He had compassion on His people and His dwelling place; but they mocked the messengers, despised His words and misused His prophets, until His wrath arose and there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:14-16). Christ was mocked, and before Him the prophets were mocked; it is nothing new. To minimise the movement because it is being mocked is a self-inflicted wound, and it means you never really believed. What happens to us today happened to our prophets yesterday (Luke 6:22-23). Jeremiah counted the years: from the thirteenth year of Josiah, twenty-three years, the Lord had spoken through him early and persistently and sent all His servants the prophets, and they would not listen or turn from their evil ways and their other gods (Jeremiah 25:1-7). Ezekiel named every rank. The priests violated the law and profaned the holy things, putting no difference between holy and profane, clean and unclean, and hid their eyes from the sabbaths, just as our people today put no difference between anything and call it Christianity. The princes were like wolves ravening the prey for dishonest gain, the prophets daubed with untempered mortar and said the Lord had spoken when He had not, the people used oppression and robbery and vexed the poor and the stranger, and the Lord sought a man to stand in the gap and found none (Ezekiel 22:26-30). The sabbaths were not kept, not the weekly sabbath and not the land’s rest every seventh year (Leviticus 25:3-4). The Lord had said that if they would not listen, the land would enjoy her sabbaths while it lay desolate and they were in their enemies’ land (Leviticus 26:34-35). The land could not rest while the people dwelt on it doing evil, so He removed the people so the land could keep its sabbaths. He brought on them the king of the Chaldees, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young or old; the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the king and his princes went to Babylon, and they burned the house of God, broke down the wall of Jerusalem, burned its palaces and destroyed its goodly vessels (2 Chronicles 36:17-19). That is exactly the fierce nation of the curses, which would not regard the old nor show favour to the young (Deuteronomy 28:49-50). The power of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and He sets over it one who is profitable (Ecclesiasticus 10:4); when Israel would not rule in righteousness, He raised a Nebuchadnezzar. With the temple destroyed, what could no longer take place? Sacrifice. From captivity to captivity there was no atonement to be had, and that is exactly why we needed a saviour, an ultimate sacrifice. Those who escaped the sword were servants to Nebuchadnezzar and his sons until Persia reigned, to fulfil the word by Jeremiah until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths, seventy years (2 Chronicles 36:20-21). They were to serve the king of Babylon seventy years, and then the Lord would punish Babylon for its iniquity (Jeremiah 25:11-12). Even when He takes us down with one kingdom, He punishes that kingdom with a new one; He used Nebuchadnezzar, and He used Cyrus. When His people repent in the land of their captivity, He remembers His covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and He remembers the land (Leviticus 26:40-42). In the first year of Cyrus the Lord stirred his spirit to proclaim that whoever was of His people could go up (2 Chronicles 36:22-23). The same record that closes on the removal opens on the return. Jeremiah was told he would lose his heritage and serve his enemies in a land he did not know (Jeremiah 17:4); he was never carried to Babylon as a slave, so it speaks of his return: Jeremiah is here in the last days, serving his enemies in the land of his captivity, and he will remember who he is, his God and his land.

name: Nineveh under Jonah
text: Wickedness come up before the Lord; and turning every one from his evil way, and from the violence that was in their hands. Jonah was sent to cry against Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, because its wickedness had come up before the Lord; after fleeing and being brought back from the belly of the fish, he went in and cried that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 1:1-2; Jonah 3:1-4). The people believed God and fasted in sackcloth, and the king decreed that every one turn from his evil way and from the violence in his hands (Jonah 3:5-9). God saw their works and did not bring the evil He had spoken, and when Jonah was angry He answered that He would spare that great city (Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:1-11). Jonah the son of Amittai prophesied in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, whose restoring of Israel’s coast from the entering of Hamath was according to the word the Lord spoke by him (2 Kings 14:23-25). He was in the same time frame as Hosea and Amos, and the prophets were all seeing the same thing: the disorder in Israel, and the Lord always sending His prophets to correct His people. The word came to him to arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for their wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Nineveh was the seat of the kings of Assyria; Sennacherib went home to dwell there after the angel struck his camp (2 Kings 19:36). But the Ninevites to whom Jonah was a sign were not the Assyrians, the teaching says (Luke 11:29-30). They were the captives of the ten tribes led into Nineveh: Tobit, of the tribe of Naphtali of the northern kingdom, was carried away in the time of Enemessar king of the Assyrians and came to Nineveh with his brethren and his nation (Tobit 1:1-3). Jonah fled toward Tarshish, and when the storm came he was asleep in the ship. When the lot fell on him he confessed he was a Hebrew who feared the Lord, and told them to cast him into the sea; that is accountability and integrity, standing up when you know you are the cause of the trouble, the opposite of Achan hiding the accursed thing (Jonah 1:3-12; Joshua 7:1). In the fish’s belly he sought the Lord, as Hosea says they will seek Him early in their affliction (Jonah 2:1-9; Hosea 5:15), and Christ made those three days and nights the sign of His own burial (Matthew 12:39-40). The word came the second time to preach the preaching the Lord gave him, and a true prophet speaks the words of the Lord, not his own (Jonah 3:1-2; 1 Peter 4:11). Nineveh was a city of three days’ journey; he went a day’s journey in and cried that in forty days it would be overthrown (Jonah 3:3-4). The king’s decree named what had to change: the evil way and the violence in their hands (Jonah 3:8). The prophets of that day named the same sins in Israel, swearing, lying, killing, stealing and adultery until blood touched blood, and selling the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes (Hosea 4:1-2; Amos 2:6-8). The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least. The king rose from his throne, laid aside his robe, sat in ashes, and decreed that neither man nor beast taste anything or drink water, but cry mightily to God and turn from their evil way and their violence (Jonah 3:5-8). That is what a true fast is: not holding back one food, but no food and no water. They did not presume on God: who could tell whether He would turn from His fierce anger (Jonah 3:9)? Judith warned the elders of Bethulia the same way not to bind the counsels of the Lord to their own time (Judith 8:12-16). God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way, and He repented of the evil He had said He would do and did not do it (Jonah 3:10). It displeased Jonah, and he said this was why he had fled, for he knew the Lord was gracious, merciful, slow to anger and of great kindness (Jonah 4:1-2). He had gone in on fire, and now he felt he would look like a false prophet, and twice he asked to die. The Lord answered with the gourd: Jonah had pity on a plant he did not labour for, and should not the Lord spare Nineveh, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand who could not discern their right hand from their left, and much cattle (Jonah 4:3-11)? His thoughts are not our thoughts (Isaiah 55:8-9). We preach so that God gets the glory, not ourselves; as He turned from punishing when the fathers provoked Him, He can turn to do well (Zechariah 8:14-17). The reprieve was not the end of the word against Nineveh. Tobit, a captive of Naphtali in Nineveh, told his son to leave the city, because what the prophet Jonah spoke would surely come to pass: the captives had heard Jonah and taken heed, and the Lord held off because His people were there, but the word still stood, and before Tobit died he heard of the city’s destruction and rejoiced over it (Tobit 14:4, 8, 15). The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment and condemn the generation that heard a greater than Jonah and did not repent (Matthew 12:41).

name: Jeremiah
text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; be not afraid of their faces: speaking all that was commanded, though the word was a burning fire shut up in his bones and his own familiars watched for his halting. Jeremiah, of the priests in Anathoth, was known and ordained a prophet to the nations before he was formed in the belly, and he prophesied from the days of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1:1-5). Told not to plead his youth or fear their faces, he spoke against kings, princes, priests and people through the stocks, the burned roll and the miry dungeon (Jeremiah 20:1-2; Jeremiah 36:23; Jeremiah 38:6). The Lord made him a fortified city against the whole land: they fought against him and did not prevail, and when the city fell the enemy set him free (Jeremiah 1:18-19; Jeremiah 40:1-6). Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, of the priests in Anathoth, a Levite city in Benjamin, and the word came to him from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem in the eleventh year of Zedekiah (Jeremiah 1:1-3; Joshua 21:17-18). The verse-by-verse teaching places his ministry at about 627 to 586 BC and calls him one of the mightiest prophets in the scriptures; he worked hand in hand with Josiah’s reform and lamented Josiah when he fell (2 Chronicles 35:25). Before the Lord formed him in the belly He knew him, set him apart and ordained him a prophet to the nations (Jeremiah 1:4-5). The teaching reads this with Paul, separated from his mother’s womb (Galatians 1:15), and the study note says the same thing is happening today: the brothers and sisters waking up were known from the beginning and are raised up to prophesy against the nations. Jeremiah answered that he could not speak, for he was a child, about eighteen by the teacher’s reckoning; the Lord told him not to say it, but to go where he was sent and speak what he was commanded, without fear of their faces (Jeremiah 1:6-8). The class puts it plainly: stop making excuses; he tried to run from it and the Lord did not let him. The Lord touched his mouth, put His words there, and set him over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant (Jeremiah 1:9-10). That is why we stay within these scriptures and never go wrong, the note says, and it is our job today, spiritual warfare. He was to gird himself and speak all he was commanded and not be dismayed, lest he be confounded before them; we cannot go out with a spirit of fear on us (Jeremiah 1:17; 2 Timothy 1:7). The opposition came from his own. When he stood in the court of the Lord’s house and said the house would become like Shiloh, the priests, the prophets and the people seized him and said he must die; he answered that he was in their hand, but they would bring innocent blood on themselves (Jeremiah 26:8-16). Urijah, who prophesied the same words, was hunted down and slain by Jehoiakim, while the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:20-24). Pashur the priest struck him and put him in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:1-2). Mocked daily, he resolved to speak no more in the Lord’s name, but the word burned inside him like fire trapped in his bones and he could not hold it in (Jeremiah 20:7-9). One class reads those verses as his thoughts in the stocks, encouraging himself; the fire is inescapable, not surface level. His familiar friends watched for him to stumble (Jeremiah 20:10): the people who watched you grow up, waiting for you to revert so they can plaster it over social media. Jehoiakim cut the roll and burned it, and the words were written again with more besides (Jeremiah 36:23-32). The princes let him down into the dungeon of Malchiah and he sank in the mire (Jeremiah 38:6); the class says that mire is dung, and it is not far fetched. The promise of his ordination was kept: they fought against him and did not prevail (Jeremiah 1:19). He had the respect of a prophet and the contempt of a prophet, the teacher says; his own king, princes and priests gave him trouble for forty years and could not stop him, and he never lost his love for his people. Ebed-melech drew him out of the mire, and he stayed in the court of the prison until the day Jerusalem was taken (Jeremiah 38:7-13; Jeremiah 38:28). Nebuchadnezzar gave charge to look after him and do him no harm (Jeremiah 39:11-12); the teaching calls this the Lord’s mercy and grace, the enemies showing him favour, as the Lord had promised to make the enemy treat him well (Jeremiah 15:11; Proverbs 16:7). Nebuzaradan, a heathen, told him the city fell because the people sinned and did not obey the voice of the Lord; the nations always knew why we went into captivity (Jeremiah 40:1-3; Judith 5:17-18). He had been bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, but he was loosed and given his choice, and he went to Gedaliah at Mizpah and dwelt among the people left in the land (Jeremiah 40:4-6). The verse-by-verse teaching stresses that Jeremiah was never a captive in Babylon. One class goes further, reading the word that he himself would lose his heritage and serve his enemies in a land he did not know as spoken to Jeremiah for the last days: that land, the class says, is called America today (Jeremiah 17:4).

name: Pashur the son of Immer
text: Smiting the prophet of the Lord and putting him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin; prophesying lies. Pashur the son of Immer, priest and chief governor in the house of the Lord, struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin after Jeremiah prophesied the breaking of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 19:14-15; Jeremiah 20:1-2). The next day Jeremiah renamed him Magor-missabib, fear round about, and told him he would see his friends fall, and would go to Babylon, die and be buried there with the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jeremiah 20:3-6). Jeremiah had come from Tophet, where he broke the potter’s vessel before the elders as a sign that the Lord would break the people and the city beyond repair, and then stood in the court of the Lord’s house and told all the people the evil was coming because they had hardened their necks and would not hear (Jeremiah 19:10-15). The class that reads chapter 19 straight into chapter 20 draws the lesson: rather than hear what the Bible says, they hit, hurt and stopped the one who said it. Pashur the son of Immer, the priest who was also chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard it, struck Jeremiah, and put him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin by the house of the Lord (Jeremiah 20:1-2). The teacher marks this as the place where the opposition to Jeremiah starts. The class explains the words: smote means he struck him, flogged him, and the stocks were public shaming, meant to break a man’s spirit. Another class set pictures of the slave stocks beside this verse: we have lived the same atrocities our forefathers went through. Pashur did it because he was tired of Jeremiah blasting them for their wickedness and corruption, and Judah was worse than the northern kingdom because they knew better. The teaching keeps him apart from Pashur the son of Malchiah, who later sought Jeremiah’s death (Jeremiah 21:1; Jeremiah 38:1); this Pashur was the priest showing that he had power and a position. He was also a false prophet. Jeremiah’s sentence names the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jeremiah 20:6), and the Luke 20 teaching sets him beside the husbandmen who beat the servants sent to them (Luke 20:10-11), giving his stance as the priest who says God is not talking to you, I am the priest. Jeremiah 23 describes the same house: prophet and priest both profane, wickedness found even in the Lord’s house, and prophets speaking a vision of their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord (Jeremiah 23:11; Jeremiah 23:16). The study note compares the pastor who says, let me tell you what God told me to tell you, when it is a lie. The class of 2026-07-18 draws the application from Pashur’s stocks: prophecy is not all loves and kisses; we are supposed to prophesy destruction so our people may wake up, and destruction is headed to America. The next day Pashur let him out, and Jeremiah told him the Lord had not called his name Pashur but Magor-missabib, which the class explains just means fear round about: he would be a terror to himself and to all his friends, and would watch them fall by the sword of their enemies (Jeremiah 20:3-4). All Judah would be given to the king of Babylon, with the strength of the city, its labours, its precious things and the treasures of the kings of Judah; the teacher notes that this shows our people had treasures, their own land and wealth (Jeremiah 20:4-5). Pashur and everyone in his house would go into captivity, and he would die in Babylon and be buried there with the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jeremiah 20:6). The stocks did not break Jeremiah’s spirit, the class says; he was emboldened by it. Jeremiah had no power of his own to give Judah to Babylon; it was the spirit of the Lord speaking. As the Luke 20 teaching puts it, do what you want to the messenger, it will not stop the judgment. When the city fell, the nobles of Judah were slain at Riblah before Zedekiah’s eyes, and the teacher turns back from that verse to the word spoken to Pashur, that his own eyes would see people he would not expect put to death (Jeremiah 39:6; Jeremiah 20:4). The chapter records the sentence and not its carrying out; the captivity that the priest’s lies denied came as Jeremiah said.

name: Jehoiakim
text: Building his house by unrighteousness and his chambers by wrong, using his neighbour’s service without wages; eyes and heart set on covetousness, innocent blood, oppression and violence; slaying Urijah the prophet; cutting the roll of the Lord’s words with a penknife and burning it. Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son Eliakim, was set on the throne by Pharaoh-nechoh and taxed the land to pay him; he did evil, built his house with unpaid labour, slew Urijah the prophet, and cut and burned the roll of Jeremiah’s words (2 Kings 23:34-37; Jeremiah 22:13-17; Jeremiah 26:20-23; Jeremiah 36:23). He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and rebelled, and the Lord pronounced that none of his would sit on David’s throne and that he would have the burial of an ass (2 Kings 24:1; Jeremiah 22:18-19; Jeremiah 36:30). Pharaoh-nechoh bound Jehoahaz at Riblah and made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in his place, turning his name to Jehoiakim; Jehoiakim taxed the land to give Pharaoh the silver and gold he demanded, and did evil as his fathers had done, not as his father Josiah (2 Kings 23:31-37). The class calls him a puppet, Pharaoh’s vassal king, the way America goes into other countries and sets up puppet rulers; he paid his taxes to Pharaoh, the teacher says, but he taxed us to do it. The renaming, the Daniel 1 teaching notes, is a practice among all the nations when we are taken over: they give us a new name. The Three Waves teaching dates his reign from about 608 BC. Jeremiah pronounced woe on the king who built his house by unrighteousness and his upper rooms by wrong, who used his neighbour’s labour without pay, and made himself a wide house panelled in cedar and painted with vermilion (Jeremiah 22:13-14). His father ate and drank and did justice, judged the cause of the poor and needy, and it was well with him; but Jehoiakim’s eyes and heart were only for covetousness, for shedding innocent blood, for oppression and violence (Jeremiah 22:15-17). The teaching reads it as Jehoiakim refusing Josiah’s example. The classes carry it to America: how was the White House built? By slaves. Did we get paid for our captivity? Not at all. The slaves who built the Capitol never lived in it, and woe means destruction. Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim prophesied the same words as Jeremiah; when Jehoiakim sought to kill him he fled to Egypt, and the king sent men who brought him back, and he struck him with the sword and threw his body among the graves of the common people (Jeremiah 26:20-23). The study note sets the two kings side by side: Hezekiah knew the word came from God and spared Micah, and this king killed his prophet (Jeremiah 26:18-19). When the roll of Jeremiah’s words was read to him in the winter house, he cut it with the penknife and burned it in the fire until it was consumed, and neither he nor his servants were afraid or tore their garments, though three of his princes pleaded with him (Jeremiah 36:21-25). God always gives warning first, the class says, and some still wish they could burn this Bible up. He ordered Baruch and Jeremiah seized, but the Lord hid them (Jeremiah 36:26). Jeremiah wrote the words again with the sentence added: Jehoiakim would have no one to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body would be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night; the Lord would punish him, his seed and his servants for their iniquity (Jeremiah 36:27-31). Congratulations, the teacher says, you played yourself. Jeremiah had already said no one would lament him, but he would be buried with the burial of an ass, dragged and thrown out beyond the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 22:18-19); the teacher reads it as dying outside the land because he was evil. His son Coniah would be pulled off like a signet ring and recorded as childless, none of his seed to prosper on David’s throne (Jeremiah 22:24-30). He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and then rebelled, and the Lord sent bands of the Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah to destroy it, the evil out of the north (2 Kings 24:1-2; Jeremiah 4:6). This man was so evil, the teacher says, the Lord was sending nations against us. The study note traces the removal of Judah to the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:3-4). Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim in fetters to carry him to Babylon and took vessels of the Lord’s house (2 Chronicles 36:6-7), and the teaching counts this as the first wave, when Daniel and the three Hebrew children were taken. The note draws the lesson: when His people will not rule in righteousness, the Most High raises up a Nebuchadnezzar over them (Ecclesiasticus 10:1-4). All these people and their offspring, the class says, paid for what this fool did.

name: Hananiah the son of Azur
text: Prophesying a lie in the name of the Lord, and breaking the yoke from off Jeremiah’s neck before the priests and all the people. In the fourth year of Zedekiah, Hananiah the son of Azur, a prophet of Gibeon, told the priests and people in the Lord’s house that the Lord had broken the yoke of Babylon and would bring back the vessels, Jeconiah and the captives within two full years, and he broke the wooden yoke off Jeremiah’s neck (Jeremiah 28:1-4; Jeremiah 28:10-11). Jeremiah told him the Lord had not sent him, that he made the people trust in a lie and taught rebellion, and that he would die that year; he died in the seventh month (Jeremiah 28:15-17). The Zedekiah teaching sets the climate: Jeconiah was still alive in Babylon and still revered as king, Zedekiah was known as a puppet, and a false hope was being spread that Jeconiah would soon return. The Lord had already told the people through Jeremiah that they would serve the king of Babylon seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11-12), and had Jeremiah wear a yoke as the sign that the nations must bring their necks under Babylon’s yoke (Jeremiah 27:2; Jeremiah 27:12). Into that setting Hananiah, a so-called prophet of Gibeon, as the study note calls him, stood in the house of the Lord before the priests and all the people and said the Lord had broken the yoke of the king of Babylon, and within two full years would bring back the vessels of the Lord’s house, Jeconiah and all the captives (Jeremiah 28:1-4). The Hammertime class, whose theme is forefathers whose sins cursed their seed, sets his two years against the seventy the people had already been given: they understood the prophecy was going to be seventy years. It was prosperity, peace, peace, the teacher says, and there was no peace (Jeremiah 23:16-17; Jeremiah 6:14). He said thus says the Lord when the Lord had told him nothing, the Zedekiah teaching says, taking the Lord’s name in vain (Exodus 20:7). Jeremiah said amen, may the Lord do so, but told him not to hold on to it: the prophets of old prophesied war, evil and pestilence against many countries, and a prophet who prophesies peace is known to be sent by the Lord only when his word comes to pass (Jeremiah 28:5-9). The class of 2026-04-11 says the war and pestilence the old prophets foretold is what you see our leadership doing today, and they will be made known when the mission is accomplished. Hananiah then took the yoke off Jeremiah’s neck and broke it before the people, saying the Lord would break Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke from all nations within two years, and Jeremiah went his way (Jeremiah 28:10-11). Jeremiah got on him, one class says, for teaching peace and safety; the prophets of the Lord come teaching that evil is coming, and the feel-good preachers are the opposite. Your pastor, another teacher says, is still telling you it is your season. The word came to Jeremiah: Hananiah had broken yokes of wood, but in their place he would make yokes of iron; the Lord had put an iron yoke on the neck of all these nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar, and had given him even the beasts of the field (Jeremiah 28:12-14). Babylon was the superpower at that time, the study note says. The Zedekiah teaching reads the yoke as vassal service and taxation to Babylon, not chattel slavery; another teaching sets the yoke of iron beside the iron yoke of the curses (Deuteronomy 28:48), which it carries forward to the chains of the later captivity. Then Jeremiah told Hananiah the Lord had not sent him, that he made this people trust in a lie, and that the Lord would cast him off the face of the earth: that year he would die, because he had taught rebellion against the Lord (Jeremiah 28:15-16). The study note explains the rebellion: he taught the people to go against the Most High instead of accepting that they had to go through captivity. Hananiah died the same year, in the seventh month (Jeremiah 28:17). The law had already set the sentence: the prophet who presumes to speak a word in the Lord’s name that He did not command shall die, and the sign is that the thing does not come to pass (Deuteronomy 18:20-22). By this law, the study note says, a lot of these pastors stand condemned, who claim Christ said what He never said. These false pastors make our people trust in lies, one teacher says; we are not here to spread peace on the earth but to prophesy against many nations. The Hammertime class shows what one man can do: it takes just one, like Theudas and Judas of Galilee, who drew people after them and perished (Acts 5:36-37), and it warns against those who corrupt the word of God (2 Corinthians 2:17) and against presumptuous sins (Psalm 19:13).

name: Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah
text: Prophesying a lie in the name of the Lord among the captives at Babylon; committing villainy in Israel and adultery with their neighbours’ wives. Jeremiah’s letter to the captives in Babylon told them to build, plant, marry and seek the peace of the city, and not to be deceived by the prophets among them, for the captivity would last seventy years (Jeremiah 29:4-10). He named two of those prophets, Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who prophesied lies in the Lord’s name and committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives; Nebuchadnezzar would slay them before the captives, and their names would become a curse, roasted in the fire (Jeremiah 29:20-23). The letter went from Jerusalem to the elders, priests, prophets and people carried away with Jeconiah, among them the carpenters and smiths; the study note says it was just like this captivity, with our talents and skills taken (Jeremiah 29:1-3). They were to build houses, plant gardens, marry, increase and not diminish, and seek the peace of the city where they were carried, for in its peace they would have peace (Jeremiah 29:4-7; Romans 13:1). One teacher explains it: get comfortable and do not fight back, because you would be fighting the Most High; and increasing means marrying within your people. After seventy years at Babylon the Lord would visit them and bring them back (Jeremiah 29:10), and the teaching on Ezra 1 marks that fulfilled at Cyrus, the land keeping her sabbaths (Ezra 1:1; 2 Chronicles 36:21). Against that word stood the prophets and diviners among the captives, whom they were not to listen to, for they prophesied falsely in the Lord’s name (Jeremiah 29:8-9). The Zedekiah teaching lays out the two sets of false prophets: in Babylon they said the captives would soon return, and in Jerusalem they said Babylon would never come. Ahab and Zedekiah were more of them, taking the Lord’s name in vain along with Hananiah; this Zedekiah, the teacher stresses, is not King Zedekiah but a false prophet. The study note sets beside them the so-called prophets of Christianity and the so-called prophecy of Islam. They committed villainy in Israel, adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and spoke lying words in the Lord’s name that He had not commanded; the Lord says He knows it and is witness (Jeremiah 29:23). That is Christianity, the teacher says: prophesying strong while smashing your wife. Jeremiah 23 describes the same prophets: prophet and priest both profane, committing adultery and walking in lies, strengthening the hands of evildoers, all of them like Sodom (Jeremiah 23:11-14). Our people in Jeremiah’s time were like Sodom and Gomorrah, the class says; it is not new, and not just one sin. Their way would be slippery ground in the dark, the class of 2026-07-26 says: whatever path they took, they would fall, and the Lord would bring the Babylonians. They were the prophets who said, I have dreamed, stealing words and telling their own dreams (Jeremiah 23:25-32); nobody was standing in the counsel of the Lord. The Lord would deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and he would slay them before the eyes of the captives (Jeremiah 29:21). Their names would become a curse among all the captives of Judah in Babylon, who would wish a man the fate of Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire (Jeremiah 29:22). The teacher explains it as a proverb: when somebody is beaten badly they become a proverb, the Lord is going to do you like He did Zedekiah. The men who used the captivity to sell a lie were put to death by the king whose rule they said would soon end. Two classes read the History of Susanna beside this chapter, where wickedness came out of Babylon from ancient judges who seemed to govern the people, of whom the Lord had spoken (Susanna 1:5); the teacher says the Lord spoke of it here, where they were cooked to death (Jeremiah 29:20-23). He carries that line of wicked elders forward to the Pharisees, who did the exact same thing, and one class sets the woman taken in adultery beside it (John 8:3-11). The teaching on the letter draws the application: captivity is chastening (Hebrews 12:6), and the prophets understood the time, and in that was their patience and their hope. It was seventy years then, one teacher says of the long captivity, and now it is hundreds; yet the Lord would be found and would gather His people from all the nations where He had driven them (Jeremiah 29:13-14). No matter where you go on the planet, the class says, you are going to find Israelites.

name: Shemaiah the Nehelamite
text: Sending letters in his own name from Babylon to have Jeremiah put in prison and in the stocks as a madman; prophesying when the Lord sent him not, and causing the people to trust in a lie. Shemaiah the Nehelamite, among the captives in Babylon, sent letters in his own name to Jerusalem and to Zephaniah the priest, demanding to know why Jeremiah had not been put in the stocks as a madman for writing that the captivity would be long (Jeremiah 29:24-28). Zephaniah read the letter to Jeremiah, and the word came back that Shemaiah prophesied when the Lord had not sent him and made the people trust in a lie; he and his seed would have no man among the people and would not see the good the Lord would do (Jeremiah 29:29-32). Jeremiah had written to the captives carried away with Jeconiah that they would be in Babylon seventy years, and must build, plant, marry and seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4-10). The Zedekiah teaching explains the setting: Ezekiel was among the captives, messengers went back and forth, and false prophets were telling the captives they would soon return, when the word was that they would serve Babylon seventy years. Shemaiah the Nehelamite was one of them. The teacher gives the name as meaning dreamer, which sets him with the prophets of Jeremiah 23 who said they had dreamed when the Lord had not shown them anything (Jeremiah 23:25-27). He sent letters in his own name to all the people at Jerusalem, to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests (Jeremiah 29:25). He told Zephaniah the Lord had made him priest in place of Jehoiada, to be an officer in the house of the Lord over every man who is mad and makes himself a prophet, to put him in prison and in the stocks, and asked why he had not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who made himself a prophet and had sent to Babylon saying the captivity would be long, so build houses and plant gardens (Jeremiah 29:26-28). He wrote in his own name, not the Lord’s, and wanted the prophet who told the truth locked up as a madman. The study note marks the difference between the two men: the Lord was dealing with Jeremiah. The long captivity was the offence. It was seventy years at that time, one teacher says, and now it is hundreds. The letter Shemaiah attacked told the captives to settle because the Lord had set the time, and to fight it, another teacher says, is to fight the Most High. Zephaniah read the letter in Jeremiah’s hearing, and the word came to Jeremiah to send to all the captivity: because Shemaiah had prophesied to them when the Lord had not sent him, and made them trust in a lie, the Lord would punish him and his seed; none of his line would live among the people, and he would not see the good the Lord would do for His people, because he had taught rebellion against the Lord (Jeremiah 29:29-32). His sentence reached his seed as well as himself. The study note names his offence with the same words as Hananiah’s: he taught rebellion (Jeremiah 28:16), leading the people against the time the Lord had set instead of accepting that they had to go through captivity. The good he would not see is the good the letter promised: after seventy years the Lord would visit His people and bring them back, for His plans toward them were for peace and not for harm, to give them a hopeful end (Jeremiah 29:10-11). The class of 2026-05-23 takes that end as the comfort of the captivity: everything you see here is temporary, and you already know the end. The teaching on the letter says the prophets understood the time, and in that was their patience and their hope (Jeremiah 29:12-14). The false prophets offered a quick return; the true word offered a sure one, and Shemaiah was cut off from it.

name: Jonadab and the Rechabites
text: Obeying the voice of Jonadab their father in all that he charged them: drinking no wine, building no house, sowing no seed, planting no vineyard, but dwelling in tents all their days. In the days of Jehoiakim the Lord sent Jeremiah to bring the house of the Rechabites into a chamber of the temple and set wine before them, and they refused, because Jonadab the son of Rechab their father had commanded them never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed or plant vineyards, but to live in tents (Jeremiah 35:1-10). The Lord set their obedience against Judah, which would not listen to Him, and promised that Jonadab would never lack a man to stand before Him (Jeremiah 35:12-19). In the days of Jehoiakim the word came to Jeremiah to go to the house of the Rechabites, bring them into one of the chambers of the house of the Lord, and give them wine to drink (Jeremiah 35:1-2). He took Jaazaniah, his brethren and all his sons, the whole house of the Rechabites, brought them into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the man of God, set bowls full of wine and cups before them, and told them to drink (Jeremiah 35:3-5). They answered that they would drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab their father had commanded them that they and their sons should drink no wine for ever, build no house, sow no seed, plant no vineyard nor own one, but live in tents all their days, that they might live many days in the land where they were strangers (Jeremiah 35:6-7). They had obeyed his voice in all he charged them: they drank no wine all their days, they, their wives, their sons and their daughters; they built no houses to live in, and had neither vineyard, field nor seed, but lived in tents (Jeremiah 35:8-10). They had come into Jerusalem only for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians, when Nebuchadnezzar came up into the land (Jeremiah 35:11). The study note says it plainly: they obeyed in all things. The wine was set before them in the house of the Lord by a prophet of the Lord, and they still kept their father’s word. Then the Lord sent Jeremiah to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem with the lesson: would they not receive instruction and listen to His words? The words of Jonadab were carried out, and his sons drank no wine to that day because they obeyed their father’s commandment; but the Lord had spoken to Judah early and often, and they did not listen to Him (Jeremiah 35:12-14). He had sent all His servants the prophets, early and often, calling every man to return from his evil way, amend his doings, and not go after other gods to serve them, and they would dwell in the land He gave their fathers; but they did not incline their ear (Jeremiah 35:15). The sons of Jonadab kept the commandment their father gave them, and this people did not listen to the Lord (Jeremiah 35:16). One class reads that verse to our people today: the Lord sent the prophets to go out and tell you to repent and not to go after other gods, and the class names Easter and Christmas among those other gods’ feasts. Therefore the Lord would bring on Judah and on all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the evil He had pronounced against them, because He had spoken and they had not heard, He had called and they had not answered (Jeremiah 35:17). To the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said that because they obeyed the commandment of Jonadab their father, kept all his precepts and did all he commanded them, Jonadab the son of Rechab would not lack a man to stand before the Lord for ever (Jeremiah 35:18-19). The study note leaves the chapter as the chapter sets it: a household that kept a father’s word was blessed, and a nation that would not keep the Lord’s word received all the evil He had spoken.

name: Baruch the scribe
text: Writing from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the Lord upon a roll, reading it in the house of the Lord and before the princes, and writing it again after the king burned it. Baruch the son of Neriah wrote in a roll all the words the Lord had spoken to Jeremiah, from Jeremiah’s own mouth, and read them in the Lord’s house on the fasting day while Jeremiah was shut up (Jeremiah 36:4-10). The princes sent him into hiding with Jeremiah; Jehoiakim cut the roll and burned it, and Baruch wrote it all again with many more words besides (Jeremiah 36:19-32). When he complained that the Lord had added grief to his sorrow, he was told not to seek great things for himself, and was promised his life wherever he went (Jeremiah 45:1-5). In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the Lord told Jeremiah to write all His words against Israel, Judah and the nations, so that Judah might hear the evil He purposed, turn every man from his evil way, and be forgiven (Jeremiah 36:1-3). The teacher applies it straight to today: the words the Lord spoke to the prophet are for us to turn from our evil ways, the same thing now. Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote in a roll from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord (Jeremiah 36:4). The teaching uses this to show how the scriptures were written: men moved by the spirit wrote at God’s command, as Moses wrote the journeys at the Lord’s commandment (Numbers 33:2). There is a book of Baruch, the teacher notes; Baruch was always with Jeremiah documenting, the way the Lord dealt with Elijah first and then Elisha. Jeremiah was shut up and could not go into the house of the Lord, so he sent Baruch to read the roll in the people’s hearing on the fasting day, and Baruch did all that Jeremiah commanded him (Jeremiah 36:5-8). In the fifth year, in the ninth month, he read it from the chamber of Gemariah at the new gate, and Michaiah carried the words to the princes (Jeremiah 36:9-13). The princes had Baruch read it again and were afraid; they asked how he wrote all these words, and he answered that Jeremiah spoke them with his mouth and he wrote them with ink in the book (Jeremiah 36:14-18). One class hears unbelief in their question: they did not believe God put His spirit on these men. The princes told Baruch and Jeremiah to go and hide and let no one know where they were (Jeremiah 36:19). The roll was read before Jehoiakim in the winter house, and as it was read he cut it with the penknife and burned it in the fire; neither the king nor his servants were afraid or tore their garments, though Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah pleaded with him not to burn it (Jeremiah 36:20-25). They always hit those who speak truth and rebuke in the gate, the teacher says; Israel does not like the consequences of its sins. Another class says some do the same thing now with their words: you wish you could burn this Bible up. The king ordered Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet seized, but the Lord hid them (Jeremiah 36:26). Baruch took another roll and wrote again from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words the king had burned, with many similar words added (Jeremiah 36:27-32). A class uses this to show why books named in scripture can be missing: many of the books of the Israelites were destroyed. In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when he had written these words, Baruch cried that the Lord had added grief to his sorrow; he was worn out with sighing and found no rest (Jeremiah 45:1-3). The Lord answered that what He had built He would break down and what He had planted He would pluck up, the whole land, and asked whether Baruch was seeking great things for himself: he should not seek them, for evil was coming on all flesh, but his life would be given him wherever he went (Jeremiah 45:4-5). The class applies it to us: that is how we are right now, with that woe is me spirit; we are already in sorrow and God says He will add grief. Seeking great things is how the people are, taught by preachers who promise increase for a tithe; God may never change your situation, but at least you know where you went wrong. The teacher on Baruch 1 puts it bluntly: now you want to seek great things for yourself, are you clueless? The study note sends the reader to the scribe’s own words, preserved in the Apocrypha, where the captives are told that in the land of their captivity they would remember themselves and turn (Baruch 2:29-33), and sets beside it the word that in their affliction they will seek Him early (Hosea 5:15). Jeremiah’s record has Baruch carried into Egypt with the prophet (Jeremiah 43:6), and the teaching on Baruch 1 places him in Babylon, reading his book to Jeconiah and the captives (Baruch 1:1-4). He did not receive great things; he received his life, and his words were kept for the captivity.

name: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian
text: Going out to the king in the gate of Benjamin and telling him the princes had done evil to Jeremiah, then drawing the prophet up out of the dungeon of mire with old cast clouts and rotten rags under his armholes. When the princes had Jeremiah let down into the miry dungeon to die, Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch of the king’s house, went to Zedekiah at the gate of Benjamin, told him the princes had done evil to the prophet, and with thirty men drew Jeremiah out with old rags under the cords (Jeremiah 38:4-13). Before the city fell the Lord sent him word by Jeremiah that he would be delivered and not fall by the sword, because he had trusted in the Lord (Jeremiah 39:15-18). Shephatiah, Gedaliah the son of Pashur, Jucal and Pashur the son of Malchiah heard Jeremiah tell the people that whoever stayed in the city would die and whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live, and told the king he must be put to death because he weakened the hands of the men of war and sought the people’s hurt; Zedekiah answered that he was in their hand, for the king could do nothing against them (Jeremiah 38:1-5). The class calls it false accusation from his own brethren, who had already charged him with defecting to the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 37:13-15), and the teacher of the Zedekiah finale sets it beside the false witnesses against Christ: the spirit of Christ was in Jeremiah. Zedekiah, he says, was a weakling and a coward. They let Jeremiah down with cords into the dungeon of Malchiah, where there was no water but mire, and he sank in it (Jeremiah 38:6). One class says the mire was dung, a hole where it came up and he could not avoid it; the Zedekiah teaching calls it quicksand, meant to give him a slow and agonizing death, and says that is what you have to be ready for. Either way the pit was meant to kill him slowly. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs in the king’s house, heard of it while the king sat in the gate of Benjamin. He went out and told the king that these men had done evil in all they had done to Jeremiah, and that the prophet was likely to die of hunger where he was, for there was no more bread in the city (Jeremiah 38:7-9). As the teacher tells it, the Ethiopian eunuch came and let the king know these men were killing Jeremiah. The king commanded him to take thirty men and lift the prophet out before he died (Jeremiah 38:10). He took the men into the king’s house under the treasury, brought old worn clothes and rotten rags, let them down by cords, and told Jeremiah to put them under his arms beneath the cords; so they drew him up, and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison (Jeremiah 38:11-13). Jeremiah was malnourished, one teacher says, barely fed in that dungeon, and the rags let him hold on so he could come up, like a harness. The class says the Lord made a way for Jeremiah because he was set to bring the word to the king at the risk of his life, and the way He made came through a servant of the king’s house who would speak. While Jeremiah was still shut up in the court of the prison, the word came to him for Ebed-melech: the Lord would bring His words on the city for harm and not for good, and they would be fulfilled before his eyes (Jeremiah 39:15-16). But in that day the Lord would deliver him; he would not be given into the hand of the men he feared, nor fall by the sword, but his life would be spared, because he had put his trust in the Lord (Jeremiah 39:17-18). The study note draws the reason: the Most High dealt with the Ethiopian because he was used to help Jeremiah, and his deliverance goes back to the hour the king told him to lift the prophet out before he died (Jeremiah 38:10). The Rise of Babylon teaching reads the promise the same way: God looked out for the one who looked out for Jeremiah. That teacher takes the men he feared to be Babylon, and hears in the promise survival rather than freedom: he would not be killed, though he would live under Babylon, because he looked out for Jeremiah when he was locked up. The city fell as it was spoken, and the king’s sons and the nobles of Judah were slain at Riblah (Jeremiah 39:6); the man who had spoken up for the prophet was spared by name. The Grace teaching tells the reader to read chapters 38 and 39 together, the rescue and the deliverance side by side.

name: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah
text: Smiting Gedaliah the governor with the sword at his own table, and all the Jews and Chaldeans with him at Mizpah; slaying seventy of the eighty men coming with offerings to the house of the Lord and casting them into the pit; carrying the residue captive toward the Ammonites. After Jerusalem fell, the king of Babylon made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor at Mizpah over the poor left in the land; Johanan warned him that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to kill him, and Gedaliah did not believe it (Jeremiah 40:7-16). In the seventh month Ishmael, of the royal seed, ate with him and then killed him and the Jews and Chaldeans with him, slew seventy of eighty pilgrims and filled Asa’s pit with them, and carried off the rest toward the Ammonites; Johanan recovered the captives at Gibeon, and Ishmael escaped with eight men (Jeremiah 41:1-15). Nebuzaradan, a heathen, told Jeremiah the evil came because the people had sinned and not obeyed the voice of the Lord; the study note says the nations always knew why we went into captivity, and sin becomes our weakness (Jeremiah 40:1-3; Judith 5:17-18). Jeremiah went to Gedaliah at Mizpah, one of his good friends, the note says (Jeremiah 40:4-6). Gedaliah swore to the captains of the forces not to fear to serve the Chaldeans, but to dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it would be well with them (Jeremiah 40:7-9). The teacher calls it obeying the powers that be, Romans 13 in the Old Testament; the war was over, the note says, and they were already conquered. The Jews who had fled among the Moabites, the Ammonites and Edom, hoping to find sanctuary there, came back and gathered wine and summer fruits in abundance (Jeremiah 40:11-12). Johanan the son of Kareah and the captains came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and warned him that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to kill him; Gedaliah did not believe them, and when Johanan offered secretly to kill Ishmael so that the remnant would not perish, Gedaliah forbade it and said he spoke falsely of Ishmael (Jeremiah 40:13-16). The teachers take the warning at its word: Ishmael was sent by the Ammonites to kill him, one says; he worked for the Ammonites, says another. A third teaching adds the people’s side: they made puppet rulers out of us and set up a governor named Gedaliah, our people hated following those orders, and Ishmael, of the royal seed, rose up and assassinated him. The two stand together: a prince of David’s line who resented the governor, sent by the king of Ammon to do it. In the seventh month Ishmael, of the royal seed and one of the princes of the king, came with ten men to Mizpah and ate bread with Gedaliah, at a banquet held in Ishmael’s honor, the study note says; then they rose up and struck him with the sword and killed him, with all the Jews who were with him and the Chaldeans and men of war found there (Jeremiah 41:1-3). The next day, before anyone knew, eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria with shaved beards, torn clothes and cut bodies, bringing offerings and incense to the house of the Lord; Ishmael went out weeping to meet them, playing a part, the note says, brought them into the city, killed them and cast them into the pit (Jeremiah 41:4-7). He killed his own people, the teacher says. Ten were spared because they said they had stores of wheat, barley, oil and honey hidden in the field; they bribed him, the teacher says (Jeremiah 41:8). The pit was the one Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel, when he built up Mizpah (Jeremiah 41:9; 1 Kings 15:22), and Ishmael filled it with the slain. Ishmael carried away captive the rest of the people at Mizpah, the king’s daughters among them, whom Nebuzaradan had committed to Gedaliah, and set out to cross over to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:10). When Johanan and the captains heard of all the evil he had done, they took their men and found him by the great waters in Gibeon; the captives were glad when they saw Johanan, and turned and went back to him (Jeremiah 41:11-14). But Ishmael escaped from Johanan with eight men and went to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:15). He ran back to the ones who sent him to kill in the first place, the teacher says. The scripture records no sentence carried out on him. The weight of his deed fell on the remnant: Johanan took the people he had recovered to the habitation of Chimham by Bethlehem, to go into Egypt, afraid of the Chaldeans because Ishmael had killed the governor the king of Babylon had set over the land (Jeremiah 41:16-18). With Gedaliah dead, the study note says, they felt they had no reason to stay. The Rise of Babylon teaching carries it further, drawing on the Igbo tradition that Judeans fled after the slaying of Gedaliah into Egypt and from there south and west into Africa: the killing of Gedaliah, the teacher says, forced them to move further into Egypt.

name: Johanan and the remnant that went down to Egypt
text: Asking Jeremiah to pray for the way wherein they should walk, swearing to obey the voice of the Lord whether it were good or evil, and then calling the prophet a liar and going into Egypt against the commandment; burning incense to the queen of heaven in the land of Egypt. After Gedaliah’s murder the captains and all the people, from the least to the greatest, asked Jeremiah to pray for the way they should go and swore to obey the Lord’s answer, good or evil (Jeremiah 42:1-6). When the answer came to stay in the land and not go into Egypt, Azariah, Johanan and all the proud men called Jeremiah a liar and carried the whole remnant, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, to Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:1-7). There they burned incense to the queen of heaven and refused the prophet, and the Lord swore that sword and famine would consume them in Egypt until only a few escaped (Jeremiah 44:15-28). Johanan the son of Kareah, Jezaniah and all the people from the least to the greatest asked Jeremiah to pray to the Lord his God for them, that He would show them the way to walk; they swore the Lord would be a true and faithful witness against them if they did not do all He sent them, whether it was good or evil (Jeremiah 42:1-6). After ten days the answer came: if they stayed in the land He would build them and not pull them down, plant them and not uproot them, for He repented of the evil He had done to them; they were not to fear the king of Babylon, for He was with them to save them (Jeremiah 42:7-12). He does not desire evil, the study note says; He only wants His laws kept. But if they went into Egypt thinking to see no war and hunger for no bread, the sword they feared would overtake them there (Jeremiah 42:13-18). Jeremiah told them plainly not to go into Egypt, and that they had deceived themselves when they sent him (Jeremiah 42:19-22). Some people speak words they do not believe, the note says; many ask for counsel with their minds already made up, and we are these same people, quick to say we will not do what the Most High commands. Azariah, Johanan and all the proud men said Jeremiah spoke falsely and that Baruch had set him against them; pride is destruction, the note says (Jeremiah 43:1-3). They took the whole remnant, men, women, children, the king’s daughters, Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt to Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:4-7). Jeremiah was always warning us about going into Egypt, the teacher says; our people loved Egypt, and we sought the Pharaohs instead of the Lord (Isaiah 30:1-3). In Egypt, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros, the Lord reminded them of Jerusalem’s desolation for burning incense to other gods, and asked why they did the same evil in Egypt (Jeremiah 44:1-8). We left our own land to do the same thing, the teacher says; we have learned nothing. The men who knew their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women, answered that they would not listen: they would burn incense to the queen of heaven as they and their fathers, kings and princes had done, for then they had plenty of food and saw no evil (Jeremiah 44:15-19). The teachers name the queen of heaven Ashtoreth, Isis, Ishtar. The women were leading the men, one class says; the men knew their wives were worshipping other gods and stood back and did nothing. The study note calls it the disorder we see in Babylon the great today, the women worshipping without their men and the men with no rule over their houses; another class calls it a failure of stewardship: set your house in order (2 Esdras 14:13). The Lord swore by His great name that it would no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in Egypt; He would watch over them for harm and not for good, and they would be consumed by sword and famine until there was an end of them (Jeremiah 44:24-27). The study note reads it with the curses, which pursue even those who sought refuge in Egypt (Deuteronomy 28:45). Yet a small number would escape the sword and return to Judah, and the remnant would know whose word would stand, the Lord’s or theirs (Jeremiah 44:28); not all of them were wicked, the teacher says, some were keeping God’s commandments. The sign was Pharaoh-hophra given into the hand of his enemies as Zedekiah had been given to Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 44:29-30); we fled there, the teacher says, thinking Egypt was a powerhouse. Nebuchadnezzar, the Lord’s servant, would set his throne on the stones Jeremiah hid at Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, strike Egypt, and burn the houses of its gods (Jeremiah 43:8-13). The teachers read going back to Egypt as more than the flight of that day. The study note on the curses says the Egypt of the ships is not the literal land, for you can walk to Egypt, but spiritual Egypt, America (Deuteronomy 28:68; Revelation 11:8), and the Passover class calls it the transatlantic slave trade. The class on Joseph reads Ephraim’s return to Egypt the same way (Hosea 9:3). America is not literally Egypt, one teacher says, but it is the shadow of Egypt, and its strength is the political system and the economy we trust. The Passover class warns against the freed brothers who talk of going back to Egypt because at least there they had good food (Numbers 11:4-6): everything you learned in Egypt, forget it (Leviticus 18:3).

name: Moab and Ammon
text: Moab: magnifying himself against the Lord, trusting in his works and his treasures, and skipping for joy at the derision of Israel. Ammon: saying Aha against the sanctuary when it was profaned, against the land of Israel when it was desolate, and against the house of Judah when they went into captivity. Jeremiah’s burden declared no more praise of Moab: because he trusted in his works and treasures, magnified himself against the Lord and skipped for joy at Israel’s derision, he would be spoiled and Chemosh carried into captivity (Jeremiah 48:1-2; Jeremiah 48:7; Jeremiah 48:26-27). Ammon, which said Aha when the sanctuary was profaned and Judah went into captivity, would be given to the men of the east (Ezekiel 25:3-4). The study note and the classes identify Moab as the so-called Chinese and Ammon as the so-called Japanese, and teach that the judgment begun under Nebuchadnezzar has a latter-day fulfilment (Jeremiah 48:47). The study note opens chapters 48 to 51 as our redemption, the judgment on the nations that held Israel, and names them: Moab the so-called Chinese, Ammon the so-called Japanese, Edom the white man, Elam the Persians and East Indians, Babylon America. The classes trace Moab and Ammon to their beginning: Lot’s daughters, thinking everyone on earth was dead, made their father drunk and bore Moab and Ben-ammi by him (Genesis 19:30-38). The class on the madmen of China reads the identification from that origin, pointing to the facial traits it says often come from such a union, which the old term mongoloidism names after the peoples of the East; it adds that the elders taught Moab and Ammon in the nineties, before books such as Thomas W. Plant’s The Japanese: Who Are They? were found. The burden begins with no more praise of Moab, and Madmen cut down (Jeremiah 48:1-2). God calls the so-called Chinese by that name, the note says; see what He calls Moab, the class adds: madmen. We praise Moab quick, everybody was kung fu fighting, but Moab does not have that love for us; people say China is the next superpower, and the prophecy says no more praise. The history the schools do not teach, the note says, is Moab enslaving us under the Tang Dynasty and building industries off our people. Moab had been at ease from his youth, settled on his lees, never poured from vessel to vessel nor gone into captivity, so his taste and scent had not changed (Jeremiah 48:11). Vessel to vessel, the teaching says, is captivity to captivity, as happened to us; it did not happen to Moab, and his hatred has not changed. He would be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was of Bethel, Jeroboam’s calf (Jeremiah 48:13; 1 Kings 12:28-29), and the class sets beside it the horned, cow-headed gods of Chinese religion. Moab magnified himself against the Lord; Israel was a derision to him, and he skipped for joy whenever he spoke of Israel (Jeremiah 48:26-27). He was glad because he helped destroy us; and if He punished His own children, the note asks, what makes the heathen think their time will not come? The Lord knew his pride, his loftiness and his lies (Jeremiah 48:29-30); the class reads a book that applies that verse to China, and whatever China says about who will be destroyed, God says it shall not be so. Ammon said Aha against the sanctuary when it was profaned, the land when it was desolate, and Judah when it went into captivity (Ezekiel 25:3; Ezekiel 25:6): Ammon laughed when we went into slavery.
