Moab with Seir said Judah is like all the heathen (Ezekiel 25:8), and the class says the nations stick together to hide the black images on the ancient walls of China. Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Moab then (Jeremiah 48:8), and the class teaches the duality: Moab is a world power today and will be destroyed again, with Asia, which shared in the hope of Babylon (2 Esdras 15:46-49); as she did to His chosen, so God would do to her (2 Esdras 15:56). Moab would dwell in the rock (Jeremiah 48:28), which the class reads as China’s bunkers in the mountains; the incense of the high places and the bald heads and clipped beards (Jeremiah 48:35-37) it reads as Buddhist incense and monks’ shaved heads, the same as the Mongolians next door. The study note reads the one who flies as an eagle over Moab as he that judges, and the class asks whose symbol is the eagle: America (Jeremiah 48:40). Fear, pit and snare would take whoever fled (Jeremiah 48:43-44): the bunker city beneath Beijing will not save them. For all that pride Moab will return to its place and serve Israel: Moab is the Lord’s washpot (Psalm 60:8), a vessel for washing the feet, a vessel of dishonour, the teaching says, and Israel will take its captors for servants and handmaids (Isaiah 14:2). The Lord would bring again Moab’s captivity in the latter days (Jeremiah 48:47); the study note says that captivity has not happened yet. Ammon would be delivered to the men of the east and cut off from the peoples, and Moab opened on its flank, so that Ammon would be remembered no more among the nations (Ezekiel 25:4-11). The classes read the men of the east as Nebuchadnezzar and then Persia and Media, as the Lord moving Moab and Ammon further east into Asia, where they are called Chinese and Japanese and not remembered by name, and as the Arabs who later took Ammon’s land. Are we promoting harm to the Chinese? No, the class says: the judgment is the Lord’s, like a ring going round all the nations (2 Esdras 5:42).

name: Babylon, the lady of kingdoms
text: Shewing no mercy to the people the Lord was wroth with and gave into her hand; laying her yoke very heavily upon the ancient; saying in her heart, I am, and none else beside me; trusting in her wickedness, her wisdom, and the multitude of her sorceries. Isaiah told the virgin daughter of Babylon to come down and sit in the dust without a throne: the Lord gave His people into her hand, and she showed them no mercy, laid her yoke heavily on the aged, and said in her heart that she was, and none beside her (Isaiah 47:1; Isaiah 47:6-8). Loss of children and widowhood would come on her in one day, and the burden of Babylon and the proverb against its king carry the same sentence (Isaiah 47:9; Isaiah 13:19; Isaiah 14:4-23). The classes teach that this is not ancient Babylon but its daughter, America. The verse-by-verse teaching opens with Psalm 137: the daughter of Babylon is Edom, the children of Edom who cried to raze Jerusalem to its foundation (Psalm 137:7-8). One class says Edom is called the daughter of Babylon because they assisted the Babylonians; another says plainly, not ancient Babylon, the daughter of Babylon, which is America; the Obadiah teaching joins them, Edom becoming Babylon the great once in power. She is told to come down from reigning over kings, feared above all kingdoms and able to manufacture a war, and sit in the dust, from richest to poor (Isaiah 47:1; Revelation 17:18). Her shame uncovered is mystery Babylon revealed, and the teacher reads the next verse as Christ returning with His armies (Isaiah 47:2-3; Jude 1:14-15). The Lord was angry with His people and gave them into her hand, and she showed them no mercy and laid her yoke very heavily on the aged (Isaiah 47:6). God was angry with us because we broke His laws, the class says; the white man showed us no mercy, laid a heavy yoke even on the old men and women, and polluted us with their holidays. The teacher sets beside it the nations that helped forward the affliction (Zechariah 1:15), naming the Klan and Jim Crow. She dwells carelessly and says in her heart that she is, and there is none besides her (Isaiah 47:8), the very words God says of Himself (Isaiah 46:9): a nation setting itself up as God. America dwells carelessly, the class says, passing laws in secret and making its citizens care less, read less, think less. She trusted in her wickedness and said none saw her (Isaiah 47:10): God saw Tulsa and Seneca Village, and their technology has perverted them into thinking they are God. Her sorceries were laboured in from her youth (Isaiah 47:12): 1776 is their youth, the sorceries are the media, military-grade witchcraft, and the stargazers are the think tanks. Isaiah 14 names the same oppressor, the golden city, the richest country on earth, who struck the peoples with a continual stroke (Isaiah 14:4-6): this land taken with bloodshed. Lucifer, who weakened the nations (Isaiah 14:12), is the king of verse 4, a man; the classes teach that Esau mixed Jude with Isaiah 14 to make a fallen-angel doctrine and that heaven here is rulership (Lamentations 2:1). He would sit on the mount of the congregation in the sides of the north (Isaiah 14:13): the stars of God are us, sat on in captivity in this hemisphere. Loss of children and widowhood would come on her in a moment, in one day, in their perfection (Isaiah 47:9). The class says it will come on America’s own soil in one day, like the plague of the firstborn in one night, and in their perfection means nothing misses; loss of children is the destruction of the citizenry, widowhood of her military and institutions. Her astrologers could not save her, and her merchants, the corporations, would wander each to his own quarter (Isaiah 47:13-15; Revelation 18:23). The study note reads the burden of Isaiah 13 as the destruction of Edom and the nations, the United States of Babylon (Isaiah 13:19). The banner is the Bible, the weapons of His indignation the nukes that will be used, the darkened stars satellites, the arrogant one brought low Esau, and the earth moved out of her place nuclear destruction (Isaiah 13:2-13). First the Lord makes a man more precious than fine gold, the Israelite man (Isaiah 13:12); He cannot bring the destruction until He has made these new men, the class says. The Medes who do not regard silver (Isaiah 13:17) destroyed ancient Babylon, and the class teaches the Lord will use Iran against mystery Babylon, America and Israel, their bows being missiles. Ancient Babylon fell from within; this one becomes as Sodom, by fire (Isaiah 13:19). Every man flees to his own land (Isaiah 13:14), where the note draws a word against mixing with the nations; we do not have that much time (Isaiah 13:22). The king of Babylon is brought down to the pit, and those who see him look closely and ask whether this is the man who made the earth tremble and would not release his prisoners (Isaiah 14:15-17). Is this the man, the class says: not a fallen angel; Lucifer is a man, and the Bible is what makes them look. We are his prisoners, and you were never free. The Lord sweeps Babylon with the besom of destruction, a broom of twigs (Isaiah 14:19-23). On the other side stands the reversal: the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and Israel will rule over their oppressors (Isaiah 14:1-2).

name: The elders with idols in the temple (Ezekiel 8)
text: The image of jealousy at the gate; seventy ancients with censers before creeping things and idols portrayed on the wall in the dark, saying, the Lord seeth us not; women weeping for Tammuz; twenty-five men with their backs to the temple worshipping the sun toward the east. Ezekiel was carried in the visions of God to Jerusalem and shown the abominations inside the Lord’s house: an image of jealousy at the gate, seventy elders burning incense before idols painted on the walls of a dark chamber, women at the north gate weeping for Tammuz, and twenty-five men with their backs to the temple bowing to the sun (Ezekiel 8:3-16). The elders said the Lord did not see them; the Lord said these things drove Him from His sanctuary and He would deal in fury and not spare, and the glory departed from the city (Ezekiel 8:12; Ezekiel 8:18; Ezekiel 11:22-23). In the sixth year, as the elders of Judah sat before Ezekiel in the captivity, the spirit carried him in the visions of God to Jerusalem (Ezekiel 8:1-3). One class says those elders sat before him like they were so righteous; the history teaching notes that the vision shows those not yet taken, for the captivity came in waves. The class on religious syncretism builds up to the chapter through Jeroboam’s calves and Manasseh’s idols in the Lord’s house (2 Kings 21:1-9): we went crazier. At the gate stood the image of jealousy, and the Lord asked whether he saw the great abominations that drove Him far from His own sanctuary (Ezekiel 8:5-6). The Lord is saying, the class says, I cannot be around you all. Ezekiel dug through the wall and saw every form of creeping thing, abominable beasts and all the idols of the house of Israel painted on the wall round about (Ezekiel 8:7-10). The class sets beside it the images of Cesare Borgia and Guadalupe on the walls today, what we grew up with in the stained glass of the churches (Deuteronomy 4:16-19). When Judah saw the Chaldeans painted in vermilion she doted on them and sent messengers to them (Ezekiel 23:14-16); the study note says she was drawn in by the flashy art as a harlot is enticed, and the class joins it to the fringes of the law, given so they would not go whoring after their own eyes (Numbers 15:39). Seventy of the elders of Israel stood before those pictures, Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan among them, each with his censer and a thick cloud of incense, saying the Lord did not see them and had forsaken the earth (Ezekiel 8:11-12). The elders were the instructors, one class says, and in the dark they were not even serving God. What do you do in the dark? Your secrets. Men loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil (John 3:19); the study note says a man can be comfortable in the darkness he was raised in, and refusing to change is what condemns him. Then greater abominations: at the north gate women sat weeping for Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:13-14). Israelite women were weeping for Tammuz, the class says. The teachers name Tammuz the son of Nimrod and Semiramis, his mother-wife, the mother and child of the old Babylonian religion carried from Babel into every nation as Isis and Osiris and the Madonna; they call him today baby Jesus, the forever baby, born at the winter solstice, December 25th. Tammuz is what you all celebrate on Christmas, one teacher says. Other classes name his mother Ashtaroth or Astarte; all make him the Babylonian mother-and-child god. In the inner court about twenty-five men stood with their backs to the temple and their faces to the east, worshipping the sun (Ezekiel 8:15-16). Where do you think you get your Sunday service from, one teacher asks: sun worship. They had also filled the land with violence and put the branch to their nose (Ezekiel 8:17), which one class reads as a lit branch that got them high. The Lord answered with one sentence: He would deal in fury, His eye would not spare, and though they cried in His ears with a loud voice He would not hear them (Ezekiel 8:18). The men who said the Lord did not see were shown to Him one by one. The eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, the teacher reads (Ecclesiasticus 23:19), and He sets our secret sins in the light of His face (Psalm 90:8). God starts first with the leaders, another class says, and an idol can be anything set before Him, even your children. The next chapter is the end result of this one, the history teaching says: the mark was set on the foreheads of those who sighed and cried over the abominations, and the slaughter began at the sanctuary, with the elders before the house (Ezekiel 9:1-6). To sigh and cry you must know the law, one class adds (Isaiah 8:16). The glory of the God of Israel went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain on the east side, and the spirit carried Ezekiel back to the captives in Chaldea, where he told them everything the Lord had shown him (Ezekiel 11:22-25). The classes bring it home at the season of Tammuz: we were born right here in Babylon the great.

name: Pelatiah and the princes at the east gate
text: Devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city: it is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh. The spirit brought Ezekiel to the east gate of the Lord’s house, where twenty-five men stood, among them Jaazaniah the son of Azur and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people, who devised mischief and gave wicked counsel, saying the judgment was not near, build houses, the city is the caldron and we are the flesh (Ezekiel 11:1-3). Ezekiel prophesied against them, and while he prophesied Pelatiah died (Ezekiel 11:4-13). The study note sets Ezekiel 11 to 14 under one theme, false security. The spirit lifted Ezekiel to the east gate of the Lord’s house, where he saw twenty-five men, among them Jaazaniah the son of Azur, not the Jaazaniah son of Shaphan of the dark chamber, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people (Ezekiel 11:1). Remember the name Pelatiah, the note says. These men devised mischief and gave wicked counsel in the city: the judgment is not near, let us build houses; this city is the caldron and we are the flesh (Ezekiel 11:2-3). Assyria had already carried away the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:6), and some of Judah was already captive in Babylon, yet the counsel was that Jerusalem, the iron pot, would protect them, giving the people a false sense of security. The class that reads this chapter turns first to chapter 8 to show how much idolatry was going on at that time. The spirit of the Lord fell on Ezekiel, and he said the Lord knew the things that came into their minds, every one of them (Ezekiel 11:4-5). They had multiplied their slain in the city and filled its streets with the dead (Ezekiel 11:6). The Lord turned their proverb around: the slain they had laid in the city were the flesh and the city the caldron, but He would bring them out of it (Ezekiel 11:7). Ezekiel names the sins of the princes of the bloody city: they used their power to shed blood, took gifts to shed blood, took usury and increase, gained by extortion and forgot the Lord (Ezekiel 22:6-12); its princes were like wolves, its prophets daubed with untempered mortar, and the Lord sought a man to stand in the gap and found none (Ezekiel 22:25-30). The study note reads those princes as breaking the laws of Leviticus 18, and asks with the psalm who will rise up for Him against the evildoers (Psalm 94:16). They feared the sword, and the Lord would bring the sword on them (Ezekiel 11:8); the sword, the study note says, means the nations. He would bring them out of the city, deliver them to strangers, and judge them in the border of Israel, because they had not walked in His statutes but had done after the manners of the heathen round about (Ezekiel 11:9-12). We are judged for not keeping the Most High’s laws, the same then as today, the note says; the manner of the heathen is the immoral laws and spiritual idolatry of Leviticus 18 (Leviticus 18:3), for which the land spewed Israel out (Leviticus 18:24-28). While Ezekiel prophesied, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died (Ezekiel 11:13), put to death by the Most High, the study note says, one of the wicked counsellors struck in the middle of the prophecy against him. Ezekiel fell on his face and cried out whether the Lord would make a full end of the remnant. The answer was for the captives, whom the people of Jerusalem had told to get far from the Lord (Ezekiel 11:14-15). Though the Lord scattered them among the countries, He would be to them a little sanctuary where they came (Ezekiel 11:16). The study note reads the little sanctuaries as the schools IUIC is setting up; there is a school near you, one teacher says, with elders in every city (Titus 1:5), and another calls it learning who we are in the sanctuaries around the globe, scattered first through the Arab slave trade and then the transatlantic trade (Deuteronomy 28:68; Deuteronomy 4:27). He would gather them, give them the land of Israel, give them one heart and a new spirit, and take the stony heart out of their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, that they might walk in His statutes (Ezekiel 11:17-20). The stony heart, the note says, is the rebellious mind; one class says we are a traumatized people and need the Spirit of God, and the heart of flesh is a new mind to keep the laws, given after the purging in the wilderness (Zechariah 13:9). But those whose heart walked after their detestable things would have their way repaid on their own heads (Ezekiel 11:21): there is a big payback, the note says, for those who will not keep His laws. Then the cherubim, the angels of the wheels of the first chapter, lifted their wings, and the glory went up from the city (Ezekiel 11:22-23).

name: Edom, in the day of his brother
text: Standing on the other side in the day that strangers carried away Jacob captive, and being as one of them; rejoicing over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; entering the gate, laying hands on the substance, standing in the crossway to cut off those that escaped, and delivering up those that remained. Obadiah’s vision is one charge against Edom: when strangers carried Jacob captive and cast lots on Jerusalem, Esau stood on the other side and was as one of them, rejoicing over Judah, looting the gate, cutting off those who escaped and handing over the survivors (Obadiah 1:10-14). The Lord would bring the proud eagle down from its nest among the stars, return his deeds on his own head, and make the house of Esau stubble for the fire of Jacob (Obadiah 1:4; Obadiah 1:15; Obadiah 1:18). The study note and the classes identify Edom as Esau, the white man (Genesis 36:1; Genesis 36:8). The Lord has made Edom small among the heathen and greatly despised (Obadiah 1:1-2). Esau is Edom, the study note says, and Edom is the white man, called red for his lack of melanin, while Jacob needed no description (Genesis 36:1). The pride of his heart deceived him, dwelling in the clefts of the rock and asking who would bring him down (Obadiah 1:3). The teachers read the clefts together: Mount Seir, where Esau dwelt (Genesis 36:8); the rock-cut city of Petra; the Caucasus mountains of the Middle Ages, which is why they call themselves Caucasian; and today the governments, the high places and the skyscrapers. He exalts himself as the eagle and sets his nest among the stars (Obadiah 1:4): Rome, Greece, Spain, France, Britain, Russia and America take the eagle for their symbol, the great seal holding arrows and an olive branch, and the nest among the stars is the moon landing, the satellites and the space force; in 1969 they said the eagle has landed. A thief steals until he has enough, and grape gatherers leave some grapes (Obadiah 1:5), but Esau, the class says, takes every grape, the stem, the root and the ground, the house, the people in the house, the land, the race and the identity; like the ocean, he is never full. His hidden things will be searched out (Obadiah 1:6), and God puts His spirit on us to search them out. The class answers from the record why he is greatly despised: the papal bulls Dum Diversas and Romanus Pontifex granted perpetual slavery over all who were not European, and perpetual slavery is perpetual hatred; then the Force Publique in the Congo and the massacres at Ponce and Utuado. The charge is his violence against his brother Jacob (Obadiah 1:10). In the day strangers carried away Jacob’s forces and cast lots on Jerusalem, Esau stood on the other side and took part, the study note says (Obadiah 1:11). The class teaches that Edom aided the Babylonians, who were Cushites, in the destruction of the first temple in 586 BC, and Esdras says the Edomites burned the temple when the Chaldees laid Judea waste (1 Esdras 4:45). He looked on the day of his brother, rejoiced over Judah in the day of its destruction, entered the gate and laid hands on its substance, and stood in the crossway to cut off those who escaped and hand over the rest (Obadiah 1:12-14): when we were escaping, Edom blocked our way and gave us up. Psalm 137 remembers the children of Edom crying to raze Jerusalem to its foundation (Psalm 137:7). Ezekiel names the same revenge (Ezekiel 25:12), and the class says he takes it through the legislative, judicial and executive branches, weaponizing the police, the original slave catchers. From his nest among the stars the Lord will bring him down (Obadiah 1:4): once you reach that height, the class says, the bringing down begins, and from 1969 the teachings started going out. The men of his confederacy will deceive him and bring him to the border, and those who eat his bread will lay a wound under him (Obadiah 1:7); the classes name the European Union and NATO, and the Obadiah teaching the ten horns that turn on the harlot (Revelation 17:12-17): his own confederacy turns on him, as it did in the world wars. The wise will perish out of Edom and the mighty men of Teman be dismayed, and for his violence against Jacob shame will cover him (Obadiah 1:8-10). The day of the Lord is near on all the heathen: as he has done, it will be done to him (Obadiah 1:15). That is justice, the class says; their reward is what they did to us. The nations will drink and be as though they had not been (Obadiah 1:16), which one class carries from America to those who came back to the land in 1948. On Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and the house of Jacob will be a fire, Joseph a flame, and Esau stubble, with none remaining (Obadiah 1:17-18). Ezekiel says the Lord will lay His vengeance on Edom by the hand of His people Israel (Ezekiel 25:13-14), and the study note says that vengeance is future: the Most High must first change our minds (Zechariah 9:13; Wisdom 3:6-8). It is written because we are soft, the class adds; the day is coming, but now is not that time. The Obadiah teaching warns that we are not to walk around with actual hatred, only to remember our history. Saviours will come up on Mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau, and the kingdom will be the Lord’s (Obadiah 1:21); we are the herald to Christ, the class says.

name: The prince of Tyre
text: Saying, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; setting his heart as the heart of God because of the riches gotten by his wisdom and his traffick. The word came to Ezekiel for the prince of Tyre, whose heart was lifted up by the riches his wisdom and trade had gathered, so that he said he was a god sitting in the seat of God in the midst of the seas, though he was a man and not God (Ezekiel 28:1-5). The Lord would bring strangers, the terrible of the nations, to bring him down to the pit, and he would die the deaths of the uncircumcised (Ezekiel 28:6-10). The classes read Tyre as the historical city in Lebanon and, as a similitude, as Edom and America (Hosea 12:10). The prince of Tyre said he was a god and sat in the seat of God in the midst of the seas, yet he was a man and not God, though he set his heart as the heart of God (Ezekiel 28:2). The class reads it as a metaphor for Edom, for America: no other nation did what America has done in the midst of the seas. Another class shows how both readings stand: God speaks in similitudes (Hosea 12:10), naming a country that did exist while speaking of another, and Tyre was a city in Lebanon; the same class of 2026-04-11 reads Tyre and Zidon in Joel and Amos as the Canaanite cities that sold Judah to the Grecians (Joel 3:4-6; Amos 1:9). The seat of God, the class says, is space and rulership, the superpower sitting among the nations like the woman who sits on many waters (Revelation 17:1). A man and not God: made of dust, water and blood, whatever the crown and seal; the classes set it beside the man of Isaiah 14 and the number of a man (Isaiah 14:16; Revelation 13:18). He was wiser than Daniel, and no secret could be hidden from him (Ezekiel 28:3). Everything you type on these devices is recorded, the class says, and will be used against you; if you entertain secret sins on your phone, he sees it. By wisdom and by his traffic, which is trade, he gathered gold and silver into his treasures, and his heart was lifted up because of his riches (Ezekiel 28:4-5). The classes give the record: treaties with the Native nations broken the minute gold was found, the forts set where the gold is, the riches of the slave trade, Haiti made to take American rice until it depended on it, and the lending of the IMF and World Bank. You read this and it sounds profound, the class says, but it is all in the negative. One teacher reads a commentary that calls it the insanity of prosperity, pride begotten of great prosperity, and carries it from Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, Pharaoh and Herod to America (Acts 12:21-23). The same spirit said Aha against Jerusalem, the gate of the peoples, expecting to grow rich from her ruin (Ezekiel 26:2); the study note says Tyre saw our loss as her come-up. The lamentation over the king of Tyre says his heart was lifted up by his beauty and he was filled with violence by the multitude of his merchandise (Ezekiel 28:16-17). Two teachings read the king of Tyre in Eden as Cain, with the harps and pipes of Jubal’s line (Genesis 4:21), and the anointed cherub that covers as the cherub set east of Eden to keep the way of the tree of life (Genesis 3:24): today that cherub is Esau, Cain again, covering the truth that we are the Israelites and whitewashing history (Ezekiel 28:13-14). Because he set his heart as the heart of God, the Lord would bring strangers, the terrible of the nations, to draw their swords against the beauty of his wisdom and bring him down to the pit, and he would die the deaths of those slain in the midst of the seas (Ezekiel 28:6-8). The classes read the terrible of the nations as the terrorists of the nations, and the strangers as his own allies turning on him. Would he still say he was God before the one who slew him? He would be a man and not God in the hand of the one who killed him (Ezekiel 28:9-10). Against the city, the Lord would bring many nations up like the waves of the sea and make her a bare rock for spreading nets, and He brought Nebuchadnezzar from the north as His sword against a nation that gained from our fall (Ezekiel 26:3-12). At her fall the princes of the sea would come down from their thrones and lament the renowned city of seafaring men (Ezekiel 26:15-18), and the study note sets beside it the shipmasters and sailors standing afar off at the burning of the great city, the seafaring city that reflects Esau’s nation (Revelation 18:17-19; Isaiah 14:12). She would be sought and never found again, the note says, because she said Aha (Ezekiel 26:21). The king of Tyre was cast out of the mountain of God as profane, which one teaching reads as cast out of Israel’s homeland, and fire from his own midst brought him to ashes before all who saw him (Ezekiel 28:16-19).

name: Pharaoh-hophra and Egypt
text: Saying, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself; being a staff of reed to the house of Israel that brake when they leaned upon it. Ezekiel was sent against Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon lying in his rivers, who said the river was his own and he had made it for himself, and who had been a staff of reed to Israel, breaking when they leaned on it (Ezekiel 29:1-7). The Lord would make Egypt desolate forty years from Syene to the border of Ethiopia and afterward restore it as the basest of kingdoms, no more Israel’s confidence; and Jeremiah gave the remnant in Egypt the sign that Pharaoh-hophra would be given to his enemies as Zedekiah had been (Ezekiel 29:8-16; Jeremiah 44:30). In the tenth year, in the tenth month, the word came to Ezekiel to set his face against Pharaoh king of Egypt and all Egypt: the great dragon lying in the midst of his rivers, who said his river was his own and he had made it for himself (Ezekiel 29:1-3). One teaching reads a commentary on the prince of Tyre that calls this the insanity of prosperity, inordinate pride begotten of great prosperity, and lists Pharaoh here beside Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar; the teacher carries it to America. We trust in democracy, one class says, we trust in America’s military, instead of the Holy One. Egypt had been a staff of reed to the house of Israel: when they took hold of it, it broke and tore their shoulder, and when they leaned on it, it snapped and made their loins shake (Ezekiel 29:6-7). The Rabshakeh had said the same of Egypt in Hezekiah’s day (Isaiah 36:6), and the teachers draw the history: we had a history of trusting in Egypt; we loved Egypt, and put all our trust in Egypt (Isaiah 30:1-3). We made a league with the Egyptians to help us fight Nebuchadnezzar, one teacher says, and Jeremiah said do not do that. Tartan was sent against Egypt and Ethiopia, another says, because Israel made the Ethiopians and Egyptians their strength (Isaiah 20:1-6). After Gedaliah’s murder the remnant ran to the same reed, and settled at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros, burning incense to other gods there (Jeremiah 44:1-8). The Lord would put hooks in his jaws, make the fish of his rivers stick to his scales, and cast him into the wilderness as food for the beasts and the birds (Ezekiel 29:4-5). He would bring a sword on Egypt and make the land desolate from the tower of Syene to the border of Ethiopia, and no foot would pass through it for forty years (Ezekiel 29:8-12); nobody lived there for forty years, the teacher says. The teachers place Syene at Aswan, and teach that the Egypt of the Bible reached down to the border of Ethiopia, taking in what is now Sudan. After forty years He would gather the Egyptians back to Pathros, the land of their origin, and they would be the basest of kingdoms, never again to lift itself above the nations, nor be the confidence of Israel, which would only call their iniquity to mind when they looked to Egypt (Ezekiel 29:13-16). The teachers gloss Pathros as Upper Egypt and, in several classes, as Sudan; the readings stand together, since they teach that the Egypt of scripture reached into Sudan. Egypt would never be exalted as a world superpower again, the teacher says, rebuking those who glorify ancient Egypt; base means the bottom of all bottoms. In the twenty-seventh year the word came that Nebuchadnezzar had made his army serve a great service against Tyre and received no wages for it, so the Lord would give him the land of Egypt as wages for his army, because they worked for Him; and in that day He would make the horn of Israel to bud (Ezekiel 29:17-21). Empires rise and fall on Israel’s account, the teaching says (Genesis 15:13-14); God destroys all that we rely on, and He will take away our confidence in America. The sign for Hophra was given to the remnant in Egypt: he would be handed to his enemies as Zedekiah was given to Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 44:29-30). The Hidden History teaching gives the history: Hophra, called Apries, was overthrown by his own general Amasis, whom the soldiers proclaimed king, in a civil war of about 570 to 567 BC, and Jeremiah prophesied it years before it happened. The study note draws the lesson: evil does not come to a city by chance, but the Lord has done it, and none can deliver out of His hand (Amos 3:6; Deuteronomy 32:39).

name: The shepherds of Israel
text: Feeding themselves and not the flock; eating the fat and clothing themselves with the wool; not strengthening the diseased, healing the sick, binding up the broken, bringing again the driven away, or seeking the lost; ruling with force and with cruelty. Ezekiel was sent against the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, ate the fat, wore the wool, did not heal, bind up, bring back or seek the lost, and ruled with force and cruelty, until the sheep were scattered and became meat for every beast (Ezekiel 34:1-6). The Lord declared Himself against the shepherds, said He would search out His sheep Himself, and would set over them one shepherd, His servant David, whom the classes teach is Christ (Ezekiel 34:10-11; Ezekiel 34:23-24). What Jeremiah prophesied, the class says, is very similar to Ezekiel: woe to the pastors who destroy and scatter the sheep of His pasture (Jeremiah 23:1-2); shepherd is another word for pastor. The class reads the denominations as the scattering, and sets beside it the promise of pastors after His own heart who feed with knowledge (Jeremiah 3:15), the knowledge of God’s laws. Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves (Ezekiel 34:2). They ate the fat, clothed themselves with the wool and killed the fed, but did not feed the flock (Ezekiel 34:3): they get the best clothes, the class says; still in gators to this day, one teacher adds; bring your tithes, bring your money, says another (Isaiah 56:11). They did not strengthen the diseased, heal the sick, bind up the broken, bring back the driven away or seek the lost, but ruled with force and cruelty (Ezekiel 34:4). The driven away are the twelve tribes scattered, and Ezekiel was writing in the Babylonian captivity. The sheep were scattered for lack of a shepherd and became meat for all the beasts of the field (Ezekiel 34:5): meat for all the nations, the class says, the slaves that were scattered over the mountains and hills, which one teacher reads as countries and cities, with none searching or seeking for them (Ezekiel 34:6). None of these pastors are searching for the twelve tribes, the class says, and there are Israelite groups too, comfortable at home on the internet, whose whole campaign is to stop the ones doing the work; one teacher names some of the urban apologists along with the Christian pastors. We think of being prey only to the nations, but our own people prey on us as well (Ezekiel 34:22). One teacher turns the chapter on his own leaders: our job is to serve you, it cannot be for money; force and cruelty is brothers being cursed out and threatened, and the leader confesses himself among the sinners, as Nehemiah did (Nehemiah 1:6-7). Esau, another says, put some of our own people over us. The hireling, the class says, flees when the wolf comes, because the sheep are not his (John 10:12-13). The Lord is against the shepherds, the teacher says, underline that: He will require His flock at their hand, make them cease from feeding it, and deliver it from their mouth (Ezekiel 34:7-10). He Himself will search out His sheep (Ezekiel 34:11). Who is that I? Christ, sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24), and after Him the apostles in the great commission (Matthew 28:19). He will deliver them out of all places where they were scattered in the cloudy and dark day (Ezekiel 34:12): when those nuclear bombs go off, the class says, the Lord is going to be here, and another reads the dark day as war blacking out sun and moon (Matthew 24:29-30). He will bring them to their own land and feed them in a good pasture on the mountains of Israel, which is the kingdom (Ezekiel 34:13-15). He will seek the lost, bring back the driven away, bind up the broken and strengthen the sick; we were broken, we are the sick ones. But He will destroy the fat and the strong and feed them with judgment (Ezekiel 34:16), which the class reads as the nations and another as the leaders among us who grew fat on the flock; feeding with judgment, a third says, is feeding with His laws. He will judge between cattle and cattle (Ezekiel 34:17; Ezekiel 34:20-22), which the class carries to Christ separating the sheep from the goats (Matthew 25:32-33) and another reads as righteous and wicked Israelites. He will set up one shepherd over them, His servant David, to feed them and be a prince among them (Ezekiel 34:23-24). That shepherd is Christ, the good shepherd, the king the Lord raises up when He breaks the yoke and saves Israel out of captivity (Jeremiah 30:8-10; Hosea 3:5; John 10:11), and His covenant of peace is why He is the Prince of Peace (Ezekiel 34:25). The showers will come in their season and the earth will yield her increase, as it would not yield to Cain, and they will be safe in their land with none to make them afraid (Ezekiel 34:26-28; Genesis 4:12): right now we live in fear, the class says, and nobody is going to make us afraid ever again. They will know that the Lord their God is with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are His people, the flock of His pasture (Ezekiel 34:30-31).

name: Jonah
text: Rising up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord instead of going to Nineveh to cry against it. The word of the Lord sent Jonah the son of Amittai to cry against Nineveh, and he rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord (Jonah 1:1-3). The storm found him asleep in the ship; he confessed he was the cause and was cast into the sea, and the Lord prepared a great fish in which he lay three days and three nights, praying, until he was put out on dry land (Jonah 1:4-17; Jonah 2:1-10). Sent the second time he went and cried against the city, and when the Lord spared it he was angry; the Lord reproved him with the gourd, and Christ made his three days the sign given to His generation (Jonah 3:1-4; Jonah 4:1-11; Matthew 12:39-40). Jonah the son of Amittai prophesied in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, who restored Israel’s border by his word (2 Kings 14:25). The word came to him to go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for its wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Christians read Ninevites and think Assyrians, the Luke 11 teaching says, but the Ninevites to whom Jonah was a sign were the captives of the ten tribes led into Nineveh, as Tobit of Naphtali shows, who was carried there and heard Jonah and took heed (Tobit 1:1-3; Tobit 14:8); the study note on Acts 1 likewise says Jonah preached to Nineveh, where the northern kingdom was exiled. Our people in Nineveh were observing lying vanities, one class says, as they keep Christmas and a white Jesus today (Jonah 2:8). Jonah said no, as the teacher puts it: he rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, went down to Joppa, found a ship, paid the fare and went aboard (Jonah 1:3). The study note on Genesis 10 places Tarshish in Spain, first among the merchants of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:12); one history teaching reads from a book that Jonah looked to it as a safe haven where Hebrew traders had been since Solomon’s time, and another says most place it at Sicily. Two classes say he fled because he was afraid of the people of Nineveh; he himself later says he fled because he knew the Lord was gracious and merciful and would relent (Jonah 4:2), and the teaching adds that he feared being taken for a false prophet. Both can stand; like Adam, one class says, he tried to hide. The Lord sent a great wind and the ship was near breaking; the mariners cried each to his own god, and Jonah lay fast asleep in the sides of the ship (Jonah 1:4-5). The study note calls him the picture of the slack spirit, asleep while the ship breaks, and America the spiritual ship going down with our people asleep in it. The lot fell on Jonah, and he confessed he was a Hebrew who feared the Lord, the God of heaven who made the sea and the dry land (Jonah 1:7-10). He told them to throw him into the sea, for the storm was on his account (Jonah 1:11-12). That is accountability and integrity, the teaching says, owning that you are the cause, the opposite of Achan, whose hidden sin troubled the camp (Joshua 7:1). They rowed hard, prayed not to be charged with innocent blood, and cast him in, and the sea ceased her raging (Jonah 1:13-16). The Lord had prepared a great fish and Jonah was in its belly three days and three nights (Jonah 1:17). He cried to the Lord out of the belly of hell, which the teaching explains is the grave; cast out of His sight, he would look again toward the holy temple and pay what he had vowed (Jonah 2:1-9). The man who fled the Lord now sought Him, as in their affliction they will seek Him early (Hosea 5:15); in the fish, one class says, he repented of his fear and his doubt, and the teaching reads his rising from the pit as pointing to Christ, whose soul would not be left in the grave (Psalm 16:10). The word came the second time, and he went and cried what he was given, that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 3:1-4). When the Lord spared the city he was very angry and asked to die (Jonah 4:1-3). Jonah had an attitude problem, one class says, self-willed, mad that God did not destroy the people, like James and John wanting fire from heaven (Luke 9:54-55). With the gourd, the worm and the east wind the Lord showed him that he pitied a plant he had not laboured for, and asked whether He should not spare Nineveh (Jonah 4:4-11). Your spirit is not right, the teacher says; we do not preach for our own glory, and His thoughts are not our thoughts (Isaiah 55:8). The Lord held off because His people were there, the Luke 11 teaching says, but the word still stood and the city was destroyed (Tobit 14:4). Christ gave that generation no sign but the sign of Jonas: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, the Son of man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, and one greater than Jonah was there (Matthew 12:39-41). Three days and three nights, the teaching says, rules out Good Friday to Sunday. Jonah is actually about us, one class says: the God who heard him in the fish does not change (Malachi 3:6), so pray.

name: Nineveh under Nahum
text: A bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose prey departeth not; the dwelling of the lions that filled his holes with prey; the wicked counsellor that imagineth evil against the Lord. Nahum’s burden of Nineveh declares the Lord jealous and avenging, slow to anger but never clearing the guilty, and names the wicked counsellor who came out of Nineveh imagining evil against Him (Nahum 1:1-3; Nahum 1:11). The lions’ den that had emptied Jacob would be flooded, spoiled and left empty, and the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, would have no healing for its wound (Nahum 2:2-13; Nahum 3:1; Nahum 3:19). The teachers read it as the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC and, in several classes, as the sentence on Mystery Babylon, America. The burden opens with who the Lord is: jealous, avenging, taking vengeance on His adversaries and reserving wrath for His enemies (Nahum 1:2). God reserves wrath for America, for China, for Europe, the class says, for what they did to our people. He is slow to anger and great in power and will not at all acquit the wicked (Nahum 1:3); somebody tell the white man, one teacher says. His way is in the whirlwind and the storm, and one teaching sees Him in today’s hurricanes and earthquakes; the mountains quake before Him, and none can stand before His indignation (Nahum 1:3-6). Nineveh had been spared once. The Lord held off because His people were there, the Luke 11 teaching says, and the Empires class says Jonah stayed the destruction but Nineveh did not change the people there, which was us, and eventually Nineveh fell. Tobit, a captive of Naphtali there, saw the bodies of Israelites thrown out about the walls of Nineveh (Tobit 1:17-18); the Assyrians did much wickedness to our people, the teacher says. The emptiers had emptied Jacob and marred his branches (Nahum 2:2). Nineveh was the den of the lions, where the lion tore enough for his whelps and filled his holes with prey (Nahum 2:11-12). Out of her came one who imagined evil against the Lord, a wicked counsellor (Nahum 1:11); one class says that is America, another a system of people (Daniel 7:8). Woe to the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose prey never departs (Nahum 3:1). Woe to the bloody city, this is America, one class says, and the heaps of carcasses are our forefathers. Another says the bloody city robbed our lands, our identity, our culture, even our minds, and we are the prey that is still here; the study note on Exodus 14 reads the prey that does not depart as the people in captivity who will not leave. She was the well-favoured harlot, mistress of witchcrafts, who sold nations through her whoredoms (Nahum 3:4), which one class reads as the harlot Mystery Babylon (Revelation 17:5). The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble, and knows those who trust Him (Nahum 1:7): trouble is coming, the class says, and the Lord is good in the day of trouble if you keep the law, and we will have to depend on each other. With an overrunning flood He would make an utter end of the place, and affliction would not rise a second time (Nahum 1:8-9); one teacher sets it with Babylon, which shall not rise again (Jeremiah 51:64). He would break the yoke from off Judah and burst the bonds (Nahum 1:13): God will break the yoke of the white man and the nations off of us, the class says. No more of Nineveh’s name would be sown, her images would be cut off, and He would make her grave (Nahum 1:14), which one teaching reads of Esau (Isaiah 14:20). To Judah it was good tidings on the mountains: keep your solemn feasts (Nahum 1:15). The one who dashes in pieces came up; the chariots raged in the streets, the gates of the rivers were opened and the palace dissolved, and though they cried stand, stand, none looked back; she was empty, void and waste (Nahum 2:1-10). The Lord of hosts was against her (Nahum 2:13; Nahum 3:5). Her shepherds would slumber and her bruise would have no healing, and all who heard of her fall would clap their hands, for her wickedness had passed on everyone continually (Nahum 3:18-19). The history teachings give the fall: Babylon and the Medes teamed up to take down the Assyrian, Cyaxares the Mede with Nabopolassar, in 612 BC after about three months of siege; the Median army stormed the city and left ruined hills and heaps of debris, and by 600 BC Assyria was gone. Tobit had told his son to leave Nineveh, because what Jonas the prophet spoke would surely come to pass, and before he died he heard of its destruction and rejoiced (Tobit 14:4; Tobit 14:8; Tobit 14:15). The Disturbing Truth class reads Nahum 1 as not about ancient Assyria but about Babylon and her allies, and the other classes read the bloody city as Mystery Babylon: Nineveh and America are one and the same, one teacher says.

name: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin
text: Weakening the hands of the people of Judah and troubling them in building; hiring counsellors against them to frustrate their purpose; writing accusations against Jerusalem to the king, and making the work cease by force and power. When the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard the returned captives were building the temple, they asked to build with them, claiming to have sought the same God since Esarhaddon brought them there, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua refused (Ezra 4:1-3). Then the people of the land weakened the hands of Judah, hired counsellors against them from Cyrus to Darius, wrote accusations to the king, and made the work cease by force and power until the second year of Darius (Ezra 4:4-24). No sentence on them is recorded; their purpose was overturned when the prophets rose up and Darius confirmed the decree of Cyrus (Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:1-12). When the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity were building the temple, they came to Zerubbabel and the chief of the fathers asking to build with them, saying they sought the same God and had sacrificed to Him since Esarhaddon king of Assyria brought them there (Ezra 4:1-2). Word travels fast, the verse-by-verse teacher says; Samaria is about sixty miles off. The scripture calls them adversaries before they even speak, the class says; the forefathers discerned in the spirit. Adversary means enemies, another class says, and this is meant for our people, not an all-inclusive thing. The study note identifies them with the nations Assyria settled in Samaria, taught only to appease the God of the land after the lions came, each nation still making its own gods (2 Kings 17:24-33); they feared the Lord and served their images, and the note says Israel as a nation does the same (2 Kings 17:41). The teacher reads 2 Kings 17 to show these nations were liars, and calls their settling real gentrification. Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the chief of the fathers answered that the strangers had nothing to do with them in building a house to their God; they themselves together would build, as Cyrus had commanded (Ezra 4:3). The work of the Most High is not shared with other nations, the study note says. Zerubbabel was not subcontracting work to the heathen, the teacher says; he knew the scriptures: make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land and no marriages (Exodus 34:12; Deuteronomy 7:2-4), and never trust your enemy, for though he pretends to help he will undermine you (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-18). We ourselves together, one captain says, is a strong four words. One history teaching sets beside the verse the FBI director’s answer that the greatest threat to the United States was Negro unity, unity under the Bible and under Christ; another says we are not on some rainbow coalition, for the heathen infiltrate and destroy. Then the people of the land weakened the hands of Judah, troubled them in building, and hired counsellors against them all the days of Cyrus until Darius (Ezra 4:4-5). The teacher reads weakened the hands through the FBI files and the infiltration of our movements from their founding, and the class names the informants planted inside, the secret plots and popular persuasions of that day (1 Esdras 5:73). Under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes they wrote accusations, and Rehum and Shimshai, with the nations Asnapper had settled, wrote that the rebellious and bad city, once built, would pay no tribute and damage the king’s revenue (Ezra 4:6-16). The heathen always keep records on the children of Israel, the study note says; the history teaching calls the letter propaganda slandering us, and the teacher sets beside it today’s labels such as black identity extremists. The king answered that the records showed Jerusalem had rebelled of old, and ordered the work to cease until he gave command (Ezra 4:17-22). Rehum and Shimshai went up in haste and made the Jews cease by force and power (Ezra 4:23); by force means military, the teacher says, and by power means legislation. Esdras tells it with horsemen halting the work (1 Esdras 2:30). The house ceased until the second year of Darius (Ezra 4:24). Esdras, the study note and one class give the full stoppage as two years, not one tool, not one brick; the Ezra 4 teacher reckons the temple delayed about twenty years, and the history teaching counts the hindrance from Cyrus to Darius. The two stand together: years of hindrance, then two years of full stoppage (1 Esdras 5:73). The record gives no sentence on the adversaries; it records their purpose overturned. When Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, Zerubbabel and Jeshua rose up and built, and the eye of God was on the elders so that the governor could not stop them (Ezra 5:1-5); the study note says the work gets done only when the prophets and the people labour together (Zephaniah 2:1-3). The search found the decree of Cyrus, and Darius ordered the work left alone, its costs paid from the king’s tribute beyond the river, and anyone who altered the word hanged on timber from his own house (Ezra 6:1-12); a Persian decree was upheld and not overturned, the note says (Esther 8:8). The house was finished in the sixth year of Darius and dedicated with joy (Ezra 6:14-18). The curses are a revolving door, the teacher says: the stranger rises above us while we disobey (Deuteronomy 28:43; Baruch 3:8).

name: Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest
text: Obeying the voice of the Lord their God and the words of Haggai the prophet; humbling themselves, fearing before the Lord, and rising up to work in the house of the Lord of hosts. In the second year of Darius the word came by Haggai to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest: the people said the time had not come to build the Lord’s house while they lived in panelled houses and His house lay waste, and their labour came to little (Haggai 1:1-11). Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the remnant obeyed the voice of the Lord and the words of Haggai and feared before Him, and the Lord stirred their spirit and they worked on His house (Haggai 1:12-14). He told them He was with them, promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former, and made Zerubbabel as a signet (Haggai 2:4-9; Haggai 2:23). Zerubbabel means born in Babylon, the class says, and that is us. He was one of the king’s bodyguards, and when the three guards contended he spoke for truth and asked nothing for himself but that Darius keep his vow to build Jerusalem and return the vessels (1 Esdras 4:13; 1 Esdras 4:42-46). With Joshua the son of Josedec he set up the altar in the seventh month despite fear of the peoples, built as it is written, and laid the foundation, and the shout of joy and the weeping of the old men who remembered the first house could not be told apart (Ezra 3:1-13). Then the adversaries’ secret plots and popular persuasions stopped the building two years (1 Esdras 5:72-73). The class teaches that Zerubbabel and Joshua fell back: battle fatigue, the top two men taking care of their own personal lives. The people said the time was not come, while they lived in panelled houses, the nice house with the new roof, and the Lord’s house lay waste (Haggai 1:2-4). Consider your ways, the Lord said (Haggai 1:5-7): examine yourselves, the class says (2 Corinthians 13:5). They sowed much and brought in little and put their wages in a bag with holes, because His house lay waste while every man ran to his own (Haggai 1:6-11); God is always second or third, the class says, after the forty-eight and fifty-two hours we give the job. In Zechariah’s vision Joshua stood before the angel in filthy garments with Satan at his right hand, and the Lord rebuked Satan and called Joshua a brand plucked from the fire (Zechariah 3:1-3). What was his iniquity? He gave up, the class says; he stopped doing what God commanded, like the guest without a wedding garment (Matthew 22:11). Then Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the remnant obeyed the voice of the Lord and the words of Haggai, and feared before the Lord (Haggai 1:12). They took heed, one class says; they did not answer, I am over you. The Lord said, I am with you, stirred up their spirit, and on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month they came and worked (Haggai 1:13-15). Haggai and Zechariah blasted the high priest and the governor, the class says, and correction is love. Joshua’s filthy garments were taken away and he was clothed in change of raiment, with a clean mitre on his head (Zechariah 3:4-5); the study note says the change of raiment is Israel becoming righteous by keeping the commandments (Psalm 132:9). The Lord promised His servant the BRANCH (Zechariah 3:8): the study note reads the Branch as the remnant of Judah, Benjamin and Levi, and the class teaches that the Branch is Christ, who would remove the iniquity of the land in one day, at the cross (Zechariah 3:9). To Zerubbabel the word was that the work would be done not by might or power but by His spirit (Zechariah 4:6): the king’s bodyguard could break bones, the class says, but the spirit overcomes; the great mountain made a plain before him is Babylon then and Babylon today, America (Zechariah 4:7; Jeremiah 51:25). His hands laid the foundation and would finish it, and the headstone is Christ (Zechariah 4:9; Psalm 118:22). One class reads the two olive trees as Moses and Elijah, and a Revelation teaching reads them in layers, Joshua and Zerubbabel among them (Zechariah 4:11-14; Revelation 11:4). To the old men who wept, Haggai said be strong, for the Lord was with them; He would shake heaven, earth and the nations, the desire of all nations would come, the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former, and there He would give peace (Haggai 2:3-9). The study note says that peace has not come to fruition yet; one class reads the shaking as the third woe, the desire of nations as gold, silver and pearls returned to Israel, not paper money, and the latter house as the third temple, and the Born in Babylon class teaches it as the house that Christ builds. Holiness does not spread by touch but uncleanness does, the note says; the desire to serve in sincerity was not there, yet from the day the foundation was laid He would bless them (Haggai 2:10-19). He would make Zerubbabel as a signet, for He had chosen him (Haggai 2:23): God chose a prominent figure, a governor, to do His work, one teacher says, and Ben Sira sets him as a signet on the right hand, with Jesus the son of Josedec (Ecclesiasticus 49:11-12). The house was finished in the sixth year of Darius, in the month Adar (Ezra 6:14-15). Walk in the footsteps of Zerubbabel, the class says.

name: Ezra
text: Preparing his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments; proclaiming a fast at the river Ahava, and being ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after saying the hand of God is upon all them that seek him. Ezra the son of Seraiah, a priest of the line of Aaron and a ready scribe in the law of Moses, went up from Babylon in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, for he had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach it in Israel (Ezra 7:1-10). At the river Ahava he proclaimed a fast and was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after saying the hand of God is on all who seek Him, and the Lord brought the company and the treasure safely to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:21-32). There he read the law to the people while the Levites gave the sense (Nehemiah 8:1-8). Ezra was the son of Seraiah, of the line of Zadok, Phinehas, Eleazar and Aaron, a priest of the true line, the study note says, and a ready scribe in the law of Moses; the king granted all he asked, for the hand of the Lord his God was on him (Ezra 7:1-6). The history teaching places his going up about 58 to 60 years after the temple was finished, with the book of Esther falling between Ezra 6 and 7, and the departure about 458 BC. Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments (Ezra 7:10). The study note says preparing the heart means setting mind and spirit in order, examining oneself and putting away the weak nature of sin before teaching others: set your house in order (2 Esdras 14:13-14). He had such skill that he left out nothing of the law (1 Esdras 8:7), which the note says came because he prayed and fasted to understand; if any lack wisdom, let him ask of God (James 1:5). The classes take the verse as a pattern: seek, do and teach; fix yourself first; pastors who do not prepare their heart cannot give the sense. Ezra understood, one teacher says, that we went into captivity for not keeping the commandments. Artaxerxes sent him with the king’s silver and gold and freed the priests and Levites from toll, tribute and custom (Ezra 7:11-24); the note sees in it the nations bringing back Israel’s substance (Isaiah 60:5-6), and teaches using the favour of those set over you without abusing it. A heathen king supported the work of the prophets, the note says, and Ezra blessed the Lord who put it in the king’s heart (Ezra 7:27-28). Ezra knew which men among him had understanding, the note says, and sent for Levites and ministers (Ezra 8:15-20). At the river Ahava he proclaimed a fast to humble themselves before God and seek a right way for themselves, their little ones and their substance, for he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen after telling him the hand of God is on all who seek Him for good (Ezra 8:21-22). To afflict the soul is to fast, taking neither food nor water, the note says (Isaiah 58:5). The Jews had enemies, the history teaching says, but he would not go back and ask for soldiers when he had just told the king that God fights for those who keep His commandments; Nehemiah, unlike Ezra, was sent with an army. They fasted and sought God, and He was entreated of them (Ezra 8:23). Ezra set apart twelve chief priests and weighed the silver, gold and vessels into their hands, and they were weighed again in the house of God, to make sure there was no foul play, the teacher says; the hand of God delivered them from the enemy and from those who lay in wait by the way (Ezra 8:24-34; 1 Esdras 8:54-64). In Jerusalem Ezra the scribe stood on a pulpit of wood above the people and read the law in the street from morning to midday, and the Levites read distinctly, gave the sense and caused them to understand (Nehemiah 8:1-8). The study note says the Most High does not favour camps and closed rooms, and teaching is meant to bring understanding, not recitation. That is the model of teaching, the class says: read distinctly, give the sense, cause the people to understand; hear the law, then learn what it means and when to apply it. The teaching calls him chief priest and reader (1 Esdras 9:49) and the men beside him teachers giving the sense, standing above the people as IUIC sets up today. The people lifted their hands and bowed their heads, and that is how you pray (Nehemiah 8:6); they kept the feast of tabernacles with great gladness (Nehemiah 8:13-18; 1 Esdras 9:37-55). The classes also credit Ezra with restoring the scriptures. The law was burnt, and the people had grown up seventy years in Babylon; Ezra knew, for he was brought up in the law, and for forty days, like Moses on Sinai, he drank the cup given him and dictated the books, two hundred and four of them, keeping the last seventy for the wise (2 Esdras 14:21-47). The spirit strengthened his memory, the class says, but it cannot strengthen your memory if you have nothing in your memory. One history episode places this in Babylon before his journey, so that Nehemiah 8 is that book being read, and a later episode places it in Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s time. The 400 Years class counts the four hundred years to Christ from the time of Ezra (2 Esdras 7:28).

name: The returned exiles who married strange wives
text: Not separating themselves from the people of the lands; taking their daughters for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy seed mingled itself with the people of those lands; the princes and rulers chief in the trespass. The princes told Ezra that the people, the priests, and the Levites had taken wives of the nations of the lands, so that the holy seed was mixed with them, and that the rulers had led the trespass (Ezra 9:1-2). Ezra mourned and confessed it as the same trespass that had carried the fathers into captivity, and the congregation covenanted to put away the strange wives and the children born of them, examining the matter family by family over three months (Ezra 9:3-15; Ezra 10:1-17). A generation later Nehemiah found the same sin again and contended with those who had done it (Nehemiah 13:23-28). The princes reported that the people, the priests, and the Levites had not separated from the peoples of the lands but had taken their daughters for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed was mingled with them, with the rulers chief in the trespass (Ezra 9:1-2). Esdras tells the same history, adding that the rulers and great men had been partakers from the beginning (1 Esdras 8:68-70). The sin is marriage with the nations, and it was not only the common people but the Levites and the leaders. The teaching calls that Israel’s issue from the days of Numbers until now: the desire to mix and mingle with the nations. The law was plain: make no marriages with them, neither giving daughters to their sons nor taking their daughters, because they would turn the sons away from following the Most High to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). The class teaches that the man follows his woman and her god. Solomon is the prime example: he made his alliances by taking the daughters of kings, and his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:1-4). Ezra tore his garment, pulled out the hair of his head and beard, and sat stunned until the evening sacrifice, and all who trembled at God’s words gathered to him (Ezra 9:3-4). On his knees he confessed that since the days of the fathers the nation had been in great trespass, and for it kings and priests had been given to the sword, to captivity, to spoil, and to confusion of face (Ezra 9:5-7). The teaching hears in it what Daniel said: confusion of face, the fruit of intermingling, so that our people now carry every complexion of the nations. He owned a little reviving in their bondage: still bondmen under Persia and not ruling, but given leave to rebuild God’s house and return to the law (Ezra 9:8-9). Having been punished less than their iniquities deserved, should they again break the commandments and join in affinity with these peoples (Ezra 9:10-14)? The class draws from it how merciful God is: Assyria, Babylon, and the burned temple were less than the nation deserved. While Ezra wept and confessed a great congregation gathered, and Shechaniah the son of Jehiel said they had trespassed, yet there was hope: let them covenant to put away all the wives and those born of them, according to the law (Ezra 10:1-4). Ezra made them all swear to it and mourned without bread or water (Ezra 10:5-6). A proclamation gave the children of the captivity three days to gather; whoever did not come forfeited his substance and was separated from the congregation (Ezra 10:7-8). They gathered in the ninth month and sat in the street trembling over the matter and the great rain (Ezra 10:9), a storm, and knowing they had sinned they were afraid, for storms come from the Lord (1 Esdras 9:6). Ezra told them to make confession and do God’s pleasure by separating from the peoples of the land and from the strange wives (Ezra 10:10-11). The study note says doing His pleasure today is the same, separating from unclean people, and the class teaches that there is no interracial marriage with God. Because the transgressors were many and the rain heavy, each city came at appointed times with its elders and judges, and men who had not taken other nations sat and judged, for one who is in the sin cannot judge it, from the first day of the tenth month to the first day of the first month: three months to clean house (Ezra 10:12-17). The teaching notes they could do it because they kept a registry of genealogies. Sons of the priests, even sons of Jeshua, gave their hands to put away their wives and offered a ram for their trespass, and the roll names Levites, singers, porters, and men of Israel, some with children by these wives (Ezra 10:18-44); Esdras says they put them away with their children (1 Esdras 9:36). The study note sets a limit: that covenant concerned those particular wives and children, and does not mean an Israelite today with a child by another nation must put away the child. The class adds its charge to anyone holding on to a heathen wife today: separate, for that pleases God. Yet the sin came back. Nehemiah later found Jews married to women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab whose children could not speak the Jews’ language, because the mothers reared them; he contended with them, reminded them that outlandish women caused even Solomon to sin, and chased away a grandson of the high priest married to the daughter of Sanballat (Nehemiah 13:23-28). No one is above the temptation that took Solomon down (1 Corinthians 10:12).

name: Nehemiah
text: Fasting and praying before the God of heaven for the remnant; building the wall in fifty-two days with a sword in one hand; taking no governor’s bread; forbidding usury; shutting the gates on the Sabbath; remember me, O my God, for good. Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes in Shushan, heard that the remnant in Judah was in affliction and the wall of Jerusalem broken down, and he wept, fasted, and prayed, pleading the promise to gather a scattered people who return (Nehemiah 1:1-11). The king sent him with letters, timber, and an armed escort, and he built the wall in fifty-two days with the builders armed, refused the governor’s bread, ended the usury, and later cleansed the temple chamber and shut the gates on the Sabbath (Nehemiah 2:1-9; Nehemiah 4:13-23; Nehemiah 5:6-18; Nehemiah 6:15; Nehemiah 13:4-22). He never claimed the work as his own, and asked God to remember him for good (Nehemiah 13:31). Nehemiah was born in captivity at Shushan and had never seen Jerusalem. He held a high place in the Persian court as cupbearer, whose work guarded the king from poison and kept him in the king’s presence every day. When Hanani came from Judah with word that the remnant was in great affliction and reproach, the wall broken down and the gates burned, he sat down and wept, mourned for days, fasted, and prayed (Nehemiah 1:1-4). No matter how high he went, he never forgot his people. He confessed the sins of Israel, his own father’s house included, and held the Most High to what He had told Moses: scattered among the nations for transgression, gathered from the uttermost parts when they turned and kept His commandments (Nehemiah 1:5-11; Deuteronomy 30:1-4). A cupbearer had to keep a cheerful face before the king, and the class compares it to how our people are expected to smile before their employers today. When the king saw his sorrow Nehemiah was very afraid. Yet he told the king that the city of his fathers’ sepulchres lay waste, and he prayed to the God of heaven before he made his request (Nehemiah 2:1-4). He asked to be sent to build it, set the king a time, and received letters to the governors and to the keeper of the king’s forest, all by the favour of his God upon him (Nehemiah 2:5-8). It is not that the heathen love Israel; the Lord moves a king to deal well with His remnant (Jeremiah 15:11). After three days in Jerusalem he viewed the ruined walls by night, telling no man what God had put in his heart, then told the rulers how God’s hand had been with him, and they set their hands to the work (Nehemiah 2:11-18). He never said the work came from his own wisdom, and he put the same vision on the men around him. Under mockery and conspiracy the people had a mind to work, and the wall rose to half its height (Nehemiah 4:1-6). He answered with prayer and a watch day and night, set the people by their families with swords, spears, and bows, and told them not to fear but to remember the Lord, who is great and to be feared, and fight for their brethren, wives, and houses; half worked and half stood guard, every builder wore his sword, and no one put off his clothes except for washing (Nehemiah 4:9-23). When the nobles exacted usury of their brethren he rebuked them and made them restore it, and for twelve years as governor he refused the governor’s portion, because the bondage was heavy on the people and because of the fear of God (Nehemiah 5:6-18). The teaching draws the lesson that leaders must always deal right with the people. When a hired prophet urged him to hide in the temple, he asked whether a man like him should flee (Nehemiah 6:10-13). The teaching says real leaders do not run and hide while other men stand in the front. On his return from the king he threw Tobiah’s goods out of the temple chamber, restored the Levites’ portions, and shut the gates at dark before the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:4-22). The wall was finished in fifty-two days, and when the enemies and the heathen round about saw it they were disheartened, for they saw that the work was done by God (Nehemiah 6:15-16). Ecclesiasticus counts him among the elect, a man of great renown who raised up the fallen walls, set up the gates and bars, and rebuilt the ruins (Ecclesiasticus 49:13), and he gathered a library of the records of the kings, the prophets, and David (2 Maccabees 2:13). Again and again he asked God to think on him for good according to all he had done for the people, and not to wipe out his good deeds for the house of God (Nehemiah 5:19; Nehemiah 13:14; Nehemiah 13:31). God is not unrighteous to forget the work and labour of love shown toward His name (Hebrews 6:10); Nehemiah is remembered for his good deeds to this day. He was humble enough to write down the names of everyone who built beside him, so that they too would be remembered by God, while the nobles of Tekoa who would not bend their necks to the work are remembered for that (Nehemiah 3:1-5). The pattern stands for today: be a people with a mind to work, and do not be the noble who would not put his hand to it.

name: Sanballat, Geshem, and Noadiah
text: Laughing the work to scorn; conspiring to fight against Jerusalem; sending four times to draw Nehemiah to the plain of Ono to do him mischief; an open letter charging rebellion; hiring Shemaiah and the prophetess Noadiah to put him in fear. Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian were grieved that a man had come to seek the welfare of Israel; they mocked the builders, accused them of rebelling against the king, and conspired to attack the city (Nehemiah 2:10; Nehemiah 2:19; Nehemiah 4:1-11). When the wall stood they tried four times to draw Nehemiah out to Ono, sent an open letter saying he meant to be king, and hired Shemaiah, with the prophetess Noadiah and other prophets, to frighten him into sin (Nehemiah 6:1-14). No sentence on them is recorded; Nehemiah left them to God and finished the wall, and they were disheartened (Nehemiah 6:14-16). When Sanballat and Tobiah heard that a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, it grieved them deeply (Nehemiah 2:10), the same spirit that had weakened the hands of Judah and hired counsellors against the temple work (Ezra 4:4-5). The teaching draws the line to today: whenever a man rises up to seek the welfare of his people, the nations count him a threat, and they will buy him off, demonize him, or kill him. J. Edgar Hoover called black unity, or a black messiah, one of the most dangerous things, and Fred Hampton, Malcolm X, Medgar Evers, and Martin Luther King show what came to men who looked after the welfare of their people. The class tells our people to stop expecting the nations to be happy that they repent and keep the commandments. When the building began, Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem laughed and asked whether the Jews would rebel against the king (Nehemiah 2:19), a lie, since Nehemiah carried the king’s own letters. He answered that God would prosper His servants, and that the mockers had no share, no right, and no memorial in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:20), which the teaching renders as: God is not dealing with you, so what we do is none of your business. Before the army of Samaria Sanballat called them feeble Jews, and Tobiah said a fox could break down their wall (Nehemiah 4:1-3). When the breaches began to be stopped, the Arabians, Ammonites, and Ashdodites joined them in a plot to fight against Jerusalem and slay the builders by surprise (Nehemiah 4:7-11). The teaching says they saw Israel being productive and did not like it, the same wrath the dragon makes against the remnant that keeps the commandments (Revelation 12:17). With the wall standing, Sanballat and Geshem sent four times for Nehemiah to meet them in the plain of Ono, meaning to kill him, then an open letter saying it was reported among the heathen that he built the wall to rebel and be king, with prophets proclaiming him (Nehemiah 6:1-7). Nehemiah understood propaganda: the aim was to make the builders afraid and weaken their hands so the work would stop (Nehemiah 6:8-9). The class notes the same charge is made today, that gathering our people means overthrowing the country. Then Tobiah and Sanballat hired Shemaiah to tell him to hide in the temple, so that he would be afraid, sin, and give them matter for an evil report (Nehemiah 6:10-13). The class teaches that the heathen hired one of his own people to convince the leader to run and hide, that he sold his people out, and that to stop the work of God out of fear is itself a sin. Nehemiah also named the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who would have put him in fear (Nehemiah 6:14), and the teaching points out that a woman of our own people joined the enemies against the work. Nehemiah answered every stage. He was doing a great work and would not come down; the charges were made up in their own hearts; a man such as he would not flee into the temple (Nehemiah 6:3; Nehemiah 6:8; Nehemiah 6:11). He prayed that their reproach be turned on their own heads (Nehemiah 4:4), and committed Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah, and the prophets to God according to their works (Nehemiah 6:14). No penalty carried out on them is recorded; the record is of their purpose defeated. The wall was finished in fifty-two days, and when the enemies heard it they were greatly disheartened, for they saw that the work was done by God (Nehemiah 6:15-16). The class says that when they see our people organized and working together, they are disheartened the same way. Yet the enemy kept a line inside: the nobles of Judah traded letters with Tobiah, being bound to him by marriage, and one of the grandsons of the high priest was son in law to Sanballat until Nehemiah chased him away (Nehemiah 6:17-19; Nehemiah 13:28). The men set over the people must fear God and hate covetousness, men who cannot be bought off or silenced with money, not hired the way Sanballat and Tobiah hired that man against Nehemiah (Exodus 18:21).

name: The nobles who exacted usury of their brethren
text: Exacting usury every one of his brother; taking their lands, vineyards, oliveyards, and houses, and bringing their sons and daughters into bondage for debt. While the wall was being built, the people cried out against their own brethren: to buy corn in the famine and pay the king’s tribute they had mortgaged their lands and houses, and their sons and daughters were going into bondage to the nobles and rulers (Nehemiah 5:1-5). Nehemiah rebuked the nobles for exacting usury, set a great assembly against them, and made them swear before the priests to restore the lands, the houses, and the hundredth part they had taken, and the people did according to the promise (Nehemiah 5:6-13). Even in the middle of the outside threat a wrong rose up inside the camp: a great cry of the people and their wives against their brethren the Jews (Nehemiah 5:1). Some had many children and took up corn to live; some had mortgaged their lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn in the dearth; some had borrowed money for the king’s tribute on their lands (Nehemiah 5:2-4). They were one flesh with their brethren, yet their sons and daughters were being brought into bondage and they had no power to redeem them, because other men held their lands (Nehemiah 5:5). The teaching puts it plainly: Israel was oppressing Israel; redeemed out of captivity and back in our own land, we were putting each other in captivity. The class identifies the nobles as the wealthy intellects, the bourgeoisie of that day, who with the rulers, the governors before Nehemiah, were exploiting and extorting their own people for their lands, their money, and the servitude of their children. The law is plain: lend to the poor of God’s people without usury (Exodus 22:25). Usury means interest; lend your brother twenty dollars and you get twenty dollars back, nothing more and nothing less.
