One teaching ties the usury to the king’s tribute the rulers laid on the people, and the class to interest on loans; the two stand together, since the people borrowed against their lands to pay the tribute. If your brother grows poor, relieve him even if he is a sojourner, and take no usury or increase from him, but fear God (Leviticus 25:35-37); lending for a profit off your own people is evil. The stranger there is your own brother away from his allotment, and brother, neighbour, and the children of your people all mean the same nation (Leviticus 19:17-18). A brother sold for poverty was to serve as a hired servant and not as a bondman, because the children of Israel are God’s servants whom He brought out of Egypt (Leviticus 25:39-42). The nobles had made the poor of their own people what the law forbade them to be. Nehemiah was very angry. He consulted with himself, rebuked the nobles and rulers for each exacting usury of his brother, and set a great assembly against them (Nehemiah 5:6-7). The class teaches that he got all Israel against the nobles, and that sometimes a show of force is needed to get the rich among our people off the backs of the poor, because they will do worse to you than the white man at times. He reminded them that he had redeemed their brethren from the heathen as far as he was able; would they now sell them? They held their peace and found nothing to answer, because they knew they were guilty (Nehemiah 5:8). What they did was not good; they ought to walk in the fear of God because of the reproach of the heathen, which, the teaching notes, shows that the heathen are our enemies (Nehemiah 5:9). He asked them to leave off the usury and restore that same day the lands, vineyards, oliveyards, and houses, with the hundredth part of the money, corn, wine, and oil they had exacted (Nehemiah 5:10-11). They promised to restore it and require nothing; he took an oath of them before the priests and shook out his lap as a sign that God would shake out every man who broke the promise, and the congregation said Amen and praised the Lord, and the people did as they had promised (Nehemiah 5:12-13). Restitution is the law’s remedy, and the principle still applies among brothers and sisters (Exodus 22:1). Nehemiah set the example himself. For twelve years as governor he did not eat the bread of the governor, unlike the former governors who were chargeable to the people and whose servants ruled over them; he bought no land and kept his men at the wall, because the bondage was heavy on the people and because of the fear of God (Nehemiah 5:14-18). He was about the work and for the people, not the usury of the people, and he asked God to think on him for good for all he had done for them (Nehemiah 5:19).

name: Eliashib and Tobiah the Ammonite
text: Preparing for Tobiah the Ammonite a great chamber in the court of the house of God, where the offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of the Levites had been laid; a grandson of the high priest son in law to Sanballat the Horonite. While Nehemiah was away with the king, Eliashib the priest, who had oversight of the chambers of the house of God and was allied to Tobiah the Ammonite, prepared for him a great chamber where the offerings, the vessels, and the tithes of the Levites had been kept (Nehemiah 13:4-6). The law read in that season shut the Ammonite out of the congregation for ever (Nehemiah 13:1-3). Nehemiah came back, threw out Tobiah’s household stuff, cleansed the chambers, restored the Levites, and chased away the high priest’s grandson who had married the daughter of Sanballat (Nehemiah 13:7-13; Nehemiah 13:28). They read in the book of Moses that the Ammonite and the Moabite should not come into the congregation of God for ever, because they did not meet Israel with bread and water but hired Balaam to curse them, and God turned the curse into a blessing; when the people heard it they separated the mixed multitude from Israel (Nehemiah 13:1-3; Deuteronomy 23:3-4; Numbers 22:5-6). But before this Eliashib the priest, set over the chambers of the house of God, was allied to Tobiah and made him a great chamber where the meat offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of corn, wine, and oil for the Levites, singers, and porters had been laid (Nehemiah 13:4-5). The priest gave a man whom the law shut out of the congregation a place to live in the courts of the house of God. The teaching explains that this is how the enemy always knew what was being done during the building. Tobiah had married into Judah: he was son in law of Shechaniah, his son had taken the daughter of Meshullam, and many in Judah were sworn to him; the nobles sent him letters, spoke of his good deeds before Nehemiah, and carried Nehemiah’s words back to him (Nehemiah 6:17-19). The class teaches that the heathen married into the noble families of our people to gain status while the nobles went about saying these were good folks, and warns that there is always a snake among us, a Judas who aligns himself with the heathen to hinder the building. Eliashib’s own house was bound to the enemy, for one of the sons of Joiada his son was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite, the same Sanballat who had plotted to kill Nehemiah (Nehemiah 13:28). All this happened while Nehemiah was not at Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes he had gone back to the king (Nehemiah 13:6). The classes teach that Malachi stood in during his absence, and it was the priests he rebuked: they had departed out of the way, caused many to stumble at the law, corrupted the covenant of Levi, and been partial in the law (Malachi 2:7-9). When Nehemiah obtained leave of the king and came back and understood the evil Eliashib had done for Tobiah, it grieved him deeply; he cast all Tobiah’s household stuff out of the chamber, had the chambers cleansed, and brought back the vessels of the house of God with the meat offering and the frankincense (Nehemiah 13:7-9). The teaching says he threw the Ammonite’s things into the street, for by the law that man should never have been in the temple at all. He found that the portions of the Levites had not been given, so that they and the singers had fled each to his field; he contended with the rulers, asked why the house of God was forsaken, set the Levites back in their place, and appointed faithful treasurers to distribute to their brethren, asking God not to wipe out his good deeds for the house of God (Nehemiah 13:10-14). The son of Joiada who was son in law to Sanballat he chased away, because he had defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites (Nehemiah 13:28-29). So he cleansed them from all strangers and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, each in his business (Nehemiah 13:30-31). The class teaches that the book is not about assimilation but separation, because the Lord made Israel a royal priesthood and a holy nation severed from all people, not to mingle that royal seed with the heathen.

name: The Sabbath traders of Jerusalem and Tyre
text: Treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in sheaves, lading asses with wine, grapes, and figs, and bringing burdens into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day; men of Tyre selling fish and all manner of ware on the Sabbath to the children of Judah. After the people had sworn not to buy wares or food from the peoples of the land on the Sabbath, Nehemiah found men of Judah treading winepresses and carrying burdens into Jerusalem on the Sabbath, and men of Tyre selling fish and all kinds of ware to the children of Judah (Nehemiah 10:31; Nehemiah 13:15-16). He contended with the nobles for profaning the Sabbath, had the gates shut at dark before it, and warned the merchants lodging outside the wall that he would lay hands on them, and they came no more on the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:17-22). When the covenant was sealed, the people swore that if the peoples of the land brought wares or food to sell on the Sabbath or a holy day, they would not buy (Nehemiah 10:31). But in those days Nehemiah saw some in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in sheaves, loading donkeys, and carrying wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of burdens into Jerusalem to sell, and men of Tyre living there sold fish and all manner of ware on the Sabbath to the children of Judah (Nehemiah 13:15-16). While Nehemiah was away the rulers had again let the other nations come in. The class likens the Tyrians to the merchants who move into our communities today and make their money off of us. The commandment says to remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy, doing no work on the seventh day, not you, your son, your daughter, your servants, or your cattle (Exodus 20:8-10). It says remember because Israel would forget it, and in this captivity it was lost through forced conversion. The Sabbath is a sign between the Most High and the children of Israel for ever, not between Him and the other nations (Exodus 31:13-17). Jeremiah had warned this same city to carry no burden in through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21-22), the very burdens Nehemiah later shut the gates against. The same heart is recorded in Amos, where Israel asked when the new moon and the Sabbath would be gone so that they could sell corn (Amos 8:5). No buying, no selling, and no burdens on the Sabbath day. Nehemiah contended with the nobles of Judah and asked what evil thing this was, that they profaned the Sabbath. Did their fathers not do the same, so that God brought all this evil on them and on the city, and now they were bringing more wrath on Israel (Nehemiah 13:17-18)? The teaching says we had gone into captivity for breaking God’s law, and on the return there were people trying to get us to sin again. When the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the Sabbath he commanded them shut until after the Sabbath and set his own servants at them, so that no burden would come in (Nehemiah 13:19). The class takes from this that the Sabbath begins when it gets dark and runs from evening to evening (Leviticus 23:32), not from sunrise. The merchants and sellers lodged outside Jerusalem once or twice, waiting to get in, and he testified against them: if they did it again he would lay hands on them (Nehemiah 13:20-21). This laying on of hands is not a blessing but a serious warning, and the merchants knew he was not joking; the teaching says our forefathers did not play games with the other nations, and from that time they came no more on the Sabbath. The captains add that the prophets of God were not soft, like the pastor who stays inside. Nehemiah commanded the Levites to cleanse themselves and keep the gates to sanctify the Sabbath day, and asked God to remember him and spare him according to the greatness of His mercy (Nehemiah 13:22).

name: Bigthan and Teresh
text: Two of the king’s chamberlains, of those which kept the door, being wroth and seeking to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. While Mordecai sat in the king’s gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s chamberlains who kept the door, were angry and sought to kill king Ahasuerus (Esther 2:21). Mordecai learned of it and told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai’s name; the matter was searched out, both men were put to death, and it was written in the chronicles (Esther 2:22-23; Rest of Esther 12:1-3). That record came up years later on a sleepless night and turned Haman’s plot back on his own head (Esther 6:1-11). Mordecai, a Benjamite carried away from Jerusalem with Jeconiah, raised Esther, his uncle’s daughter, as his own, and when she was made queen she still kept his charge not to show her people (Esther 2:5-7; Esther 2:10; Esther 2:20). The class teaches that they were cousins, not uncle and niece, and that they came of the mighty Benjamite line of Kish, the same line as Saul (1 Samuel 9:1-2). Mordecai served in the king’s court and sat in the king’s gate. In those days two of the king’s chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those who kept the door, were angry and sought to lay hands on king Ahasuerus (Esther 2:21): a coup against the king by men trusted to guard him. The Rest of Esther calls them Gabatha and Tharra, two eunuchs of the king and keepers of the palace, and the teaching explains that chamberlains were eunuchs, made so that they would not lie with the women they kept (Rest of Esther 12:1). Mordecai heard their devices and searched out their purposes before he spoke (Rest of Esther 12:2). The same chapter says that Haman the Agagite, already in great honour with the king, sought to harm Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs (Rest of Esther 12:6). The teaching draws the line from there: Greece was always trying to overthrow Persia, Haman’s aim was to translate the kingdom of the Persians to the Macedonians, and the two eunuchs were part of that plan (Rest of Esther 16:12-14). Asked in class whether Haman was plotting with them, the teacher answered that he possibly was. The thing was known to Mordecai, who told Esther the queen, and Esther told the king in Mordecai’s name; when the matter was searched out it was found true, both men were hanged on a tree, and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king (Esther 2:22-23). The Rest of Esther adds that the king examined them, that after they confessed they were strangled, and that he rewarded Mordecai with service in the court (Rest of Esther 12:3-5). The teaching holds the two records together: they were strangled, they were hung on a tree. Mordecai told, and the class says that is what a man is supposed to do. Israel in captivity was commanded to seek the peace of the city where they were carried and to pray for it, for in its peace they would have peace, which is why Mordecai kept the king safe (Jeremiah 29:7). These nations kept records, and so did Israel, and the study note marks that this deed of Mordecai’s would later help the whole nation. On the night Haman came to ask for Mordecai’s death, the king could not sleep, had the chronicles read, found that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, and learned that nothing had been done for him (Esther 6:1-3). The teaching calls the Lord a mastermind in how He moves, using even a king’s sleeplessness to set His purpose in motion. Haman, asked what should be done for the man the king wished to honour, described the highest honour he could think of, sure it was for himself, and was made to parade Mordecai through the city in it (Esther 6:4-11). What Haman planned for himself was given to the man he hated.

name: Haman the Agagite
text: Thinking scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone, and seeking to destroy all the Jews throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus; offering ten thousand talents of silver for their destruction; making a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai. King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite above all the princes, and when Mordecai would not bow to him Haman disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone and sought to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom (Esther 3:1-6). He cast Pur, offered ten thousand talents of silver, had letters sealed with the king’s ring to kill every Jew, young and old, in one day, and built a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai (Esther 3:7-15; Esther 5:9-14). His plot turned on him: he was made to honour Mordecai, was named by Esther as the enemy, and was hanged on his own gallows (Esther 6:1-13; Esther 7:1-10). After Mordecai had saved the king’s life, the king promoted Haman the Agagite and set his seat above all the princes, and the king’s servants bowed to him by the king’s command, but Mordecai would not bow (Esther 3:1-2). The class teaches that this is a descendant of the same Agag whom Saul spared when he was commanded to destroy Amalek, and whom Samuel hewed in pieces (1 Samuel 15:20); Agag came of Amalek, and Amalek of Esau (Genesis 36:12). Haman is an Amalekite, an Edomite, at the king’s right hand. The Rest of Esther calls him a Macedonian, a stranger to the Persian blood (Rest of Esther 16:10), and the teaching joins the two: a Macedonian Edomite, living among the Greeks but of the line of Amalek. When the servants told him that Mordecai, a Jew, would not bow, Haman was full of wrath and thought it too small a thing to lay hands on Mordecai alone; he sought to destroy all the Jews in the whole kingdom (Esther 3:3-6). The Purim teaching says one man’s vendetta became a sentence on a whole race. Why all of them? The class answers: remember what Saul was sent to do to Amalek. Haman’s people kept the records, and he knew Mordecai’s line of Kish was the line sent to destroy his forefathers. Esau forgave Jacob, but his children hold the grudge from generation to generation; they do not forget, and we do. They cast Pur, the lot, before Haman from Nisan to Adar, and he told the king there was a people scattered in every province whose laws differed from all people and who did not keep the king’s laws, so that it did not profit the king to let them live; he would pay ten thousand talents of silver for their destruction (Esther 3:7-9). His letter called Israel a malicious people with laws contrary to all nations, standing in the way of the uniting of the kingdoms (Rest of Esther 13:4-5). The class calls it the same slander used on our people today, and asks whether it is malicious to teach that a man should not kill, or for a woman to dress modestly; the nations call it so because when Israel keeps the commandments they cannot rule. The king gave him his ring, and letters went out to kill every Jew, young and old, little children and women, on the thirteenth of Adar and take their goods (Esther 3:10-15). With riches, rank, and a seat at the queen’s banquet, nothing satisfied him while Mordecai sat in the gate, and at the counsel of his wife Zeresh and his friends he built a gallows fifty cubits high for him (Esther 5:9-14). The study note marks that it was the wife’s idea: the enemy’s women are in league with the work against Israel. That night the king could not sleep, read in the chronicles how Mordecai had saved his life, and when Haman came in to ask for Mordecai’s death, asked him what should be done for the man the king wished to honour. Full of himself, Haman thought it meant him and named the king’s robe, horse, and crown, and he was ordered to do all of it for Mordecai the Jew (Esther 6:1-11). He hurried home mourning, and his wise men and his wife told him that if Mordecai was of the seed of the Jews, before whom he had begun to fall, he would not prevail but would surely fall (Esther 6:12-13). At Esther’s second banquet she asked for her life and her people’s, sold to be destroyed, and named the adversary: this wicked Haman (Esther 7:1-6). The king went out in wrath; Haman fell on the couch where Esther was, pleading for his life, and the king took it as an assault on the queen in his own house; they covered his face, and at Harbonah’s word about the gallows the king had him hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai (Esther 7:7-10). The study note calls this the Most High, a man of war, and how He moves. His house went to Esther and his ring to Mordecai (Esther 8:1-2), a second decree let the Jews stand for their lives (Esther 8:11), his ten sons were slain and hanged (Esther 9:10-14), and the days were kept as Purim, because the lot Haman cast to consume the Jews returned on his own head (Esther 9:24-26). The second letter says he meant to translate the kingdom of the Persians to the Macedonians, and the teaching calls him a sleeper cell in the Persian government (Rest of Esther 16:12-14).

name: Mordecai and Esther
text: Mordecai: bowing not to Haman, nor doing him reverence. Esther: gathering the Jews to fast three days, and going in to the king not according to the law: if I perish, I perish. Mordecai would not bow to Haman, and when Haman’s wrath became a decree against all the Jews he mourned in sackcloth, prayed, and charged Esther to go in to the king for her people (Esther 3:2; Esther 4:1-8; Rest of Esther 13:8-18). Esther feared the law against coming to the king uncalled, but at Mordecai’s word she had the Jews of Shushan fast three days with her, prayed, and went in against the law, ready to perish (Esther 4:10-16; Rest of Esther 14:1-19). God turned the king’s heart, Haman fell, the Jews were delivered, Purim was ordained, and Mordecai was made next to the king (Esther 7:10; Esther 9:1-32; Esther 10:3). All the king’s servants bowed to Haman, but Mordecai would not bow, for he had told them he was a Jew (Esther 3:2-4). The class teaches that it is not our custom to bow to any man, the same as the three Hebrew children would not bow to the image. Mordecai’s own prayer gives the reason: not contempt, pride, or a desire for glory; he could have kissed the soles of Haman’s feet for the salvation of Israel, but he would not set the glory of man above the glory of God (Rest of Esther 13:12-14). The teaching sets it beside our people at work today, where the co-worker asks in front of everyone why you dress as you do and keep the Sabbath, and then goes to the supervisor. When Mordecai learned of the decree he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and cried out through the city, and in every province there was mourning, fasting, and weeping (Esther 4:1-3). This was a law passed to kill every Israelite, and the teaching warns that such laws will be passed again. He prayed that the whole world is in God’s power and that if He has appointed to save Israel no man can stand against it, and all Israel cried out with him (Rest of Esther 13:8-18). He refused the clothes Esther sent and gave her messenger a copy of the decree, charging her to go to the king for her people (Esther 4:4-8). Esther answered that whoever came to the king uncalled died unless he held out the golden sceptre, and she had not been called in thirty days (Esther 4:10-11); the study note says she made an excuse. Mordecai would not take a weak answer: she would not escape in the king’s house more than the other Jews; if she kept silent, deliverance would come from another place and she and her father’s house would perish; and who could say she had not come to the kingdom for such a time as this (Esther 4:13-14). The deliverance of Israel cannot be held back, and the teaching applies it to anyone slothful in the work: the Lord will raise up somebody else. Esther had all the Jews in Shushan fast three days, she and her maidens with them, and resolved to go in against the law, and if she perished, she perished (Esther 4:15-17). She put off her royal apparel for mourning, covered her head with ashes, confessed that Israel was given to its enemies for worshipping their gods, asked for boldness and eloquent speech, and told God she abhorred the sign of her high estate (Rest of Esther 14:1-19). The teaching notes she was raised right, taught from her youth how the Lord took Israel from among all people. On the third day she put on her royal apparel and stood in the inner court; the king looked on her fiercely and she fainted, and God changed his spirit into mildness, so that he held out the golden sceptre and comforted her (Esther 5:1-2; Rest of Esther 15:1-16). At her second banquet she named Haman, and he was hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai (Esther 7:3-10). The king gave Esther the house of Haman and Mordecai his ring, and a second decree let the Jews in every city stand for their lives (Esther 8:1-11). Mordecai went out in royal blue and white with a great crown of gold, and many of the people of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell on them (Esther 8:15-17): a picture, the study note says, of the time when the fear of Israel will be on all nations. The day their enemies hoped to rule them was turned the other way, and no man could stand before them (Esther 9:1-2). Mordecai and Esther wrote to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar every year as Purim, days turned from sorrow to joy, and the Jews bound it on their seed so that it would not fail (Esther 9:20-32). The teaching reminds that Purim is a memorial of the destruction of Israel’s enemies and of the Lord’s deliverance, not a day about presents (Rest of Esther 16:21-23). Mordecai was made next to the king, great among the Jews, seeking the wealth of his people and speaking peace to all his seed (Esther 10:3), and he confessed that God had done all these things (Rest of Esther 10:4-5). What was written before was written for our learning (Romans 15:4): days of sorrow now, and joy coming for those who stay in the commandments.

name: Daniel
text: Purposing in his heart not to defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat nor with the wine which he drank; kneeling and praying three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, as he did aforetime, after the decree was signed. Daniel, of the king’s seed of Judah, was carried to Babylon with the best of Israel’s youth to be trained for the king’s service, and he resolved not to defile himself with the king’s meat and wine; God gave him favour, and he and his companions were found ten times wiser than all the king’s wise men (Daniel 1:1-20). Under Darius, when his rivals could find no fault in him except concerning the law of his God, he kept praying three times a day toward Jerusalem after the decree was signed, and God shut the lions’ mouths (Daniel 6:1-23). He prospered under Darius and Cyrus and was told he would stand in his lot at the end of the days (Daniel 6:28; Daniel 12:13). When Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem he carried off vessels of the house of God, as the prophets had warned, and Isaiah had told Hezekiah that his sons would be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (Daniel 1:1-2; 2 Kings 20:16-18). The king had the master of his eunuchs bring children of the king’s seed and the princes, without blemish and skilled in wisdom, to be taught the tongue of the Chaldeans and fed from the king’s table (Daniel 1:3-5). The class teaches that Babylon did not take any old body; they took the best and most educated to build up their kingdom, and Esau did the same when he took the best of our people and put them in North America. The study note adds that our people still serve in governments and are used to build a system that is not their own, often assimilated and well rewarded for it. The prince of the eunuchs renamed Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah as Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Daniel 1:6-7), part of the assimilation; the study notes compare it to Hadassah made Esther, and the teaching to our fathers in slavery whose names were changed. But Daniel resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s meat or his wine, and asked the prince of the eunuchs to spare him (Daniel 1:8). God brought him into favour, for the Lord causes the enemy to treat His remnant well in the time of evil (Jeremiah 15:11). The officer feared for his head if they looked worse than the others, so Daniel asked for a ten day proof on pulse, which the teaching explains as vegetables, the green herb given for meat in the beginning (Genesis 1:29), and water; at the end they looked fairer and fuller than all who ate the king’s meat (Daniel 1:9-16). Under Darius, Daniel was first of three presidents over a hundred and twenty princes, preferred because an excellent spirit was in him, and when the others sought occasion against him they found no error or fault (Daniel 6:1-4). The study note says this is how our forefathers rolled, keeping a clear conscience before God and men (Acts 24:16), and the class says he lived up to a name, integrity. They could find nothing against him except concerning the law of his God, so they had Darius sign a decree that no one petition any god or man but the king for thirty days (Daniel 6:5-9). When Daniel knew it was signed he went home, and with his windows open toward Jerusalem he knelt three times a day and prayed and gave thanks, as he had done before (Daniel 6:10). God gave the four children knowledge and skill in all learning, and Daniel understanding in all visions and dreams; the king found them ten times better than all his magicians and astrologers (Daniel 1:17-20). The verse by verse teaching says the Most High gave them that understanding and they could not be outdone, as with Moses before the magicians, and points to Susanna, where young Daniel exposed the lying elders (Susanna 1:45-62). He continued to the first year of Cyrus (Daniel 1:21). Cast into the den, he told the king that God had sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths, because he was found innocent, and he came up unharmed because he trusted in his God (Daniel 6:16-23). The study note joins to this the account of Habakkuk carried by an angel with food for Daniel in the den, for God does not forsake those who seek and love Him (Bel and the Dragon 1:33-39). His accusers went into the den in his place (Daniel 6:24), for when a man’s ways please the Lord He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). Darius commanded all his dominion to tremble before the God of Daniel, and Daniel prospered under Darius and Cyrus the Persian (Daniel 6:25-28); a reference work read in class calls him one of the few well known men of the Bible of whom nothing negative is written. Daniel was told that he would rest, and at the end of the days stand in his lot (Daniel 12:13). The study note reads rest as his death and the promise as the Most High sending these leaders back to us, and the verse by verse class teaches that Daniel is on the earth in the time of the end, raising up his people and understanding what was sealed from him, though no one knows who he is.

name: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego
text: Not serving the king’s gods nor worshipping the golden image which he had set up; not careful to answer the king in this matter: but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods. Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image in the plain of Dura and commanded every people to fall down and worship it at the sound of the music, on pain of the burning fiery furnace (Daniel 3:1-6). Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, whom he had set over the province, would not bow, and told the raging king that their God was able to deliver them, and that even if He did not, they would not serve his gods (Daniel 3:12-18). They were cast bound into a furnace heated seven times over, walked unhurt in the fire with a fourth, and came out without the smell of fire; the king blessed their God and promoted them (Daniel 3:19-30). Nebuchadnezzar made an image of gold sixty cubits high, about a hundred and ten feet by the class’s reckoning, and gathered the princes, governors, judges, treasurers, sheriffs, and rulers to its dedication (Daniel 3:1-3). The study note likens it to the ribbon cutting at a new monument, and the Agree Together class calls it a one world religion, the same thing they are trying to do today, reading in class how evangelical pastors dedicated a towering gold statue of Donald Trump in Miami: Daniel 3 coming to life. When the music sounded all were to fall down and worship or be cast into the furnace (Daniel 3:4-6); the study note compares it to the national anthem at ball games, hat off and hand over heart, a form of worshipping the image of the eagle. The class sets it beside the image the whole world is made to worship in the last days (Revelation 13:6-8). Certain Chaldeans accused the three men (Daniel 3:8-12). They were high up in the government, over the affairs of the province, and still refused; the verse by verse teaching contrasts the believer who goes to the job’s Christmas party so as not to be fired. The study note gives the reason plainly: they did not bow because of the law, which forbids other gods, graven images, and bowing to them (Exodus 20:3-5). Brought before the king in his rage, they were asked what god could save them from his hand (Daniel 3:13-15), talking big and challenging our God, though the teaching recalls he had already confessed Daniel’s God as a God of gods (Daniel 2:47). They answered that they had no need to answer him: their God was able to deliver them from the furnace and from his hand, but if not, they still would not serve his gods nor worship the image (Daniel 3:16-18). Whatever happened, they were never bowing. The king had the furnace heated seven times more and his mightiest men bind them in their coats and cast them in, and the flame slew the men who took them up (Daniel 3:19-22). The Song of the Three Holy Children records Azariah’s prayer in the fire, confessing that all that came on the nation was true judgment for its sins, and that they had been given to lawless enemies and an unjust king (Song of the Three Holy Children 1:1-9). The class notes that even facing death they prayed for the whole nation, and that high office in the king’s government never made them call the enemy a friend. The flame streamed forty-nine cubits above the furnace and burned the Chaldeans it found about it, but the angel of the Lord came down, drove the flame out, and made the midst of the furnace like a moist whistling wind (Song of the Three Holy Children 1:23-27). The teaching says the fire did not simply get out of control: fire is a spirit created for vengeance (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-29), and the Lord killed those men. The king saw four men loose and unhurt in the fire, and the fourth looked like the Son of God (Daniel 3:24-25). The Agree Together class says the translators understood the fourth was Christ; the verse by verse teaching speaks of the angel who came down into the furnace, and the king himself said their God had sent His angel (Daniel 3:28). The fire had not singed their hair or changed their coats, and they did not even smell of smoke (Daniel 3:26-27). The king blessed their God, who delivered the servants who trusted in Him and yielded their bodies rather than serve any god but their own, decreed that anyone who spoke against their God be cut in pieces, since no other god can deliver like this, and promoted them in the province (Daniel 3:28-30). The study note says he understood then that we had our own God, and that when the nations get jacked up they come to know who has the true and living God; the Most High is in the midst of Israel, and His people shall never be ashamed (Joel 2:27). The class warns that Nebuchadnezzar did not hold to it but went back to his idols, and that these events will occur again. The teaching’s charge is that nothing should stop us from keeping the laws of God.

name: The Chaldeans who accused the Jews
text: Coming near and accusing the Jews to the king, that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego regarded not the king, served not his gods, nor worshipped the golden image, to have them cast into the furnace for keeping the second commandment. When all the peoples fell down before the golden image, certain Chaldeans came near and accused the Jews, reminding the king of his decree and naming Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, the men he had set over the province, as refusing his gods and his image (Daniel 3:8-12). The three were cast into the furnace and came out unharmed while the flame slew the men about it, and the king blessed their God and decreed that anyone who spoke against Him be cut in pieces (Daniel 3:19-30). The class teaches that the Lord killed the Chaldeans about the furnace. When the music sounded and every people, nation, and language fell down before the image, certain Chaldeans came near and accused the Jews (Daniel 3:7-8). The verse by verse teaching says they accused them because the righteous would not bend themselves down and worship. They reminded the king of his own decree and its penalty, then named Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, whom he himself had set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, as men who did not regard him, did not serve his gods, and did not worship the golden image (Daniel 3:9-12). The teaching renders their message: these men you have set up are not listening to you, they are a poor example, and you have to do something. The only fault they could bring was obedience. The study note says the reason the three did not bow was according to the law, which forbids other gods, graven images, and bowing down to them (Exodus 20:3-5). The Agree Together class calls the image a one world religion, the same thing they are trying to do today, and the accusers were its enforcers. The same kind of law came again under the Greeks, when it was no longer lawful to keep the Sabbath or profess to be a Jew and whoever would not conform to the manners of the Gentiles was put to death (2 Maccabees 6:6-9); the class says such a law was passed in France and used to dissolve the school there, and warns our people not to think it cannot happen here. Full of fury, Nebuchadnezzar had the furnace heated seven times more than usual, and the flame slew the men who took the three up to it (Daniel 3:19-22). The Song of the Three Holy Children records that the flame streamed out and burned the Chaldeans it found about the furnace, while the angel of the Lord made the midst of it like a moist whistling wind for the three (Song of the Three Holy Children 1:23-27). The teaching says the fire did not simply get out of control: fire is a spirit created for vengeance, and the Lord killed those Chaldeans; the king, who had just seen his own men burned up, did not care, for to him they were only soldiers (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-29). The charge ended in the opposite of its aim. The men it named came out unsinged, without even the smell of smoke, and the king blessed their God, decreed that anyone of any people who spoke amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be cut in pieces and his house made a dunghill, and promoted the three in the province (Daniel 3:26-30). The study note says that when the nations get jacked up they come to know who has the true and living God. The Agree Together class warns that Nebuchadnezzar went back to his idols and that these events will occur again. The decree hung over anyone who spoke against the God of Israel, and the Chaldeans who brought the charge the Lord had already killed in the flame.

name: Nebuchadnezzar
text: Pride: is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?. Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a great tree hewn down and left a stump till seven times passed, and Daniel told him the tree was he, counselling him to leave his sins by doing righteousness and showing mercy to the poor (Daniel 4:4-27). A year later he boasted of the great Babylon he had built by his own power, and while the word was in his mouth the kingdom departed from him; he was driven out to eat grass as oxen until he knew that the Most High rules (Daniel 4:28-33). At the end of the days his understanding and his kingdom returned, and he praised the King of heaven, who can bring down the proud (Daniel 4:34-37). Nebuchadnezzar proclaimed to all nations the signs the Most High had worked toward him. Resting and flourishing in his palace, he dreamed and was afraid, and none of his wise men could interpret it until Daniel came, renamed Belteshazzar after the king’s god (Daniel 4:1-9). He saw a tree reaching to heaven that fed all flesh, and a watcher, a holy one, commanded it hewn down, its stump bound with iron and brass and a beast’s heart given it till seven times passed, so that the living would know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men and sets over it the basest of men (Daniel 4:10-17). The study note says that is what we see today, the basest of men ruling the earth, and the class adds that the king acknowledged he was that base man whom God had set up. Daniel, astonished for an hour, told him the tree was he: he would be driven from men to eat grass as oxen until he knew the Most High rules, and the stump meant his kingdom would be kept for him (Daniel 4:18-26). He counselled him to leave his sins by doing righteousness and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor (Daniel 4:27), and one class teaches that the poor were the Israelites. A 2026 class on pride notes that Daniel warned him a year in advance and he did not listen. The teaching traces the pattern: he had confessed Daniel’s God after the first dream, then set up the image and threw the three Hebrews into the furnace; he kept bucking against the Lord. At the end of twelve months, walking in his palace, he boasted that this great Babylon was built by his own power for the honour of his majesty (Daniel 4:28-30). The study note calls him very proud and boastful, and the class says there was no recognition of the Most High even after the dream; he was still delusional. The same class asks whether you think there is no God listening when you run your mouth. While the word was in his mouth a voice from heaven said the kingdom had departed from him, and the same hour he was driven from men, ate grass as oxen, and was wet with the dew of heaven till his hair grew like eagles’ feathers and his nails like birds’ claws (Daniel 4:31-33). The teaching says the Lord made him lose his mind, and ties it to Titus, whom the Lord likewise judged while he was speaking. At the end of the days he lifted his eyes to heaven, his understanding returned, and he blessed the Most High, before whom all the inhabitants of the earth count as nothing and whom no one can hinder (Daniel 4:34-35), for all nations before Him are counted less than nothing (Isaiah 40:17). His reason, his glory, and his kingdom returned, and he praised the King of heaven, who is able to humble the proud (Daniel 4:36-37); the Most High brings low and lifts up (1 Samuel 2:7). The study note says Israel already understood this, but the heathen had to learn it by being jacked up. The teaching calls it divine intervention, and observes that the dark nations keep some sense of a God above them, while Edom will not be humbled this way but has to be destroyed. Daniel later set this very judgment before Belshazzar (Daniel 5:18-21). The class sums it up: you only rule because God put you there, so humble yourself before He draws the picture for you.

name: Belshazzar
text: Drinking wine from the gold and silver vessels taken out of the temple of the house of God at Jerusalem, with his princes, his wives, and his concubines, and praising the gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone; lifting himself up against the Lord of heaven, having known how his father was humbled. At a feast for a thousand lords, Belshazzar had the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple at Jerusalem brought in, and he, his princes, his wives, and his concubines drank from them and praised gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone (Daniel 5:1-4). A hand wrote on the wall, and Daniel read it: God had counted out his kingdom and ended it, he was weighed and found lacking, and his kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:5-28). That same night Belshazzar was slain, and Darius the Mede took the kingdom (Daniel 5:30-31). Belshazzar the king, not Belteshazzar, which is Daniel, made a great feast, and while tasting the wine commanded that the vessels of the temple be brought so that his lords, wives, and concubines might drink from them, and they praised gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone (Daniel 5:1-4). The study note recalls that even before the captivity Israel was warned it would see these gods of silver and gold in Babylon and was told not to fear or worship them (Baruch 6:3-6). The class says they were mocking the vessels stolen from the temple of the Lord. The text calls Nebuchadnezzar his father; the classes teach that Belshazzar was a later descendant, the margin reading father as grandfather, and one class names him the son of Nabonidus, the king then reigning. Daniel set his sin before him. The Most High had given Nebuchadnezzar his kingdom and majesty, so that he slew whom he would and set up whom he would, the same power, the teaching says, that America has; but when his heart was lifted up in pride he was put down from his throne and driven out until he knew that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men (Daniel 5:18-21). Belshazzar knew all this and did not humble his heart, but lifted himself against the Lord of heaven, drank from His vessels, and praised gods that neither see nor hear, and did not glorify the God who holds his breath in His hand (Daniel 5:22-23). The teaching puts it to him plainly: you knew about your father being driven out of his kingdom and losing his mind, and you still chose to be arrogant. The study note adds that gods of silver and gold cannot even save themselves (Baruch 6:12-16). In the same hour the fingers of a man’s hand wrote on the plaster of the palace wall, and the king’s face changed, his joints were loosed, and his knees knocked together (Daniel 5:5-6). The study note pictures him sitting back with his lords, wives, and concubines having a good time when a hand starts writing on the wall, and he is terrified out of everything. None of his wise men could read it, and he offered scarlet, a chain of gold, and the third place in the kingdom (Daniel 5:7-9); the class explains the third place, since Nabonidus ruled first and Belshazzar second as co-regent. The queen told him of Daniel, in whom was the spirit of the holy gods (Daniel 5:10-12), which the class identifies as the Holy Spirit, the spirit of truth given to those who keep the commandments (John 14:15-17). Daniel, old now after the seventy years in Babylon, told him to keep his gifts (Daniel 5:13-17). Daniel read the writing: God had counted out the days of the kingdom and ended it; the king was weighed and found lacking; his kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:24-28). The class reads it as the end of Babylon’s seventy years: your time is up. Belshazzar clothed Daniel in scarlet and proclaimed him third ruler, and that night Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans was slain, and Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old (Daniel 5:29-31). The study note marks that the kingdom passed to the Medes and Persians immediately after the interpretation. The teaching says it was an inside job, for the Medes had long been allied with Babylon and lived among them, so Babylon was taken rather than burned; the Babylon prophesied to burn is the one still to come, the one we live in now.

name: Daniel’s accusers
text: Seeking occasion against Daniel and finding none; procuring a decree by the law of the Medes and Persians that no man petition any god or man for thirty days save the king, to take him in the law of his God; assembling to find him praying and pressing the king to cast him to the lions. The presidents and princes under Darius sought occasion against Daniel and found no fault in him except concerning the law of his God, so they had the king sign an unchangeable decree that no one petition any god or man but the king for thirty days (Daniel 6:4-9). They found Daniel praying toward Jerusalem as before, reported him, and pressed the king until Daniel was cast to the lions (Daniel 6:10-17). God shut the lions’ mouths, and the king had the accusers, their children, and their wives cast into the den, where the lions broke their bones before they reached the bottom (Daniel 6:22-24). Darius set a hundred and twenty princes over the kingdom and three presidents over them, Daniel first, and thought to set him over the whole realm because an excellent spirit was in him (Daniel 6:1-3). The presidents and princes sought occasion against him concerning the kingdom and found none, because he was faithful and no error or fault was in him (Daniel 6:4). The class renders their thinking: we cannot find fault with his work, so we will use his religion against him. The study note says they really hated Daniel and knew the only way to find fault was concerning the law of his God (Daniel 6:5). They came to the king claiming that all the rulers had agreed, and persuaded him to sign a decree that anyone who asked a petition of any god or man but the king for thirty days be cast into the den of lions, by the law of the Medes and Persians, which does not change (Daniel 6:6-9). The teaching explains that in the Persian empire a decree once sent out could not be reversed, and the king’s counsellors held him to it. They gathered, found Daniel praying and making supplication to his God, reminded the king of his decree, and reported that Daniel, of the captivity of Judah, did not regard him or his decree (Daniel 6:10-13). The king laboured till sundown to deliver him, but they pressed him that no decree of the Medes and Persians could be changed (Daniel 6:14-15). The class reads beside this the account in Bel and the Dragon, where the people of Babylon said the king had become a Jew and threatened to destroy him and his house unless he delivered Daniel to them (Bel and the Dragon 1:28-30). The king, displeased with himself, commanded Daniel cast in, saying that the God he served continually would deliver him, and the den was sealed (Daniel 6:16-17). The king passed the night fasting, with no music and no sleep, and hurried to the den at dawn; Daniel answered that God had sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths, because he was found innocent before God and had done the king no hurt (Daniel 6:18-22). The class sets beside it the Bel and the Dragon account, in which seven lions were kept hungry so they would devour Daniel, the prophet Habakkuk was carried by an angel to feed him in the den, and the king cried that the God of Daniel is great and there is none other (Bel and the Dragon 1:31-41). Then the king commanded that the men who had accused Daniel be cast into the den, they, their children, and their wives, and the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones before they came to the bottom (Daniel 6:24). The class says the lions that had been held back from Daniel devoured those who set him up. The law of the false witness is to do to him as he thought to do to his brother (Deuteronomy 19:16-19), and the study note on that law says that whoever falsely accuses a man of a crime worthy of death is put to death, because that is what he intended for his neighbour, and that false witnesses arising among our own people were part of why the nation fell into captivity. When a man’s ways please the Lord, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). Darius then wrote to every people that in all his dominion men should tremble before the God of Daniel, the living God whose kingdom shall not be destroyed (Daniel 6:25-27).

name: The priests who despised the Name
text: Offering polluted bread upon the altar, and the blind, the lame, and the sick for sacrifice; saying the table of the Lord is contemptible and its service a weariness; departing out of the way, causing many to stumble at the law, and being partial in the law. While Nehemiah was away with the king, the priests despised the name of the Lord, offering polluted bread and blind, lame, and sick animals on His altar and calling His table contemptible (Malachi 1:6-13). The Lord sent Malachi to rebuke them: He would curse their blessings, and because they had left the way, caused many to stumble at the law, corrupted the covenant of Levi, and been partial in the law, He made them contemptible and base before all the people (Malachi 2:1-9). The classes place Malachi in the years of Nehemiah’s absence: when Nehemiah went back to the king, the Lord raised up Malachi to keep the people in line until he returned, and with the governor gone the priests went back to doing as they pleased (Nehemiah 13:6). Malachi opens with the Lord’s love for Israel: He loved Jacob and hated Esau, laid Edom’s mountains waste, and though Edom said it would return and build, He would throw it down, and it would be called the border of wickedness, a people the Lord is angry with for ever (Malachi 1:1-5). The teaching reads Edom’s rebuilding as Europe rising to power, and the border of wickedness as the source of the confusion spread in the earth. Esau dwelt in mount Seir (Genesis 36:8), and the study note joins it to Obadiah, where the pride of Edom’s heart deceived him (Obadiah 1:3). The Lord reminded the priests that sons honour fathers and servants their masters, and asked where His honour and His fear were, since they despised His name; and they asked how they had despised it (Malachi 1:6). They offered polluted bread on His altar and said His table was contemptible; they brought the blind, the lame, and the sick for sacrifice, and the Lord told them to offer that to their governor and see whether he would accept them (Malachi 1:7-8). The classes say the governor was Nehemiah, who with his men would have laid hands on anyone who brought him such a thing. They called the service a weariness and brought the torn, the lame, and the sick, and the Lord cursed the deceiver who vowed a male of his flock and sacrificed a blemished thing (Malachi 1:12-14). The tithing class adds that they were giving lame animals to Levi when the Lord required the best. The teaching says that during the Persian captivity many of the chief priests and leaders made leagues with the other nations and caused the people to sin. The priest was to keep knowledge and teach the law as the Lord’s messenger, but they had left the way, caused many to stumble at the law, and corrupted the covenant of Levi (Malachi 2:7-8). Judah dealt treacherously and married the daughter of a strange god, and the class teaches that the wife of his youth is the woman of his own people, whom Israel was putting away for the women of other nations (Malachi 2:11-16). The Lord told the priests that if they would not take it to heart to give glory to His name He would send a curse on them and curse their blessings, and He had cursed them already; He would corrupt their seed and spread the dung of their feasts on their faces (Malachi 2:1-3). The class teaches that giving glory to His name means the offerings on His altar, going back to the first chapter, not saying the name with some special pronunciation. His covenant with Levi had been one of life and peace, when the law of truth was in Levi’s mouth and he turned many away from iniquity (Malachi 2:4-6). But because they had not kept His ways and had been partial in the law, He made them contemptible and base before all the people (Malachi 2:9). The classes teach that this debasement is seen in Levi today, living in base conditions in Haiti, the seed corrupted and dung spread on their faces. When Nehemiah returned he chased away the high priest’s grandson who had married Sanballat’s daughter and asked God to remember those who had defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites (Nehemiah 13:28-29), and the classes read Malachi’s rebuke alongside that cleansing: Levi had been partial in the law.

name: Judah robbing God in tithes and offerings
text: Going away from the Lord’s ordinances and not keeping them; robbing God in tithes and offerings, so that there was no meat in His house and the Levites fled every one to his field. From the days of their fathers Judah had gone away from the Lord’s ordinances, and when He called them to return and they asked how, He answered that they had robbed Him in tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:7-8). The whole nation was under a curse for it; He told them to bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there might be food in His house, and He would open the windows of heaven, rebuke the devourer, and bless the land (Malachi 3:9-12). In Nehemiah’s day the portions of the Levites had not been given, and the Levites had fled to their fields (Nehemiah 13:10-12). The Lord does not change, and so the sons of Jacob were not consumed; from the days of their fathers they had gone away from His ordinances, and He told them to return and He would return to them, but they asked how they should return (Malachi 3:6-7). He asked whether a man would rob God, for they had robbed Him, and when they asked how, He said in tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:8). The captains teach that the tithe of the law was the increase of the seed, the corn, the wine, the oil, and the firstlings of the herd and flock, eaten before the Lord in the place He chose, which was Jerusalem; if the way was too far it could be turned into money, but that money was spent in Jerusalem on food again, and the Levite within the gates was not to be forsaken, for he had no inheritance (Deuteronomy 14:22-29; 2 Chronicles 6:6). The class teaches that the robbery was not taking care of Levi. Levi had no land and served at the altar, atoning for the nation’s sins, and the tithes were his portion, but the other tribes were not showing charity to their brothers the Levites, and were giving lame animals when the Lord required the best. Nehemiah met exactly this: the people had sworn to bring the firstfruits and the tithes to the chambers of the house of God for the Levites (Nehemiah 10:37), yet on his return the Levites’ portions had not been given, so the Levites and singers had fled every one to his field; he contended with the rulers, asked why the house of God was forsaken, set the Levites back in their place, brought the tithe into the treasuries, and made faithful men treasurers over it (Nehemiah 13:10-13). They were cursed with a curse, the whole nation, because they had robbed Him (Malachi 3:9). The class explains the curse through the law: when Levi is not cared for, there is no rain, the locust consumes what is sown, and the worm eats the vines (Deuteronomy 28:38-39). The Lord told them to bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there might be food in His house, and to prove Him (Malachi 3:10). The captains show that the storehouse held the increase of corn, wine, and oil (2 Chronicles 32:28), food and not a bank account, and that the windows of heaven are the rain, as at the flood (Genesis 7:11), the good treasure the Lord opens to give rain in its season and bless the work of the hand (Deuteronomy 28:12). He would rebuke the devourer for their sake, so that it would not destroy the fruit of their ground nor the vine drop its fruit early, and all nations would call them blessed (Malachi 3:11-12). The captains teach that the pastors misuse this scripture to shame their congregations into giving money, when it speaks of food for Levi in Jerusalem. They add that the tithe cannot be kept that way now: Israel is scattered among all people, the Lord Himself will set them in their own land again, and the priesthood has been changed out of Levi to Judah in Christ (Deuteronomy 28:64; Isaiah 14:1; Hebrews 7:11-14). The nation that neglected the house of God and its servants stood under the curse until it returned, and the promise to return was open to it (Malachi 3:7).

name: Tobit
text: Walking in truth and justice all his days; alms, tithes, and burying the dead of his people at the risk of his own life. Tobit was carried into Assyria with the tribe of Nephthali, and while his tribe sacrificed to the calf he alone kept the feasts at Jerusalem and brought the firstfruits and the tenths, giving the third year tithe to the orphans as his grandmother Debora had taught him (Tobit 1:3-8). In Nineveh he clothed the naked and buried the brethren the king had killed and left lying about the walls, and for it he was informed on, hunted, and stripped of everything he owned (Tobit 1:16-20). After one such burial he slept beside his courtyard wall and lost his sight, and the affliction stood until Raphael was sent, who told him that his prayers and his burials had been carried up before the Holy One (Tobit 2:1-10; Tobit 12:12-15). Tobit says of himself that he walked all the days of his life in the way of truth and justice and did many alms deeds to his brethren (Tobit 1:3). His whole tribe revolted to the calf, and he alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts with the firstfruits and the tenths, giving the first tenth to the sons of Aaron, spending the second at Jerusalem, and giving the third to those it was owed to, as Debora his father’s mother had commanded him, because he had been left an orphan himself (Tobit 1:4-8). That third year tithe is the provision the law names for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:22-29), and the teaching carries it across: our fathers stopped paying what belonged to them, and the record says we are still in captivity and subject to payments because of it (Baruch 3:8). A man keeping that tithe in a strange land is keeping the nation. In Nineveh he gave his bread to the hungry and his clothes to the naked, and when he saw any of his nation dead or cast about the walls he buried him, including the men Sennacherib had killed in his wrath and thrown out (Tobit 1:16-18). The nation has a law on this: wherever the dead are found they are to be taken up and buried (2 Esdras 2:23), with tears over the dead, the body covered according to the custom, and the burial not neglected (Ecclesiasticus 38:16). The teaching sets it beside our own captivity, where our dead were left hanging and displayed on purpose. To present the body a living sacrifice is not a private religion, it is a life spent on the nation (Romans 12:1). A Ninevite reported him, he was sought to be put to death, and all his goods were taken by force (Tobit 1:19-20), just as the captivity warns that they will spoil those that fear God and take their goods, and then the chosen are tried as gold in the fire (2 Esdras 16:71-73). At Pentecost he sent his son to bring in a poor man of their brethren who was mindful of the Lord, which is the wisdom of knowing to whom a man does good (Tobit 2:1-2; Ecclesiasticus 12:1-4). Word came instead that one of the nation had been strangled and cast into the marketplace; he left his meal untasted, took up the body, and ate afterward in heaviness because the prophet had said the feasts would be turned into mourning (Tobit 2:3-6). His neighbours mocked him, and that night the sparrows blinded him and the physicians could not help (Tobit 2:7-10). Blind, he still kept order in his house, telling his wife to take back a kid she had been given rather than eat what might be stolen. She answered him by naming his alms and his righteous deeds and telling him that all his works were known (Tobit 2:11-14). Blessed is the man that considers the poor, for the Lord will deliver him in the time of trouble (Psalms 41:1), and the righteous considers the cause of the poor while the wicked does not care to know it (Proverbs 29:7). Out of that same mind he charged his son to be mindful of the Lord all his days, to give alms of his substance, and not to turn his face from any poor man, because alms deliver from death (Tobit 4:5-11). Raphael told them that it is honourable to reveal the works of God, that prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness, and that it is better to give alms than to lay up gold (Tobit 12:6-9). Treasure laid up according to the commandments brings more profit than gold, and alms stored up deliver from affliction and fight against the enemy better than a mighty shield and a strong spear (Ecclesiasticus 29:11-13). Then he told Tobit why he had come: when Tobit prayed, and when he buried the dead, and when he did not delay to rise up and leave his dinner to go and cover a body, the angel was with him and carried the remembrance of those prayers before the Holy One (Tobit 12:12-15). He charged them to praise God and not to be slack in it, and to write everything in a book, which is why the account is here at all (Romans 15:4). Tobit received his sight and saw his son (Tobit 11:7-15). At the end he told Tobias to keep the law and the commandments, to show himself merciful and just, and to leave Nineveh because what the prophet Jonas spoke would surely come to pass; his son obeyed him, departed, and lived to hear of the destruction of the city (Tobit 14:1-2; Tobit 14:11-15).

name: Aman, who ensnared Achiacharus
text: Treachery against the man who brought him up. Achiacharus was Tobit’s brother’s son, cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of the accounts under the king at Nineveh, and it was he who interceded for Tobit and brought him home, and who nourished him while he was blind (Tobit 1:21-22; Tobit 2:10). Tobit’s dying counsel holds up one case against that kindness: remember how Aman handled Achiacharus who brought him up, how out of light he brought him into darkness, and how he was rewarded for it (Tobit 14:10). Achiacharus was saved, and the man who laid the snare fell into it and perished. The record first shows Achiacharus in office. He was Anael’s son, Tobit’s brother’s son, and the king set him next to himself as cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of the accounts, and he entreated for Tobit so that Tobit could return to Nineveh after his goods had been seized and his life sought for burying the dead (Tobit 1:21-22). When Tobit was blinded, it was Achiacharus who nourished him until he went into Elymais (Tobit 2:10). Everything the man had, Aman had from him. That is the weight of the charge. The teaching on this chapter puts it in one line: you do good and good follows you, you do evil and evil follows you. The injury was not hostility between strangers; it was the return made for the care that had raised him. Tobit sets the case down at the very end of his life, in the middle of his charge to his son to keep the law and the commandments and to show himself merciful (Tobit 14:9-10). He does not tell the story for its own sake. He tells it as the counterweight to the instruction, because a son who has just been told to be merciful and just needs also to be told what it looks like when a man takes kindness and turns it into an opportunity. The whole book has been arguing that alms and righteousness are what a man is measured by, and here is the man who was fed by another man’s righteousness and used it against him. Aman brought his benefactor out of light into darkness, and the reward came back on him: Achiacharus was saved, and the other had his reward, for he went down into darkness (Tobit 14:10). Tobit names the pattern twice over in the same breath, setting Manasses, who gave alms and escaped the snare of death, beside Aman, who fell into the snare and perished (Tobit 14:10). The same two ends are what the wisdom of the fathers teaches about a pit dug for another man and a net laid in secret (Proverbs 26:27; Psalms 35:7-8), and the deliverance of Achiacharus is of a piece with the deliverance of Tobit himself, who was restored and whose nephew came to rejoice with him (Tobit 11:18). Tobit draws the conclusion himself and gives it to his son as the last thing he says before he dies: consider what alms do, and how righteousness delivers (Tobit 14:11). The teaching on the chapter reads the case exactly that way, as a father’s final advice rather than a story about a villain. The betrayer did not obtain what he intended. The man he wronged lived, the snare took its own maker, and the lesson set beside the charge to keep the law and be merciful is that a man is not saved by his position at the king’s right hand but by what he does with the mercy he has received.

name: Holofernes
text: Making Nebuchadnezzar a god; blasphemy against the God of Israel; lust and drunkenness. Nabuchodonosor sent his chief captain Holofernes with a great host to bring every nation under him and to destroy all their gods, so that he alone should be called god (Judith 2:4-13; Judith 3:8). When Achior warned him that this people is only overcome when it sins against its own God, he answered that Nabuchodonosor alone is god and gave Achior over to the men of Bethulia (Judith 6:2-4). He besieged the city, and the widow Judith came down to his camp; he drank more wine at her banquet than he had ever drunk in one day, and she took his own sword and struck off his head (Judith 12:16-20; Judith 13:6-10). The teaching sets this campaign in the Persian period, after the return. The temple was standing and newly sanctified, the people were lately gathered out of the Babylonian captivity, and Joacim, the son of Jeshua the son of Josedec, was high priest and wrote to the men of Bethulia to keep the passages of the hill country (Judith 4:1-8; Nehemiah 12:10; Nehemiah 12:26). The king had just broken Arphaxad in the plain of Ragau, taken Ecbatane, and turned its beauty into shame, and out of that victory he commissioned Holofernes to take vengeance on all the earth (Judith 1:13-15; Judith 2:1-6). The commission was not tribute only. Every place was to destroy its own gods so that all nations should serve Nabuchodonosor and all tongues call on him as a god (Judith 3:8). That is the charge: a man made the instrument of turning worship itself over to a king. Achior, the captain of the Ammonites, gave him the history of the nation plainly, that as long as they did not sin before their God it went well with them, and that when they departed from the way he had appointed they were destroyed and carried away, but that if there is no iniquity in them their Lord will defend them (Judith 5:17-21). The teaching lingers on that warning because the nations have always known it. It is the same counsel the enemy’s own records preserve, where men who came against this people were told by their own advisers to leave them alone because their God is the true God and the writing on their tablets is true; the enemy studies to know when we are in sin, because that is the only ground he has. Holofernes would not hear it. He asked who is God but Nabuchodonosor, said the God of Israel would not save his people, and had Achior bound and carried to Bethulia to perish with the people he had defended (Judith 6:2-4; Judith 6:10-13). His confidence was in the numbers of his army, and his answer to a true report was to punish the man who brought it. The thing that undid him was not the siege. Judith came down with her maid and was received into his tent, and on the fourth day he made a banquet to his own servants and called for her, saying in his heart that it would be a shame to let such a woman go; and he drank much more wine than he had ever drunk in any one day since he was born (Judith 12:10-20). The captain who had frightened cities into surrender was left alone and helpless in his own tent, filled with wine and lying along on his bed. Judith stood by his bed and prayed for strength, took down his own sword from the pillar, took him by the hair of his head, and struck twice upon his neck and took away his head (Judith 13:4-8). She gave it to her maid, who put it in the bag of meat, and the two of them went out through the camp by the way they had gone every night to prayer, so that nobody stopped them (Judith 13:9-10). At Bethulia she called the watchmen to open the gate and gave God the praise (Judith 13:11-14), and she had the head hung on the highest place of the wall and told the men to go out at dawn as though they would come down to the plain (Judith 14:1-4). When Bagoas went in to wake his lord and found the body with the head taken away, he cried out, and the whole army was struck with fear and confusion and fled, and Israel pursued and took the spoil (Judith 14:14-19; Judith 15:1-7). Judith’s song puts the whole account in one sentence: the Almighty Lord disappointed them by the hand of a woman (Judith 16:5-6), which is the very thing she had asked for when she prayed that the strength of a woman would smite the man who had purposed cruel things against the sanctuary (Judith 9:7-10).

name: Judith
text: A widow who feared God greatly, fasting all the days of her widowhood; going out to Holofernes in the name of the Lord. Judith was a widow of Bethulia who had kept sackcloth and fasted every day of her widowhood except the eves of the sabbaths and feasts, and who had refused every man since her husband died (Judith 8:4-8). When the governors promised to surrender the city in five days if God did not help, she told them they were tempting God and putting his counsel to a term of their own making (Judith 8:11-17). She prayed, went down to the Assyrian camp with her maid, kept her own food and her own hours of prayer, and came back with the head of Holofernes (Judith 9:1-14; Judith 12:1-9; Judith 13:4-10). She gave his goods to the sanctuary, and nobody made Israel afraid in her days or for a long time after her death. The account is careful to say what she was before the crisis came. Her husband Manasses had died in the barley harvest and left her gold and silver, menservants and maidservants, cattle and lands, and she remained upon them, a woman of goodly countenance and very beautiful to look upon (Judith 8:2-8). She made a tent on the roof of her house, put sackcloth on her loins, wore her widow’s apparel, and fasted all the days of her widowhood except the eves of the sabbaths and the sabbaths, the eves of the new moons and the new moons, and the feasts and solemn days of the house of Israel, and none gave her an ill word, for she feared God greatly (Judith 8:5-8). The teaching reads that as loyalty, and reads it both ways: her husband had been loyal to her in leaving the house in order, and she answered it by refusing to give another man what he had provided, and by giving that time to God and to the people instead. When Ozias and the governors had sworn to deliver the city in five days unless God sent rain, she sent for them and told them that they had no right to bind the counsel of God to a term, that God is not as a man to be threatened, and that they should call on him and remember how the fathers were tried; she set before them what the loss of the city and the sanctuary would mean, and asked them to look to her instead (Judith 8:11-27). Then she prayed, rehearsing what God had done by the hand of Simeon, and asked for the power of a widow’s hand against the man who had purposed to defile the sanctuary and to cast down the horn of the altar with a sword (Judith 9:1-14). She put off the sackcloth and the garments of her widowhood only for this, washed and anointed herself, braided her hair and put on the garments of gladness she had worn while her husband lived, and decked herself to draw the eyes of every man who should see her (Judith 10:3-4). In the camp she kept the distinction she had made. She would not eat the king’s meat but ate what her maid carried, and she asked leave to go out every night into the valley to wash and pray, which is how she walked out of the camp at the end with nobody stopping her (Judith 12:1-9). On the fourth night the captain was left alone with her, full of wine, and she prayed for strength, took his own sword from the pillar of the bed, and struck off his head; her maid carried it out in the bag of meat and the two of them walked out as they had walked out every other night (Judith 13:4-10). She would take no credit for it; she told the men at the gate that God had not taken away his mercy from the house of Israel, and Ozias blessed her above all the women upon the earth, and all the people said amen (Judith 13:14-20). When the host was broken, the people of every coast fell on it, and the men of Israel returned from the slaughter and gave her the tent of Holofernes and all his plate and beds and vessels and furniture (Judith 15:8-11). The last chapter is where the teaching puts the weight. Judith dedicated all the stuff of Holofernes that the people had given her, and gave the canopy she had taken out of his bedchamber for a gift to the Lord (Judith 16:19). She gave the spoil back. Then she returned to Bethulia and remained in her own possession, honourable in all the country; many desired her and no man knew her all the days of her life after Manasses died, and she set her maid at liberty and distributed her goods to her husband’s kindred before she died at a hundred and five years old (Judith 16:21-24). Israel lamented her seven days, and there was none that made the children of Israel afraid in the days of Judith, nor a long time after her death (Judith 16:24-25). Deliverance did not end in a monument to herself. It ended in the sanctuary being paid, her house set in order, and the nation left unafraid.

name: Susanna
text: Choosing to fall into the hands of the elders rather than sin in the sight of the Lord. Susanna was the daughter of Chelcias and the wife of Joacim in Babylon, a woman that feared the Lord, whose righteous parents had taught her according to the law of Moses (Susanna 1:1-4). Two elders appointed judges that year hid in her husband’s garden and demanded that she lie with them, threatening to swear that they had caught her with a young man if she refused (Susanna 1:19-21). She answered that if she did it, it was death, and if she did not, she could not escape their hands, and that it was better for her to fall into their hands than to sin in the sight of the Lord; she cried out with a loud voice, and they cried out against her (Susanna 1:22-24). The account begins with how she was raised. Her parents were righteous and taught their daughter according to the law of Moses, and she feared the Lord (Susanna 1:2-3). The teaching stops there to say what that is worth, that a woman trained from a youth in the law is a different woman under pressure, and that the training is the whole reason the next scene goes the way it does. The two elders appointed judges that year kept much at her husband’s house, where every suit at law came before them (Susanna 1:4-6). They saw her walking in the garden every day and their lust was inflamed, and they perverted their own mind and turned away their eyes so as not to look toward heaven or remember just judgments (Susanna 1:7-9). The sin is named in the teaching before it is acted: it begins as coveting a neighbour’s possession, and it is already adultery in the heart before any hand is laid on anybody (Matthew 5:27-28). When she had sent the maids for oil and washing balls and shut the garden doors, the two ran to her and said that nobody could see them, and that if she would not consent they would bear witness that a young man had been with her (Susanna 1:15-21). She sighed and said that she was straitened on every side, that to do this thing was death, and that not to do it would not save her from their hands, and then said the sentence the charge is drawn from, that it was better for her to fall into their hands and not do it than to sin in the sight of the Lord (Susanna 1:22-23). She made the calculation deliberately, and chose the death she could see over the guilt she could not undo. Then she cried with a loud voice, and the elders cried out against her, and one ran and opened the garden door so that the servants rushed in and heard their version first (Susanna 1:24-27). The next day the assembly gathered at her husband’s house and the two elders came full of mischievous imagination to put her to death (Susanna 1:28-29). She came with her father and mother, her children and all her kindred, and the wicked men commanded that her face be uncovered, for she was covered, so that they might be filled with her beauty (Susanna 1:30-32). Her friends wept, the elders laid their hands on her head, and she, weeping, looked up toward heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord (Susanna 1:33-35). That is the exact contrast the teaching draws with the two men who had turned their eyes away so as not to look toward heaven. They told the assembly that they had seen her with a young man too strong for them to hold, and the assembly believed them because they were the elders and judges of the people, and condemned her to death (Susanna 1:36-41).
