Trust no brother and put no confidence in a friend is not cynicism but the warning of the prophets for exactly such a day (Jeremiah 9:4-6; Micah 7:5). Then Susanna cried out with a loud voice to the everlasting God that knows the secrets and knows all things before they be, saying that they had borne false witness against her and that she must die having never done the things they had maliciously invented, and the Lord heard her voice (Susanna 1:42-44). The teaching makes the practical point here for anyone accused where there is no evidence either way and it is one word against another: the matter has to be taken to God and left with him until he reveals it, and he did. As she was led out to die, God raised up the holy spirit of a young youth whose name was Daniel, who cried out that he was clear from the blood of this woman and rebuked the assembly for condemning a daughter of Israel without examination (Susanna 1:45-49). He had the two put apart, asked each under what tree he saw them, and got a mastick tree from one and a holm tree from the other, and told each that he had lied against his own head (Susanna 1:50-59). The assembly praised God that saves them that trust in him, and did to the two men what they had maliciously intended to do to their neighbour, according to the law of Moses (Susanna 1:60-62). Innocent blood was saved that day, her parents and her husband and all her kindred praised God because there was no dishonesty found in her, and from that day Daniel was held in great reputation in the sight of the people (Susanna 1:63-64).

name: The two elders who accused Susanna
text: Attempted adultery by extortion; false witness against an innocent woman. Two ancients of the people were appointed judges that year, of whom the Lord had said that wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges who seemed to govern the people (Susanna 1:5). They saw Susanna walking daily in her husband’s garden, perverted their own mind, and turned away their eyes so as not to look toward heaven nor remember just judgments (Susanna 1:6-9). They hid themselves, demanded that she lie with them, and when she refused they swore before the assembly that they had taken her with a young man (Susanna 1:19-21; Susanna 1:36-41). Daniel examined them apart, their answers did not agree, and the assembly did to them what they had intended for her. The record marks them as judges before adulterers, and the teaching sets the case among leaders bound in their own sin: Eli’s sons, who lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle and made the Lord’s people to transgress (1 Samuel 2:22-25), and the man who says a man should not commit adultery and commits it, through whom the name of God is blasphemed (Romans 2:21-24). These two kept much at Joacim’s house, where every suit at law came, and used the standing it gave them (Susanna 1:6). Their lust was inflamed by watching her, and the teaching traces the order of it: coveting comes first and is already adultery in the heart, and the watching day after day carries a man from the thought to the act (Matthew 5:27-28; Susanna 1:7-12). They were ashamed to declare it even to each other until they were caught in the same place, and then appointed a time together (Susanna 1:10-14). A man who goes on until he is bound with his sins is past the reach of a scripture (2 Esdras 16:77). They hid in the garden, and when she sent the maids away they rose up and ran to her, saying that nobody could see them, and that if she would not consent they would bear witness that a young man had been with her (Susanna 1:15-21). When she cried out, they cried out against her, and one of them opened the garden door so that the servants would come in on their account of it (Susanna 1:24-27). The next day they came to the assembly full of mischievous imagination to put her to death, and commanded that her face be uncovered, that they might be filled with her beauty even while they were killing her (Susanna 1:28-32). Then they laid their hands upon her head and testified that a young man had come to her and been too strong for them to hold, and the assembly believed them as the elders and judges of the people and condemned her to death (Susanna 1:34-41). It is what the law forbids in one line, not to raise a false report nor put the hand with the wicked (Exodus 23:1). The Lord heard her voice and raised up the spirit of a young youth named Daniel, who cried that he was clear from the blood of this woman and rebuked the assembly for condemning a daughter of Israel without examination, and he had the two put apart, one far from another (Susanna 1:44-52). To the first he said that he was waxen old in wickedness, that the sins he had committed before were come to light, and that he had pronounced false judgment, condemning the innocent and letting the guilty go free; then he asked under what tree he had seen them, got a mastick tree, and told him he had lied against his own head and that the angel of God had the sentence to cut him in two (Susanna 1:52-55). To the second he said that beauty had deceived him and lust had perverted his heart, that this was how the two had dealt with the daughters of Israel, who for fear kept company with them, but that the daughter of Juda would not abide their wickedness; he asked the same question, got a holm tree, and gave the same answer (Susanna 1:56-59). The teaching notes the name Daniel uses for him, seed of Chanaan and not of Juda, read the way Ezekiel reads it, that a man of the nation who goes on in this becomes another nation in his conduct (Ezekiel 16:3). The whole assembly praised God that saves them that trust in him and rose up against the two elders, because Daniel had convicted them of false witness by their own mouth; then, according to the law of Moses, they did to them as they had maliciously intended to do to their neighbour and put them to death, and innocent blood was saved that day (Susanna 1:60-62). That is the statute exactly: when a witness testifies falsely against his brother, what he thought to have done to his brother is done to him, and the evil is put away (Deuteronomy 19:16-19). The teaching closes on what a lying tongue can do, that a backbiting tongue has disquieted many, pulled down strong cities and cast out virtuous women (Ecclesiasticus 28:14-15), and on the company such a charge puts a man in, since false witnesses rose against David, against Christ, and against the apostles (Psalms 27:12; Psalms 35:11; Matthew 26:59-60; Acts 6:13). It adds one warning to everyone else in the room: the man who sees an unrighteous judgment and stays quiet will answer for it with the one who began it (Proverbs 24:10-12).

name: The priests of Bel
text: Deceiving the king and the people with an idol that seemed to eat. When Astyages was gathered to his fathers and Cyrus of Persia received his kingdom, Daniel was the king’s companion and honoured above all his friends, and the Babylonians had an idol called Bel on which twelve great measures of fine flour, forty sheep and six vessels of wine were spent every day (Bel and the Dragon 1:1-3). The king worshipped it and went daily to adore it, and asked Daniel why he did not, since Bel ate and drank so much every day; Daniel answered that it was clay within and brass without and had never eaten or drunk anything (Bel and the Dragon 1:4-7). The seventy priests had made a privy entrance under the table, by which they and their wives and children came in continually and consumed the provision (Bel and the Dragon 1:10-13). The history of the destruction of Bel and the Dragon was cut off from the end of Daniel, and it opens where Astyages, Cyrus’s grandfather on his mother’s side, died and Cyrus received the kingdom, with Darius the Mede reigning under him, the same Darius who set Daniel first of the three presidents (Bel and the Dragon 1:1-2; Daniel 6:1-3). Bel is Baal, the same name shortened, and when the Medes and Persians took Babylon they kept the gods of the city they had conquered; one landlord replaced another and the tenants went on with the same worship. The expense is the point of the record: twelve great measures of fine flour, forty sheep and six vessels of wine, every day, out of the king’s own revenue, for a thing that could not move (Bel and the Dragon 1:3). The prophets say what such a thing is: the idols of the heathen are upright as a palm tree and cannot speak, and must be carried (Jeremiah 10:3-5); they cannot hear a prayer or move a foot (Epistle of Jeremy 1:26-28); and they that make a graven image are all of them vanity (Isaiah 44:9-11). The king asked why Daniel did not worship, and he answered that he worshipped no idols made with hands but the living God who created heaven and earth (Bel and the Dragon 1:4-6), which is the second commandment kept in front of a king (Exodus 20:4-5). When the king insisted that Bel was living because of how much he ate and drank, Daniel smiled and said it was clay within and brass without (Bel and the Dragon 1:7). The king then called his priests and told them that if they did not say who devoured the expenses they would die, and that if they could certify him that Bel devoured them, Daniel would die for blasphemy against Bel; and Daniel agreed to those terms (Bel and the Dragon 1:8-9). The seventy priests set the trap themselves. They told the king to go out, to set on the meat and the wine himself, and to shut the door and seal it with his own signet, and promised to suffer death if the food were not eaten (Bel and the Dragon 1:10-12). They regarded it little, because under the table they had made a privy entrance by which they entered in continually and consumed those things (Bel and the Dragon 1:13). Daniel had his servants bring ashes and strew them throughout the temple in the presence of the king alone, and then they went out, shut the door and sealed it (Bel and the Dragon 1:14). In the night the priests came with their wives and children, as they were accustomed, and ate and drank up all (Bel and the Dragon 1:15). The king rose early, was told that the seals were whole, opened the doors, saw the table empty and cried out that Bel was great and that there was no deceit at all in him (Bel and the Dragon 1:16-18). Then Daniel laughed, held him back from going in, and told him to mark the footsteps on the pavement; and the king said that he saw the footsteps of men, women and children (Bel and the Dragon 1:19-20). The witness against them was the floor. The king was angry and took the priests with their wives and children, and they showed him the privy doors by which they came in and consumed the things upon the table, and he slew them (Bel and the Dragon 1:21-22). The teaching does not soften the sentence on the households, and explains what it turns on: they were all of one consent, the whole family in the enterprise together night after night, which is how a charge falls on everyone who kept it running and not only on the man at the head of it. The law gives the same sentence for a man who turns people away from the living God, that the evil be put away from among them (Deuteronomy 13:5). Bel himself was delivered into Daniel’s power, and he destroyed the idol and its temple (Bel and the Dragon 1:22). Then the king pressed him with the great dragon the Babylonians worshipped, saying that this one at least was alive; Daniel asked leave to kill it without sword or staff, made lumps of pitch, fat and hair, put them in its mouth, and it burst asunder (Bel and the Dragon 1:23-27). The men of Babylon then came against Daniel and had him cast into the lions’ den, and he was fed there by Habbacuc, taken up unhurt on the seventh day, and his accusers were cast in and devoured before him (Bel and the Dragon 1:28-32; Bel and the Dragon 1:40-42).

name: The Hellenizers who forsook the holy covenant
text: Covenanting with the heathen; removing circumcision; profaning the Sabbath; sacrificing to idols. In the days of Antiochus Epiphanes wicked men went out of Israel and persuaded many, saying that they should make a covenant with the heathen round about, because since they had departed from them they had had much sorrow (1 Maccabees 1:11-12). They got the king’s licence to live after the ordinances of the heathen, built a place of exercise at Jerusalem after the custom of the heathen, made themselves uncircumcised and forsook the holy covenant (1 Maccabees 1:13-15). When the king wrote that all should be one people and every man leave his own laws, many of Israel consented to his religion, sacrificed to idols and profaned the sabbath (1 Maccabees 1:41-43; 1 Maccabees 1:52). The complaint that started it is the oldest one we have, the same reasoning our fathers used in the wilderness about Egypt: the mind that measures the nation by how comfortable it is among the nations will always argue for the covenant that ends the discomfort. The device pleased them, certain of the people were forward in it, and they went to the king, who gave them licence (1 Maccabees 1:11-13). What they built with the licence was a place of exercise at Jerusalem according to the custom of the heathen, the gymnasium, the word itself meaning to exercise naked (1 Maccabees 1:14). Jason bought the office of high priest and paid extra for leave to set up that place, to train up the youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to have the men of Jerusalem written by the name of Antiochians, so that we could be entered on the register as Greeks (2 Maccabees 4:7-10). He brought his own nation to the Greekish fashion, put down the governments that were according to the law, brought the chief young men under his subjection and made them wear the hat, so that the priests had no courage to serve any more at the altar but despised the temple, neglected the sacrifices and hurried out after the game of the discus, not setting by the honours of their fathers but liking the glory of the Grecians best of all (2 Maccabees 4:11-15). The teaching says that sentence is still describing our people: the glory of another society preferred to our own fathers, and men who will fight you for saying so. Then they made themselves uncircumcised and forsook the holy covenant and joined themselves to the heathen, and were sold to do mischief (1 Maccabees 1:15). The law makes that a cutting off from the people (Genesis 17:14), as profaning the sabbath is a capital matter (Exodus 31:14), and the prophet had already said what the real condition was, that the house of Israel is uncircumcised in the heart (Jeremiah 9:25-26). When the king’s decree came that all should be one people and every man should leave his own laws, the heathen agreed, and many also of Israel consented to his religion, sacrificed to idols and profaned the sabbath (1 Maccabees 1:41-43), and many of the people resorted to the men who forsook the law and joined them (1 Maccabees 1:52). They also rent in pieces the books of the law that they found, and burnt them (1 Maccabees 1:56), which the teaching reads as the whole object of the campaign: cut the connection and the heritage goes, as the prophet said we would discontinue from the heritage given to us (Jeremiah 17:4), the law of life being that heritage (Ecclesiasticus 17:11). Paul is writing about this very history when he reminds the congregation that they were once carried away to dumb idols (1 Corinthians 12:2). Sore calamity came upon them, and the writer names the form of it exactly: they had those to be their enemies and avengers whose custom they had followed so earnestly and whom they had desired to be like in all things (2 Maccabees 4:16-17). The men who had asked for the covenant got the covenant and everything in it. Apollonius came with a pretence of peace and slew them on the sabbath, the temple they had traded away was called by the name of Jupiter Olympius and filled with riot, and the citizens they had made Greeks were sold as slaves like everybody else (2 Maccabees 5:24-26; 2 Maccabees 6:1-6). Against them Mattathias and his company went about and pulled down the altars, circumcised by force the children that they found uncircumcised, pursued after the proud men, and recovered the law out of the hand of the Gentiles and of the kings (1 Maccabees 2:44-48); and Judas went through the cities of Juda destroying the ungodly out of them and turning away wrath from Israel (1 Maccabees 3:5-8). The end of the men who had led it is set down one by one. Jason, who had undermined his own brother, was undermined by Menelaus and fled to the Ammonites; he obtained not the principality but at the last received shame for the reward of his treason, fled from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws and abhorred as an open enemy of his country, was cast out into Egypt, and he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land, and he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him (2 Maccabees 5:5-10). The teaching draws the plain moral: nobody honours a traitor, not even the people he sold his own to.

name: Apollonius
text: Falling upon Jerusalem on the Sabbath under a pretence of peace; slaying a great multitude; taking women and children captive. Two years after Antiochus had spoiled the sanctuary, the king sent his chief collector of tribute to the cities of Juda, and he came to Jerusalem with a great multitude and spoke peaceable words to them, but all was deceit (1 Maccabees 1:29-30). He was Apollonius, sent with twenty and two thousand men and commanded to slay all those that were in their best age and to sell the women and the younger sort; coming to Jerusalem and pretending peace, he waited for the sabbath, and when he took the Jews keeping the holy day he commanded his men to arm themselves and slew a great multitude (2 Maccabees 5:24-26). Judas met him in the field and killed him, and carried his sword all his life long (1 Maccabees 3:10-12). The office he came in is part of the charge. He came as the chief collector of tribute, and the teaching stops on that word: tribute is the mark of a people in subjection, which is why Christ answered that the kings of the earth take custom of strangers and not of their own children (Matthew 17:24-27), why the question about the penny with Caesar’s image on it settled who the money belonged to (Mark 12:14-17), and why the record of the captivity says that we are scattered for a reproach and a curse and subject to payments (Baruch 3:8), the curse itself standing for a sign upon us and upon our seed (Deuteronomy 28:46). The Greeks who sent him were themselves vassals paying Rome, and they paid it with us, selling our people to make up what they owed. He spoke peaceable words, but all was deceit (1 Maccabees 1:30). The psalm the teaching sets beside this describes the man exactly: he put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him and broke his covenant, the words of his mouth were smoother than butter but war was in his heart, his words were softer than oil, and they were drawn swords (Psalms 55:20-21). The teaching says this is not a single bad ambassador but a settled habit, and names the modern form of it, the smooth words spoken to our preachers and our neighbourhoods by men who deliver nothing afterward, and help that arrives carrying sickness. He timed the attack for the day he knew we would not fight, and killed men who had gone up to keep the sabbath (2 Maccabees 5:25-26; Exodus 31:14). When they had given him credence he fell suddenly upon the city, smote it very sore, destroyed much people of Israel, took the spoils, set it on fire, pulled down the houses and the walls on every side, took the women and children captive, and possessed the cattle (1 Maccabees 1:30-32). Then he fortified the city of David with a great wall and mighty towers and put there a sinful nation, wicked men, so that it became a sore snare and a place to lie in wait against the sanctuary, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them (1 Maccabees 1:33-38). The teaching reads the garrison as the thing we still live with, an armed presence quartered in our own streets whose work is to make the place unlivable. Her sanctuary was laid waste, her feasts were turned into mourning, her sabbaths into reproach, and her honour into contempt (1 Maccabees 1:39-40). Judas Maccabeus rose up in his father’s place, and his brethren helped him, and they fought the battle of Israel with cheerfulness (1 Maccabees 3:1-2). The reason the account gives for what followed is not numbers. Salvation prospered in his hand because he had taken to himself those that observed the law, as his father had charged him, and the workers of iniquity were troubled (1 Maccabees 2:67; 1 Maccabees 3:6). He received to himself such as were ready to perish, men who had already given up their own lives for the nation (1 Maccabees 3:9). Then Apollonius gathered the Gentiles together and a great host out of Samaria to fight against Israel, and Judas, when he perceived it, went forth to meet him and smote him and slew him; many also fell down slain and the rest fled (1 Maccabees 3:10-11). Judas took their spoils, and he took the sword of Apollonius and fought with it all his life long (1 Maccabees 3:12). The man who had come in under a pretence of peace and struck on the holy day was met in the open field and killed, and his own weapon was carried afterward by the man who had kept the law he came to destroy.

name: Antiochus Epiphanes
text: Defiling the temple; forbidding the law; murdering the faithful. Antiochus Epiphanes came out of the Seleucid line as a wicked root, a hostage at Rome who took the kingdom after his brother died, entered proudly into the sanctuary, carried off the golden altar, the candlestick and the hidden treasures, and made a great massacre and spoke very proudly (1 Maccabees 1:10; 1 Maccabees 1:20-24). He wrote to his whole kingdom that all should be one people and that every man should leave his own laws, forbade the burnt offering, the sabbath and the festivals, set the abomination of desolation upon the altar, and put to death the women who had circumcised their children (1 Maccabees 1:41-50; 1 Maccabees 1:54-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-2). He died in a strange country of an incurable plague, eaten with worms and unbearable to his own army (2 Maccabees 9:5-12). He called himself God manifest, and his own people renamed him Epimanes, the madman. The prophet had already drawn him: a little horn out of one of the four, waxing exceeding great toward the pleasant land, casting down some of the host and of the stars, magnifying himself even to the prince of the host, and taking away the daily sacrifice (Daniel 8:9-12; Daniel 11:31). After he had taken Egypt he turned on Jerusalem, went into the sanctuary and stripped it of the golden altar, the candlestick, the vessels, the table of the shewbread, the censers of gold, the veil, the crowns and the golden ornaments, and the hidden treasures he found (1 Maccabees 1:20-23). The teaching notes that he did not do this in Egypt: he went for the altar because he knew what our hearts were fixed on. Great mourning came on Israel in every place, and the house of Jacob was covered with confusion (1 Maccabees 1:25-28). Then he made it law. He wrote that all should be one people and every man leave his own laws, forbade the offerings in the temple, commanded that the sabbaths and festival days be profaned, that altars of idols be set up, that swine’s flesh be offered, and that whoever would not do according to the word of the king should die (1 Maccabees 1:41-50). An old man of Athens was sent to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers; the temple was called by the name of Jupiter Olympius and filled with riot, the altar with profane things, and it was not lawful to keep the sabbath days or the ancient feasts or to profess oneself a Jew (2 Maccabees 6:1-6). On the king’s birthday they were compelled to eat of the sacrifices, and at the feast of Bacchus to go in procession with ivy (2 Maccabees 6:7). The teaching names the object: suppress the identity and the people forget who they are and who their God is, which is why the books of the law were rent in pieces and burnt (1 Maccabees 1:56-57). On the fifteenth day of Casleu the abomination of desolation was set upon the altar; they put to death the women who had caused their children to be circumcised and hanged the infants about their necks, and many in Israel chose rather to die than to be defiled with unclean meats (1 Maccabees 1:54-64). He went into Persia for money, the war in Judea having drained him, tried to rob the temple at Persepolis, was driven out and returned with shame; at Ecbatane he was told that Nicanor and Timotheus had been beaten (2 Maccabees 9:1-3). Swelling with anger, he drove without stopping and spoke proudly that he would make Jerusalem a common burying place of the Jews (2 Maccabees 9:4). As soon as he had said it, the Lord Almighty smote him with an incurable and invisible plague, a pain of the bowels that was remediless, and the writer says it was most just, since he had tormented other men’s bowels (2 Maccabees 9:5-6). He fell out of his chariot, so that every member of his body was in pain; worms rose up out of him, his flesh fell away while he lived, and the filthiness of his smell was so intolerable that no man could carry him (2 Maccabees 9:7-10). The man who thought he could weigh the mountains in a balance was carried in a horse litter. Plagued, he began to leave off his great pride and to come to the knowledge of himself by the scourge of God, saying that it is fitting to be subject to God and that a mortal man should not proudly think of himself as if he were God (2 Maccabees 9:11-12). He vowed to set the holy city at liberty, to make the Jews equal with the citizens of Athens, to garnish the temple out of his own revenue, and even to become a Jew himself; but for all this his pains would not cease, for the just judgment of God was come upon him (2 Maccabees 9:13-18). So the murderer and blasphemer, having suffered as he had made other men suffer, died a miserable death in a strange country in the mountains (2 Maccabees 9:28). The first book tells the same end from inside his own mind: he fell sick for grief, said that he remembered the evils he did at Jerusalem and that he sent to destroy the inhabitants of Judea without a cause, and perceived that for this cause these troubles were come upon him (1 Maccabees 6:8-13). The teaching precepts that confession with the rule that he that leads into captivity goes into captivity (Revelation 13:10), and observes how late such men come to it.

name: Mattathias
text: Zealous for the law: refusing the king’s commandment at Modin, and executing the apostate on the altar as Phinehas did Zambri. Mattathias, a priest of the sons of Joarib, left Jerusalem and dwelt at Modin with his five sons, and when he saw the blasphemies committed in Juda and Jerusalem he said that it would have been better not to have been born than to see the misery of his people (1 Maccabees 2:1-7). The king’s officers came to Modin to make them sacrifice and offered him rank, gifts and the friendship of the king, and he answered that though all the nations under the king obeyed him, he and his sons and his brethren would walk in the covenant of their fathers (1 Maccabees 2:15-22). When a Jew came in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar at Modin, he ran and slew him on the altar, killed the king’s commissioner, and pulled the altar down (1 Maccabees 2:23-25). He saw the temple made as a man without glory, the vessels carried into captivity, the infants slain in the streets, and asked what nation had not had a part in her kingdom; he and his sons rent their clothes and mourned very sore (1 Maccabees 2:7-14). Every nation confederate against us is the psalm exactly (Psalms 83:1-8). The teaching holds this up as the qualification: oppression makes a wise man mad (Ecclesiastes 7:7), the mark is set on the men that sigh and cry for the abominations done in the city (Ezekiel 9:4), and men who see their people so and are not moved are the men Christ compared to children in the marketplace (Luke 7:31-32). Against that, the Lord has always raised up deliverers when the people cried (Judges 3:9; 2 Kings 13:5; Nehemiah 9:27). The officers came to Modin with flattery and with a price. They told him that he was a ruler, honourable and great, strengthened with sons and brethren, that the men of Juda and those left at Jerusalem had already done it, and that if he came first he and his house would be numbered among the king’s friends and honoured with silver and gold (1 Maccabees 2:17-18). A gift destroys the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:7), and the apostle’s rule is not to be partaker of other men’s sins (1 Timothy 5:22). Mattathias answered with a loud voice that though all the nations under the king obeyed him and fell away from the religion of their fathers, he and his sons and his brethren would walk in the covenant of their fathers, and would not go from their religion on the right hand or the left (1 Maccabees 2:19-22). It is the answer the three children gave in Babylon (Daniel 3:16-18), and the answer of the apostles, that we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Then one of the Jews came in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar at Modin according to the king’s commandment. Mattathias was inflamed with zeal, his reins trembled, and he ran and slew him upon the altar, killed the king’s commissioner who compelled men to sacrifice, and pulled down the altar (1 Maccabees 2:23-25). The writer measures him by the statute, that he dealt zealously for the law of God as Phinees did to Zambri (1 Maccabees 2:26; Numbers 25:7-13), the sentence the law gives for the man who entices the people to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6-11). He cried through the city that whoever was zealous of the law and maintained the covenant should follow him, and he and his sons fled into the mountains (1 Maccabees 2:27-28). When a thousand in the wilderness let themselves be killed on the sabbath rather than defend themselves, he and his friends decided to fight any man who came against them on that day (1 Maccabees 2:29-41). The Assideans and all who fled from the evils joined him, and they went about pulling down the altars, circumcising the children they found uncircumcised, and recovered the law out of the hand of the Gentiles and the kings (1 Maccabees 2:42-48). When his time came to die he charged them to be zealous for the law, to give their lives for the covenant, and to call to remembrance what acts the fathers did in their time (1 Maccabees 2:49-51). He named them one by one, Abraham, Joseph, Phinees, Josue, Caleb, David, Elias, the three saved out of the flame, and Daniel delivered from the lions, and drew the conclusion, that none that put their trust in him shall be overcome, and that the words of a sinful man are not to be feared (1 Maccabees 2:52-62). Then he told them who each was. Simon is a man of counsel, and shall be a father to them; Judas Maccabeus has been mighty and strong from his youth, let him be their captain and fight the battle of the people; take to you all those that observe the law, avenge the wrong of your people, recompense fully the heathen, and take heed to the commandments of the law (1 Maccabees 2:65-68). The teaching calls that what a father is for, to tell his children who to follow and what to hold on to. So he blessed them and was gathered to his fathers, died in the hundred forty and sixth year, was buried at Modin, and all Israel made great lamentation for him (1 Maccabees 2:69-70). The blessing of a father establishes the houses of the children (Ecclesiasticus 3:9), and the wisdom says of such a man that though he die, he is as though he were not dead, for he has left one behind him like himself, an avenger against his enemies (Ecclesiasticus 30:4-6).

name: The Jew who sacrificed at Modin
text: Sacrificing on the heathen altar at the king’s command. The king’s officers came to Modin to compel the people to revolt and to make them sacrifice, and offered Mattathias rank and rewards if he would be the first to fulfil the king’s commandment (1 Maccabees 2:15-18). Mattathias refused for himself, his sons and his brethren, and while he was still speaking one of the Jews came in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar which was at Modin, according to the king’s commandment (1 Maccabees 2:19-23). Mattathias was inflamed with zeal, ran, and slew him upon the altar, and pulled the altar down (1 Maccabees 2:24-25). What makes this case is the timing and the audience. The refusal had just been made publicly, in front of the officers and in front of the men of the city; Mattathias had said out loud that though every nation under the king obeyed him and fell away from the religion of their fathers, he and his house would walk in the covenant of their fathers and would not go from their religion on the right hand or the left (1 Maccabees 2:19-22). The offer that had been refused was the flattery and the price together, that he was an honourable and great man with sons and brethren, that the men of Juda and those left at Jerusalem had already done it, and that silver and gold and many rewards and the friendship of the king were waiting (1 Maccabees 2:17-18). Then this man stepped out in the sight of all and took the terms that had just been turned down (1 Maccabees 2:23). The teaching says a gift destroys the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:7), and that a man is not to lay his hand with another man’s sin but to keep himself pure (1 Timothy 5:22); this man did in public the very thing the nation had just been told not to do, and gave the officers the example they had come for. The law does not treat that as a private failure. The man who is found doing wickedly in the sight of the Lord in transgressing his covenant, who has gone and served other gods and worshipped them, is to be brought out and stoned, on the word of two or three witnesses, and the hands of the witnesses are to be first upon him to put him away (Deuteronomy 17:2-7). Where the enticement comes from a brother, a son, a daughter, a wife or a friend, saying let us go and serve other gods, the sentence is the same and the hand of the man who heard it is to be first upon him, so that all Israel hears and fears (Deuteronomy 13:6-10). The altar at Modin was the test case set up in the town precisely so that the rest would follow. Mattathias saw it, was inflamed with zeal, and his reins trembled; he could not forbear to show his anger according to judgment, and he ran and slew the man upon the altar, and the king’s commissioner who compelled men to sacrifice he killed at that time also, and the altar he pulled down (1 Maccabees 2:24-25). The writer gives the precedent in the same breath: thus he dealt zealously for the law of God, as Phinees did to Zambri the son of Salom (1 Maccabees 2:26). Phinees rose up from among the congregation, took a javelin in his hand, and thrust both of them through, and the plague was stayed, and he was given the covenant of an everlasting priesthood because he was zealous for his God and made an atonement for the children of Israel (Numbers 25:7-8; Numbers 25:11-13). The execution was not the end of the day but the beginning of the revolt. Mattathias cried through the city with a loud voice that whoever was zealous of the law and maintained the covenant should follow him, and he and his sons left everything they had in the city and fled into the mountains (1 Maccabees 2:27-28). The teaching reads the whole scene as one lesson about company: the father’s last charge to his sons was to take to themselves all those that observe the law, because the men around you are what decides whether the work stands, and the man on the altar at Modin is the other kind. One man taking the reward in front of everybody was what the king’s policy needed, and the answer to it set the nation in motion.

name: Judas Maccabeus
text: Going to battle with prayer and the law, keeping the ordinances of war, and cleansing the sanctuary. Judas rose up in his father’s place, and his brethren helped him, and they fought the battle of Israel with cheerfulness; salvation prospered in his hand because he took to himself those that observed the law (1 Maccabees 3:1-6; 1 Maccabees 2:67). Facing Seron with a small company he told them that the victory of battle does not stand in the multitude of a host but that strength comes from heaven, and that they fight for their lives and their laws (1 Maccabees 3:18-22). He set captains over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens and sent home the men the law excuses from war (1 Maccabees 3:55-60), and after the victories he cleansed the sanctuary and dedicated the new altar with eight days of gladness (1 Maccabees 4:36-59). The account says why he prospered before saying what he won. All his brethren helped him, and so did all that held with his father; the wicked shrank for fear of him, because salvation prospered in his hand (1 Maccabees 3:2-6). That goes back to the charge his father gave him, to take to himself all those that observe the law (1 Maccabees 2:67), and the teaching will not let the point go: he had no sinners in his company, and the men he received were such as were ready to perish, men who had given up their own lives for the nation (1 Maccabees 3:9). Before the battle at Maspha the congregation gathered where they had prayed of old, fasted, put on sackcloth, cast ashes on their heads, brought out the priests’ garments and the firstfruits and the tithes, and cried toward heaven (1 Maccabees 3:44-53), the assembly the prophet commands when the land is in that condition (Joel 2:16-17). To men who asked how so few could fight so great a multitude, he answered that with the God of heaven it is all one to deliver with a great multitude or a small company, that the victory of battle stands not in the multitude of a host but that strength comes from heaven, and that they come in pride to destroy us and our children, but we fight for our lives and our laws (1 Maccabees 3:17-22). Then he kept the ordinances of war as they are written, ordaining captains over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens, and sending home the men building houses, betrothing wives, or planting vineyards, and the fearful, according to the law (1 Maccabees 3:55-56; Deuteronomy 20:5-9). At Emmaus he armed them with good words and said that as the will of God is in heaven, so let him do (1 Maccabees 3:58-60). The second book shows the same discipline: he told them that the enemy trusted in weapons and boldness but that our confidence is in Almighty God, recounted the deliverances under Sennacherib and among the Galatians, divided the army into four parts with his brothers over the bands, appointed Eleazar to read the holy book, and gave the watchword, the help of God (2 Maccabees 8:16-23). After the victory they broke off the pursuit because it was the day before the sabbath, and kept the sabbath giving thanks (2 Maccabees 8:24-28). He also kept the army clean. After a battle at Odollam they purified themselves and kept the sabbath, and when they came the next day to bury their own slain, they found under the coats of every one of the dead things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which the law forbids, and every man saw why they had been slain (2 Maccabees 12:38-40). Judas turned it into an exhortation to the living to keep themselves from sin, and sent two thousand drachms of silver to Jerusalem for a sin offering, being mindful of the resurrection (2 Maccabees 12:41-45). The teaching is careful here: it was a good thought made in hope, and does not put in a man’s hand what only Christ can give; what it shows is a captain who reckoned sin in the camp as the reason for the losses. When the enemies were discomfited, he told his brethren to go up and cleanse and dedicate the sanctuary, and they found it desolate, the altar profaned, the gates burnt, shrubs growing in the courts as in a forest, and the priests’ chambers pulled down (1 Maccabees 4:36-38). He chose priests of blameless conversation, such as had pleasure in the law, to cleanse it; they pulled down the profaned altar and laid up its stones in the mountain of the temple until there should come a prophet to show what to do with them, and built a new altar of whole stones according to the law (1 Maccabees 4:42-47). On the twenty and fifth day of Casleu, the same day the heathen had profaned it, they rose early and offered sacrifice on the new altar, dedicated it with songs and citherns and harps, and kept the dedication eight days with gladness (1 Maccabees 4:52-59). They kept it as the feast of tabernacles, bearing branches and palms, and ordained by a common statute that the nation should keep those days every year (2 Maccabees 10:6-8). It is the feast Christ is found at in Jerusalem in winter (John 10:22). The second book gives him the vision that goes with the charge: Onias the former high priest praying for the whole body of the Jews, and Jeremias, a lover of the brethren, giving Judas a sword of gold to wound the adversaries (2 Maccabees 15:11-16), after which Nicanor’s host was broken and the day kept yearly (2 Maccabees 15:25-29).

name: Alcimus
text: Slandering Judas to the king; slaying sixty Asideans under a sworn peace; pulling down the wall of the inner court. When Demetrius was set on the throne, all the wicked and ungodly men of Israel came to him, having Alcimus, who desired to be high priest, for their captain, and they accused the people, saying that Judas and his brethren had slain the king’s friends and driven them out of their own land (1 Maccabees 7:5-7). The king sent Bacchides with Alcimus, whom he made high priest, commanding him to take vengeance on the children of Israel (1 Maccabees 7:8-9). Under a sworn peace Alcimus took sixty of the Assideans and slew them in one day, and afterward, when he commanded the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary to be pulled down, he was struck with a palsy and died in great torment (1 Maccabees 7:12-18; 1 Maccabees 9:54-56). The teaching keeps a list running through this period and puts him at the end of it: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, Jason, Menelaus, Rhodocus, and now Alcimus. The wicked among our own always seek position. The men who came with him to Demetrius had been driven out of the land, because they were of no use to their own people and of no use to the king they sold them to; their complaint was that Judas had slain the king’s friends (1 Maccabees 7:5-7). The king made him high priest and sent Bacchides with him and a great power into the land of Judea, with a commandment to take vengeance on the children of Israel (1 Maccabees 7:8-9). They sent to Judas and his brethren with peaceable words deceitfully, but he gave no heed, seeing that they had come with a great power (1 Maccabees 7:10-11). The Assideans were the first among the children of Israel to seek peace of them, saying that one that is a priest of the seed of Aaron had come with the army and would do them no wrong (1 Maccabees 7:12-14). The teaching stops on that reasoning, because it is the mistake: he was in the line, but he had defiled himself willingly in the times of their mingling with the Gentiles, and a man in the line who has done that is not what the line says he is. He spoke to them peaceably and swore that he would not seek harm to them or to their friends, and they believed him, and he took sixty of them and slew them in one day (1 Maccabees 7:15-16). The writer reaches for the psalm to say what it looked like, that the flesh of the saints was cast out and their blood shed round about Jerusalem with none to bury them (1 Maccabees 7:17; Psalms 79:2-3). Then the fear and dread of them fell on all the people, who said that there was neither truth nor righteousness in them, for they had broken the covenant and the oath they had made (1 Maccabees 7:18). Bacchides slew many and cast them into the great pit, committed the country to Alcimus, and left him a power to aid him (1 Maccabees 7:19-20). Alcimus contended for the high priesthood, and all such as troubled the people resorted to him, and when they had gotten the land of Juda into their power they did much hurt in Israel, so that Judas saw that Alcimus and his company had done among the Israelites even above the heathen (1 Maccabees 7:21-23). The teaching does not flinch from that verse: a man of the nation can do us worse than the nations. When Judas took vengeance on the men who had revolted, and Alcimus saw that he had the upper hand and could not abide his force, he went again to the king and said all the worst of them that he could (1 Maccabees 7:24-25). The second book shows the same speech. He came to Demetrius with a crown of gold and a palm and boughs used solemnly in the temple, and in council he said that those called Assideans, whose captain is Judas Maccabeus, nourish war and will not let the realm be in peace, that he himself had been deprived of his ancestors’ honour, meaning the high priesthood, and that as long as Judas lives it is not possible that the state should be quiet (2 Maccabees 14:3-10; 2 Maccabees 14:26-27). In the hundred fifty and third year, in the second month, Alcimus commanded that the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary should be pulled down, and he pulled down also the works of the prophets (1 Maccabees 9:54). That is where it ended. As he began to pull down, at that very time he was plagued and his enterprises hindered, for his mouth was stopped and he was taken with a palsy, so that he could no more speak nor give order concerning his house (1 Maccabees 9:55). So Alcimus died at that time with great torment (1 Maccabees 9:56). The mouth that had slandered his own nation to two kings was stopped first, and the man who had sworn a peace and killed sixty men under it was left unable to give an order about his own house. When Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead he returned to the king, and the land of Juda was in rest two years (1 Maccabees 9:57). The teaching reads the case as a warning to men who want the office more than the work: he had the pedigree, took the title from a foreign king, held the country with a foreign garrison, and the record of it is four verses about how he died.

name: Nicanor
text: Blasphemy against the temple; breaking covenant with Judas; resolving to attack on the Sabbath. The king sent Nicanor, one of his honourable princes, a man that bare deadly hate to Israel, with a commandment to destroy the people (1 Maccabees 7:26). He sent to Judas with friendly words asking for a meeting in peace, while his men were prepared to take Judas away by violence (1 Maccabees 7:27-30). When the priests came out of the sanctuary to salute him, he mocked them, abused them shamefully and swore that unless Judas were delivered into his hands he would burn up the house (1 Maccabees 7:33-35). He purposed to fall on the Jews on the sabbath day, and on the thirteenth of Adar his host was broken and he himself was the first man slain in the battle (2 Maccabees 15:1-5; 1 Maccabees 7:39-43). The teaching notes that the hatred was not there from the first day. Nicanor had first appeared with friendly words, and the relationship between him and Judas ran from good to bad; the second book shows him made governor, bearing Judas good will and loving the man from his heart, advising him to marry and live quietly, until Alcimus accused him to the king of appointing Judas as his successor (2 Maccabees 14:23-27). Forced by the king’s letter to send Judas prisoner, he was troubled and loath to break with a man who had done him no wrong; but he went through with it, and from that point he set himself against the people (2 Maccabees 14:28-30). He sent to Judas and his brethren deceitfully with friendly words, saying that there should be no battle between them and that he would come with a few men to see him in peace, and they saluted one another peaceably, while his enemies were prepared to take Judas away by violence; Judas learned of the deceit and would not see his face again (1 Maccabees 7:27-30). What the charge turns on is what he said in front of the temple. When he came up to mount Sion and certain of the priests and of the elders came out of the sanctuary to salute him peaceably and to show him the burnt sacrifice that was offered for the king, he mocked them, laughed at them, abused them shamefully and spoke proudly, and swore in his wrath that unless Judas and his host were delivered into his hands he would burn up this house; and he went out in a great rage (1 Maccabees 7:33-35). The second book has him stretching out his right hand toward the temple and swearing that if they did not deliver Judas he would break down the house of God, cast down the altar and set up a temple to Bacchus there (2 Maccabees 14:31-33). The priests went in and stood before the altar weeping, and asked God to remember this man’s blasphemies and to suffer him not to continue (1 Maccabees 7:36-38), which is the psalm’s own plea, that God arise and plead his own cause, and remember the reproach of the foolish man and the tumult of those that rise up against him continually (Psalms 74:22-23). Then he resolved to set upon Judas on the sabbath day, and when the Jews compelled to follow him asked him to honour the day which he that sees all things had honoured with holiness above other days, he asked whether there were a mighty one in heaven that had commanded the sabbath to be kept, and when they answered that there is a living Lord in heaven that commanded the seventh day, he replied that he was mighty upon earth and commanded them to take weapons (2 Maccabees 15:1-5). Judas pitched at Adasa with three thousand men and prayed that, as the angel had gone out against the messengers of the king of the Assyrians and smitten a hundred fourscore and five thousand of them, so this host might be destroyed, and that the rest might know that this man had spoken blasphemy against the sanctuary (1 Maccabees 7:39-42). So on the thirteenth day of the month Adar the hosts joined battle, and Nicanor’s host was discomfited, and he himself was the first man slain in the battle (1 Maccabees 7:43). When his host saw that he was slain they cast away their weapons and fled, and the Jews pursued them a day’s journey from Adasa to Gazara, sounding an alarm with trumpets, so that the people came out of all the towns of Judea round about and closed them in, and they were all slain with the sword, and not one of them was left (1 Maccabees 7:44-46). Then they took the spoils and the prey, and smote off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had stretched out so proudly, and brought them away and hanged them up toward Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 7:47). The second book adds that they hanged the head from the tower as a manifest token of the help of God, and cut out the tongue that had spoken against the holy place and gave it to the fowls (2 Maccabees 15:28-35). For this cause the people rejoiced greatly and kept that day as a day of great gladness, and they ordained to keep it yearly, the thirteenth day of Adar (1 Maccabees 7:48-49; 2 Maccabees 15:36). The teaching reads that ordinance without embarrassment: our forefathers kept a feast over it, told their children what was done to the man who threatened the house, and would do the same again. Thus the land of Juda was in rest a little while (1 Maccabees 7:50).

name: Tryphon
text: Taking Jonathan the high priest by treachery under a covenant of friendship; slaying him and the young king Antiochus. Tryphon went about to get the kingdom of Asia and to kill the young king Antiochus, whom he himself had set up, but he was afraid that Jonathan would not suffer him, so he sought a way to take Jonathan and kill him (1 Maccabees 12:39-40). At Bethsan he received Jonathan honourably, gave him gifts, persuaded him to send his forty thousand men home, and then shut the gates of Ptolemais on him, took him, and slew the thousand that had come with him (1 Maccabees 12:41-48). He took a hundred talents of silver and Jonathan’s two sons from Simon on a promise of release, kept them, and killed Jonathan at Bascama; then he slew the young king and crowned himself (1 Maccabees 13:12-24; 1 Maccabees 13:31-32). The teaching sets out who he was. Diodotus was an official under Alexander Balas who revolted against Demetrius, took Alexander’s infant son out of Arabia, proclaimed him king as Antiochus, and acted as his regent while he gathered most of Syria to himself. The boy he was protecting was the obstacle to his own crown, and Jonathan, in league with the boy king, was the obstacle to removing him; so he went about to get the kingdom and kill the king, and because he feared that Jonathan would fight him, he sought a way to take Jonathan first (1 Maccabees 12:39-40). Jonathan came out to meet him at Bethsan with forty thousand chosen men (1 Maccabees 12:41). When Tryphon saw the size of the force he did not stretch out his hand against him, but received him honourably, gave him gifts, and commanded his men of war to obey him as himself (1 Maccabees 12:42-43). Then he asked why he had put all these people to so great trouble, seeing there was no war between them, and told him to send them home and come to Ptolemais with a few men, promising to give him the city and the rest of the strongholds and forces (1 Maccabees 12:44-45). Jonathan believed him, sent away his hosts, kept three thousand, sent two thousand into Galilee, and went with a thousand (1 Maccabees 12:46-47). As soon as he entered Ptolemais they shut the gates, took him, and slew all that came in with him (1 Maccabees 12:48). The teaching precepts the whole scene with the psalm: he put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him and broke his covenant, the words of his mouth were smoother than butter but war was in his heart, and his words, softer than oil, were drawn swords (Psalms 55:20-21). It reads this as the settled nature of the enemy rather than the character of one man, and the reason we are told to cast our burden on the Lord (Psalms 55:22-23). Simon rose up in his brother’s place, told the people that he would not spare his own life in a time of trouble, and they answered that he should be their leader (1 Maccabees 13:1-9). Tryphon sent to him saying that he held Jonathan for money owing to the king’s treasury, and that if Simon would send a hundred talents of silver and Jonathan’s two sons for hostages he would let him go (1 Maccabees 13:12-16). Simon perceived that they spoke deceitfully, but sent the money and the children, so that the people could not say that Jonathan had died because he would not send them (1 Maccabees 13:17-18). Tryphon took both and would not let him go, marched into the country, was turned back by a great snow, went into Galilee, and at Bascama slew Jonathan, who was buried there (1 Maccabees 13:19-23). Simon took the bones of his brother to Modin and built the monument with seven pyramids for his father, his mother and his four brethren, with pillars and armour for a perpetual memory (1 Maccabees 13:25-29). Then Tryphon dealt deceitfully with the young king Antiochus and slew him, reigned in his stead, crowned himself king of Asia, and brought a great calamity upon the land (1 Maccabees 13:31-32). The book does not record a sentence executed on him. It records the kingdom turning against him. Antiochus the son of Demetrius came into the land of his fathers, and the forces gathered to him, so that few were left with Tryphon (1 Maccabees 15:1-10). He pursued him, and Tryphon fled to Dora by the sea, knowing that troubles were come on him all at once and that his forces had forsaken him (1 Maccabees 15:10-11). The king besieged Dora with a hundred and twenty thousand men of war and eight thousand horsemen, joined his ships to the town, and pressed it by sea and land, so that no man could go out or in (1 Maccabees 15:13-14). From there Tryphon got away, took ship and fled to Orthosias, and the account leaves him there (1 Maccabees 15:37). What the record shows is the end of everything he killed for. The treachery at Ptolemais and the murder at Bascama were meant to clear his way to the crown of Asia, and what he held at the last was a divided kingdom and a coast he could not defend, while the house he had tried to destroy went on: the yoke of the heathen was taken away from Israel, and the people began to write in their instruments and contracts in the first year of Simon the high priest (1 Maccabees 13:41-42). The sentence on the man is deferred; the judgment on the purpose is on the page.

name: Ptolemy the son of Abubus
text: Murdering Simon the high priest and two of his sons at a banquet in his own castle. Ptolemeus the son of Abubus was made captain in the plain of Jericho and had abundance of silver and gold, for he was the high priest’s son in law; his heart was lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself, and he consulted deceitfully against Simon and his sons to destroy them (1 Maccabees 16:11-13). When Simon came down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, Ptolemeus received them deceitfully into a little hold called Docus which he had built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there; and when they had drunk largely he and his men rose up, took their weapons, came upon Simon in the banqueting place, and slew him and his two sons and certain of his servants (1 Maccabees 16:14-16). The teaching gives this case a name from the street, the back door, and defines it exactly: being taken down by somebody close to you, a family member or a friend, because that is the one direction you are not watching. The reason it names for it is the same one the record gives, which is that the man has watched you get something and cannot stand it: his heart being lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself (1 Maccabees 16:13). He had the position, the money and the marriage, and he had all three from the man he killed. The setting was ordinary and the victim was at work. Simon was visiting the cities that were in the country and taking care for the good ordering of them, and came down himself to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, in the hundred threescore and seventeenth year, in the eleventh month, called Sabat (1 Maccabees 16:14). Ptolemeus received them deceitfully into a little hold called Docus which he had built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there; and when Simon and his sons had drunk largely, he and his men rose up and took their weapons and came upon Simon in the banqueting place and slew him and his two sons and certain of his servants (1 Maccabees 16:15-16). The writer says plainly what was done: in doing this he committed a great treachery and recompensed evil for good (1 Maccabees 16:17). The law curses the man that smites his neighbour secretly and the man that takes a reward to slay an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:24-25), and the wisdom says that whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house (Proverbs 17:13); and the psalm had already described the shape of it, a familiar friend, trusted, who ate bread with him (Psalms 41:9). The teaching sets the wise man’s rule against the whole scene, that an enemy is never to be trusted, that though he humble himself and go crouching a man should take good heed and beware of him, that he is not to be set beside you nor allowed to sit at your right hand, because when he has overthrown you he will stand up in your place and seek your seat; that he will speak sweetly with his lips while in his heart he imagines how to throw you into a pit, and that he will weep with his eyes but if he finds opportunity he will not be satisfied with blood (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-16). The banquet hall was built for it, and the men were already in the room. The book records no sentence executed on him. It records the rest of the plot failing. He wrote to the king to send him a host to aid him, promising to deliver him the country and the cities; he sent others to Gazara to kill John, and letters to the captains to come to him for silver and gold and rewards, and others to take Jerusalem and the mountain of the temple (1 Maccabees 16:18-20). But one ran before to Gazara and told John that his father and his brethren were slain, and that Ptolemeus had sent to slay him also (1 Maccabees 16:21). Hearing it, John was sore astonished, and he laid hands on the men that had come to destroy him and slew them, for he knew that they sought to make him away (1 Maccabees 16:22). So the country the man had reached for was not his, and the son he had sent men to kill took his father’s place and his father’s work, and the acts of John and his wars are written in the chronicles of his priesthood from the day he was made high priest after his father (1 Maccabees 16:23-24). The teaching uses the case as a warning about who is allowed near the seat: the treachery was possible only because Ptolemeus had been given rank, wealth and a place in the family, and the record leaves his own end unwritten while it keeps writing about the house he tried to destroy.

name: Onias the high priest
text: Godliness and hatred of wickedness, so that the laws were kept very well and the city lived in peace. While Onias was high priest the holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were kept very well, because of his godliness and his hatred of wickedness, so that even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts (2 Maccabees 3:1-3). When Simon the governor of the temple could not overcome him he betrayed the treasury to the Greeks, and Onias told Heliodorus plainly that the money was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children (2 Maccabees 3:4-12). After Heliodorus was struck down, Onias prayed and offered a sacrifice for the life of the man who had come to rob him (2 Maccabees 3:31-35). He was murdered in the end by Andronicus at the persuasion of Menelaus, and the Jews and many of other nations were grieved for the unjust murder of the man (2 Maccabees 4:33-38). The verse the case turns on makes one man the reason for a city’s obedience: the laws were kept very well because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness (2 Maccabees 3:1). The teaching will not let that pass as a compliment. One man’s faith holds up other people’s faith, and the second half of the sentence is the working part: loving the Lord means hating evil (Psalms 97:10), setting no wicked thing before the eyes (Psalms 101:3), and not putting a hand to the plough to look back (Luke 9:62). The result was that even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts, and Seleucus of his own revenues bore all the cost of the sacrifices (2 Maccabees 3:2-3). The trouble came from inside. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city, and when he could not overcome Onias he told Apollonius the governor of Celosyria that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money and that it could all be brought into the king’s hand (2 Maccabees 3:4-6). The teaching calls that what it is, a friend which is only a friend in name, a companion that rejoices in the prosperity of a friend but in the time of trouble will be against him (Ecclesiasticus 37:1-4); and it is an offence against the multitude of a city, which the wisdom warns a man not to commit (Ecclesiasticus 7:7). What Simon offered to hand over was not a king’s revenue. It was the third year tithe, laid up for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:28-29), the same provision Tobit kept in Assyria (Tobit 1:6-8), and the teaching adds the reckoning we are still under, that we are subject to payments because our fathers stopped paying it (Baruch 3:8). When Heliodorus came and asked whether the report was true, the high priest did not hide it: there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and it was wrong to injure those who had committed it to the holy place (2 Maccabees 3:9-12). The first thing the record shows him doing after Heliodorus was struck down is praying for him. When the man lay speechless and his friends asked Onias to call on the Most High, the high priest offered a sacrifice for his health; and the messengers who had scourged him appeared again and told him to give Onias great thanks, since for his sake the Lord had granted him life (2 Maccabees 3:31-36). Simon answered that by slandering Onias as if he had terrified Heliodorus, and was bold to call him a traitor, a man who had deserved well of the city and was zealous of the laws (2 Maccabees 4:1-2). When the hatred went so far that murders were committed by Simon’s faction, Onias went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both public and private (2 Maccabees 4:3-6). The teaching marks the restraint: he had every cause to accuse, and went to seek the good of all. His brother Jason bought the priesthood from under him and turned the nation to the Greekish fashion; Menelaus bought it from under Jason and began to steal the vessels of gold out of the temple (2 Maccabees 4:7-10; 2 Maccabees 4:23-32). When Onias knew of it he reproved him and withdrew into a sanctuary at Daphne by Antioch; and Menelaus persuaded Andronicus to get him into his hands; Andronicus came in deceit, gave him his right hand with an oath, persuaded him out of the sanctuary, and killed him without regard of justice (2 Maccabees 4:33-34). What follows is the blessing on the man’s name. Not only the Jews but many of other nations took great indignation and were much grieved for the unjust murder; the king himself was heartily sorry and wept because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead, took away Andronicus his purple, led him through the city to the very place where he had committed the impiety, and there slew the cursed murderer, the Lord rewarding him as he had deserved (2 Maccabees 4:35-38). The teaching reads that as the report a man ought to have of them that are without (1 Timothy 3:7; 1 Thessalonians 4:12; Colossians 4:5; 1 Peter 2:12): he would not join the nations, and they still could say nothing against him. Long afterward Judas is given a dream of him, a virtuous and good man, reverend in conversation and gentle in condition, holding up his hands and praying for the whole body of the Jews (2 Maccabees 15:12-14).

name: Heliodorus
text: Attempting to plunder the temple treasury. While Onias was high priest the holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were kept very well, so that even the heathen kings honoured the temple. Simon the governor of the temple fell out with him, could not overcome him, and reported the treasury to Apollonius, so the king sent Heliodorus his treasurer to bring the money away. Onias told him it was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children and for property left in trust, and the whole city lay in sackcloth, but he went in anyway. A horse with a terrible rider and two young men struck him down at the treasury; he lived only because Onias sacrificed for him, and he went back to tell the king that anyone sent to that place as an enemy would return well scourged. The class makes a city at peace the starting point. The holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were kept very well because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness, so that even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts, and Seleucus king of Asia bore the charges of the sacrifices out of his own revenues (2 Maccabees 3:1-3). Because of the faith of one man, his strength and his love for the laws of God, everybody around him was lifted, and the nations themselves respected what he guarded. That king is the one Daniel called a raiser of taxes, who would be destroyed neither in anger nor in battle (Daniel 11:20). Then Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about the disorder of the city, and when he could not overcome him he got him to Apollonius and told him the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money; Apollonius told the king, and the king chose Heliodorus his treasurer and sent him to bring it away (2 Maccabees 3:4-7). Heliodorus took his journey under a colour of visiting the cities of Coelosyria and Phenice, but in truth to fulfil the king’s purpose, which is what everybody was told while he surveyed the temple. The class settles what that money was before it weighs the crime. Every third year the tithe of the increase was brought in so that the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow within the gates might eat and be satisfied (Deuteronomy 14:28-29), and Tobit gave the third part of his increase to those to whom it was meet, having been left an orphan himself (Tobit 1:6-8). That fund was our own relief for our own poor, and the prophet names the failure to keep it up as part of why we are this day in captivity, subject to payments (Baruch 3:8). Onias told Heliodorus that the money was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, that part of it belonged to Hircanus the son of Tobias, four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold in all, and that such a wrong could not be done to them that had committed it to the holiness of the place; Heliodorus answered that in any wise it must be brought into the king’s treasury (2 Maccabees 3:10-13). The measure the class applies is the saying that the bread of the needy is their life, and he that takes away his neighbour’s living slays him (Ecclesiasticus 34:21-22). Taking that money was murder. The priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their vestments and called to heaven, the women girt with sackcloth abounded in the streets, and the virgins ran to the gates and walls; whoever looked the high priest in the face would have been wounded in heart, because Onias was in agony knowing what the loss of that money meant for the widows and orphans of Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 3:15-21). Heliodorus executed what was decreed anyway. As he stood with his guard about the treasury, the Lord of spirits caused a great apparition: a horse with a terrible rider smote at him with his forefeet, and two young men scourged him continually, so that he fell compassed with great darkness and was carried out, unable to help himself with his weapons, and they that were with him acknowledged the power of God (2 Maccabees 3:24-28). His friends begged Onias to call on the Most High to grant him his life. The high priest, suspecting that the king might think some treachery had been done by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the health of the man, and while he was making the atonement the same young men appeared again and told Heliodorus to give Onias great thanks, since for his sake his life was granted him, and, having been scourged from heaven, to declare the mighty power of God to all men (2 Maccabees 3:31-34). When the king asked whom he might send to Jerusalem once more, he answered that an enemy or a traitor should be sent, for he would come back well scourged if he escaped with his life, because he that dwells in heaven has his eye on that place and destroys them that come to hurt it (2 Maccabees 3:35-39). The reprieve came through the prayer of the man he had been sent to rob. The history class follows him afterward: it was Heliodorus who killed the king who had sent him, exactly as Daniel had written of that king, and he was then put out of the way himself.

name: Simon the governor of the temple
text: Betraying the temple treasury to the king out of a private quarrel; slandering Onias the high priest. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin was made governor of the temple, and when he could not prevail against Onias in a quarrel over the disorder of the city he went to the nations and reported the treasury as money lying there for the king. After Heliodorus was driven off, he slandered Onias as the worker of those evils and called a traitor the man who had deserved well of the city, and murders were committed by men of his faction. Onias went to the king seeking the good of all rather than to accuse his countrymen, and the record gives no sentence upon Simon. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about the disorder of the city (2 Maccabees 3:4). The class read out what that office carried: management of the temple resources, maintenance of the temple, administration of the worship, the handling of disputes, coordination with the other authorities, and security. Whatever the dispute was, Onias as high priest had the last say. When Simon could not overcome him he got him to Apollonius, the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice, and told him the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money (2 Maccabees 3:5-6). He ran to the other nations. They were working together on that temple, and because of one argument he carried the nations against the man set over him. One man had a problem with one man, and because he could not have his way he thought to tear down the whole nation. The class measures the offense by the proverbs read with it. Every friend says he is a friend, but there is a friend which is only a friend in name, and it is a grief to death when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy (Ecclesiasticus 37:1-4). Offend not against the multitude of a city; bind not one sin upon another, for in one you shall not go unpunished; and say not that God will look upon the multitude of your offerings, as though a man may sin on purpose and be forgiven anyway (Ecclesiasticus 7:7-9). The money he exposed was for the widows, the orphans, the strangers and the Levites, and the bread of the needy is their life, so that he who takes away his neighbour’s living slays him (Ecclesiasticus 34:21-22). Three things the wise man said his heart feared are the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation, all of them worse than death (Ecclesiasticus 26:5-7). Simon did all three: he slandered the city, he gathered the Greeks to get the money out of Jerusalem, and he falsely accused Onias. When the seizure failed, Simon, having been a betrayer of the money and of his country, slandered Onias as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils, and was so bold as to call a traitor the man who had deserved well of the city, tendered his own nation and was zealous of the laws; and their hatred went so far that murders were committed by one of his faction (2 Maccabees 4:1-3). The class reading this in another year puts the killing plainly: men under Simon took it upon themselves to go and kill men who were with Onias, and they had that spirit because it was the spirit on the man over them. That is the pattern traced through the whole lesson: he coveted the upper hand, from there it turned to anger, from there to slander, and from there to murder, one sin knocking over the next. Wars and fightings come out of lusts that war in a man, who kills and desires to have and cannot obtain, and asks amiss (James 4:1-3); a man angry with his brother without a cause is in danger of the judgment, and the name calling carries the sin further (Matthew 5:21-22); and a man who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). The men who saw it and said nothing were not clear either, since a witness who hears and does not utter it bears the iniquity (Leviticus 5:1), and he that is partner with a thief hates his own soul (Proverbs 29:24). Onias, seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius as governor did rage and increase Simon’s malice, went to the king, not as an accuser of his countrymen but seeking the good of all, both publicly and privately, because he saw it was impossible for the state to continue quiet or for Simon to leave his folly unless the king looked to it (2 Maccabees 4:4-6). Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and a man is to live peaceably with all men as much as lies in him (Romans 12:18), but the qualifier is there for a reason; some spirits do not want peace, and some men cannot be reasoned with, because all men have not faith (2 Thessalonians 3:1-2). No sentence upon Simon is written. Three years afterward his brother Menelaus bought the priesthood, so that the high priest of Israel was now of the tribe of Benjamin (2 Maccabees 4:23-24), and what Simon set in motion went on working after him.

name: Jason the high priest
text: Buying the priesthood; setting up a Greek gymnasium; drawing his countrymen to heathen customs. When Antiochus called Epiphanes took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias worked underhand for the priesthood, promising the king three hundred and threescore talents of silver and more besides for licence to set up a place of exercise and train the youth in the fashions of the heathen. Having the rule, he put down the governments which were according to the law, built the gymnasium under the tower, brought the chief young men under the Greek hat, and the priests left the altar for the games. Menelaus outbid him and drove him out; he died in a strange land with no mourning and no burial with his fathers. After the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus called Epiphanes took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest, promising the king three hundred and threescore talents of silver and fourscore talents of another revenue (2 Maccabees 4:7-8). The class calls that what it is: bribery, and the priesthood goes by bloodline, so the lot had already fallen to Onias. Sometimes it is not good enough for a man to be the support brother; Jason reckoned he could do better, and would have the money besides. Look at a man’s motives. Seek not of the Lord preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour (Ecclesiasticus 7:4-5); a man who strives for masteries is not crowned except he strive lawfully (2 Timothy 2:5); the prophet numbered bribe taking among the mighty sins of the nation (Amos 5:12), and all bribery is blotted out (Ecclesiasticus 40:12). Onias already had his friend Simon turned against him. Now it was his own blood brother. He promised a hundred and fifty talents more for licence to set up a place of exercise and train the youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians (2 Maccabees 4:9). The history class puts the offer plainly: he could bring Israel into the Greek games and make them Greek, which Onias would never have done. Having got the rule, he brought his own nation to the Greek fashion, put down the governments which were according to the law, brought up new customs against the law, built a place of exercise under the tower itself, brought the chief young men under his subjection, and made them wear a hat (2 Maccabees 4:10-12). The hat was shown in class beside the statue of the discus thrower: the hat of Hermes, and gymnasium means a place to be naked. The wicked men of that time did the same, building a place of exercise at Jerusalem after the customs of the heathen, making themselves uncircumcised and forsaking the holy covenant (1 Maccabees 1:11-15); to make yourself uncircumcised is to forsake the covenant, because circumcision is the sign that a man will keep the law (Deuteronomy 10:16).
