Through Jason, that ungodly wretch and no high priest, the priests lost the courage to serve at the altar; despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices they hurried to the place of exercise when the game of discus called them, liking the glory of the Grecians better than the honours of their fathers (2 Maccabees 4:13-15). The class applies it without softening: our people love that society more than their own forefathers, and in the colleges they love Greek society best of anything. Sore calamity came of it, for they had those to be their enemies and avengers whose custom they followed and whom they desired to be like in all things; it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God (2 Maccabees 4:16-17). That is the history Paul pointed back to when he told his readers they had been carried away to dumb idols even as they were led (1 Corinthians 12:1-2). At the games at Tyre he sent silver to the sacrifice of Hercules (2 Maccabees 4:18-20). Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus to bear the money to the king, and Menelaus got the priesthood by offering three hundred talents of silver more; so Jason, who had undermined his brother, was undermined by another and fled to the Ammonites (2 Maccabees 4:23-26). On a false rumour that Antiochus was dead he came back with a thousand men and assaulted the city; Menelaus fled into the castle, and Jason slew his own citizens without mercy, thinking them enemies and not countrymen, because he despised his own people (2 Maccabees 5:5-6). The king thought Judea had revolted, and the bidder for an office became the occasion of the slaughter that followed. For all this he obtained not the principality, but received shame for his treason and fled again to the Ammonites. Accused before Aretas king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws and an open enemy of his own country, he was cast out into Egypt; he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land, and he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him, nor sepulchre with his fathers (2 Maccabees 5:7-10). The history class marks where he ran at the end: he retired to the Lacedemonians, hoping for safety by reason of kindred, since the Spartans were of the stock of Abraham (1 Maccabees 12:20-21). Even there he found nothing. Nobody likes a traitor, and all the evil he did came back on him.

name: Menelaus
text: Buying the priesthood over Jason; stealing the temple vessels; procuring the murder of Onias; bribing his way past the king’s judgment. Sent by Jason to carry money to the king, Menelaus offered three hundred talents more and took the priesthood for himself, bringing nothing worthy of the office but the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast. He stole vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some to Andronicus, and got Onias drawn out of sanctuary and killed; when accused he bought the king’s favour, and the three men who pleaded for the city were condemned instead. He guided Antiochus into the most holy temple, and was later brought to Berea and thrust into the tower of ashes, with no burial in the earth. Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of that same Simon, to bear the money to the king; being brought before him he magnified the king for the glorious appearance of his power and got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver. He came bringing nothing worthy of the high priesthood, but having the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast (2 Maccabees 4:23-25). The class marks what has now happened to the office: the high priest of Israel is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, put there by a bid, and his own brother Simon is the man who first carried the temple to the nations. He took no good order for the money he had promised, and being called to account he left his brother Lysimachus as his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:27-29). Supposing that he had a convenient time, he stole certain vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some of them to Andronicus, and sold others into Tyre and the cities round about; and when Onias knew it of a surety he reproved him and withdrew himself into a sanctuary at Daphne beside Antioch, whereupon Menelaus took Andronicus apart and prayed him to get Onias into his hands (2 Maccabees 4:32-34). After his brother’s sacrilege was answered by the people (2 Maccabees 4:39-42), an accusation was laid against Menelaus, and when the king came to Tyre three men sent from the senate pleaded the cause; but Menelaus promised Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes much money to pacify the king toward him and was discharged, while the men who followed the matter for the city, for the people and for the holy vessels were condemned to death, and even they of Tyre, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, buried them honourably. So through the covetousness of them that were in power he remained still in authority, increasing in malice and a great traitor to the citizens (2 Maccabees 4:43-50). The history class names it without softening: this is a man of Israel killing his own people for greed. When Antiochus was not content with the slaughter of the city but presumed to go into the most holy temple of all the world, Menelaus, that traitor to the laws and to his own country, was his guide (2 Maccabees 5:15). The class names that plainly: one of our own showed the other nation what to take, and the governors left behind afterward were worse than all the rest, bearing a heavy hand over his own countrymen and having a malicious mind against them (2 Maccabees 5:22-23). That is why to this day they look for the ones who will be harder on us than Esau, because they have something to prove. Even in the letters of peace that came later, when the king wrote that the nation should be at rest and have their temple restored and use their own kind of meats and laws, it was Menelaus who was named as the man declaring the people’s mind and sent to comfort them (2 Maccabees 11:29-32). The traitor was still the go-between. What became of him is not told until the thirteenth chapter. He joined himself with Antiochus Eupator and with great dissimulation encouraged him, not for the safeguard of the country but because he thought to be made ruler; but the King of kings moved the king’s mind against this wicked wretch, and when Lysias informed him that this man was the cause of all the mischief the king commanded to bring him to Berea and to put him to death there, where a tower of fifty cubits high stands full of ashes, into which whoever is condemned of sacrilege is thrust. So he died, not having so much as burial in the earth, and most justly, because he had committed many sins about the altar whose fire and ashes were holy, and he received his death in ashes (2 Maccabees 13:3-8). If he could not be high priest again he meant to be governor, and one day you are the king’s friend and the Most High says that is not your friend. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap (Galatians 6:7).

name: Andronicus
text: Murder of Onias the high priest under a sworn assurance. Andronicus was left in authority as the king’s deputy, and Menelaus had given him some of the gold vessels stolen out of the temple. When Onias reproved the theft and took sanctuary at Daphne, Menelaus took Andronicus apart and prayed him to get the high priest into his hands; he came in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary though he was suspected, and shut him up without regard of justice. The king stripped him of his purple, led him through the whole city to the place of the murder, and slew him there. Antiochus went in haste to settle a rising in Tarsus and Mallos and left Andronicus, a man in authority, for his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:30-31). Menelaus, having stolen certain vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some of them to Andronicus and sold others into Tyre and the cities round about; and when Onias knew the theft of a surety he reproved him and withdrew himself into a sanctuary at Daphne beside Antioch (2 Maccabees 4:32-33). The class showed on the map how far the high priest of Israel had to flee to be safe, out of Jerusalem and up into Syria, which is exactly what the wise man said a backbiting tongue does: it has disquieted many and driven them from nation to nation, pulled down strong cities and overthrown the houses of great men (Ecclesiasticus 28:13-15). Menelaus then took Andronicus apart and prayed him to get Onias into his hands. He came to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, and though he was suspected by him, persuaded him to come forth of the sanctuary, and shut him up immediately without regard of justice (2 Maccabees 4:34). He killed the true high priest, the man whose godliness had kept the city in peace (2 Maccabees 3:1), the man seen afterward in the vision holding up his hands and praying for the whole body of the Jews, virtuous and good, reverend in conversation, gentle in condition, well spoken, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue (2 Maccabees 15:12-14). Not only the Jews but many also of other nations took great indignation and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man (2 Maccabees 4:35), because Onias had a good report even among the nations. The class draws the standard for office out of that: a man must have a good report of them which are without (1 Timothy 3:7), walk honestly toward them that are without (1 Thessalonians 4:12), walk in wisdom toward them (Colossians 4:5), and keep his conversation honest among the Gentiles, so that they who speak against him as an evildoer may see his good works (1 Peter 2:12). Onias had that report without ever joining himself to them. When the king came back and heard the complaint he was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger he took away the purple from Andronicus, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city to that very place where he had committed the impiety against Onias, and there slew the cursed murderer (2 Maccabees 4:37-38). The record calls that the Lord rewarding him his punishment as he had deserved. The class set the plain sayings beside it. For the work of a man shall he render to him, and cause every man to find according to his ways (Job 34:11). He that does wrong shall receive for the wrong which he has done, and there is no respect of persons (Colossians 3:25). God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap; it might not be this year, and it might be next year, but it is coming (Galatians 6:7). The oath and the offered right hand were what drew the victim out of safety, and they did not cover the man who gave them. The king who had been served by the murder was the one who carried out the sentence, and he carried it out on the spot where the murder was done.

name: Lysimachus
text: Sacrilege: robbing the temple with Menelaus’ consent. Left as his brother’s deputy, Lysimachus committed many sacrileges in the city by the consent of Menelaus, and much gold was already carried away when the report of it spread. The multitude gathered against him, and he armed about three thousand men and began the violence himself, with an old man named Auranus leading them. The people answered with stones, clubs and handfuls of dust, wounded and scattered the force, and killed the temple robber beside the treasury. Menelaus, called to account for the money he had promised the king, left his brother Lysimachus in his place as his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:29). The temple was handed to the same house that had already sold it, and the brother of the man who first betrayed the treasury was now guarding the door of it. Many sacrileges were committed in the city by Lysimachus with the consent of Menelaus, and the report of it was spread abroad, many vessels of gold being already carried away (2 Maccabees 4:39). The history class puts it bluntly: this man was robbing the place openly, and the gold was gone before anyone moved. When the multitude gathered themselves together against him, the common people rose filled with rage, and Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began first to offer violence, Auranus being the leader of them, a man far gone in years and no less in folly (2 Maccabees 4:40). An old man, the class said, and evil with it; age had taught him nothing. Rather than restore what was taken, the plunderer answered the protest of his own countrymen with an army of three thousand. They that saw the attempt of Lysimachus caught up stones, and others clubs, and some took handfuls of dust that was next at hand and cast them all together upon Lysimachus and those that set upon them; many of them they wounded, some they struck to the ground, and all of them they forced to flee. As for the temple robber himself, him they killed beside the treasury (2 Maccabees 4:41-42). The people had no weapons and used what was under their feet. The place he had plundered was the place where his hired force could no longer keep him. The corruption did not die with him. Of these matters an accusation was laid against Menelaus, and when the king came to Tyre three men sent from the senate pleaded the cause before him; but Menelaus, being convicted, promised Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes much money to pacify the king toward him and was discharged, while they that followed the matter for the city, for the people and for the holy vessels were condemned to death, and they of Tyre, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, buried them honourably (2 Maccabees 4:43-49). So through the covetousness of them that were in power Menelaus remained still in authority (2 Maccabees 4:50). The man who guarded the sacrilege with soldiers fell at the treasury; the man who bought the king kept the office. The history class reads the whole run of it as one covetousness working its way through a single family until every man in it was dead in disgrace.

name: Eleazar the scribe
text: Choosing to die gloriously rather than eat swine’s flesh, or pretend to, at ninety years old. When the king sent to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, Eleazar, one of the principal scribes and an aged man, was forced to open his mouth to eat swine’s flesh and spat it out, choosing to die gloriously rather than live stained. His old acquaintance offered him a way out: bring his own lawful meat and only appear to eat the king’s. He refused, so that no young person should think that Eleazar at ninety years old had gone over to a strange religion, and he went to the torment and died, leaving his death as an example to the nation. The king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and to pollute the temple at Jerusalem and call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius (2 Maccabees 6:1-2). It was no longer lawful for a man to keep the sabbath days or the ancient feasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Jew, and on the day of the king’s birth every month they were brought by bitter constraint to eat of the sacrifices (2 Maccabees 6:6-7). The class marks what that programme really was: suppression of identity. Do not keep the feast days, do not circumcise your children, do not say what you are, to the end that we might forget the law; and if a man could not profess himself a Jew, what was he called instead. Eleazar, one of the principal scribes, an aged man and of a well favoured countenance, was constrained to open his mouth and eat swine’s flesh; he spat it out and came of his own accord to the torment, choosing rather to die gloriously than to live stained with such an abomination (2 Maccabees 6:18-19). The class explains why they picked him: he was one of the main men of that time, and the people looked to him for strength and guidance, so corrupting him in front of everybody would corrupt the whole nation at once. His stand is the same answer Mattathias gave, that though all the nations under the king fell away every one from the religion of their fathers, he and his sons would walk in the covenant of their fathers and not go from their religion, to the right hand or the left (1 Maccabees 2:19-22). Our religion is keeping the commandments. They that had the charge of that wicked feast, being his old acquaintance, took him aside and urged him to bring flesh of his own provision, such as was lawful for him to use, and make as if he did eat of the king’s meat, that in so doing he might be delivered from death (2 Maccabees 6:21-22). The meat would have been clean; only the appearance would have been a lie, and the appearance was the whole point of the exercise. He began to consider discreetly, as became his age and the excellency of his ancient years, the honour of his gray head, and his most honest education from a child in the holy law made and given by God, and told them straightway to send him to the grave (2 Maccabees 6:23-24). It did not become his age in any wise to dissemble, so that many young persons should think that Eleazar, being fourscore years old and ten, was now gone to a strange religion. Ninety years old, and he would not so much as pretend, because the old are the example the younger generation copies. The class sets his answer beside the charge to Timothy, that a man continuing in the doctrine saves himself and them that hear him (1 Timothy 4:15-16), and beside the proverb that the just man walks in his integrity and his children are blessed after him (Proverbs 20:7). He added that if he were delivered for the present from the punishment of men, he could not escape the hand of the Almighty, alive or dead (2 Maccabees 6:26). They that led him changed the good will they bore him into hatred, because the words he spoke proceeded, as they thought, from a desperate mind. Ready to die with stripes he groaned and said that he suffered grievous pains in body from the beating, but in soul was well content to suffer these things because he feared God (2 Maccabees 6:29-30). So he died, leaving his death for an example of noble courage and a memorial of virtue, not only to young men but to all his nation (2 Maccabees 6:31). The class set that end beside what Esdras saw: a great multitude upon mount Sion praising the Lord with songs, and in the midst of them a young man of high stature, taller than all the rest, setting crowns upon their heads, because it is the Son of God whom they confessed in the world; these are they that have put off the mortal clothing and put on the immortal, and the commendation is for those who stood so stiffly for the name of the Lord (2 Esdras 2:42-47). That is what Eleazar was doing. He was not going to go against the commandments of God, and the record keeps his name for it. Not long after, Judas Maccabeus gathered about six thousand men and called upon the Lord, and the persecution this old man refused to bow to began to break (2 Maccabees 8:1-5).

name: The seven brethren and their mother
text: Refusing to taste swine’s flesh under torture, seven times over, in hope of the resurrection. Seven brothers and their mother were taken and compelled by the king, against the law, to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips when they refused. Each chose death rather than transgress the laws of the fathers, and each spoke to the king before he died, of the correction of their own people, of the resurrection, and of the punishment waiting for the persecutor. Their mother saw all seven slain within the space of one day and bore it with good courage, exhorting every one of them in her own language, and she died last of all. Seven brethren with their mother were taken and compelled by the king, against the law, to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips when they would not (2 Maccabees 7:1-2). One of them spoke for the rest: they were ready to die rather than transgress the laws of their fathers. The class asked the question the record puts to us now, why swine’s flesh is all through the church today, when these are the ones who stood stiffly for the law and died for it. It also weighed what that answer costs: you truly cannot desire anything left in this world. We are already captives, with the bills and the fourteen hour days; what is it you are leaving behind? There has to be something better. The king and they that were with him marvelled at the young man’s courage (2 Maccabees 7:12). They marvel, the class said, because they understand there is a certain spirit in these people, something they know. The brothers answered in turn while they watched what was done to the ones before them. The fourth told the king it is good, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God to be raised up again by him, and that for the persecutor there would be no resurrection to life (2 Maccabees 7:14). The sixth told him not to be deceived without cause, for they suffered these things for themselves, having sinned against their God, but that he who strives against God should not think to escape unpunished (2 Maccabees 7:18-19). The mother was marvellous above all, and worthy of honourable memory, for she saw her seven sons slain within the space of one day and bore it with good courage because of the hope that she had in the Lord. She exhorted every one of them in her own language, filled with a courageous spirit, and took no credit for them: she neither gave them breath nor life, neither was it she that formed the members of every one of them, but the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man and found out the beginning of all things, would also of his own mercy give them breath and life again (2 Maccabees 7:20-23). The class reads her as the pattern for a house. Children are to be nurtured in the law (2 Esdras 8:12), and fathers are charged not to provoke them to wrath but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). What she had put in them from childhood is what stood up under the whips. The hope is written plainly in their own answers. The King of the world would raise up those who die for his laws to everlasting life (2 Maccabees 7:9). That is the hope Daniel wrote of, that they who sleep in the dust of the earth awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt, and that they who turn many to righteousness shine as the stars (Daniel 12:2-3), and the reason a man is told to fear the one able to destroy both soul and body rather than them that kill the body (Matthew 10:28). The class drew the mercy of God out of the other half of the fourth brother’s answer: what kind of mercy would it be if the same people who tormented us received an equal reward in the kingdom? That is not a merciful God, if he allows them to do that to us and then gives them the same portion. The youngest was offered riches, happiness and the friendship of the king, and the mother was called to counsel him; she bowed herself toward the tyrant, laughed him to scorn, and spoke to her son in her own country language instead, telling him not to fear the tormentor but to take his death as his brethren had (2 Maccabees 7:24-29). Last of all, after the sons, the mother died (2 Maccabees 7:41). Nothing in the account promises that the torments would stop short of death. What it promises is that the One who formed them will form them again, and the record keeps the whole household as one witness to it (Hebrews 11:35-38).

name: Timotheus
text: Gathering the heathen to root out the Jews; a second campaign after being once spared. Timotheus was captain of the heathen forces gathered to root out the Jews, and he was beaten in the field more than once, gathering another host each time, hiring the Arabians, and at last bringing foreign forces and horses out of Asia to take Judea by arms. Judas and his company answered him with prayer, sackcloth and earth upon their heads before they took up their weapons. His army was destroyed, he fled to the stronghold at Gazara, and when it was taken he was found hidden in a pit and killed with his brother. The campaign begins with the temple. When the nations round about heard that the altar was built and the sanctuary renewed as before, it displeased them very much, so they thought to destroy the generation of Jacob that was among them and began to slay and destroy the people (1 Maccabees 5:1-2). The history class sets that beside the same thing in the Persian captivity: when the walls of Jerusalem were made up and the breaches began to be stopped, Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabians and the Ammonites were very wroth and conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem (Nehemiah 4:7-9). The temple was the sign of our connection to our God, and its renewal is exactly what angered them. Judas passed over to the children of Ammon, where he found a mighty power and much people with Timotheus their captain, and fought many battles with them (1 Maccabees 5:6-8). Then the heathen at Galaad assembled themselves together against the Israelites that were in their quarters, to destroy them, with Timotheus as captain of their host, and those who fled to the fortress at Dathema sent letters to Judas and his brethren saying that many of them were already slain and that the enemy was coming to take the stronghold (1 Maccabees 5:9-13). Simon was sent into Galilee and Judas and Jonathan into Gilead. When the battle was begun and the cry of the city went up to heaven, Judas told his host to fight that day for their brethren, and the host of Timotheus, knowing that it was Maccabeus, fled from him, and about eight thousand men were killed of them that day (1 Maccabees 5:30-34). Being beaten, he gathered another host, hired the Arabians to help him, and pitched beyond the brook, ready to come and fight (1 Maccabees 5:37-39). Beaten again, he gathered a great multitude of foreign forces and horses out of Asia not a few, and came as though he would take Jewry by force of arms. When he drew near, they that were with Maccabeus turned themselves to pray, sprinkled earth upon their heads, girded their loins with sackcloth, fell down at the foot of the altar, and besought God to be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, as the law declares (2 Maccabees 10:24-26). The history class sets the two sides against each other: the one part had their courage and their refuge in the Lord, and the other side made their own rage the leader of their battle. There were slain of the footmen twenty thousand and five hundred, and six hundred horsemen; and Timotheus himself fled into a strong hold called Gazara, where Chereas was governor. They that were with Maccabeus laid siege to the fortress four days, and they that were within, trusting to the strength of the place, blasphemed exceedingly and uttered wicked words. Upon the fifth day early, twenty young men of Maccabeus’ company, inflamed with anger because of the blasphemies, assaulted the wall manfully, and others likewise ascending after them burnt the towers and kindled fires and burnt the blasphemers alive, while others broke open the gates. They killed Timotheus, who was hid in a certain pit, and Chereas his brother, with Apollophanes; and when this was done they praised the Lord with psalms and thanksgiving, who had done so great things for Israel and given them the victory (2 Maccabees 10:28-38). The governors named afterward, who would not suffer the people to be quiet and live in peace, include a man of the same name (2 Maccabees 12:2). The history class settles it at that point: the Timotheus of the tenth chapter is dead, and this is a different man. That second commander fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, and talked his way out with much craft, because he held many of the parents and brethren of the Jews and could tell them that if he were put to death they would never be found again; so on his undertaking to restore them without hurt they let him go for the saving of their brethren (2 Maccabees 12:24-25). The class calls that his trump card. Two captains of the same name, two outcomes; and in both, what was gathered against Judah failed of its purpose, and the pit a man digs for others is the net his own foot is taken in (Psalms 9:15-16).

name: The men of Joppa
text: Drowning two hundred of the Jews that dwelt among them, under a pretence of peace. The men of Joppa asked the Jews who dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into boats they had prepared, as though they meant them no hurt. The Jews accepted according to the common decree of the city, desiring to live in peace and suspecting nothing, and when they were out in the deep no less than two hundred of them were drowned. Judas called upon God the righteous Judge, burned the haven and the boats by night, and dealt with Jamnia the same way when he learned they intended the like. The case stands at a moment of settled peace. The covenants had been made, Lysias had gone up to the king, and the Jews were about their husbandry (2 Maccabees 12:1). But the governors of the several places would not suffer them to be quiet and live in peace (2 Maccabees 12:2). The history class reads that verse as the standing history of our people among the nations: they do not want us living peaceably among them, and when we are left to ourselves and begin to prosper they are angered. It named Black Wall Street and Rosewood in the same breath as Joppa. The men of Joppa did an ungodly deed: they prayed the Jews that dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into the boats which they had prepared, as though they had meant them no hurt (2 Maccabees 12:3). The class gives the setting that made it work. Joppa was a port, and the sailing went by a common decree of the city, so there was nothing in the request that looked out of the ordinary. They accepted it according to the common decree of the city, being desirous to live in peace and suspecting nothing. When they were gone forth into the deep, the men of Joppa drowned no less than two hundred of them (2 Maccabees 12:4). The boats that carried them were the murder, and the wives and the children went out in them. When Judas heard of the cruelty done to his countrymen, he had his men make ready, called on God the righteous Judge, and came against the murderers of his brethren: he burned the harbour by night, set the boats on fire and killed those who had fled there, and because the town was shut against him he withdrew, meaning to return and root out the whole city of Joppa (2 Maccabees 12:5-7). The prayer came before the weapons did, and the class marks that order as the whole difference between this campaign and a reprisal. He heard also that they of Jamnia were minded to do the like to the Jews that dwelt among them, so he came upon the Jamnites by night and set fire on the haven and the navy, so that the light of the fire was seen at Jerusalem two hundred and forty furlongs off (2 Maccabees 12:8-9). He went through the places where our people were living among the nations and were being set upon, and he did not wait for the second city to carry out what it had planned. Nine furlongs further on their journey, no fewer than five thousand men on foot and five hundred horsemen of the Arabians set upon them; there was a very sore battle, and the side of Judas got the victory by the help of God, so that the Arabians, being overcome, besought him for peace and promised to give him cattle, and Judas, thinking they would be profitable in many things, granted them peace, and they shook hands and departed (2 Maccabees 12:10-12). The appeal to the righteous Judge reached the deed already done, the plan to repeat it, and the ambush laid on the road afterward; and where the nation that met them asked for peace instead of pretending it, peace was given.

name: Judas’ soldiers with idol tokens under their coats
text: Carrying things consecrated to idols into battle. After the fight with Gorgias, Judas and his company kept the sabbath at Odollam and came the day following to take up their dead and bury them with their kinsmen. Under the coat of every slain man they found things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which the law forbids the Jews, and every man then saw why they had been slain. They praised the righteous Judge who had opened the things that were hid, prayed that the sin might be put out of remembrance, and Judas sent two thousand drachms of silver to Jerusalem for a sin offering. When they that were with Gorgias had fought long and were weary, Judas called upon the Lord to show himself their helper and leader of the battle, began in his own language and sang songs with a loud voice, and rushing unawares upon the men of Gorgias put them to flight (2 Maccabees 12:36-37). He gathered his host and came into the city of Odollam, and when the seventh day came they purified themselves as the custom was and kept the sabbath in that place (2 Maccabees 12:38). Wherever they were, and whatever had happened the day before, they kept the sabbath. Upon the day following, as the use had been, Judas and his company came to take up the bodies of them that were slain and to bury them with their kinsmen in their fathers’ graves; and under the coats of every one that was slain they found things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which is forbidden the Jews by the law. Then every man saw that this was the reason they had been killed (2 Maccabees 12:39-40). Men inside the army of Israel were carrying idols under their clothes. The class draws the plain reason for the losses out of it: he was losing men because some of the men he lost were in the midst of that evil. The law had said the graven images of the gods of the nations were to be burnt with fire, and that a man was not to desire the silver or gold on them nor take it, lest he be snared by it and become a cursed thing (Deuteronomy 7:25-26); Israel had already lost a battle at Ai over one accursed thing taken at Jericho, and was told that they could not stand before their enemies until it was taken away (Joshua 6:18; Joshua 7:11-13). All men therefore praised the Lord, the righteous Judge, who had opened the things that were hid, and betook themselves to prayer, beseeching him that the sin committed might wholly be put out of remembrance (2 Maccabees 12:41-42). The class reads that as mercy asked for men who had been caught in idolatry and yet had died fighting for their people. Judas also exhorted the people to keep themselves from sin, for so much as they saw before their eyes the things that came to pass for the sins of those that were slain. He made a gathering throughout the company to the sum of two thousand drachms of silver and sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sin offering, doing therein very well and honestly in that he was mindful of the resurrection; for if he had not hoped that they that were slain should have risen again, it had been superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. He perceived that there was great favour laid up for those that died godly, and it was a holy and good thought, and he made a reconciliation for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43-45). The class weighs that wording carefully. The record calls it a good thought, and a good thought is not a guarantee; Judas could not promise the kingdom to a man who died in the middle of that sin, and no man can. He prayed and hoped, the way David fasted and prayed for the child while there was still hope (2 Samuel 12:22), because he knew out of the prophet that they who sleep in the dust of the earth awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt (Daniel 12:2). The class also answers the use that is made of this passage against the apocrypha, that praying for the dead proves the writer was a pagan. The offering went to Jerusalem for the living as much as for the dead, and the exhortation bound up with it is that the men still standing keep themselves from the same sin. The exposure brought warning to the living and intercession for the dead in one act.

name: Joseph, the husband of Mary
text: A just man; doing as the angel of the Lord bade him, four times, without a word recorded. Joseph stands in the record as the husband of Mary and the last name in the king’s line that runs through Zerubbabel, the heir to a throne he could not sit on because the nation was in captivity. Betrothed to a woman found with child, and a just man, he meant to put her away privately rather than make her a public example, and when the angel told him in a dream whose the child was he took her. He was told to flee into Egypt and went by night, told to return and returned, warned again and turned aside into Galilee, and he kept the circumcision, the purification and the yearly passover for the child according to the law. Scripture records nothing he said, only what he did. Matthew runs the line from the captivity down, from Jechonias to Salathiel to Zorobabel, and on through the generations to Jacob, the father of Joseph the husband of Mary (Matthew 1:12-16). The class works that line carefully, because it settles who Joseph was: it is Solomon’s line, the king’s line, and Zerubbabel stands in the middle of it. God said he would bring forth his servant the Branch, and that Zerubbabel would bring forth the headstone (Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 4:7); Zerubbabel laid the foundation of the second temple, and through his loins brought forth the stone the builders refused, the head of the corner (Psalms 118:22; Ephesians 2:20-22). Joseph was therefore heir to the throne of David and could not sit on it, because Rome ruled and had set an Edomite over Judea instead. Luke reckons the same man through Heli (Luke 3:23), and the class settles why there are two lines: Luke comes down through Nathan and not through Solomon, and no man has two fathers’ fathers. Heli was Mary’s father and had no sons, so his son in law was written in the record as his son, as Tobias inherited the substance of Raguel, who had only a daughter (Tobit 14:13). That marriage had been arranged by her father long before. Betrothed to a woman found with child, and being a just man, he would not make her a public example but was minded to put her away privately; and when the angel of the Lord appeared in a dream and told him not to fear taking Mary as his wife, he did as he was bidden, and took her (Matthew 1:18-25). Then a decree from Caesar Augustus sent every man to his own city to be taxed, and he went from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David (Luke 2:1-5). The verse by verse class marks two things in that journey. Paying tribute to a foreign king is the proof of captivity, which is why the prophet wrote that we are yet this day in our captivity, subject to payments, and why Christ said the children are free and the strangers pay the tribute (Baruch 3:8; Matthew 17:24-26). And it explains how a man of Judah came to live in Galilee: that was Naphtali’s portion, emptied in the Assyrian captivity and joined to Judea again in the days of the Maccabees (Tobit 1:1-2; 1 Maccabees 10:30). The angel told him to take the young child and his mother into Egypt, because Herod would seek the child to destroy him, and he arose and took them by night (Matthew 2:13-14). The study notes make the point about that hiding: they hid among the Egyptians, and a family that did not look like the people of that land would have been no more hidden there than anywhere. Told to return, he came into the land of Israel; hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in his father’s room he was afraid to go there, and being warned of God in a dream he turned aside into Galilee and dwelt in Nazareth, a town with no reputation (Matthew 2:19-23; John 1:45-46). The prophet’s word, that God called his son out of Egypt, was written long before that flight, and the return fulfilled it (Matthew 2:15; Hosea 11:1). The study notes call it twofold: Israel came out of Egypt, and the son came out after. Protection came to that household as instructions Joseph had to carry out, by night, with a ruler hunting the child. The house kept the law for the child it was given. On the eighth day he was circumcised and named as the angel had said, as the law appoints for a man child (Luke 2:21; Leviticus 12:2-3). When the days of purifying were fulfilled, seven days and thirty and three more, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, forty days in all (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:4-6); he was born under the law, and everything done for him was done after it (Galatians 4:4-5). They returned into Galilee to Nazareth (Luke 2:39), and went up every year at the passover, as the law required of the men three times in the year (Luke 2:41; Deuteronomy 16:16). The class marks that he was twelve at a passover, and that the custom of the feast was the feast, not a birthday. He was subject to them, and increased in wisdom and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:51-52). By the time of the cross Joseph was gone, and Christ committed his mother to the disciple he loved (John 19:25-27). The promise concerning the child was never treated in that house as leave to let the commandments go undone.

name: Herod the Great and the children of Bethlehem
text: Slaying all the male children of Bethlehem from two years old and under. Herod was set over Judea by Rome and was an Edomite, not of Israel, and when the wise men asked after the one born King of the Jews he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. He got the birthplace out of the chief priests, enquired privately after the time of the star, and sent the wise men to search under a pretence that he also wished to worship. When they did not come back he was exceeding wroth and slew all the children in Bethlehem and its coasts from two years old and under. Matthew reports his death and no sentence explaining it, and joins the mourning to Jeremiah’s word about Rachel. Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, and wise men came from the east to Jerusalem asking where he was that is born King of the Jews, and when Herod heard it he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matthew 2:1-3). The study notes press the reason: Herod was set up as king over Judea by Rome, and he was an Edomite, not of Israel. If the messiah were coming to save all nations, there would be nothing in his birth to trouble a ruler of the nations. He is troubled because the messiah coming to Israel means judgment on those who hold Israel down. The class traces the house behind the name. Antipater, a native of Idumea, founded the Herodian dynasty and was the father of Herod; he rose under the later Hasmonean kings, became a client of Pompey, was made chief minister of Judea by Julius Caesar, and set his sons over Jerusalem and Galilee. That family had converted to Judaism, so they were schooled in the customs and prophecies of Israel without being of Israel, and the Herodians of the gospels were that same stock, the ones spoken of as saying they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9). Herod married a Hasmonean princess to give himself a claim and then killed her, and destroyed the old priestly line and the men who might have been rivals. The history class puts it sharply: this is the man who now says he also wishes to worship the child. He gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people and demanded of them where Christ should be born, and they answered at once out of the prophet, Bethlehem of Judea (Matthew 2:4-6; Micah 5:2). They knew the scriptures concerning the messiah, and the same men who could quote where he would be born were blinded when he walked among them; Israel obtained not that which he sought for, and the rest were blinded (Romans 11:7-10). Then Herod called the wise men privily, enquired what time the star appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem to search for the young child and bring him word, saying that he would come and worship also (Matthew 2:7-8). What he did next showed what he had in mind. Being warned of God in a dream, they departed into their own country another way (Matthew 2:12); and when Herod saw that he was mocked of the wise men, he was exceeding wroth, and sent forth and slew all the children in Bethlehem and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired (Matthew 2:16). The history class explains the age he chose: the star had been standing out about two years, so he killed every child of two years and under in hope that the messiah was among them; that is why Luke shows an infant and Matthew a child already walking. The study notes set the pattern beside Egypt, where the ruler charged that every son born be cast into the river, the same attempt to cut off a deliverer before he could rise (Exodus 1:22), and beside the great red dragon standing before the woman ready to be delivered, to devour her child as soon as it was born (Revelation 12:3-4), that dragon being the old serpent, the Devil and Satan (Revelation 12:9), and red the colour Esau was born (Genesis 25:25). The design failed. The angel had already told Joseph to take the young child and his mother into Egypt, and he departed by night and remained there until the death of Herod, so that the prophet’s word, that God called his son out of Egypt, was fulfilled (Matthew 2:13-15; Hosea 11:1). When Herod was dead the angel told Joseph to return to the land of Israel, because they were dead which sought the young child’s life (Matthew 2:19-20). Matthew reports the death of the king and nothing of the manner of it, and he pronounces no separate sentence upon him. What Matthew does set down is the mourning, written beforehand by Jeremiah: a voice heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they were not (Matthew 2:17-18; Jeremiah 31:15). The ruler died and the promised child lived. The children of Bethlehem were still murdered, and neither the failure of the plot nor the fulfilling of the prophecy touches the guilt of the hand that shed their blood; hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-17), and the man that takes reward to slay an innocent person is under the curse pronounced before all the people (Deuteronomy 27:25).

name: John the Baptist
text: Telling a king it is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife. John came preaching repentance in the wilderness of Judea, in the raiment and the spirit of Elijah, and demanded the works that go with repentance from the crowds, the publicans, the soldiers and the rulers alike. He took no title for himself, confessing that he was not the Christ but the voice sent before him. He told Herod the tetrarch that it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife and was imprisoned for it, and at a birthday feast the king, for his oath’s sake, sent the executioner. Christ called him more than a prophet, and named him the Elias that was to come. John the Baptist preached in the wilderness of Judea, saying repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand; he is the messenger the prophets said would go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah (Matthew 3:1-2; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5-6). His raiment of camel’s hair and the leathern girdle about his loins were Elijah’s manner, marking him as of the same spirit (2 Kings 1:8). The voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord is Isaiah’s word spoken of him (Isaiah 40:3-5). They were baptized of him in Jordan confessing their sins, which the study notes mark as more than a dipping in water; a man must be taught the law to know what he is confessing (Matthew 3:5-6). To the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism he said to bring forth fruits meet for repentance, and not to say within themselves that they had Abraham to their father, since God can raise up his children of stones (Matthew 3:7-9). The study notes settle what those fruits are: works, the same works Paul preached (Acts 26:20). Descent from Abraham without the works of Abraham counts for nothing, and those works are to believe God and keep his commandments, his charge, his statutes and his laws (Genesis 26:5; John 8:39). The works he named were practical: a man with two coats to give to the man with none, the publicans to exact no more than was appointed, the soldiers to do violence to none, accuse none falsely, and be content with their wages (Luke 3:10-14). He took no title, confessing that he was not the Christ, nor Elias, nor that prophet, but the voice in the wilderness (John 1:19-23). His own baptism with water was not the baptism of the one coming after him, who would baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire, gathering the wheat and burning the chaff (Luke 3:16-17; Psalms 1:4). The class ties that promise to the commandments: the Comforter is given to them that obey him and brings the words of Christ to remembrance (John 14:15-16; John 14:26; Acts 5:32). He reproved the ruler as plainly as the crowds, telling Herod the tetrarch that it was not lawful for him to have his brother Philip’s wife, and reproving him for all the evils he had done (Mark 6:17-18; Luke 3:19; Leviticus 18:16; Leviticus 20:21). The class marks who that ruler was: an Idumean, a convert raised in the customs of the Jews and set over Judea, who knew the law well enough to be accused by it (Acts 26:3). John rebuked him anyway, and Herod added this above all, that he shut him up in prison (Luke 3:20). Herod feared John, knowing him a just man and holy, and heard him gladly; Herodias had a quarrel against him and would have killed him, but could not (Mark 6:19-20). At the birthday feast the oath was made before the guests, the girl asked her mother what to ask and was told to ask the head of John the Baptist, and the king, exceeding sorry, sent the executioner for his oath’s sake (Mark 6:21-29). The killing was no sentence of God upon John. A ruler who knew him righteous valued his own word above a righteous man’s blood. From the prison John sent two disciples to ask whether Jesus was he that should come, and Christ answered by the works, quoting Isaiah: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have the gospel preached to them (Matthew 11:2-6; Isaiah 35:5-6). He then asked the multitude what they went out into the wilderness to see: not a reed shaken with the wind nor a man in soft clothing, but a prophet, and more than a prophet, the messenger sent before the face of the Lord (Matthew 11:7-10). Among them born of women none greater had risen, and yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater; the law and the prophets prophesied until John, and he is the Elias that was to come (Matthew 11:11-14). The class carries that word past the grave. The disciples were told that Elias had come already, and that men knew him not but did to him whatever they wished, and they understood he spoke of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:10-13). A short time later, on the mount, two men talked with Christ in glory, and they were Moses and Elias (Luke 9:28-31). The man beheaded in a prison was standing there, comforting the one he had been sent before, which is the promise Christ made to the living, that a man believing in him shall never die (John 11:25-26). The executioner ended the ministry and did not end the man.

name: The centurion of Capernaum
text: Loving the nation and building the synagogue; not counting himself worthy that the Lord should come under his roof: speak the word only. A centurion at Capernaum had a servant who was dear to him and ready to die, and he sent elders of the Jews to plead for him; they said of him that he loved their nation and had built them their synagogue. He himself sent word that he was not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof, and asked him to say the word only, reasoning from the authority he himself exercised over soldiers and servants. Christ marvelled and said he had not found so great faith, no, not in Israel, and the servant was found whole. When Christ had ended all his sayings in the audience of the people he entered into Capernaum (Luke 7:1). The verse by verse class begins with where that is, because it settles who the man in this case is. Capernaum lies upon the sea coast in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim, the country the prophet calls Galilee of the Gentiles, which is the northern kingdom of Israel and not another nation (Matthew 4:13-16; Isaiah 9:1-2). Christ came there when Nazareth thrust him out (Luke 4:28-31), and he said plainly in that same gospel that he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24). A certain centurion’s servant, who was dear to him, was sick and ready to die, and when he heard of Jesus he sent elders of the Jews to plead for him; and they besought him instantly, saying that the man was worthy for whom he should do this, for he loved their nation and had built them a synagogue (Luke 7:2-5). A centurion is a man set over a hundred soldiers, which is how two of them could be told to make ready two hundred men (Acts 23:23), and this one had the standing and the means to build the people a sanctuary. The class reads him as one of our own, a commandment keeping man of the scattered northern kingdom, and sets him beside Cornelius the centurion of the Italian band, a devout man who feared God with all his house, gave much alms to the people, and whose prayers and alms came up for a memorial before God (Acts 10:1-4). That is the test the class applies: God hears not sinners, but if a man be a worshipper of God and does his will, him he hears (John 9:31). And what both men did with what they had is exactly what the rich are charged to do, not to be highminded nor to trust in uncertain riches, but to be rich in good works, ready to distribute (1 Timothy 6:17-18). He did not rest the petition on that commendation. When Jesus was not far from the house he sent friends to say that he was not worthy that he should enter under his roof, and that he had not thought himself worthy even to come out to him, but to say in a word, and his servant would be healed. He gave his reason out of the thing he knew: he was himself a man set under authority, having soldiers under him, and he said to one to go and he went, and to another to come and he came, and to his servant to do this and he did it (Luke 7:6-8). The class marks the humility in a man who could move a hundred soldiers and would not walk up to Christ himself: the fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom, and before honour is humility (Proverbs 15:33), and all are to be subject one to another and clothed with humility, because God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5-6). When Jesus heard these things he marvelled at him, and turned about and said to the people that followed him that he had not found so great faith, no, not in Israel (Luke 7:9). They that were sent returned to the house and found the servant whole that had been sick (Luke 7:10), and Matthew sets down that he was healed in the selfsame hour (Matthew 8:13). The class answers the reading that makes this a heathen praised above Israel: the town is in Zabulon and Nephthalim, the elders of the Jews carried his petition, and he had built the synagogue the nation worshipped in. Matthew tells the same account with the centurion himself speaking to Christ (Matthew 8:5-10), and the class settles the apparent contradiction with a rule taken out of the record itself. What one man does by another, he does by himself. The friends and the servants who carried the words were the very men he commanded to go and to come, so the words are his words whoever carried them; and the Lord said he would save his people Israel out of the hand of the Philistines by the hand of his servant David, though David did it with an army under him (2 Samuel 3:18). What is praised here is the faith, and what answered it was a word spoken at a distance, to a house Christ never entered.

name: Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum
text: Not repenting after the mighty works done in them. Most of Christ’s mighty works were done in Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, and those cities did not repent. He upbraided them and measured them against Tyre, Sidon and Sodom, saying those cities would have repented at what these had seen, and that it would be more tolerable for them in the day of judgment. Capernaum, which had been exalted to heaven, was to be brought down to hell. Luke sets the same woes beside the sending of the seventy and the rule that to despise the messenger is to despise the one who sent him. When John was cast into prison Christ departed into Galilee, left Nazareth, and came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim, and from that time he began to preach the same word John had preached, that men should repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matthew 4:13-17). The study notes mark what the prophet calls that country: Galilee of the Gentiles (Isaiah 9:1-2). Zabulon and Nephthalim are tribes of the northern kingdom, and that is the key to who the gentiles are that the gospel goes to after the southern kingdom rejects it. These towns were not outsiders looking on. They were where the ministry lived. Then he began to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not. Woe to Chorazin and woe to Bethsaida, for if the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. And Capernaum, which was exalted to heaven, would be brought down to hell, for if the mighty works done in her had been done in Sodom, it would have remained to that day (Matthew 11:20-24). The study notes put the charge in plain terms: men watched works no ordinary man could do and still would not turn, and other nations would have turned at what Israel watched and did not turn at. That is what a stiffnecked people looks like. Christ said the same thing another way, that if he had not come and spoken to them they had not had sin, but now they have no cloke for their sin (John 15:22-24). It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment than for Chorazin and Bethsaida, and more tolerable for the land of Sodom than for Capernaum (Matthew 11:20-24). The comparison takes away the comfort of measuring yourself against a city with a worse name; the greater the light given, the greater the reckoning for it. The class is careful about the timing: the judgment spoken of here is the one at the return of Christ, not a report that every part of the sentence had already fallen. And that is why the epistle asks how a man shall escape if he neglects so great salvation, spoken first by the Lord and confirmed by them that heard him (Hebrews 2:1-3). Luke sets the same woes beside the sending out of the seventy, whom the Lord appointed and sent two and two before his face into every city and place where he himself would come (Luke 10:1-2). The class explains the pairing out of the law: no matter is established except at the mouth of two or three witnesses, so the men were sent in twos because they were being sent to bear witness, and to bear witness against a city is to bring judgment on it. Where they were received they said that the kingdom of God is come nigh; where they were not received they were to go out into the streets of that city and wipe off the very dust of it against them, and it would be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city (Luke 10:8-12). The teaching class puts the working edge on that: the same word is carried into the cities now, and a man who walks past it cannot say afterward that he was never told. What is done to the messenger is done to the one who sent him. He that hears them hears Christ, and he that despises them despises Christ, and he that despises Christ despises the one that sent him (Luke 10:13-16). That has been the standing answer of the nation to the men sent to gather it; the Lord said he had sent his servants the prophets, and they had been taken and slain and their bodies torn in pieces, and the house was left desolate (2 Esdras 1:32-33; Matthew 23:37-38). To be exalted to heaven and thrust down to hell is the prophet’s own language for Zion cast down from heaven to the earth in the day of his anger (Lamentations 2:1). And when the seventy came back with joy, Christ answered that he beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven (Luke 10:17-18): the going out of the witnesses was the beginning of the fall of the kingdom that held them.

name: The Canaanite woman
text: Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table. A woman of Canaan came out of the coasts of Tyre and Sidon crying after him for a daughter grievously vexed with a devil, and he answered her not a word. The disciples asked him to send her away, and he said he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; she came and worshipped and asked for help, and he told her it was not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to dogs. She agreed with him and asked only for the crumbs, and he called her faith great and healed the daughter from that hour. Jesus departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, and a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts and cried after him, asking mercy of the son of David for a daughter grievously vexed with a devil (Matthew 15:21-22). The history class takes the name Canaan for the land and not for her nation: Tyre and Sidon stand in the land of Canaan, so calling her a woman of Canaan tells you where she lived. Mark gives her nation plainly: she was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, and she heard of him and came and fell at his feet (Mark 7:25-26). The class also marks what she called him. She said son of David, because everyone in that country knew he was born of a man out of a known line. He answered her not a word. The disciples came and asked him to send her away because she cried after them, and he said that he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:23-24). The class presses the question that a reading of a messiah for all nations cannot answer: he was going through that country healing and teaching, so why would he not so much as speak to this woman, and why would his own disciples ask him to send her off. Then she came and worshipped him and said, Lord, help me (Matthew 15:25), and he told her to let the children first be filled, for it is not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to the dogs (Matthew 15:26; Mark 7:27). The study notes mark the point exactly there: the order is stated plainly, and he does not soften it for her. She did not argue with the order; she asked inside it, saying that the dogs under the table eat of the children’s crumbs (Matthew 15:27; Mark 7:28). The class weighs what that admission was. Israel was told they were a holy people, chosen to be a special people above all people on the face of the earth (Deuteronomy 7:6), and the nations were counted as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance, as nothing before him (Isaiah 40:15-17). You never find an Israelite in the scriptures calling himself a dog. This woman did, and what she asked for was the dust of the balance, a crumb off the table. Jesus answered that her faith was great and told her it would be to her as she would, and her daughter was made whole from that very hour (Matthew 15:28). Mark records that he sent her away on the strength of that saying, and that when she came to her house she found the devil gone out and her daughter laid upon the bed (Mark 7:29-30). The class marks both what she was commended for and what she was not given. She was not told to go and sin no more, and nothing was said to her about everlasting life. Set beside the woman of Samaria, who claimed Jacob as her father and was offered water springing up into everlasting life without even asking for it (John 4:12-14), the difference between the two answers is the difference between the two nations. The class closes without malice in it. The crumb was still given; Christ showed her no hate, and the rule that follows for us is to live peaceably with all men as much as lies in us (Romans 12:18). The blessing did not come by overturning what he had said about the order of the house; it came to a woman who accepted the order and still believed mercy could reach her child. Matthew has already set down the only other faith commended in those words, and that was the centurion of Capernaum (Matthew 8:10).

name: The wicked husbandmen
text: Beating and killing the servants sent for the fruit, and killing the heir to seize the inheritance. A certain man planted a vineyard, let it out to husbandmen and went into a far country, and at the season sent a servant for the fruit; the husbandmen beat him and sent him away empty, and beat and wounded the servants who followed (Luke 20:9-12). Last of all the owner sent his beloved son, and the husbandmen reasoned among themselves that this was the heir and killed him to seize the inheritance (Luke 20:13-15). Asked what the lord of the vineyard would do, the chief priests and elders passed the sentence out of their own mouths, and then perceived that the parable had been spoken against them (Matthew 21:40-41; Luke 20:19-20). A parable is opened by precept upon precept, which is the only way the dark sayings are understood (Isaiah 28:9-10; Psalms 78:1-2). The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel and the men of Judah his pleasant plant (Isaiah 5:7). The husbandmen are the leaders set over that vineyard, the shepherds who were to feed the flock and instead fed themselves, eating the fat and clothing themselves with the wool (Ezekiel 34:1-3). The servants sent at the season are the prophets, sent rising early and often because God had compassion on his people (Jeremiah 25:4-5; 2 Chronicles 36:15-16). What was done to them is on record: Pashur the priest smote Jeremiah and put him in the stocks for prophesying the judgment, and Jeremiah told him the beating would not turn the judgment aside (Jeremiah 20:1-4). The same office did the same thing after Christ was gone, laying hands on the apostles and putting them in hold for teaching the people and preaching the resurrection (Acts 4:1-3). The parable describes a pattern the leaders of the nation had kept for centuries. Then the owner said he would send his beloved son, which is the word spoken over Christ at the Jordan and again in the mount (Matthew 3:16-17; Matthew 17:5). When the husbandmen saw him they said among themselves that this was the heir, and that killing him would make the inheritance theirs (Luke 20:13-15). That saying carries the weight of the case, because to call him the heir they had to know who he was. The council said as much: if they let him alone all men would believe on him and the Romans would take away their place and nation, and Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said it was expedient that one man die for the people, which was itself a prophecy of the thing they were plotting (John 11:47-53). Even among the chief rulers many believed on him and would not confess him, for fear of being put out of the synagogue (John 12:42). The killing was not done in ignorance of the son. It was done because of who he was, to keep a place and a position. Asked what the lord of the vineyard would do, they answered that he would miserably destroy those wicked men and let the vineyard to other husbandmen who would render him the fruits in their seasons, and in Luke the hearers recoiled from the sentence as soon as it was spoken (Matthew 21:40-41; Luke 20:16). They had judged themselves. He answered out of the scriptures that the stone the builders rejected is become the head of the corner, that the kingdom of God would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth its fruits, and that the stone would break some and grind others to powder (Matthew 21:42-44; Luke 20:17-18). Peter afterward named the builders to their faces, telling the rulers and elders of Israel that this was the stone set at nought of them which is become the head of the corner (Acts 4:5-11). That stone is Christ, the chief corner stone, the only foundation any man may build on (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Corinthians 3:11), and the stone cut out without hands that breaks every kingdom in pieces and stands for ever (Daniel 2:44-45). The account against that generation was reckoned from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zacharias, slain between the temple and the altar, and their house was left desolate (Matthew 23:35-38). Pilate was told he could have no power at all except it were given from above, and that the men who delivered Christ to him had the greater sin (John 19:10-11). The chief priests and scribes sought to lay hands on him that same hour, feared the people, and then sent spies who pretended to be just men, so they might deliver him to the power of the governor (Luke 20:19-20). Notice what the sentence does not say. The vineyard is not destroyed. It is let out again to husbandmen who will render the fruit, which is why Paul described his own work and that of Apollos in the same figure, one planting and another watering while God gives the increase, and called the people God’s husbandry (1 Corinthians 3:6-9). The office was not abolished. It was taken from men who would not render the fruit and given to men who would.

name: The marriage of the king’s son
text: Making light of the call, and killing the servants who brought it. A king made a marriage for his son and sent his servants to call those who were bidden, and they would not come; at the second sending they made light of it, one going to his farm and another to his merchandise, while the rest took the servants, treated them spitefully and killed them (Matthew 22:1-6). The king sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city, then filled the wedding from the highways with guests both bad and good (Matthew 22:7-10). One guest was found without a wedding garment, had nothing to answer, and was bound and cast into outer darkness: many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:11-14). The servants in this parable are not any man who says he loves God. The law names them: the children of Israel are the servants of the Most High, the people he brought out of the land of Egypt (Leviticus 25:55). So both the refusal and the killing fall on a nation called by name, and on the messengers sent to that nation. Luke carries the same parable as a great supper and sets down the excuses one by one, a piece of ground just bought, five yoke of oxen to prove, a wife just married (Luke 14:16-24). Those three are lifted straight out of the law of war, where the man who had built a house and not dedicated it, planted a vineyard and not eaten of it, or betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent home from the battle (Deuteronomy 20:5-7). But the weapons of this warfare are not carnal (2 Corinthians 10:4-5), and Paul told the brethren the time is short, so that those who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Corinthians 7:29). What was once a lawful release from a physical battle is here called what it now is. A sinful man will not be reproved, but finds an excuse according to his own will (Sirach 32:17). The second offense is inside the wedding. When the king came in to see the guests he found a man with no wedding garment on, and the man was speechless (Matthew 22:11-14). The garment is not cloth. It is righteousness, the keeping of the laws of the Most High, the clothing the psalm asks for when it prays that the priests be clothed with righteousness (Psalms 132:9). A man can be gathered in off the highway and still be missing the one thing the king came in to look for. The king was wroth, sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city, and said that those who were bidden were not worthy (Matthew 22:7-10). The honour of the invitation did not shield them; it measured them. Then the servants went out into the highways and gathered as many as they found, both bad and good, and the wedding was furnished with guests. Luke names who is gathered in: the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind, and the poor of his people are Zion (Isaiah 14:32). The order of that gathering is set down in Acts, where Paul said it was necessary that the word be spoken to them first, and since they judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life he turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13:44-46), who are named in the same gospel as Zebulun and Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles, the northern kingdom (Matthew 4:15). The last servant is sent into the highways and hedges to compel them to come in, and to compel is to press and to force, which is what the preaching in the street is for. The man without the garment was bound hand and foot, taken away and cast into outer darkness where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, and the parable closes with its own reason: many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:11-14). Luke closes the same teaching by saying that none of the men who were bidden would taste of that supper. Not every man of the nation will answer, for they are not all Israel which are of Israel (Romans 9:6). The refusal has an answer written long before: the Lord called and they refused, he stretched out his hand and no man regarded, and he will laugh at their calamity when their fear comes as desolation, and they will seek him early and not find him (Proverbs 1:24-28). Both halves of the sentence stand together. Refusing the call brought the armies on the city, and coming in without righteousness brought the binding at the table.

name: The scribes and Pharisees
text: Shutting up the kingdom against men; devouring widows’ houses; tithing mint and omitting judgment, mercy and faith; whited sepulchres. Christ told the multitude and his disciples that the scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat, so whatever they bid the people observe they should observe and do, but they were not to follow their works, for they say and do not (Matthew 23:1-4). The woes that follow name the crimes: shutting up the kingdom of heaven against men, devouring widows’ houses and making long prayer for a pretence, tithing mint and anise and cummin while omitting judgment, mercy and faith, and appearing as whited sepulchres, beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within (Matthew 23:13-15; Matthew 23:23-24; Matthew 23:25-28). This is the plainest speaking in the gospel, and Christ was no soft man with these teachers of the law who did not believe it. They sat in Moses’ seat, and that seat is the law; they were the judges of the people, which is why the instruction was to observe what they taught and not to do after their works. They bound heavy burdens grievous to be borne and laid them on men’s shoulders, and would not move them with one of their fingers (Matthew 23:1-4). All their works they did to be seen of men, loving the uppermost rooms at feasts, the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the markets, when the greatest among them was to be the servant (Matthew 23:5-12). Luke keeps the same charge and adds the lawyers, who took away the key of knowledge, entered not in themselves, and hindered those who were entering (Luke 11:45-52). That key is understanding, and Christ is the one who opens and no man shuts (Revelation 3:7). Taking it away is teaching a man he need not keep what was commanded, when the answer given to the man who asked how to enter into life was plain: keep the commandments (Matthew 19:16-17). The cup was clean outside and full of extortion and excess within, and the order given was to cleanse first that which is within (Matthew 23:25-28). Washing does not reach it. Though a man wash with nitre and take much soap, his iniquity is still marked before the Lord (Jeremiah 2:22); a man cleanses his way by taking heed to the word (Psalms 119:9), and Christ told the disciples they were clean through the word he had spoken (John 15:3). They paid tithe of mint and rue and all manner of herbs and passed over judgment and the love of God, and both were to be done (Matthew 23:23-24; Luke 11:42). The love of God is walking after his commandments (2 John 1:6), and to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); what the Lord desires is mercy and the knowledge of God, and the priest’s lips should keep that knowledge and seek the law at his mouth (Hosea 6:6; Malachi 2:7). They were told instead to give alms of such things as they had, which is the counsel Tobit gave his son, that alms delivers from death (Luke 11:41; Tobit 4:7-11). The sentence in this chapter is a curse pronounced in the open, woe after woe, on men who held the office and would not keep the law they taught. Those who shut up the kingdom and devoured widows’ houses under a pretence of long prayer were told they would receive the greater damnation (Matthew 23:13-15). They compassed sea and land to make one proselyte and made him twofold more the child of hell than themselves, and their rules about swearing by the gold rather than the temple are called blindness, because the temple sanctifies the gold (Matthew 23:15-22). Christ called them serpents and a generation of vipers and asked how they could escape the damnation of hell (Matthew 23:33). Their leaven was named beside the leaven of Herod, which shows whose manner they were following, and leaven is an influence that spreads, which is why the warning was given to the multitude and the disciples before it was said to the men themselves (Mark 8:15). Luke records the same men as graves which appear not, so that the men who walk over them are not aware of them (Luke 11:44). The outside is handsome and the people walking among them do not know what they are standing on. That is the mark of the perilous times, when men are lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, having a form of godliness and denying the power of it (2 Timothy 3:1-5). The blood of all the prophets, from Abel to Zacharias who perished between the altar and the temple, was required of that generation (Luke 11:50-51; Matthew 23:35-36). When the teaching ended, the scribes and Pharisees began to urge him vehemently and to lay wait for him, seeking to catch something out of his mouth that they might accuse him (Luke 11:53-54). The office did not shield the conduct. It raised the account against them.

name: Jerusalem, that killeth the prophets
text: Killing the prophets and stoning them that are sent; not knowing the time of her visitation. Christ named the city by what it did: it killed the prophets and stoned those sent to it, and he said how often he would have gathered her children together as a hen gathers her brood, and they would not (Luke 13:34-35). The sentence follows in the same breath, that her house is left desolate (Matthew 23:37-38). He told the disciples that of all the buildings of the temple there would not be left one stone upon another (Matthew 24:1-2), and Luke gives the cause: she knew not the time of her visitation (Luke 19:41-44). They built the tombs of the prophets and garnished the sepulchres of the righteous and said that if they had lived in the days of their fathers they would not have been partakers in the blood of the prophets, and by saying it they witnessed against themselves that they were the children of those who killed the prophets (Matthew 23:29-32).
