The record of the kings says the messengers were sent early and often because God had compassion on his people, and they mocked them and despised his words until there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:15-16); Nehemiah says the same, that they cast the law behind their backs and slew the prophets that testified against them (Nehemiah 9:26). The account was reckoned from righteous Abel to Zacharias, whom they slew between the temple and the altar, and it was required of that generation (Matthew 23:33-36). They followed that man into the temple to kill him, which is what hatred does when it is let run; it does not stop at the door of a holy place. Of the prophets and wise men and scribes he would send, some they would kill and crucify and some they would scourge in their synagogues and persecute from city to city. That spirit comes back on the earth in every generation, and it is the reason a man can be laid hands on today for opening a Bible in the street. Coming near the city he wept over it, because the things belonging to her peace were hidden from her eyes (Luke 19:41-44). He had just been told by some of the Pharisees to rebuke his disciples for calling him the king that comes in the name of the Lord, and he answered that if these held their peace the stones would immediately cry out (Luke 19:37-40; Habakkuk 2:11). Then he said the stones of the city would be thrown down. The weeping was not sentiment over buildings. It was over a people who had the visitation standing in front of them and did not know the day of it. The disciples came to show him the buildings of the temple, and he told them not to be taken with what they were looking at, because there would not be left one stone upon another that would not be thrown down (Matthew 24:1-2). Luke gives the sign to watch for: when Jerusalem is seen compassed with armies, then the desolation of it is near, and those in Judaea are to flee to the mountains and those in the midst of it to depart out (Luke 21:20-21). Those who took the word left. Those who came up to the passover anyway were shut inside it. These are the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled (Luke 21:22), and what was written is the curse in the law: a nation brought from far, swift as the eagle flies, of fierce countenance, which would besiege them in all their gates until their high and fenced walls came down, and they would eat the flesh of their own sons and daughters in the siege (Deuteronomy 28:49-53). The eagle was the standard of Rome. Christ had already said woe to those who give suck in those days, and told the daughters of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and for their children (Luke 23:28-31). The people would fall by the edge of the sword and be led away captive into all nations, and the city would be trodden down of the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). That is the same word given in the law, that the Lord would scatter them among the nations and leave them few in number (Deuteronomy 4:27; Deuteronomy 28:64), and it is the reason the great multitude that no man could number is gathered out of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues (Revelation 7:9). The siege of 70 AD did not end the nation; it scattered it, first into Africa and from there into the hands of every empire that followed, which is how a people came to be mingled among the heathen and to learn their works (Psalms 106:35). Perpetual hatred stood behind the armies, the hatred of Esau who shed the blood of the children of Israel in the time of their calamity (Ezekiel 35:5). The house was pulled down and the nation was not. The word left standing is the one Christ gave with the sentence: they would not see him again until they said he was blessed who came in the name of the Lord, and they would look on the one they had pierced and mourn for him (Luke 13:35; Zechariah 12:10).

name: Peter’s denial
text: Denying Christ three times with cursing and swearing. Peter said that though all men should be offended because of him he would never be offended, and that though he should die with him he would not deny him (Matthew 26:33-35). In the high priest’s hall he denied it to a damsel, then with an oath, and then with cursing and swearing that he did not know the man, and the cock crew (Matthew 26:69-75). The Lord turned and looked on Peter, and he remembered the word that had been spoken to him, and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60-62). Before the denial he was warned and he was prayed for. Satan had desired to have them, to sift them as wheat, and Christ told Peter he had prayed for him that his faith fail not, and that when he was converted he should strengthen his brethren (Luke 22:31-32). Peter had walked with him and was not yet converted. What converts a man is named in the psalm: the law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul (Psalms 19:7), and that is also what he was to strengthen his brethren with. Peter answered out of his own confidence that he was ready to go both into prison and to death, and was told what he would do before the cock crew (Luke 22:33-34). A man does not know tomorrow, for his life is a vapour that appears for a little time and then vanishes away (James 4:14-15). He denied three times. The third time he was picked out by his speech, because he was a Galilaean; the way he talked gave him away, so that he sounded like the man he was denying (Luke 22:54-60). Matthew records the oath, and then the cursing and swearing that he did not know the man (Matthew 26:69-75). The warning about that stands in the same gospel: whoever confesses him before men, him will he confess before his Father, and whoever denies him before men will be denied (Matthew 10:32-33). It was the hour given to the other side, as Christ told the chief priests and the captains of the temple when they came out against him with swords and staves, that this was their hour and the power of darkness (Luke 22:52-53). Isaiah had written it plainly of the servant: he was despised and rejected of men, and we hid as it were our faces from him, and we esteemed him not (Isaiah 53:3). That verse is Peter in the courtyard. The look and the tears are the first part of the answer. The Lord turned and looked on Peter, and Peter remembered the word and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60-62). The difference between this case and the traitor in the same chapter is what came after the weeping. When Judas saw what he had done he did not go back and reconcile; he went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). Peter reconciled. Godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death (2 Corinthians 7:10). The reconciliation is recorded. After the resurrection Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved him and three times charged him to feed his lambs and his sheep, once for each denial, and Peter was grieved at the third asking (John 21:15-17). Then he was told by what death he should glorify God, that when he was old another would gird him and carry him where he would not (John 21:18-19), which answers what he had been told in the upper room, that where Christ was going he could not follow then but should follow afterwards (John 13:36). The history says he was held nine months in prison at Rome, converted the keepers and others while he was in there, and was scourged and crucified with his head downward, a position he asked for because he did not count himself worthy to die as his master died. The man who bounced back from that courtyard is the same man who stood at the gate called Beautiful and told a lame beggar that he had no silver and gold, but gave him what he had (Acts 3:1-8). The charge given with the warning stood: once converted, he was to strengthen his brethren. The fall did not cancel the man, and it did not cancel what he was sent to teach.

name: The chief priests, and the watch at the sepulchre
text: Paying the soldiers large money to report a lie about the resurrection. The day after the preparation the chief priests and Pharisees came to Pilate, called Christ a deceiver, and asked that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, because they remembered his saying that after three days he would rise; Pilate gave them a watch, and they sealed the stone and set it (Matthew 27:62-66). When some of the watch came into the city and told the chief priests all the things that were done, the priests assembled with the elders, took counsel, and gave large money to the soldiers to say that the disciples came by night and stole him away while they slept (Matthew 28:11-13). They remembered the saying better than the disciples did. That is the weight of the request: the men who had him put to death were the men who took his words about the third day seriously enough to post a guard against them. There was an earthquake, and the angel of the Lord came down and rolled back the stone and sat on it, and the keepers shook and became as dead men, and the angel told the women he was not there, for he was risen as he said (Matthew 28:1-6). At that point the matter was settled in front of witnesses, and the men who had asked for the guard could have conceded it. They did not. They assembled, took counsel, and bought the report they had set the watch to prevent (Matthew 28:11-13). Men love darkness rather than light, because their deeds are evil (John 3:19). The money had a reason behind it. A soldier who lost a prisoner under his watch answered for it with his own life, which is why the priests added that if it came to the governor’s ears they would persuade him and secure them (Matthew 28:14). So the soldiers were bought with money and with a promise of protection from the same men who had just been shown that the promise was worth nothing, since they had made a covenant with death and an agreement with hell, saying the overflowing scourge would not come to them (Isaiah 28:15). Never trust an enemy, whatever the terms (Sirach 12:10). The bargain itself broke the law twice over, against raising a false report and against bearing false witness (Exodus 23:1; Exodus 20:16). The soldiers took the money and did as they were taught, and that saying was commonly reported among the Jews until the day the account was written (Matthew 28:15). No sentence on the chief priests, on the elders, or on the soldiers is recorded in the passage. What is recorded is the bargain, with their names attached to it, in a book that has outlived every copy of the story they bought. The report also could not hold, because of how the resurrection was shown. God raised him the third day and showed him openly, not to all the people, but to witnesses chosen before, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:40-41). He was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve, and after that of above five hundred brethren at once, most of whom were still alive when Paul wrote it down (1 Corinthians 15:5-6). He showed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs over forty days (Acts 1:3). A crucifixion was a public thing in that city, and so was the darkness and the earthquake that went with this one, so the men who were paid to say they had slept through the one event everyone was talking about were given a story that could not survive the witnesses. The standing rule on such a report is written: a false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaks lies shall not escape (Proverbs 19:5).

name: The woman with the issue of blood
text: Believing that if she might but touch his clothes she should be whole. A woman had an issue of blood twelve years, had suffered many things of many physicians and spent all her living on them, and was nothing bettered but rather grew worse (Mark 5:25-26). She came behind him in the press and touched the border of his garment, and straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up (Luke 8:43-44). He would not let the touch pass, and when she came trembling and told all the truth before the people he called her daughter, told her that her faith had made her whole, and sent her away in peace, whole of her plague (Mark 5:30-34). The law puts a woman apart seven days for her issue, and anyone who touches her or what she sits on is unclean until the evening; if the issue runs beyond the time of her separation, all those days are counted as the days of her separation and she remains unclean (Leviticus 15:19-25). Twelve years of that is what this woman had carried. The gospel calls it a plague, and a sickness of long continuance that is not written in the book of the law is one of the things named in the curses that would cleave to the nation (Deuteronomy 28:59-61; Mark 5:29). She was not a woman with an inconvenience. She was a woman under a curse, cut off from the congregation, out of money, and worse than when she started. What she reached for was not his sleeve or his hand. It was the border of the garment (Luke 8:43-44; Matthew 9:20-21), and of all the things on a man walking through a crowd it is the hardest to take hold of, which means she went down for it on purpose. The fringe on the border with the ribband of blue is commanded in the law, to be looked on so that the people remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them (Numbers 15:38-39). She knew what was in those fringes. The people of that country knew the same thing, and wherever he entered they laid the sick in the streets and asked that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment, and as many as touched were made whole (Mark 6:56). The issue stopped straightway, and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague (Mark 5:29). He would not let it pass as one more press of the crowd. When Peter said the multitude thronged him and pressed him, he answered that somebody had touched him, for he perceived that virtue had gone out of him (Luke 8:45-46). The distinction matters, because a whole crowd was touching him and one woman was healed. The chapter is one work of power after another and every one of them turns on faith; healing came by faith and by the works that go with it, and not by the touching of a hand. She came trembling, fell down before him, and declared before all the people why she had touched him and how she was healed immediately (Luke 8:47). He did not let her keep it quiet, and the reason is in what she was given. A woman who had been put apart for twelve years was named daughter in front of the congregation, told that her faith had made her whole, and sent away in peace, whole of her plague (Luke 8:48; Mark 5:34). The verdict was public because the uncleanness had been public. What years of physicians and all her living could not buy was given for nothing, and the one thing she brought was the thing the Lord named.

name: Herod Antipas and Herodias
text: Taking his brother’s wife; beheading John for saying so. Herod the tetrarch had married Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and John told him plainly that it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife (Mark 6:17-18). For that word Herod shut John up in prison, adding it above all the other evils he had done (Luke 3:19-20). Herodias held a quarrel against John and would have killed him but could not, because Herod feared him, knowing that he was a just man and holy; at the birthday feast an oath sworn before the guests put the prophet’s head on a charger and into her hands (Mark 6:19-28). When Herod the Great died his kingdom was split among three sons, and Herod Antipas was made tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea (Luke 3:1). That house was Idumaean, of the stock of Esau, put in place by Rome to rule over Israel, and its head had already killed the children of Bethlehem trying to reach the child (Matthew 2:16). They were not strangers to the law. They were raised and groomed in the customs of Israel, which is exactly why Rome used them, and Paul said as much to Agrippa, that he knew him to be expert in all customs and questions among the Jews (Acts 26:3). Herod knew the law well enough to be accused by it. The statute is written plainly: the nakedness of a brother’s wife is not to be uncovered (Leviticus 18:16), and a man who takes his brother’s wife has done an unclean thing (Leviticus 20:21). John reproved him for Herodias and for all the evils he had done, and Herod added this above all, that he shut John up in prison (Luke 3:19-20). Mark records that Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just man and holy, observed him, heard him gladly and did many things at his word (Mark 6:19-20). Hearing him gladly never turned into obeying him, and the whole case turns on that gap. On his birthday he made a supper for his lords, his high captains and the chief estates of Galilee; the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him and those who sat with him, and he swore to give her whatever she asked, to the half of his kingdom. She asked her mother what to ask and was told, the head of John the Baptist. The king was exceeding sorry, and for his oath’s sake and for the sake of the company at the table he would not reject her, and sent an executioner (Mark 6:21-28). A rash oath sworn in front of guests did not make the killing lawful. The fear of looking small in front of his own table outweighed everything he knew about the man in his prison. No sentence on Herod or on Herodias is recorded in these accounts. What is recorded is a conscience that would not settle. When Herod heard of the fame of Jesus he said that this was John the Baptist, whom he had beheaded, risen from the dead (Mark 6:14-16). When certain of the Pharisees came telling Christ to depart because Herod would kill him, he told them to go and tell that fox that he cast out devils and did cures that day and the next, and the third day he would be perfected, and that it could not be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem (Luke 13:31-33). To call a man a fox in that day was to call him a crafty and cruel enemy of God’s servants, not to flatter him. A threat from that house did not move Christ off his work by a single day. At the trial Herod was exceeding glad to see him, because he had heard many things of him and hoped to see some miracle done. He questioned him in many words, and Christ answered him nothing; then Herod with his men of war set him at nought, mocked him, arrayed him in a gorgeous robe and sent him back to Pilate (Luke 23:8-12). He had nothing to say to that house at all. Its head had sought his life as a child, and this one had beheaded John. The man who would not lose face in front of his dinner guests got no word out of the Son of God in front of a whole court. The charge in this case is proved and the sentence is not executed in the record.

name: The rich young ruler
text: Going away sorrowful, because he had great possessions. A ruler came running and kneeled to him and asked what he should do to inherit eternal life, and was answered that if he would enter into life he should keep the commandments, which were then named to him (Mark 10:17-19; Luke 18:18-20). He said he had observed all these from his youth. Christ, looking on him, loved him, and named the one thing he lacked: sell what he had, give to the poor, take up the cross and follow him. He was sad at that saying and went away grieved, for he had great possessions (Mark 10:20-22). Luke sets the case immediately after the word that a man must receive the kingdom of God as a little child or he will not enter it (Luke 18:16-17). That is the measure the ruler is laid against. Coming into this truth means putting down what a man thought he knew, and a man who says he is grown and nobody can teach him is a man who will not make it. The answer to his question came out of the law: keep the commandments, and the ones named to him were the commandments of loving a neighbour, do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness, defraud not, honour his father and his mother (Mark 10:19). Money buys nothing here, and what is paid week by week to a preacher washes away no sin. Matthew adds the one that the list was building toward, to love a neighbour as himself (Matthew 19:19). He answered that he had observed all these from his youth. That is the arrogancy the scripture warns about: talk no more so exceedingly proudly, for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed (1 Samuel 2:3). He was wise in his own conceit (Romans 12:16). So the one thing lacking was named, and it was drawn straight out of the commandment he had just claimed to keep: sell what he had, give to the poor, and come and follow (Mark 10:21). He had kept the letter of what was named to him and had not loved his neighbour as himself, or he would already have given to the poor of his own people. What that looked like when men did it is written in Acts, where those who were possessors of lands and houses sold them and laid the price at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to every man according as he had need, and none of them lacked (Acts 4:32-35). He was sad at that saying and went away grieved, for he had great possessions (Mark 10:22). Nothing further is recorded of the man and no sentence is passed on him. What follows is the warning drawn out of his case. Christ looked round about and said how hardly those who have riches shall enter into the kingdom of God, and that it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter in (Mark 10:23-25). The eye of a needle is the low gate a camel has to stoop and unload to get through, and the point of the picture is that a rich man will not stoop. He that trusts in his riches shall fall, but the righteous shall flourish as a branch (Proverbs 11:28), and riches profit not in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death (Proverbs 11:4). The prayer in Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches, lest a man be full and deny the Lord, or be poor and steal (Proverbs 30:8-9). The danger is named again in Revelation, where a man says he is rich and increased with goods and has need of nothing, and does not know that he is wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked (Revelation 3:17). The disciples were astonished out of measure and asked who then could be saved, and he answered that with men it is impossible, but not with God, for with God all things are possible (Mark 10:26-27). Wealth is not the charge in itself; blessed is the rich that is found without blemish and has not gone after gold (Sirach 31:8), and rich men in the body are charged not to be high minded nor to trust in uncertain riches, but to be rich in good works, ready to distribute and willing to communicate (1 Timothy 6:17-18). Peter said they had left all and followed him, and the answer names what the exchange is worth: no man who has left house or brethren or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or lands for his sake and the gospel’s shall fail to receive a hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and in the world to come eternal life (Mark 10:28-30). What is forsaken coming into this truth is repaid in the nation. A man may lose one parent and gain a congregation, and beyond that a whole people. That exchange was set in front of the ruler, and he kept what he had instead.

name: The widow and her two mites
text: Casting in all that she had, even all her living. Jesus sat over against the treasury and watched how the people cast money into it, and many that were rich cast in much; a certain poor widow came and threw in two mites, which make a farthing (Mark 12:41-42). He called his disciples and said that this poor widow had cast in more than all those who had cast into the treasury, because they all cast in of their abundance, but she of her want cast in all that she had, even all her living (Mark 12:43-44; Luke 21:1-4). The treasury was not a collection plate. It was the store in the temple, and what was laid up in it is stated in the history: when a governor came to seize the money, the high priest told him it was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, with some of it the private deposit of a man of great dignity, and that it was impossible such a wrong should be done to those who had committed it to the holiness of the place (2 Maccabees 3:4-12). The custom carried down to the day in this chapter, when the giving was done in the open and everyone could see what went in. So this is a widow putting her last coin into the fund that existed to relieve widows. The two mites together make a farthing, the smallest coins in circulation in that country, worth a fraction of a penny. Measured against the sums going in around her it was nothing. Measured against what she held it was everything, because it was not a portion of her living, it was all her living (Mark 12:44). The law measures a gift that way: every man is to give as he is able, according to the blessing of the Lord his God given to him (Deuteronomy 16:17), and a willing mind is accepted according to that a man has, and not according to that he has not (2 Corinthians 8:12). Tobit told his son to give alms of his substance, and if he had but little, not to be afraid to give according to that little, because alms delivers from death (Tobit 4:7-11). The blessing recorded here is the verdict he spoke over her in front of the disciples. He called them to him and said that this poor widow had cast in more than all those who had cast into the treasury (Mark 12:43; Luke 21:3). The rich cast in much. She cast in more than all of them together, and the reason is given with the verdict: they all cast in of their abundance, but she of her want cast in all the living that she had. Nothing is said against the rich men in the passage. They were doing what they were supposed to do with an abundance, and the charge laid on such men is not to be high minded nor to trust in uncertain riches but to be rich in good works, ready to distribute (1 Timothy 6:17-18). The comparison is not between a good giver and bad ones. It is between what a gift costs and what it counts, and by that measure the smallest sum that went into the treasury that day was the largest gift given in it. He which sows sparingly shall reap also sparingly, and he which sows bountifully shall reap also bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6). The verdict is also the warning, because it stands in the same chapter as the scribes who devoured widows’ houses and for a pretence made long prayers (Mark 12:40). Christ had just named the men who eat widows like her, and then pointed at her and called her the greatest giver in the room.

name: Barabbas
text: Insurrection and murder. At the feast the governor released one prisoner to the people, and there was a notable prisoner named Barabbas, who lay bound with those who had made insurrection with him and had committed murder in the insurrection (Matthew 27:15-16; Mark 15:6-7). Luke states the charge plainly: he had been cast into prison for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder (Luke 23:18-19). The chief priests moved the people to ask for Barabbas, and Pilate released him and delivered Jesus to their will (Mark 15:11; Luke 23:25). Barabbas was not an unknown man. He was a notable prisoner, taken with a band that had risen against the government and killed in the rising (Mark 15:6-7; Luke 23:18-19). John calls him a robber (John 18:40). He was not brought out because his cause had been heard and he was found innocent; he was brought out because the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude to ask for him and to destroy Jesus (Matthew 27:20). Peter afterward set the exchange before the people in plain words: they denied the Holy One and the Just, desired a murderer to be granted to them, and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, of which the apostles were witnesses (Acts 3:14-15). That is the offense of this case as the apostles preached it. Peter said in the same breath that through ignorance they did it, as did also their rulers, and then called them to repent and be converted so that their sins might be blotted out (Acts 3:17-19). The crowd that shouted for a murderer was not written off. It was preached to. Pilate said a third time that he found no cause of death in him, and asked what evil the man had done (Luke 23:22). He knew the man was innocent and gave sentence anyway. Matthew records how the choice was put, whether he should release Barabbas or Jesus which is called Christ, and gives the governor’s own reading of the court: he knew that for envy they had delivered him (Matthew 27:17-18). His own wife sent word to him while he sat on the judgment seat, telling him to have nothing to do with that just man (Matthew 27:19). The envy was written on their faces and in their spirit and they could not hide it, and a heathen governor could see it from the bench. So the guilty man went free and the innocent man was delivered to their will (Mark 15:15; Luke 23:25). No further history of Barabbas is given, and no penalty on him is recorded anywhere in the gospels. He stands in the book as a man spared, and spared in the very proceeding that laid the sentence he had earned on another. The rule the court broke is written: he that justifies the wicked, and he that condemns the just, are both an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 17:15). And the release is not the end of the reckoning, because the same word that named the exchange also named the day when he whom they pierced will be looked on and mourned for (Zechariah 12:10).

name: Joseph of Arimathaea
text: Going in boldly unto Pilate and craving the body; and not having consented to the counsel and deed of them. Joseph of Arimathaea was an honourable counsellor who waited for the kingdom of God, a good man and a just, and he had not consented to the counsel and deed of the council he sat in (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50-51). When the evening was come, because it was the preparation, he went in boldly to Pilate and craved the body. He took it down, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb hewn out of a rock, where no man had been laid before (Matthew 27:57-60). He sat in the council that condemned Christ and did not consent to their counsel and deed (Luke 23:50-51). Not every man was let into that room, so the record is telling you he had standing among the Pharisees and was a follower of Christ at the same time. John says he was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). That fear has a definition in the gospel: Christ had sent them out as sheep among wolves and told them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, and warned that men would deliver them up to the councils and scourge them in their synagogues (Matthew 10:16-18). Joseph was inside one of those councils. He is named with Nicodemus, who came to Christ by night and told him plainly that they knew he was a teacher come from God (John 3:1-2), and the two of them together are the proof that the rejection of Christ was the work of the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, and not of every man in the nation (Mark 8:31; John 8:31). When the evening was come he went in boldly to Pilate and craved the body, which was the dangerous part of it (Mark 15:43). It takes position and standing to walk into that hall and ask a Roman governor for the corpse of a man his own court had just executed as a rebel, and to be heard. He used what he had, the way Esther used her place for the nation and Daniel used his. He bought fine linen, took the body down, wrapped it, laid it in a sepulchre hewn out of a rock, and rolled a stone to the door; Nicodemus came with him bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pound weight (Mark 15:46; John 19:39-40). The burial was made the same day, which is the custom written in the law: the body of a man hanged on a tree shall not remain all night, but shall be buried that day, that the land be not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). There is no waiting days over a body. The prophet had written that he would make his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death (Isaiah 53:9). He was crucified between two malefactors, and then a rich man buried him in his own new sepulchre (Matthew 27:57-60). Joseph is how that word came to pass, and the passage names him as rich in the same sentence that names what he did with it. The women who came with him out of Galilee followed after and beheld the sepulchre and how the body was laid, then returned and prepared spices and ointments, and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment (Luke 23:55-56). Their witness of the place is what makes the report bought from the watch worthless, because they knew exactly where the body had been put. Nothing is promised to Joseph in the text beyond the record itself. A counsellor who did not consent, who spent his standing, his linen and his own tomb on a body nobody else would claim, is named in all four gospels and set beside Nicodemus as proof that some of those men did change. The honour is in what he did, and in the word it fulfilled.

name: Zacharias
text: Not believing the words of the angel Gabriel, and asking for a sign. While Zacharias executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his course, his lot was to burn incense, and the angel Gabriel stood on the right side of the altar and told him his prayer was heard, that Elisabeth would bear him a son, and that he should call his name John (Luke 1:8-13). Zacharias asked how he should know this, since he was an old man and his wife well stricken in years (Luke 1:18). Gabriel answered that because he did not believe the words, which would be fulfilled in their season, he would be dumb and unable to speak until the day these things were performed (Luke 1:19-20). Everything about his position argued against the question. He was of the course of Abia, the eighth of the twenty-four courses of the sons of Aaron that David set in order when he was preparing the house, by a pattern the Lord gave him in writing (Luke 1:5; 1 Chronicles 24:7-10; 1 Chronicles 28:11-19). His wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and among the priests a man who could not be reckoned by genealogy was put from the priesthood as polluted (Ezra 2:61-63). He was standing at the altar of incense at the hour the law appointed, with the whole multitude praying outside (Exodus 30:7-8; Luke 1:9-10). He was in the exact place the Most High had built for that conversation, and the answer to his own prayer was handed to him there. The question had been asked and answered before, in the same circumstances. Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age when they were told she would have a son, and the answer given then was that nothing is too hard for the Lord (Genesis 18:11-14). Here the promise came with the name of the messenger attached to it: Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, sent to speak and to show him these glad tidings (Luke 1:19). The fault named in the sentence is not the asking of a question. It is the not believing. The words would be fulfilled in their season whatever he made of them (Luke 1:20). He was a righteous man, blameless in the commandments and ordinances, serving in his appointed course, and he doubted the one thing he had been praying for (Luke 1:6-7). He was struck dumb and unable to speak until the day the things spoken were performed (Luke 1:20). The people outside waited and marvelled that he tarried so long in the temple; when he came out he could not speak to them, and they perceived that he had seen a vision, for he beckoned to them and remained speechless. As soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished he departed to his own house, and after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived (Luke 1:21-24). The performance the angel spoke of took place in its order, and the sentence had a stated cause and a stated limit. His unbelief cost him his speech; it did not cost Elisabeth the child, and it did not delay the promise by a day. The judgment ended exactly where the angel said it would. At the circumcision on the eighth day the neighbours and cousins would have called the child Zacharias after his father, and Elisabeth said he should be called John. They made signs to his father, and he asked for a writing table and wrote that his name is John, and they all marvelled. At once his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke and praised God (Luke 1:57-64). The tongue that was stopped for unbelief was given back to prophesy: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people and raised up a horn of salvation in the house of his servant David, to perform the mercy promised to the fathers and the oath sworn to Abraham, that being delivered out of the hand of their enemies they might serve him without fear (Luke 1:67-75). The child would go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1:76-79), and that shadow is the affliction and the iron of captivity (Psalms 107:10). The first words out of his mouth were about the deliverance of the nation, not about the year he had spent silent.

name: Zacharias and Elisabeth
text: Both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. Zacharias was a priest of the course of Abia and Elisabeth was of the daughters of Aaron, and they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless; they had no child, because Elisabeth was barren, and they were both now well stricken in years (Luke 1:5-7). The answer came at the altar of incense: a son named John, great in the sight of the Lord, filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother’s womb, who would turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God and go before him in the spirit and power of Elias (Luke 1:13-17). Luke states the verdict on this household before he states its trouble. Both were righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless; and they had no child, because Elisabeth was barren, and they were both well stricken in years (Luke 1:5-7). The childlessness is set down beside the blamelessness, not against it. It is the commandments that make a man righteous (Deuteronomy 6:25), and a house without children was not therefore a house under judgment. Both of them were found in their place. Zacharias was executing the priest’s office in the order of his course when the answer came, at the hour of incense that the law fixed, with the whole multitude of the people praying outside (Luke 1:8-10; Exodus 30:7-8). That course was one of the twenty-four David had set in order by the pattern the Lord gave him (1 Chronicles 24:7-10). Elisabeth held the same line at the other end of it. When the neighbours and kinsfolk would have named the child after his father, she said he should be called John and would not be moved from it, though none of her kindred was called by that name (Luke 1:59-61). Neither of them took an unanswered prayer as a licence to leave off what they had been keeping all their lives. What was promised was more than a child in the house. There would be joy and gladness and many would rejoice at his birth; he would be great in the sight of the Lord, drink neither wine nor strong drink, be filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother’s womb, turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and make ready a people prepared for the Lord (Luke 1:13-17). That is the word Malachi had left standing at the end of the prophets (Malachi 4:5-6), and it is the child of whom Christ said that among those born of women there had not risen a greater (Matthew 11:11). A man filled with the Spirit from the womb is spoken of the same way Jeremiah was, known before he was formed in the belly and ordained a prophet to the nations (Jeremiah 1:5). The answer to one household’s prayer was sent for the whole nation. Elisabeth conceived and hid herself five months, saying that the Lord had dealt with her so in the days wherein he looked on her, to take away her reproach among men (Luke 1:24-25). Her reproach was that she was called barren, and what was done for her is what was done for Sarah, which is what the angel meant in telling Mary that with God nothing shall be impossible: an old woman past the age was carrying a child and was already in her sixth month (Luke 1:36-37; Genesis 18:11-14). When Mary came into the house and greeted her, the child leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost and cried out with a loud voice (Luke 1:41-42). Her neighbours and kin heard how greatly the Lord had shown her mercy, and they rejoiced with her (Luke 1:57-58). Her husband’s silence did not withdraw any of it, and when his mouth was opened the house that had been childless was filled with prophecy of the covenant sworn to Abraham and of salvation from the hand of their enemies (Luke 1:67-75).

name: Mary, the mother of Jesus
text: Be it unto me according to thy word; blessed is she that believed. The angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. She was told she would bring forth a son and call his name Jesus, that he would be great and be called the Son of the Highest, and that with God nothing shall be impossible; she asked how it should be, and then answered as the handmaid of the Lord, that it be to her according to his word (Luke 1:26-38). Elisabeth gave the verdict on that answer: blessed is she that believed, for there shall be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:39-45). Her answer was the answer of a servant. She called herself the handmaid of the Lord and said, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38). The same messenger had stood in the temple six months earlier and told Zacharias that his wife would bear a son, and the promise was performed in its season, in the order the Most High set, and the same order holds here (Luke 1:13; Luke 1:23-24). Mary went from there into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah, and saluted Elisabeth, who was then six months with child (Luke 1:39-40). Everything done for the child was done after the law. He was circumcised when eight days were accomplished and his name was called Jesus, as the law of circumcision requires on the eighth day, a covenant older than the Levitical priesthood and given to Abraham (Luke 2:21; Leviticus 12:3; Genesis 17:9-12; John 7:22). When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which is the offering the law appoints for a woman who cannot bring a lamb (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:6-8). He was made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those that were under the law (Galatians 4:4-5), and his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover (Luke 2:41). She kept the sayings spoken of him and pondered them in her heart (Luke 2:19). At the marriage in Cana she told him they had no wine, and when he answered that his hour was not yet come she turned to the servants and told them to do whatever he said (John 2:1-5). After the ascension she is named in the upper room with the eleven and the women and his brethren, continuing with one accord in prayer and supplication (Acts 1:14). Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, called her blessed among women and blessed for believing, because there should be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:41-45). Mary answered with the song that magnifies the Lord for regarding the low estate of his handmaiden, and said that from that time all generations would call her blessed (Luke 1:46-48). The song does not stop with her. Her song says that God had shown the strength of his arm against the proud, brought the mighty down from their thrones and lifted the lowly, fed the hungry and sent the rich away empty, and helped Israel his servant in remembrance of his mercy, as he had promised the fathers, Abraham and his seed for ever (Luke 1:51-55). The mercy she was given is the mercy promised to the nation she belonged to. Christ himself fixed where the honour goes. When a woman in the crowd blessed the womb that bare him, he answered that rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27-28), and when he was told his mother and his brethren stood outside, he said that his mother and his brethren are those who hear the word of God and do it (Luke 8:21). He turned the honour off the mother and onto the keeping of the word, which is the same thing his mother had done at Cana when she pointed the servants at him. And the blessing came with a sword in it. Simeon told her that this child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, and that a sword should pierce through her own soul also (Luke 2:34-35). John places her standing by the cross, and records the care of her committed to the disciple whom he loved (John 19:25-27). She was called blessed, and she was not spared the grief that came with it.

name: Simeon and Anna
text: Just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel; a widow who departed not from the temple, serving God with fastings and prayers night and day. Simeon was a man in Jerusalem, just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and it was revealed to him by the Holy Ghost that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ (Luke 2:25-26). He came by the Spirit into the temple when the parents brought in the child to do for him after the custom of the law, took him up in his arms and blessed God (Luke 2:27-28). Anna, a prophetess of the tribe of Aser who never left the temple but served God with fasting and prayer night and day, came in at that moment and spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem (Luke 2:36-38). Simeon is described before he is heard, and the two words used of him have definitions in the scriptures. A just man is a man made perfect in his generations, the way Noah is called just and perfect (Genesis 6:9), and the perfecting is the law of the Lord, which is perfect, converting the soul (Psalms 19:7). A devout man is a man who feared God with all his house, the way Cornelius is described, giving much alms and praying always (Acts 10:1-2). So the man waiting in the temple was a keeper of the law and a man in the fear of God, and what he was waiting on was not a private comfort. It was the consolation of a nation, at a time when there was no New Testament and everything anyone knew about the Messiah came out of the prophets they read every sabbath. He came into the temple by the Spirit at the hour the parents brought the child in to do for him after the custom of the law, which is the same hour they came to present him to the Lord and to offer the pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons written in the law (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:6-8). Anna is named by her tribe: a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser. Asher was still there in that day, and the proof of it is set down in this chapter. She was of a great age, had lived with a husband seven years from her virginity, and was a widow of about fourscore and four years, who departed not from the temple but served God with fastings and prayers night and day (Luke 2:36-37). That is how the two of them were found ready: one waiting on a promise, and one in the house fasting and praying. Simeon took the child up in his arms and blessed God, saying that his servant could now depart in peace according to the word, for his eyes had seen the salvation prepared before the face of all people, a light to lighten the Gentiles and the glory of his people Israel (Luke 2:28-32). The light is Christ, the light that is come and the glory of the Lord risen on the people (Isaiah 60:1), given for a covenant of the people and for a light of the Gentiles (Isaiah 42:6-7). Who those Gentiles are is named in the prophecy itself and in the gospel that quotes it: the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, the people that walked in darkness and sat in the region and shadow of death (Isaiah 9:1-2; Matthew 4:15-16). The consolation of Israel and the light of the Gentiles are not two errands. They are the gathering of one nation that had been split in two. Joseph and his mother marvelled at the things spoken of him, and Simeon blessed them, and then said the harder part to the mother: this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, and a sword shall pierce through her own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed (Luke 2:33-35). Set that beside the sign the angel gave the shepherds, which was a babe wrapped in swaddling clothes lying in a manger (Luke 2:12). The child is the sign, not the woman. Anna came in at that moment, gave thanks to the Lord as well, and spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem (Luke 2:38). She did not keep what she had seen to herself. Both of them received the thing they had waited on, and both of them turned it straight into testimony to people who were waiting for the same thing.

name: Nazareth, his own country
text: Being offended at him; seeking to cast him down the hill. As his custom was, he went into the synagogue of his own country on the sabbath day and stood up to read, and after reading from Esaias he told them that the scripture was fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:16-21). They wondered at the gracious words and then asked whether this was not Joseph’s son, and when he named the widow of Sarepta and Naaman the Syrian they were filled with wrath, thrust him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill to cast him down headlong; he passed through the midst of them and went his way (Luke 4:22-30). Mark records that he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands on a few sick folk and healed them, and that he marvelled because of their unbelief (Mark 6:1-6). What he read to them was the commission itself: the Spirit of the Lord was on him, because he had anointed him to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, and to set at liberty them that are bruised (Luke 4:18-19; Isaiah 61:1-2). Every clause of it is about a people in bondage; the bruising is the hard bondage a nation was made to serve under, and the same prophet promises rest from that sorrow and fear and a proverb taken up against the king that ruled them (Isaiah 14:3-6). He closed the book, sat down, and said that this day the scripture was fulfilled in their ears, and the eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him (Luke 4:20-21). It began with astonishment. They wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth, which is the grace poured into the lips of the king in the psalm (Psalms 45:1-2), and then they went through his family: is not this Joseph’s son, the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joses and Simon and Judas, and are not his sisters here with us (Luke 4:22; Mark 6:2-3). They knew the whole household. They had seen him small, and that was the whole of their argument. A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house (Mark 6:4). That happens to the men teaching today; the people who knew you before you repented are the ones who ask who you think you are. In Luke the offense goes past words. He reminded them that many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, and none of them was he sent to but the widow of Sarepta, and many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus, and none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:25-27). Both prophets had to go outside to be received. At that the whole synagogue was filled with wrath, and they rose up, thrust him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, to cast him down headlong (Luke 4:28-29). That is still how it goes when the word is carried into a man’s own neighbourhood. He passed through the midst of them and went his way (Luke 4:30). The judgment on that town is in what they lost by their own hand. He could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands on a few sick folk and healed them, and Matthew says he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief (Mark 6:5; Matthew 13:58). The record does not say the town got nothing. It says the works stopped where the believing stopped. He marvelled because of their unbelief (Mark 6:6). Consider what that means: the unbelief of his own people was such that it made the Son of the Most High marvel. In the very next town the contrast is set down for you. He went down to Capernaum and taught on the sabbath days, and they were astonished at his doctrine, for his word was with power; and a man with the spirit of an unclean devil cried out that he knew him, the Holy One of God (Luke 4:31-34). The demon in the synagogue knew who he was while his own town was walking him to a cliff. When it was day he departed and the people sought him and would have kept him from leaving, and he told them he must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also, for that was what he was sent to do (Luke 4:42-43). It is written of him more widely than one town, that he came to his own and his own received him not (John 1:11), and that word is defined by the gospels themselves, which say he was rejected of the elders and the chief priests and the scribes (Mark 8:31; Luke 9:22), while other men of the nation believed on him and were told to continue in his word (John 8:31). Nazareth had the first hearing and the closest knowledge of him, and came away with the least.

name: The Samaritan village, and the sons of thunder
text: Refusing to receive him because his face was toward Jerusalem; James and John asking for fire from heaven. A village of Samaria would not take him in because he was travelling toward Jerusalem, and James and John asked leave to call fire out of heaven and consume it as Elias had done (Luke 9:51-54). The village was of the northern kingdom, and the refusal was the old grudge between the two houses. He rebuked the two disciples rather than the village, told them they did not know what manner of spirit was on them, and said the Son of man came to save lives and not to destroy them, and they went on to another village (Luke 9:55-56). When the time came that he should be received up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem and sent messengers ahead into a village of the Samaritans to make ready, and they would not receive him because of where he was going (Luke 9:51-53). That village was of the northern kingdom. Samaria was the head of Ephraim (Isaiah 7:9), and the Samaritans were Israelites, which is why the woman at the well appealed to their father Jacob and why the record notes that the Jews had no dealings with them (John 4:9; John 4:12). This was the beef between the two houses, not a stranger turning away a stranger. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom he had surnamed the sons of thunder, asked leave to command fire out of heaven and consume the village, as Elias had done to the captains sent against him (Luke 9:54; 2 Kings 1:9-12). In plain terms they wanted to burn their own brothers over a slight. Their anger came dressed as loyalty. Just before this, John had reported that they forbade a man casting out devils in Christ’s name because he did not walk with them, and was told to forbid him not, since the man who is not against us is on our side (Luke 9:49-50). The same spirit was still running. Men teaching the same identity who do not speak against Christ are not to be hindered merely because they do not stand with us, and a brother who will not receive a labourer is not thereby marked for destruction. Rejection is real, and it falls back on the one who rejects: the man who despises the labourer despises the one who sent him, and despises not man but God (Luke 10:16; 1 Thessalonians 4:8). It was not theirs to avenge. He turned and rebuked the two, not the village, telling them they did not know what manner of spirit was on them, for the Son of man came to save men’s lives and not to destroy them, and they went to another village (Luke 9:55-56). John records the same purpose in other words, that the Son was sent to save the world and not to condemn it (John 3:17). The correction fell on the disciples who proposed the fire. The work is to win the soul, not to end it: a true witness delivers souls (Proverbs 14:25), and the man who wins souls is wise (Proverbs 11:30). The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle toward all men, able to teach, patient, instructing in meekness those who oppose themselves, so that God may give them repentance and they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil (2 Timothy 2:24-26). Those two brothers had no patience, and that is exactly what the name they carried meant. The rebuke prepared them. The same two had been taken up into the mountain with Peter (Luke 9:28), and they became an integral part of building up the believers and teaching them, which they could not have done carrying the temper they had on that road. John afterward went with Peter into Samaria when its people received the word of God, and prayed for them (Acts 8:14-17), serving the very people he had once asked to burn. Where a house or a city will not receive the labourer, the instruction was to shake off the dust from the feet for a testimony and go on, and the account is left with God, who will settle it in the day of judgment (Luke 9:5; Matthew 10:14-15). No fire fell on that village. The only sentence in the record is the one spoken to the men who asked for it.

name: Mary of Bethany
text: Sitting at his feet to hear his word; anointing his body aforehand to the burying. While Martha was taken up with much serving, Mary sat at Christ’s feet and heard his word, and was told she had chosen the good part that would not be taken from her (Luke 10:38-42). At Bethany she anointed his feet with costly spikenard and wiped them with her hair, and Judas objected in the name of the poor, being a thief who carried the bag (John 12:1-6). Christ defended the act and said she had kept the ointment against the day of his burying, and the promise given her was a memorial wherever the gospel is preached (John 12:7-8; Mark 14:3-9). Martha received him into her house and was cumbered about much serving, while her sister Mary sat at his feet and heard his word; when Martha asked that Mary be told to help, she was answered that she was careful and troubled about many things, that one thing was needful, and that Mary had chosen that good part which would not be taken away from her (Luke 10:38-42). The serving was not wrong. People have to eat, and the body needs it. But man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God (Luke 4:4), and Job said he esteemed the words of God’s mouth more than his necessary food (Job 23:12). A man can be so taken up with the business of the day that the word never gets in him. Mary put the word first, and that is what was commended. At Bethany she took a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, anointed his feet and wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the smell of it (John 12:1-3). Judas Iscariot objected that the ointment could have been sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor; John says plainly that he did not say it because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and had the bag and took what was put in it (John 12:4-6). The bag is where the money was kept. Concern spoken in another man’s name covered his own appetite. Mary answered nothing; Christ answered for her. He told them to let her alone, that she had kept the ointment against the day of his burying, and that they had the poor always with them but would not always have him (John 12:7-8; Matthew 26:6-13). She had poured it on his body for his burial. Burying a man decently is an old custom among our people and it runs through the scriptures: Jacob made Joseph swear to carry him out of Egypt and bury him with his fathers, and Joseph went up and did it (Genesis 47:29-31; Genesis 50:4-5), and Tobit charged his son to bury him decently and to lay his mother by him in one grave (Tobit 4:3-4; Tobit 14:9). Mary honoured that custom beforehand and at her own cost, while men at the table were counting the price of it. Defending her gift did not cancel the duty to the poor. Mark preserves the whole of it: the anointing at Bethany, the indignation over the waste, the word that they could do the poor good whenever they would, that she had done what she could, and the promise that what this woman had done would be told for a memorial wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world (Mark 14:3-9). What was exposed was the wrong of condemning an honourable act by invoking another duty insincerely. The law asks the whole heart and soul and might (Deuteronomy 6:5), and both of the acts recorded of her, the sitting and the anointing, were that. Neither was taken from her.

name: The barren fig tree
text: Cumbering the ground three years without fruit. Answering the news of Galilaeans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices, Christ refused to rank the dead as worse sinners than the rest, and warned twice that without repentance they would all likewise perish (Luke 13:1-5). He then gave the parable of a fig tree in a vineyard that had been sought for fruit three years and found barren, and the order to cut it down (Luke 13:6-7). The dresser asked for one more year to dig about it and dung it, and if it still bore nothing, then it would be cut down (Luke 13:8-9). Word was brought of Galilaeans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices, and he refused to let the hearers rank those men as sinners above all other Galilaeans, and said the same of the eighteen killed when the tower in Siloam fell; twice, in the same words, he answered that without repentance they would all likewise perish (Luke 13:1-5). He was not speaking of dying in the body, because every man dies. Ezekiel makes the same demand and names what is at stake: repent and turn from all transgressions, so that iniquity is not your ruin, and make a new heart and a new spirit, for why will a house of Israel die (Ezekiel 18:30-32). The perishing in view is of the soul. Comparing themselves favourably with men who died suddenly took nothing off their own account. Then the parable. A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, came three years seeking fruit on it and found none, and told the dresser to cut it down, since it was only taking up the ground (Luke 13:6-7). The vineyard is named in the prophets: the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant, and what he looked for in it was judgment and righteousness (Isaiah 5:1-7). The three years is the length of his own ministry among the people, who began to be about thirty years of age (Luke 3:23). The fruit sought is what John required of those coming to his baptism, fruits meet for repentance (Matthew 3:7-8), and what is named as the fruit of the spirit: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness and temperance (Galatians 5:22-23). A tree standing in the vineyard, tended and watered, and returning nothing, is the charge. The dresser asked that it be let alone one more year, until he should dig about it and dung it, and if it bore fruit, well; and if not, then it would be cut down (Luke 13:8-9). Digging and dunging is cultivation: feeding the tree, working the ground, giving it time. That added year is the longsuffering of God, the same longsuffering that waited in the days of Noah while the ark was preparing (1 Peter 3:20). The extra time came with labour spent on the tree and with an expectation attached to it, not with a ruling that barrenness no longer mattered. The parable stops on that condition. It never reports that this tree bore, and it never reports the axe. The history reports what the parable leaves open: three years was the length of the ministry, and the city was cut down after it, the house left desolate as he said standing over it (Luke 13:34-35). Time given is time to turn. Men grow bold in evil because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, and yet it shall be well with them that fear God (Ecclesiastes 8:11-13). The reprieve here was real, it was worked for, and it was measured.

name: The Samaritan leper who returned
text: One of ten: turning back to glorify God with a loud voice, and giving thanks at his feet. Ten lepers stood far off and cried for mercy, and were sent to show themselves to the priests as the law requires, and were cleansed as they went (Luke 17:11-14). Nine kept going. One turned back, glorified God with a loud voice and fell on his face at Christ’s feet giving thanks, and Luke names him a Samaritan, that is, an Israelite of the northern kingdom (Luke 17:15-16). He alone was asked after and told that his faith had made him whole (Luke 17:17-19). Passing through the midst of Samaria and Galilee, he entered a village and ten men that were lepers met him, standing far off, and lifted up their voices for mercy; he told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were cleansed (Luke 17:11-14). The order was the law. When he cleansed a leper earlier he charged the man to tell no one, but to go and show himself to the priest and offer for his cleansing according as Moses commanded, for a testimony (Luke 5:12-14), and that offering is set out in the law of the leper (Leviticus 14:2-4). Christ did not set the statute aside; he sent men to keep it. They moved on his word before the record says a thing about them being healed. One of them, seeing that he was healed, turned back and glorified God with a loud voice, and fell down on his face at his feet giving thanks; and Luke adds that he was a Samaritan (Luke 17:15-16). That does not mean another nation. Samaria held Israelites: the woman at the well asked whether he was greater than their father Jacob, and the record notes that the Jews had no dealings with the Samaritans (John 4:9; John 4:12). The man Christ goes on to call a stranger is an Israelite of the northern kingdom, and the scriptures use the word that way. The sons of the stranger who join themselves to the Lord, keep the sabbath and take hold of his covenant are brought to the holy mountain and their sacrifices accepted (Isaiah 56:6-7), and the strangers gathered with Judah and Benjamin came out of Ephraim and Manasseh and Simeon, and entered into a covenant to seek the Lord with all their heart (2 Chronicles 15:9; 2 Chronicles 15:12). He asked whether there were not ten cleansed, where the other nine were, and why none was found returning to give glory to God except this stranger, and then told the man to arise and go his way, for his faith had made him whole (Luke 17:17-19). All ten were cleansed; one was commended. The thing named is faith, and faith is what marks the children of Abraham, for they which are of faith are the children of Abraham (Galatians 3:7). Israel did not obtain that which it sought, but the election obtained it and the rest were blinded (Romans 11:7). The nine were of the blood. The one who came back had the faith with it. The account does not announce the end of the nine or take back what was given them. It makes their absence a question that has to be answered. Thanksgiving belongs together with the mercy received: the man who offers praise glorifies God (Psalms 50:23), and the charge is to bless the Lord and forget none of his benefits, who forgives all iniquities and heals all diseases (Psalms 103:1-3). This man did not forget once the trouble was lifted off him. He turned around and went back to the one who lifted it.

name: Zacchaeus
text: Extortion as chief of the publicans. Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans at Jericho and rich, could not see Christ for the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree, and was called down by name and received him joyfully while the people murmured (Luke 19:1-7). Standing before him he said he gave half of his goods to the poor, and that if he had taken anything from any man by false accusation he restored it fourfold, which is the rate the law names (Luke 19:8; Exodus 22:1). Salvation came to his house, and he was named a son of Abraham, since the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:9-10). Jesus entered and passed through Jericho, and a man named Zacchaeus, who was chief among the publicans and rich, sought to see who he was and could not for the press, because he was little of stature; so he ran before and climbed up into a sycamore tree on the road he would take (Luke 19:1-4). He had been hearing the reports. A cleansed leper had published the matter and blazed it abroad until Christ could no more openly enter a city (Mark 1:40-45), and this man wanted to see for himself who everybody was talking about. The office and the money are the setting of the case; the interest that put him up that tree was already faith. Christ came to the place, looked up, called him by his name and told him to make haste and come down, for he must abide at his house that day; he made haste and came down and received him joyfully, while the onlookers murmured that he had gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner (Luke 19:5-7). Receiving a man carries a promise with it: he that receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward, and even a cup of cold water given in the name of a disciple does not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40-42). That cold water is good news from a far country to a thirsty soul (Proverbs 25:25). The murmurers had already been answered once: the whole need no physician, but they that are sick, and they were sent to go and learn what it means that God will have mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:11-13; Hosea 6:6). Zacchaeus stood and said that half of his goods he gave to the poor, and that if he had taken anything from any man by false accusation he restored him fourfold (Luke 19:8). That is a man applying the law to himself. Fourfold is the rate the statute names for a stolen sheep, where an ox requires five (Exodus 22:1); the law of the trespass requires the principal restored with a fifth part added, paid to the man who was wronged (Leviticus 6:1-5; Numbers 5:6-7); and David passed the same fourfold sentence on himself when Nathan set the parable before him (2 Samuel 12:5-6). John had already told publicans coming to his baptism to exact no more than was appointed them, and to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance (Luke 3:8; Luke 3:12-13). A sacrifice cannot stand in the place of dealing justly with the man a person has robbed. Salvation came to that house that day, and he was called a son of Abraham, because the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:9-10). Sonship there is by faith, not by the sacrifice: Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, and circumcision was afterward the seal of a righteousness of faith he already had (Romans 4:1-3; Romans 4:11). A rich young ruler heard a like word about selling and giving to the poor and went away sorrowful because he had great possessions (Matthew 19:16-22); a rich man hardly enters the kingdom, and yet this rich man did, because his hand was already open. And the salvation spoken over the house is the one Zacharias named, to be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all that hate us (Luke 1:68-74), for the lost that the Son of man came after are the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24).

name: Pontius Pilate
text: Condemning a man he had three times pronounced innocent. The council brought Christ to Pilate on charges they had made up, that he perverted the nation, forbade tribute to Caesar and called himself a king, every one of which the record refutes (Luke 23:1-3; Matthew 22:15-22; John 18:33-34). Pilate examined him, said he found no fault in the man, said it again, and a third time asked what evil he had done, finding no cause of death in him (Luke 23:4; Luke 23:13-16; Luke 23:20-25). Knowing that they had delivered him for envy, and warned by his wife’s dream, he still gave sentence when releasing the prisoner was turned into disloyalty to Caesar (Matthew 27:18-19; John 19:12-16). The whole multitude led him to Pilate and began to accuse him, saying they had found this fellow perverting the nation, forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ a king (Luke 23:1-2). Every count was a slander. He had been asked plainly whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar, had called the men who asked it hypocrites, and had told them to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, so that they marvelled and left him (Matthew 22:15-22). And when Pilate asked whether he was the King of the Jews, his answer was to ask whether Pilate said that of himself, or whether others had told it to him (John 18:33-34; Luke 23:3). He never claimed the title they charged him with. Pilate examined him and told the chief priests and the people that he found no fault in this man; when they grew the more fierce he said it again, and a third time asked what evil the man had done, finding no cause of death in him (Luke 23:4; Luke 23:13-16; Luke 23:20-25; John 18:38; John 19:4). Matthew gives the reason he could see it: he knew that for envy they had delivered him, and his wife sent word of what she had suffered in a dream (Matthew 27:18-19). He tried to move the case out of his hands to Herod’s jurisdiction, and Herod, whose house had sought the child’s life and who had beheaded John, got no answer at all (Luke 23:6-11). The governor who said three times that the prisoner was innocent is the governor who handed him over, and he handed him over when releasing him was cast as disloyalty to Caesar (John 19:12-16). Washing his hands before the multitude did not undo the sentence he gave (Matthew 27:22-26). The law forbids following a multitude to do evil, and forbids slaying the innocent and righteous (Exodus 23:2; Exodus 23:7). No divine sentence upon Pilate is recorded in the Gospels. What is recorded is the company he was put in: against the holy child Jesus, Herod and Pontius Pilate were gathered together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel (Acts 4:27-28). That their gathering fulfilled what God’s counsel had determined before did not turn a false judgment into a just one. And the weight of the record does not fall on the Roman. Even he said he found no fault in the man; it was his own nation that grew the more fierce and pressed the case (Luke 23:5). The apostles kept his name in the testimony: Christ witnessed a good confession before Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6:13). The contrast stands there, between a prisoner bearing witness to the truth and a judge who announced innocence and then yielded to pressure. To justify the wicked and to condemn the just are both an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 17:15). What was done to the Master sets the pattern for the servants: the followers of Christ are brought before governors on invented charges and have all manner of evil said against them falsely, and are told to rejoice and be exceeding glad, for so were the prophets persecuted before them (Matthew 5:10-12).

name: The penitent thief
text: Robbery, under sentence of crucifixion. Two malefactors were crucified with Christ, one on either side, and one of them railed on him while the other rebuked his fellow, owned that they received the due reward of their deeds, and said that this man had done nothing amiss (Luke 23:32-33; Luke 23:39-41). He then asked to be remembered when Christ came into his kingdom, which is not the speech of a man who thought him a common prisoner (Luke 23:42). He was answered with the promise of paradise that same day (Luke 23:43). Two other malefactors were led with him to be put to death, and they crucified him at the place called Calvary, one criminal on the right hand and one on the left (Luke 23:32-33). The soldiers mocked him and offered him vinegar, the superscription over him was written in letters of Greek and Latin and Hebrew, and one of the two railed on him, telling him to save himself and them if he was the Christ (Luke 23:36-39). The other rebuked his companion, asked whether he did not fear God seeing he was under the same condemnation, said that they were there justly and received the due reward of their deeds, and that this man had done nothing amiss (Luke 23:40-41). He did not use his own suffering as an argument for his innocence. He judged himself first, and he judged his fellow for railing. Then he asked to be remembered when Christ came into his kingdom (Luke 23:42). That petition tells what the man already knew. A prisoner who thought this was just another condemned man would not have spoken of a kingdom that was coming. The rulers of his nation had said they had no king but Caesar (John 19:15), having settled into their place under Rome and their share of its comfort; this man, with nothing left and hours to live, was still looking for the kingdom the scriptures promised. He had broken Rome’s law and Rome was killing him for it. His repentance showed itself in the rebuke he gave, the guilt he owned and the mercy he asked for. The answer was that he would be with him that day in paradise (Luke 23:43). The promise did not take him off the cross and did not declare his former deeds harmless. Nor is it a general rule that every man goes somewhere at death. Esdras was told he would be taken away from all and would remain with the Son and with such as were like him until the times were ended (2 Esdras 14:9), and Christ said that where he is, there also shall his servant be (John 12:26). John saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, speaking, asking how long until their blood was avenged, receiving white robes and told to rest yet for a little season (Revelation 6:9-11), while the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished (Revelation 20:5). The righteous is taken away from the evil to come, and enters into peace (Isaiah 57:1-2). The promise is particular, and it was spoken over a man who had just acknowledged that his punishment was just. Isaiah had written that the servant would be numbered with the transgressors and make intercession for the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), and here is the scene in the flesh: the innocent man between two guilty ones, the one railing and the other receiving mercy. There was darkness over all the earth from the sixth hour to the ninth, the sun was darkened and the veil of the temple was rent, and when it was over the centurion glorified God and said that certainly this was a righteous man, and all the people that had come to the sight beat their breasts and went home (Luke 23:44-48). The last hour was not out of reach of repentance. It is no warrant for counting on a last hour that has not been promised to anybody.

name: The traders in the temple
text: Making the house of prayer a den of thieves. At the passover Christ found in the temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting, made a scourge of small cords and drove them all out, poured out the money and overthrew the tables (John 2:13-16).
