The other account names what the place had become, a house of prayer turned into a den of thieves, in the words of Isaiah and Jeremiah (Matthew 21:12-13; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11). The trade was put out, the disciples remembered the writing about the zeal of God’s house, and the scribes and chief priests answered the correction by seeking how to destroy him (John 2:17; Mark 11:18). The passover was at hand and he went up to Jerusalem, and found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting (John 2:13-14). This was during the feast, in the court of the house, and no man had business trading in there at the passover. What they had made of the place is named in the later account: the house of prayer turned into a den of thieves (Matthew 21:12-13; Mark 11:15-17), the words taken out of the prophets (Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11). A den is where robbers go to divide what they have taken and to plan the next one. That is what the house of the Lord had been turned into. Jeremiah had already described the leadership that let it get that way. They were waxen fat, they shone, they overpassed the deeds of the wicked, they judged not the cause of the fatherless, and they judged not the right of the needy, and still they prospered (Jeremiah 5:27-28). Men who live off the people will overlook the wickedness of whoever pays them. And the warning that stands next to the den of thieves is the place God had already destroyed for the wickedness of his people (Jeremiah 7:12): the house itself protects nobody who steals, murders, commits adultery and swears falsely and then comes and stands in it (Jeremiah 7:8-11). Zechariah said the day would come when there would be no more the trader in the house of the Lord of hosts (Zechariah 14:21). He made a scourge of small cords and drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and the oxen, poured out the changers’ money and overthrew the tables, and told those that sold doves to take those things away and not make his Father’s house a house of merchandise (John 2:15-16). He drove grown men out of the temple with a whip. The Christ who did that was not the soft and mealy mouthed figure of the films; Mark adds that he would not allow a vessel to be carried through the temple, and that the scribes and chief priests heard it and sought how they might destroy him, because they feared him, since all the people were astonished at his doctrine (Mark 11:16-18). The men whose trade was overturned answered the correction with a plot. His disciples remembered that it was written, that the zeal of God’s house had eaten him up (John 2:17; Psalms 69:9). When they demanded a sign for what he had done he spoke of the temple of his body raised up in three days, which went over their heads at the time and which false witnesses carried into his trial later on (John 2:18-22; Matthew 26:59-61). The judgment in this record is temporal and immediate: the trade driven out, the money on the floor, the tables turned over, the house cleared. The same trade goes on wherever money is extracted from our people in the name of the house, and the seat is defended instead of the flock, and the same correction stands written against it.

name: Nicodemus
text: Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?; and bringing a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes. A Pharisee and ruler of the Jews came to Christ by night, acknowledged that his works showed God was with him, and was told that a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God (John 3:1-3). He was asked whether he was a master of Israel and did not know these things (John 3:9-10). When the council raged that no ruler had believed, he put their own law to them about hearing a man before judging him, and at the burial he came with a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes and wound the body with Joseph (John 7:45-52; John 19:38-42). There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, who came to Christ by night and said they knew he was a teacher come from God, because no man could do those miracles unless God were with him (John 3:1-2). Those men taught the synagogues, and coming openly would have cost him his standing, so he came in the dark; he was a secret disciple. The answer he got was not a welcome but a requirement: except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). He took it in the flesh and asked how a man can be born when he is old, and enter the second time into his mother’s womb, and was told that a man must be born of water and of the Spirit (John 3:4-5). Being born again is by the word of God, an incorruptible seed that lives and abides for ever (1 Peter 1:23); what is born of the flesh is flesh, and they that are in the flesh cannot please God (John 3:6-8; Romans 8:8). Esdras puts the same demand plainly: subdue your own understanding and reform your hearts (2 Esdras 14:34). That is a hard word to a man who already believes he is right, which is why sinners and publicans received Christ sooner than a ruler did. He was asked whether he was a master of Israel and did not know these things (John 3:9-10). Men depended on him for the understanding of the law. Later, when the council sent officers to take Christ and raged that none of the rulers had believed on him, Nicodemus asked them whether their law judges a man before it hears him, and was answered with a sneer about Galilee (John 7:45-52). The law he invoked is written: hear the causes between brethren and judge righteously, and make diligent inquisition (Deuteronomy 1:16-17; Deuteronomy 19:18). At the burial he came bringing about a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes, and wound the body with Joseph in the linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury (John 19:38-42). His appearances move from a night visit, to a demand for a lawful hearing, to costly service in the daylight. The teaching he was given is the heart of that chapter. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (John 3:14-15). The history behind it is plain and so is who it was for: it was Israel in the wilderness that spoke against God and against Moses, Israel that was bitten, and Israel that looked and lived (Numbers 21:5-9). The serpent of brass was a sign of salvation, given to put them in remembrance of the commandment of the law (Wisdom of Solomon 16:5-6), so the looking was never apart from repentance. The verse that follows, that God so loved the world (John 3:16), comes straight off the serpent and has the same people in view: the world John names elsewhere is the one Christ was made manifest to (John 1:29-31), the one the Pharisees said was gone after him (John 12:19), and the one he taught openly in the synagogue and the temple (John 18:20). Then the condemnation: light is come into the world and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil, while the man who does truth comes to the light so that his deeds may be made manifest (John 3:19-21). A man can be comfortable and even do well in the darkness he was raised in, and coming into the light costs him change. Christ did not condemn the rulers; they condemned themselves by not humbling down to repent. Nicodemus is the one of them who did come to the light, and the record of it is his deeds, not a sentence pronounced over him. The man first identified as coming by night is named again at the tomb (John 19:39). What he lacked at the first meeting he was still being called out of, and in the end he answered, at his own risk and his own cost.

name: The woman taken in adultery
text: Adultery, in the very act. While Christ was teaching in the temple early in the morning, the scribes and Pharisees brought in a woman taken in adultery, set her in the middle, cited Moses on stoning and asked what he said, tempting him so they might have something to accuse him of (John 8:1-6). Their own words condemned them, because adultery takes two and the law puts both to death, and they brought only the woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22-24). He told them that the man among them without sin should cast the first stone, and they went out one by one beginning at the eldest, and he told her that neither did he condemn her, and to sin no more (John 8:7-11). Early in the morning he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them, as he did daily, lodging at the mount of Olives at night (John 8:1-2; Luke 21:37). Into that teaching the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery and set her in the midst, saying that Moses in the law commanded that such should be stoned, and asking what he said; John states their purpose outright, that they said it tempting him, so that they might have something of which to accuse him (John 8:3-6). Their own mouths condemned them (Job 15:6). Adultery takes two. The law they were quoting forbids the man to lie carnally with his neighbour’s wife (Leviticus 18:20), puts both the adulterer and the adulteress to death (Leviticus 20:10), and orders that both of them die, and that both be brought out to the gate of the city and stoned (Deuteronomy 22:22-24). If she was taken in the very act, then a man was taken with her, and they brought the woman only. These were the men who sat in Moses’ seat (Matthew 23:2-3), the judges and officers the law requires in every gate, charged to judge the people with just judgment and not to wrest judgment (Deuteronomy 16:18-19), and evil men understand not judgment (Proverbs 28:5). They were willing to have a woman killed in order to catch a man in his speech and charge him with speaking against the law, which is the one accusation they believed would not be forgiven (Matthew 12:31). He stooped down and with his finger wrote on the ground as though he did not hear them, and the record never says what he wrote; there is no room in it to invent the words. When they continued asking, he lifted himself up and said that the man among them that is without sin should first cast a stone at her (John 8:7-8). Sin is the transgression of the law (1 John 3:4), and the law he was pointing them back to is their own procedure: at the mouth of two or three witnesses a man is put to death, and the hands of the witnesses are to be first upon him, and afterward the hands of all the people (Deuteronomy 17:6-7). They had come with witnesses. They were being told to throw. Convicted by their own conscience, they went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, until he was left alone with the woman standing in the midst (John 8:9). The eldest knew what the next statute says: if a false witness rises up, both parties stand before the priests and the judges, diligent inquisition is made, and what the false witness thought to do to his brother is done to him, so that the rest hear and fear (Deuteronomy 19:16-21). The law also forbids going up and down as a talebearer among the people and standing against the blood of a neighbour (Leviticus 19:16). Blessed is the man whose conscience has not condemned him (Ecclesiasticus 14:2); theirs had. He asked her where her accusers were and whether no man had condemned her, and she said no man, and he told her that neither did he condemn her, and to go and sin no more (John 8:10-11). That is the mercy those men had omitted, one of the weightier matters of the law along with judgment and faith (Matthew 23:23). She was spared; adultery was not made lawful. The Son of man came to save men’s lives and not to destroy them (Luke 9:56), and the last word spoken to her was an order to stop.

name: Caiaphas and the council
text: Seeking false witness against Christ; condemning him by night; delivering him to the Gentiles; forbidding the apostles; stoning Stephen. The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said that if they let this man alone all would believe on him and the Romans would take away their place and nation, and Caiaphas told them it was expedient that one man die for the people (John 11:47-53). From that day they took counsel to put him to death, sought false witness and found none that agreed, condemned him and carried him to Pilate with invented charges (Matthew 26:59-61; Luke 23:1-2). Afterward they threatened and beat the apostles, forbade them to speak in that name, and killed Stephen (Acts 4:13-21; Acts 5:40; Acts 7:57-60). The chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a council and asked what they were doing, since this man did many miracles; if they let him alone all men would believe on him, and the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation (John 11:47-48). The motive is stated there in their own words. Rome kept them in their seat of authority; without Rome they had nothing. Caiaphas, being the high priest that year, told them they knew nothing at all, and that it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and from that day they took counsel together to put him to death (John 11:49-53). The verdict was settled before there was any hearing. Annas had held the office and kept the title after the Romans put him out, and Caiaphas his son in law was the high priest the year Christ was killed; both are named with John and Alexander and the kindred of the high priest (Acts 4:5-6). These were the very men who procured the death. The council sought false witness to put him to death and found none that agreed together, two coming at the last with the saying about destroying the temple (Matthew 26:59-62; Mark 14:55-59). They condemned him on his own answer and then carried accusations to Pilate that contradicted what he had taught, that he perverted the nation and forbade tribute to Caesar (Matthew 26:63-66; Luke 23:1-2). The law they administered forbids raising a false report and joining hands with the wicked as an unrighteous witness, forbids following a multitude to do evil, and forbids slaying the innocent (Exodus 23:1-2; Exodus 23:7), and it requires diligent inquisition, with the false witness punished as he intended (Deuteronomy 19:15-19). Peter set it before their faces in their own chamber: the stone which was set at nought of the builders had become the head of the corner, and there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:7-12). It was the builders’ own office to build and bind the nation, to feed the flock and bind up the brokenhearted; when the stone came, envy and vainglory put it out. They could say nothing against the healed man standing there with the apostles, and they still conferred and threatened, because it was never about the miracle but about their position and their following (Acts 4:13-18). Told to judge for themselves whether it is right to hearken to men rather than to God, they let the apostles go for fear of the people (Acts 4:19-21), and afterward beat them and commanded them again not to speak in that name (Acts 5:27-28; Acts 5:40). Stephen named them the betrayers and murderers of the Just One, men who received the law by the disposition of angels and did not keep it, and they answered by killing him also (Acts 7:51-53; Acts 7:54-60). Their allegiance was to Rome and to a kingdom here; Paul writes of those who both killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, who please not God and are contrary to all men (1 Thessalonians 2:14-16). Christ had said the kingdom would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits of it, and that their house was left to them desolate (Matthew 21:43; Matthew 23:38). Office did not cover them, and the whole council was not of one mind: Joseph of Arimathaea had not consented to their counsel and deed (Luke 23:50-51), and Nicodemus had called for a lawful hearing (John 7:51).

name: Judas Iscariot
text: Theft from the common purse; betraying innocent blood for thirty pieces of silver. One of the twelve, he carried the bag and took what was put in it, and his objection to the ointment at Bethany was made in the name of the poor although he cared nothing for them (John 12:4-6). Satan entered into him, he asked the chief priests what they would give him, they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver as the prophet had written, and he delivered Christ with a kiss (Luke 22:3-6; Zechariah 11:12-13; Luke 22:47-48). When he saw that Christ was condemned he brought the money back, confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood, threw the silver into the temple and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). He was one of the twelve and he kept the bag, which is where the money was, and he took what was put in it (John 12:4-6; John 13:29). His objection to Mary’s ointment at Bethany was spoken in the name of the poor, and John says plainly that it was not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief. He walked with Christ, saw the healing, was around the commandment keeping, and never repented of what he was. The commandment on it is one line: do not steal (Exodus 20:15). Riches are not comely for a niggard, and what should an envious man do with money (Ecclesiasticus 14:3)? They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts which drown men in destruction and perdition, for the love of money is the root of all evil, and some coveting after it have erred from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:9-10). Then Satan entered into him, and he went to the chief priests and captains and asked what they would give him, and they were glad and covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver, and from that time he sought opportunity to betray him away from the multitude (Luke 22:3-6; Matthew 26:14-16). Men are not in their right mind when they can be glad over a thing like that. The price was written beforehand: thirty pieces of silver, cast to the potter in the house of the Lord (Zechariah 11:12-13), which Matthew credits to Jeremy because Zechariah was repeating what the earlier prophet had said in a writing that did not survive. Judas delivered him with a kiss, and was asked whether he betrayed the Son of man with a kiss (Luke 22:47-48). The statute names the act without disguise: cursed is the man that takes reward to slay an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:25), and the psalm had said it would be the familiar friend who lifted up his heel (Psalms 41:9). When he saw that Christ was condemned, he repented himself, brought the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders and said he had sinned in that he had betrayed innocent blood; they told him to see to it himself, and he cast the silver down in the temple, departed, and went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). Giving the money back did not give back the life he had sold. The priests would not put it into the treasury because it was the price of blood, and bought the potter’s field with it to bury strangers in, so that the field is called the field of blood to this day (Matthew 27:6-10). Acts records the fearful end there and the office given to another man, as the psalm had said (Acts 1:16-20; Acts 1:25; Psalms 109:8). The warning had been spoken at the table: the Son of man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed, and it had been good for that man if he had never been born (Mark 14:21; Matthew 26:24). He was sorry afterward, and sorrow by itself is not repentance: godly sorrow works repentance to salvation not to be repented of, but the sorrow of the world works death (2 Corinthians 7:10). He that loves gold shall not be justified, and gold has been the ruin of many, their destruction being present with them (Ecclesiasticus 31:5-6). A place among the twelve, three years in the company of Christ and the trust of the bag did not make a hidden covetousness safe. Money was his demise, and men will still give a brother up for it.

name: Barnabas
text: Selling his land and laying the money at the apostles’ feet; a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith. Joses, whom the apostles surnamed Barnabas, a Levite of Cyprus, sold his land and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, in a congregation where none lacked because distribution was made to every man according to his need (Acts 4:32-37). When the disciples feared Saul, Barnabas brought him to the apostles and told them what had happened on the road and at Damascus, and afterward sought him at Tarsus to share a year of teaching at Antioch (Acts 9:26-28; Acts 11:22-26). Luke calls him a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith, and the church commended him and Paul as men that had hazarded their lives for the name of the Lord (Acts 15:25-26). The multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul, and no man said that anything he possessed was his own, but they had all things common; none among them lacked, because those who owned lands or houses sold them and laid the money down at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to every man according as he had need (Acts 4:32-35). Joses, whom the apostles surnamed Barnabas, which is the son of consolation, a Levite of the country of Cyprus, sold his land and brought the money and laid it at their feet (Acts 4:36-37). This was never a prosperity arrangement where a man gives in order to get rich. The congregation was the centre of the community, and the alms circulated through it, so that when one lacked, the rest supplied him, whether the need was food, a rent or a proper burial. The law had long required the open hand toward a poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:7-8). Barnabas was a ranked man and he still gave, and his gift stands in the record immediately before the deceit of Ananias and Sapphira; giving and the appearance of giving are not the same thing. His consolation reached further than his purse. When Saul came to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, they were all afraid of him and did not believe that he was a disciple, until Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared how he had seen the Lord in the way, and how he had preached boldly at Damascus in that name (Acts 9:26-28). He did not ask them to forget what Saul had done; he brought them the witness of what had happened since. Sent out from Jerusalem to Antioch when a great number there turned to the Lord, he saw the grace of God and was glad, and exhorted them all that with purpose of heart they would cleave to the Lord; then he departed to Tarsus to seek Saul, brought him to Antioch, and for a whole year they assembled with the congregation and taught much people (Acts 11:22-26). Luke describes him there as a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith, and adds that much people was added to the Lord. To be full of the Holy Ghost is first and foremost to be keeping the laws; the wisdom and understanding come after that, and then the power. The name the apostles gave him, the son of consolation, matches both his giving and his care for the brethren. When the prophet Agabus signified by the spirit that a great dearth was coming, which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar, the disciples at Antioch determined, every man according to his ability, to send relief to the brethren in Judaea, and they sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:27-30). The same care for need bound congregations together across distance. The Holy Ghost afterward separated Barnabas and Saul for the work to which they were called, and the congregation sent them away with fasting and prayer and the laying on of hands (Acts 13:1-3). The work cost them. At Antioch in Pisidia they told the rulers that the word of God had to be spoken to them first, and turned to the scattered when it was put from them, and the two were raised persecution against and expelled out of the coasts by their own countrymen (Acts 13:46-50). When certain men came down from Judaea teaching that no man could be saved without circumcision after the manner of Moses, Barnabas and Paul had no small dissension with them and carried the matter up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, and the letter that came back out of that council named them men that had hazarded their lives for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 15:1-2; Acts 15:25-26). Money, reputation, teaching and life itself were all put into the work.

name: Ananias and Sapphira
text: Vowing a possession to the Lord, keeping back part of the price, and lying to the Holy Ghost about it. Ananias, with his wife Sapphira knowing of it, sold a possession, kept back part of the price, and laid the remainder at the apostles’ feet as though it were the whole (Acts 5:1-2). Peter told him the land was his before the sale and the money was in his own power after it, so the offence was not the amount but the lie, which was not to men but to God (Acts 5:3-4). He fell down and died, and three hours later his wife repeated the same figure and fell down also, and great fear came on the whole congregation (Acts 5:5-11). This follows straight on from the end of the previous chapter, where none of the believers lacked, because as many as owned lands or houses sold them and laid the price at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to every man according as he had need (Acts 4:34-35). A certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession and kept back part of the price, his wife being privy to it, and brought a certain part and laid it at the apostles’ feet as though it were the whole (Acts 5:1-2). Peter stated their freedom plainly: while the land remained, it was their own, and after it was sold the money was in their own power (Acts 5:3-4). Nobody demanded the property. Money is only a tool for the work, and a man gives as much as he has, with wisdom, so that he does not strip himself and end up a burden. The offence was not the amount. It was the account they gave of it. The spirit on them was covetousness and lying together. They saw the full value and wanted it, and they also wanted the standing of a whole offering. A vow is not required of any man, but once it is spoken it binds: when a man vows a vow he is not to be slack in paying it, and what has gone out of his lips he must keep and perform (Deuteronomy 23:21-23; Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). It is better to say that a thing cannot be done than to swear to what will not be performed, and the instruction is that our communication be yes and no (Matthew 5:33-37). The renewed mind is required to put away lying and speak truth with the neighbour, because we are members one of another (Ephesians 4:23-25), and the law says not to steal, nor deal falsely, nor lie one to another (Leviticus 19:11). Peter carried the charge past appearances before men: the lie was to the Holy Ghost and to God. Ananias heard those words, fell down and gave up the ghost, and the young men wound him up, carried him out and buried him (Acts 5:5-6). About three hours after, his wife came in, not knowing what was done, and Peter asked her directly whether they had sold the land for so much; she confirmed the figure, was told that the feet of the men who had buried her husband were at the door, and fell down straightway and was buried by him (Acts 5:7-10). Her agreement with her husband did not shield her. A wife submits in righteousness, not in wickedness; had she refused the thing, or carried it to the leadership, she could have saved his life, the way Abigail saved her house (1 Samuel 25:23-33). Great fear came upon all the congregation and upon as many as heard these things (Acts 5:11). This happened after the death of Christ, among the people gathered around the apostles, under grace, and grace was never a licence to sin. The Most High commanded no man to do wickedly, and gave no man licence to sin (Ecclesiasticus 15:20). The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), and the question whether we should continue in sin so that grace may abound is answered with God forbid (Romans 6:1-2). If a man sins wilfully after he has received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:26-27). Measures differ, and other men were spared for worse, since grace is given according to the measure of the gift of Christ (Ephesians 4:7). But the witness in this matter was not two or three men; the eyes of the Most High are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, seeing all the ways of men (Ecclesiasticus 23:19). The gift was voluntary. Truthfulness was not.

name: Stephen
text: Full of faith and of the Holy Ghost; a face like an angel before the council; forgiving those who stoned him. When the widows of the Grecians were neglected in the daily ministration, the twelve told the congregation to look out seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, and Stephen was named first among them (Acts 6:1-6). Full of faith and power he did great wonders, and men who could not resist the wisdom by which he spoke bribed witnesses to accuse him of blasphemy (Acts 6:8-14). Before the council he rehearsed the history of the fathers, charged his hearers with receiving the law and not keeping it, saw the glory of God, and was stoned praying that the sin not be laid to their charge (Acts 7:51-60). The complaint that began it was that the widows of the Grecians were neglected in the daily ministration (Acts 6:1). The Grecians are Greek speaking Israelites of the dispersion, our people scattered into the Greek provinces and named after the land that held them, the same way our people carried across the water are named for the place of their captivity now. There was money laid up for widows and there was an order for it, with a standard for who was taken into the number (1 Timothy 5:9-12). Those widows were being neglected because these were followers of Christ, and the rulers had already agreed that any man who confessed him should be put out of the synagogue (John 9:22). The twelve said it was not reason that they should leave the word of God and serve tables, and told the multitude to look out seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and of wisdom, whom they would appoint over the business, so that the apostles could give themselves continually to prayer and the ministry of the word (Acts 6:2-4). The measure used is the one written for deacons: grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre, first proved and then found blameless (1 Timothy 3:8-10). Stephen is named first of the seven, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and the apostles prayed and laid hands on them (Acts 6:5-6). Full of faith and power, he did great wonders and miracles among the people, and men of the synagogue of the Libertines, with the Cyrenians and Alexandrians and them of Cilicia and of Asia, rose up disputing with him and were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spoke (Acts 6:8-10). Every group named there is Greek speaking Israelites, and the Libertines were freedmen out of Roman slavery. Beaten on the scriptures, they suborned men to say that he had spoken blasphemous words against Moses and against God, stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, caught him and brought him to the council, and set up false witnesses (Acts 6:11-14). He was not teaching men to break the laws. He was teaching them to receive Christ in the place of the animal sacrifice, and they could not tell the difference between mercy and the keeping of the law. Before the council he recited the history of the fathers from Abraham in Mesopotamia through Joseph and Moses, off the top of his head, and brought it to its point: Moses said that God would raise up a prophet of their brethren like himself, and that prophet is the Christ (Acts 7:2-8; Acts 7:35-37). Our forefathers read more than a few chapters a day, and a man who has read can recite. The fathers would not obey that prophet in the wilderness, and the children would not obey him now. Then he turned it on them: stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, always resisting the Holy Ghost as their fathers did; which of the prophets had their fathers not persecuted; they had received the law by the disposition of angels and had not kept it (Acts 7:51-53). The charge was never that the law was evil. It was that the men who received it did not keep it. They were cut to the heart and gnashed on him with their teeth, and he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, and said so out loud (Acts 7:54-56). Their sentence did not overturn what heaven had shown him. They stopped their ears, ran upon him with one accord, cast him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul; and Stephen called on the Lord to receive his spirit, and kneeled down and cried that this sin should not be laid to their charge, and fell asleep (Acts 7:57-60). It is the same spirit Christ had when he asked the Father to forgive them. Devout men carried him to his burial and made great lamentation over him, and the great persecution that rose that day scattered the congregation abroad, and they that were scattered went everywhere preaching the word (Acts 8:1-4). His blessing was not escape from death. It was a face like the face of an angel before the council (Acts 6:15), the heavens opened to him, and the promise that belongs to those persecuted for righteousness (Matthew 5:10-12).

name: The false witnesses against Stephen
text: Suborning witnesses and stirring up the council against a man they could not answer. Men of the synagogues of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicia and Asia disputed with Stephen and could not resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spoke (Acts 6:9-10). Beaten on the scriptures, they suborned men to charge him with blasphemy against Moses and against God, stirred up the people and the rulers, and set up false witnesses before the council against the holy place and the law (Acts 6:11-14). Acts records no penalty on them; it records that the man they accused was cast out and stoned, and that they laid their clothes at Saul’s feet (Acts 7:54-58). The dispute began in the synagogue of the Libertines, with the Cyrenians and Alexandrians and them of Cilicia and of Asia, and they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which Stephen spoke (Acts 6:9-10). Losing on the scriptures, they suborned men, which is to bribe and induce them, to say that they had heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God (Acts 6:11). They stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, came upon him, caught him and brought him to the council, and set up false witnesses who said he did not cease to speak blasphemous words against the holy place and the law (Acts 6:12-13). A losing argument was turned into a prosecution. The solemnity of the council did not clean the testimony carried into it. The witnesses said he taught that Jesus of Nazareth would destroy the place and change the customs Moses delivered (Acts 6:14). Christ said he came not to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfil (Matthew 5:17), and the only thing set aside was the burnt offering, which the prophets had already put in its place: God spoke not to the fathers concerning burnt offerings when he brought them out of Egypt, he desired mercy and not sacrifice, and to obey is better than sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:22; Hosea 6:6; 1 Samuel 15:22). The same method had been used on the Master, where the council sought false witness and the witnesses agreed not together (Matthew 26:59-61; Mark 14:55-59), and it was used again on Paul, charged with teaching men to forsake Moses and to speak against the law and the place (Acts 21:21; Acts 21:28). The law these men claimed to be defending forbids false witness outright (Exodus 20:16), and Stephen named the contradiction in one sentence: they had received the law and had not kept it (Acts 7:53). Acts records no penalty carried out upon these witnesses. It records what their testimony did. The council was cut to the heart and gnashed on him, they cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, ran upon him with one accord, cast him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul (Acts 7:54-58). Under the statute, the men who witness in a capital cause cast the first stones, and afterward the hands of all the people (Deuteronomy 17:6-7), so their own hands were on it. And the statute written for their case is equally plain: if a false witness rises up, both parties stand before the priests and the judges, diligent inquisition is made, and what the false witness thought to do to his brother is done to him, so that the rest hear and fear and do no more such evil (Deuteronomy 19:16-21). Stephen’s last prayer asked that this sin should not be laid to their charge (Acts 7:59-60). That did not rename what they had done. It asked mercy for men who were guilty of it. One of the men standing there received that mercy and said so afterward: Saul was consenting to his death, and stood by and kept the clothes of those who killed him (Acts 8:1; Acts 22:20). That one persecutor repented does not supply an unwritten acquittal for everyone who took part. The statute stands against the testimony they gave, and the end of the men who gave it is not disclosed, which is where it is left: judge nothing before the time (1 Corinthians 4:5).

name: Saul of Tarsus
text: Persecuting the church; consenting to Stephen’s death; compelling the saints to blaspheme. The witnesses who stoned Stephen laid their clothes at his feet, and he was consenting to the death; from that day he made havock of the congregation, entering every house and committing men and women to prison (Acts 7:58; Acts 8:1-3). Breathing out threatenings and slaughter, he went to the high priest for letters to Damascus so that he might bring any he found of that way bound to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). A light out of heaven struck him down on the road, and the voice asked why he was persecuting Christ; the man who came to lead others bound was led by the hand into the city, blind, and afterward was told he was a chosen vessel who would suffer for that name (Acts 9:3-9; Acts 9:15-16). The witnesses who stoned Stephen laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul, and he was consenting to his death (Acts 7:58; Acts 8:1). From that day he made havock of the congregation, entering into every house and haling men and women and committing them to prison (Acts 8:3). Still breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples, he went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). Before the followers of Christ were called Christians at Antioch they were called this way, after the one who said he is the way (John 14:6). Authority from the chief priests gave the campaign an official face. It did not make it obedience to God. His own account is heavier than Luke’s summary. He persecuted this way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women (Acts 22:4-5). He shut up many of the saints in prison, gave his voice against them when they were put to death, punished them often in every synagogue and compelled them to blaspheme, and being exceedingly mad against them, persecuted them even to strange cities (Acts 26:9-11). He thought he ought to do it. He had been brought up at the feet of Gamaliel and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers (Acts 22:3); he was of the stock of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, a Pharisee, and by his own reckoning blameless touching the righteousness which is in the law (Philippians 3:5-6); and he profited in that religion above many of his equals, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of his fathers, while he wasted the church of God beyond measure (Galatians 1:13-14). Learning, zeal and certainty did not keep him out of the gravest sin. As he came near Damascus a light from heaven shined round about him, he fell to the earth and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him (Acts 9:3-5). Christ was already dead at that time, and the question still stands in the present tense, because what is done to one of his little ones is done to him. Trembling and astonished, the man who had set out to lead others bound asked what he would have him do, and was led by the hand into the city, and was three days without sight and neither ate nor drank (Acts 9:6-9). The men with him stood speechless, hearing a voice and seeing no man, while his own retelling says they saw the light and heard not the voice, the other half of one event and no contradiction (Acts 22:9). Ananias objected that he had heard by many how much evil this man had done to the saints at Jerusalem, and was told to go, for he was a chosen vessel to bear the name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, and would be shown how great things he must suffer for it (Acts 9:13-16). Ananias went in, called him Brother Saul, and there fell from his eyes as it had been scales, and he received sight and was baptized (Acts 9:17-18). He did it in ignorance, which is why the scripture says to judge nothing before the time (1 Corinthians 4:5). The things any of us did before this truth were worthy of death, so no man is written off as beyond repentance, and the enemies who can still repent are the ones inside our own nation (Romans 11:28). Straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, and all that heard him were amazed and asked whether this was not the man who destroyed them which called on that name; but he increased the more in strength and confounded the Jews at Damascus (Acts 9:20-22). The mercy did not cancel the cost. They took counsel to kill him and watched the gates day and night, and the disciples took him by night and let him down the wall in a basket (Acts 9:23-25). He afterward called himself the least of the apostles, not meet to be called an apostle, because he persecuted the church of God (1 Corinthians 15:9), and a blasphemer and a persecutor and injurious, who obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly in unbelief, and was set forth as a pattern of Christ’s longsuffering to them which should believe after (1 Timothy 1:12-16). The gospel he preached was not taught him by any man; he had it by revelation, went into Arabia, and only after three years went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and James (Galatians 1:11-12; Galatians 1:17-19).

name: Simon Magus
text: Offering money for the gift of the Holy Ghost. A certain man called Simon had used sorcery in Samaria and gave out that he was some great one, and all gave heed to him, from the least to the greatest, calling him the great power of God. When Philip preached, Simon believed and was baptized and kept company with him, wondering at the miracles. Then he saw the Holy Ghost given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands and offered them money for the same power, and Peter told him his heart was not right and that he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity. He was commanded to repent and pray, and he asked the apostles to pray for him. Before Philip came down to Samaria there was a certain man called Simon who used sorcery and bewitched the people, giving out that he himself was some great one, and they all gave heed to him, from the least to the greatest, saying that this man was the great power of God, because of long time he had bewitched them with sorceries (Acts 8:9-11). That bewitching is what Christianity does to our people today, a binding spell that covers the eyes from seeing the truth, where a man can read the plain scripture that Christ is black and that he came first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and walk away not believing, or say he does not want the Bible, only your opinion, and then reject that too. It is an enchantment to the highest level, where a man reads one thing in front of him and sees something else. Then the people believed Philip and were baptized, both men and women, and Simon himself believed also and was baptized and continued with Philip, wondering at the miracles and signs (Acts 8:12-13). The apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word and sent Peter and John, who prayed for them and laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost (Acts 8:14-17). Notice the order: Philip the deacon woke the city up and planted, but the apostles had to come and put the spirit on them, the same order kept today when the bishop and the apostles visit the cities where new schools open and pray over the congregation. Paul described that order when he said he planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6). What those men received with the laying on of hands was the spirit and the remission of sins, because Christ appeared once in the end of the world to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26). When Simon saw that the Holy Ghost was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money and asked for the same power, that on whomever he laid hands the man might receive the Holy Ghost (Acts 8:18-19). Simon had the spirits of covetousness, envy, preeminence, and vainglory. He had held status as the great power of God, and when he lost it those spirits rose up in him and he wanted to buy back what he once had, thinking, I have the money, I will pay you for what you have. His art was itself forbidden in Israel, which suffers no enchanter or user of divination among the people (Deuteronomy 18:10-11). Peter answered that his money would perish with him because he had thought the gift of God could be purchased with money, that he had neither part nor lot in the matter because his heart was not right, and that he should repent and pray, for Peter perceived he was in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity (Acts 8:20-23). The gall of bitterness is deep resentment and bitterness of spirit; the bond of iniquity is sin holding a man fast. It was a foolish thought in his head, that the spirit of God could be bought. Simon became jealous because the signs God worked through the apostles overshadowed what the people had known him for. That thing did not come overnight. He fed envy, preeminence, vainglory, and covetousness day by day until the roots of bitterness took hold and bound him, and he became a prisoner of his own mind, trapped and sinning. Simon answered and asked them to pray to the Lord for him, that none of the things they had spoken would come upon him (Acts 8:24-25). This is why, when people come into the truth, some who had status, fame, or money as celebrities, pastors, or deacons have to come up as a member and clean themselves. Some get jealous, hold on to the envy, and try to bring different doctrines to sway members away, the same spirit of bitterness that moved the Pharisees to kill Christ because the disciples came from nowhere and went to the scriptures better without the status. The history outside the Bible says Simon Magus followed Peter performing tricks and became known as the father of heretics, teaching salvation by grace alone without works and claiming that he had manifested himself as the father in Samaria, the son in Judaea, and the holy spirit to the Gentiles, making himself a trinity. The validity of that account is uncertain, but some of our brothers recover themselves, and this one, by that record, never did.

name: Ananias of Damascus
text: Going to the street called Straight and putting his hands on the man who had come to bind him: Brother Saul. Saul was still breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples and had gone to the high priest for letters to Damascus, so that any of this way, men or women, could be brought bound to Jerusalem. A disciple at Damascus named Ananias was told in a vision to go to the street called Straight, to the house of Judas, and lay hands on Saul of Tarsus. He answered that he had heard by many how much evil this man had done to the saints at Jerusalem and that he held authority from the chief priests, and he was told to go, because Saul was a chosen vessel. He went in, called him Brother Saul, and laid his hands on him. Saul was still breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord and went to the high priest for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any of this way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). Before the followers of Christ were called Christians at Antioch they were called this way, meaning the way of Christ; and the sisters were hunted with the men, so this was not a persecution of the men only. These letters came from the same office that had the Messiah put to death, so it is no surprise that they were now having his disciples killed. On the road the light shone and the voice asked why he persecuted him; Saul never laid a hand on the Messiah himself, but he was laying hands on the elect, and to persecute the elect is to persecute Christ. Then the Lord spoke in a vision to a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias and sent him to the street called Straight, to the house of Judas, to ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying and had himself seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming in and putting his hand on him (Acts 9:3-12). Ananias objected, saying he had heard by many of this man, how much evil he had done to the saints at Jerusalem, and that here he had authority from the chief priests to bind all that called on the name (Acts 9:13-14). The objection was honest: this man held what amounted to a licence to kill from the high priest, and he had consented to Stephen’s death, shut up the saints in prison, punished them in every synagogue, and persecuted them even to strange cities (Acts 26:10-11). Was Saul doing it in ignorance? He was, and that is why the scripture says to judge nothing before the time (1 Corinthians 4:5). The scriptures and the power of the spirit can fix the worst of us, the murderers, the thieves, the covetous, the adulterers, and the fornicators. Paul later called himself a blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious, and said he obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13). This is the true meaning of loving your enemies (Matthew 5:43-45): not the ones who enslaved and colonized your ancestors, which is what Christianity twists it into, but the enemies within your own nation, because Paul, who persecuted and killed the disciples, was one of those enemies, and he could still repent. The Lord told Ananias to go his way, because Saul was a chosen vessel to bear his name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel, and that he would be shown how great things he must suffer for that name (Acts 9:15-16). Ananias went his way and entered into the house, and putting his hands on him called him Brother Saul, saying that the Lord, even Jesus, who had appeared to him in the way, had sent him so that he might receive his sight and be filled with the Holy Ghost (Acts 9:17). He had heard the report and stated the danger, and then he obeyed anyway. Something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, he received sight, arose, and was baptized; and he spent certain days with the disciples at Damascus, and straightway preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God (Acts 9:18-20). At that time there was no New Testament, so he preached Christ out of the law and the prophets and confounded the Jews that dwelt at Damascus, proving that this is very Christ (Acts 9:22). People discredit Paul’s writings, but Acts credits and justifies them, so to throw out Paul a man would have to throw out Acts with him. Paul was not taught by Peter or the other apostles; Christ himself taught him directly, which is why he told the Galatians that he neither received the gospel of man nor was taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:11-12). Paul kept the man in his own account years later, calling Ananias a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews that dwelt at Damascus, who told him that the God of our fathers had chosen him to know his will, and to see the Just One, and to be his witness of what he had seen and heard (Acts 22:12-16). A devout man is a man according to the laws of the Most High who has a good report, and that is the measure by which Ananias is remembered: not by his fear, but by his keeping of the law and by the name he gave the man the whole congregation was afraid of.

name: Dorcas (Tabitha)
text: Full of good works and almsdeeds which she did; the coats and garments she made for the widows. At Joppa there was a certain disciple named Tabitha, called Dorcas, full of good works and almsdeeds. She fell sick and died, and they washed her and laid her in an upper chamber, and sent two men to Lydda for Peter. When he came the widows stood by him weeping and showing the coats and garments she had made while she was with them. He put them all out, kneeled down and prayed, and told her to arise, and he presented her alive to the saints and widows. As Peter passed throughout all quarters he came down to the saints at Lydda and found a man named Aeneas who had kept his bed eight years, sick of the palsy, and told him that Jesus Christ made him whole and that he should arise and make his bed, and he arose immediately, and all that dwelt at Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord (Acts 9:32-35). The saints are the children of Israel, and turning to the Lord there means they repented. At Joppa there was a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas, and this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did (Acts 9:36). Women were disciples too, students and followers of Christ. The sisters were not elders, but they were disciples, and the scripture names this one by her works. Our sisters are recorded for their good works; when our sisters have faith, their almsdeeds follow them. She fell sick and died, and they washed her and laid her in an upper chamber (Acts 9:37). The washing of the dead shows our own customs of purifying the body, kept among our people long before the nations we were scattered into taught us anything. Because Lydda was near Joppa and the disciples had heard Peter was there, they sent two men asking him not to delay, and when he came they brought him into the upper chamber, and all the widows stood by him weeping and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them (Acts 9:38-39). She had a trade, and she made the garments for the brothers and the widows out of it. Dorcas made coats and garments and gave almsdeeds, so she had a good name and no covetous spirit; what she took in she gave back. That is the opposite of the opportunists who look at thousands gathered at Passover and think only of what they can get from the people, coveting to live off of them. And why did the disciples send for this particular apostle? Because Peter and the apostles had a reputation for healing, so much that the sick were laid in the streets on beds and couches so that even his shadow passing by might fall on some of them (Acts 5:12-16). Peter put them all out, kneeled down and prayed, and turning to the body told Tabitha to arise; she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up, and he gave her his hand and lifted her up, and called the saints and widows and presented her alive (Acts 9:40-41). The woman who had clothed the widows was given back to the widows who wept for her. It is no surprise to see an apostle raise the dead, because Christ had said that he that believed on him would do the works that he did, and greater works than these (John 14:12). It was known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord, and Peter tarried many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner (Acts 9:42-43). What was known was that Peter had brought her back, and on that report much of Israel believed at that time. For us today the Lord said it would not come that way; the record is that he would give his houses to a people who had seen no signs and no prophets, and would yet believe him and do what he commanded (2 Esdras 1:35-37). We come by the spirit and by faith, not by watching the dead rise. And the house Peter stayed in at Joppa is the same house he was lodging in when the vision of the sheet came down and the men from Cornelius came to the gate. A woman’s almsdeeds and a raising at Joppa stand at the front of that history, and the account gives her good report as the reason the disciples sent for the apostle at all.

name: Cornelius
text: A devout man, one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway. There was a certain man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band, a devout man who feared God with all his house, gave much alms to the people, and prayed always. An angel told him his prayers and his alms had come up for a memorial before God and sent him to Joppa for Simon called Peter. Peter, who had been given the vision of the sheet let down by four corners, came and said that God had showed him not to call any man common or unclean, and preached to the household. While he yet spoke the Holy Ghost fell on all that heard, and he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. There was a certain man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band (Acts 10:1). Our people read Italian band and picture a Caucasian; settle first where the man lived. This is Caesarea Maritima, the port Rome built over Strato’s Tower, and scripture puts that coast under Dor in the allotment of Manasseh the son of Joseph, in the same Samaria where Christ sat at the well (Joshua 17:7-11, John 4:20-26). Peter sailed some thirty or forty miles up that coast from Joppa to reach him. Cornelius was an Israelite officer in the Roman army, not a man of another nation. Our people of the diaspora took Greek and Latin names and built careers in the Roman military, the same as our people serve in the American military today. He is called a devout man that feared God with all his house, gave much alms, and prayed always (Acts 10:2). To be devout is to be devout according to the law, and to fear the Most High is to keep his commandments; the statutes and the judgments were showed to Jacob and to Israel only and to no other nation (Psalms 147:19-20). Scholars record that Esau is the forefather of the Roman Empire, and Esau found no place of repentance, so a Roman by nation could have had no salvation opened to him at all. An angel told him his prayers and his alms were come up for a memorial before God and sent him to Joppa for Simon called Peter (Acts 10:3-6). God remembered the good work the man was doing, and he was not penny pinching when he did it. The Most High regards the prayer of the destitute and the groaning of the prisoner (Psalms 102:16-20), and Israel were the prisoners of Rome; he hears the prayer of the oppressed, not of the oppressor. Meanwhile Peter fell into a trance and saw a vessel like a great sheet knit at the four corners, full of beasts and creeping things and fowls, and refused the voice that told him to rise, kill, and eat, and was answered that what God has cleansed he should not call common (Acts 10:9-16). Christians use that to justify unclean food, but it is an allegory. The vessel is Israel swallowed up among the nations as a vessel wherein is no pleasure (Hosea 8:8); the sheet let down from four corners is the diaspora gathered from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:11-12); and the beasts are men. What was cleansed was man, the northern kingdom, saved out of all the dwelling places where they had sinned (Ezekiel 37:21-23). The men reported that Cornelius was a just man, one that feared God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews (Acts 10:21-22). To be just is to keep the law that is holy, just, and good; even the southern kingdom, which had no dealings with the north, vouched for this man. Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet and worshipped him, and Peter took him up, saying that he himself also was a man (Acts 10:24-26). Then Peter said it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company with one of another nation, but that God had showed him not to call any man common or unclean (Acts 10:28). One of another nation is not other races; it is the northern kingdom, and the whole verse rests on the split between Judah and Ephraim. Peter said that God is no respecter of persons, but that in every nation he that fears him and works righteousness is accepted with him, and then named the audience in the next breath: the word which God sent to the children of Israel (Acts 10:34-36). No respecter of persons does not mean the nations are equal, because he plainly had respect to the children of Israel; it means no partiality in judgment, and replacement theology lives on reading verses thirty-four and thirty-five while skipping verse thirty-six. While Peter yet spoke, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word, and he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord (Acts 10:44-48); the spirit is poured out on the house of Israel, and Ephraim is the wild olive tree grafted back in among the branches (Romans 11:17-21). When they of the circumcision contended with him at Jerusalem he rehearsed the matter and expounded it by order, and they held their peace and glorified God (Acts 11:1-3, Acts 11:17-18). And James answers this same case by quoting the raising up of the tabernacle of David that is fallen (Acts 15:15-17, Amos 9:11), which would make no sense over Cornelius if he were not of the twelve tribes.

name: Peter at Antioch
text: Dissembling: withdrawing from the Gentiles for fear of them of the circumcision. At Antioch Peter had eaten with the Gentiles until certain men came from James, and then he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision, and the other Jews dissembled with him, so that even Barnabas was carried away. Paul withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed, and said before them all that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel. This history is not recorded in Acts; Paul tells it himself to the Galatians. When James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace given to Paul, they gave him and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, that they should go to the heathen and the pillars to the circumcision (Galatians 2:9). The heathen there is the northern kingdom, the same people called the Gentiles and the uncircumcision; the scripture itself calls the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali Galilee of the Gentiles, and those are two tribes of Israel (Matthew 4:15-16). Paul was already at Antioch doing his ministry when Peter came along later. But when Peter was come to Antioch, Paul withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed; for before certain men came from James he did eat with the Gentiles, and when they were come he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision, and the other Jews dissembled likewise with him, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their dissimulation (Galatians 2:11-13). This history is not recorded in Acts at all. Peter was the head apostle, second in command from Christ, and he still made mistakes. Four words carry the charge: he withdrew, he separated himself, the others dissembled, and Barnabas was carried away with their dissimulation. To dissimulate is to disguise or conceal under a false appearance, to hide the real motive behind a pretense; dissimulation is feigning and hypocrisy. In plain speech, Peter was being fake, and the reason given is fear. The men he had been eating with were Israelites of the northern kingdom living in a Gentile way of life; when the southern kingdom arrived he separated himself from them out of respect of persons, not wanting to be seen eating with them, and Barnabas withdrew with him and would not sit or eat with them either. That withdrawing is the very thing that broke the nation in the first place, when the ten tribes told Rehoboam they had no portion in David and every man went to his tent (1 Kings 12:16). The law forbids respect of persons in judgment, neither respecting the person of the poor nor honouring the person of the mighty (Leviticus 19:15). And Peter knew better than any man there, because he was the one who had been told by God not to call any man common or unclean, and the one who had watched the same gift of the Holy Ghost fall on that household (Acts 10:28, Acts 11:2-3, Acts 15:7-9). When Paul saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, he said to Peter before them all that if he, being a Jew, lived after the manner of Gentiles and not as do the Jews, he had no business compelling the Gentiles to live as do the Jews (Galatians 2:14). Paul confronted him in front of everybody. The charge was plain: you claim to be a Jew, salvation is of the Jews, you are supposed to be the example, and you are following their footsteps instead of setting one, showing respect of persons and living like them while trying to teach them to follow after the Jews. You are being a hypocrite in your actions. Paul did not let things slide; he had no respect of persons and feared no man regardless of his status. You already learned this, Peter. God showed you that you cannot call any man common or unclean. You sat with them, and you convinced many of the Jews that these men were all right, and now you are wavering. The correction went no further than the rebuke. Galatians records no sentence taking Peter out of his work, and the next words of the letter are Paul including himself with him: we who are Jews by nature, knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ (Galatians 2:15-16). Peter was corrected in front of them all and would have been embarrassed and ashamed, and he repented; and as a teacher, what does a man teach after that? What he repented from. Do not be fake. Reproof between brethren is the law and not an injury, since the commandment is to rebuke a brother plainly and not to hate him in the heart (Leviticus 19:17), and Peter himself afterward wrote of the wisdom given to our beloved brother Paul (2 Peter 3:15-16). The case is kept in the book so that a so-called Christian cannot use it to excuse breaking the commandments, and so that a man with rank among us knows that rank is no cover for hypocrisy.

name: James the brother of John
text: Killed with the sword by Herod, to please the people. About that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church, and killed James the brother of John with the sword; and because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also. It was the days of unleavened bread. James is one of the two who had asked to sit on the right hand and the left and were told they would drink of the cup that Christ drank of; no accusation against him is recorded, only the sword. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to Christ asking that they might sit, one on his right hand and the other on his left, in his glory, and were told they knew not what they asked, and were asked whether they could drink of the cup he drank of; they said they could, and he told them they would indeed drink of it, but that the seats were not his to give (Mark 10:35-40). Matthew tells the same request through the mother of Zebedee’s children, and the same answer, that the places belong to them for whom they are prepared of the Father (Matthew 20:20-23). That cup is drunk in this day as well. The people are reproached and reviled for this word, and it will grow sharper, not lighter. When the ten heard it they were displeased with the two brothers, and Christ called them and said that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them and their great ones exercise authority, but it should not be so among them: whoever would be great among them must be their minister, and whoever would be chief, the servant of all, because the Son of man came not to be ministered to but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many (Mark 10:41-45). The higher the rank, the heavier the load. The same two brothers had been rebuked before, when a village of the Samaritans would not receive him and they asked whether they should command fire to come down from heaven; he turned and told them they knew not what manner of spirit they were of, for the Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives but to save them (Luke 9:51-56). The men who asked for the seats and for the fire were taught, corrected, and kept, and the record of their correction stands beside the record of their death. Now about that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church, and he killed James the brother of John with the sword; and because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also, and it was then the days of unleavened bread (Acts 12:1-3). One of the twelve was finally martyred, and the elders of his own nation were glad of it. The government attacked the Israelites because it pleased a portion of the very people. Do not think the ones we hand flyers to will not side with the government when it turns on us. And they waited until the highest holy days to attack. Christ was killed on the Passover, and Peter was arrested on the Passover. Picture our own men snatched up on a Passover, or something happening to the brothers travelling all over the world for the feast. Herod put Peter in prison and delivered him to four quaternions of soldiers, groups of four, to keep him, intending after Easter to bring him out to the people; Passover was already past, so the king meant to make a public display of the apostle on the Roman holiday, and prayer was made without ceasing of the church to God for him (Acts 12:4-5). The angel of the Lord came upon him, a light shined in the prison, his chains fell off, the angel walked him past the first and the second ward, and the iron gate opened of its own accord; and when Peter was come to himself he said he knew of a surety that the Lord had sent his angel and delivered him out of the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews (Acts 12:6-11). The government and his own people were against him, and all we have is the prayer of the church and the angels answering those prayers. The two outcomes in one chapter must not be confused. Peter was delivered; James had already been killed with the sword, and Christ had told him beforehand that he would drink of that cup (Mark 10:39). The history sets this in the reign of Herod Agrippa the first, in the days of Claudius Caesar, just after the assassination of Caligula.

name: Herod Agrippa
text: Accepting worship due to God alone. Herod had killed James with the sword and taken Peter, and when Peter was delivered he examined the keepers and commanded that they should be put to death. Then upon a set day, arrayed in royal apparel, he sat upon his throne and made an oration to the men of Tyre and Sidon, and the people shouted that it was the voice of a god and not of a man. Immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory, and he was eaten of worms and gave up the ghost. The next line of the record says the word of God grew and multiplied. This is Herod Agrippa the first, the king who stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church, killed James the brother of John with the sword, and took Peter also because it pleased the people (Acts 12:1-4). When Peter was delivered out of the prison by the angel there was no small stir among the soldiers about what was become of him, and Herod sought for him and found him not, and examined the keepers and commanded that they should be put to death (Acts 12:18-19). A man who could not reach the prisoner killed his own guards for it, because the standing custom was that a keeper who lost a prisoner died in his place. Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon, but they came with one accord to him and, having made Blastus the king’s chamberlain their friend, desired peace, because their country was nourished by the king’s country. That is how America feeds the islands and then owns them. Upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne and made an oration to them, and the people gave a shout, saying that it was the voice of a god and not of a man (Acts 12:20-22). He had just lost his prisoner, and he came out dressed in his best and sat in his elegance to be praised for it. That is the same spirit as calling a president the savior and asking God to bless him and the country in the same sentence, and God is still listening to these empires talk. Peter had already refused that honour in the house at Caesarea, standing a man up off his feet and saying that he himself also was a man (Acts 10:25-26). What an apostle would not take, a king took. Immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory, and he was eaten of worms and gave up the ghost (Acts 12:23). Most likely he was given a disease and dropped dead. The scripture does not leave the death to be explained as the end of a political career; it names the cause, and the cause is the glory he took. That was his honour on the earth, and that is his legacy. The pattern is old and it does not change, and in each case the man’s own mouth brought the destruction on him. Nebuchadnezzar walked in his palace and said, is not this great Babylon that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty; and while the word was yet in the king’s mouth there fell a voice from heaven saying the kingdom was departed from him, and the same hour he was driven from men and ate grass as oxen until he knew that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomsoever he will (Daniel 4:29-33). Daniel had warned him a year in advance to break off his sins by righteousness and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor, and he did not listen (Daniel 4:27). Antiochus swore to make Jerusalem a common burying place and was struck with an incurable and invisible plague, a pain of the bowels without remedy, eaten with worms, his flesh falling away, and died in a strange country in the mountains (2 Maccabees 9:4-28). Sennacherib ran his mouth about touching the Israelites and one angel emptied his camp. Pride is pride, and it cannot hide, from your house, to the congregation, to the White House. And the next sentence after Herod’s death is the answer to everything he had done: the word of God grew and multiplied, and Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had fulfilled their ministry and took with them John whose surname was Mark (Acts 12:24-25).

name: Elymas the sorcerer
text: Withstanding the apostles; seeking to turn the deputy from the faith. At Paphos Barnabas and Saul found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew whose name was Bar-jesus, who was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man. The deputy called for Barnabas and Saul and desired to hear the word of God, but Elymas the sorcerer withstood them, seeking to turn the deputy away from the faith. Paul, filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him and told him the hand of the Lord was upon him and that he would be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. As the brethren at Antioch ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Ghost said to separate Barnabas and Saul for the work he had called them to, and they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews at Salamis (Acts 13:2-5). When they had gone through the isle to Paphos they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew whose name was Bar-jesus, who was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, who called for Barnabas and Saul and desired to hear the word of God; but Elymas the sorcerer, for so is his name by interpretation, withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith (Acts 13:6-8). Read who these men are. The sorcerer is called a Jew, one of our own, and the deputy sent for the apostles and desired to hear the word, which no man of another nation would have done. Both of them are Israelites, and the whole case is a fight inside the house. The office Elymas held was not a small one either. He had the ear of the man who governed the island, and he used that place to keep another man from hearing. Then Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him and said that he was full of all subtilty and all mischief, a child of the devil, an enemy of all righteousness, and asked whether he would not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord (Acts 13:9-10). He called an Israelite a child of the devil, the same words Christ used on the men of his own nation who sought to kill him, telling them they were of their father the devil and would do the lusts of their father, who was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). Those words are also the pattern of the man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God: Elymas opposed God, the scriptures, and all righteousness, and Paul names the spirit in him by the same terms (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). Israel suffers no enchanter, no user of divination, and no witch to live among the people (Deuteronomy 18:10-12, Exodus 22:18). Paul told him that the hand of the Lord was upon him, and that he would be blind, not seeing the sun for a season; and immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness, and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand (Acts 13:11). The man who had stood between another man and the word could no longer find his own way across a room without help. The blindness was stated as being for a season, and the account records neither its end nor any repentance afterward. Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord (Acts 13:12). The hindrance was removed and the hearing went forward. This is the living picture of what Paul wrote afterward, that the preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish, but to us which are saved it is the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:18). One man in that room heard it as the power of God and believed; the other blasphemed and contradicted and was struck blind in front of him. And the same thing runs today, where men who will not come to the light because their deeds would be reproved spend their strength trying to talk other people out of hearing (John 3:19-20). No sentence of death is carried out by the apostles in the account, and nothing further is told of Elymas.

name: They that troubled the churches with circumcision
text: Preaching another gospel, subverting souls with a commandment the apostles never gave. Certain men came down from Judaea and taught the brethren that except they were circumcised after the manner of Moses they could not be saved, and Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, so the matter went up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem. There rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying it was needful to circumcise them and to command them to keep the law of Moses. The council gave its sentence and sent letters saying that certain which went out from them had troubled the brethren with words, subverting their souls, to whom they gave no such commandment.
