Whoever will save his life shall lose it, and what is a man advantaged if he gain the whole world and lose himself (Luke 9:24-25). The thing he went back for was the thing that passes away. He was not alone in that season, which is the sober part of the case. All they which are in Asia had turned away, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them (2 Timothy 1:15); Crescens went to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia, and only Luke stayed with Paul (2 Timothy 4:11). Christ had already prophesied that many would be offended, would betray one another, and would hate one another (Matthew 24:10), which is why Paul was not undone by it. The application made in class is not comfortable: we have watched brothers and sisters who were called friends, who ate in our homes and knew our families, turn and try to pull the work down, and some who left to start their own assemblies saw them fall overnight, because God does not bless a hand that did that much evil to its own brethren. The sentence on Demas is deferred. Paul left the name in the book, and that by itself is a record.

name: Alexander the coppersmith
text: Doing Paul much evil; greatly withstanding his words. In the uproar at Ephesus the Jews put Alexander forward out of the multitude to make a defence, and the crowd shouted him down for about two hours once they knew what he was (Acts 19:33-34). Paul later names Alexander with Hymenaeus among those who made shipwreck of the faith and were delivered to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:19-20), and at the end writes that Alexander the coppersmith did him much evil and greatly withstood their words, and that the Lord would reward him according to his works (2 Timothy 4:14-15). Alexander first appears in the city of the silversmiths. Demetrius had stirred the craftsmen over the shrines of Diana, the town was in confusion, and the Jews pushed Alexander forward; he beckoned with his hand and would have made his defence to the people, but when they knew he was a Jew they cried up their goddess for about two hours instead (Acts 19:24-27; Acts 19:33-34). The teaching reads him plainly: he was a coppersmith in the city where the trade was making idols, which is where Paul met him, and for a moment he stood between Paul’s companions and a mob. One teacher takes it further and says that once the crowd turned he went along with the foolishness. Whatever he was then, he did not stay. Paul names him with Hymenaeus among those who put away faith and a good conscience and made shipwreck concerning the faith, and delivered them to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:19-20), after charging Timothy with the same commission that he might war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18). In the last chapter Paul ever wrote he returns to him: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil, and Timothy is told to beware of him also, for he greatly withstood our words (2 Timothy 4:14-15). Put the weight where it belongs. Imagine being in the ministry and then turning against the ministry. That was this man, and Paul writes it in the same breath as the line that at his first answer no man stood with him and all men forsook him (2 Timothy 4:16). Paul did not lift a hand and did not ask anybody else to. He said, the Lord reward him according to his works (2 Timothy 4:14). That is the law he taught: avenge not yourselves, for vengeance belongs to God, who will repay (Romans 12:19), and mercy belongs to the Lord, for he renders to every man according to his work (Psalms 62:12). Paul had been the chief of persecutors himself and obtained mercy, so he was not looking to destroy this man. He was keeping order and leaving the account where accounts are settled. What Paul does command is separation. Mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which you have learned, and avoid them (Romans 16:17). Under Moses a man who drew the people after another doctrine was to be stoned and the hand of the witness first upon him (Deuteronomy 13:6-10); in Christ the body cuts him off and nothing more, and the words passed to Timothy are a warning to a young leader, not an execution. In the same passage where he asks the Lord to repay Alexander, Paul prays that the forsaking of the others be not laid to their charge, and records that notwithstanding, the Lord stood with him and strengthened him, so that the preaching might be fully known and he was delivered out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:16-17). The case stands as cursed on the word Paul spoke over him. The carrying out of it is not in the book.

name: Gaius, the wellbeloved
text: Walking in the truth; doing faithfully to the brethren and to strangers; bringing them forward on their journey after a godly sort. John wrote his third epistle to the wellbeloved Gaius, whom he loved in the truth, and rejoiced greatly when the brethren came and testified of the truth that was in him, because he walked in the truth (3 John 1:1-4). He did faithfully whatever he did to the brethren and to strangers, who bore witness of his charity before the congregation, and John told him he would do well to bring them forward on their journey after a godly sort (3 John 1:5-6). A whole doctrine turns on how John words the greeting. He does not merely say the truth was in the man; he says he loved him in the truth, then says the brethren testified of the truth that was in him, even as he walked in the truth (3 John 1:1,3-4). A man is in the truth because he walks in it, and the truth is in him because he learned it from somewhere and from somebody. The teaching raises this against a doctrine going around that a man only needs the truth to be in him and does not need to be in the body: that is the subtle way of telling people they do not need a congregation and do not need the elders who taught them, and the very verse they lean on answers them. John also prayed that he would prosper and be in health even as his soul prospered (3 John 1:2), which puts the state of the soul first and makes the rest follow it. What he actually did is set down without decoration. He did faithfully whatever he did to the brethren and to strangers, and they bore witness of his charity before the whole congregation (3 John 1:5-6). Those men had gone out for the Name’s sake, taking nothing of the Gentiles, so we ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth (3 John 1:7-8). Bringing them forward on their journey after a godly sort means paying the road, feeding them, and sending them on able to keep working. This is the plain law of the body: given to hospitality, distributing to the necessity of the saints (Romans 12:13), continuing in brotherly love and not forgetful to entertain strangers (Hebrews 13:1-2). Christ himself set the price on it: he that receives you receives me, and he that receives me receives him that sent me, and even a cup of cold water given in the name of a disciple does not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40-42). John’s word over him is beloved, and the charge attached is the standard he is to keep: follow not that which is evil, but that which is good, because he that does good is of God, and he that does evil has not seen God (3 John 1:11). In the same short letter Demetrius is given a good report of all men and of the truth itself (3 John 1:12), so the commendation is not flattery, it is testimony the congregation could verify. The setting matters. John, the apostle who walked with Christ, is writing as a father to a household, the way Paul called Timothy his own son in the faith and Titus his own son after the common faith, and told the Corinthians that though they had ten thousand instructors they had not many fathers, for he had begotten them through the gospel (1 Timothy 1:2; Titus 1:4; 1 Corinthians 4:15). Gaius is not praised for rank; there is no office named for him. He kept the brethren moving, paid their way forward, and had the whole congregation testify to it. The reward Christ named for that work is the one that is never lost.

name: Diotrephes
text: Loving the preeminence; prating against the apostle with malicious words; casting the brethren out of the church. John wrote to the congregation, but Diotrephes, who loved to have the preeminence among them, received them not (3 John 1:9). John said that if he came he would remember the deeds: prating against them with malicious words, refusing to receive the brethren, forbidding those who would, and casting them out of the congregation (3 John 1:10). No sentence is pronounced; John gives the rule instead, to follow not that which is evil but that which is good (3 John 1:11). The teaching will not let the verse pass lightly. This was a man the apostles themselves had set up, an overseer over a congregation, and the men he would not receive had walked with Christ, eaten with him, and been taught by him. The sin is named as covetousness, and not of money or a garment: he coveted power. He wanted to be the top teacher in Israel and to be known as number one, and he could not work with anybody who might be greater or know more than he did. Zimri had the same spirit and killed a drunken king to sit on the throne, and then destroyed the whole house of Baasha (1 Kings 16:8-12). Diotrephes did not receive the apostles because he thought he was over them. John lists the deeds. Prating against the apostles with malicious words is verbal abuse and name calling, the same evil that fills the internet now, men who learned a few scriptures running their mouths at the men who taught them. Refusing the brethren, forbidding them that would, and casting people out of the congregation is what it looks like on the ground (3 John 1:10). A man like this builds a clique out of the brothers who will not question him, raises them up, and pushes away the ones who come asking from the scriptures; the clique keeps evil quiet in the midst and the whole thing turns into partiality. Then, when brothers are sent to check on a school, he tells them today is not a good day, come back another time, and any member who goes over his head is put out. Paul warned the overseers of it at Miletus: after his departing grievous wolves would enter in, not sparing the flock, and of their own selves men would arise speaking perverse things to draw away disciples after them (Acts 20:28-30). John pronounces no sentence on him. He gives the congregation the rule instead: follow not that which is evil, but that which is good; he that does good is of God, but he that does evil has not seen God (3 John 1:11). The standard for a leader is the one Christ set. The princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion and the great ones authority, but it shall not be so among us; whoever will be great shall be the minister, and whoever will be chief shall be the servant (Matthew 20:25-27). He that is greatest among you shall be your servant, and the man who exalts himself shall be abased while the man who humbles himself shall be exalted (Matthew 23:11-12). Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). The answer the teaching keeps returning to is that there is only one preeminent. Christ is the head of the body, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence (Colossians 1:18). Not the bishop, not the captain, not Diotrephes. Gamaliel’s test applies to every man who rises up boasting himself to be somebody: Theudas drew four hundred after him and was slain, Judas of Galilee drew much people and perished, and all that obeyed them were scattered and brought to nothing, because if the work is of men it comes to nothing, and if it is of God it cannot be overthrown (Acts 5:34-39). Cursed is the man that trusts in man and makes flesh his arm (Jeremiah 17:5), so the men who followed such a leader away from the scriptures carry their own judgment. And the class sets him among the hirelings: the hireling is not the shepherd, the sheep are not his own, so he sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, because he cares not for the sheep (John 10:12-13). The brethren he shut out were the very strangers the body is commanded to entertain (Hebrews 13:2).

name: The churches of Ephesus, Sardis, and Laodicea
text: Leaving the first love; a name to live while dead; lukewarm, and saying, I am rich. To Ephesus Christ granted the works, the labour, the patience, and the trying of false apostles, then charged them with leaving their first love and told them to remember, repent, and do the first works, or the candlestick would be removed (Revelation 2:1-5). Sardis had a name that it lived and was dead (Revelation 3:1). Laodicea said it was rich and increased with goods and in need of nothing, and did not know it was wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17). Each of the three is given space to repent. The seven were real congregations in Asia Minor, in what is now Turkey, built up by Paul and the brothers who travelled with him, and the angel addressed in each letter is the man set over the congregation, since the word means messenger, which is what Malachi’s own name means (Revelation 1:11,20; Malachi 2:7; 2 Esdras 1:38-39). The teaching insists these seven are alive today in the various congregations, and that the point of reading them is to examine which one you are. To Ephesus Christ first granted the works, the labour, the patience, that they could not bear them which are evil, that they had tried the false apostles and found them liars, and had laboured for his name and not fainted (Revelation 2:1-3). Not bearing the evil is itself commanded: a mark is set on the men that sigh and cry for the abominations done in the midst of the city (Ezekiel 9:4), and we are to have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness but rather reprove them (Ephesians 5:11). Then came the charge: they had left their first love (Revelation 2:4). We all know what the first love was, when we first repented and could not get enough of studying. The first love is Christ, who is the word made flesh, and it is the love David spoke of when he said how he loved the law, that it was his meditation all the day and sweeter than honey (Psalms 119:97,103; 1 John 4:19). Even David left it once from a rooftop, and had to repent and come back. Sardis had a name that it lived and was dead (Revelation 3:1). Laodicea was neither cold nor hot, and because it was lukewarm he would spue it out of his mouth (Revelation 3:15-16). The lukewarmness is double mindedness: no man can serve two masters, and a double minded man is unstable in all his ways (Matthew 6:22-24; James 1:8). The city’s own history explains the talk. Laodicea was granted free city status by Rome and its golden age of prosperity ran on trade, so the congregation said it was rich, increased with goods, and had need of nothing, not knowing it was wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17). Blindness is the state Isaiah described, groping for the wall at noonday like dead men (Isaiah 59:10). Paul had already had to write to that city and to Colossae about men creeping in with philosophy and vain deceit, beguiling them of their reward and not holding the head (Colossians 2:8,18-19). None of the three is destroyed. Each is told to repent. Ephesus is told to remember from where it had fallen, repent, and do the first works, or he comes quickly and removes the candlestick out of its place (Revelation 2:5). The first works are the commandments heard from the beginning, since this is love, that we walk after his commandments (2 John 1:5-6), and they were given from the beginning to men who afterwards despised his law and denied his covenants (2 Esdras 7:24). Ephesus is commended in the same breath for hating the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which Christ says he hates also (Revelation 2:6). Sardis is told to be watchful, strengthen the things that remain that are ready to die, remember how it had received and heard, hold fast, and repent, or he comes as a thief at an hour it will not know (Revelation 3:2-3). Sardis also had a few names that had not defiled their garments, and they would walk with him in white (Revelation 3:4); spots and clean garments sat in the same congregation. The counsel to Laodicea is to buy of him gold tried in the fire, white raiment to cover the shame of nakedness, and eyesalve for the eyes (Revelation 3:18). The buying is Isaiah’s buying, without money and without price, the wisdom and understanding that rested on the branch out of the stem of Jesse (Isaiah 55:1; Isaiah 11:1-3). Then comes the reason for the whole letter: as many as he loves, he rebukes and chastens, so be zealous and repent (Revelation 3:19). That is the same doctrine as the chastening of the son in whom the father delights, which is not to be despised or fainted under (Hebrews 12:5-11; Proverbs 3:11-12). He stands at the door and knocks, and the door is opened by keeping the commandments, since he said that if you love him you keep them, and promised the comforter to them that do (Revelation 3:20; John 14:15-17). Israel’s ancient charge was that they forsook the kindness of their youth and walked after vanity and became vain (Jeremiah 2:2-5). These three letters are that charge again, with a space to repent attached to each one, which is why the verdict is reprieve.

name: Antipas, Smyrna, and Philadelphia
text: Faithful unto death; keeping the word of his patience; not denying his name in the place where Satan’s seat is. To Smyrna Christ said he knew their works, tribulation, and poverty, and that they were rich, and told them to fear none of the things they were about to suffer, to be faithful even to death, and he would give them a crown of life (Revelation 2:8-10). At Pergamos, where Satan’s seat is, they held fast his name and had not denied his faith even in the days when Antipas his faithful martyr was slain among them (Revelation 2:12-13). Philadelphia had a little strength, kept his word, and had not denied his name, and an open door was set before it that no man can shut (Revelation 3:7-8). To Smyrna he granted the works, the tribulation, and the poverty, and then said they were rich (Revelation 2:9). All the promises belonged to them whatever their purse held. In the same verse he named the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. The history identifies them: the house of Herod, Edomites converted in generations before and sitting in the congregations, which is how Drusilla the daughter of Herod Agrippa is called a Jewess, and how men brought up with Herod the tetrarch are found among the teachers at Antioch (Acts 13:1). Judah means the praise of the Lord, and Edom was never called that. Then the warning: fear none of those things they should suffer, for the devil would cast some of them into prison that they might be tried, and they would have tribulation ten days, and they were to be faithful even to death for a crown of life (Revelation 2:10). Christ had said the same: hands would be laid on them, they would be delivered to the synagogues and into prisons, and it would turn to them for a testimony (Luke 21:12-13); and they were not to fear them which kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28). The trying is the point: then shall they be known who are my chosen, and they shall be tried as the gold in the fire (2 Esdras 16:73). He that endures to the end shall be saved (Matthew 10:22), and blessed is the man that endures temptation, for when he is tried he shall receive the crown of life (James 1:12). At Pergamos the record names one man. Christ knew where they dwelt, where Satan’s seat is, and that they held fast his name and had not denied his faith even in the days when Antipas his faithful martyr was slain among them (Revelation 2:12-13). The account preserved of him is that John the apostle ordained him bishop of Pergamon, and that he was put to death under Nero for casting out the demons the local population worshipped, roasted inside a brazen bull shaped altar. It was not a quick death, and it came under the emperor known for burning our people alive. The city was given over to the same idolatry the apostles met at Lystra, where the people called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius and brought oxen and garlands to sacrifice to them, and stoned Paul when he told them to turn from those vanities to the living God (Acts 14:11-19). The teaching draws the line hard: nobody threatens a man who goes along with what everybody else does. Antipas spoke against the worship of that city and they cooked him for it. To Smyrna: he that overcomes shall not be hurt of the second death (Revelation 2:11). The ones beheaded for the witness of Jesus and for the word of God, who had not worshipped the beast nor his image nor received his mark, live and reign with Christ, and on such the second death has no power (Revelation 20:4-6). That is what a crown of life is worth. To Philadelphia, the city whose name means brotherly love, he writes as the one that is holy and true, that has the key of David, that opens and no man shuts (Revelation 3:7). That key is Isaiah’s, laid upon his shoulder (Isaiah 22:22), and it is the book sealed with seven seals that no man was found worthy to open until the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, prevailed to open it (Revelation 5:1-5), after which he opened the understanding of the disciples (Luke 24:44-45). So the open door set before them is the understanding itself, and no man can shut it, though the scribes and Pharisees shut up the kingdom of heaven against men (Revelation 3:8; Matthew 23:13). They had a little strength, kept his word, and did not deny his name. He promised to make them of the synagogue of Satan come and worship before their feet and know that he had loved them (Revelation 3:9), and because they kept the word of his patience, to keep them from the hour of temptation that comes upon all the world (Revelation 3:10). The patience is the keeping of the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus (Revelation 14:12), the law kept as the apple of the eye (Proverbs 7:1-2), and the hour is the hour in which the judgment of Babylon comes and so great riches come to nothing (Revelation 18:10,17-19). He told them to hold fast what they had, that no man take their crown, and promised the overcomer would be made a pillar in the temple of his God and go no more out (Revelation 3:11-12).

name: The church in Pergamos
text: Holding among them the doctrine of Balaam and the doctrine of the Nicolaitans. Christ granted that the congregation at Pergamos, dwelling where Satan’s seat is, held fast his name and had not denied his faith even when Antipas was slain among them, and then charged them with having there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, and them that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans (Revelation 2:13-15). The sentence is repentance or the sword of his mouth, and the promise to the one who repents is hidden manna and a white stone with a new name (Revelation 2:16-17). The doctrine of Balaam is not a mystery; the history is in Numbers. Balaam could not curse Israel and knew it, so he gave counsel instead, and the counsel was women. The daughters of Moab called the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down and joined themselves to Baalpeor, and a plague ran through the congregation (Numbers 25:1-3), and Moses afterwards said these were the very women who caused the children of Israel through the counsel of Balaam to commit trespass in the matter of Peor (Numbers 31:15-16). Our enemies have always known this is the weakness. Holofernes was told plainly that if there is sin in this people it will be their ruin, and if there is no iniquity in the nation then pass them by, lest their Lord defend them (Judith 5:20-21). Keep the people in sin and you can overtake them, because the connection with God is severed. Peter describes the man himself: forsaking the right way, gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness (2 Peter 2:15). There were men in the body who wanted nothing but money. The second thing was them that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, which Christ says outright that he hates (Revelation 2:15). Nicolas was a proselyte of Antioch, one of the seven chosen out to serve when the widows were being neglected (Acts 6:5), a man converted first to the sacrifices and then to Christ and then set over an office. The accounts read in class say the sect that carried his name lived in unrestrained indulgence and held it a matter of indifference what a man ate and how he lived, shameless in uncleanness, which is the same fornication and the same idolatry named in the verse before it, and the same seduction of Israel into immoral and idolatrous unions with the women of Moab. It is also the exact opposite of what the apostles had settled: abstain from pollutions of idols, from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood (Acts 15:28-29). God hates it because it is the worship of other gods, and his name is Jealous (Exodus 34:14). Ephesus is commended in the same chapter for hating those deeds (Revelation 2:6). Repent, or else he comes quickly and will fight against them with the sword of his mouth (Revelation 2:16). That sword is the sharp sword that goes out of his mouth to smite the nations and rule them with a rod of iron (Revelation 19:15); with righteousness he judges the poor, and with the breath of his lips he slays the wicked (Isaiah 11:4), and the wicked whom he consumes with the spirit of his mouth and destroys with the brightness of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The warning is for our own nation as much as for the heathen: follow what the other nations do and you get what the other nations get. There is no exemption for unrepentant Israel. On the other side of the repentance is the promise: hidden manna, a white stone, and in the stone a new name written which no man knows except the one who receives it (Revelation 2:17). The manna is Christ. Their fathers ate manna in the wilderness and are dead; he is the bread of life which comes down from heaven, that a man may eat of it and not die (John 6:31-35,48-51). It is hidden because the gospel is hid to them that are lost (2 Corinthians 4:3), which is why the world still cannot say who the black Messiah is or who he came for, and why undoing what was taught about it is the work. The verdict here is reprieve, not sentence. Christ set down what was right with them before he named what was wrong, and the sword only comes out if they will not turn.

name: Jezebel of Thyatira
text: Calling herself a prophetess; teaching the servants of God to commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols. Christ granted Thyatira its works, charity, service, faith, and patience, and said the last were more than the first, then charged the congregation with suffering that woman Jezebel, who called herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce his servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols (Revelation 2:19-20). He gave her space to repent and she repented not, so the sentence is that he will cast her into a bed, cast them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation except they repent, and kill her children with death (Revelation 2:21-23). He grants the good first, as he does with every one of the seven. He knew their works, charity, service, faith, and patience, and said the last works were more than the first: the congregation had grown, fruitful in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God (Revelation 2:18-19; Colossians 1:10). Then the charge, and the first word in it does the work. They suffered that woman, which means they allowed her, and the letter is addressed to the man set over the congregation (Revelation 2:20). The teaching states it plainly: that spirit cannot operate without a man weak enough to let it, and what was going on at Thyatira was male leadership allowing women a voice in the congregation and letting doctrine be pushed through the men. That is why the charge given to Timothy at Ephesus was that the woman learn in silence with all subjection, not teaching, not usurping authority over the man (1 Timothy 2:11-12), and why a bishop must be the husband of one wife who rules his own house well, since a man who knows not how to rule his own house cannot take care of the congregation of God (1 Timothy 3:1-5). The fornication is not only sexual. Jehoram made high places in the mountains of Judah and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, which was idolatry, and he did it because he had the daughter of Ahab to wife (2 Chronicles 21:11-13). Behind that daughter stood Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, married to Ahab as part of the league Omri made with Tyre and Zidon; she brought Baal worship into Samaria and multiplied it, and four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of the groves ate at her table, men taking orders from a witch (1 Kings 16:29-33; 1 Kings 18:19). Her daughter Athaliah carried the same spirit into Judah and was counsellor to her son to do wickedly, then destroyed the royal seed so she could rule alone (2 Chronicles 22:2-3,10). Spirits come back. The thing that has been is that which shall be, and there is no new thing under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:9; Ecclesiastes 6:10). That is how a queen out of the book of Kings is named in a congregation in Asia centuries later. The idolatry prevalent in that province was woman worship, which is why the rest in Thyatira are said not to have known the depths of Satan. He gave her space to repent of her fornication, and she repented not (Revelation 2:21). That space is the whole mercy of the present time, and Esdras describes what becomes of those who waste it: they that loathed his law while they had yet liberty, when the place of repentance was open to them, understood not but despised it, and the same must know it after death by pain (2 Esdras 9:11). So the sentence follows: he will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds, and he will kill her children with death, and all the congregations shall know that he is he which searches the reins and hearts and gives to every one according to their works (Revelation 2:22-23). He knows what men think in their hearts, searches out all their works, and will put them to shame (2 Esdras 16:63). Her children are the ones who carried her doctrine, as the sons of Belial who sat before Naboth and bore false witness against him at her letters were her children in that sense (1 Kings 21:11-13). In the old account they were killed with death literally. Jehu gathered all the prophets and priests of Baal to a great feast and then sent in the guard and the captains to slay them and pull down the house of Baal (2 Kings 10:18-27), and Jehoiada had Athaliah and all that followed her put to the sword, the house of Baal broken down, and Mattan the priest of Baal slain before the altar (2 Kings 11:15-18). To the rest in Thyatira, as many as had not this doctrine and had not known the depths of Satan, he put no other burden, only to hold fast till he come (Revelation 2:24-25). There was a remnant there as there was in Elijah’s day, when he thought he alone was left and seven thousand had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:14,18). And the apostles had already settled what the servants of God abstain from, meats offered to idols and fornication (Acts 15:28-29), because the things the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to devils, and we cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils (1 Corinthians 10:19-21).
